The Story of King Shahryar and His Brother

In the name of Allah, the Compassionate, the Merciful!

	Praise be to Allah,
	the Beneficent King,
	the Maker of the world,
	Lord of the three worlds,
	who set the sky up over us with no pillars to hold it,
	and spread the earth out flat beneath us like a bed;
	and blessing and peace upon our lord Mohammed,
	lord of all the prophets,
	and upon his family and his companions,
	blessing and peace enduring to the day of judgement.
	Amen!
	O Sovereign of the three worlds!

And now to begin. The doings and the sayings of the people who came before us have become lessons and examples for the people of today. A man can look at what befell other men and take warning from it; he can read through the records of the ancient peoples and everything that happened to them, and be steadied and governed by what he reads. Praise, then, to Him who made the histories of the past a warning to the present.

Among such stories are the tales called A Thousand Nights and a Night, with all their famous legends and their wonders.

It is told — though Allah alone knows what is hidden, and He alone rules, and to Him belong all honour and all giving and all grace and all mercy — that in the old days, and in the old time before them, there was a king among the kings of the house of Sasan, in the islands of India and China, a lord of armies and guards and servants and dependants. He left two sons, one in the prime of his manhood and the other still a boy; and both were fine horsemen and brave men, though the elder was the better rider of the two.

The elder came to the throne, and he ruled the land and governed his people so justly that he was loved by everyone in his capital and everyone in his kingdom. His name was King Shahryar, and he made his younger brother, whose name was Shah Zaman, king of Samarkand, away in the outer lands.

The two of them stayed in their separate kingdoms, and the law was carried out in both, and each governed his own people with fairness and a straight hand, and lived in great ease and contentment. Things went on that way for twenty years.

But at the end of the twentieth year the elder king began to long for a sight of his younger brother, and felt he had to look at him once more. So he asked his vizier what he thought of paying a visit, and the vizier, who did not think the journey a good idea, suggested instead that a letter be written and a present sent, in his own charge, inviting the younger brother to come to the elder.

The king took the advice. He had handsome gifts got ready at once — horses with saddles of gold crusted with gems, Mamluks, which is to say soldiers who are also slaves, beautiful serving girls, splendid and costly cloth — and he wrote his brother a letter full of his love for him and how badly he wanted to see him. It ended:

"So we hope, out of the affection and the kindness of our beloved brother, that he will trouble himself to turn his face towards us. We have sent our vizier to make all the arrangements for the march. Our one and only wish is to see you before we die; and if you delay, or disappoint us, we shall not survive the blow. And peace be upon you."

Then King Shahryar sealed the letter and gave it to the vizier along with the gifts, and told him to tuck up his skirts and put out his strength and lose no time going or coming back.

"Hearing and obedience!" said the vizier, and he set about getting ready without a pause, and packed his loads and had everything he needed prepared without delay. It took him three days, and at dawn on the fourth he took his leave of the king and marched off — over desert and hill road, over stony waste and pleasant meadow, never stopping by night or by day. Wherever he came into a country whose ruler was subject to his own king, and was met with magnificent presents of gold and silver and every fine and rare thing, he would stay three days, which is the term a guest is owed, and when he left on the fourth he would be escorted in honour for a full day's march.

When the vizier drew near Shah Zaman's court at Samarkand, he sent ahead one of his senior officers to announce that he had come. The officer presented himself, kissed the ground before the king, and delivered his message; and the king sent out a party of his nobles and lords to meet his brother's vizier a full day's journey from the city. They met him respectfully, wished him every good thing, and formed an escort and a procession around him.

When he entered the city he went straight to the palace and presented himself to the king. He kissed the ground, prayed for the king's health and happiness and for victory over all his enemies, and told him that his brother was longing to see him and begged for the pleasure of a visit. Then he handed over the letter.

Shah Zaman took it and read it. It had hints and turns in it that needed thinking about; but once he had taken in what it meant, he said, "I hear and I obey the commands of my beloved brother!" And to the vizier he added, "But we will not march until you have had three days' hospitality."

He gave the vizier good quarters in the palace, pitched tents for the troops, and had them supplied with everything they might want in the way of food and drink and the rest. On the fourth day he made ready for the road, put together magnificent presents worthy of his elder brother's rank, and appointed his own chief vizier to govern the country while he was away. Then he had his tents and his camels and his mules brought out, and the whole camp — bales and loads, servants and guards — pitched within sight of the city, ready to set out for his brother's capital the next morning.

But when the night was half over, he remembered something he had meant to bring and had left behind in the palace. So he went back quietly and let himself into his own rooms — and found the queen his wife asleep on his own bed, with both arms around a black cook, a loathsome man, greasy and filthy from the kitchen.

The world went dark in front of him. He said, "If this is going on while I am still within sight of my own city, what will this damned woman be doing during the months I am away at my brother's court?"

He drew his scimitar and cut the two of them into four pieces with a single stroke, and left them lying on the bed, and went back to the camp without letting anyone know what had happened. Then he gave the order to move, and set off at once.

But he could not stop thinking about his wife's treachery. He kept saying to himself, "How could she do this to me? How could she work her own death?" — until grief took hold of him so hard that his colour turned yellow and his body went weak, and he looked like a man sickening for something that kills. So the vizier shortened the day's marches and lingered long at the watering places, and did what he could to comfort him.

When Shah Zaman came near his brother's capital he sent runners and messengers ahead with the good news of his arrival, and Shahryar came out to meet him with his viziers and his emirs and all the lords and great men of his kingdom. He greeted him, and was overjoyed to see him, and had the city decorated in his honour.

But when the brothers came face to face, the elder could not miss the change in the younger's colour, and asked what was wrong.

"It is only the wear of the road," Shah Zaman said, "and my health needs looking after. The change of water and air has told on me. But praise be to Allah, who has brought me back to a brother so dear and so rare!" That was how he covered it and kept his secret. And he added, "O King of the age, it is nothing but toil and travel that have turned my face yellow with bile and sunk my eyes back in my head."

So the two of them entered the capital in state, and the elder brother lodged the younger in a palace that looked out over the pleasure garden. After a while, seeing that his condition had not changed, Shahryar put it down to being away from his own country and his own kingdom, and left him to go his own way and asked him nothing — until one day he said again, "Brother, I see you are getting weaker in body and yellower in the face."

"Brother," Shah Zaman answered, "I have a wound inside me." But still he would not tell him what he had seen his wife do.

So Shahryar sent for doctors and surgeons and had them treat his brother by the rules of their art, and they worked on him for a whole month; but their syrups and their medicines did nothing at all, because he went on dwelling on what his wife had done, and instead of easing, his misery got worse. The doctors' treatment failed entirely.

One day the elder brother said to him, "I am going out hunting and coursing, to take some pleasure and pass the time. Perhaps it will lighten your heart."

But Shah Zaman refused. "Brother," he said, "my soul wants nothing of the kind. Let me have the favour of staying quietly here. I am wholly taken up with my illness."

So Shah Zaman spent the night in the palace, and next morning, when his brother had ridden out, he left his room and sat down at one of the latticed windows overlooking the pleasure grounds. He sat there thinking the saddest thoughts he had about his wife's betrayal, and burning sighs came up out of his tortured chest.

And while he was sitting like that — a small private door of the palace, one that was carefully kept shut, swung open, and out of it came twenty slave girls, and in the middle of them his brother's wife. She was extraordinarily beautiful, a model of grace and symmetry and perfect loveliness, and she walked with the step of a gazelle going down to water.

Shah Zaman drew back from the window, but kept the whole party in sight, watching from a place where he could not be seen himself.

They walked directly under his lattice and went a little way into the garden, until they came to a fountain jetting up in the middle of a great basin of water. There they stripped off their clothes — and of the twenty, ten turned out to be women, the king's concubines, and the other ten were young men, slaves, who had been dressed as women all along.

Then they paired off, each with each. But the queen was left by herself, and after a moment she called out loudly, "Here to me, Saeed, my lord!"

And down out of one of the trees, in a single dropping leap, came a huge Black man, slack-mouthed, the whites of his eyes showing as they rolled — a hideous sight, as Shah Zaman saw him from the window. He walked straight up to her and threw his arms round her neck, and she held him just as tightly; and he kissed her, and wound his legs round hers the way a loop of thread winds round a button, and threw her down and had her. The other slaves did the same with the girls, until they had all satisfied themselves; and they went on kissing and clinging and coupling and carousing until the day began to fade. Then the Mamluks got up off the women, and the Black slave got up off the queen; the young men put their disguises on again; and all of them went back into the palace and shut the private door behind them, exactly as before — all except the Black man, who went back up his tree.

When Shah Zaman had seen his sister-in-law behave like this, he said to himself, "By Allah, my trouble is lighter than his! My brother is a greater king among kings than I am, and this shameful business is going on inside his own palace, and his own wife is in love with the filthiest slave in his household. But it only shows that they all do it, and that there is not a woman alive who does not cheat her husband. The curse of Allah on every one of them, and on the fools who lean on them for support, or put the reins of their conduct into their hands."

So he put away his misery and his low spirits, his regret and his brooding, and eased his own sorrow by repeating those words over and over. He added, "It is my settled opinion that no man in this world is safe from the malice of women."

When supper time came they brought in the trays, and he ate ravenously, because he had gone a long time without touching meat and had not been able to face any dish, however fine. Then he gave grateful thanks to Almighty Allah, praising Him and blessing Him, and he slept a thoroughly restful night — it had been a long while since he had tasted the sweetness of sleep. The next day he ate a good breakfast and began to get his health and his strength back, and before long he was in excellent condition again.

His brother came back from the hunt ten days later, and Shah Zaman rode out to meet him, and they greeted one another. When King Shahryar looked at King Shah Zaman he saw that the colour of health had come back into him, that his face had gone ruddy, and that he was eating with an appetite after living on so little. He wondered at it a good deal, and said, "Brother, I was so worried that you would not come out hunting and chasing with me and take your pleasure in my country!"

Shah Zaman thanked him and made his excuses. Then the two of them took horse and rode into the city, and when they were sitting comfortably in the palace the food trays were set in front of them and they ate their fill. When the dishes had been taken away and they had washed their hands, King Shahryar turned to his brother.

"My mind is full of astonishment at the state of you," he said. "I wanted to take you hunting with me, but I saw you changed in colour, pale and worn to look at, and in real distress of mind besides. And now — alhamdulillah, praise be to Allah — I see your natural colour has come back into your face and you are in the best of health. I believed your sickness came from being cut off from your family and your friends, and from being away from your capital and your country, and so I held back from troubling you with any more questions. But now I beg you: explain to me what caused your illness and the change in your colour, and explain to me the reason for your recovery and the ruddy health I am used to seeing in you. Speak out, and hide nothing."

Shah Zaman bowed his head towards the ground for a while, then lifted it and said, "I will tell you what caused my illness and the loss of my colour. But excuse me from telling you the cause of its coming back and the reason for my recovery. I beg you not to press me for an answer."

Shahryar was very much surprised at this. "Let me hear first what made you so pale and brought you so low," he said.

"Know then, brother," Shah Zaman answered, "that when you sent your vizier with the invitation to come to you, I made ready and marched out of my city. But then I remembered a string of jewels I had left behind in the palace, which I meant as a present for you. I went back for it alone, and found my wife on my own bed in the arms of a hideous black cook. So I killed the pair of them and came on to you — and my mind kept working over the business, and I lost my bloom and grew weak. But excuse me if I still refuse to tell you the reason my colour came back."

Shahryar shook his head, marvelling at it beyond measure, and with the fire of anger flaring up in his heart he cried, "The malice of woman is a mighty thing indeed!" Then he took refuge from them with Allah, and said, "In plain truth, brother, you have escaped a great deal of evil by putting your wife to death, and your rage and your grief were entirely excusable — a thing like that has never yet happened to a crowned king. By Allah, if it had happened to me, I would not have been satisfied with less than killing a thousand women, and that way lies madness. But praise be to Allah, who has softened your trouble for you. And now you really must tell me what it was that suddenly gave you back your colour and your health, and explain to me why you are hiding it."

"O King of the age, again I beg you to excuse me."

"No. You must."

"Brother, I am afraid the telling of it will cause you more anger and more sorrow than it caused me."

"All the more reason," said Shahryar, "to tell me the whole story. And I charge you by Allah to keep nothing back."

So Shah Zaman told him everything he had seen, from beginning to end, and finished: "When I saw your calamity, brother, and the treachery of your wife, and thought about it — that you are older than I am and greater than I am in sovereignty — my own sorrow was made small by the comparison, and my mind came back into balance and good temper. And so, throwing off my misery and my low spirits, I could eat and drink and sleep, and got my health and strength back quickly. That is the truth, and the whole of it."

When King Shahryar heard this he flew into a rage so great that it nearly choked him; but he mastered himself and said, "Brother, I would not call you a liar in this matter, but I cannot believe it until I see it with my own eyes."

"If you want to look at your own calamity," said Shah Zaman, "get up at once and make ready for hunting and coursing again, and then hide yourself here with me. You will see it, and your own eyes will prove it."

"True," said the king.

So he had it proclaimed that he was going travelling, and the troops and the tents went out of the city and camped within sight of it, and Shahryar rode out with them and took his place in the middle of his army, ordering the slaves to let no one in to him. When night came he called for his vizier and said, "Sit in my place, and let no one know I am gone for the next three days."

Then the two brothers disguised themselves and came back to the palace by night, in complete secrecy, and passed the dark hours there. At dawn they settled themselves at the lattice overlooking the pleasure grounds, and before long the queen and her women came out as before, passed under the windows, and made for the fountain. There they stripped, ten of them men and ten of them women, and the king's wife called out, "Where are you, Saeed?"

The Black man dropped straight down out of the tree, and rushing into her arms without any pause at all, called out, "I am Sa'ad al-Din Saood!" The queen laughed out loud, and they all fell to satisfying their lusts, and stayed at it a couple of hours. Then the white slaves got up off the serving women, and the Black slave got up off the queen; and they all went down into the basin, and after performing the full washing they put their clothes on and went away as they had done before.

When King Shahryar saw this shame done by his wife and his concubines, he went out of his mind. "Only in complete solitude," he cried, "can a man be safe from what goes on in this vile world! By Allah, life is nothing but one great wrong."

Then he said, "Do not cross me, brother, in what I am about to propose."

"I will not," said the other.

"Then let us get up exactly as we are and go away from here at once. We have no business with kingship. Let us wander over Allah's earth and worship the Almighty until we find somebody the same calamity has happened to; and if we find nobody, then death will be more welcome to us than life."

So the two brothers went out through a second private door of the palace, and never stopped travelling by night or by day until they came to a tree standing in the middle of a meadow, beside a spring of sweet water on the shore of the salt sea. They both drank, and sat down to rest.

An hour of the day had gone by when they heard a roaring and an uproar out in the middle of the sea, as if the heavens were falling in on the earth; and the sea broke into waves in front of them, and out of it there rose a black pillar, which grew and grew until it towered up to the sky and began to come towards that meadow.

They were terrified, and climbed to the top of the tree, which was a tall one, and looked out from there to see what was happening. And it was a jinni — one of the jinn, the spirits that people nowadays call genies — enormously tall, huge in the chest and the body, broad-browed and black as pitch, carrying a crystal chest on his head. He waded to shore through the deep water, came to the tree the two kings were in, and sat himself down under it.

Then he set the chest upright and drew out of it a casket with seven steel padlocks, which he unlocked with seven steel keys that he took from beside his thigh. And out of the casket came a young woman, white-skinned and lovely-faced, slender and finely made, and as bright as the moon of the fourteenth night, which is the full moon, or as the sun pouring down its light. As the poet Utayyah put it, and put it well:

	She rose like the morning breaking through the night,
	and gilded the whole grove with her graciousness;
	the sun itself takes light from her radiance
	when she puts back her veil and shames the moon.
	Every creature bows down between her hands
	when she unveils and shows what she is.
	And she floods whole cities with a torrent of tears
	when the lightning of her glance goes over them.

The jinni sat her down under the tree at his side, and looked at her and said, "Dearest love of this heart of mine! Lady of the noblest family — I carried you off on your wedding night so that nobody could get in ahead of me and take your maidenhead before I did, and nobody has ever loved you or had you but me. Sweetheart, I should like to sleep a little."

Then he laid his head on the lady's thighs, and stretched out his legs, which reached all the way down to the sea, and slept, and snored, and rumbled like rolling thunder.

After a while she lifted her head towards the top of the tree and saw the two kings perched near the summit. So she carefully slid the ifrit's head off her lap — she was tired of holding it up, and an ifrit is a jinni of the fiercer kind — and set it down on the ground, and stood up under the tree, and signalled to them: Come down, you two. Don't be afraid of this ifrit.

They were in a terrible fright, finding they had been seen, and signalled back, "In Allah's name, and by your own modesty, madam — excuse us from coming down."

"In Allah's name," she signalled, "come down this instant. If you don't, I will wake my husband here, this ifrit, and he will kill you by the worst death there is." And she went on making signs at them.

So, out of fear, they came down to her. She stood up in front of them and said, "Take me, and be quick about it. Otherwise I will wake this ifrit and set him on you, and he will kill you where you stand."

"Madam," they said, "we beg you by Allah, let us off this. We are runaways from exactly this sort of thing, and we are in absolute terror of this husband of yours. How can we possibly do what you want?"

"No more talk," she said. "It has to be." And she swore to them by Him who raised the skies up with no prop and no pillar that if they did not do what she wanted, she would have them killed and thrown into the sea.

So Shahryar, in his fear, said to his brother, "Do what she tells you."

"I will not," said Shah Zaman, "until you do it first."

And they stood there arguing about which of them was going to have her.

"What is this?" she said. "Why are you arguing and hanging back? If you two do not come forward like men and do what men do, I will wake the ifrit on you."

At that, in their terror of the jinni, they both did what she told them to do. And when they had got up off her she said, "Well done."

Then she took a purse out of her pocket and drew out a knotted string, with five hundred and seventy signet rings threaded on it. "Do you know what these are?" she asked.

"We do not," they said.

"These," she said, "are the seals of five hundred and seventy men, and every one of them has had me on the horns of this foul, stupid, filthy ifrit. So give me your two seal rings as well, the pair of you."

When they had pulled the rings off their hands and given them to her, she said, "The truth is that this ifrit carried me off on my wedding night, and put me in a casket, and set the casket inside a chest, and fastened seven strong steel padlocks on the chest, and laid me down on the floor of the raving sea, where the waves crash and clash over me. He guarded me so that I should stay chaste and honest — as he puts it — and so that nobody but him should ever have me. And I have lain with as many of my own kind as I pleased. This miserable jinni does not understand that destiny cannot be turned aside or held back by anything, and that whatever a woman wants she gets, however unwilling a man may be. As one of the poets says:

	Do not rely on women;
	do not trust their hearts.
	Their joys and their sorrows
	both hang below the belt.
	They will swear you a love
	that guile never leaves.
	Look at what happened to Yusuf —
	beware of their tricks, beware of the sting.
	Was it not through their arts
	that Iblis got Adam thrown out?

And another says:

	Ease off your blame, man — it only drives the passion higher.
	My fault is not so heavy as the fault you have found in it.
	If I have become a true lover, nothing has come to me
	but what has come to a great many others before now.
	For the man is a wonder and well worth our praise
	who has kept himself safe and sound out of the wiles of women."

Hearing all this, the two of them marvelled beyond marvelling. And she went back to the ifrit and took his head up on her thigh as before, and said to them quietly, "Now go your ways, and get yourselves out of the reach of his malice."

So they went off, saying to one another, "Allah! Allah!" and, "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great — and with Him we take refuge from the malice and the cunning of women, which has no equal on earth. Think about it, brother: look at what this astonishing woman has done to an ifrit, who is a great deal more powerful than we are. Something worse has happened to him than happened to us, and that ought to be consolation enough. So let us go back to our countries and our capitals — and let us settle it that we will never marry a woman again. And soon enough we will show them what we intend to do."

Then they rode back to King Shahryar's camp, which they reached on the morning of the third day; and having called together the viziers and the emirs, the chamberlains and the senior officials, the king gave a robe of honour to his deputy and gave orders to return to the city at once.

There he sat down on his throne and sent for his chief minister — the father of the two girls who, Allah willing, will be spoken of shortly — and said, "I order you to take my wife and put her to death. She has broken her word and her faith."

So the vizier carried her off to the place of execution and killed her.

Then King Shahryar took a sword in his hand and went to the women's quarters and killed all the concubines and all their Mamluks. And he swore a binding oath that from now on, whatever wife he married, he would take her maidenhead at night and kill her the next morning, to make certain of his honour. "Because," he said, "there never was and there is not now one chaste woman on the face of the earth."

Then Shah Zaman asked leave to go home, and he was fitted out and escorted, and travelled until he reached his own country.

Meanwhile Shahryar ordered his vizier to bring him that night's bride, so that he could go in to her. The vizier produced a most beautiful girl, the daughter of one of the emirs; the king went in to her in the evening, and when morning came he told his minister to strike her head off. And the vizier did it, for fear of the king.

He went on like that for three years. Every night he married a girl, and every morning he killed her — until the people raised an outcry against him and cursed him and prayed to Allah to destroy him and his rule utterly. The women wailed and the mothers wept and parents fled the city with their daughters, until there was not a girl left in the whole place old enough to be taken to bed.

Then the king ordered his chief vizier — the same man who was charged with the executions — to bring him a virgin as usual. The minister went out and searched and could not find one; and he came home in sorrow and dread, afraid for his own life.

Now this vizier had two daughters, whose names were Shahrazad and Dunyazad. Shahrazad is the name English has usually spelled Scheherazade, and she was the elder. She had read the books and the annals and the legends of earlier kings, and the stories and examples and lessons of men and things long gone by; indeed it was said that she had collected a thousand volumes of histories about ancient peoples and dead rulers. She had read the poets and knew them by heart. She had studied philosophy and the sciences and the arts and every accomplishment; and she was pleasant and polite, wise and witty, well read and well brought up.

That day she said to her father, "Why do I see you so changed, and so loaded down with worry and care? About such things one of the poets said:

	Tell anyone who is grieving:
	grief will never last.
	Just as joy has no tomorrow,
	so sorrow will go past."

When the vizier heard this from his daughter he told her, from beginning to end, everything that had passed between himself and the king.

Then she said, "By Allah, father — how long is this slaughter of women going to go on? Shall I tell you what is in my mind, to save both sides from destruction?"

"Say on, daughter," he said.

"I want you to give me in marriage to this King Shahryar," she said. "Either I live, or I am the ransom for the virgin daughters of the Muslims and the reason they are delivered out of his hands and out of yours."

"In Allah's name!" he cried, in a rage that needed no feeding. "You little fool — do not put your life in that kind of danger! How dare you speak to me in words so far from wisdom and so close to stupidity? Understand this: a person with no experience of the world falls into trouble easily, and whoever does not consider how a thing ends does not keep the world for a friend. As the common people say — I was sitting at my ease, and nothing but my own meddling brought me unease."

"You must," she broke in, "let me do this good deed. And let him kill me if he likes. I shall only die as a ransom for others."

"Daughter," he asked, "how does that do you any good, once you have thrown your life away?"

"Father," she answered, "it has to be, whatever comes of it."

The vizier flew into a fury again and scolded her and reproached her, and finished with, "In plain truth, I am afraid the same thing will happen to you that happened to the Bull and the Ass with the Farmer."

"And what happened to them, father?" she asked.

Whereupon the vizier began the

Tale of the Bull and the Ass

Know, my daughter, that there was once a merchant who had a great deal of money and a great many men under him, and who was rich in cattle and camels. He had a wife and children too, and he lived out in the country, where he was an experienced farmer and devoted to his land.

Now Allah Most High had given him the gift of understanding the speech of every kind of beast and bird — but on pain of death if he ever told anyone he had it. So he kept it secret, out of plain fear.

In his cowshed he had a Bull and an Ass, each tied up in his own stall, right next to one another. And one day, as the merchant was sitting nearby with his servants and his children were playing around him, he heard the Bull say to the Ass:

"Health and joy to you, Father of Waking! You get rest and good service. Everything under you is swept clean and freshly watered. Men wait on you and feed you, and your ration is sifted barley and your drink is clean spring water — while I, wretched creature, am taken out in the middle of the night, and they put the plough on my neck and a thing they call a Yoke, and I wear myself out splitting the ground from sunrise to sunset. I am made to do more than I can, and to put up with every sort of ill-treatment from one night to the next; and then they take me back with my sides torn and my neck flayed and my legs aching and my eyelids raw with tears. Then they shut me in the byre and throw me beans and chopped straw with dirt and chaff in it, and I lie in dung and filth and stink all night long.

"But you — you are always in a place that has been swept and watered and cleaned out, and you are always lying at your ease, except now and then, and rarely enough, when the master has business and rides you into town and comes straight back with you. So it works out that I am worked and worn while you take your rest; you sleep while I lie awake; I am hungry while you eat your fill; and I get contempt while you get goodwill."

When the Bull had finished, the Ass turned to him and said, "Broad-Brow, you poor lost creature — whoever named you Bull-head was not lying. You have no forethought and no cunning, Father of a Bull; you are the simplest of simpletons, and you know nothing about taking good advice. Have you never heard what the wise man said?

	For other men I carry these hardships and this work,
	and theirs is the pleasure and mine is the care —
	like the bleacher who blackens his own face in the sun
	to whiten the clothes that other men will wear.

"But you, you fool, are full of eagerness. You slave and sweat in front of the master; you tear yourself and wear yourself out and kill yourself for somebody else's comfort. Have you never heard the saying, no one to guide you and you wander off the road? You go out at the call to dawn prayer and you do not come back until sundown, and all the long day you put up with every kind of hardship — beating and belabouring and foul language.

"Now listen to me, Sir Bull. When they tie you to that stinking manger, you paw the ground with your front hooves and lash out with your back ones and butt with your horns and bellow, and so they think you are contented. And when they throw down your fodder you fall on it greedily and hurry to line that fine fat belly of yours.

"If you take my advice it will go better for you, and you will have an easier life than mine. When you go out to the field and they lay that thing called a Yoke on your neck, lie down and do not get up again, even if they thrash you; and if you do get up, lie down a second time. And when they bring you home and offer you your beans, fall over backwards and only sniff at your food and back away from it and do not taste it, and be content with the chopped straw and the chaff. That way you can pretend to be ill. Keep it up for a day, or two days, or even three, and you will get a rest from all your toil and trouble."

When the Bull heard all this he knew the Ass was his friend, and thanked him. "Your advice is sound," he said, and prayed that every blessing might repay him, and cried, "Father of Waking, you have made up for everything I lack!"

(And the merchant, my daughter, understood every word of it.)

The next day the driver took the Bull and settled the plough on his neck and set him to work as usual; but the Bull began to shirk his ploughing, exactly as the Ass had advised. The ploughman beat him until he broke the yoke and bolted; but the man caught him and leathered him until the beast despaired of his life. Even so, he would do nothing but stand still and then drop down again, and he kept it up until the evening.

Then the herdsman led him home and put him in his stall. But he backed away from his manger, and did not stamp or rear or butt or bellow the way he usually did, which puzzled the man. He brought him the beans and the husks, and the Bull sniffed at them and left them, and lay down as far from them as he could get, and passed the whole night without eating.

The farmhand came back next morning, and seeing the manger still full of beans, the chopped straw untouched, and the ox lying on his back in a pitiful state with his legs stuck out and his belly swollen, he was worried about him and said to himself, "By Allah, he has certainly fallen sick — that is why he would not plough yesterday."

So he went to the merchant and reported, "Master, the Bull is ailing. He refused his fodder last night, and what is more he has not touched a scrap of it this morning."

Now the merchant knew perfectly well what all this meant, because he had overheard the conversation between the Bull and the Ass. So he said, "Take that rascal of a donkey, and put the yoke on his neck, and tie him to the plough, and make him do the Bull's work."

So the ploughman took the Ass and worked him the whole day long at the Bull's task; and when he flagged from weakness the man fed him the stick until his ribs were sore and his sides were sunken and his neck was flayed by the yoke. When he came home in the evening he could hardly drag one leg after another, front or back.

The Bull, meanwhile, had spent the day lying stretched out at full length and had eaten his fodder with an excellent appetite, and he never stopped calling down blessings on the Ass for his good advice — not knowing what had happened to the Ass on his account.

So when night came and the Ass came back into the byre, the Bull rose up to honour him and said, "May good news gladden your heart, Father of Waking! Thanks to you I have rested all day and eaten my food in peace and quiet."

But the Ass did not answer a word, for rage and heartburning and exhaustion and the beating he had taken; and he repented with the bitterest repentance there is, and said to himself, "This is what comes of my folly in giving good advice. As the saying goes — I was sitting at my ease, and nothing but my own meddling brought me unease. But I will keep my own worth in mind, and the nobility of my nature. For what does the poet say?

	Does the beautiful colour of the basil fail
	because a beetle has crawled over the leaf?
	And if a spider and a fly are living in it,
	does disgrace attach to the royal hall?
	The cowrie shell, I know, will pass as currency —
	but does that make the clear drop of the pearl worth less?

"And now I must think, and play a trick on him, and get him back to his place, or else I die."

Then he went wearily to his manger, while the Bull thanked him and blessed him.

"And in just the same way, my daughter," said the vizier, "you will die for want of sense. So sit still and say nothing, and do not put your life in this kind of danger — for by Allah, I am giving you the best advice I have, and it comes out of my love for you and my care for you."

"Father," she answered, "I must go up to this King, and I must be married to him."

"Do not do it," he said.

"I truly will," she said.

"If you will not be quiet and stay where you are," he replied, "I will do to you exactly what the merchant did to his wife."

"And what did he do?" she asked.

Know then, said the vizier, that after the Ass came back the merchant went out onto the terrace roof with his wife and his children, because it was a moonlit night with the moon at the full. The terrace looked down over the cowshed; and as he sat there with his children playing round him, the trader heard the Ass say to the Bull:

"Tell me, Father Broad-Brow — what do you mean to do tomorrow?"

"What else," the Bull answered, "but go on following your advice? It could not have been better, and it has given me rest and quiet, and I shall not depart from it by a hair. So when they bring me my food I shall refuse it, and blow my belly out, and play sick."

The Ass shook his head. "Do nothing of the sort, Father of a Bull."

"Why not?" asked the Bull.

"Because," said the Ass, "I am about to give you the best advice you have ever had. I heard our owner say to the herdsman: If the Bull does not get up from his place and do his work this morning, and if he backs off from his fodder again today, hand him over to the butcher to have his throat cut, and give the meat to the poor and make a bit of leather out of the hide. Now I am afraid for you on account of that. So take my advice before a disaster falls on you: when they bring your fodder, eat it, and get up, and bellow, and paw the ground — or our master will most certainly kill you. And peace be with you."

At that the Bull got up and lowed aloud and thanked the Ass, and said, "Tomorrow I will go out with them gladly." And he ate up all his food at once and licked the manger clean.

(All of this happened, and the owner was listening to every word.)

Next morning the trader and his wife went and sat down by the Bull's crib, and the driver came and led the Bull out; and the Bull, seeing his owner, whisked his tail and broke wind and frisked about so energetically that the merchant burst out laughing, and went on laughing until he fell over on his back.

His wife asked him, "What are you laughing at like that?"

"I laughed," he said, "at a secret something I heard and saw, and I cannot tell you or I shall die."

"You must tell me," she said, "and you must say why you were laughing, even if it kills you."

"I cannot reveal what beasts and birds say in their own language," he answered. "I would die."

"By Allah, you are lying," she said. "This is a mere excuse. You are laughing at nobody but me, and now you want to hide something from me. But by the Lord of the Heavens, if you do not tell me why, I will not live with you another day. I am leaving." And she sat down and cried.

"Curse it," said the merchant, "what are you crying for? Fear Allah, and leave this alone, and ask me no more questions."

"You have got to tell me why you laughed," she said.

"You know," he replied, "that when I prayed to Allah to grant me the understanding of the speech of beasts and birds, I swore a vow never to tell the secret to anybody, on pain of dropping dead on the spot."

"Never mind that," she cried. "Tell me what passed between the Bull and the Ass, and die this very hour if that is what you want." And she went on badgering him until he was worn out and quite beside himself.

So at last he said, "Send for your father and your mother, and our relatives, and some of the neighbours." Which she did; and he sent for the judge and his witnesses, meaning to make his will, and tell her the secret, and die.

He loved her very much — she was his cousin, his father's brother's daughter, and the mother of his children, and he had lived with her for a hundred and twenty years.

So when the whole family and all the neighbours had assembled, he said to them, "There is a strange business hanging over me, and it is of such a kind that if I tell the secret to anybody, I am a dead man."

At that every single person there said to the woman, "In Allah's name, drop this sinful obstinacy and admit that this is how the matter stands, before you end up killing your husband and the father of your children."

But she answered, "I will not let go of it until he tells me, even if it kills him."

So they gave up urging her; and the trader got up from among them and went off to an outbuilding to wash for prayer, meaning to come back afterwards and tell them the secret and die.

Now, daughter Shahrazad, that merchant kept about fifty hens in his outbuildings with a single rooster over them. And while he was getting himself ready to say goodbye to his household, he heard one of his many farm dogs address the Rooster in the Rooster's own language. The Rooster was flapping his wings and crowing at the top of his voice and jumping from one hen's back to another and treading them all in turn.

"Rooster," said the Dog, "how small your wits are, and how shameless your behaviour is! Bad luck to whoever raised you. Are you not ashamed of yourself, carrying on like that on a day like this?"

"And what," asked the Rooster, "has happened today?"

"Do you not know," said the Dog, "that our master is getting ready to die today? His wife is determined that he shall tell her the secret Allah taught him, and the moment he does, he dies. We dogs are all in mourning. And you clap your wings and crow your loudest and tread one hen after another. Is this an hour for amusing yourself and taking your pleasure? Have you no shame?"

"Then by Allah," said the Rooster, "our master is a half-wit and a man with no sense in him. If he cannot manage one single wife, his life is not worth keeping. Now I have about fifty ladies of my own. I please this one and cross that one; I starve one and stuff another; and by good government I have the lot of them well under control. And this master of ours claims to have wit and wisdom, and he has one wife, and does not know how to manage her."

"Then what," asked the Dog, "should the master do to get himself out of this fix?"

"He should get up this instant," said the Rooster, "and take a few switches off that mulberry tree, and give her a good thorough beating across the back and the ribs until she cries: I repent, my lord! I will never ask you a question as long as I live! And then let him beat her once more, and soundly. And when he has done that he can sleep without a care and enjoy his life. But this master of ours has neither sense nor judgement."

"Now, daughter Shahrazad," the vizier went on, "I will do to you what that husband did to that wife."

"And what did he do?" said Shahrazad.

He replied: When the merchant heard the wise words his Rooster spoke to his Dog, he got up in a hurry and went to his wife's room, cutting some mulberry switches on the way and hiding them there. Then he called to her, "Come into the inner room, so that I can tell you the secret where nobody can see me, and then die."

She went in with him, and he locked the door, and came down on her with such a beating — back and shoulders, ribs, arms and legs — saying all the while, "Are you going to spend your life asking questions about what does not concern you?" — that she was very nearly senseless.

Presently she cried out, "I am one of the repentant! By Allah, I will never ask you another question. I repent, truly and thoroughly."

Then she kissed his hands and his feet, and he led her out of the room as obedient as a wife should be. Her parents and the whole company were delighted, and the sadness and the mourning turned into joy and gladness. So the merchant learned how to run a household from his Rooster, and he and his wife lived together as happily as any two people until they died.

"And you too, my daughter," the vizier went on. "Unless you turn back from this business I will do to you what that trader did to his wife."

But she answered him very firmly. "I will never give it up, father, and this tale is not going to change my mind. Leave off this talk and this chatter. I will not listen to you; and if you refuse me, I will marry myself to him in spite of your nose. And I will go up to the King myself, alone, and say to him: I begged my father to marry me to you, and he refused, because he was determined to disappoint his lord and grudged the like of me to the like of you."

Her father asked, "Does it have to be?"

"It does," she answered.

At which the vizier, worn out with lamenting and arguing and persuading and dissuading her, all to no purpose, went up to King Shahryar and blessed him and kissed the ground before him, and told him the whole story of the dispute with his daughter from beginning to end, and how he intended to bring her to him that night.

The King was astonished beyond measure, because he had made a particular exception of the vizier's daughter. "Most faithful of my counsellors," he said, "how can this be? You know I have sworn by the Raiser of the Heavens that after I have gone in to her tonight I shall say to you tomorrow morning: Take her and kill her. And if you do not kill her, I will kill you in her place, without fail."

"May Allah guide you to glory and lengthen your life, O King of the age," the vizier answered. "It is she who has decided this. I have told her all that and more, but she will not listen to me, and she insists on spending this coming night with the King's Majesty."

So Shahryar was greatly pleased, and said, "Very well. Go and get her ready, and bring her to me tonight."

The vizier went back to his daughter and reported the order, saying, "May Allah not leave your father desolate by the loss of you!"

But Shahrazad was overjoyed. She got ready everything she needed, and said to her younger sister Dunyazad, "Pay close attention to what I am asking you to do. When I have gone in to the King I will send for you; and when you come to me, and see that he has had what he wants of me, then say to me: Sister, if you are not sleepy, tell me some new story, something delightful and delicious, to help the waking hours along. And I will tell you a tale which will be our deliverance, if it pleases Allah, and which will turn the King away from this blood-thirsty habit of his."

Dunyazad answered, "With love and gladness."

So when night came their father the vizier brought Shahrazad to the King, who was pleased at the sight of her and asked, "Have you brought me what I need?"

"I have," he answered.

But when the King took her to his bed and began to play with her and wanted to go in to her, she wept; which made him ask, "What is the matter?"

"O King of the age," she replied, "I have a younger sister, and I should dearly like to say goodbye to her tonight before I see the dawn."

So he sent for Dunyazad at once, and she came and kissed the ground between his hands, and he let her take a seat near the foot of the bed. Then the King got up and took his bride's maidenhead, and the three of them fell asleep.

But at midnight Shahrazad woke, and signalled to her sister Dunyazad, who sat up and said, "In Allah's name, sister, tell us some new story, something delightful and delicious, to pass away the waking hours of the last of the night."

"With joy and goodwill," answered Shahrazad, "if this pious and fortunate King will permit me."

"Tell on," said the King, who happened to be sleepless and restless and was therefore pleased at the prospect of hearing a story.

So Shahrazad was glad; and on the first night of the Thousand Nights and a Night she began with the

Tale of the Trader and the Jinni

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that there was once a merchant among the merchants, a man of great wealth with business in a number of cities.

One day he mounted his horse and rode out to collect money owed him in certain towns; and the heat came down on him hard, so he sat down under a tree, and put his hand into his saddlebag and took out some broken bread and a few dry dates, and began to eat.

When he had finished the dates he flung the stones away, hard — and there in front of him stood an ifrit, an enormous one, brandishing a drawn sword. The ifrit came up to him and said, "Stand up, so that I can kill you, exactly as you killed my son."

"How have I killed your son?" asked the merchant.

"When you ate those dates and threw away the stones," he answered, "they struck my son full in the chest as he was walking past, and he died on the spot."

"Truly we come from Allah, and to Allah we are returning," said the merchant. "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great! If I killed your son, I killed him by pure accident. I beg you to pardon me."

"There is no help for it," said the jinni. "I have to kill you."

Then he seized him and dragged him along, and threw him down on the ground, and raised the sword to strike. And the merchant wept and said, "I commit my case to Allah," and began to recite:

	Time holds two sorts of day, this one a blessing and that one a curse,
	and life holds two halves, this one all pleasure and that one all pain.
	Do you not see, when the hurricane blows, stripping and striking hard,
	that nothing but the great tree of the forest feels the strain of it?
	How many trees does the earth feed, the dry ones and the green —
	and none but the ones bearing fruit get stones thrown at them.
	Do you not see how corpses rise and float on the top of the tide,
	while the pearls worth having lie hidden in the deepest part of the sea?
	The stars in heaven are past counting,
	but no star is ever eclipsed except the sun and the moon.
	You judged well of the days that saw you going about safe and sound,
	and never counted the pangs and the pains that Fate is always ready with.
	The nights kept you safe, and being safe made you proud —
	but the good things of the night are the very things that breed the bad.

When the merchant had finished his verses the jinni said to him, "Cut it short, by Allah. I have to kill you."

But the merchant spoke to him like this. "Understand, ifrit, that I have debts owed to me and a great deal of property, and children and a wife, and a number of things left in my keeping. Let me go home and settle with every man who has a claim on me; and I will come back to you at the head of the new year. Let Allah be my witness and my guarantor that I will return to you, and then you may do with me whatever you like. And Allah is witness to what I say."

The jinni took a firm promise from him and let him go.

So he went back to his own city and put his affairs in order and paid every man what he was owed; and after telling his wife and children what had happened to him, he appointed a guardian for them and lived with them for a full year.

Then he got up, and washed himself clean as a man does before death, and took his shroud under his arm, and said goodbye to his household and his neighbours and every one of his relations, and went out — though every part of him refused to go. They began weeping and wailing and beating their breasts over him; but he travelled on until he came to the same garden, and the day he arrived was the head of the new year.

As he sat there weeping over what had happened to him, an old man came up, a very ancient man, leading a gazelle on a chain. He greeted the merchant and wished him a long life, and said, "What has brought you to sit in this place, all by yourself, when it is a haunt of evil spirits?"

The merchant told him everything that had passed between himself and the ifrit; and the old man, the owner of the gazelle, marvelled at it and said, "By Allah, brother, your faith is nothing short of extraordinary, and your story is a strange one. If it were engraved with needles on the inner corners of the eye, it would be a warning to anyone willing to take warning."

Then he sat down beside the merchant and said, "By Allah, brother, I am not leaving you until I see what happens between you and this ifrit."

And as he sat there and the two of them talked, the merchant began to feel fear and terror, and a grief past all easing, and a care that kept growing, and the last extremity of despair.

The owner of the gazelle was still at his side when a second old man came up to them, and with him two dogs, both greyhounds and both black. This second old man greeted them and asked their news as well, and said, "What has brought you to sit in this place, which is a dwelling of the jinn?"

So they told him the tale from beginning to end. And they had not been sitting there long before a third old man came up, with him a she-mule of a bright bay colour; and he greeted them and asked why they were sitting there. So they told him the story from first to last — and there is no use, my lord, in telling a tale twice.

He sat down with them. And then a cloud of dust came on, and a great dust-devil rose up in the middle of the waste ground; and the cloud opened, and inside it was that same jinni, with a drawn sword in his hand and his eyes throwing off sparks of rage.

He came up to them and hauled the merchant out from among them and shouted at him, "Get up, so that I can kill you, exactly as you killed my son, the life-blood of my liver."

The merchant wailed and wept, and the three old men began sighing and crying and weeping and wailing along with their companion.

Then the first old man, the owner of the gazelle, stepped out from among them and kissed the ifrit's hand and said, "Jinni — Crown of the Kings of the Jinn — if I were to tell you the story of myself and this gazelle, and you found it a wonder, would you give me a third part of this merchant's blood?"

"I would," said the jinni. "If you tell me this tale and I hold it to be a marvel, then I will give you a third of his blood."

At which the old man began to tell

The First Old Man's Story

Know, jinni, that this gazelle is my father's brother's daughter, my own flesh and blood. I married her when she was a young girl, and I lived with her for the best part of thirty years, and she never gave me a child. So I took a concubine, and she gave me the gift of a son, a boy as handsome as the full moon, with beautiful shining eyes and eyebrows that met in a single line, and every limb of him perfectly made.

Little by little he grew, and grew tall; and when he was a lad of fifteen I had to travel to certain cities, and I set off with a great stock of goods.

But my cousin — this gazelle — had learned magic and sorcery and the black arts from her childhood. So she turned that son of mine into a calf, and turned my slave girl, his mother, into a heifer, and handed the pair of them over to the herdsman.

When I came home after a long absence and asked after my son and his mother, she said, "Your slave girl is dead, and your son has run off, and I do not know where he has gone."

So I stayed a whole year with a grieving heart and streaming eyes, until the time came round for the Great Feast of Allah. Then I sent to my herdsman and told him to pick me out a fat heifer; and he brought me one — and it was the girl, my slave, whom this gazelle had bewitched.

I tucked up my sleeves and my skirts and took a knife and started to cut her throat. But she bellowed aloud and wept bitter tears. It astonished me, and pity took hold of me, and I stayed my hand and said to the herdsman, "Bring me a different one."

Then my cousin cried out, "Kill her! I have none fatter and none finer."

So I went forward to sacrifice her a second time, and a second time she bellowed aloud; and out of pity I held back again, and told the herdsman to kill her and skin her himself. He killed her and skinned her, and found neither fat nor flesh on her, nothing but hide and bone. And I was sorry, when being sorry was no use to me at all.

I gave her over to the herdsman and said, "Fetch me a fat calf." And he brought my son, under the spell.

When the calf saw me he broke his tether and ran to me and fawned on me and cried, and shed tears; so that I took pity on him and said to the herdsman, "Bring me a heifer, and let this calf go."

At that my cousin — this gazelle — shouted at me, "You must kill this calf. This is a holy day and a blessed one, and nothing is sacrificed on it that is not perfect and pure; and we have no calf fatter or finer than this one."

"Look at the state of the heifer I slaughtered at your bidding," I said, "and how we turned away from her in disappointment, and how she was no good to us at all. I regret killing her bitterly. So this time I will not do what you tell me and sacrifice this calf."

"By Allah the Most Great, the Compassionate, the Merciful," she said, "there is no help for it. You must kill him on this holy day; and if you do not kill him, then you are no husband to me and I am no wife to you."

Now when I heard those hard words — not understanding what she was after — I went up to the calf with the knife in my hand:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

Then her sister said to her, "How lovely your tale is, and how pleasing, and how sweet, and how good to listen to!"

And Shahrazad answered, "And what is this compared to what I could tell you tomorrow night, if I am alive and the King spares me?"

Then the King said to himself, "By Allah, I will not kill her until I have heard the rest of her tale."

So they slept the rest of that night in each other's arms until the day was fully up. Then the King went out to his audience hall, and the vizier went up with his daughter's shroud under his arm. The King gave out his orders, and promoted this man and dismissed that one, until the end of the day; and he said not one word to the vizier about what had happened. The minister wondered at it beyond all wondering. And when the court broke up, King Shahryar went into his palace.

When it was the Second Night,

Dunyazad said to her sister Shahrazad, "Sister, finish that story of the Merchant and the Jinni for us."

And she answered, "With joy and goodwill, if the King permits me."

Then the King said, "Tell your tale."

And Shahrazad began: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the merchant meant to sacrifice the calf, and saw it weeping, his heart softened, and he said to the herdsman, "Keep the calf with the rest of my cattle."

All this the old man told the jinni, who marvelled a good deal at such strange words. Then the owner of the gazelle went on:

Lord of the Kings of the Jinn, all this happened, and my uncle's daughter, this gazelle, stood watching and saw it, and said, "Butcher this calf for me. It is certainly a fat one." But I told the herdsman to take it away, and he took it and turned for home.

Next day, as I was sitting in my own house, in came the herdsman, and he stood in front of me and said, "Master, I am going to tell you something that will gladden your heart, and it should earn me the reward that goes with good news."

"So it shall," I answered.

"Merchant," he said, "I have a daughter, and she learned magic in her childhood from an old woman who lived with us. Yesterday, when you gave me the calf, I took it into the house to her, and she looked at it and covered her face; and then she wept, and then she laughed, and then wept again, and at last she said: Father, has my honour become so cheap to you that you bring strange men in to me?

"I asked her: Where are these strange men, and why were you laughing and crying? And she answered: The truth is that this calf you have with you is the son of our master the merchant. He is under a spell put on him by his stepmother, who bewitched both him and his mother. That is why I laughed. And the reason I wept is his mother — because his father killed her without knowing what he was doing.

"I marvelled at this beyond all marvelling, and I could hardly wait for daylight before coming to tell you."

When I heard my herdsman's words, jinni, I went out with him — drunk without any wine, out of the sheer joy and gladness that had come over me — and we went to his house. There his daughter welcomed me and kissed my hand, and at once the calf came and fawned on me as before.

"Is this true, what you say about this calf?" I asked the herdsman's daughter.

"It is, my lord," she said. "He is your son, the very core of your heart."

I was overjoyed, and said to her, "Girl, if you will free him, everything I own that is in your father's hands, cattle and property both, shall be yours."

She smiled and answered, "My lord, I have no greed for the goods, and I will not take them except on two conditions. The first is that you marry me to your son. The second is that I may put a spell on the woman who put a spell on him, and shut her up — because otherwise I cannot be safe from her malice and her mischief."

When I heard the herdsman's daughter say this, jinni, I answered, "Besides what you are asking for, all the cattle and the household goods in your father's charge are yours; and as for my uncle's daughter, her blood is lawful to you."

When I had said it, she took a cup and filled it with water, and recited a spell over it, and sprinkled it on the calf, saying, "If Almighty Allah created you a calf, then stay in this shape and do not change; but if you are under a spell, then come back to the shape you had before, by the command of Allah Most High!"

And the calf shuddered — and became a man.

Then I fell on his neck and said, "In Allah's name, tell me everything my uncle's daughter did to you and to your mother." And when he had told me what had passed between them, I said, "My son, Allah favoured you with somebody to give you back to yourself, and what was yours has come back to you."

Then, jinni, I married the herdsman's daughter to him; and she turned my wife into this gazelle, saying, "This shape is a pretty one, and not loathsome at all."

After that she lived with us night and day and day and night, until the Almighty took her to Himself. When she died, my son set out for the cities of India — for the very city, in fact, that belongs to this man here, the one who has had done to him what has been done. And I took this gazelle, my cousin, and wandered with her from town to town looking for news of my son, until Destiny drove me to this place, where I found the merchant sitting here in tears.

That is my tale.

"That story is strange indeed," said the jinni, "and so I grant you the third part of his blood."

Then the second old man, the one who owned the two greyhounds, came up and said, "Jinni, if I tell you what happened to me because of my brothers, these two hounds, and you find it a tale more wonderful and more marvellous than the one you have just heard, will you grant me a third of this man's blood as well?"

"You have my word on it," the jinni replied, "if your adventures are more marvellous and more wonderful."

At which he began

The Second Old Man's Story

Know, Lord of the Kings of the Jinn, that these two dogs are my brothers, and I am the third of us.

When our father died he left us a capital of three thousand gold pieces. I opened a shop with my share and traded in it, and my two brothers did the same, each setting up a shop of his own.

But I had not been in business long before the eldest sold his stock for a thousand dinars, and bought an outfit and goods, and went off to foreign parts. He was away a whole year with the caravan.

Then one day, as I was sitting in my shop, a beggar came and stood in front of me asking for charity. "May Allah open another door to you," I said.

At which he answered, weeping, "Am I so changed that you do not know me?"

I looked at him closely — and it was my brother. So I got up and made him welcome, and sat him down in the shop and asked him what had happened.

"Do not ask," he said. "My money is all gone, and my situation is beyond describing."

So I took him to the baths and dressed him in a suit of my own clothes and gave him a room in my house. What is more, when I went over my stock accounts and the profits of my business, I found that hard work had earned me a thousand dinars, and that my capital, the head of my wealth, came to two thousand. So I split the whole lot with him, and said, "Suppose that you never went abroad at all, but stayed at home. And do not let your bad luck weigh on you."

He took his share very gladly and opened a shop of his own; and things went quietly along for a few days and nights.

But then my second brother — that other dog there — set his heart on travelling too, and sold off what goods and stock he had; and though we tried to stop him, he would not be stopped. He got himself an outfit for the journey and set off with a party of travellers.

After a whole year away he came back to me, exactly as my elder brother had.

"Brother," I said, "did I not try to talk you out of travelling?"

He burst into tears and cried, "Brother, this is what destiny has decreed. Here I am, a plain beggar, without a penny and without a shirt to my back."

So I took him to the baths as well, jinni, and dressed him in new clothes of my own, and took him along to my shop and gave him food and drink. And I said to him, "Brother, it is my habit to cast up my shop accounts at the head of every year, and whatever surplus I find is to be shared between you and me."

So I struck a balance, ifrit, and found two thousand dinars of profit; and I gave praise to the Creator, be He extolled and exalted, and made over half of it to my brother and kept the other half myself. Then he set about opening a shop, and so we went on for a long while.

After a time my brothers began pressing me to travel with them. I refused. "What did the two of you gain by travelling," I said, "that I should expect to gain by it?" And since I would not listen to them, we each went back to our own shop and bought and sold as before.

They kept on urging me to travel for a whole twelve months, and I kept refusing, until six full years had gone by. Then I agreed, and said, "Brothers, here I am, ready to travel with you. Now let me see what money you have between you."

I found they did not have a farthing. They had squandered everything on rich food and drink and pleasures of the flesh. But I did not say a word of reproach to them. Far from it: I went over my shop accounts once more, and sold what goods and stock were mine; and finding myself the owner of six thousand gold pieces, I gladly divided the sum in half.

"These three thousand gold pieces are for you and me to trade with," I said to my brothers. And I added, "Let us bury the other half in the ground, so that it will be there if any harm comes to us — and in that case each of us takes a thousand and opens a shop again."

"Your reckoning is right," they both said. So I gave each of them his thousand gold pieces and kept the same for myself, a thousand dinars.

Then we got suitable goods together and hired a ship, and loaded our merchandise, and sailed on day after day for a full month, until we came to a city where we sold our venture; and for every gold piece we took ten.

And as we were turning back to our ship we found on the seashore a girl in worn and ragged clothes, and she kissed my hand and said, "Master, is there kindness in you, and charity? I can make you a fitting return for both."

"There is," I answered. "There is goodwill in me and a wish to do right, even if you make me no return at all."

Then she said, "Take me as your wife, master, and carry me to your city, for I have given myself to you. Do me this kindness, and I am one of those who deserve kindness and charity: I will make you a fitting return for it. And do not be ashamed of the state you find me in."

When I heard her say this my heart went out to her, as Allah willed it — be He extolled and exalted. So I took her and clothed her and had a good place made ready for her on the ship, and treated her with honour.

So we sailed on; and my heart became attached to her past all attaching, and I was not away from her by night or by day, and I paid more attention to her than to my brothers. So they grew cold towards me, and became jealous of my wealth and the quantity of goods I had, and they looked greedily at everything I owned. They took counsel together to murder me and seize my money, saying, "Let us kill our brother, and all his money will be ours." And Satan made the deed look fine to them. So when they found me alone — and I asleep beside my wife — they picked the two of us up and threw us into the sea.

My wife woke with a start out of her sleep, and instantly became an ifritah, and lifted me up and carried me to an island; and she vanished for a short time, and came back in the morning and said:

"Here I am, your faithful servant, who has made you a fitting return. I carried you up out of the water and saved you from death by the command of the Almighty. You should know that I am a jinniyah; and the moment I saw you my heart loved you, by the will of the Lord — for I am a believer in Allah and in His Apostle, on whom be blessing and peace. So I came to you in the state you saw me in, and you married me; and now, you see, I have saved you from drowning. But I am angry with your brothers, and I certainly must kill them."

When I had heard her story I was astonished, and I thanked her for everything she had done, and said, "But as for killing my brothers — that must not happen."

Then I told her the whole tale of what had passed between us, from the beginning of our lives to the end of it; and when she had heard it she said, "Tonight I will fly over them as a bird, and sink their ship, and kill them."

"In Allah's name," I said, "do not. The proverb says: you who do good to the man who does evil — leave the evildoer to his own evil deeds. And besides, they are still my brothers."

But she came back at me: "By Allah, there is no help for it. I shall kill them."

I humbled myself in front of her, begging their pardon; at which she lifted me up and flew off with me, and at last set me down on the terrace roof of my own house.

I opened the doors and dug up what I had hidden in the ground; and after greeting the neighbours I opened my shop and bought goods.

Now when night came I went home, and there I saw these two hounds tied up. When they caught sight of me they got up and whined and fawned on me — and before I could understand what had happened, my wife said, "These two dogs are your brothers."

"And who has done this to them?" I said.

"I sent a message to my sister," she answered, "and she treated them like this. And these two will not be released from the shape they are in until ten years have gone by."

And now I have arrived at this place on my way to my wife's sister, so that she can deliver them from this condition, after they have endured it for a full ten years. And as I was going along I saw this young man, who told me what had happened to him, and I decided not to go on from here until I had seen what might happen between you and him.

That is my tale.

Then the jinni said, "This is certainly a strange story, and so I give you the third part of his blood and his crime."

At which the third old man, the master of the she-mule, said to the jinni, "I can tell you a tale more wonderful than either of these, if you will grant me the rest of his blood and the rest of his offence."

And the jinni answered, "So be it."

Then the old man began

The Third Old Man's Story

Know, Sultan and head of the jinn, that this mule was my wife.

It happened that I went away and was gone for a whole year; and when I came back from my journey I came to her at night, and saw a Black slave lying with her on the carpet bed. They were talking and playing with one another, laughing and kissing and coupling.

When she saw me she got up and came at me in a hurry with a water jar; and muttering spells over it, she sprinkled me and said, "Come out of this shape of yours and into the shape of a dog." And that instant I was a dog.

She drove me out of the house, and I ran out through the doorway and did not stop running until I came to a butcher's stall, where I stopped and started eating the bones that were lying there.

When the owner of the stall saw me he took me and led me into his house; but the moment his daughter caught sight of me she covered her face and cried out, "Are you bringing men in to me? Do you walk in here with them?"

"Where is the man?" her father asked.

"This dog," she said, "is a man whose wife has put a spell on him. And I can release him."

When her father heard that, he said, "In Allah's name, daughter — release him."

So she took a water jar and, after saying words over it, sprinkled a few drops on me and said, "Come out of that shape and into the shape you had before." And I went back to being myself.

Then I kissed her hand and said, "I wish you would transform my wife the way she transformed me."

At that she gave me some water and said, "As soon as you see her asleep, sprinkle this on her and say the words you heard me say, and she will become whatever you want her to be."

I went to my wife and found her fast asleep; and as I sprinkled the water on her I said, "Come out of that shape and into the shape of a she-mule." And that instant she became a she-mule — and she is the one you are looking at now with your own eyes, Sultan and head of the Kings of the Jinn.

Then the jinni turned to her and said, "Is this true?"

And she nodded her head and answered by signs: It is the truth. That is my story, and that is what happened to me.

Now when the old man had finished speaking, the jinni shook with pleasure and gave him the third part of the merchant's blood:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

Then Dunyazad said, "Sister, how pleasant your tale is, and how good to listen to — how sweet, and how welcome!"

She answered, "And what is this compared to what I could tell you tomorrow night, if I live and the King spares me?"

Then the King thought, "By Allah, I will not kill her until I have heard the rest of her tale, for it is truly a wonder."

So they rested that night in each other's arms until dawn. After that the King went out to his Hall of State, and the vizier and the troops came in and the court filled up; and the King gave his orders and gave judgement, appointed men and dismissed men, commanding and forbidding through the rest of the day. Then the council broke up, and King Shahryar went into his palace.

When it was the Third Night,

and the King had had his will of the vizier's daughter, her sister Dunyazad said to her, "Finish that tale of yours for us."

And she answered, "With joy and goodwill! It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the third old man had told the jinni a tale more wonderful than the two before it, the jinni marvelled beyond all marvelling and, shaking with delight, cried, 'There — I have given you what was left of the merchant's punishment, and for your sake I have let him go.'"

At which the merchant embraced the old men and thanked them; and the three of them wished him joy of his deliverance, and each went off to his own city.

But this tale is not so wonderful as the fisherman's story.

The King asked, "What is the fisherman's story?"

And she answered by telling the tale of

The Fisherman and the Jinni

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that there was once a fisherman well on in years, who had a wife and three children and was in poor circumstances. It was his habit to cast his net four times a day, and no more.

One day he went out about noon to the seashore and set down his basket; and tucking up his shirt and wading into the water, he made a cast with his net and waited for it to settle on the bottom. Then he gathered the cords together and hauled — and found it heavy. However hard he pulled towards the shore, he could not get it up. So he carried the ends of it up the beach and drove a stake into the ground and made the net fast to it. Then he stripped and dived into the water all round the net, and did not stop working at it until he had brought it up.

He was delighted, and put his clothes back on and went to the net — and found in it a dead donkey which had torn the meshes.

When he saw it he cried out in his grief, "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah the Glorious, the Great!" And then he said, "This is a strange way of earning a day's bread." And he began making up verses on the spot:

	You who work through the dark of the night in danger and in pain —
	the work you do for a day's bread does not come by strength or effort.
	Do you not see the fisherman going out on the sea after his bread
	while the stars of night glimmer overhead like a tangled skein?
	Down he goes into the water, and the waves knock him about,
	and all the while his eyes strain to see the net belly out;
	till, glad of a good night's work, he carries home a fish
	whose throat the hook of Fate had caught and cut in two.
	And a man buys that fish from him — a man who spent the night hours
	warm and comfortable, out of the cold and the wet and the dark.
	Praise to the Lord who gives to this one and denies that one his wish,
	and dooms one man to do the work and catch it, and another to eat it.

Then he said, "Up and get on with it. I am certain of His generosity, if Allah wills." And he went on:

	When Evil Fate has hold of you, put on
	the long patience of a noble soul: it is your best.
	Do not complain to your fellow creatures; that is complaining
	from the most merciful of them to the least merciful of all.
