The fisherman, having looked at the dead donkey, got it free of the tangle and wrung out his net and spread it; then he waded into the sea saying, "In Allah's name!" and made a cast and pulled — and it grew heavy, and settled down even more firmly than the first time.

Now he thought there must be fish in it, so he made it fast, and took off his clothes and went into the water and dived and hauled until he had dragged it up onto dry land. And this time he found in it a large earthenware pitcher full of sand and mud.

Seeing this he was greatly upset, and began reciting:

	Leave off, troubles of the world —
	and if you will not leave off, then forgive.
	I went out to look for my day's bread
	and I find I must go breadless.
	Neither does my craft bring me anything
	nor does Fate allot me a share.
	How many fools reach up to the Pleiades
	while the dark swallows the wise and the careful.

So he begged Allah's pardon and threw the jar away, and wrung out his net and cleaned it, and went back to the sea a third time to cast, and waited until it had sunk. Then he pulled it in and found in it broken crockery and broken glass; at which he began to speak these lines:

	Your daily bread is His to give: you can neither tie it up nor loose it,
	and neither pen nor writing will help you find it.
	Joy and daily bread are what Fate condescends to allow;
	this is sad and barren ground, while that makes the farmer glad.
	The arrows of Time and Life bring down a great many worthy men
	while they lift up to high position men of no worth at all.
	So come, Death — for truly life is not worth a straw
	when the falcon falls low and the mallard rides the wind.
	It is no wonder to see the great in soul and mind
	go poor, while many a worthless clown is marked out for luck.
	This bird will fly over the whole world from east to furthest west,
	and that one gets every wish it has without leaving the nest.

Then he raised his eyes to heaven and said, "My God, You know very well that I cast my net only four times a day. The third is done, and so far You have granted me nothing. So this time, my God, be pleased to give me my daily bread."

Then, having called on Allah's name, he threw his net again and waited for it to sink and settle; and then hauled at it, and could not draw it in, because it had caught fast on the bottom. He cried out in his vexation, "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah!" and began reciting:

	Curse this wretched world, if this is how it is —
	that I must be swamped by grief and misery.
	Though a man's lot look cheerful when the morning breaks,
	he drains the cup of sorrow before he sees the evening.
	And yet I was the very man of whom the world, when asked
	whose lot was happiest, would say: his.

At that he stripped and dived down to the net and worked away at it until he got it to land. Then he opened the meshes — and found in it a jar shaped like a cucumber, made of yellow copper, plainly full of something, its mouth closed with a lead cap stamped with the seal ring of our lord Solomon, son of David, may Allah accept them both.

At the sight of it the fisherman was delighted, and said, "If I sell this in the brass market it is worth ten gold dinars." He shook it, and finding it heavy went on, "I wish I knew what was inside. But I must and will open it and look at what is in it, and then put it in my bag and sell it in the brass market."

So he took out a knife and worked at the lead until he had loosened it off the jar; and he laid the cap on the ground and tipped the jar up to pour out whatever might be inside.

Nothing came out at all, which astonished him a great deal. But then a smoke came out of the jar and went spiralling up into the sky — which astonished him a great deal more — and trailed along the surface of the ground; and when it had reached its full height the thick vapour drew itself together and became an ifrit, enormous in bulk, whose head touched the clouds while his feet were still on the earth. His head was like a dome, his hands like pitchforks, his legs as long as masts and his mouth as big as a cave; his teeth were like boulders, his nostrils like water jugs, his eyes like two lamps, and his whole look was fierce and black.

Now when the fisherman saw the ifrit the muscles in his sides quivered, his teeth chattered, his mouth went dry and he could not think what to do.

At this the ifrit looked at him and cried, "There is no god but God, and Solomon is the prophet of God!" and then added, "Apostle of Allah, do not kill me. Never again will I contradict you in a word or sin against you in a deed."

"Marid," said the fisherman — for that is the name of the mightiest and most rebellious of the jinn — "did you say Solomon, the Apostle of Allah? Solomon has been dead for a thousand and eight hundred years, and we are living in the last days of the world. What is your story, and what account do you give of yourself, and how did you come to be inside this jar?"

Now when the evil spirit heard the fisherman's words he said, "There is no god but God. Be of good cheer, fisherman!"

"Why do you tell me to be of good cheer?" said the fisherman.

"Because," he replied, "you are going to die a bad death within the hour."

"For such good news as that," said the fisherman, "you deserve to have Heaven's protection taken off you, you distant one. Why should you kill me? What have I done to deserve death — I, who freed you out of the jar and saved you from the bottom of the sea and brought you up onto dry land?"

"Ask me one thing only," the ifrit answered, "which death you would like to die, and by what manner of killing I am to kill you."

"What is my crime," said the fisherman, "and why should I be paid back like this?"

"Hear my story, fisherman," said the ifrit.

"Say on," he answered, "and keep it short, for truly my life is in my nostrils this minute."

So the jinni said: Know that I am one of the jinn who fell into heresy, and I sinned against Solomon son of David, on the two of them be peace, along with the famous Sakhr the Jinni. So the Prophet sent his minister, Asaf son of Barkhiya, to seize me; and this vizier brought me against my will and led me to him in chains — and I went with him though every part of me refused to go — and stood me in front of him like a beggar.

When Solomon saw me he took refuge with Allah, and ordered me to embrace the True Faith and obey his commands. I refused. So he sent for this jar and shut me up in it and stopped it with lead, and stamped on it the Most High Name, and gave his orders to the jinn, who carried me off and threw me into the middle of the ocean.

There I stayed a hundred years, and all that time I said in my heart, "Whoever sets me free, I will make him rich for ever and ever." But the full century went by, and nobody set me free.

So I began the second hundred, saying, "Whoever sets me free, for him I will open the treasure hoards of the earth." Still nobody set me free, and so four hundred years went past.

Then I said, "Whoever sets me free, for him I will grant three wishes." And still nobody set me free.

At that I flew into a rage past all raging, and said to myself, "Whoever sets me free from this time on, I will kill him, and I will give him his choice of what death he dies." And now, since you are the one who has set me free, I give you your full choice of deaths.

The fisherman, hearing all this, said, "O Allah — the wonder of it, that I should not have come along to free you until now!" And he added, "Spare my life, and may Allah spare yours; and do not kill me, or Allah will set somebody on to kill you."

"There is no help for it," the stubborn creature replied. "Die you must. So ask me, as a favour, what manner of death you will die."

Even so certain of it, the fisherman tried once more. "Forgive me my death," he said, "as a generous reward for having freed you."

"I would certainly not be killing you," said the ifrit, "except on account of that same freeing."

"Chief of the ifrits," said the fisherman, "I do you good and you pay me back with evil. Truly the old saying does not lie:

	We did them good, and they met our good with ill;
	such, on my life, is every bad man's work.
	Whoever does a kindness to people who do not deserve it
	gets what the man got who took in the hyena."

Now when the ifrit heard this he answered, "No more of this talk. I have to kill you."

At which the fisherman said to himself, "This is a jinni, and I am a man, and Allah has given me a reasonably cunning wit. So I will now find a way to bring about his destruction by my own contrivance and my own intelligence — just as he has taken counsel of nothing but his malice and his perversity."

He began by asking the ifrit, "Have you really made up your mind to kill me?"

And getting no answer but "I have," he cried, "Now, by the Most Great Name engraved on the seal ring of Solomon son of David, peace be on the holy two — if I ask you about a certain matter, will you give me a truthful answer?"

The ifrit replied, "I will." But at the mention of the Most Great Name his wits were shaken, and he said, trembling, "Ask, and be quick about it."

"How," said the fisherman, "did you fit into this bottle, which would not hold your hand — no, nor even your foot? And how did it come to be big enough to hold the whole of you?"

"What!" said the ifrit. "Do you not believe I was all in there?"

And the fisherman answered, "No. I will never believe it until I see you inside it with my own eyes":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Fourth Night,

her sister said to her, "Please finish this tale for us, if you are not sleepy!" So she took it up again:

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the fisherman said to the ifrit, "I will never in any way believe you until I see you inside it with my own eyes," the evil spirit instantly shook himself and became a vapour, which drew together and went into the jar little by little, until all of him was well inside. And at that the fisherman snatched up the lead cap with the seal on it and stoppered the mouth of the jar, and called out to the ifrit:

"Ask me, as a favour, what death you would like to die! By Allah, I am going to throw you into the sea here in front of us, and I will build myself a hut on this spot; and whoever comes here I shall warn him off fishing and tell him: In these waters there lives an ifrit who offers the man who rescues him a choice of deaths and a choice of ways of being killed."

Now when the ifrit heard this from the fisherman, and saw himself shut in, he wanted to escape; but Solomon's seal prevented him. So he understood that the fisherman had cheated him and outwitted him, and he became meek and submissive, and began humbly saying, "I was only joking with you."

But the other answered, "You are lying, vilest of the ifrits, and meanest, and filthiest." And he set off with the bottle for the shore; the ifrit calling out "No! No!" and the fisherman calling out "Yes! Yes!"

At that the evil spirit softened his voice and smoothed his speech and abased himself, and said, "What will you do with me, fisherman?"

"I will throw you back into the sea," he answered, "where you have been housed and homed for a thousand and eight hundred years; and now I shall leave you there till Judgement Day. Did I not say to you: spare me and Allah will spare you, and do not kill me or Allah will kill you? And you rejected my plea and had no intention but to deal ungraciously with me. And now Allah has thrown you into my hands, and I am the cunninger of the two of us."

"Open the jar for me," said the ifrit, "and I will do you good."

"You are lying, you accursed thing," said the fisherman. "My case with you is the case of the vizier of King Yunan with the sage Duban."

"And who was the vizier of King Yunan, and who was the sage Duban, and what was the story about them?" said the ifrit.

At which the fisherman began to tell

The Tale of the Wazir and the Sage Duban

Know, ifrit, that in the old days, and in the old time before them, a king called Yunan ruled over the city of Fars in the land of Rum. He was a powerful ruler and a rich one, with armies and guards and allies among every nation of men; but his body was afflicted with a leprosy that the doctors and the men of science could not heal. He drank potions and swallowed powders and rubbed on ointments, and none of it did him any good, and not one of the whole host of physicians could manage a cure.

At last there came to his city a great healer of men, well on in years, whose name was the sage Duban. This man was a reader of books — Greek, Persian, Roman, Arabic and Syriac. He was skilled in astronomy and in medicine, the theory as well as the practice; he knew everything that heals the body and everything that harms it; he was familiar with the properties of every plant and grass and herb, what good it did and what damage; and he understood philosophy, and had gone round the whole range of medical science and of the other branches on the tree of knowledge.

This physician had spent only a few days in the city before he heard of the King's illness and all the suffering the leprosy caused him, and how every doctor and wise man had failed to heal him. So he sat up through the night thinking hard; and when the dawn broke and the morning appeared and the light was born again, and the sun greeted the good, whose beauty adorns the world, he put on his handsomest clothes and went in to King Yunan and kissed the ground before him. Then he prayed in the finest language for the long continuance of his honour and his prosperity, and made himself known.

"O King," he said, "news has reached me of what has befallen you in your own body, and of how the whole host of physicians have proved unable to reduce it. And I can cure you, O King — and I will not make you drink a draught or rub you with any ointment."

Now when King Yunan heard this he said, in enormous surprise, "How will you do it? By Allah, if you make me whole I will make you rich, and your son's sons after you, and I will give you magnificent presents; and whatever you wish for shall be yours, and you shall be my drinking companion and my friend."

The King then robed him in a dress of honour and treated him graciously, and asked, "Can you really cure me of this complaint without drug or ointment?"

"I can," he answered. "I will heal you without the pains and penalties of medicine."

The King marvelled beyond all marvelling, and said, "Physician, when will this be that you speak of, and in how many days will it happen? Hurry, my son!"

"I hear and I obey," he replied. "The cure will begin tomorrow."

And so saying he went out of the presence, and rented a house in the city so as to have somewhere better to keep his books and scrolls, his medicines and his aromatic roots. Then he set to work choosing the fittest drugs and simples; and he made a polo mallet, hollow inside and fitted with a handle outside, and he made a ball to go with it, and both were prepared with consummate art.

Next day, when the two of them were ready for use and wanted nothing more, he went up to the King and kissed the ground between his hands and told him to ride out onto the parade ground and play polo. The King went, and his suite went with him — emirs and chamberlains, viziers and lords of the realm. And before he had even taken his seat, the sage Duban came up to him and handed him the mallet.

"Take this mallet," he said, "and grip it the way I do — so. And now push out onto the field, and lean well over your horse, and drive the ball with all your might until your palm is damp and your body sweats. Then the medicine will pass through your palm and go all through you. When you have finished playing, and can feel the medicine working, go back to your palace, and wash yourself completely at the baths, and lie down to sleep; and so you will be made whole. And now, peace be with you."

At that King Yunan took the mallet from the sage and gripped it firmly. Then he mounted, and drove the ball before him, and galloped after it until he caught it up, and struck it with all his strength, his palm gripping the mallet handle all the while; and he did not stop knocking the ball about until his hand was damp and his skin, sweating, took the medicine in out of the wood.

Then the sage Duban knew the drugs had gone through him, and told him to go back to the palace and get into the baths at once, without any delay. So King Yunan went straight back and gave orders to clear the baths for him. They did it — the carpet-spreaders hurrying and the slaves hurrying — and got out a change of clothes for the King. He went in and washed himself long and thoroughly; then he dressed inside the bathhouse, and rode from there to his palace, and lay down, and slept.

So much for King Yunan. As for the sage Duban, he went home and slept as usual, and when morning broke he went to the palace and asked for an audience. The King ordered him admitted; and then, having kissed the ground between his hands, he recited these lines about the King, speaking them solemnly:

	Eloquence is happy when you are named as her father,
	but she goes into mourning when any other man claims the title.
	Lord of the fairest face, whose shining rays
	clear off the fogs of doubt that hang over famous deeds —
	may your face never stop shining like the dawn and the sunrise,
	and may you never show Time a face hot with anger.
	Your favour has given us gifts that did such work in us
	as rain clouds do raining on hills that frame the open country.
	Freely you spent your wealth so as to rise high,
	until you won from Time the very heights your greatness aimed at.

Now when the sage had finished reciting, the King got quickly to his feet and fell on his neck; then, seating him at his side, he ordered him dressed in a magnificent robe. For it had happened that when the King came out of the baths he looked at his body and saw no trace of the leprosy: the skin was all as clean as new silver. He was overjoyed at it, and his chest opened with delight, and he felt thoroughly happy.

Presently, when it was full day, he came into his audience hall and sat on the throne of his kingship, and his chamberlains and great men flocked into the presence, and the sage Duban with them. Seeing the doctor, the King rose to honour him and seated him at his side; and then the food trays were brought in loaded with the choicest dishes, and the physician ate with the King, and stayed in his company all that day.

What is more, at nightfall he gave the physician Duban two thousand gold pieces, besides the usual robe of honour and a great many other gifts, and sent him home on his own horse.

After the sage had gone out, King Yunan said again how astonished he was at the doctor's art. "This man treated my body from the outside," he said, "and never rubbed me with any ointment at all. By Allah, this is nothing short of perfect skill. I am bound to honour a man like that with rewards and distinctions, and take him as my companion and my friend for the rest of my days."

So King Yunan passed the night in joy and gladness, because his body had been made whole and had thrown off so destructive a disease.

Next morning the King came out from his private apartments and sat on his throne, and the lords of the realm stood about him, and the emirs and viziers sat as usual on his right hand and his left. Then he asked for the sage Duban, who came in and kissed the ground before him; and the King rose to greet him and seated him at his side, and ate with him and wished him a long life. What is more he robed him again and gave him presents, and did not stop talking with him until the evening drew on. Then the King ordered him, by way of salary, five robes of honour and a thousand dinars. And the physician went home to his own house full of gratitude to the King.

Now when the next morning came the King went to his audience hall, and his lords and nobles gathered round him, and his chamberlains and his ministers, the way the white of the eye encloses the black.

Now the King had a vizier among his viziers who was unpleasant to look at, an ill-omened sight, mean and ungenerous, full of envy and ill will. When this minister saw the King put the physician next to him and give him all these presents, he grew jealous of him and planned to do him harm — as the saying on the subject goes, "Envy lurks in everybody"; and as the other saying goes, "Oppression is hidden in every heart: power reveals it and weakness conceals it."

So the minister came before the King and kissed the ground between his hands and said, "O King of the age and of all time, in whose kindness I grew to manhood — I have serious advice to offer you, and if I hold it back I am a bastard and no true-born man. So if you order me to disclose it, I will do it at once."

The King, who was troubled at the way the minister put it, said, "And what is this advice of yours?"

"O glorious monarch," he said, "the wise men of old said: whoever does not consider how a thing ends will not have Fortune for a friend. And indeed I have lately seen the King going down a road that is anything but the right one; for he is lavishing gifts on his enemy, on a man whose whole object is the downfall and ruin of his kingship. To this man he has shown favour, honouring him beyond all honouring and making an intimate of him. And so I fear for the King's life."

The King, much troubled, and changing colour, asked, "Who is it you suspect, and who is it you are hinting at?"

And the minister answered, "O King, if you are asleep, wake up! I am pointing at the physician Duban."

"Shame on you," the King retorted. "This is a true friend, whom I favour above all men, because he cured me with something I held in my own hand, and healed the leprosy that had baffled every physician there is. He is a man whose like is not to be found these days — not in the whole world, from the furthest east to the furthest west. And it is of such a man that you say such hard things.

"Now from this day forward I allot him a fixed salary and allowance, a thousand gold pieces every month; and if I were to share my kingdom with him it would be a small enough matter. I cannot help suspecting that you speak this way out of nothing but envy and jealousy — as they tell of King Sindibad":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

Then Dunyazad said, "Sister, how pleasant your tale is, and how good to listen to — how sweet, and how welcome!"

She answered, "And what is this compared to what I could tell you tomorrow night, if the King is pleased to spare my life?"

Then the King said to himself, "By Allah, I will not kill her until I have heard the rest of her tale, for it is truly a wonder."

So they rested that night in each other's arms until dawn. Then the King went out to his Hall of Rule, and the vizier and the troops came in, and the audience chamber filled up; and the King gave his orders and gave judgement, appointed men and dismissed men, commanding and forbidding through the rest of that day, until the court broke up and King Shahryar went back to his palace.

When it was the Fifth Night,

her sister said, "Do finish your story for us, if you are not sleepy." And she took it up again:

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that King Yunan said to his minister, "Vizier, you are a man possessed by the evil spirit of envy on account of this physician, and you are scheming to have me put him to death — after which I should be very bitterly sorry, exactly as King Sindibad was sorry for killing his falcon."

"Pardon me, O King of the age," said the vizier. "How was that?"

So the King began the story of

King Sindibad and His Falcon

It is said — though Allah alone knows — that there was once a king among the kings of Fars who was fond of amusement and diversion, and especially of coursing and hunting. He had raised a falcon which he carried all night on his fist, and whenever he went hunting he took the bird with him; and he had a little golden cup made for her, hung round her neck, so that she could be given water out of it.

One day, as the King was sitting quietly in his palace, the chief falconer of the household suddenly spoke up: "O King of the age, this is a day made for hunting birds."

So the King gave the orders and set out with the hawk on his fist; and they rode cheerfully on until they came to a valley, where they set out a ring of nets for the hunt. And a gazelle came into the trap, and the King cried, "Whoever lets that gazelle spring over his head and loses her — that man I shall certainly kill."

They drew the nets in tighter round the gazelle, and she came near the King's own position; and there she planted herself on her haunches and crossed her forelegs over her breast, as though she were about to kiss the ground in front of him. He bent his head low to the creature in acknowledgement — and she bounded high over his head and made off into the waste.

At which the King turned round to his troops and saw them winking at one another and pointing at him. "Vizier," he asked, "what are my men saying?"

And the minister answered, "They are saying that you proclaimed that whoever let the gazelle spring over his head should be put to death."

"Now by the life of my own head," said the King, "I will go after her until I bring her back."

So he set off at a gallop on the gazelle's trail, and did not give up tracking her until he came to the foothills of a mountain range, where the quarry made for a cave. Then the King cast the falcon off at it, and she caught the gazelle up at once and swooped down and drove her talons into its eyes, dazing it and blinding it; and the King drew his mace and struck a blow that rolled the animal over. Then he dismounted, and cut the gazelle's throat and skinned the body and hung it from the pommel of his saddle.

Now this was the hour of the midday rest, and the country was parched and dry, and there was no water to be found anywhere; and the King was thirsty, and so was his horse. So he went about looking, until he saw a tree with water dripping from its branches, like melted butter.

The King was wearing leather gauntlets to protect him against poisons. He took the cup from the hawk's neck and filled it with the water and set it down in front of the bird — and the falcon struck at it with her claws and knocked the liquid over.

The King filled it a second time from the falling drops, thinking his hawk was thirsty; and again the bird struck the cup with her talons and overturned it.

Then the King grew angry with the hawk, and filled the cup a third time and offered it to his horse; and the hawk knocked it over with a flick of her wings.

"Allah confound you," said the King, "unluckiest of all flying things! You keep me from drinking, and you deprive yourself as well, and the horse too."

And he struck the falcon with his sword and cut off her wing. But the bird lifted her head and said to him by signs, "Look at the thing hanging in that tree."

So the King lifted his eyes, and saw a nest of vipers, whose drops of poison he had taken for water. And he was sorry then that he had struck off his falcon's wing; and he mounted and rode on with the dead gazelle until he reached the camp he had started from.

He threw the game to the cook, saying, "Take this and grill it," and sat down in his chair with the falcon still on his fist — and suddenly the bird gasped, and died. At which the King cried out in sorrow and remorse for having killed the falcon that had saved his life.

Now that is what happened in the case of King Sindibad; and I am certain that if I did what you want me to do, I should be as sorry as the man who killed his parrot.

"And how was that?" said the vizier.

And the King began to tell

The Tale of the Husband and the Parrot

There was a certain man, a merchant into the bargain, who had married a beautiful wife — a woman of perfect beauty and grace, of fine proportions and great loveliness — and he was insanely jealous of her, and she managed very successfully to keep him from travelling anywhere.

At last something came up that forced him to leave her. So he went to the bird market and bought himself, for a hundred gold pieces, a parrot, which he set up in the house to act as a chaperone; he expected her to tell him, when he came back, everything that had gone on the whole time he was away. For the bird was knowing and clever, and never forgot anything she had seen or heard.

Now his beautiful wife had fallen in love with a young Turk who used to visit her, and she feasted him by day and slept with him by night.

When the man had made his journey and got what he wanted from it he came home, and at once had the parrot brought to him and questioned her about his wife's behaviour while he had been abroad.

"Your wife has a man friend," she said, "who spent every night with her while you were away."

At that the husband went to his wife in a violent rage and gave her a beating thorough enough to satisfy anybody.

The woman, suspecting that one of the slave girls had been telling tales to the master, called them all together and questioned them on their oaths; and every one of them swore she had kept the secret — but that the parrot had not. "And we heard her with our own ears," they said.

So the woman told one of the girls to set a hand-mill under the cage and grind with it; and a second to sprinkle water down through the roof of the cage; and a third to run about, right and left, flashing a mirror of bright steel — and to keep it up all night long.

Next morning the husband came home, having been entertained by one of his friends, and told them to bring the parrot to him, and asked what had happened while he was out.

"Forgive me, master," said the bird, "but I could neither hear nor see anything, on account of the tremendous darkness, and the thunder and the lightning, which went on all night."

As it happened to be summer, the master was amazed. "But we are in the middle of July," he cried. "This is not the season for rain and storms."

"By Allah, it is so," the bird answered. "I saw with these eyes what my tongue has told you."

At this the man, not understanding the situation and not smelling the plot, flew into a tremendous rage; and reckoning that his wife had been wrongly accused, he put out his hand and pulled the parrot out of her cage and dashed her on the ground so hard that he killed her on the spot.

Some days afterwards one of the slave girls confessed the whole truth to him; and even then he would not believe it, until he saw the young Turk, his wife's lover, coming out of her room. Then he drew his blade and killed him with a blow to the back of the neck; and he did the same to the adulteress. And so the two of them went, loaded with mortal sin, straight to the Everlasting Fire.

Then the merchant knew that the parrot had told him the truth about everything she had seen, and he grieved bitterly over losing her — when grieving was no use to him at all.

The minister, hearing King Yunan out, replied, "O Monarch, high in dignity — and what harm have I done this man, or what evil have I ever had from him, that I should be plotting his death? I would not be doing it except to serve you, and you will see soon enough that I am right. And if you take my advice you will be saved, and if you do not you will be destroyed — exactly like the vizier who dealt treacherously with the young prince."

"How was that?" asked the King.

And the minister began

The Tale of the Prince and the Ogress

There was a certain King whose son was far too fond of hunting and coursing, and he ordered one of his viziers to attend on the boy wherever he went.

One day the young man set out for the chase with his father's minister; and as they jogged along together a big wild animal came into view.

"Up and after that fine quarry!" cried the vizier to the King's son.

So the prince went after it until he was out of everyone's sight, and the animal got away from him in the wilderness; and he was left confused, not knowing which way to turn. And then a girl appeared ahead of him, in tears.

"Who are you?" the King's son asked.

"I am the daughter of a king among the kings of India," she answered, "and I was travelling with a caravan through the desert when drowsiness came over me and I fell off my mount without knowing it. So I am cut off from my people and thoroughly lost."

The prince, hearing this, pitied her, and mounted her behind him on his horse's crupper; and they rode until they passed an old ruin, where the girl said, "Master, I need to relieve myself."

So he set her down at the ruin, and she took so long there that the King's son thought she was simply wasting time. So he followed her without her knowing it — and she was a ghulah, an ogress, and she was saying to her brood:

"Children, today I am bringing you a fine fat young man for dinner."

To which they answered, "Bring him quickly, mother, so that we can browse on him till our bellies are full."

The prince, hearing this talk, gave himself up for dead, and the muscles in his sides quivered in fear for his life; so he turned away and was about to run.

The ogress came out, and seeing him in such a fright — for he was trembling in every limb — cried, "What are you afraid of?"

"I have run into an enemy," he replied, "and I am very much afraid of him."

"Did you not tell me you were a King's son?" asked the ogress.

"I did," he answered.

"Then why not give this enemy of yours some money and satisfy him that way?"

"He will not be satisfied with my purse," he said, "only with my life. And I am mortally afraid of him, and I am a man being wronged."

"If you are as distressed as you think you are," she replied, "then ask Allah for help against him. He will certainly protect you from the man's mischief and from the evil you are afraid of."

Then the prince raised his eyes to heaven and cried, "You who answer the needy man when he calls on You, and drive his distress away — my God, grant me victory over my enemy, and turn him away from me, for You are Almighty over all things."

The ogress, hearing his prayer, turned away from him; and the prince went back to his father and told him the whole story about the vizier — at which the King summoned the minister into his presence and killed him then and there.

And you likewise, O King: if you go on trusting this doctor, you will be made to die the worst of deaths. The very man you have made so much of, and treated as an intimate, will bring about your destruction. Do you not see how he cured the disease from outside your body, with something gripped in your hand? Do not be so sure he will not destroy you with something held the same way.

"You have spoken truly, vizier," King Yunan replied. "It may well be as you hint, my good advising minister. Perhaps this sage has come as a spy, looking to put me to death — for if he certainly cured me with a something held in my hand, he can certainly kill me with a something given me to smell."

Then King Yunan asked, "Minister, what is to be done with him?"

And the vizier answered, "Send after him this very instant and summon him into your presence; and when he comes, strike him across the neck. So you will be rid of him and his wickedness, and will deceive him before he can deceive you."

"You have spoken truly again, vizier," said the King. And he sent a man to call the sage, who came in a cheerful mood, not knowing what the Compassionate One had appointed for him. As a certain poet says, by way of illustration:

	You who go in fear of Fate — travel trusting;
	commit the whole of it to Him who built the world, and wait.
	What Fate says "Be" to must be, my lord;
	and from what Fate has not decreed you are safe.

As Duban the physician came in, he addressed the King in these lines:

	If I fail of my thanks to you, and do not thank you day after day,
	then for whom did I ever put together prose and verse, my speech and my song?
	You lavished your generous gifts before ever I asked for them;
	you lavished your favours unasked, with no pretext and no delay.
	How shall I stint my praise of you, how shall I stop praising
	your graciousness, in private and in the most open show?
	No; I will thank your kindnesses, for your favours always lie
	light on my thought and my tongue, though they weigh heavy on my back.

And he said further, on the same theme:

	Turn away from grief and do not care a jot!
	Commit what you need to Fate and to your Lot.
	Enjoy the present, and enjoy it thoroughly,
	and let the past be entirely forgotten.
	For what happens to look like the worst
	shall work out for your good, as Allah knows.
	Allah will do whatever He wills,
	and in His will do not oppose Him.

And further still:

	To the All-wise, the Subtle One, trust the things of this world;
	rest yourself from everything the worldly man clings to.
	Learn well and wisely that nothing comes about by your will,
	but only as Allah wills it, the King of Kings.

And lastly:

	Be cheerful and glad, and forget every grief you have.
	Grief has worn out the wisest hearts often enough.
	Thinking is only folly in a feeble slave:
	shun it, and so be saved for ever.

The King's only reply was, "Do you know why I have sent for you?"

And the sage answered, "Allah Most High alone knows hidden things."

But the King retorted, "I sent for you only to take your life and destroy you utterly."

Duban the Wise wondered at this strange address beyond all wondering, and asked, "O King — and why would you kill me? What harm have I done you?"

"Men tell me you are a spy," the King answered, "sent here with the intention of killing me. And so I will kill you before I am killed by you." And he called to his headsman and said, "Strike me off this traitor's head and deliver us from his evil practices."

"Spare me and Allah will spare you," said the sage. "Do not kill me, or Allah will kill you." And he said those very words to him, ifrit, exactly as I said them to you — and yet you would not let me go, being bent on my death.

King Yunan only answered, "I shall not be safe unless I kill you; for just as you healed me with something held in the hand, so I am not secure against your killing me with something given me to smell, or by some other means."

"So this, O King," said the physician, "is my recompense and my reward? You return nothing but evil for good."

"There is no help for it," the King replied. "Die you must, and without delay."

Now when the physician was certain the King would kill him without waiting, he wept, and regretted the good he had done to the man who did not deserve it. As somebody has said on this subject:

	Maymunah is bare of wit and wisdom,
	whose own father outstrips every wit in wisdom.
	A man cannot walk on mud or dust or clay
	except by good sense — otherwise he trips and slips.

At that the headsman stepped forward and bound the sage Duban's eyes and bared his blade, saying to the King, "By your leave." And the physician wept and cried, "Spare me and Allah will spare you; do not kill me, or Allah will kill you," and began reciting:

	I was kind, and did not escape; they were cruel, and escaped;
	and my kindness led me nowhere but to the Hall of Ruin.
	If I live I will never be kind again; and if I die, then damnation
	on all who come after me, and a curse on their kindliness.

"Is this," Duban went on, "the return I get from you? It seems to me you are paying me the crocodile's kindness."

"What is the tale of the crocodile?" said the King.

"It is impossible for me to tell it in the state I am in," said the physician. "In Allah's name, spare me, as you hope Allah will spare you." And he wept beyond all weeping.

Then one of the King's favourites stood up and said, "O King, grant me this physician's blood. We have never seen him sin against you, or do anything but heal you of a disease that baffled every doctor and man of science."

"You do not know why I am putting this physician to death," said the King, "and it is this. If I spare him, I doom myself to certain death; for a man who healed me of such a malady with something held in my hand can certainly kill me with something held to my nose. And I am afraid he may kill me for a price, since he may well be a spy whose only purpose in coming here was to bring about my destruction. So there is no help for it. Die he must — and only then shall I be sure of my own life."

Again Duban cried, "Spare me and Allah will spare you; do not kill me, or Allah will kill you." But it was no use.

Now when the physician knew for certain that the King would kill him, ifrit, he said, "O King, if there is no help for it and I must die, then grant me a little delay, so that I can go down to my house and settle my obligations and tell my household and my neighbours where to bury me and how to distribute my medical books. Among them I have one that is the rarest of rarities, which I should like to present to you as a gift: keep it as a treasure in your treasury."

"And what is in the book?" asked the King.

"Things past counting," the sage answered. "And the least of its secrets is this: that if, directly after you have cut off my head, you open three leaves and read three lines of the page on your left hand, my head will speak, and answer every question you care to ask it."

The King wondered beyond all wondering, and shaking with delight at the strangeness of it, said, "Physician, are you really telling me that when I cut off your head it will speak to me?"

"Yes, O King," he replied.

"This is a strange matter indeed," said the King. And he sent him home at once under close guard, and Duban settled all his obligations then and there.

Next day he went up to the King's audience hall, where emirs and viziers, chamberlains and governors, grandees and lords of the realm were all gathered together, making the presence chamber as gay as a garden of flower beds. And the physician came up and stood before the King, carrying a worn old volume and a little metal case full of powder, like the powder used for the eyes.

Then he sat down and said, "Give me a tray." So they brought him one, and he poured the powder onto it and levelled it off, and at last he spoke:

"O King, take this book, but do not open it until my head falls. Then set the head on this tray and have it pressed down onto the powder, and at once the blood will stop flowing. That is the moment to open the book."

So the King took the book and made a sign to the headsman, who rose and struck off the physician's head and set it in the middle of the tray and pressed it down onto the powder. The blood stopped flowing; and the sage Duban opened his eyes and said, "Now open the book, O King."

The King opened the book and found the leaves stuck together; so he put his finger to his mouth, and by moistening it he managed to turn over the first leaf, and the second the same way, and the third, each leaf opening with a good deal of trouble. And when he had unstuck six leaves he looked them over and, finding nothing written on them, said, "Physician, there is no writing here."

"Turn over more," Duban replied. And he turned over three more in the same way.

Now the book was poisoned; and before long the venom worked into his system, and he fell into violent convulsions and cried out, "The poison has done its work!"

At which the sage Duban's head began to improvise:

	There have been rulers who ruled with a foul and tyrannical hand,
	and soon they were as though they had never, never been.
	Had they been just, they would have had justice done to them; they
	oppressed, and were oppressed in turn by Fortune, who paid them back
	with ruin and bane and misery. So they faded like the morning,
	and the tongue of things repeats: take this for that,
	and do not vent your spleen on the ways of Fortune.

No sooner had the head stopped speaking than the King rolled over dead.

Now I would have you know, ifrit, that if King Yunan had spared the sage Duban, Allah would have spared him; but he refused to do it and decreed his death, and so Allah killed him. And you too, ifrit — if you had spared me, Allah would have spared you:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

Then Dunyazad said, "Sister, how pleasant your tale is, and how good to listen to — how sweet, and how welcome!"

She answered, "And what is this compared to what I could tell you tomorrow night, if I live and the King spares me?"

The King said to himself, "By Allah, I will not kill her until I have heard the rest of her story, for it is truly a wonder."

They rested that night in each other's arms until dawn. Then the King went out to his court; the viziers and the troops came in and the audience hall filled up; and the King gave his orders and gave judgement, appointed men and dismissed men, commanding and forbidding through the rest of that day, until the court broke up and King Shahryar went into his palace.

When it was the Sixth Night,

her sister Dunyazad said to her, "Please finish your story for us." And she answered, "I will, if the King gives me leave."

"Say on," said the King. And she went on:

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the fisherman said to the ifrit, "If you had spared me I would have spared you; but nothing would satisfy you except my death. So now I will put you to death by shutting you up in this jar, and I will hurl you into this sea."

Then the marid roared aloud and cried, "In Allah's name, fisherman — don't! Spare me, and pardon what I have done; and as I have been tyrannical, be you generous. For it is said, among the sayings that go about: You who do good to the man who has done you evil — let the evildoer's own evil deeds be enough for him. And do not deal with me as Umamah dealt with Atikah."

"And what happened between them?" asked the fisherman.

"This is no time for storytelling," the ifrit answered, "and me in this prison. Set me free and I will tell you the tale."

"Leave off this talk," said the fisherman. "There is no help for it: you must be thrown back into the sea, and there is no way of your ever getting out of it, for ever and ever. I put myself under your protection for nothing; I humbled myself to you in tears, and all you wanted was to kill me — me, who had done you no injury to deserve it. Far from injuring you by any evil act, I did you nothing but good in releasing you from that prison of yours.

"Now I knew you for an evildoer when you did to me what you did. And know this: when I have thrown you back into the sea, I shall warn whoever fishes you up about what happened to me with you, and I shall advise him to toss you straight back in again. So you shall stay here under these waters until the End of Time makes an end of you."

But the ifrit cried out, "Set me free! This is a fine occasion for generosity, and I make a covenant with you and vow never to do you hurt or harm. On the contrary, I will help you to something that will put you beyond want."

The fisherman accepted his promises on both conditions — that he should not trouble him as before, but on the contrary do him a service; and after making the pledge firm and swearing him a solemn oath by Allah Most High, he opened the jar.

At that the pillar of smoke rose up until the whole of it was out; and then it thickened and once more became an ifrit, hideous to look at, who promptly gave the bottle a kick and sent it flying into the sea.

The fisherman, seeing how the jar was treated and making sure his own death was next, wet himself, and said to himself, "This looks bad." But he steadied his heart and cried:

"Ifrit, Allah has said: keep your covenant, for the keeping of your covenant shall be inquired into hereafter. You have made a vow to me and sworn an oath not to play me false, in case Allah plays you false — for truly He is a jealous God, who gives the sinner time but does not let him escape. I say to you what the sage Duban said to King Yunan: spare me, so that Allah may spare you."

The ifrit burst out laughing and stalked away, saying to the fisherman, "Follow me." And the man walked after him at a safe distance, not being at all sure of getting away, until they had gone right round the outskirts of the city.

From there they struck out into uncultivated ground, and crossed it, and came down into a broad wilderness; and in the middle of it stood a mountain tarn.

The ifrit waded into the middle of it and again cried, "Follow me." And when that was done he took his stand in the centre and told the man to cast his net and catch his fish.

The fisherman looked into the water and was astonished to see fish of different colours in it, white and red, blue and yellow. But he cast his net, and hauling it in, saw he had netted four fish, one of each colour.

He was overjoyed at it, and more so when the ifrit said, "Carry these to the Sultan and set them in front of him; and he will give you what will make you a wealthy man. And now accept my apology, for by Allah I know no other way of doing you good at present, seeing that I have lain in this sea for eighteen hundred years and have not seen the face of the world until this hour. But I would not have you fish here more than once a day."

Then the ifrit wished him well, saying, "Allah grant we meet again," and struck the ground with one foot; and the earth split open and swallowed him up.

The fisherman, marvelling a great deal at what had happened to him with the ifrit, took the fish and made for the city; and as soon as he got home he filled an earthenware bowl with water and dropped the fish into it, and they began to struggle and wriggle about.

Then he carried the bowl off on his head and went to the King's palace, as the ifrit had told him to, and laid the fish before the presence. And the King marvelled beyond all marvelling at the sight, for never in his life had he seen fish like these, in colour or in shape.

So he said, "Give those fish to the foreign slave girl who is cooking for us now" — meaning the bondmaid whom the King of Rum had sent him only three days before, so that he had not yet tested her talents in the dressing of meat.

At which the vizier carried the fish to the cook and told her to fry them, saying, "Girl, the King sends you this message: I have not stored you up, O treasure of mine, except against a hard time of mine. So show us today your delicate handiwork and your savoury cooking; for this dish of fish is a present sent to the Sultan, and plainly a rarity."

The vizier, having instructed her carefully, went back to the King, who ordered him to give the fisherman four hundred dinars. He gave them accordingly, and the man clutched them to his chest and ran off home, stumbling and falling and getting up again and thinking the whole thing was a dream. Anyway, he bought his family everything they needed, and at last he went in to his wife in enormous joy and gladness.

So much for him. As for the cook, she took the fish and cleaned them and set them in the frying pan, basting them with oil until one side was done. Then she turned them over — and the kitchen wall split apart, and out of it came a young lady, beautiful in shape, oval in the face, perfect in grace, with eyelids that lines of kohl enchase.

Her dress was a silk head-kerchief fringed and tasselled with blue; a large ring hung from each ear; a pair of bracelets went round her wrists; there were rings with priceless gems in their settings on her fingers; and she held in her hand a long rod of rattan cane, which she thrust into the frying pan, saying, "Fish! Fish! Are you keeping your covenant?"

When the cook saw this apparition she fainted away. The young lady repeated her words a second time and a third time; and at last the fish raised their heads out of the pan and said, in words anyone could understand, "Yes! Yes!" And they began, all in one voice, to recite:

	Come back and so will I! Keep faith and so will I!
	And if you choose to abandon us, I will pay you back till we are quits!

After this the young lady turned the frying pan over and went out the way she had come in, and the kitchen wall closed behind her.

When the cook came round from her fainting fit she saw the four fish burnt black as charcoal, and cried out, "His staff broke at the first blow!" — and fell down in a faint again.

While she was lying there the vizier came for the fish; and seeing her senseless on the floor, not knowing Sunday from Thursday, he shoved her with his foot and said, "Bring the fish for the Sultan!"

At that she came round, and wept, and told him her situation and everything that had happened to her. The vizier marvelled greatly and exclaimed, "This is nothing short of an extraordinary business!" And he sent for the fisherman and said to him, "You, fisherman, must fetch us four more fish like the ones you brought before."

So the man went off to the tarn and cast his net; and when he landed it, there were four fish in it exactly like the first. He carried them straight to the vizier, who took them in to the cook and said, "Up with you, and fry these in front of me, so that I can see this business for myself."

The girl got up and cleaned the fish and set them in the frying pan over the fire. But they had not been there long before the wall split apart and the young lady appeared, dressed as before and holding the wand, which she again thrust into the frying pan, saying, "Fish! Fish! Are you keeping to your old covenant?"

And the fish lifted their heads and answered, "Yes! Yes!" and recited the couplet:

	Come back and so will I! Keep faith and so will I!
	But if you choose to abandon us, I will pay you back till we are quits!

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Seventh Night,

she went on: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the fish had spoken, and the young lady had upset the frying pan with her rod and gone out the way she came in, and the wall had closed up behind her, the vizier cried, "This is not a thing that can be kept from the King."

So he went and told him what had happened; at which the King said, "There is no help for it. I must see this with my own eyes."

Then he sent for the fisherman and ordered him to bring four more fish like the first, and to take three men with him as witnesses. The fisherman brought the fish at once; and the King, after ordering that he be given four hundred gold pieces, turned to the vizier and said, "Up, and fry me these fish here in front of me."

The minister answered, "To hear is to obey," and had the frying pan brought, and threw the cleaned fish into it and set it over the fire. And then the wall split apart, and out burst a Black slave, huge as a boulder, or like something left over from the ancient giants of the tribe of Ad, with a branch of a green tree in his hand; and he cried in a loud and terrible voice, "Fish! Fish! Are you all keeping to your old covenant?"

At which the fish lifted their heads out of the frying pan and said, "Yes! Yes! We are true to our vow." And they recited the couplet again:

	Come back and so will I! Keep faith and so will I!
	But if you choose to abandon us, I will pay you back till we are quits!

Then the huge man came up to the frying pan and turned it over with the branch, and went out the way he had come in.

When he had vanished from their sight the King inspected the fish; and finding them all burnt black as charcoal, he was utterly bewildered, and said to the vizier, "This is truly a matter that cannot be kept quiet; and as for these fish, there is certainly some marvellous adventure attached to them."

So he had the fisherman brought, and asked him, "Confound you, man — where did these fish come from?"

"From a tarn between four heights," he answered, "lying behind that mountain there, which is in sight of your city."

"How many days' march?" asked the King.

"Our lord the Sultan," he said, "it is half an hour's walk."

The King was astonished, and immediately ordered his men to march and his horsemen to mount, and led off with the fisherman going in front as guide — privately cursing the ifrit as he went.

They travelled on until they had climbed the mountain and come down into a great desert which none of them had ever seen in all their lives; and the Sultan and all his company marvelled at this open country set among four mountains, and at the tarn, and at its fish of four colours, red and white, yellow and blue.

The King stood rooted to the spot in wonder, and asked his troops and everyone else there, "Has any one of you ever seen this piece of water before now?"

And they all answered, "O King of the age, we never set eyes on it in all our days."

They questioned the oldest inhabitants they could find as well, men well on in years; and every one of them replied, "We have never seen a little lake like this in this place."

At which the King said, "By Allah, I will not go back to my capital or sit on the throne of my forefathers until I have learned the truth about this tarn and the fish in it."

Then he ordered his men to dismount and camp all round the mountain, which they did; and he summoned his vizier, a minister of great experience, shrewd, sharp-witted and well versed in affairs, and said to him:

"There is something in my mind that I mean to do, and I will tell you what it is. My heart tells me to go out alone tonight and get to the root of the mystery of this tarn and its fish. You take your seat at my tent door, and say to the emirs and viziers, the governors and the chamberlains — in short, to everybody who asks you — that the Sultan is unwell and has ordered me to admit nobody. And take care that no one learns what I am doing."

And the vizier could not oppose him.

Then the King changed his clothes and his ornaments and slung his sword over his shoulder, and took a path that led up one of the mountains, and marched the rest of the night until the day dawned; and he did not stop travelling until the heat was too much for him. After his long walk he rested a while, and then took up the march again and went on through the second night until dawn — when suddenly a black point appeared in the distance.

He was delighted at it and said to himself, "Perhaps somebody here will tell me the mystery of the tarn and its fish."

Coming closer to the dark object, he found it was a palace built of black stone plated with iron; and one leaf of the gate stood wide open while the other was shut.

The King's spirits rose as he stood before the gate and rapped a light rap. But hearing no answer, he knocked a second and a third time; and there was still no sign of anyone. Then he knocked as loud as he could, and still no answer. So he said, "It must be empty."

At that he gathered up his resolution and walked boldly in through the main gate into the great hall, and there called out, "Hello, people of the palace! I am a stranger and a traveller. Have you anything here in the way of food?"

He repeated his call a second and a third time, and still no reply came. So, steadying his heart and making up his mind, he went on through the entrance hall into the very middle of the palace, and found not a soul in it.

And yet it was furnished with silks starred with gold, and hangings were let down over the doorways. In the middle was a spacious court, off which stood four open rooms, each with its raised dais, room facing room; a canopy shaded the court, and in the centre was a jetting fountain with four figures of lions in red gold, spouting out water as clear as pearls and as transparent as gems. Round about the palace birds had been let loose, and over the whole of it was stretched a net of golden wire to stop them flying away. In short, there was everything there except human beings.

The King marvelled greatly at it, and yet felt sad at heart, because he could see nobody to give him any account of that waste land and its tarn, of the fish, the mountains, or the palace itself.

Presently, as he sat between the doors deep in thought, he heard a voice of lamentation, as if from a heart worn out with grief, and it was chanting these verses:

	I hid what I suffered from him, and even so it came to light,
	and sleep fled from my eyelids every night and turned into sleeplessness.
	O world! O Fate! hold back your hand and stop your hurting and harming;
	look and see my luckless spirit, the colour of it and the terror of it.
	Will you never show pity to a high-born young man who lost himself
	on the road of Love, and fell from wealth and fame to the lowest and basest state?
	I used to be jealous of the west wind as it breathed over your body —
	but when Destiny comes down it blinds a man's sight.
	What can the unlucky archer do who faces his enemy
	and bends his bow to loose the arrow, and finds his bowstring gone?
	And when cares and troubles bear so heavily on a young man of generous heart,
	how is he to escape his lot, and where is his place of refuge from Fate?

Now when the Sultan heard the mournful voice he sprang to his feet, and following the sound, found a curtain let down over the door of a room. He raised it and saw behind it a young man sitting on a couch about a foot and a half above the floor — a young man beautiful to look at, well made, and finely spoken. His forehead was flower-white and his cheek was rosy bright, and there was a mole on the width of his cheek like a speck of ambergris. As the poet writes:

	A slim-waisted youth, from whose hair and forehead
	the world takes both its blackness and its light.
	In the whole round of Creation there is no fairer show,
	no rarer sight your eye has ever met:
	a nut-brown mole sits enthroned on a cheek
	of the rosiest red, beneath an eye of jet.

The King was glad, and greeted him; but the young man stayed sitting where he was, in his caftan of silk edged with Egyptian gold and his crown studded with gems of every kind; and his face was sad with the marks of sorrow. He returned the royal greeting most courteously and added, "My lord, your dignity demands that I rise to you; and my only excuse is to beg your pardon."

"You are excused, young man," said the King. "Look on me as your guest, come here on a particular errand. I want you to tell me the secrets of this tarn and its fish, and of this palace, and of your being alone in it, and the cause of your groaning and grieving."

When the young man heard this he wept bitterly, until his breast was soaked with tears, and began reciting:

	Say to the man who sleeps carelessly while the arrow of Fortune flies:
	how many does this shifting world lay low, and how many raise up?
	Though your own eye is sealed in sleep, the eyes of the Almighty do not sleep.
	And who has ever found Time fair, or Fate constant in its ways?

Then he heaved a long-drawn sigh and recited:

	Trust your case to Him, the Lord who made mankind;
	leave off worry and care and cultivate a contented mind.
	Do not ask about the past, or how or why it came about:
	all human things were designed by Fate and Destiny.

The King marvelled, and asked him, "What makes you weep, young man?"

And he answered, "How should I not weep, when this is my situation?"

Then he put out his hand and lifted the skirt of his robe — and the lower half of him was stone, all the way down to his feet, while from the navel up to the hair of his head he was a man.

The King, seeing the state he was in, grieved sorely, and out of compassion cried, "Alas and alack! Truly, young man, you are heaping sorrow on top of my sorrow. I meant to ask you only about the mystery of the fish, and now I am concerned to learn your story as well as theirs. But there is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great! Lose no time, young man — tell me your whole tale at once."

"Lend me your ears," he said, "and your sight, and your understanding."

"They are all at your service," said the King.

At which the young man began. "My case, and the case of these fish, is a wonder and a marvel; and if it were engraved with needles on the inner corners of the eye, it would be a warning to anyone willing to take warning."

"How is that?" asked the King.

And the young man began to tell

The Tale of the Ensorcelled Prince

Know then, my lord, that once my father was King of this city, and his name was Mahmud, and he was called Lord of the Black Islands, and owner of what are now these four mountains. He ruled seventy years, and then went to the mercy of the Lord, and I reigned as Sultan in his place.

I took as my wife my cousin, my father's brother's daughter, and she loved me with such an overflowing love that whenever I was away she would not eat and would not drink until she saw me again. She lived with me for five years — until a certain day when she went out to the baths, and I told the cook to hurry and get everything ready for our supper.

And I came into this palace and lay down on the bed where I usually slept, and told two of the girls to fan my face, one sitting at my head and the other at my feet. But I was troubled and made restless by my wife's absence and could not sleep; for although my eyes were shut, my mind and my thoughts were wide awake.

Presently I heard the slave girl at my head say to the one at my feet, "Mas'udah, how miserable our master is, and how wasted in his youth — and oh, the pity of his being betrayed like this by our mistress, the accursed whore."

The other answered, "Yes indeed. Allah curse every faithless and adulterous woman. But a man like our master, with all his fine qualities, deserves something better than this harlot who lies out every night."

Then the one at my head said, "Is our lord dumb, or good for nothing but blowing bubbles, that he never questions her?"

And the other said, "Shame on you. Does our lord know her ways? Does she leave him any choice? Why, does she not drug the cup she gives him every night before bedtime, and put bhang in it? So he sleeps and knows nothing about where she goes or what she does. But we know that after giving him the drugged wine she puts on her richest clothes and perfumes herself and goes out and stays out till daybreak; and then she comes back to him and burns a pastille under his nose, and he wakes out of that deathlike sleep."

When I heard what the slave girl said, the light went black in front of my eyes, and I thought night would never come.

Presently my uncle's daughter came back from the baths; and they laid the table for us, and we ate, and sat together a good half hour drinking our wine as we always did. Then she called for the particular wine I used to drink before sleeping, and handed me the cup; and I seemed to drink it as usual, but poured the contents into the breast of my robe, and lay down, and let her hear that I was asleep.

And then she cried, "Sleep out the night and never wake again! By Allah, I loathe you, and I loathe your whole body, and my soul turns in disgust from lying with you; and I cannot see the moment when Allah will snatch your life away."

Then she got up and put on her finest dress and perfumed herself and slung my sword over her shoulder; and opening the gates of the palace, she went out on her wicked way.

I got up and followed her out of the palace, and she threaded through the streets until she came to the city gate, where she spoke words I could not understand, and the padlocks dropped off by themselves as though they had been broken, and the leaves of the gate swung open. Out she went — and I after her, without her noticing anything — until at last she came to the mounds outside the city, and a reed fence built round a round-roofed hut of mud brick.

As she went in at the door I climbed onto the roof, from where I could see into the inside — and there my beautiful cousin had gone in to a hideous slave, a Black man whose upper lip was like the lid of a pot and whose lower lip was like the pot itself, lips that could have swept the gravel up off the floor of the hut. He was a leper besides, and a paralytic, lying on a heap of sugar-cane trash and wrapped in an old blanket and the filthiest rags and tatters.

She kissed the ground in front of him, and he lifted his head far enough to see her and said, "Damn you — what call had you to stay away all this time? Several of my brothers have been here, and drank their wine, and each of them had his young woman with him, and I was not willing to drink, because you were not here."

Then she said, "My lord, love of my heart, coolness of my eyes — do you not know that I am married to my cousin, whose very look I loathe, and that I hate myself when I am in his company? And if I were not afraid on your account, I would not let a single sun rise before I made his city a heap of ruins, where the raven would croak and the owl hoot, and the jackal and the wolf would den and hunt; no, I would have carried its very stones to the far side of Mount Kaf."

"You are lying, damn you," the slave answered. "Now I swear an oath by the courage and the honour of Black men — and do not imagine our manhood is the poor manhood of white men — that from this day on, if you stay away till this hour again, I will not keep company with you, and I will not put my body against your body. Do you play fast and loose with us, you cracked pot, so that we can satisfy your dirty lusts? Stinker! Bitch! Vilest of the vile whites!"

When I heard what he said, and saw with my own eyes what passed between those two wretches, the world went dark in front of my face and my soul did not know what place it was in.

But my wife stood there humbly weeping in front of him, and coaxing him, and saying, "My beloved, the very fruit of my heart — there is nobody left to cheer me but your dear self; and if you cast me off, who will take me in, my beloved, light of my eyes?" And she went on weeping and abasing herself to him until he condescended to be reconciled with her.

Then she was delighted, and got up and took off her clothes, down to her petticoat trousers, and said, "My master, what have you here for your servant to eat?"

"Uncover the basin," he grumbled. "You will find at the bottom of it the grilled bones of some rats we had for dinner. Pick at those. And then go to that slop pot, where you will find some leavings of beer you can drink."

So she ate, and drank, and washed her hands, and went and lay down beside the slave on the cane trash; and stripping herself stark naked, she crept in with him under his filthy coverlet and his rags and tatters.

When I saw my wife, my cousin, my uncle's daughter, do this thing, I clean lost my wits; and climbing down from the roof I went in and took the sword she had brought with her and drew it, determined to cut the pair of them down. I struck first at the slave's neck, and thought the sentence of death had fallen on him:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Eighth Night,

she went on: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the young enchanted prince said to the King:

When I struck the slave, meaning to take his head off, I thought I had killed him, for he gave a loud hissing groan. But I had cut only the skin and flesh of the throat and the two arteries. It woke my uncle's daughter; so I sheathed the sword and went out and back to the city, and came into the palace and lay down on my bed and slept till morning — when my wife roused me, and I saw she had cut off her hair and put on mourning clothes.

She said, "Cousin, do not blame me for what I am doing. Word has just reached me that my mother is dead, and that my father has been killed in a holy war, and that of my brothers one has died of a snakebite and the other by falling down a precipice. I can do nothing and should do nothing but weep and lament."

When I heard this I held back from any reproach, and said only, "Do as you like. I certainly will not thwart you."

She went on sorrowing and weeping and wailing for a whole year from one end of its circle to the other; and when the year was up she said to me, "I want to build myself a tomb in your palace, with a dome on it, which I will set apart for my mourning and will call the House of Lamentations."

And again I said, "Do as you like."

So she built herself a memorial tomb to mourn in, and set at the centre of it a dome, under which there showed a grave like a holy man's sepulchre. And there she carried the slave, and lodged him; but he was exceedingly weak from his wound and could do her no love service. He could only drink wine; and from the day he was hurt he never spoke a word, and yet he lived on, because his appointed hour had not come.

Every day, morning and evening, my wife went to him and wept and wailed over him and gave him wine and strong soups; and she did not leave off doing this for a second year. And I bore with her patiently and paid no attention.

One day, however, I went in to her unexpectedly, and found her weeping and beating her face and crying, "Why are you gone from my sight, delight of my heart? Speak to me, my life. Talk to me, my love." And then she recited:

	For love of you my patience fails, and though you may forget,
	I cannot, nor can my heart answer to any other love.
	Carry my body and carry my soul wherever you go,
	and where you pitch the camp let my body be buried;
	call my name over my grave, and an answer will come back —
	the moaning of my bones answering your cry.

Then she recited, weeping bitterly all the while:

	The day of my delight is the day when you come near,
	and the day of my terror is the day when you turn away.
	Though I tremble all night in my bitter dread of death,
	when I hold you in my arms I am free of all fear.

And once more she began:

	Though I might wake one morning with every happiness in my hand,
	though the whole world were mine and I reigned like the kings of Persia,
	all of it would be worth the wing of a gnat to me
	if I could not see your face, if I looked for you in vain.

When she had finished her words and her weeping for a moment, I said to her, "Cousin, let this mourning of yours be enough. There is little profit in pouring out tears."

"Do not thwart me," she answered, "in anything I do, or I will lay violent hands on myself."

So I held my peace and left her to go her own way; and she went on crying and keening and indulging her grief for yet another year.

At the end of the third year I grew weary of this long-drawn-out mourning; and one day I happened to go into the tomb chamber vexed and angry about some matter that had crossed me, and I suddenly heard her say, "My lord, I never hear you grant me a single word. Why do you not answer me, my master?" And she began reciting:

	O tomb! O tomb! is his beauty put into shadow?
	Have you darkened that face that was as bright as noon?
	O tomb! you are neither earth to me nor heaven —
	then how does it come about that in you my sun and my moon are joined?

When I heard verses like that, rage was heaped on top of my rage, and I cried out, "Well away! How long is this sorrow going to last?" And I began reciting back at her:

	O tomb! O tomb! is his horribleness put into shadow?
	Have you darkened that face that turns the stomach?
	O tomb! you are neither cesspool to me nor cooking pot —
	then how does it come about that in you soil and coal are joined?

When she heard this she sprang to her feet, crying, "Shame on you, you dog! All this is your doing. You wounded my heart's darling and worked me this bitter grief; and you have wasted his youth, so that for these three years he has lain in bed more dead than alive."

In my fury I cried, "You foulest of harlots and filthiest of whores — you who have been had by every slave you hire to have at you! Yes indeed, it was I who did this good deed." And snatching up my sword I drew it and went at her to cut her down.

But she laughed my words and my intention to scorn, and cried, "To heel, dog that you are! Alas for the past, which will never come again — and nobody can raise the dead. Allah has now delivered into my hand the man who did this to me, a deed that has burnt my heart with a fire that has not died and a flame that could not be quenched."

Then she stood up, and pronouncing some words I could not understand, she said, "By virtue of my sorcery, become half stone and half man." And I became what you see — unable to stand or to sit, neither dead nor alive.

What is more, she put a spell on the city with all its streets and gardens; and by her magic she turned the four islands into the four mountains round the tarn you were asking me about. And the citizens, who were of four different faiths — Muslim, Christian, Jew and Magian — she transformed by her enchantments into fish: the Muslims are the white ones, the Magians the red, the Christians the blue and the Jews the yellow.

And every day she tortures me and flogs me with a hundred strokes, each one of which draws floods of blood and cuts the skin of my shoulders into strips; and last of all she puts a hair shirt on my upper half and then throws these robes over it.

At this the young man shed tears again and began reciting:

	In patience, O my God, I endure my lot and my fate;
	I will bear whatever state You will for me.
	They oppress me; they torture me; they make my life a misery —
	and yet perhaps the happiness of Heaven will make up for my hard case.
	Yes, my life is narrowed by the ruin and the hatred of enemies,
	but Mustafa and Murtaza shall open Heaven's gate to me.

After this the Sultan turned to the young prince and said, "Young man, you have taken one grief away only to add another. But now, my friend — where is she? And where is the tomb the wounded slave is lying in?"

"The slave lies under that dome," said the young man, "and she sits in the chamber facing that door. Every day at sunrise she comes out and first strips me and whips me with a hundred strokes of the leather scourge, and I weep and shriek, but there is no power of movement in my lower limbs to keep her off me. When she has finished tormenting me she goes and visits the slave, bringing him wine and boiled meat. And tomorrow she will be here early."

"By Allah, young man," said the King, "I shall certainly do you a good turn that the world will not willingly let die, and an act of daring that will be talked about long after I am dead and gone."

Then the King sat down beside the young prince and talked with him until nightfall, when he lay down and slept. But as soon as the false dawn showed he got up and took off his outer clothes and bared his blade and hurried to the place where the slave lay.

There he found candles and lamps lit, and the smell of incense and ointments; and guided by these, he made for the slave and struck him one blow and killed him on the spot. After which he lifted him onto his back and threw him into a well in the palace. Then he came back, and putting on the slave's clothes, lay down full length inside the tomb chamber with the drawn sword close along his side.

An hour or so later the accursed witch came. First she went to her husband and stripped his clothes off, and taking a whip, flogged him cruelly while he cried out, "Ah — the state I am in is enough for me! Take pity on me, cousin!"

But she answered, "Did you take pity on me, and spare the life of the man I truly loved?"

Then she drew the hair shirt over his raw and bleeding skin, and threw the robe over the top of it, and went down to the slave with a goblet of wine and a bowl of meat broth in her hands. She came in under the dome weeping and wailing, "Well away!" and crying, "My lord, speak a word to me! My master, talk to me a while!" And she began to recite:

	How long is this harshness, this unlovingness, going to last?
	Are the floods of tears you have seen not enough for you?
	You draw out our separation on purpose —
