	and if you meant to please my enemy, then you are satisfied.

Then she wept again and said, "My lord, speak to me! Talk to me!"

The King lowered his voice, and twisted his tongue, and spoke thickly and indistinctly, the way a man speaks who is very weak and whose throat has been cut: "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great."

Now when she heard the words she shouted for joy, and fell to the ground in a faint; and when her senses came back she asked, "My lord, can it be true that you have the power of speech?"

And the King, making his voice small and faint, answered, "My curse — do you deserve that I should talk to you and speak with you?"

"Why? What do you mean?" she said.

And he replied, "What I mean is that all the livelong day you torment your husband, and he keeps calling on heaven for help, until sleep is a stranger to me from evening till morning; and he prays and swears, cursing the two of us, you and me, and gives me no quiet and a great deal of trouble. If it were not for that I should have got my health back long ago. And that is what prevents me from answering you."

"With your leave," she said, "I will release him from the spell he is under."

"Release him," said the King, "and let us have some rest."

"To hear is to obey," she cried. And going from the tomb chamber to the palace, she took a metal bowl and filled it with water and spoke certain words over it that made the contents bubble and boil as a cauldron seethes over a fire. And with this she sprinkled her husband, saying, "By virtue of the dreadful words I have spoken — if you became like this by my spells, then come out of that form into your own former form."

And the young man shivered and shook; and then he rose to his feet, and rejoicing at his deliverance, cried aloud, "I testify that there is no god but God, and that truly Mohammed is His Apostle, whom Allah bless and keep!"

Then she said to him, screaming it into his face, "Get out, and do not come back here — for if you do I shall certainly kill you."

So he went out from between her hands; and she went back to the dome, and down into the tomb, and said, "My lord, come out to me, so that I can look at you and at your handsomeness."

The King answered in a faint, low voice, "What have you done? You have rid me of the branch but not of the root."

"My darling! My black one!" she asked. "What is the root?"

And he answered, "Shame on you, my curse. The people of this city and of the four islands, every night when it is half over, lift their heads out of the tank you have turned them into fish in, and cry to Heaven and call down its anger on me and on you; and that is the reason my body is baulked of its health. Go at once and set them free; then come to me and take my hand and raise me up, for a little strength is already coming back into me."

When she heard the King's words — and she still thought he was the slave — she cried joyfully, "My master, on my head and on my eyes be your command. In Allah's name!"

So she sprang to her feet, full of joy and gladness, and ran down to the tarn and took a little of its water in the palm of her hand:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Ninth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the young woman, the sorceress, took some of the tarn water in her hand and spoke words over it that could not be understood, the fish lifted their heads and stood up in that instant like men, the spell on the people of the city being lifted.

What had been a lake became a crowded capital again; the markets were thronged with people buying and selling, every citizen busy with his own trade; and the four hills became islands as they had been before.

Then the young woman, the wicked sorceress, went back to the King and — still thinking he was the slave — said to him, "My love, stretch out your honoured hand so that I can help you up."

"Come nearer to me," said the King in his faint, feigned voice.

She came close, as if to embrace him — and he took up the sword that lay hidden by his side and struck her across the breast, so that the point showed gleaming out behind her back. Then he struck her a second time and cut her in two, and threw her on the ground in two halves.

After that he went out and found the young man, now free of the spell, waiting for him, and wished him joy of his release; and the prince kissed his hand with many thanks.

"Will you stay in this city," said the King, "or come with me to my capital?"

"O King of the age," said the young man, "do you not know how far it is between you and your city?"

"Two and a half days," he answered.

At which the other said, "If you are asleep, O King, wake up. Between you and your city is a year's march for a well-girt walker; and you would not have come here in two and a half days except that the city was under enchantment. And I, O King, will never leave you — not even for the blink of an eye."

The King was delighted at this and said, "Thanks be to Allah, who has bestowed you on me! From this hour you are my son, and my only son, for in all my life I have never been blessed with a child."

At which they embraced and were overjoyed. And reaching the palace, the prince who had been under the spell informed his lords and his great men that he was about to visit the Holy Places as a pilgrim, and told them to get ready everything necessary for the occasion.

The preparations took ten days, after which he set out with the Sultan, whose heart was burning with longing for the city he had been absent from for a whole twelvemonth. They travelled with an escort of Mamluks carrying all sorts of precious gifts and rarities, and they did not stop travelling day or night for a full year, until they came near the Sultan's capital and sent messengers on ahead to announce that they were coming.

Then the vizier and the whole army came out to meet him in joy and gladness, for they had given up all hope of ever seeing their King again; and the troops kissed the ground before him and wished him joy of his safe return. He came in and took his seat on his throne, and the minister came before him; and when he had been told everything that had happened to the young prince, he congratulated him on his narrow escape.

When order had been restored throughout the land, the King gave gifts to a great many of his people, and said to the vizier, "Bring me the fisherman who brought us the fish."

So he sent for the man who had been the first cause of the city and its citizens being delivered from enchantment; and when he came into the presence, the Sultan gave him a robe of honour and asked him about his circumstances and whether he had any children. The fisherman told him he had two daughters and a son. So the King sent for them, and took one daughter as his wife and gave the other to the young prince, and made the son his head treasurer.

Furthermore he invested his vizier with the sultanate of the City in the Black Islands, which had belonged to the young prince, and sent with him the escort of fifty armed slaves, together with robes of honour for all the emirs and grandees. The vizier kissed his hands and went on his way; while the Sultan and the prince stayed at home in all the comfort and delight of life. And the fisherman became the richest man of his age, and his daughters were married to kings, until death came to them all.

And yet, O King — this is not more wonderful than the story of

The Porter and the Three Ladies of Baghdad

Once upon a time there was a porter in Baghdad, a bachelor, and one who meant to stay unmarried.

It happened one day, as he was standing about in the street leaning idly on his carrying-crate, that a respectable woman came and stood in front of him, in a cloak of Mosul silk embroidered with gold and edged with brocade; her walking shoes were worked with gold as well, and her hair hung down in long plaits. She lifted her face veil and showed two black eyes fringed with jet lashes, whose glances were soft and languishing and whose perfect beauty never stopped coaxing; and she spoke to the porter in the smoothest tones and the choicest language.

"Take up your crate and follow me."

The porter was so dazzled he could hardly believe he had heard her right, but he shouldered his basket in a great hurry, saying to himself, "O day of good luck! O day of Allah's grace!" And he walked after her until she stopped at the door of a house.

There she knocked, and an old man came out to her, a Christian, to whom she gave a gold piece and got in return what she wanted of strained wine, as clear as olive oil; and she set it carefully in the hamper and said, "Lift, and follow."

"By Allah," said the porter, "this is a lucky day indeed, a day fit for the granting of everything a man could wish for."

He hoisted the crate up again and followed her, until she stopped at a fruiterer's shop and bought Syrian apples and Ottoman quinces and Omani peaches, and cucumbers grown on the Nile, and Egyptian limes and Sultani oranges and citrons; and besides these, jasmine from Aleppo, scented myrtle berries, Damascus water lilies, privet flower and camomile, blood-red anemones, violets, pomegranate blossom, sweet briar and narcissus. She set the whole lot in the porter's crate and said, "Up with it."

So he lifted, and followed her, until she stopped at a butcher's stall and said, "Cut me ten pounds of mutton." She paid him his price, and he wrapped it in a banana leaf, and she laid it in the crate and said, "Hoist, porter."

He hoisted accordingly, and followed her as she walked on until she stopped at a grocer's, where she bought dried fruit and pistachio kernels, raisins from Tihamah, shelled almonds and everything else wanted for dessert; and she said to the porter, "Lift, and follow me."

So up he went with his hamper and after her, until she stopped at the confectioner's, and there she bought an earthenware platter and piled it with every kind of sweet in the shop — open-worked tarts and fritters scented with musk, and soap-cakes, and lemon loaves and preserved melon, and Zaynab's combs, and ladies' fingers, and judge's titbits, and goodies of every description — and put the platter in the porter's crate.

At which he said, being a cheerful man, "You should have told me, and I would have brought a pony or a she-camel along to carry all this shopping."

She smiled, and gave him a little cuff on the back of the neck, and said, "Step out, and do not overdo the talking. Your wage will not be lacking, Allah willing."

Then she stopped at a perfumer's and took ten sorts of scented water from him — rose scented with musk, orange flower, water lily, willow flower, violet and five others. She also bought two loaves of sugar, a bottle for spraying perfume, a lump of male incense, aloe-wood, ambergris and musk, and candles of Alexandrian wax; and she put the whole lot into the basket, saying, "Up with your crate, and after me."

He did it, and followed until she stood in front of the greengrocer's, where she bought pickled safflower and olives, in brine and in oil, with tarragon and cream cheese and hard Syrian cheese; and she stowed them away in the crate and said, "Take up your basket and follow me."

He did, and went after her until she came to a fine mansion fronted by a spacious court — a tall, handsome place to which columns gave both strength and grace; and the gate had two leaves of ebony inlaid with plates of red gold.

The lady stopped at the door and, turning her face veil aside, knocked softly with her knuckles, while the porter stood behind her thinking of nothing at all except her beauty and her loveliness.

Presently the door swung back and both leaves opened; and he looked to see who had opened it — and it was a lady of tall figure, some five feet high, a model of beauty and loveliness, brilliance and symmetry and perfect grace. Her forehead was flower-white; her cheeks like the anemone, ruddy and bright; her eyes were the eyes of the wild heifer or the gazelle, with eyebrows like the crescent moon that ends Sha'aban and begins Ramadan; her mouth was the ring of Solomon; her lips coral red, and her teeth like a line of strung pearls or of camomile petals. Her throat recalled the antelope's; and her breasts, like two pomegranates of exactly the same size, stood as though at bay; her body rose and fell in waves under her dress like the folds of a length of brocade; and her navel would have held an ounce of benzoin ointment. In short she was the woman the poet meant when he said:

	Cast your eye on the sun and moon of the palace;
	enjoy her flower-like face and her fragrant light.
	Your eyes will never see hair so black
	framing a brow so purely white.
	The ruddy rose of her cheek makes her claim for her,
	though we cannot name the name of the beauty we describe.
	As her walk sways, I smile at hips so wide
	and weep to see how slight the waist is that carries them.

When the porter looked at her his wits were waylaid and his senses stormed, so that the crate very nearly fell off his head; and he said to himself, "Never in my life have I seen a day more blessed than this one."

Then the lady who kept the door said to the lady who had done the shopping, "Come in from the gate and relieve this poor man of his load."

So the caterer went in, followed by the doorkeeper and the porter, and they went on until they reached a spacious ground-floor hall, built with admirable skill and decorated with every kind of colour and carving, with upper balconies and groined arches and galleries and cupboards and alcoves with curtains hanging in front of them. In the middle stood a great basin full of water with a fine fountain in it; and at the upper end, on the raised dais, was a couch of juniper wood set with gems and pearls, with a canopy over it like mosquito curtains, of red satin silk, looped up with pearls as big as filberts and bigger.

And on the couch sat a lady bright of face, with a brow beaming brilliance, the dream philosophy dreams of; whose eyes were loaded with the magic of Babylon and whose eyebrows were arched like a bow for archery; whose breath breathed ambergris and perfume, and whose lips were sugar to taste and carnelian to look at. Her figure was straight as a single upright stroke of the pen, and her face shamed the noon sun's radiance; and she was like a galaxy, or a dome with golden inlay, or a bride displayed in her choicest finery, or a noble girl of Arabia. The poet sang of her exactly right when he said:

	Her smiles show two rows of pearls,
	camomile buds or a spray of frost.
	Her hair strays down like night let loose
	and her light shames the light of dawn.

The third lady rose from the couch and came forward with a gracefully swaying walk until she reached the middle of the room, and said to her sisters, "Why are you standing about? Take it down off this poor man's head."

So the caterer went and stood in front of him, and the doorkeeper behind him, while the third helped them; and they lifted the load off the porter's head, and emptied it of everything in it, and put each thing in its place. And finally they gave him two gold pieces and said, "Off you go, porter."

But he did not go. He stood looking at the ladies and admiring what uncommon beauty they had, and what pleasant manners and kind natures — he had never seen better — and he looked wistfully at that good store of wines and sweet-scented flowers and fruit and everything else. He was astonished too, beyond all astonishment, particularly at seeing no man about the place; and he lingered.

At which the eldest lady said, "What is the matter with you, that you do not go? Perhaps your wage is too small?" And turning to her sister the caterer, she said, "Give him another dinar."

But the porter answered, "By Allah, my lady, it is not the wage. My hire is never more than two dirhams. But the truth is that my heart and my soul are taken up with you and with your situation. I wonder to see you on your own with never a man about you, and not a soul to keep you company. And you know perfectly well that a minaret topples over unless it stands on four legs — and you are wanting that same fourth. And women's pleasure without a man is short measure, as the poet said:

	Do you not see that for our joy we want four things in all:
	the harp and the lute, the flute and the flageolet;
	and let them be companioned by four scents —
	rose, myrtle, anemone and violet.
	And all eight will not please if you withhold four more:
	good wine, and youth, and gold, and a pretty companion.

"You are three, and you want a fourth, who should be a person of good sense and discretion, sharp-witted and able to keep a secret carefully."

His words pleased them and amused them a great deal, and they laughed at him and said, "And who is going to give us any guarantee of that? We are unmarried women, and we are afraid to trust our secret where it may not be kept — for we have read in a certain chronicle the lines of one Ibn al-Sumam:

	Hold your secret fast and unfold it to nobody;
	a secret is lost the moment that secret is told.
	If your own breast fails to hold your secret in,
	how can you hope that another man's breast will hold it?

"And Abu Nowas said it well on the same subject:

	Whoever puts his secret into another man's hand
	deserves to have the brand burnt on his forehead."

When the porter heard this he answered, "By your lives! I am a man of sense and discretion, who has read books and studied chronicles. I reveal what is fair and conceal what is foul, and I act as the poet advises:

	None but the good keep a secret,
	and good men keep it unrevealed.
	With me it is a well-shut house
	with the locks keyless and the door sealed."

When the young women heard his verse and the way he applied it to them, they said, "You know we have laid out all our money on this place. Now tell us — have you anything to offer us in return for entertainment? For we certainly will not let you sit in our company and be our drinking companion and look at faces as fair and rare as ours without paying a round sum. Do you not know the saying:

	Without hope of gain, Love is not worth a grain?"

To which the doorkeeper added, "If you bring something, you are something; if nothing, be off with you — you are nothing."

But the caterer broke in and said, "No, sisters, leave off teasing him. By Allah, he has not failed me today; anyone else would never have kept his patience with me. Whatever his charge comes to, I will take it on myself."

The porter, overjoyed, kissed the ground before her and thanked her, saying, "By Allah, this money is the first fruit this day has given me."

Hearing this they said, "Sit down, and welcome to you." And the eldest lady added, "By Allah, we cannot let you join us except on one condition, and this is it: that no questions are asked about what does not concern you, and that being contrary is soundly flogged."

"I agree to that, my lady," the porter answered. "On my head and my eyes be it. Look — I am dumb. I have no tongue."

Then the caterer got up, and tightening her girdle, set the table by the fountain and put the flowers and sweet herbs in their jars, and strained the wine and ranged the flasks in a row and made everything else ready. Then she sat down, she and her sisters, with the porter in the middle of them — and he kept thinking he must be dreaming.

She took up the wine flagon and poured the first cup and drank it off, and a second, and a third. After that she filled a fourth cup and handed it to one of her sisters; and last of all she crowned a goblet and passed it to the porter, saying:

	"Drink the dear draught, drink free and glad —
	the drink that heals every grief and pain."

He took the cup in his hand and, bowing low, gave her his best thanks, and improvised:

	"Do not drain the bowl except with a trusted friend,
	a man of worth whose good old blood is known to everybody.
	For wine, like the wind, takes its sweetness from what is sweet,
	and stinks when it happens to blow over a stench."

And he added:

	"Do not drain the bowl except from a dear hand like yours.
	The cup calls your gifts to mind — and you are the gift of wine."

After reciting this couplet he kissed their hands and drank, and was drunk, and sat swaying from side to side, and went on:

	"Every drink with blood in it the Law holds unclean
	except one — the blood shed by the vine.
	Fill! Fill! take all my wealth, inherited or earned;
	you fawn! a willing ransom for those eyes of yours."

Then the caterer crowned a cup and gave it to the doorkeeper, who took it from her hand and thanked her and drank. Then she poured again and passed it to the eldest lady, sitting on the couch; and filled yet another and handed it to the porter. He kissed the ground before them, and after drinking and thanking them began reciting again:

	"Here! Here! by Allah, here!
	Cups of the sweet, the dear!
	Fill me a brimming bowl —
	it is the Fountain of Life I ask for."

Then the porter stood up in front of the mistress of the house and said, "My lady, I am your slave, your Mamluk, your bondsman, your very own property." And he began reciting:

	"A slave of slaves is standing at your door,
	praising your generous kindness and your gifts.
	Beauty! may he come in a while to enjoy
	your charms? for Love and I will never part."

She said to him, "Drink; and health and happiness go with your drinking."

So he took the cup and kissed her hand and recited these lines in a sing-song:

	"I gave her good old wine that, like her cheeks,
	blushed red, or like flame flaring up out of a furnace.
	She kissed the brim and said, smiling all over,
	how dare you serve people's cheeks for people to drink?
	'Drink!' said I. 'These are my tears, and their colour
	is heart's blood that sighs have boiled in the cup.'"

She answered him with this couplet:

	"If you have shed tears of blood for me, my friend,
	then let me drink them up, by your head and your eyes!"

Then the lady took the cup and drank it off to her sisters' health; and they did not stop drinking, with the porter in the middle of them, and dancing and laughing and reciting verses and singing ballads and refrains.

All this time the porter was carrying on with them — kissing, playing, biting, handling, groping, fingering; while one of them thrust a dainty morsel into his mouth and another slapped him, and this one cuffed his cheeks and that one threw sweet flowers at him. And he was in the very paradise of pleasure, as though he were sitting in the seventh sphere among the houris, who are the maidens of Heaven.

They went on like this until the wine started playing tricks in their heads and getting the better of their wits. And when the drink had beaten them, the doorkeeper stood up and pulled her clothes off until she was stark naked. She did let her hair down over her body by way of a shift; and then she threw herself into the basin and disported herself and dived like a duck and swam up and down, and took water into her mouth and squirted it all over the porter, and washed her limbs, and between her breasts, and inside her thighs, and all round her navel.

Then she came up out of the cistern and threw herself down on the porter's lap and said, "My lord, my love, what do you call this?" — pointing to herself.

"I call that your slit," said the porter.

"Wah! wah!" she said. "Are you not ashamed to use a word like that?" And she caught him by the collar and cuffed him soundly.

"Your womb, then," he said; and she struck him a second slap, crying, "Oh fie, oh fie — that is another ugly word. Have you no shame in you at all?"

"Your cunny," he said; and she cried, "You! Are you completely destitute of modesty?" and thumped him and bashed him.

Then the porter cried, "Your clitoris" — at which the eldest lady came down on him with a still sorer beating, and said, "No."

"It is so," he said. And the porter went on calling the same article by a variety of other names; and whatever he said, they beat him more and more, until his neck ached and swelled with the blows he had taken. And in this way they made a butt of him and a laughing stock.

At last he turned on them and asked, "And what do you women call it?"

To which the girl answered, "The basil of the bridges."

"Thank Allah for my safety!" cried the porter. "Help me and be kind to me, O basil of the bridges!"

They passed the cup round and tossed the bowl off again; and then the second lady stood up, and stripping off all her clothes, threw herself into the cistern and did as the first had done. Then she came out of the water and threw her naked body down on the porter's lap and pointed to herself and said, "Light of my eyes, do tell me the name of this."

He answered as before, "Your slit."

"Has a word like that no shame for you?" she said; and cuffed him and buffeted him until the room rang with the blows. And then she said, "Oh fie! Oh fie! How can you say that without blushing?"

He suggested, "The basil of the bridges." But she would not have it, and said, "No! No!" and struck him and slapped him on the back of the neck.

So he began calling out every name he knew — "Your slit, your womb, your cunny, your clitoris" — and the girls kept saying, "No! No!"

So he said, "I stick to the basil of the bridges." And all three of them laughed until they fell over on their backs, and laid slaps on his neck, and said, "No! No! That is not its proper name."

At which he cried, "Sisters — what is its name?"

And they answered, "What do you say to the husked sesame seed?"

Then the caterer put her clothes back on, and they fell to carousing again; but the porter kept moaning, "Oh! and Oh!" over his neck and shoulders, and the cup went merrily round and round for a good hour.

After that the eldest and handsomest lady stood up and stripped her clothes off — at which the porter took his own neck in his hands and rubbed it and massaged it, saying, "My neck and shoulders are on the way of Allah!"

Then she threw herself into the basin and swam and dived, disported herself and washed; and the porter looked at her naked figure as though she were a slice of the moon, and at her face with the sheen of the full moon on it, or like the dawn when it brightens; and he took in her noble height and shape and those glorious forms that quivered as she moved, for she was as naked as the Lord made her.

Then he cried, "Alack! Alack!" and began to address her, putting it into these couplets:

	"If I compare your shape to the green bough
	my comparison fails and I make a bad mistake;
	for the bough is at its finest the more it is clothed
	and you are at your finest stark naked."

When the lady heard his verses she came up out of the basin and, seating herself on his lap and knees, pointed to herself and said, "My little lord, what is the name of this?"

"The basil of the bridges," he said.

"Bah, bah!" she said.

"The husked sesame," he said.

"Pooh, pooh!" she said.

Then he said, "Your womb"; and she cried, "Fie, fie! Are you not ashamed of yourself?" and cuffed him on the back of the neck.

And whatever name he gave, declaring, "That is it," she beat him and cried, "No! no!" — until at last he said, "Sisters, what is its name?"

She replied, "It is called the Inn of Abu Mansur."

At which the porter said, "Ha, ha! Allah be praised for a safe deliverance! O Inn of Abu Mansur!"

Then she came out and dressed, and the cup went round for a full hour.

At last the porter got up and stripped off all his clothes and jumped into the tank, and swam about and washed under his bearded chin and under his arms, exactly as they had done. Then he came out and threw himself into the first lady's lap, and rested his arms on the doorkeeper's lap, and laid his legs in the caterer's lap, and pointed to himself and said, "My mistresses — what is the name of this article?"

They all laughed at him until they fell over on their backs, and one said, "Your pintle!"

But he answered, "No!" and gave each of them a bite by way of a forfeit.

Then they said, "Your pizzle!" and he cried, "No," and gave each of them a hug:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Tenth Night,

her sister Dunyazad said, "Finish your story for us." And she answered, "With joy and goodwill."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the girls did not stop saying to the porter, "Your prickle, your pintle, your pizzle," and he did not stop kissing and biting and hugging until his heart was satisfied, and they laughed until they could laugh no more.

At last one of them said, "Well then, brother — what is it called?"

"Do you not know?" said he.

"No!" said they.

"Its true name," he said, "is the mule Burst-all, which browses on the basil of the bridges, and munches the husked sesame, and spends the night at the Inn of Abu Mansur."

Then they laughed until they fell over on their backs, and went back to their carousing; and they went on like this until night began to fall.

Then they said to the porter, "In Allah's name, master — up, and on with those sorry old shoes of yours, and turn your face and show us the breadth of your shoulders."

"By Allah," he said, "parting with my soul would be easier for me than parting from you. Come, let us join the night to the day, and tomorrow morning each of us will go his own way."

"On my life," said the caterer, "let him stay with us, so that we can laugh at him. We could live out our whole lives and never meet his like; he really is a merry rogue and a witty one."

So they said, "You may not stay with us tonight except on the condition that you submit to our orders, and that whatever you see, you ask no questions about it and do not inquire into the reason for it."

"All right," he answered.

And they said, "Go and read the writing over the door."

So he got up and went to the entrance, and there he found written in gold wash: Whoever speaks of what does not concern him shall hear what does not please him.

The porter said, "Be witnesses against me that I will not speak of what does not concern me."

Then the caterer got up and set food in front of them and they ate; after which they moved from one drinking place to another, and she lit the lamps and the candles and burned ambergris and aloe-wood, and set out fresh fruit and the wine service; and they fell to carousing and talking about their lovers.

And they did not stop eating and drinking and chatting, nibbling dried fruit and laughing and playing tricks, for a good hour — when there came a knock at the gate.

The knocking did not disturb the party in the least, but one of them got up to see what it was, and came back presently saying, "Truly our pleasure tonight is going to be perfect."

"How is that?" they asked.

"At the gate," she answered, "there are three Persian kalandars — wandering holy beggars under a vow — with their beards and their heads and their eyebrows all shaved off; and all three of them blind in the left eye, which is certainly a strange coincidence. They are foreigners from the land of Rum, with the marks of travel plain on them; they have only just arrived in Baghdad, this being their first visit to our city; and the reason they are knocking at our door is simply that they cannot find a lodging.

"Indeed one of them said to me: perhaps the owner of this house will let us have the key of his stable, or some old outbuilding where we can pass the night. For evening had caught them out, and being strangers in the country they knew nobody who would shelter them. And sisters — each one of them is a figure of fun in his own way; and if we let them in we shall have something to make sport of."

She went on persuading them until they said, "Let them in — and make the usual condition with them, that they do not speak of what does not concern them, in case they hear what does not please them."

So she was delighted, and went to the door, and came back with the three one-eyed men, whose beards and moustaches were shaved clean off. They gave their greetings and stood well back out of respect; but the three ladies rose to them and welcomed them and wished them joy of their safe arrival, and made them sit down.

The kalandars looked round the room and saw it was a pleasant place, swept clean and decorated with flowers, the lamps burning and the smoke of the perfumes spiralling up into the air; and besides the dessert and the fruit and the wine there were three lovely girls who might well be unmarried. So they exclaimed all in one voice, "By Allah, this is good!"

Then they turned to the porter and saw he was a merry-faced fellow, though by no means sober, and sore after his slappings. So they took him for one of themselves and said, "A beggar like us — Arab or foreigner, whichever."

But when the porter heard this he got up and, fixing his eyes fiercely on them, said, "Sit there and do not overdo the talking! Have you not read what is written over the door? It hardly suits fellows who come to us like paupers to wag their tongues at us."

"We beg your pardon, fakir," they answered, "and our heads are between your hands."

The ladies laughed themselves silly at the squabble; and making peace between the kalandars and the porter, they seated their new guests in front of food, and they ate. Then they all sat together, and the doorkeeper served them with drink; and as the cup went merrily round, the porter said to the beggars, "And you, brothers — have you no story or rare adventure to entertain us with?"

Now the warmth of the wine had gone to their heads, and they called for musical instruments; and the doorkeeper brought them a tambourine from Mosul, a lute from Iraq and a Persian harp. And each beggar took one and tuned it — this one the tambourine and those two the lute and the harp — and struck up a merry tune, while the ladies sang so lustily that there was a tremendous noise.

And while they were carrying on, somebody knocked at the gate, and the doorkeeper went to see what the matter was.

Now the reason for that knocking, O King (said Shahrazad), was this. The Caliph, Harun al-Rashid, had come out of the palace as he did now and then, to amuse himself in the city that night and to see and hear what new thing was stirring. He was dressed as a merchant, and he was attended by Ja'afar his vizier and by Masrur his executioner.

As they walked about the city their way led them towards the house of the three ladies, where they heard the loud noise of musical instruments and singing and merriment. So the Caliph said to Ja'afar, "I have a great desire to go into this house and hear those songs and see who is singing them."

"O Commander of the Faithful," said Ja'afar, "these people are certainly drunk on wine, and I am afraid some mischief may come to us if we get among them."

"There is no help for it, I must go in," the Caliph replied. "And I want you to think up some pretext for our turning up among them."

"I hear and I obey," said Ja'afar; and he knocked at the door, at which the doorkeeper came out and opened it.

Then Ja'afar came forward and, kissing the ground before her, said, "My lady, we are merchants from the town of Tiberias. We arrived in Baghdad ten days ago, and put up at the merchants' caravanserai, and sold all our goods. Now a certain trader invited us to an entertainment tonight; so we went to his house and he set food before us and we ate; then we sat drinking with him for an hour or so, when he gave us leave to go. And we went out from him in the darkness of the night, and being strangers we could not find our way back to our inn. So perhaps out of your kindness and courtesy you will let us stay with you tonight — and Heaven will reward you."

The doorkeeper looked them over, and seeing them dressed as merchants and looking grave and substantial men, she went back to her sisters and repeated Ja'afar's story; and they took pity on the strangers and said to her, "Let them in."

She opened the door to them, and they said, "Have we your leave to come in?"

"Come in," she said. And the Caliph came in, followed by Ja'afar and Masrur; and when the girls saw them they rose in respect and made them sit down and saw to their wants, saying, "Welcome, and well come, and good cheer to our guests — but on one condition."

"What is that?" they asked.

And one of the ladies answered, "Do not speak of what does not concern you, in case you hear what does not please you."

"Just so," they said; and sat down to their wine and drank deep.

Presently the Caliph looked at the three kalandars and, seeing every one of them blind in the left eye, wondered at the sight; then he looked at the girls and was startled, and marvelled beyond all marvelling at their beauty and loveliness.

They went on carousing and talking, and said to the Caliph, "Drink!"

But he replied, "I am under a vow to go on pilgrimage," and drew back from the wine.

At that the doorkeeper got up and spread a tablecloth worked with gold in front of him, and set a porcelain bowl on it, into which she poured willow-flower water with a lump of snow and a spoonful of sugar candy. The Caliph thanked her, and said to himself, "By Allah, I will repay her tomorrow for the kindness she has done me."

The others turned back to talking and carousing; and when the wine had got the better of them, the eldest lady, who ruled the house, stood up and made them a bow and took the caterer by the hand and said, "Get up, sister, and let us do what we have to do."

They both answered, "Just so."

Then the doorkeeper stood up and set about removing the table service and the remains of the feast; and she renewed the pastilles and cleared the middle of the room. Then she made the kalandars sit on a sofa at the side of the dais, and seated the Caliph and Ja'afar and Masrur on the other side of the room; after which she called the porter and said, "How poor your manners are! You are not a stranger now — you are one of the household."

So he stood up and, tightening his waistcloth, asked, "What would you like me to do?"

And she answered, "Stand where you are."

Then the caterer got up and set a low chair in the middle of the room; and opening a closet, called to the porter, "Come and help me."

So he went to help her — and saw two black bitches with chains round their necks.

"Take hold of them," she said. And he took them and led them into the middle of the room.

Then the lady of the house got up and tucked her sleeves back above her wrists, and taking a scourge, said to the porter, "Bring one of the bitches forward."

He brought her forward, dragging her by the chain, and the bitch wept and shook her head at the lady; but the lady came down on her with blows on the skull, and the bitch howled, and the lady did not stop beating her until her own forearm gave out.

Then, throwing the scourge out of her hand, she pressed the bitch to her breast and wiped away her tears with her hands and kissed her head.

Then she said to the porter, "Take her away and bring the second." And when he brought her, she did to her exactly as she had done to the first.

Now the Caliph's heart was touched at these cruel doings; his chest tightened and he lost all patience in his desire to know why the two bitches were beaten like that. He threw a wink at Ja'afar, wanting him to ask; but the minister turned to him and said with a sign, "Be silent."

Then the doorkeeper said to the mistress of the house, "My lady, get up and go to your place, so that I in my turn can do what I have to do."

She answered, "Just so"; and taking her seat on the couch of juniper wood, decorated with gold and silver, she said to the doorkeeper and the caterer, "Now do what you have to do."

At which the doorkeeper sat down on a low seat by the side of the couch; but the caterer went into a closet and brought out of it a satin bag with green fringes and two gold tassels. She stood in front of the lady of the house and shook the bag and drew a lute out of it, which she tuned by tightening the pegs; and when it was in perfect order she began to sing these verses:

	"You are what I wish for, you are what I aim at,
	and when, O Love, I see your face
	the mansion of heaven opens;
	but I see Hell when I lose the sight of you.
	From you comes madness — and no less
	from you come the highest joy and ecstasy.
	Nor, in my love for you, do I fear
	shame or blame, hatred or spite.
	When Love was enthroned inside my heart
	I tore the veil of modesty apart;
	and Love does not stop tearing that veil
	and bringing disgrace down on grace.
	I put on the robe of sickness then,
	but secrecy was torn to rags.
	And so my love and my longing heart
	proclaim your highest and most supreme power;
	the teardrop running down my cheek
	tells the tale of my dishonour;
	and everything hidden was seen by everybody
	and my whole riddle was read out right.
	Heal me of my sickness, then, for you
	are both the sickness and the cure!
	But the woman whose cure is in your hand
	will never be free of ruin and blight.
	Burn me with those eyes that rain light down;
	kill me with the swords of imagination.
	How many has the sword of Love laid low
	for all their high position?
	And yet I will never stop pining,
	nor will I run away into forgetting.
	Love is my health, my faith, my joy,
	in public and in private, right or wrong.
	Happy are the eyes that see your charms,
	that gaze on you as much as they please!
	Yes — of my purest wish and my own will,
	the slave of Love is what I shall always be called."

When the girl heard this lament in quatrains she cried out, "Alas! Alas!" and tore her clothes, and fell to the ground in a faint. And the Caliph saw the scars of the palm rod on her back and the welts of the whip, and marvelled beyond all wondering.

Then the doorkeeper got up and sprinkled water on her and brought her a fresh and very fine dress and put it on her.

But when the company saw all this their minds were troubled, because they had no idea of the situation and did not know the story behind it. So the Caliph said to Ja'afar, "Did you not see the scars on that girl's body? I cannot keep quiet or be easy until I learn the truth about her condition, and the story of this other girl, and the secret of the two black bitches."

But Ja'afar answered, "Our lord, they made it a condition with us that we should not speak of what does not concern us, in case we hear what does not please us."

Then the doorkeeper said, "By Allah, sister, come here and finish this service for me."

"With joy and goodwill," the caterer replied. So she took the lute and leaned it against her breast and swept the strings with her fingertips, and began to sing:

	"Give my eyes back the sleep that has been stolen from them so long,
	and tell me where my reason has fled to.
	I learned that once I gave your love a place,
	sleep became the mortal enemy of my eyelids.
	They said, 'We used to think you an upright woman — who waylaid
	your soul?' 'Go and ask his glorious eyes,' I said.
	I pardon him all the blood he chose to spill,
	granting that his own troubles drove him to shed it.
	He cast a sunlike brightness on the mirror of my mind
	whose keen reflection bred a fire in my vitals.
	Let Allah waste the Waters of Life however He likes;
	those dewy red lips are wage enough for me.
	If you speak to my love you will find cause enough
	for complaint and tears, or for pity, or for desire.
	His face will greet your eyes in clear water
	when the bowl fails and you need not drink wine at all."

Then she quoted from the same ode:

	"I drank, but the draught was his glance, not wine,
	and his swaying walk swayed these eyes of mine to sleep.
	It was not grape juice that gripped me but the grip of the past;
	it was not the bowl that overcame me but gifts from heaven.
	His coiling little curls netted my soul
	and his cruel will outwitted all my wits."

After a pause she went on:

	"If we complain of absence, what are we to say?
	Or if pain afflicts us, which way are we to go?
	If I hire an interpreter to tell my tale —
	a lover's complaint is not told for pay.
	If I put on patience, a lover's life
	will not last a day after love is lost.
	Nothing is left me now but regret and repining
	and tears flooding my cheeks for ever and ever.
	O you who have fled from the babies of these eyes,
	you are housed in a heart that will never stray.
	Would to heaven I knew — have you kept our pact,
	to hold firmest faith as long as the stream flows?
	Or have you forgotten the weeping slave
	whom groans afflict and whom griefs waylay?
	Ah, when the separation ends and we lie side by side,
	I will blame you for your hardness and scold you for your pride!"

Now when the doorkeeper heard her second ode she shrieked aloud and said, "By Allah, that is very good!" — and laying hands on her clothes, tore them as she had the first time, and fell to the ground in a faint.

At which the caterer rose and sprinkled water on her and brought her a second change of clothes. She came round and sat up, and said to her sister the caterer, "On you go, and help me with my duty, for there is only this one song left."

So the caterer brought out the lute again and began to sing these verses:

	"How long is this to last, how long this hardness full of grief?
	Are all these tears you see running not enough for you?
	You deliberately draw out our parting with a cruel purpose —
	is it not enough to gladden the heart of an envious enemy?
	If this lying world had once been true to a lover's heart
	he would not have watched out the weary night in tears.
	Oh pity me, whom your cruel will has overwhelmed;
	my lord, my king, it is time you showed me some mercy.
	To whom shall I tell my wrongs, you who have murdered me?
	Sad is the one who must suffer the pangs of broken faith.
	My wild love for you grows hour by hour,
	and the days of exile lengthen minute by slow minute.
	O Muslims, claim vengeance for this slave of Love,
	whose sleep Love always wastes, whose patience Love lays low.
	Does the law of Love allow you, my heart's desire, to lie
	wrapped in another's arms and cry Go! to me?
	And yet in your presence — tell me — what joys shall I enjoy
	when the man I love works only to overthrow my love?"

When the doorkeeper heard the third song she cried out aloud, and laying hands on her clothes, tore them right down to the hem and fell to the ground in a faint for the third time, showing the scars of the scourge again.

Then the three kalandars said, "Would to Heaven we had never come into this house, but had spent the night on the rubbish mounds outside the city! Truly our visit has been spoiled by sights that cut a man to the heart."

The Caliph turned to them and asked, "Why is that?"

And they answered, "Our minds are badly troubled by this business."

"Are you not of the household?" said the Caliph.

"No," they said, "nor did we ever set eyes on the place until an hour ago."

At this the Caliph marvelled, and said, "This man sitting next to you — would he not know the secret of the matter?" And saying it he winked and made signs at the porter.

So they questioned the man, but he answered, "By the Almighty power of Allah, in love we are all alike! I am Baghdad born and bred, and yet in all my born days I never darkened these doors until today; and my keeping company with them was a curious business."

"By Allah," they said, "we took you for one of them, and now we see you are one like ourselves."

Then the Caliph said, "We are seven men, and they are only three women without even a fourth to help them; so let us question them about their situation. And if they will not answer us, we shall be answered by force."

Every one of them agreed to this except Ja'afar, who said, "That is not my reckoning. Let them be. We are their guests, and as you know they made a compact and a condition with us which we accepted and promised to keep. So it is better that we say nothing about the matter; and since there is little of the night left, let each and every one of us go his own way."

Then he winked at the Caliph and whispered to him, "There is only one hour of darkness left, and I can bring them before you tomorrow, when you can question them all about their story as much as you like."

But the Caliph raised his head haughtily and cried out at him in anger, "I have no patience left, for my longing to hear about them. Let the kalandars ask them straight away."

"That is not my advice," said Ja'afar.

Then words ran high and talk answered talk, and they argued about who should put the question first; but at last they all settled on the porter.

And as the racket grew, the mistress of the house could not help noticing it, and asked them, "You people — what is this matter you are all talking so loudly about?"

Then the porter stood up respectfully in front of her and said, "My lady, this company earnestly wants you to tell them the story of the two bitches, and what makes you punish them so cruelly, and then makes you fall to weeping over them and kissing them; and last of all they want to hear the tale of your sister, and why she has been beaten with palm rods like a man. These are the questions they have charged me to put. And peace be with you."

At which the lady of the house said to her guests, "Is this true, what he says on your behalf?"

And all of them answered, "Yes" — except Ja'afar, who kept silent.

When she heard this she cried, "By Allah, guests, you have wronged us, and grievously. When you came in to us we made a compact and a condition with you: that whoever spoke of what did not concern him should hear what did not please him. Was it not enough for you that we took you into our house and fed you with the best food we had? But the fault is not so much yours as hers, who let you in."

Then she pulled her sleeves back from her wrists and struck the floor three times with her hand, crying, "Come quickly!"

And a closet door opened, and out of it came seven Black slaves with drawn swords in their hands, to whom she said, "Pinion these chatterers' elbows and tie them to one another."

They did as she said, and asked her, "O veiled and virtuous one, is it your high command that we strike off their heads?"

But she answered, "Leave them a while, so that I can question them about their situation, before their necks feel the sword."

"By Allah, my lady!" cried the porter, "do not kill me for somebody else's sin. All these men gave the offence and deserve the penalty for the crime, except me. By Allah, our night would have been charming if we had escaped the mortification of these one-eyed kalandars, whose arrival in a crowded city would turn it into a howling wilderness."

Then he recited these verses:

	"How fine a thing is pity that a strong man does not smother —
	and finest of all when it is shown to the weakest brother.
	By the holy tie of Love itself between the two of us,
	let one man not suffer for the sin of another."

When the porter had finished his verse the lady laughed:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Eleventh Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the lady, having laughed at the porter in spite of her anger, came up to the party and spoke to them.

"Tell me who you are," she said, "for you have only an hour to live. And if you were not men of rank, and perhaps notables among your own people, you would not have been so contrary, and I would have hurried your doom along."

Then the Caliph said, "Confound you, Ja'afar — tell her who we are, or we shall be killed by mistake; and speak fair to her before some horror comes down on us."

"It is no more than you deserve," he replied.

At which the Caliph cried out at him, "There is a time for witty words and there is a time for serious work."

Then the lady turned to the three kalandars and asked them, "Are you brothers?"

"No, by Allah," they answered. "We are nothing but beggars and foreigners."

Then she said to one of them, "Were you born blind in one eye?"

"No, by Allah," he said. "It was a marvellous business and a strange mischance that caused my eye to be torn out; and my tale is one which, if it were engraved with needles on the inner corners of the eye, would be a warning to anyone willing to take warning."

She questioned the second and the third kalandar, and both answered like the first. "By Allah, mistress, each one of us comes from a different country, and all three of us are the sons of kings, sovereign princes ruling over vassals and capital cities."

At that she turned to them and said, "Let every one of you tell me his tale in turn, and explain what brought him to our house; and if his story pleases us, let him rub his head and be on his way."

The first to come forward was the porter, who said, "My lady, I am a man, and a porter. This lady, the caterer, hired me to carry a load, and took me first to a wine-seller's shop, then to a butcher's stall; from there to a fruiterer's; from there to a grocer who also sold dried fruit; from there to a confectioner and a perfumer-and-druggist; and from him to this place, where what happened to me with you happened. That is my story, and peace be on us all."

At this the lady laughed and said, "Rub your head and be on your way."

But he cried, "By Allah, I will not stir a foot until I have heard my companions' stories."

Then one of the one-eyed men came forward and began to tell her

The First Kalandar's Tale

Know, my lady, that the reason my beard was shaved off and my eye was torn out was this.

My father was a king, and he had a brother who was king over another city; and it happened that my cousin — my father's brother's son — and I were both born on one and the same day.

The years and the days rolled on, and as we grew up I used to visit my uncle now and then and spend some months with him. My cousin and I were sworn friends, for he always treated me with tremendous kindness: he killed the fattest sheep for me and strained the best of his wines, and we enjoyed long hours of talking and drinking.

One day, when the wine had got the better of us, my uncle's son said to me, "Cousin, I have a great service to ask of you, and I want you not to stop me in anything I mean to do."

"With joy and goodwill," I answered.

Then he made me swear the most binding oaths, and left me. But after a little while he came back leading a lady, veiled and richly dressed, with jewellery on her worth a great deal of money.

Presently he turned to me — the woman still standing behind him — and said, "Take this lady with you and go ahead of me to such and such a burial ground" (and he described it, so that I knew the place), "and go into such and such a tomb chamber, and wait there for me to come."

The oaths I had sworn to him kept me quiet and would not let me argue with him. So I led the woman to the cemetery, and she and I sat down inside the tomb chamber; and we had hardly sat down before in came my uncle's son with a bowl of water, a bag of mortar, and an adze rather like a hoe.

He went straight to the tomb in the middle of the chamber and broke it open with the adze and set the stones to one side; and then he began digging into the earth of the tomb until he came to a large iron plate the size of a wicket door. Raising it, there appeared underneath a vaulted, winding staircase.

Then he turned to the lady and said, "Come now, and make your final choice."

She went straight down the stairs and disappeared. And then he said to me:

"Cousin, by way of completing your kindness — when I have gone down into this place, put the trapdoor back where it was and heap the earth back over it as it was before. And then, of your great goodness, mix this unslaked lime that is in the bag with this water that is in the bowl, and after building the stones back up, plaster the outside, so that nobody looking at it can say: this is a new opening in an old tomb. I have worked at this place for a whole year, and nobody knows about it except Allah. And this is the service I need from you."

And presently he added, "May Allah never take you from your friends or leave them desolate by your absence, cousin — my dear cousin!"

And he went down the stairs and disappeared for ever.

When he was out of sight I put the iron plate back and did everything he had told me until the tomb was as it had been before; and I worked almost without knowing what I was doing, for my head was hot with wine.

Going back to my uncle's palace, I was told he had gone out hunting and hawking; so I slept that night without seeing him. And when the morning dawned I remembered the scenes of the evening before and what had passed between me and my cousin, and I was sorry I had obeyed him, when being sorry was no use at all. Still, I half thought it had been a dream.

So I began asking after my uncle's son; but there was nobody who could answer me about him. And I went out to the graveyard and the tomb chambers and looked for the tomb he was under, and could not find it. And I did not stop wandering from tomb chamber to tomb chamber and from grave to grave, all without success, until night came on.

So I went back to the city, and I could neither eat nor drink; my thoughts were entirely taken up with my cousin, because I did not know what had become of him. And I grieved beyond all grieving, and passed another sorrowful night, lying awake until morning.

Then I went a second time to the cemetery, turning over what my uncle's son had done, and bitterly regretting having listened to him; and I went round all the tombs and could not find the tomb I was looking for. I mourned over the past, and stayed in my mourning seven days, looking for the place and always missing the path.

Then my torment of scruples grew on me until I very nearly went mad; and I could find no way to shake off my grief except to travel, and go back to my father.

So I set off and journeyed homewards. But as I was coming into my father's capital, a crowd of rioters sprang on me and pinioned my arms.

I wondered at it with every kind of wonder, seeing that I was the Sultan's son and these men were my father's subjects, and some of them my own slaves. A great fear fell on me and I said to myself, "I wish to heaven I knew what has happened to my father."

I asked the men who had bound me why they were doing it, but they gave me no answer. However, after a while one of them said to me — and he had been a hired servant of our household — "Fortune has been false to your father. His troops betrayed him, and the vizier who killed him now reigns in his place; and we were lying in wait to seize you at that man's bidding."

I was very nearly out of my mind, and felt ready to faint at the news of my father's death; and they carried me off and set me in front of the usurper.

Now there was an old grudge between him and me, and the cause of it was this. I was fond of shooting with the pellet bow; and it happened one day, as I was standing on the terrace roof of the palace, that a bird settled on the top of the vizier's house at a moment when he happened to be there. I shot at the bird and missed my mark — and hit the vizier in the eye and knocked it out, as fate and fortune decreed. As the poet says:

	We tread the path that Fate has led us down;
	the path Fate wrote is the path we must tread.
	And a man doomed to die in one country
	will be put to death nowhere else.

And another says the same thing:

	Let Fortune have her wanton way;
	take heart, and obey everything she says.
	Do not rejoice or mourn at anything,
	for all things pass and nothing stays.

Now when I knocked the vizier's eye out he could not say a single word, because my father was king of the city; but he hated me from then on, and the grudge between the two of us was a bitter one.

So when I was set in front of him with my hands bound and my arms pinioned, he gave orders at once for me to be beheaded.

"For what crime will you put me to death?" I asked.

And he answered, "What crime is greater than this?" — pointing all the while at the place where his eye had been.

"I did that by accident," I said, "and not out of deliberate malice."

"If you did it by accident," said he, "I shall do the same to you on purpose."

Then he cried, "Bring him forward." And they brought me up to him, and he thrust his finger into my left eye and gouged it out; and that is how I became one-eyed, as you see me.

Then he ordered me bound hand and foot and put into a chest, and said to the swordsman, "Take charge of this fellow, and go off with him to the waste ground outside the city; then draw your scimitar and kill him, and leave him for the beasts and the birds to feed on."

So the headsman went out with me; and when he was in the middle of the desert he took me out of the chest — my hands pinioned and my feet in fetters — and was about to bandage my eyes before striking off my head.

But I wept so bitterly that I made him weep with me; and looking at him, I began to recite:

	"I thought you a coat of mail that would stand up
	to the enemy's arrows — and you turned out to be the enemy's sword.
	I hoped for your help in every chance that came,
	though my left hand should fail to help my right;
	but you stand aside and listen to the mocker's gibes
	while the whole gang of mockers rains their shafts on me.
	Well — if you will not guard me from my enemies,
	then stand clear, and help neither them nor me."

And I also quoted:

	"I thought my brothers were mail of the strongest steel —
	and so they were, at fending off my own arrows from my enemies.
	I thought their arrows the surest of aim —
	and so they were, when they aimed at my heart."

When the headsman heard my lines — and he had been swordsman to my father, and he owed me a debt of gratitude — he cried, "My lord, what can I do? I am only a slave under orders."

And presently he added, "Fly for your life, and never come back to this country, or they will kill you and kill me along with you. As the poet said:

	Take your life and fly when trouble threatens;
	let the ruined house tell the tale of its owner's fate.
	You will look for a new country and find one instead of the old,
	but you must not wait about to find a new life.
	It is strange that men should sit down in a place of shame
	when Allah's world is so wide and so great.
	And in serious matters do not trust anybody else:
	life itself must act for a life under threat.
	The lion with the maned neck would never go out hunting
	if he counted on help or took thought of other creatures."

Hardly able to believe I had escaped, I kissed his hand, and thought the loss of my eye a light matter considering that I had got away without being killed.

I reached my uncle's capital; and going in to him, I told him what had happened to my father and to myself. At which he wept bitterly and said, "Truly you are adding grief to my grief and woe to my woe; for your cousin has been missing these many days, and I do not know what has happened to him, and nobody can give me news of him." And he wept until he fainted.

I grieved with him and offered him what comfort I could; and he wanted to put certain medicines on my eye, but he saw that it had become like a walnut with an empty shell. Then he said, "My son, better to lose an eye and keep your life."

After that I could not keep silent any longer about his son, who was his only son and dearly loved; so I told him everything that had happened. He was overjoyed to hear news of the boy and said, "Come now, and show me the tomb."

But I answered, "By Allah, uncle, I do not know where it is; I have hunted for it carefully a great many times and could never find the place."

However, my uncle and I went to the graveyard and looked right and left, until at last I recognised the tomb, and we were both overjoyed. We went into the chamber and loosened the earth round the grave; then, raising the trapdoor, we went down some fifty steps until we came to the foot of the staircase — and there we were stopped by a blinding smoke.

At which my uncle said the saying whose sayer shall never come to shame: "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great!"

And we went on, and suddenly came out into a large room whose floor was strewn with flour and grain and provisions and all sorts of necessaries; and in the middle of it stood a canopy sheltering a couch.

My uncle went up to the couch, and looking at it, found his son and the lady who had gone down into the tomb with him, lying in each other's arms — but the two of them had turned black as charred wood, as though they had been thrown into a pit of fire.

When my uncle saw this sight he spat in his son's face and said, "You have what you deserve, you pig! This is your judgement in the passing world, and the judgement in the world to come is still waiting for you — harsher, and longer-lasting":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Twelfth Night,

she went on: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the kalandar carried on with his story in front of the lady and the Caliph and Ja'afar:

My uncle struck his son with his slipper as he lay there, a black heap of coal. I marvelled at his hardness of heart, and grieving for my cousin and for the lady, said, "By Allah, uncle, calm your anger. Can you not see that all my thoughts are taken up with this misfortune, and how sorry I am for what has happened to your son, and how horrible it is that nothing is left of him but a black heap of charcoal? Is that not enough, without your striking him with your slipper as well?"

He answered, "Nephew, this boy was madly in love with his own sister from his boyhood. Time and time again I forbade him to go near her, saying to myself: they are only little ones. But when they grew up, sin happened between them; and although I could hardly believe it, I shut him up and scolded him and threatened him with the severest threats.

"And the eunuchs and the servants said to him: beware of such a foul thing, which nobody before you has ever done and nobody after you will ever do; and take care you are not dishonoured and disgraced among the kings of the day, to the end of time.

"And I added: a report like this will be carried abroad by the caravans, so take care not to give them anything to talk about, or I shall certainly curse you and put you to death.

"After that I lodged them apart and shut her up. But the accursed girl loved him with a passionate love, for Satan had got the mastery of her as well as of him and made their foul sin look fine to them both.

"Now when my son saw that I had separated them, he secretly built this underground place and furnished it and carried provisions down to it, exactly as you see. And when I had gone out hunting he came here with his sister and hid from me. Then Allah's righteous judgement fell on the pair of them and burnt them up with fire out of Heaven; and truly the last judgement will deal them harsher pains, and longer-lasting."

Then he wept, and I wept with him; and he looked at me and said, "You are my son in his place."

And I thought for a while about the world and the chances of it: how the vizier had killed my father and taken his place and put out my eye, and how my cousin had come to his death by the strangest chance of all. And I wept again, and my uncle wept with me.

Then we climbed the steps and let down the iron plate and heaped the earth up over it; and after putting the tomb back the way it had been, we returned to the palace.

But we had hardly sat down before we heard the drumming of kettledrums and the blaring of trumpets and the clash of cymbals, and the rattle of fighting men's lances, and the shouting of attackers, and the clanking of bits and the neighing of horses; while the whole world was canopied in thick dust and clouds of sand thrown up by the horses' hooves.

We were astonished at the sight and the sound, not knowing what the matter could be; so we asked, and were told that the vizier who had usurped my father's kingdom had marched his men against us — that after raising his army and taking a host of desert Arabs into his service, he had come down on us with forces like the sands of the sea, whose number nobody could count and against whom nobody could stand.

They attacked the city without warning; and the citizens, powerless to resist them, surrendered the place. My uncle was killed, and I made for the outskirts, saying to myself, "If you fall into this villain's hands he will certainly kill you."

And so all my troubles began again; and I turned over everything that had happened to my father and my uncle, and I did not know what to do. For if the townspeople or my father's troops had recognised me, they would have done their best to win favour by destroying me; and I could think of no way of escape except by shaving off my beard and my eyebrows.

So I shaved them off, and changing my fine clothes for a kalandar's rags, I set out from my uncle's capital and made for this city, hoping that somebody might help me into the presence of the Commander of the Faithful, the Caliph, who is the Viceregent of Allah upon earth. And so I have come here, to tell him my tale and lay my case before him.

I arrived this very night, and was standing in doubt about which way to go, when suddenly I saw this second kalandar; so I greeted him, saying, "I am a stranger!" and he answered, "I am a stranger too!"

And as we were talking, up came our companion here, this third kalandar, and greeted us, saying, "I am a stranger!" And we answered, "We are strangers too!"

Then the three of us walked on together until the dark overtook us, and Destiny drove us to your house.

So that is the reason my beard and my moustaches and my eyebrows were shaved off, and that is how I lost my left eye.

They marvelled a great deal at this tale, and the Caliph said to Ja'afar, "By Allah, I have neither seen nor heard the like of what has happened to this kalandar."

Then the lady of the house said, "Rub your head and be on your way."

But he replied, "I will not go until I have heard the history of the other two."

At which the second kalandar came forward, and kissing the ground, began to tell

The Second Kalandar's Tale

Know, my lady, that I was not born one-eyed, and mine is a strange story; if it were engraved with needles on the inner corners of the eye, it would be a warning to anyone willing to take warning.

I am a king and the son of a king, and I was brought up like a prince. I learned to chant the Koran according to the seven schools; I read books of every kind and held disputations on what was in them with the scholars and the men of science; I studied the lore of the stars and the fine sayings of the poets; and I trained myself in every branch of learning until I surpassed everybody of my time. My skill in calligraphy was greater than any scribe's, and my fame was carried abroad over every region and city, and all the kings came to know my name.

Among others, the King of India heard of me, and sent to my father to invite me to his court, with offerings and presents and rarities such as suit royalty. So my father fitted out six ships for me and my people; and we put to sea and sailed for a full month until we made land. Then we brought out the horses we had with us in the ships, and after loading the camels with our presents for the prince, we set off inland.

But we had gone only a little way when a cloud of dust flew up and grew until it walled off the whole horizon. After an hour or so the veil lifted, and showed underneath it fifty horsemen, ravening lions to look at, dressed in steel armour.

We watched them closely — and they were highwaymen, wild as the wildest of the desert Arabs. When they saw that we were only four, and had nothing with us but the ten camels carrying the presents, they charged down on us with their lances levelled.

We signalled to them with our fingers, as if to say, "We are messengers of the great King of India, so do us no harm." But they answered the same way, "We are not in his dominions to obey him, and we are not subject to his rule."

Then they set on us and killed some of my slaves and put the rest to flight; and I fled too, after taking a wound, a bad one, while the Arabs were busy with the money and the presents we had with us.

I went off without knowing where I was going, having become as poor as I had been powerful; and I travelled until I came to the crest of a mountain, where I sheltered for the night in a cave. When day came I set out again, and did not stop until I arrived at a fine, well-filled city.

Now it was the season when winter was turning away with his frost, and spring was coming to greet the world with his flowers, and the young blossoms were opening and the streams were running and ringing and the birds were singing sweetly — as the poet says about a certain city, describing it:

	A place secure from every thought of fear;
	safety and peace lord it here for ever.
	Its beauties seem to make its people beautiful,
	and its happy folk look as though they were in Heaven.

I was glad to have arrived, for I was worn out with the road and yellow in the face with weakness and want; but my situation was pitiable and I had no idea where to turn.

So I went up to a tailor sitting in his little shop and greeted him. He returned my greeting and made me kindly welcome and wished me well and spoke gently to me, and asked how I came to be a stranger there. I told him my whole past from beginning to end; and he was concerned for me and said, "Young man, do not tell your secret to anybody. The king of this city is your father's greatest enemy, and there is a blood feud between them, and you have reason to fear for your life."

Then he set food and drink in front of me, and I ate and drank and he with me; and we talked freely until nightfall, when he cleared a place for me in a corner of his shop and brought me a carpet and a coverlet.

I stayed with him three days, at the end of which he said to me, "Do you know no trade you could earn a living by, my son?"

"I am learned in the law," I replied, "and a doctor of doctrine; an adept in art and science, a mathematician, and a notable penman."

"Your calling is worth nothing in our city," he answered, "where not a soul understands science, or even writing, or anything at all except making money."

"By Allah," I said, "I know nothing but what I have told you."

And he answered, "Gird up your middle, and take a hatchet and a rope, and go and cut wood in the country for your daily bread, until Allah sends you relief. And tell nobody who you are, or they will kill you."

Then he bought me an axe and a rope and put me in the charge of some woodcutters; and with these guardians I went out into the forest, where I cut firewood all day long and came back in the evening carrying my bundle on my head. I sold it for half a dinar, and with part of that I bought food and laid the rest by.

I spent a whole year at this work. And when the year was over I went out one day as usual into the wilderness, and wandering away from my companions, I came across a thickly grown hollow where there was plenty of wood.

So I went in, and found the gnarled stump of a great tree, and loosened the ground round it and shovelled the earth away. And presently my hatchet rang on a copper ring; so I cleared the soil away, and there was the ring, fixed to a wooden trapdoor.

I raised it, and underneath there appeared a staircase. I went down the steps to the bottom and came to a door, which I opened — and found myself in a noble hall, strongly made and beautifully built, where there was a girl like a pearl of great price, whose face banished every grief and care and trouble from my heart, and whose soft speech healed a soul in despair, and captivated the wise and the wary.

Her figure measured five feet in height; her breasts were firm and upright; her cheek was a very garden of delight; her colour was lively and bright; her face gleamed like the dawn through curly hair that was dark as night, and above the snows of her breast glittered teeth of a pearly white. As the poet said about somebody like her:

	A slim-waisted darling crowned with jet-black hair,
	a willow wand growing on a sandy mound.

And as another says:

	Four things that never meet, unless they meet here,
	to shed my heart's blood and carry off my soul:
	the most brilliant forehead; hair jet and bright;
	cheeks red as roses; and a figure dressed in beauty.

When I looked at her I bowed down before Him who had created her, for the beauty and loveliness He had shaped in her; and she looked at me and said, "Are you a man or a jinni?"

"I am a man," I answered.

"Then who brought you to this place," she said, "where I have lived twenty-five years without ever yet seeing a man in it?"

I said — and I found her words wonderfully sweet, and my heart was melted to the core by them — "My lady, my good fortune led me here, to drive away my cares and troubles."

Then I told her all my misfortunes from beginning to end, and my case struck her as terribly hard; so she wept and said, "I will tell you my story in my turn.

"I am the daughter of King Ifitamus, lord of the Ebony Islands, who married me to my cousin, my father's brother's son. But on my wedding night an ifrit named Jirjis son of Rajmus — first cousin, that is, mother's sister's son, of Iblis the Foul Fiend — snatched me up and flew away with me like a bird and set me down in this place, and brought here everything I needed of fine stuffs, clothing and jewels and furniture, and food and drink and the rest.

"Once every ten days he comes here and lies a single night with me, and then goes his way; for he took me without his family's consent. And he has agreed with me that if ever I need him, by night or by day, I have only to pass my hand over those two lines engraved on the alcove there, and he will appear to me before my fingers have stopped touching.

"Four days have gone by now since he was here; and since there are six days left before he comes again — tell me, will you stay with me five days, and go away the day before he comes?"

I replied, "Yes, and yes again! And how wonderful, if all this is not a dream."

At this she was delighted, and springing to her feet she took my hand and led me through an arched doorway to a bathhouse, a fine hall and richly decorated. I took off my clothes and she took off hers; then we bathed and she washed me. And when that was done we came out of the bath, and she seated me at her side on a high divan and brought me sherbet scented with musk.

When we had cooled after the bath she set food in front of me, and we ate, and fell to talking. But presently she said, "Lie down and rest, for you must certainly be tired."

So I thanked her, my lady, and lay down and slept soundly, forgetting everything that had happened to me. When I woke I found her rubbing and massaging my feet; so I thanked her again and blessed her, and we sat a while and talked.

She said, "By Allah, I have been sad at heart, having lived alone underground these twenty-five years; and praise be to Allah, who has sent me somebody to talk to!"

Then she asked, "Young man, what do you say to wine?"

And I answered, "Do as you like."

At which she went to a cupboard and took out a sealed flask of good old wine, and set out the table with flowers and scented herbs, and began to sing these lines:

	"Had we known you were coming, we would gladly have spread out
	the cores of our hearts or the balls of our eyes;
	we would have thrown down our cheeks as a carpet to greet you
	and strewn our eyelids for your feet to walk on."

Now when she had finished her verse I thanked her; for indeed love of her had taken hold of my heart, and my grief and my anguish were gone.
