We sat talking and drinking until nightfall, and I spent the night with her — such a night as I never spent in all my life. And next day delight followed delight until midday, by which time I had drunk wine so freely that I had lost my wits; and I stood up, staggering to right and to left, and said, "Come, my charmer, and I will carry you up out of this underground vault and deliver you from your jinni's spell."

She laughed and answered, "Content yourself and hold your peace. Of every ten days, one is for the ifrit and the other nine are yours."

Said I — and in good truth the drink had got the better of me — "This very instant I will break down the alcove with the talisman engraved on it, and summon the ifrit so that I can kill him; for killing ifrits is a practice of mine."

When she heard this her colour went pale and she said, "By Allah, do not!" And she began reciting:

	"This is a thing with destruction lying in it;
	I advise you to shun it, if your wits are sound."

And these lines too:

	"You who go looking for separation, draw in the rein
	of your swift horse and do not press so far forward.
	Ah, stop! for treachery is the rule of life,
	and the sweets of meeting end in parting."

I heard her verse and paid no attention to her words — no, I raised my foot and gave the alcove a mighty kick:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Thirteenth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the second kalandar went on with his tale to the lady:

But when I kicked that alcove with a mighty kick, my mistress, the air went stark and dark and thundered and lightened; the earth trembled and quaked and the world went out of sight. In that instant the fumes of the wine left my head, and I cried to her, "What is the matter?"

And she answered, "The ifrit is on us! Did I not warn you of this? By Allah, you have brought ruin on me. But fly for your life, and go up the way you came down."

So I fled up the staircase; but in the excess of my fear I forgot my sandals and my hatchet. And when I had climbed two steps I turned to look for them — and I saw the earth split apart, and out of it rose an ifrit, a monster of hideousness, who said to the girl, "What trouble and uproar is this that you disturb me with? What misfortune has come on you?"

"No misfortune has come on me," she answered, "except that my chest was tight and my heart heavy with sadness; so I drank a little wine to open it and hearten myself; and then I got up to relieve myself, but the wine had gone to my head and I fell against the alcove."

"You are lying, like the whore you are!" shrieked the ifrit. And he looked round the hall, right and left, until he caught sight of my axe and my sandals, and said to her, "What are these but the belongings of some mortal who has been in your company?"

She answered, "I never set eyes on them until this moment; they must have been carried in here clinging to your own clothes."

"These words are absurd, you harlot! you strumpet!" said the ifrit.

Then he stripped her stark naked and stretched her out on the floor and tied her hands and feet to four stakes, like someone crucified, and set about torturing her and trying to make her confess.

I could not bear to stand there listening to her cries and her groaning; so I climbed the stair shaking with fear, and when I reached the top I put the trapdoor back and covered it with earth.

Then I was sorry for what I had done, sorry beyond all sorrow; and I thought of the lady and her beauty and loveliness, and the tortures she was suffering at the hands of that accursed ifrit after her quiet life of twenty-five years, and how everything that had happened to her had happened because of me. And I thought of my father and his royal position, and how I had become a woodcutter; and how, after my life had been calm for a while, the world had gone thick and troubled on me again.

So I wept bitterly and repeated this couplet:

	When the tyranny of Fate weighs on you hardest,
	consider: one day will gladden you and one will grieve you.

Then I walked on until I reached the house of my friend the tailor, whom I found anxiously waiting for me — he was, as the saying goes, on coals of fire on my account. And when he saw me he said, "All night long my heart has been heavy, fearing for you from wild beasts or some other mischance. Now praise be to Allah for your safety."

I thanked him for his kind concern and, going off to my corner, sat pondering and brooding on what had happened to me, and blamed and scolded myself for my meddling folly and my perversity in kicking the alcove.

I was calling myself to account when my friend the tailor came to me and said, "Young man, there is an old man in the shop, a Persian, who is looking for you. He has your hatchet and your sandals, which he had taken to the woodcutters, saying: I was going out at the hour when the muezzin began the call to dawn prayer, when I came across these things and do not know whose they are; so direct me to their owner. The woodcutters recognised your hatchet and directed him to you. He is sitting in my shop, so go out to him and thank him and take your axe and your sandals."

When I heard this I turned yellow with fear and felt stunned as though by a blow; and before I could recover myself, the floor of my private room split apart, and up out of it rose the Persian — who was the ifrit.

He had tortured the lady with terrible tortures, and even so she would confess nothing to him; so he had taken the hatchet and the sandals and said to her, "As surely as I am Jirjis of the seed of Iblis, I will bring you back the owner of these!" Then he had gone to the woodcutters with the pretence I have described and, being directed to me, and having waited a while in the shop until the fact was confirmed, he now suddenly snatched me up as a hawk snatches a mouse, and flew high into the air; and then came down and plunged with me under the earth — I in a dead faint all the while — and at last set me down in the underground palace where I had spent that blissful night.

And there I saw the lady stripped to the skin, her limbs bound to four stakes, and blood welling from her sides. At the sight my eyes ran over with tears; but the ifrit covered her body and said, "You wanton — is this man not your lover?"

She looked at me and answered, "I do not know him, and I have never seen him before this hour."

"What!" said the ifrit. "All this torture and still no confession?"

And she said, "I have never seen this man in all my born days, and it is not lawful in Allah's sight to tell lies about him."

"If you do not know him," said the ifrit, "then take this sword and strike off his head."

She took the sword in her hand and came right up to me; and I signalled to her with my eyebrows, my tears running down my cheeks all the while. She understood me and answered, also by signs, "How could you bring all this evil down on me?" And I answered the same way, "This is the moment for mercy and forgiveness."

And the mute tongue of my situation spoke aloud, saying:

	My eyes were interpreters for my tongue when it was tied
	and told out clearly the love I would gladly have hidden.
	When last we met and tears came down in torrents,
	my glances gave evidence for a tongue struck dumb.
	She signed with a glance of the eye while her lips were silent;
	I signed with my fingers and she knew what was meant.
	Our eyebrows did all the work between the two of us —
	and we being speechless, Love spoke loud and plain.

Then, my mistress, the lady threw the sword away and said, "How am I to strike the neck of a man I do not know, and who has done me no harm? Such a deed would not be lawful by my law." And she held her hand.

Said the ifrit, "It is hard for you to kill your lover; and because he has lain with you, you endure these torments and obstinately refuse to confess. After this it is clear enough to me that only like loves and pities like."

Then he turned to me and asked, "Man — perhaps you do not know this woman either?"

To which I answered, "And who might she be? I certainly never saw her until this instant."

"Then take the sword," said he, "and strike off her head, and I will believe you do not know her, and I will leave you free to go and will not deal harshly with you."

"That I will do," I replied. And taking the sword I went forward briskly and raised my hand to strike.

But she signalled to me with her eyebrows, "Have I failed you in any part of love? And is this how you pay me back?"

I understood what her looks meant, and answered her with a glance, "I will sacrifice my soul for you." And the tongue of the situation wrote these lines in our hearts:

	How many a lover speaks with his eyebrows
	to the woman he loves, as his passion pleads:
	with flashing eyes he breathes his passion into her
	and she sees perfectly well what his pleading needs.
	How sweet is the look when each one gazes at the other,
	and with what swiftness and what certainty it travels:
	and this one writes out all his passion with his eyebrows,
	and that one reads all his passion with her eyes.

Then my eyes filled with tears and overflowed, and I threw the sword out of my hand and said, "Mighty ifrit and hero — if a woman, lacking wits and lacking faith, thinks it unlawful to strike off my head, how can it be lawful for me, a man, to strike the neck of a woman I have never seen in my whole life? I cannot do such a wrong, though you make me drink the cup of death and destruction."

Then said the ifrit, "The two of you are showing me how well you understand one another. But I will let you see how such doings end."

He took the sword and struck off the lady's hands first, with four strokes, and then her feet; while I stood looking on and made certain of my own death, and she said goodbye to me with her dying eyes.

So the ifrit shouted at her, "You play the whore and make a cuckold of me with your eyes!" — and struck her so that her head went flying.

Then he turned to me and said, "Mortal, we have it in our law that when a wife commits adultery it is lawful for us to kill her. As for this girl, I snatched her away on her wedding night when she was twelve years old, and she knew nobody but me. I used to come to her once every ten days and lie with her the night, in the shape of a man, a Persian; and when I was well satisfied that she had cuckolded me, I killed her.

"But as for you, I am not well satisfied that you have wronged me in her. All the same I must not let you go unharmed; so ask a favour of me and I will grant it."

Then I rejoiced, my lady, beyond all rejoicing, and said, "What favour shall I ask of you?"

He replied, "Ask me this: what shape I am to bewitch you into. Will you be a dog, or an ass, or an ape?"

I answered — and indeed I had been hoping some mercy might be shown me — "By Allah, spare me, so that Allah may spare you for sparing a Muslim, and a man who never wronged you." And I humbled myself before him with the utmost humility, and stood there in his presence saying, "I am sorely oppressed by circumstance."

He replied, "Do not talk me a long talk. It is in my power to kill you; but instead I am giving you your choice."

Said I, "Ifrit, it would become you to pardon me, exactly as the Envied man pardoned the Envier."

"And how was that?" said he.

And I began to tell him

The Tale of the Envier and the Envied

They tell, ifrit, that in a certain city there were two men who lived in houses next door to one another, sharing a party wall; and one of them envied the other and looked on him with an evil eye, and did everything he could to injure him. And although he was jealous of his neighbour all the time, his malice grew on him at last until he could hardly eat or enjoy the sweetness of sleep.

But the Envied man did nothing except prosper; and the harder the other tried to injure him, the more he got and gained and throve.

At last the malice of his neighbour, and the man's constant efforts to do him harm, came to his notice. So he said, "By Allah, God's earth is wide enough for the people in it." And leaving the neighbourhood, he went to another city, where he bought himself a piece of land with a dried-up draw-well on it, old and in ruins. There he built himself a place of prayer, and furnishing it with a few necessaries, took up his home in it and gave himself over to praying and worshipping Allah Almighty. And holy beggars and mendicants flocked to him from every quarter, and his fame went abroad through the city and the country round it.

Presently the news of what good fortune had come to him, and how the notables of the city had become his disciples, reached his envious neighbour. So he travelled to the place and presented himself at the holy man's hermitage, and was met by the Envied man with welcome and greeting and every honour.

Then the Envier said, "I have a word to say to you; that is why I have come here, and I want to give you a piece of good news. So come with me to your cell."

At which the Envied man got up and took the Envier by the hand, and they went into the innermost part of the hermitage. But the Envier said, "Tell your beggars to go back to their cells, for I will not tell you what I have to say except in private, where nobody can hear us."

So the Envied man said to his beggars, "Go back to your own cells." And when they had all done as he told them, he set off with his visitor and walked a little way, until the two of them reached the ruinous old well.

And as they stood on the brink of it, the Envier gave the Envied man a push that tumbled him headlong into it, with nobody to see it; and then he came out and went his way, thinking he had killed him.

Now this well happened to be haunted by the jinn, who, seeing what had happened, held him up and lowered him little by little until he reached the bottom, and then seated him on a large stone.

Then one of them asked the others, "Do you know who this man is?"

And they answered, "No."

"This man," the speaker went on, "is the one called the Envied, who ran from the Envier and came to live in our city, and founded this holy house here; and he has edified us with his prayers and his readings from the Koran. But the Envier set out and travelled until he found him again, and cunningly contrived to trick him and throw him into the well we are in now.

"But the fame of this good man has this very night reached the Sultan of our city, who means to visit him tomorrow on account of his daughter."

"What is wrong with his daughter?" asked one.

And another answered, "She is possessed by a spirit; for Maymun, son of Damdam, is madly in love with her. But if this pious man knew the remedy, curing her would be as easy as anything."

At which one of them asked, "And what is the medicine?"

And he replied, "The black tomcat that is with him in the oratory has, on the end of his tail, a white spot the size of a dirham. Let him pluck seven white hairs out of that spot, and then fumigate her with them, and the marid will flee out of her and not come back; and she will be in her right mind for the rest of her life."

All this took place, ifrit, within earshot of the Envied man, who listened eagerly.

When dawn broke and the morning rose in its brightness and shone, the beggars went to look for their master, and found him climbing up the wall of the well — which made him greater still in their eyes. Then, knowing that nothing but the black tomcat could supply him with the remedy he needed, he plucked the seven tail hairs from the white spot and laid them by him.

And hardly had the sun risen before the Sultan came into the hermitage with the great lords of his court, telling the rest of his retinue to wait outside. The Envied man gave him a hearty welcome, and seating him at his side, asked him, "Shall I tell you why you have come?"

The King answered, "Yes."

He went on, "You have come on the pretext of paying a visit; but what is in your heart is to ask me about your daughter."

"That is exactly so, holy man," replied the King.

And the Envied man went on, "Send and fetch her, and I trust to heal her at once — if such is the will of Allah."

The King, overjoyed, sent for his daughter, and they brought her in with her arms pinioned and her feet fettered. The Envied man made her sit down behind a curtain, and taking out the hairs, fumigated her with them — at which the thing that was in her head cried out and left her.

The girl was restored to her right mind that instant, and veiling her face, said, "What has happened? Who brought me here?"

The Sultan rejoiced with a joy nothing could exceed, and kissed his daughter's eyes and the holy man's hand; then, turning to his great lords, he asked, "What do you say? What fee does the man deserve who has made my daughter whole?"

And they all answered, "He deserves to have her as his wife."

And the King said, "You speak truly."

So he married him to her, and the Envied man became the King's son-in-law.

And after a little the vizier died, and the King said, "Whom can I make minister in his place?"

"Your son-in-law," replied the courtiers. So the Envied man became a vizier.

And after a while the Sultan died too, and the people said, "Whom shall we make king?" And they all cried, "The vizier." So the vizier was made Sultan straight away, and he became a reigning king, and a true ruler of men.

One day, when he had mounted his horse and was riding in all the eminence of his kingship among his emirs and viziers and the great men of his realm, his eye fell on his old neighbour, the Envier, standing on foot in his path. So he turned to one of his ministers and said, "Bring that man here, and do not frighten him."

The vizier brought him, and the King said, "Give him a thousand gold miskals out of the treasury, and load him ten camels with goods to trade with, and send him back to his own town under escort."

Then he said goodbye to his enemy and sent him away, and held back from punishing him for all the many and great evils he had done him.

See, ifrit, the mercy of the Envied man to the Envier, who had hated him from the beginning, and had borne him such bitter malice, and had never met him without causing him trouble; who had driven him out of house and home, and had then made a journey for the sole purpose of taking his life by throwing him into the well. And yet he did not pay back his injurious dealing, but forgave him, and was generous to him.

Then I wept in front of him, my lady, and wept bitterly — never was there bitterer weeping — and I recited:

	"Pardon my fault, for it is the wise man's custom
	to pardon every fault and let revenge go.
	Truly I contain in myself every kind of fault —
	so be pleased of your goodness to show mercy and grace.
	Whoever begs pardon from on High
	should hold his own hand back from the sinners down here."

Said the ifrit, "Do not lengthen your words. As for my killing you, do not fear it; and as for my pardoning you, do not hope for it. But from my bewitching you there is no escape."

Then he tore me from the ground, which closed under my feet, and flew up with me into the sky until I saw the earth like a great white cloud, or a saucer in the middle of the waters. Presently he set me down on a mountain, and taking a little dust and muttering some magic words over it, sprinkled me with it, saying, "Leave that shape and take the shape of an ape!"

And in that instant I became an ape — a tailless baboon, a hundred years old.

Now when he had left me, and I saw myself in this ugly and hateful shape, I wept for myself; but I resigned my soul to the tyranny of Time and Circumstance, knowing well that Fortune is fair and constant to nobody.

I came down the mountain and found a desert plain at the foot of it, long and broad, over which I travelled for a month, until my course brought me to the edge of the salt sea. After standing there a while, I noticed a ship out in the offing, running before a fair wind and making for the shore. I hid myself behind a rock on the beach and waited until the ship came near, and then I leaped aboard.

I found her full of merchants and passengers, and one of them cried, "Captain, this ill-omened brute will bring us bad luck!" And another said, "Turn this ill-omened beast out from among us." The captain said, "Let us kill it." Another said, "Kill it with a sword"; a third, "Drown it"; and a fourth, "Shoot it with an arrow."

But I sprang up and took hold of the captain's skirt, and shed tears that poured down my chops. The captain took pity on me and said, "Merchants! this ape has appealed to me for protection and I will protect him. From now on he is in my charge; so let nobody do him any hurt or harm, or there will be bad blood between us."

Then he treated me kindly; and whatever he said I understood, and I saw to his every want and served him like a servant, although my tongue would not obey my wishes — so that he came to love me.

The ship sailed on with a fair wind for fifty days, at the end of which we anchored under the walls of a great city, in which there was a world of people, and learned men above all, whose number nobody could tell but Allah.

No sooner had we arrived than we were visited by certain Mamluk officials from the King of that city, who came aboard and greeted the merchants and wished them joy of their safe arrival, and said, "Our King welcomes you, and sends you this roll of paper, on which each and every one of you must write a line. For you should know that the King's minister, a calligrapher of great renown, is dead, and the King has sworn a solemn oath that he will make nobody vizier in his place who cannot write as well as he could."

Then he gave us the scroll, which measured ten cubits long by one wide; and each of the merchants who knew how to write wrote a line on it, down to the last of them. After which I stood up — still in the shape of an ape — and snatched the roll out of their hands.

They were afraid I would tear it or throw it overboard, so they tried to stop me and scare me off; but I signed to them that I could write, at which they all marvelled, saying, "We have never yet seen an ape write."

And the captain cried, "Let him write; and if he scribbles and scrawls we will kick him out and kill him; but if he writes a fair and scholarly hand, I will adopt him as my son. For I certainly never yet saw a more intelligent and better-mannered monkey than this one. Would to Heaven my own son were his match in morals and manners."

I took the reed pen, and stretching out my paw, dipped it in ink and wrote, in the hand used for letters, these two couplets:

	Time has recorded the gifts she gave to the great,
	but she never recorded yours, which are far higher.
	May Allah never orphan men by the loss of you,
	who are the mother of Goodness and the father of Bounty.

And I wrote in Rayhani, the larger and elegantly curving letters:

	You hold a reed of good counsel for every land,
	whose driving makes the whole world thrive.
	The Nile of Egypt is nothing beside your gifts,
	you who make misery smile with five fingers.

Then I wrote in the Thuluth character:

	There is no writer who shall escape from Death,
	but what his hand has written men will repeat.
	Write nothing, therefore, but what will serve you when
	you see it on Judgement Day — if see it you do.

Then I wrote in the Naskh character:

	When Fate dooms our love to a bitter parting
	and Destiny decrees a life far off,
	we make the lips of the inkhorn complain of our pains
	and give our speech a tongue with the talking reed.

And I wrote in the Tumar character:

	Kingdom lasts with nobody; and if you deny
	this truth, then where are the kings of the earlier earth?
	Plant trees of goodness while your rule lasts,
	and when you have fallen they will speak your worth.

And I wrote in the Muhakkak character:

	When the inkhorn of your wealth and fame is opened,
	take ink from a generous heart and a gracious hand;
	write brave and noble deeds while you still can write,
	and win yourself praise from the point of the pen and of the sword.

Then I gave the scroll to the officials; and after we had all written our lines, they carried it before the King.

When he saw the paper, no writing pleased him except mine; and he said to the assembled courtiers, "Go and find the writer of these lines, and dress him in a splendid robe of honour; then mount him on a she-mule, and let a band of music go in front of him, and bring him into my presence."

At these words they smiled, and the King was angry with them and cried, "You accursed people! I give you an order and you laugh at me?"

"O King," they replied, "if we laugh it is not at you, and not without a reason."

"And what is it?" he asked.

And they answered, "O King, you order us to bring into your presence the man who wrote these lines. Now the truth is that the one who wrote them is not one of the sons of Adam, but an ape, a tailless baboon belonging to the ship's captain."

"Is this true, what you say?" said he.

"It is — by the rights of your own munificence!" said they.

The King marvelled at their words and shook with laughter, and said, "I have a mind to buy this ape from the captain."

Then he sent messengers to the ship with the mule, the robe, the guard and the state drums, saying, "All the same, you are to dress him in the robe of honour and mount him on the mule and let him be surrounded by the guards and preceded by the band."

They came to the ship and took me from the captain and robed me in the robe of honour, and mounting me on the she-mule, carried me in a state procession through the streets, while the people were amazed and amused. And people said to one another, "Hello! is our Sultan about to make an ape his minister?" And they all came crowding agog to stare at me, and the town was astir and turned upside down on my account.

When they brought me up to the King and set me in his presence, I kissed the ground before him three times, and once before the High Chamberlain and the great officers; and he told me to be seated, and I sat respectfully back on my shins and knees, and everybody there marvelled at my fine manners, and the King most of all.

At that he ordered the rest to withdraw; and when nobody was left except His Majesty, the eunuch on duty and a little white slave, he had the table of food set before me, with every kind of bird on it — everything that hops and flies and treads in a nest, such as quail and sand grouse.

Then he signed to me to eat with him; so I got up and kissed the ground before him, and then sat down and ate with him. And when the table had been taken away I washed my hands in seven waters, and took the pen case and the reed, and wrote these lines instead of speaking:

	Wail for the little partridges on porringer and plate;
	cry for the ruin of the fries and the well-marinated stews.
	Keen as I keen for the loved and lost daughters of the sand grouse,
	and for omelette heaped round fine browned fowls.
	O the fire in my heart for fish — those two fine fish I saw
	bedded on new-made scones and cakes piled up to be torn apart.
	For you, O vermicelli, my very stomach aches! I hold
	that without you every taste and joy is clean annihilated.
	Those eggs rolled their yellow eyes in the torturing pains of the fire
	before they came served with hash and hot fritters, that daintiest dish.
	Praise be to Allah for His baked meats and His roast — and ah! how good
	are these pulses, these pot-herbs steeped in oil and mixed with vinegar.
	When my hunger was satisfied I propped myself on an elbow and fell back
	on the meat pudding, in which gleamed the bangles that confound my wits.
	Then I woke my sleeping appetite to eat as though in play
	sweets from brocaded trays, and the most elaborate of trifles.
	Be patient, soul of mine! Time is a haughty, jealous creature;
	today he looks dark and lowering, and tomorrow fair to see.

Then I got up and seated myself at a respectful distance while the King read what I had written; and he marvelled and exclaimed, "The miracle of it — that an ape should be gifted with this graceful style and this power of penmanship! By Allah, it is a wonder of wonders."

Presently they set choice wines before the King in glass flagons, and he drank; and then he passed the cup on to me, and I kissed the ground and drank and wrote on it:

	With fire they boiled me to loosen my tongue,
	and gave me pain and patience for company.
	And so it comes about that the hands of men hold me up high
	and I sip honey-dew from the lips of a girl.

And these lines as well:

	Morning says to Night, "Withdraw, and let me shine";
	so let us drain draughts that dull all pain and pining.
	The glass is so fine and the wine so clear, I am in doubt
	whether it is the wine in the glass or the glass in the wine.

The King read my verse and said with a sigh, "If these gifts were in a man, he would surpass everybody of his time and his age."

Then he called for the chessboard and said, "Tell me — will you play with me?" And I signed with my head, "Yes."

Then I came forward and set out the pieces and played two games with him, and won them both. He was speechless with surprise; so I took the pen case and, drawing out a reed, wrote these two couplets on the board:

	Two armies go fighting the whole day long
	and their battling is never finished,
	until, when the dark closes round about them,
	the two of them go and sleep in a single bed.

The King read these lines with wonder and delight and said to his eunuch, "Mukbil, go to your mistress, Sitt al-Husn, and say to her: come, the King calls you here to amuse yourself with the sight of this truly wonderful ape."

So the eunuch went out and came back presently with the lady; and when she saw me she veiled her face and said, "Father! have you lost all sense of honour? How is it you are pleased to send for me and show me to strange men?"

"Sitt al-Husn," said he, "there is no man here except this little foot page, and the eunuch who brought you up, and I, your father. So who are you veiling your face from?"

She answered, "The one you take for an ape is a young man — clever and polite, wise and learned, and the son of a king. But he is under a spell; the ifrit Jirjis, who is of the seed of Iblis, laid it on him, after putting his own wife to death — the daughter of King Ifitamus, lord of the Ebony Islands."

The King marvelled at his daughter's words, and turning to me, said, "Is this true, what she says about you?"

And I signed with a nod of my head, "Yes, truly," and wept bitterly.

Then he asked his daughter, "How did you know he was under a spell?"

And she answered, "Dear father, when I was a child there was an old woman with me, a cunning and a wise one and a witch besides, and she taught me the theory of magic and its practice; and I took notes in writing and grew perfect in it, and I have committed to memory a hundred and seventy chapters of magical formulas, by the least of which I could carry the stones of your city away behind Mount Kaf and the encircling ocean, or turn the site of it into a pit of sea and its people into fish swimming about in the middle of it."

"My daughter," said her father, "I beg you, by my life — disenchant this young man, so that I may make him my vizier and marry you to him; for he is an ingenious young man and a deeply learned one."

"With joy and goodwill," she replied. And taking in her hand an iron knife with the name of Allah inscribed on it in Hebrew characters, she drew a wide circle:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Fourteenth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the kalandar went on with his tale like this:

My lady, the King's daughter took in her hand a knife with Hebrew characters inscribed on it and drew a wide circle in the middle of the palace hall, and inside it wrote mysterious names and talismans in Kufic letters; and she spoke words and muttered charms, some of which we understood and some of which we did not.

Presently the world went dark in front of our eyes, until we thought the sky was falling on our heads — and the ifrit presented himself in his own shape and appearance. His hands were like many-pronged pitchforks, his legs like the masts of great ships, and his eyes like torches of gleaming fire.

We were in terrible fear of him; but the King's daughter shouted at him, "No welcome to you and no greeting, dog!"

At which he changed into the shape of a lion and said, "Traitress, how is it you have broken the oath we swore, that neither of us would cross the other?"

"Accursed thing," she answered, "how could there be any agreement between me and the like of you?"

Then he said, "Take what you have brought on yourself." And the lion opened his jaws and rushed at her. But she was too quick for him; and plucking a hair from her head, she waved it in the air, muttering over it as she did — and the hair became instantly a keen sword blade, with which she struck the lion and cut him in two.

Then the two halves flew away into the air, and the head changed into a scorpion; and the princess became a huge serpent and set on the accursed scorpion, and the two of them fought, coiling and uncoiling, a stiff fight for a good hour.

Then the scorpion changed into a vulture, and the serpent became an eagle which set on the vulture and hunted him for an hour, until he became a black tomcat, which yowled and grinned and spat.

At that the eagle changed into a piebald wolf, and these two battled about the palace for a long time, until the cat, seeing himself beaten, changed into a worm and crept into a huge red pomegranate lying beside the jetting fountain in the middle of the palace hall.

At which the pomegranate swelled up in the air to the size of a watermelon; and falling on the marble pavement of the palace, it broke to pieces, and all the seeds fell out and were scattered about until they covered the whole floor.

Then the wolf shook himself and became a snow-white cock, which fell to picking up the seeds, meaning not to leave a single one. But by the doom of destiny one seed rolled to the edge of the fountain and lay there hidden.

The cock fell to crowing and clapping his wings and signing to us with his beak, as if to ask, "Are there any seeds left?" But we did not understand what he meant; and he called out to us with so loud a cry that we thought the palace would fall on us.

Then he ran all over the floor until he saw the seed that had rolled to the fountain's edge, and rushed eagerly to pick it up — and it sprang into the middle of the water and became a fish and dived to the bottom of the basin.

At which the cock changed into a big fish and plunged in after the other, and the two of them disappeared for a while; and then we heard loud shrieks and cries of pain that made us tremble.

After this the ifrit rose up out of the water, and he was like a burning flame, throwing fire and smoke out of his mouth and his eyes and his nostrils. And immediately the princess came out of the basin too, and she was one live coal of flame; and these two, she and he, battled for the space of an hour, until their fires completely surrounded them and their thick smoke filled the palace.

As for us, we panted for breath, being very nearly suffocated, and we longed to plunge into the water for fear of being burnt up and utterly destroyed.

And the King said, "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah the Glorious, the Great! Truly we are Allah's and to Him we are returning. Would to Heaven I had never urged my daughter to try to disenchant this ape fellow, by which I have laid on her the terrible task of fighting that accursed ifrit, against whom all the ifrits in the world could not prevail. And would to Heaven we had never seen this ape — may Allah never bless the day he came! We thought to do a good deed by him in the sight of Allah, and to release him from enchantment, and now we have brought this trouble and travail down on our own hearts."

But I, my lady, was tongue-tied and powerless to say a word to him.

Suddenly, before we knew anything about it, the ifrit yelled out from under the flames and, coming up to us as we stood on the dais, blew fire in our faces. The girl overtook him and breathed blasts of fire at his face, and the sparks from her and from him rained down on us. Her sparks did us no harm; but one of his sparks landed on my eye and destroyed it, making me a one-eyed ape; and another fell on the King's face, scorching the lower half of it, burning off his beard and his moustaches and making his lower teeth fall out; while a third landed on the eunuch's chest and killed him on the spot.

So we despaired of life and made certain of death — when a voice repeated the saying, "Allah is Most High! Allah is Most High! Help and victory to all who believe the Truth; and disappointment and disgrace to all who do not believe the religion of Mohammed, the Moon of Faith."

The speaker was the princess, who had burnt the ifrit up; and he had become a heap of ashes.

Then she came up to us and said, "Bring me a cup of water." They brought it to her, and she spoke words over it that we did not understand, and sprinkling me with it, cried, "By virtue of the Truth, and by the Most Great Name of Allah, I charge you to return to your former shape."

And I shook, and became a man as before — except that I had entirely lost one eye.

Then she cried out, "The fire! The fire! Dear father, an arrow from the accursed one has wounded me to death, for I am not used to fighting the jinn. If he had been a man I would have killed him at the beginning. I had no trouble at all until the moment the pomegranate burst and the seeds scattered; but I overlooked the seed that had the jinni's very life in it. If I had picked it up he would have died on the spot; but as Fate and Fortune decreed, I did not see it. So he came on me completely unawares, and there was a hard struggle between him and me under the earth and high in the air and in the water; and every time I opened one gate on him he opened another and a stronger one on me, until at last he opened on me the gate of fire — and few are saved on whom the door of fire opens.

"But Destiny willed that my cunning should beat his cunning; and I burned him to death, after urging him in vain to embrace the religion of Islam. As for me, I am a dead woman. May Allah supply my place to you."

Then she called on Heaven for help and did not stop begging for relief from the fire — when a black spark shot up from her robed feet to her thighs; and then it flew to her breast and from there to her face.

When it reached her face she wept and said, "I testify that there is no god but God, and that Mohammed is the Apostle of God."

And we looked at her and saw nothing but a heap of ashes, beside the heap that had been the ifrit.

We mourned for her, and I wished I had been in her place, so that I might not have seen that lovely face, which had done me so much good, turned into ashes. But there is no gainsaying the will of Allah.

When the King saw his daughter's terrible death he plucked out what was left of his beard and beat his face and tore his clothes; and I did as he did, and we both wept over her.

Then the chamberlains and the great men came in and were amazed to find two heaps of ashes and the Sultan in a dead faint; so they stood round him until he revived and told them what had happened to his daughter through the ifrit. At which their grief was very grievous, and the women and the slave girls shrieked and keened; and they kept up their lamentations for seven days.

What is more, the King ordered a great vaulted tomb built over his daughter's ashes, and wax tapers and funeral lamps to be burnt in it. But as for the ifrit's ashes, they scattered them on the winds and sent them off to the curse of Allah.

Then the Sultan fell into a sickness that very nearly brought him to his death, and it lasted a month. And when his health came back to him, and his beard grew again, and he had been converted by the mercy of Allah to Islam, he sent for me and said:

"Young man, Fate had decreed for us the happiest of lives, safe from all the chances and changes of Time — until you came to us, when troubles fell on us. Would to Heaven we had never seen you, or that foul face of yours! For we took pity on you, and by doing it we have lost everything we had.

"On your account I have lost, first, my daughter, who was worth a hundred men to me; secondly I have suffered what happened to me by the fire and the loss of my teeth; and my eunuch was killed as well.

"I do not blame you, for it was out of your power to prevent it: the doom of Allah was on you as it was on us, and thanks be to the Almighty that my daughter delivered you, even though she lost her own life doing it.

"Go out now, my son, from this city of mine; and let what has happened to us through you be enough, even though it was decreed for us. Go in peace — and if I ever see you again, I shall certainly kill you." And he shouted at me.

So I went out of his presence, my lady, weeping bitterly and hardly able to believe in my escape, and not knowing which way to go. And I recalled everything that had happened to me — my meeting with the tailor, my love for the girl in the palace under the earth, and my narrow escape from the ifrit even after he had determined to put me to death; and how I had entered the city as an ape and was now leaving it a man again.

Then I gave thanks to Allah and said, "My eye and not my life!" And before leaving the place I went into the baths and shaved my head and my beard and my moustaches and my eyebrows; and I threw ashes on my head and put on the coarse black woollen robe of a kalandar.

Then I set out, my lady; and every day I turned over all the disasters that had come on me, and I wept and repeated these lines:

	"I am distraught, and yet truly His mercy stays with me,
	though whole armies of troubles gather round me from I cannot see where.
	Patient I will be, until Patience herself grows impatient with me;
	patient for ever, until the Lord fulfils my destiny.
	Patient I will stay without complaining, a wronged and beaten man;
	patient as a sun-parched creature crossing the desert's sea of sand.
	Patient I will be until the aloe itself admits, without knowing it,
	that I am patient under bitterer things than the bitterest aloes.
	There is nothing bitterer for mankind than aloes or than patience —
	and yet bitterer to me than either was the treachery of Patience.
	My dry and seamed and scorched forehead would interpret my pain
	if a soul could search my spirit and unlock the secret there.
	If the hills had to carry the load I carry they would crumble under it;
	it would still the roaring wind, it would quench the flame's hot tongue.
	And whoever says the world is sweet will certainly see a day
	with more than the bitterness of aloes and more than their pungency."

Then I journeyed through many regions and saw many a city, making for Baghdad, so that I might get an audience in the House of Peace with the Commander of the Faithful and tell him everything that had happened to me.

I arrived here this very night and found my brother in Allah, this first kalandar, standing about like a man at a loss; so I greeted him with "Peace be upon you," and we fell into conversation. Presently up came our brother, this third kalandar, and said to us, "Peace be with you! I am a stranger"; to which we replied, "And we are strangers too, who have come here this blessed night."

So all three of us walked on together, none of us knowing the others' history, until Destiny drove us to this door and we came in to you.

So that is my story, and that is the reason for my shaving my beard and my moustaches, and that is what caused the loss of my eye.

Said the mistress of the house, "Your tale is a rare one indeed. So rub your head and be on your way."

But he replied, "I will not budge until I have heard my companions' stories."

Then the third kalandar came forward and said, "Illustrious lady, my history is not like these comrades' of mine, but stranger and far more marvellous. In their case Fate and Fortune came down on them without warning; but I drew destiny down on my own head and brought sorrow on my own soul, and shaved my own beard and lost my own eye. Hear then

The Third Kalandar's Tale

Know, my lady, that I too am a king and the son of a king, and my name is Ajib son of Khazib.

When my father died I succeeded him; and I ruled and did justice and dealt fairly with all my subjects. I took great delight in sea trips, for my capital stood on the shore with the ocean stretching far and wide in front of it; and close at hand were many great islands with forts and garrisons on them out in the middle of the water. My fleet numbered fifty merchantmen, and as many yachts for pleasure, and a hundred and fifty sail fitted out and ready for holy war against the unbelievers.

It happened that I had a mind to enjoy myself among those islands, so I took ship with my people in ten vessels; and carrying a month's provisions with me, I set out on a twenty-day voyage.

But one night a head wind struck us, and the sea rose against us in huge waves; the billows buffeted us badly and a thick darkness settled round us. We gave ourselves up for lost, and I said, "Whoever puts his days in danger deserves no praise, even if he escapes."

Then we prayed to Allah and begged Him; but the gale did not stop blowing against us, nor the surges striking us, until morning broke, when the wind fell and the seas sank to a mirror stillness and the sun shone kindly and clear on us.

Presently we made an island, where we landed and cooked some food and ate heartily and rested for a couple of days. Then we set out again and sailed another twenty days, the seas broadening and the land shrinking.

Presently the current ran against us, and we found ourselves in strange waters, where the captain had lost his reckoning and was completely bewildered in that sea. So we said to the lookout man, "Get to the masthead and keep your eyes open."

He swarmed up the mast and looked out, and cried aloud, "Captain, I see something dark to starboard, very like a fish floating on the surface of the sea; and to larboard there is a looming shape out in the middle of the water, now black and now bright."

When the captain heard the lookout's words he dashed his turban down on the deck and plucked out his beard and beat his face, saying, "Good news indeed! We are all dead men; not one of us can be saved."

And he began to weep, and all of us wept at his weeping, and for our own lives besides. And I said, "Captain, tell us what it is the lookout saw."

"My prince," he answered, "you must know that we lost our course on the night of the storm, which was followed next day by a two-day calm during which we made no way; and we have been going astray for eleven days from that night, with never a wind to bring us back onto our proper course.

"Tomorrow, by the end of the day, we shall come to a mountain of black stone called the Magnet Mountain; for the currents are carrying us there whether we like it or not. As soon as we are under its lee, the ship's sides will open, and every nail in every plank will fly out and stick fast to the mountain; for Almighty Allah has given the loadstone a mysterious power and a love for iron, and because of it everything made of iron travels towards it. And on this mountain there is a great deal of iron — how much nobody knows but the Most High — from all the vessels that have been lost there since the old days.

"The bright spot on the summit is a dome of yellow brass from Andalusia, vaulted on ten columns; and on the crown of it is a horseman riding a horse of brass and holding a brass lance in his hand; and there hangs on his breast a tablet of lead engraved with names and talismans."

And presently he added, "And, O King, nobody destroys people except that rider on his horse; and the enchantment will not be broken until he falls from his mount."

Then, my lady, the captain wept beyond all weeping, and every one of us made certain of our doom, and each said goodbye to his friend and charged him with his last will and testament, in case he should be the one saved.

We did not sleep that night; and in the morning we found ourselves much closer to the Magnet Mountain, where the waters were driving us with a violent set. When the ships were close under its lee they opened, and the nails flew out, and all the iron in them made for the Magnet Mountain and clung to it like a net; so that by the end of the day we were all struggling in the waves round about the mountain.

Some of us were saved, but more were drowned; and even the ones who escaped did not know one another, they were so stupefied by the beating of the billows and the raving of the winds.

As for me, my lady, Allah — exalted be His name — preserved my life so that I might suffer whatever He willed for me of hardship and misfortune and calamity; for I scrambled onto a plank from one of the ships, and the wind and the water threw it up at the foot of the mountain.

There I found a practicable path, leading up by steps carved out of the rock to the summit; and I called on the name of Allah Almighty:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Fifteenth Night,

she went on: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the third kalandar said to the lady — the rest of the party sitting there tied up, and the slaves standing over them with drawn swords:

And after calling on the name of Almighty Allah and passionately begging Him for help, I breasted the climb, clinging to the steps and notches cut in the stone, and mounted little by little. And the Lord stilled the wind and helped me in the climb, so that I managed to reach the summit.

There I found nowhere to rest but the dome, which I went into, overjoyed at my escape; and I made the ritual washing and prayed a prayer of two prostrations, in thanks to God for preserving me. Then I fell asleep under the dome, and in my dream I heard a mysterious voice saying:

"Son of Khazib! When you wake from your sleep, dig under your feet and you will find a bow of brass and three leaden arrows, inscribed with talismans and magical characters. Take the bow and shoot the arrows at the horseman on the top of the dome, and free mankind from this terrible calamity.

"When you have shot him he will fall into the sea, and the horse will drop at your feet: then bury it in the place where the bow was. That done, the sea will swell and rise until it is level with the mountain top, and there will appear on it a skiff carrying a man of brass — not the one you shot — holding a pair of oars in his hands. He will come to you, and you are to go aboard with him; but beware of saying In Allah's name, or of naming Allah Almighty in any other way.

"He will row you for ten days, until he brings you to certain islands called the Islands of Safety, and from there you will easily reach a port and find people to carry you to your own country. And all this will be fulfilled for you provided you do not call on the name of Allah."

Then I started up out of my sleep in joy and gladness; and hurrying to do what the mysterious voice had told me, I found the bow and the arrows and shot at the horseman and tumbled him into the sea, while the horse dropped at my feet; so I took it and buried it.

Presently the sea surged up and rose until it reached the top of the mountain; and I had not long to wait before I saw a skiff out in the offing coming towards me. I gave thanks to Allah; and when the skiff came up to me I saw in it a man of brass with a tablet of lead on his breast inscribed with talismans and magical characters; and I went aboard without saying a word.

The boatman rowed on with me through the first day and the second and the third, ten whole days in all, until I caught sight of the Islands of Safety — at which I was overjoyed, and in the stress of my gladness exclaimed, "Allah! Allah! In the name of Allah! There is no god but God, and Allah is Almighty."

At which the skiff instantly turned over and threw me into the sea; and then it righted itself and sank down into the depths.

Now I am a good swimmer, so I swam the whole day until nightfall, when my forearms and shoulders were numb with exhaustion and I felt as though I were dying; so I made my profession of faith, expecting nothing but death.

The sea was still surging under the violence of the winds; and presently there came a billow like a hill, and lifting me high in the air, threw me with a long cast onto dry land, so that His will might be fulfilled.

I crawled up the beach and took my clothes off and wrung them out to dry and spread them in the sun; then I lay down and slept the whole night.

As soon as it was day I put my clothes on and got up to see which way I should walk. Presently I came to a thicket of low trees; and making a circuit of it, I found that the place I was standing on was an islet, a mere holm, ringed on all sides by the ocean. At which I said to myself, "Whatever frees me from one great calamity throws me into a greater one."

But while I was pondering my situation and longing for death, I saw a ship in the distance making for the island; so I climbed a tree and hid myself among the branches.

Presently the ship anchored and put ten Black slaves ashore, carrying iron hoes and baskets, who walked on until they reached the middle of the island. There they dug deep into the ground until they uncovered a metal plate, which they lifted, opening a trapdoor.

After this they went back to the ship and brought from it bread and flour, honey and fruit, clarified butter, leather bottles of liquor and a great many household goods; and furniture too, and table service and mirrors, rugs and carpets — in fact everything needed to furnish a dwelling. And they kept going to and fro and down through the trapdoor until they had carried everything that was in the ship into the dwelling.

After this the slaves went aboard again and came back with the richest clothing you could imagine; and in the middle of them came an old, old man, of whom very little was left, for Time had dealt hard and harshly with him, and all that remained of him was a bone wrapped in a rag of blue cloth with the winds whistling through it, east and west. As the poet says of such a man:

	Time makes me tremble — ah, how sore the check —
	while Time in the pride of his strength goes stalking on.
	Time was when I walked and never once felt tired;
	now I am tired, though I never walk at all.

And the old man held by the hand a young man cast in beauty's own mould, all elegance and perfect grace, so fair that his good looks deserved to become proverbial; for he was like a green bough, or the young of the roe deer, ravishing every heart with his loveliness and subduing every soul with his coquetry and his charm. It was of him the poet spoke when he said:

	They brought Beauty along with him to make a comparison,
	but Beauty hung her head in shame and confusion.
	They said, "Beauty, have you ever seen his like?"
	And Beauty cried, "His like? Nowhere at all!"

They did not stop their coming and going, my lady, until all of them had gone down through the trapdoor; and they did not reappear for an hour or more, at the end of which the slaves and the old man came up without the young man. And replacing the iron plate and carefully closing the door slab as it had been before, they went back to the ship and made sail and were lost to my sight.

When they had turned away to go, I came down from the tree and, going to the place I had seen them fill in, scraped off and cleared away the earth; and I possessed my soul in patience until I had cleared the whole of it away.

Then the trapdoor appeared, which was made of wood and was the shape and size of a millstone; and when I lifted it, it disclosed a winding staircase of stone.

At this I marvelled; and going down the steps until I reached the last, I found a fine hall spread with all kinds of carpets and silks, in which a young man was sitting on a raised couch and leaning back on a round cushion, with a fan in his hand and nosegays and posies of sweet-scented herbs and flowers in front of him. But he was alone, without a soul near him in that great vault.

When he saw me he turned pale; but I greeted him courteously and said, "Set your mind at ease and calm your fears; no harm will come near you. I am a man like yourself, and the son of a king into the bargain, whom the decrees of Destiny have sent to keep you company and cheer you in your loneliness. But now tell me — what is your story, and what makes you live like this, alone under the ground?"

When he was satisfied that I was of his own kind and not a jinni, he was delighted and his good colour came back; and drawing me close to him he said:

"Brother, my story is a strange one, and it is this. My father is a merchant-jeweller with great wealth, who has white slaves and Black slaves travelling and trading on his account in ships and on camels, and dealing with the most distant cities; but he was not blessed with a child, not even one.

"Now on a certain night he dreamed a dream that he would be given a son who would be short-lived; and so the morning dawned on my father bringing him grief and weeping. On the following night my mother conceived, and my father noted down the date she became pregnant.

"When her time was up she bore me — at which my father rejoiced and gave banquets and called the neighbours together and fed the holy beggars and the poor, because he had been blessed with a child near the end of his days.

"Then he assembled the astrologers and the astronomers who knew the places of the planets, and the wizards and the wise men of the time, and the men learned in horoscopes and nativities; and they drew up the scheme of my birth and said to my father:

"'Your son will live to fifteen years, but in his fifteenth there is a sinister aspect; and if he gets safely past it he will reach a great age. And the thing that threatens him with death is this. In the Sea of Peril there stands a mountain called the Magnet Mountain, on the summit of which is a horseman of yellow brass seated on a horse of brass and carrying a tablet of lead on his breast. Fifty days after that rider falls from his horse, your son will die; and his killer will be the man who shoots the horseman down, a prince named Ajib son of King Khazib.'

"My father grieved beyond all grieving to hear this; but he brought me up in the tenderest way and educated me excellently well until my fifteenth year was reached.

"Ten days ago news came to him that the horseman had fallen into the sea, and that the man who shot him down was named Ajib son of King Khazib. At which my father wept bitterly at having to part with me, and became like a man possessed by a jinni. However, being in mortal fear for me, he built me this place under the earth; and stocking it with everything needed for the few days still to run, he brought me here in a ship and left me.

"Ten of them have gone by already; and when the forty have passed without harm coming to me, he will come and take me away — for he has done all this only out of fear of Prince Ajib. So that is my story, and that is the reason I am here alone."

When I heard his history I marvelled, and said to myself, "I am the very Prince Ajib who has done all this; but as Allah is with me, I certainly will not kill him."

So I said to him, "My lord, may this hurt and harm stay far from you; and then, please Allah, you shall suffer no care or worry or unease at all. For I will stay here with you and serve you as a servant, and then go on my way; and after keeping you company through the forty days, I will go with you to your home, where you shall give me an escort of some of your Mamluks to travel back with me to my own city. And the Almighty will repay you on my behalf."

He was glad to hear this; and I got up and lit a large wax candle and trimmed the lamps and the three lanterns, and set out food and drink and sweets. We ate and drank and sat talking about one thing and another until most of the night was gone; and then he lay down to rest, and I covered him up and went to sleep myself.

Next morning I got up and warmed a little water; then I lifted him gently so as to wake him, and brought him the warm water, and he washed his face and said to me, "Heaven repay you on my behalf with every blessing, young man! By Allah, if I get clear of this danger and am saved from the man whose name is Ajib son of Khazib, I will make my father reward you and send you home healthy and wealthy; and if I die, then my blessing be on you."

I answered, "May the day never dawn on which any evil comes to you; and may Allah make my last day come before your last day."

Then I set some food in front of him and we ate; and I got perfumes ready to fumigate the hall with, which pleased him. What is more I made him a mancala board; and we played and ate sweets and played again and enjoyed ourselves until nightfall, when I got up and lit the lamps and set something in front of him to eat, and sat telling him stories until the hours of darkness were far gone. Then he lay down to rest, and I covered him up and rested too.

And I went on doing this, my lady, for days and nights; and affection for him took root in my heart and my sorrow was eased, and I said to myself, "The astrologers lied when they predicted that he would be killed by Ajib son of Khazib. By Allah, I will not kill him."

I did not stop looking after him and talking with him and drinking with him and telling him all kinds of tales for thirty-nine days.

On the fortieth night the young man was overjoyed and said, "Brother — praise be to Allah, who has preserved me from death; and this is by your blessing and the blessing of your coming to me. And I pray God that He restores you to your own country. But now, brother, I should like you to warm me some water for a washing, and be kind enough to bathe me and change my clothes."

I replied, "With love and gladness"; and I heated plenty of water and carried it in to him and washed his whole body, the washing of health, with lupin meal, and rubbed him well and changed his clothes and spread him a high bed, on which he lay down to rest, being drowsy after the bath.

Then he said, "Brother, cut me up a watermelon and sweeten it with a little sugar candy."

So I went to the storeroom, and bringing out a fine watermelon I found there, set it on a platter and laid it before him and said, "My master, have you not a knife?"

"Here it is," he answered, "over my head, on the high shelf."

So I got up in a hurry and took the knife and drew it out of its sheath; but my foot slipped as I stepped down, and I fell heavily onto the young man with the knife in my hand — which hurried to fulfil what had been written on the Day the destinies of men were decided, and buried itself, as though it had been planted there, in the young man's heart.

He died that instant.

When I saw that he was killed, and knew that I had killed him in spite of myself, I cried out with a loud and bitter cry and beat my face and tore my clothes and said:

"Truly we are Allah's and to Him we are returning! Muslims! People who love Allah! There was only one day left of the forty dangerous days that the astrologers and the learned men had foretold for him — and the predestined death of this beautiful boy had to come at my hand. Would to Heaven I had never tried to cut that watermelon.

"What a dreadful misfortune this is that I must bear, whether I like it or not! What a disaster! What an affliction! O my Allah, I beg your pardon and declare to You that I am innocent of his death. But what God wills — let that come to pass":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Sixteenth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Ajib went on with his tale to the lady:

When I was certain I had killed him, I got up and went up the stairs and replaced the trapdoor and covered it with earth as before. Then I looked out to sea and saw the ship cleaving the water and making for the island; at which I was afraid, and said, "The moment they come and see the young man put to death, they will know it was I who killed him, and they will kill me without any delay."

So I climbed up into a tall tree and hid myself among the leaves. And I had hardly done it before the ship anchored and the slaves landed with the old man, the young man's father, and made straight for the place; and when they cleared the earth away they were surprised to find it loose.

Then they raised the trapdoor and went down, and found the young man lying at full length, dressed in fine new clothes, with his face glowing after the bath and the knife deep in his heart.

At the sight of it they shrieked and wept and beat their faces, cursing the murderer out loud; while a fainting fit came over the old man, so that the slaves thought him dead, unable to survive his son.

At last they wrapped the murdered young man in his clothes and carried him up and laid him on the ground and covered him with a shroud of silk. And while they were making for the ship the old man came round; and looking at his son stretched out there, he fell to the ground and threw dust over his head and struck his face and plucked out his beard; and his weeping redoubled as he thought of his murdered son, and he fainted away once more.

After a while a slave went and fetched a strip of silk, and they laid the old man on it and sat down at his head.

All this took place, and I was up in the tree above them watching everything that happened; and my heart turned grey before my head did, at the hard lot that was mine and the distress and anguish I had been through. And I fell to reciting:

	"How many a joy has fled by Allah's will
	with a flight that escapes the sight of the wisest head!
	How many a sadness begins the day
	and grows quite cheerful before the day is out!
	How many a good thing treads on the heels of an ill one,
	making the mourner's heart thrill with joy!"

But the old man, my lady, did not come out of his faint until near sunset; when he came to himself and looked at his dead son and remembered what had happened, and how the thing he had dreaded had come to pass. And he beat his face and his head and recited these lines:

	"My heart is racked by parting from my friends
	and two streams run for ever out of my eyelids.
	My hopes went out with them — alas, and well away!
	What way is left me now to speak or act?
	Would I had never looked on the sight of them.
	What way, good sirs, when the paths grow narrower and narrower?
	What charm shall calm my pangs when the longings of love
	burn like this and glow in my very vitals?
	Would I had trodden the road of Death along with them!
	Then this parting blow would never have fallen on us.
	Allah — I pray the Merciful to show me mercy
	and mix our lives and never part them again.
	How blessed we were, living together under one roof,
	joined in our joys and reckoning nothing of grief;
	until Fortune shot us with the arrow of separation.
	Ah, who shall bear such a parting-pang with patience?
	And the dart of Death struck down in the middle of the tribe
	the pearl of the age, whom the Morning saw shining brightest.
	I cried out, while his very case found a tongue and spoke:
	Would to Heaven, my son, that Death had let his doom run late!
	Which is the readiest road for me to meet with you,
	my son, for whom I would give away my own soul?
	If I call him the sun — no; the sun goes down.
	If I call him the moon — the moons wane. Ah, no.
	O sad mischance of you, O doom of the days;
	your place no other love will ever know.
	Your father, out of his mind, looks at you and despairs
	of overthrowing Fate by any wit or wisdom.
	Some evil eye has cast its spell this day —
	and may it fall foul on him as it has fallen foul on us."

Then he gave one single sob, and his soul fled his body.

The slaves shrieked aloud, "Alas, our lord!" and showered dust on their heads and redoubled their weeping and wailing. Presently they carried their dead master to the ship side by side with his dead son; and having moved all the goods out of the dwelling into the vessel, they set sail and disappeared from my sight.

I came down from the tree and, raising the trapdoor, went down into the underground dwelling, where everything reminded me of the young man; and I looked at the poor remains of him and began repeating these verses:

	"I see their tracks, and pine with pain and pang,
	and weep and yearn over hearths they have left.
	And I pray to Him who doomed them to depart
	that some day He may grant the gift of a safe return."

Then, my lady, I went up again through the trapdoor; and every day I used to wander round about the island, and every night I came back to the underground hall.

I lived like this for a month; until at last, looking at the western side of the island, I noticed that every day the tides ebbed and left shallow water which the flow did not make up for; and by the end of the month the sea had shown dry land in that direction.

At this I was overjoyed, making certain of my safety; so I got up and forded what little water was left and reached the mainland — where I fell in with great heaps of loose sand in which even a camel's hoof would sink to the knee.

However, I put heart into my soul, and wading through the sand, saw a fire shining a long way off and burning with a blazing light. So I made for it, hoping perhaps to find help, and broke out into these verses:

	"Perhaps my Fortune may turn her bridle round
	and Time bring me good, jealous though he is called;
	may forward my hopes and further everything I need,
	and pay for the ills that are past with present good."

And when I got near the fire — it was a palace, with gates of copper burnished red, which, when the rising sun shone on them, gleamed and glittered a long way off and had looked to me like a fire.

I was glad at the sight, and sat down opposite the gate; but I was hardly settled in my seat before I was met by ten young men in sumptuous clothes, and every one of them blind in the left eye, which looked as though it had been plucked out. They had with them an old man, an old, old man; and I marvelled a great deal at the look of them, and at their all being blind in the same eye.

When they saw me they greeted me with the salutation of peace and asked me about my circumstances and my history; at which I told them everything that had happened to me and what a full measure of misfortune had been mine.

Marvelling at my tale, they took me into the mansion, where I saw ten couches ranged round the hall, each with its blue bedding and a coverlet of blue cloth; and in the middle stood a smaller couch furnished like the rest with blue and nothing else.

As we came in, each of the young men took his seat on his own couch, and the old man seated himself on the smaller one in the middle and said to me, "Young man, sit down on the floor, and do not ask about our situation or about the loss of our eyes."

Presently he got up and set some meat in a large dish and drink in a big bowl in front of each young man, and treated me the same way; and after that they sat questioning me about my adventures and what had happened to me, and I went on telling them my tale until the night was far gone.

Then the young men said, "Master, will you not set our usual thing before us? The time has come."

He replied, "With love and gladness," and got up and went into a closet and disappeared; but presently he came back carrying ten trays on his head, each covered with a strip of blue cloth. He set a tray in front of each young man, and lighting ten wax candles, stuck one on each tray, and drew off the covers — and underneath there was nothing but ashes and powdered charcoal and kettle soot.

Then all the young men tucked their sleeves up to the elbow and fell to weeping and wailing; and they blackened their faces and smeared their clothes and beat their brows and struck their breasts, exclaiming over and over, "We were sitting at our ease, and nothing but our own meddling brought us unease!"

They did not stop doing this until the dawn drew near, when the old man got up and heated water for them; and they washed their faces and put on other, clean clothes.

Now when I saw this, my lady, my senses left me for sheer wonderment and my wits went wild, and my heart and my head were so full of it that I forgot what had happened to me. And I could not keep quiet — I felt I simply had to speak out and ask them about these strange things; so I said to them:

"How is it you do this, after we have been so open-hearted and cheerful together? Thanks be to Allah, you are all sound and sane, and yet actions like these suit nobody but madmen, or people possessed by an evil spirit. I beg you, by everything dearest to you — why do you refuse to tell me your history, and the reason for losing your eyes and for blackening your faces with ashes and soot?"

At this they turned to me and said, "Young man, do not listen to the promptings of your youth, and ask us no questions."

Then they slept, and I with them; and when they woke the old man brought us something to eat; and after we had eaten and the plates and goblets had been taken away, they sat talking until nightfall, when the old man got up and lit the wax candles and the lamps and set food and drink in front of us.

After we had eaten and drunk we sat talking and drinking in good company until midnight, when they said to the old man, "Bring us our usual thing, for the hour of sleep is at hand."

So he got up and brought them the trays of soot and ashes; and they did as they had done the night before, no more and no less.

I stayed with them like this for a month, during which they blackened their faces with ashes every night and washed and changed their clothes when the morning was young; and I only marvelled the more, and my scruples and my curiosity grew to such a pitch that I had to give up even eating and drinking.

At last I lost command of myself, for my heart was aflame with a fire that could not be put out and a flame that could not be hidden, and I said, "Young men, will you not relieve my trouble and tell me the reason for blackening your faces like this, and the meaning of your words — we were sitting at our ease, and nothing but our own meddling brought us unease?"

They said, "It would be better to keep these things secret."

Still I was so bewildered by what they did that I stopped eating and drinking altogether; and at last, losing patience entirely, I said to them, "There is no help for it. You must tell me the reason for all this."

They replied, "We kept our secret only for your own good. Gratifying you will bring evil down on you, and you will become one-eyed, exactly as we are."

I repeated, "There is no help for it; and if you will not tell me, then let me leave you and go back to my own people and be spared the sight of these things. For the proverb says:

	Better that you stay and I take my leave:
	for what the eye does not see, the heart will never grieve."

At this they said to me, "Remember, young man, that if harm comes to you we will not take you in again or let you stay among us." And bringing a ram, they slaughtered it and skinned it.

Last of all they gave me a knife, saying: "Take this skin and stretch yourself out on it, and we will sew it up around you. Presently there will come to you a certain bird called the roc, which will catch you up in its claws and tower high in the air and then set you down on a mountain. When you feel that it is no longer flying, rip the hide open with this blade and come out of it; the bird will be startled and will fly away and leave you free.

"After this, travel for half a day, and the march will bring you to a palace, wonderful to look at, towering high in the air and built of khalanj wood and aloes-wood and sandalwood, plated with red gold and studded with every kind of emerald and costly gem fit for a seal ring. Go into it and you will get what you want — for we have all gone into that palace; and that is the reason for our losing our eyes and for blackening our faces. If we were to tell you our stories now it would take far too long, for every one of us lost his left eye by an adventure of his own."

I was delighted at their words; and they did with me as they had said, and the bird, the roc, carried me off and set me down on the mountain. Then I came out of the skin and walked on until I reached the palace.

The door stood open as I came up, and I found myself in a spacious and handsome hall, exceedingly wide — as wide as a racecourse; and around it were a hundred rooms with doors of sandalwood and aloes-wood plated with red gold and fitted with silver rings for knockers.

At the upper end of the hall I saw forty girls, sumptuously dressed and ornamented, and every one of them as bright as the moon; nobody could ever tire of gazing at them, and they were all so lovely that the strictest hermit alive, on seeing them, would have become their slave and obeyed their will.

When they saw me the whole company came up to me and said, "Welcome, and well come, and good cheer to you, our lord! This whole month we have been expecting you. Praised be Allah, who has sent us someone worthy of us, as we are worthy of him."

Then they made me sit down on a high divan and said, "Today you are our lord and master, and we are your servants and your handmaids; so order us as you like."

And I marvelled at their situation.

Presently one of them got up and set food in front of me, and I ate and they ate with me; while others heated water and washed my hands and feet and changed my clothes, and others made sherbets ready and gave us to drink; and they all gathered round me, full of joy and gladness at my coming.

Then they sat down and talked with me until nightfall, when five of them got up and laid the trays and spread them with flowers and fragrant herbs and fruit, fresh and dried, and sweets in profusion. At last they brought out a fine wine service with rich old wine; and we sat down to drink, and some sang songs and others played the lute and the psaltery and the recorder and other instruments, and the bowl went merrily round.

At this such gladness took hold of me that I forgot every sorrow in the world, and said, "This is what life is; how sad that it passes!"

I enjoyed their company until the time came for rest, and our heads were all warm with wine, when they said, "Our lord, choose from among us the one who is to share your bed tonight, and who is not to lie with you again until forty days have gone by."

So I chose a girl with a lovely face and a perfect figure, her eyes edged with kohl by nature's own hand; hair long and jet black, teeth slightly parted and eyebrows meeting. She was like some limber, graceful young branch, or the slender stalk of sweet basil, made to amaze a man and bewilder his imagination — just as the poet said about such a woman:

	To match her with a green bough would be useless;
	he is a fool who finds her beauties in the roe deer.
	When did the roe have those lively, lovely limbs,
	or honey-dew those lips of hers alone can give?
	Those eyes — those soul-piercing eyes, that kill with love,
	that bind their victim with the arrows that lay him low?
	They coaxed my heart back into a second childhood.
	No wonder: a love-sick man is a child again.

And I repeated to her the poet's words:

	"No other charms but yours shall meet my eyes,
	no other image can take my heart by surprise.
