	Your love, my lady, has captured all my thoughts,
	and on that love I shall die and shall rise again."

So I lay with her that night; I never knew a lovelier. And when it was morning the girls carried me off to the baths and bathed me and dressed me in the finest clothes. Then they served food, and we ate and drank and the cup went round until nightfall, when I chose from among them one lovely in form and face, soft-sided and a model of grace — the kind of woman the poet described when he said:

	On her fair breast I saw two caskets,
	sealed fast with seals of musk to hold lovers off;
	her eyes stand guard over them with arrowy glances
	whose shafts would shoot whoever dared put out a hand.

With her I spent a very fine night. And, to be brief, my mistress, I stayed with them in all the comfort and delight of life, eating and drinking, talking and carousing, and every night lying with one or another of them.

But at the head of the new year they came to me in tears and said goodbye, weeping and crying out and clinging to me; at which I wondered, and said, "What can be the matter? Truly you are breaking my heart."

They exclaimed, "Would to Heaven we had never known you! For though we have kept company with a great many, we never saw a pleasanter man than you or a more courteous." And they wept again.

"But tell me more clearly," I asked, "what is causing this weeping, which is making my gall bladder ready to burst?"

And they answered, "Our lord and master, it is separation that makes us weep; and you, and only you, are the cause of our tears. If you will listen to us we need never be parted; and if you will not listen, we part for ever. But our hearts tell us that you will not listen to what we say, and that is the cause of our tears and our crying."

"Tell me how the matter stands."

"Know, our lord, that we are the daughters of kings, who have met here and lived together for years; and once every year we are obliged to be away for forty days; and afterwards we come back and stay here for the rest of the twelve months, eating and drinking and taking our pleasure and enjoying ourselves.

"We are about to go, according to our custom; and we are afraid that once we are gone you will go against our charge and disobey what we tell you. Now here we put into your hands the keys of the palace, which has forty rooms; and of these you may open thirty-nine — but beware, and we beg you by Allah and by our own lives, of opening the fortieth door, for behind it is the thing that will separate us for ever."

Said I, "I certainly will not open it, if it holds the cause of my being separated from you."

Then one of them came up to me and fell on my neck and wept and recited these lines:

	"If Time brings us together after a while apart,
	the world will stop frowning harshly and smile on our lot;
	and if your face will condescend to adorn my eyes,
	I will pardon Time its past wrongs and its old deceits."

And I recited the following:

	"When she drew near to say goodbye, with her heart unstrung,
	while care and longing wrung her breast that day,
	she wept wet pearls, and mine rolled down like red carnelians,
	and joined in a sad necklace, they hung about her throat."

When I saw her weeping I said, "By Allah, I will never open that fortieth door — never, and in no way at all." And I said goodbye to her.

At which they all departed, flying away like birds, signalling their farewells with their hands as they went, and leaving me alone in the palace.

When evening drew near I opened the door of the first room, and going in, found myself in a place like one of the pleasure gardens of Paradise. It was a garden with trees of the freshest green and ripe fruit of a yellow sheen; and its birds were singing clear and keen, and rills ran winding through the fair terrain.

The sight and the sounds brought comfort to my spirit; and I walked among the trees and smelt the breath of the flowers on the breeze, and heard the little birds singing their melodies, hymning the One, the Almighty, in the sweetest litanies. And I looked at the apple, whose colour is part red and part yellow, as the poet says:

	Apple, whose colour joins in a mellow union
	my beloved's red cheek and her luckless lover's yellow one.

Then I looked at the quince, and breathed in its fragrance, which puts musk and ambergris to shame, as the poet has said:

	The quince joins every taste in one; in her are found
	the gifts that have crowned the quince queen of the fruits.
	Her taste is wine, her scent the waft of musk;
	her colour pure gold, and her shape the moon's fair round.

Then I looked at the pear, whose taste surpasses sherbet and sugar; and at the apricot, whose beauty strikes the eye with admiration, as though she were a polished ruby.

Then I went out of the place and locked the door as it had been before.

Next day I opened the second door; and going in, I found myself on a spacious plain set with tall date palms and watered by a running stream, whose banks were bushed with rose and jasmine, while privet and sweet briar, ox-eye, violet and lily, narcissus, marjoram and the winter gillyflower carpeted the borders. And the breath of the breeze swept over all these sweet-smelling growths, spreading their delicious scents right and left, perfuming the world and filling my soul with delight.

After enjoying myself there a while I went out and, having shut the door as it had been before, opened the third door — where I saw a high open hall inlaid with parti-coloured marbles and costly stonework and other precious stones, and hung with cages of sandalwood and eagle-wood, full of birds making sweet music: the thousand-voiced nightingale, and the wood pigeon, the blackbird, the turtle dove and the Nubian ring dove.

My heart was filled with pleasure at it; my grief was driven off, and I slept in that aviary until dawn.

Then I unlocked the door of the fourth room, and inside found a grand saloon with forty smaller chambers opening off it. All their doors stood open; so I went in, and found them full of pearls and jacinths and beryls and emeralds and corals and carbuncles, and every kind of precious gem and jewel that the tongue of man cannot describe.

My thoughts were stunned at the sight, and I said to myself, "These, I think, are things gathered together that could not be found except in the treasuries of a King of Kings; nor could all the monarchs of the world have collected the like of them."

And my heart swelled and my sorrows stopped. "For," said I, "now truly I am the monarch of the age, since by Allah's grace all this enormous wealth is mine; and I have forty girls under my hand, and there is nobody to claim them but myself."

Then I did not leave off opening one place after another until thirty-nine days had gone by, and in that time I had gone into every room except the one whose door the princesses had charged me not to open.

But my thoughts, my mistress, ran always on that forbidden fortieth, and Satan urged me to open it for my own undoing; and I had not the patience to hold back, although there was only a single day left before they were due.

So I stood in front of that room and, after a moment's hesitation, opened the door, which was plated with red gold, and went in.

I was met by a perfume the like of which I had never smelt before; and the scent was so sharp and so subtle that it made my senses drunk as with strong wine, and I fell to the ground in a fainting fit that lasted a full hour.

When I came to myself I put strength into my heart and, going in, found myself in a chamber whose floor was strewn with saffron and blazing with light from branched candelabra of gold and lamps fed with costly oils, which gave off the scent of musk and ambergris. I saw there two great censers as well, each as big as a drinking bowl, flaming with aloes-wood, nadd perfume, ambergris and honeyed scents; and the place was full of their fragrance.

Presently, my lady, I caught sight of a noble horse, black as the murk of the murkiest night, standing ready saddled and bridled — and his saddle was of red gold — in front of two mangers, one of clear crystal holding husked sesame, and the other also of crystal holding rose water scented with musk.

When I saw this I marvelled, and said to myself, "There must certainly be some wonderful mystery in this animal." And Satan tricked me; so I led him out of the palace and mounted him — but he would not stir from the spot.

So I hammered his sides with my heels, and he did not move; and then I took the rein-whip and struck him with it. And when he felt the blow he neighed a neigh with a sound like deafening thunder, and opening a pair of wings, flew up with me into the sky, far beyond the reach of any man's eyesight.

After a full hour of flight he came down and landed on a terrace roof; and shaking me off his back, he lashed me across the face with his tail and gouged out my left eye, so that it rolled down my cheek. Then he flew away.

I came down from the terrace and found myself among the ten one-eyed young men again, sitting on their ten couches with the blue covers; and they cried out when they saw me, "No welcome to you, and nothing of good cheer! We all lived the happiest of lives, and ate and drank of the best; we took our rest on brocades and cloth of gold and slept with our heads on beauty's breast — and we could not wait one day to gain the delights of a whole year."

Said I, "Look — I have become one like you; and now I want you to bring me a tray full of blackness, so that I can blacken my face and be received into your society."

"No, by Allah," they said. "You shall not stay with us. Now get out."

So they drove me away. And finding them reject me like that, I foresaw that things would go hard with me; and I remembered all the miseries that Destiny had written on my forehead, and I went out from among them heavy-hearted and with tears in my eyes, repeating to myself the words, "I was sitting at my ease, and nothing but my own meddling brought me unease."

Then I shaved my beard and my moustaches and my eyebrows, renouncing the world, and wandered about Allah's earth in a kalandar's clothes; and the Almighty decreed safety for me until I reached Baghdad, which was on the evening of this very night.

Here I met these other two kalandars standing about at a loss; so I greeted them, saying, "I am a stranger!" and they answered, "And we are strangers too!" By the freak of Fortune we were like to like — three kalandars and three one-eyed men, all blind in the left eye.

Such, my lady, is the reason for the shearing of my beard, and that is how I lost an eye.

Said the lady to him, "Rub your head and be on your way."

But he answered, "By Allah, I will not go until I have heard the stories of these others."

Then the lady turned to the Caliph and Ja'afar and Masrur and said, "You men — give an account of yourselves as well."

At which Ja'afar stood forward and told her what he had told the doorkeeper as they were coming into the house; and when she heard his story of their being merchants and Mosul men who had outrun the watch, she said, "I grant you your lives, each for the other's sake. And now away with you, all of you."

So they all went out; and when they were in the street the Caliph said to the kalandars, "Where are you going now, my friends, seeing that the morning has not yet dawned?"

They said, "By Allah, our lord, we do not know where to go."

"Come and spend the rest of the night with us," said the Caliph. And turning to Ja'afar, "Take them home with you, and tomorrow bring them into my presence, so that we can put their adventures on record."

Ja'afar did as the Caliph ordered him, and the Commander of the Faithful went back to his palace; but sleep gave no sign of visiting him that night, and he lay awake turning over the misfortunes of the three kalandar princes and impatient to know the history of the ladies and the two black bitches.

No sooner had morning dawned than he went out and sat on the throne of his sovereignty; and turning to Ja'afar, after all his grandees and officers of state had assembled, he said, "Bring me the three ladies and the two bitches and the three kalandars."

So Ja'afar went out and brought them all before him — the ladies veiled. Then the minister turned to them and said in the Caliph's name:

"We pardon you for your ill treatment of us and your lack of courtesy, in consideration of the kindness that went before it, and because you did not know who we were. However, I would have you know now that you are standing in the presence of the fifth of the sons of Abbas — Harun al-Rashid, brother of the Caliph Musa al-Hadi, son of Al-Mansur, son of Mohammed the brother of Al-Saffah son of Mohammed, who was the first of the royal house. So speak before him the truth, and the whole truth."

When the ladies heard Ja'afar's words about the Commander of the Faithful, the eldest came forward and said, "O Commander of the Faithful, my story is one which, if it were engraved with needles on the inner corners of the eye, would be a warning to anyone willing to take warning, and an example to anyone who can profit by an example":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Seventeenth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that she stood forward before the Commander of the Faithful and began to tell

The Eldest Lady's Tale

Truly my tale is a strange one, and it is this.

Those two black bitches are my eldest sisters, by the same mother and father; and these two others — the one who carries the marks of the whip on her, and the third, our caterer — are my sisters by another mother.

When my father died, each of us took her share of the inheritance; and after a while my mother died too, leaving me and my full sisters three thousand dinars, so that each daughter received a thousand, and I the same, although I was the youngest.

In due course my sisters married with the usual festivities and went to live with their husbands, who bought merchandise with their wives' money and set out travelling together. And so they threw me off.

My brothers-in-law were away with their wives five years, in which time they spent all the money they had; and going bankrupt, they abandoned my sisters in foreign parts among strangers.

After five years my eldest sister came back to me in beggar's clothes, her dress in rags and tatters and a dirty old cloak over it; and truly she was in the foulest and sorriest state. At first sight I did not know my own sister; but presently I recognised her and said, "What state is this?"

"Sister," she answered, "words cannot undo what is done; and the pen of Destiny has run through what Allah decreed."

Then I sent her to the baths and dressed her in a suit of my own, and boiled her a broth and brought her some good wine, and said to her:

"Sister, you are the eldest, and you still stand to us in the place of father and mother. And as for the inheritance that came to me as it did to you two, Allah has blessed it and prospered it and made it grow; and my circumstances are comfortable, for I have made a good deal of money spinning and cleaning silk. You and I will share what I have equally."

I treated her with every kindness, and she stayed with me a whole year, during which our thoughts and our imaginations were always on our other sister.

Not long afterwards she came home too, in an even fouler and sorrier state than the eldest; and I dealt with her still more generously than I had with the first, and each of them had her share of what I had.

After a time they said to me, "Sister, we want to marry again; truly we have not the patience to drag out our days without husbands and live the lives of widows under a spell."

And I replied, "My dears! You have seen precious little good in marriage so far; these days good men and true have become rarities and curiosities. And I do not think your plans are advisable, since you have already tried matrimony and it failed."

But they would not take my advice, and married without my consent — although I gave them their outfits and their dowries out of my own money; and off they went with their husbands.

In a very little while their husbands played them false and, taking whatever they could lay hands on, absconded and left them in the lurch. At which they came to me ashamed and in an abject state, and made their excuses, saying:

"Pardon our fault and do not be angry with us; for though you are younger in years, you are older in sense. From now on we will never mention marriage again; so take us back as your servants, so that we may have a mouthful to eat."

Said I, "Welcome to you, sisters; there is nothing dearer to me than you." And I took them in and redoubled my kindness to them.

We went on living in this loving way for a full year, when I decided to sell my goods abroad, and first of all to fit out a passage to Basra. So I equipped a large ship and loaded her with merchandise and valuable goods for trading, and with provisions and everything needed for a voyage, and said to my sisters, "Will you stay at home while I travel, or would you rather come with me on the voyage?"

"We will travel with you," they answered, "for we cannot bear to be parted from you."

So I divided my money into two parts, one to come with me and the other to be left with a trustworthy person — for, as I said to myself, "Some accident may happen to the ship and we still be alive; in which case we shall find something on our return to stand us in good stead."

I took my two sisters and we voyaged some days and nights; but the master was careless enough to lose his course, and the ship went astray with us and entered a sea other than the sea we were making for.

For a time we knew nothing about it; and the wind blew fair for us ten days, after which the lookout man went aloft to look about him and cried, "Good news!" Then he came down rejoicing and said, "I have seen what seems to be a city, no bigger than a pigeon."

At this we were delighted; and before an hour of the day had gone by the buildings showed plain in the offing, and we asked the captain, "What is the name of that city?"

And he answered, "By Allah I do not know, for I never saw it before and never sailed these seas in my life. But since our troubles have ended safely, all that remains is for you to land there with your merchandise; and if you find selling profitable, then sell and make your market of what is there; and if not, we will rest two days and provision ourselves and go on."

So we entered the port, and the captain went up into the town and was gone a while, after which he came back to us and said, "Get up; go up into the city and marvel at the works of Allah with His creatures, and pray to be preserved from His righteous anger."

So we landed, and going up into the city, saw at the gate men holding staves in their hands; but when we came close to them, they had been transformed by the anger of Allah and had become stone.

Then we went into the city and found everyone who lived there turned into black stone. Not one inhabited house was to be seen by anybody looking for one, and there was not a soul blowing up a fire.

We were awestruck at the sight, and threaded through the market streets, where we found the goods and the gold and the silver left lying where they were; and we were glad, and said, "There must be some mystery in all this."

Then we scattered about the thoroughfares, and every one of us busied himself with collecting the wealth and the money and the rich stuffs, taking very little notice of friend or companion.

As for me, I went up to the castle, which was strongly fortified; and going into the King's palace by its gate of red gold, found all the plate of gold and silver, and the King himself seated in the middle of his chamberlains and governors and emirs and viziers, all dressed in clothing that confounded the art of man.

I came nearer and saw him sitting on a throne encrusted and inlaid with pearls and gems; and his robes were of cloth of gold decorated with jewels of every kind, each one flashing like a star. Around him stood fifty Mamluks, white slaves, dressed in silks of various sorts and holding their drawn swords in their hands — but when I came close to them, every one of them was black stone.

My understanding was confounded at the sight; but I walked on and came into the great hall of the harem, whose walls I found hung with tapestries of gold-striped silk and spread with silk carpets embroidered with flowers of gold.

Here I saw the Queen lying at full length, dressed in robes edged with fresh young pearls; on her head was a diadem set with all sorts of gems, each one fit for a ring, and round her neck hung collars and necklaces. All her clothing and her ornaments were in their natural state, but she had been turned to black stone by Allah's anger.

Presently I noticed an open door and made straight for it, and found a flight of seven steps leading up to it. So I walked up and came upon a place floored with marble and spread and hung with gold-worked carpets and tapestries, in the middle of which stood a throne of juniper wood inlaid with pearls and precious stones and set with bosses of emerald.

In the far wall was an alcove whose curtains, strung with pearls, were let down; and I saw a light coming out of it. So I went nearer, and saw that the light came from a precious stone as big as an ostrich egg, set at the upper end of the alcove on a little couch of gold and ivory; and this jewel, blazing like the sun, cast its rays far and wide. The couch too was spread with every kind of silk, amazing anyone who looked at it with their richness and their beauty.

I marvelled a great deal at all this, and most of all at seeing candles there ready lit; and I said in my mind, "Somebody must have lit these candles."

Then I went out and came to the kitchen, and from there to the pantry and the King's treasure chambers; and I went on exploring the palace and walking from place to place. I forgot myself in my awe and wonder at all this, and I was drowned in thought until the night came on.

Then I would have gone out; but not knowing where the gate was, I lost my way. So I went back to the alcove, where the lit candles guided me, and sat down on the couch; and wrapping myself in a coverlet, after repeating something from the Koran, I would have slept — but I could not, for restlessness had hold of me.

When night was at its middle I heard a voice chanting the Koran in the sweetest tones; but the sound of it was weak. So I got up, glad to hear the silence broken, and followed the sound until I came to a small room whose door stood ajar.

Then, peeping through a chink, I looked at the place — and it was a place of prayer, with a prayer niche and two wax candles burning and lamps hanging from the ceiling. And in it a prayer carpet was spread, on which a young man was sitting, fair to look at; and in front of him on its stand was a copy of the Koran, which he was reading from.

I marvelled to see him alive, alone among all the people of the city; and going in, I greeted him, at which he raised his eyes and returned my greeting.

Said I, "Now by the truth of what you are reading in Allah's Holy Book, I beg you to answer my question."

He looked at me with a smile and said, "Handmaid of Allah, first tell me why you have come here, and I in my turn will tell you what has happened to me and to the people of this city, and why I escaped their doom."

So I told him my story, at which he wondered; and I questioned him about the people of the city, and he replied, "Have patience with me a moment, sister." And reverently closing the Holy Book, he laid it up in a satin bag.

Then he sat me down at his side; and I looked at him — and he was like the moon at the full, fair of face and rare of form, soft-sided and slight, of well-proportioned height, and with a cheek smoothly bright and giving off light; in short a sweet thing, a sugar stick — just as the poet says of somebody like him:

	That night the astrologer drew a scheme of the planets,
	and there appeared in view a graceful shape of a young man.
	Saturn had stained his hair with the most saturnine jet
	and blown spots of nut-brown musk on the rose of his cheek;
	Mars tinctured both cheeks with the tincture of martial red;
	Sagittarius shot arrows out of his eyelids;
	Mercury endowed him with a bright mercurial wit;
	and the Bear carried off whatever ill men's glances grew.
	The star-lover stood amazed to see this marvel born
	when the Moon at the full bowed low to kiss the Earth.

And truly Allah the Most High had robed him in the raiment of perfect grace, and had edged it and fringed it with a cheek all beauty and loveliness — just as the poet says of such a man:

	By his eyelids shedding perfume and his fine slim waist I swear,
	by the shooting of his arrows barbed with rare sorcery;
	by the softness of his sides, and the lingering light of his glances,
	and his brow of dazzling daylight with the night inside his hair;
	by his eyebrows, which deny all rest to whoever looks at them,
	now bidding, now forbidding, always dealing joy and care;
	by the rose that decks his cheek and the myrtle of its down,
	by the jacinths bedded in his lips and the pearls his smile lays bare;
	by his gracefully bending neck and the curving of his breast,
	whose polished surface carries that lovely pair of pomegranates;
	by his heavy hips that quiver as he passes in his pride,
	or as he rests on that waist that is slim beyond compare;
	by the satin of his skin, by that fine unsullied spirit;
	by the beauty in him that contains everything bright and debonair;
	by that ever-open hand, by the candour of his tongue;
	by noble blood and high degree, of which he is the hope and heir —
	musk borrows its muskiness from him and loves to breathe it out,
	and all the airs of ambergris perfume the air through him.
	The sun, I think — the broad bright sun — would go pale beside my love,
	and without his splendour would look like a paring of his nail.

I glanced at him with one glance of the eyes that cost me a thousand sighs, and my heart was taken captive that instant; so I asked him, "My lord and my love, tell me what I asked you."

And he answered, "To hear is to obey. Know, handmaid of Allah, that this city was my father's capital; and my father is the King you saw on the throne, transformed by Allah's anger into black stone; and the Queen you found in the alcove is my mother.

"They and all the people of the city were Magians who worshipped fire instead of the Omnipotent Lord, and used to swear by flame and heat, by shade and light, and by the spheres revolving day and night.

"My father had no son until he was blessed with me near the end of his days; and he brought me up, and I grew, and prosperity ran ahead of me in everything.

"Now it happened that there was with us an old woman well on in years, a Muslim who, believing inwardly in Allah and His Apostle, outwardly conformed to the religion of my people. And my father trusted her completely, because he knew her to be trustworthy and virtuous, and he treated her with more and more kindness, believing her to be of his own faith.

"So when I was nearly grown up my father put me in her charge, saying: take him and educate him and teach him the rules of our faith; give him the best instruction, and do not leave off your fostering care of him.

"So she took me and taught me the tenets of Islam, with the divine ordinances of the ritual washing and the five daily prayers; and she made me learn the Koran by heart, saying over and over: serve nobody but Allah Almighty.

"When I had mastered this much she said to me: my son, keep this matter hidden from your father, and reveal nothing to him, or he will kill you. So I hid it from him.

"I lived like this for a while, until the old woman died; and the people of the city redoubled in their impiety and their arrogance and their error.

"One day, while they were going on as usual, they heard a loud and terrible sound, and a crier crying out with a voice like rolling thunder, so that every ear could hear it, far and near: 'People of this city, leave off your fire-worshipping and worship Allah, the All-compassionate King!'

"At this, fear and terror fell on the citizens, and they crowded to my father, he being King of the city, and asked him, 'What is this awful voice we have heard? It has confounded us with the excess of its terror.'

"And he answered, 'Do not let a voice frighten you or shake your steadfast spirit or turn you back from the faith that is right.'

"Their hearts inclined to what he said, and they did not stop worshipping the fire; and they persisted in their rebellion for a full year from the time they heard the first voice. And on the anniversary came a second cry, and a third at the head of the third year, each year once.

"Still they persisted in their evil practices, until one day at daybreak judgement and the anger of Heaven came down on them all of a sudden; and by the visitation of Allah they were all turned into black stones — they and their beasts and their cattle — and nobody was saved except me, who at that hour was busy at my devotions.

"From that day to this I have been in the state you see, constant in prayer and fasting and reading and reciting the Koran; but I have truly grown weary of my loneliness, with nobody to keep me company."

Then said I to him — for in very truth he had won my heart and was the lord of my life and my soul:

"Young man, will you come with me to the city of Baghdad, and visit the learned men and the men skilled in the law and the doctors of divinity, and get yourself an increase of wisdom and understanding and theology? And know that the woman standing in front of you will be your servant, although she is the head of her family and mistress over men and eunuchs and servants and slaves. Truly my life was no life before it met with your youth. I have a ship here loaded with merchandise; and in very truth Destiny drove me to this city so that I should come to know all this, for it was fated that we should meet."

And I did not stop persuading him and speaking him fair and using every art until he consented:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Eighteenth Night,

she went on: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the lady did not stop persuading the young man with soft speech to go away with her until he consented and said yes. She slept that night lying at his feet, hardly knowing where she was for the excess of her joy.

As soon as the next morning dawned (she went on, addressing the Caliph), I got up, and we went into the treasuries and took from them whatever was light in weight and great in worth; and then we went down side by side from the castle into the city, where we were met by the captain and my sisters and the slaves, who had been looking for me.

When they saw me they were delighted, and asked what had kept me; and I told them everything I had seen, and told them the story of the young prince and the transformation that had justly come on the citizens. At which they all marvelled — but when my two sisters (these two bitches, Commander of the Faithful!) saw me at the side of my young lover, they grew jealous of me on his account and were angry, and plotted mischief against me.

We waited for a fair wind and went on board rejoicing, and ready to fly for joy at the goods we had got; but my own greatest joy was in the young man. And we waited a while until the wind blew fair for us, and then we set sail and went on our way.

Now as we sat talking, my sisters asked me, "And what will you do with this handsome young man?"

And I answered, "I mean to make him my husband." Then I turned to him and said, "My lord, I have something to propose to you in which you must not cross me; and it is this: that when we reach Baghdad, my native city, I offer you my life as your servant in holy matrimony, and you shall be my husband and I will be your wife."

He answered, "I hear and I obey. You are my lady and my mistress, and whatever you do I will not gainsay."

Then I turned to my sisters and said, "This is my gain; I am content with this young man, and those who have got any of my property, let them keep it as their gain with my goodwill."

"You speak and do well," the two of them answered; but they were imagining mischief against me.

We sailed on before a fair wind until we had exchanged the sea of peril for the seas of safety; and in a few days we made the city of Basra, whose buildings loomed clear in front of us as the evening fell.

But after we had gone to bed and were sound asleep, my two sisters got up and picked me up, bed and all, and threw me into the sea. They did the same to the young prince, who, being unable to swim, sank and was drowned; and Allah enrolled him in the noble army of Martyrs.

As for me — would to Heaven I had drowned with him; but Allah judged that I should be one of the saved. So when I woke and found myself in the sea, and saw the ship making off like a flash of lightning, He threw a piece of timber in my way, which I got astride of; and the waves tossed me to and fro until they cast me up on the coast of an island, a high land and an uninhabited one.

I landed and walked about the island the rest of the night; and when the morning dawned I saw a rough track, barely fit for a child of Adam to walk on, leading to what turned out to be a shallow ford joining the island to the mainland.

As soon as the sun had risen I spread my clothes out to dry in it, and ate some of the island's fruit and drank its water; then I set out along the footpath, and did not stop walking until I reached the mainland.

Now when there was only a two hours' journey left between me and the city, a great serpent, as big round as a date palm, came fleeing towards me in a tremendous hurry, gliding along now to the right and now to the left until she was close on me, her tongue lolling a span long towards the ground and sweeping the dust as she went.

She was being pursued by a dragon no longer than two lances, of slender build, about as thick as a spear; and although her terror lent her speed and she kept wriggling from side to side, he overtook her and seized her by the tail — at which her tears streamed down and her tongue was thrust out in her agony.

I took pity on her; and picking up a stone and calling on Allah for help, I threw it at the dragon's head with such force that he died then and there. And the serpent opened a pair of wings and flew up into the sky and disappeared from in front of my eyes.

I sat down marvelling at this adventure; but I was tired, and drowsiness came over me, and I slept where I was for a while.

When I woke I found a jet-black girl sitting at my feet massaging them; and by her side stood two black bitches — my sisters, Commander of the Faithful!

I was embarrassed in front of her; and sitting up, I asked her, "Sister, who and what are you?"

And she answered, "How quickly you have forgotten me! I am the one you did a good turn for and sowed the seed of gratitude in, and killed her enemy; for I am the serpent whom by Allah's aid you delivered just now from the dragon.

"I am a jinniyah, and he was a jinni who hated me, and nobody saved my life from him but you. As soon as you freed me from him I flew on the wind to the ship your sisters threw you from, and moved everything in it to your house. Then I ordered my attendant marids to sink the ship, and I transformed your two sisters into these black bitches — for I know everything that has passed between them and you. But as for the young man, the truth is that he is drowned."

So saying, she flew up with me and the bitches, and presently set us down on the terrace roof of my house, where I found the whole of the property that had been in my ship already stored, with nothing missing.

"Now," the serpent that was went on, "I swear by everything engraved on the seal ring of Solomon, on whom be peace: unless you give each of these bitches three hundred stripes every day, I will come and imprison you for ever under the earth."

I answered, "Hearing and obedience!" And away she flew. But before going she charged me again, saying, "I swear again by Him who made the two seas flow — and let this be my second oath — that if you disobey me I will come and transform you as I have your sisters."

Since then I have never once failed, Commander of the Faithful, to beat them with that number of blows, until their blood flows along with my tears — and I pitying them all the while. And they know perfectly well that their being scourged is no fault of mine, and they accept my excuses.

And this is my tale and my history.

The Caliph marvelled at her adventures, and then signed to Ja'afar, who said to the second lady, the doorkeeper, "And you — how did you come by the welts and the weals on your body?"

So she began the

The Doorkeeper's Tale

Know, Commander of the Faithful, that I had a father who, when his time was up, died and left me a great store of wealth. I stayed single a short while and then married one of the richest men of his day. I lived with him a year, when he died too; and my share of his property came to eighty thousand gold dinars, according to the holy law of inheritance.

So I became extremely rich, and my reputation spread far and wide, for I had ten changes of clothing made for me, each one worth a thousand dinars.

One day, as I was sitting at home, in came an old woman with a lantern jaw and sunken cheeks, and eyes puckered up, and eyebrows scant and scabby, and a head bare and bald; teeth broken by time and mauled, back bending and neck-nape nodding, face blotched, nose running, hair speckled black and white like a snake, and in complexion a perfect fright — just as the poet says of such a woman:

	Ill-omened hag! May her sins never be shriven
	nor mercy visit her on her dying bed.
	Her wiles could lead a thousand of the strongest mules,
	bolt as they might, on a thread of spider silk.

And as another says:

	A hag to whom the unlawful is the most lawful thing there is,
	and witchcraft has grown into wisdom in her sight.
	A mischief-making brat, a demon girl,
	a whorish woman and a pimping crone.

When the old woman came in she greeted me and kissed the ground before me and said:

"I have an orphan daughter at home, and tonight is her wedding and her displaying. We are poor folk and strangers in this city, and we know nobody who lives here, and we are broken-hearted. So earn yourself a reward and a recompense in Heaven by being present at her displaying; and when the ladies of this city hear that you are going to put in an appearance, they will come too. And so you will comfort her affliction, for she is badly bruised in spirit and has nobody to look to but Allah the Most High."

Then she wept and kissed my feet, reciting these lines:

	"Your presence brings a grace on us
	that we acknowledge before your winsome face;
	and if you were absent there is not one
	who could stand in your stead or take your place."

So pity and compassion took hold of me, and I said, "To hear is to consent; and please Allah I will do more than that for her, and she shall not be shown to her bridegroom except in my own clothes and ornaments and jewellery."

At this the old woman rejoiced and bowed her head to my feet and kissed them, saying, "Allah repay you with good and comfort your heart as you have comforted mine! But, my lady, do not trouble yourself to do me this service now; be ready by supper time, and I will come and fetch you."

And saying that, she kissed my hand and went her way.

I set about stringing my pearls and putting on my brocades and doing my face, little reckoning what Fortune had in her womb for me — when suddenly the old woman stood in front of me, simpering and smiling until she showed every tooth stump, and said, "My mistress, the city ladies have arrived; and when I told them you had promised to be present, they were delighted, and they are waiting for you now and looking eagerly for your coming and for the honour of meeting you."

So I threw on my cloak, and making the old crone walk in front of me and my maids behind me, I went on until we came to a street well watered and swept neat, where the winnowing breeze blew cool and sweet.

Here we were stopped by a gate arched over with a dome of marble, firmly seated on the solidest foundation, and leading to a palace whose walls rose tall and proud from the ground and whose pinnacle was crowned by the clouds. And over the doorway these lines were written:

	I am the house where Mirth shall always smile,
	the home of Joy for as long as I last.
	And in my courtyard a fountain jets and flows
	that neither tears nor troubles shall defile.
	Its margin is decked with the royal anemone,
	with myrtle, and narcissus flower, and camomile.

Arriving at the gate, which had a black curtain hanging in front of it, the old woman knocked, and it was opened to us; and we went in and found a hallway spread with carpets and hung all round with lamps, all of them lit, and wax candles in candelabra decorated with pendants of precious gems and noble metals.

We passed on through this passage until we came into a great room whose like for grandeur and beauty is not to be found in this world. It was hung and carpeted with silks, and lit with branched sconces and tapers ranged in a double row — an avenue running up to the upper and noble end of the room, where stood a couch of juniper wood encrusted with pearls and gems and topped by a canopy with mosquito curtains of satin looped up with pearls.

And we had hardly taken all this in when there came out from under the canopy a young lady — and I looked, Commander of the Faithful, on a face and a figure more perfect than the moon at its fullest, with a countenance brighter than the dawn and gleaming with saffron-coloured light, exactly as the poet sang when he said:

	You pace the palace, a marvel to see,
	a bride fit for a Chosroes or a Caesar.
	The rose plays wanton on your rosy cheek,
	O cheek as bright as dragon's blood!
	Slim-waisted, languorous, sleepy-eyed,
	with charms that promise every delight of love.
	And the head-dress that dresses your crowned brow
	is a night of grief laid over a glad morning's light.

The lovely young girl came down from the dais and said to me, "Welcome, and well come, and good cheer to my sister, the dearly beloved, the illustrious — and a thousand greetings!" And then she recited these lines:

	"If the house could only know who is coming it would rejoice
	and would kiss the very dust your foot has stood on;
	and with the tongue of circumstance the walls would say,
	Welcome and hail to one graced with generous gifts!"

Then she sat down and said to me, "Sister, I have a brother who has caught sight of you at various wedding feasts and festivals. He is a young man handsomer than I am, and he has fallen desperately in love with you, because generous Destiny has gathered up all beauty and perfection in you; and he has given money to this old woman so that she might visit you, and she has contrived in this way to bring the two of us together.

"He has heard that you are one of the notables of your family, and he is nothing less in his; and being anxious to join his lot to yours, he has practised this device to bring me into your company. For he is eager to marry you according to the ordinance of Allah and His Apostle; and in what is lawful and right there is no shame."

When I heard this, and saw myself fairly trapped in the house, I said, "To hear is to consent."

She was delighted and clapped her hands; at which a door opened and out came a young man in the flower of his youth, exquisitely dressed, a model of beauty and loveliness and symmetry and perfect grace, with gentle winning manners, and eyebrows like a bent bow with the arrow on the string, and eyes that bewitched every heart with a sorcery that is lawful in the sight of the Lord — as some rhymer says, describing his like:

	His face shines like the face of the young moon
	and Fortune stamps him with pearls for signs.

And Allah favour the man who said:

	Blessed be his beauty; blessed the Lord's decree
	who cast and shaped a thing of such brightness.
	He joins all the gifts of beauty into one;
	all humanity is lost in loving him;
	for Beauty herself has written on his forehead,
	"I testify that there is no Good but he."

When I looked at him my heart inclined to him and I loved him; and he sat down at my side and talked with me a while, when the young lady clapped her hands again — and a side door opened, and out came the judge with his four assessors as witnesses; and they greeted us and sat down and drew up and wrote out the marriage contract between me and the young man, and withdrew.

Then he turned to me and said, "May our night be blessed"; and presently added, "My lady, I have a condition to lay on you."

Said I, "My lord, what is that?"

At which he got up and fetched a copy of the Holy Book and handed it to me, saying, "Swear on this that you will never look at any man but me, and never incline your body or your heart to another."

I swore to it readily enough, and he was overjoyed and put his arms round my neck, while love for him took possession of my whole heart.

Then they set the table in front of us, and we ate and drank until we were satisfied; but I was dying for the night to come. And when night did come he led me to the bridal chamber and slept with me on the bed, and went on kissing and holding me till the morning — such a night as I had never seen even in my dreams.

I lived with him a life of happiness and delight for a full month, at the end of which I asked his leave to go on foot to the market and buy myself certain particular stuffs; and he gave me permission.

So I put on my cloak, and taking with me the old woman and a slave girl, went to the silk merchants' hall, where I sat down in the shop front of a young merchant whom the old woman recommended, saying to me:

"This young man's father died when he was a boy and left him a great store of wealth. He has a very fine stock of goods by him, and you will find what you are looking for with him, for nobody in the market has better stuffs than he has."

Then she said to him, "Show this lady the most costly stuffs you have"; and he replied, "Hearing and obedience!"

Then she whispered to me, "Say a civil word to him." But I replied, "I am pledged to speak to no man except my husband." And as she started sounding his praises I said sharply to her, "We want none of your sweet speeches; what we want is to buy whatever we need from him and go home."

So he brought me everything I was looking for and I offered him his money; but he refused to take it, saying, "Let it be a gift offered to my guest today."

Then I said to the old woman, "If he will not take the money, give him back his stuff."

"By Allah," he cried, "I will take nothing from you. I do not sell it for gold or for silver; I give the whole lot as a gift, for a single kiss — a kiss more precious to me than everything in this shop."

The old woman asked, "And what will the kiss profit you?" And turning to me, she whispered, "Daughter, you hear what this young fellow says. What harm will it do you if he gets a kiss from you and you get what you were looking for at that price?"

I replied, "I take refuge with Allah from any such thing! Do you not know that I am bound by an oath?"

But she answered, "Now hush! Just let him kiss you, and neither speak to him nor lean over him; so you will keep your oath and your silver, and no harm at all will come to you."

And she did not stop persuading me and pressing me and making light of the matter, until evil got into my mind; and I put my head in the sack and, declaring I would never consent, consented.

So I veiled my eyes and held up the edge of my cloak between me and the people going past, and he put his mouth to my cheek under the veil. But while he was kissing me he bit me — so hard a bite that it tore the flesh off my cheek, and the blood ran fast, and I fainted.

The old woman caught me in her arms; and when I came round I found the shop shut up and her grieving over me and saying, "Thank Allah for averting what might have been worse."

Then she said to me, "Come, take heart, and let us go home before the matter becomes public and you are dishonoured. And when you are safe inside the house, pretend to be ill and lie down and cover yourself up; and I will bring you powders and plasters to cure this bite with, and your wound will be healed in three days at the most."

So after a while I got up, in extreme distress and with terror full upon me; but I went on little by little until I reached the house, when I pleaded illness and lay down.

When it was night my husband came in to me and said, "What has happened to you, my darling, on this excursion of yours?"

And I replied, "I am not well; my head is aching badly."

Then he lit a candle and came close to me and looked hard at me and asked, "What is that wound I see on your cheek — and in the tenderest part of it too?"

And I answered, "When I went out today with your permission to buy stuffs, a camel loaded with firewood jostled me, and one of the pieces tore my veil and wounded my cheek as you see; for the streets of this city are truly narrow."

"Tomorrow," he cried, "I will go and complain to the Governor, and he shall hang every firewood seller in Baghdad."

"In Allah's name," I said, "do not burden your soul with such a sin against any man. The fact is that I was riding on a donkey and it stumbled and threw me to the ground, and my cheek landed on a stick or a piece of glass and got this wound."

"Then," said he, "tomorrow I will go up to Ja'afar the Barmecide and tell him the story, and he shall kill every donkey boy in Baghdad."

"Would you destroy all these men because of my wound," I said, "when what happened to me was by the decree of Allah and His destiny?"

But he answered, "There is no help for it." And springing to his feet, he plied me with words and pressed me until I was confused and frightened; and I stuttered and stammered and my speech grew thick, and I said, "This is a mere accident, by the decree of Allah."

Then, Commander of the Faithful, he guessed my case, and said, "You have been false to your oath."

He cried out at once with a loud cry, at which a door opened and in came seven Black slaves, whom he ordered to drag me from my bed and throw me down in the middle of the room. Then he ordered one of them to pinion my elbows and squat on my head; and a second to sit on my knees and hold my feet; and drawing his sword, he gave it to a third and said:

"Strike her, Sa'ad, and cut her in two, and let each of you take half and throw it into the Tigris for the fish to eat. For that is the retribution due to those who violate their vows and are unfaithful to their love."

And he redoubled in fury, and recited these lines:

	"If there were somebody who shared her love with me,
	I would strangle Love, though my life were killed by Love,
	saying, O Soul, Death would be the nobler choice,
	for Love is a bad thing when shared between two partners."

Then he repeated to the slave, "Strike her, Sa'ad!"

And when the slave who was sitting on me was sure of the order, he bent down to me and said, "My mistress, repeat the profession of faith, and think whether there is anything you would like done; for truly this is the last hour of your life."

"Good slave," I said, "wait just a little, and get off my head so that I can charge you with my last instructions."

Then I raised my head and saw the state I was in — how I had fallen from a high position into the lowest disgrace, and into death after such a life as I had had; and how I had brought my punishment on myself by my own sin. And at that the tears streamed from my eyes and I wept beyond all weeping.

But he looked at me with eyes full of anger and began repeating:

	"Tell the woman who turns away from our love to work it a sore injury,
	and takes herself a fine new love and tosses the old one over:
	we have had enough of you before you shall cry enough of us.
	What passed between us is sufficient, and perhaps something more."

When I heard this, Commander of the Faithful, I wept and looked at him and began repeating these lines:

	"You doom my love to separation and stay unmoved yourself;
	you make my sore lids sleepless and sleep while I complain.
	You make a firm friendship reign between my eyes and insomnia,
	and yet my heart cannot forget you, nor can I hold back my tears.
	You made me swear with many an oath to keep my faith for ever;
	but when you reigned as the lord of my breast you worked me a traitor's ruin.
	I loved you like a silly child who does not know what Love is;
	so spare the learner, do not let her be killed by the master.
	By the name of Allah I beg you, when I am dead and gone,
	write on my tomb: this woman died of Love, whose senses Love had taken.
	Then perhaps somebody will pass that way who has felt the fire of Love,
	and treading on a lover's heart will melt with pity and with grief."

When I had finished my verses the tears came again; but the poetry and the weeping only added fury to his fury, and he recited:

	"It was not satiety that made me leave the darling of my soul,
	but that she sinned a mortal sin that caught me in its grip:
	she tried to let another man share the love between the two of us,
	but my true Faith in Unity refuses any partnership."

When he had stopped reciting I wept again, and begged his pardon and humbled myself in front of him and spoke to him softly, saying to myself, "I will work on him with words; and perhaps he will hold back from killing me, even if he takes everything I have."

So I complained of my sufferings and began to repeat these lines:

	"Now, by your life — if you were just, you would not have taken my life;
	but who can break the law of separation that parts two lovers?
	You load me with the heavy weight of longing love, when I
	can hardly bear the weight of my own shift for weakness and for pain.
	I do not marvel to see my life and soul laid in ruins;
	I marvel much to see my body bear such pangs of separation."

When I had finished my verse I wept again; and he looked at me and reviled me in abusive language, repeating these lines:

	"You were all taken up with the love of another man, not me;
	it was yours to show me the face of separation, mine only to see it.
	I will leave you, because you were the first of us to take your leave,
	and bear that parting blow as patiently as you bore it.
	Just as you went looking for another love, so I will look for another,
	and make the crime of murdering love your own atrocity."

When he had finished his verses he cried out to the slave again, "Cut her in half and free us from her, for we have no profit of her."

So the slave came close to me, Commander of the Faithful; and I stopped bandying verses and made certain of death, and despairing of life, committed my affairs to Almighty Allah — when the old woman rushed in and threw herself at my husband's feet and kissed them and wept and said:

"My son, by the rights of my having nursed you and by my long service to you, I beg you to pardon this young lady, for truly she has done nothing to deserve such a doom. You are a very young man, and I am afraid her death may be laid at your door; for it is said: whoever kills shall be killed. As for this wanton — since that is what you think her — drive her out of your doors, out of your love and out of your heart."

And she did not stop weeping and pressing him until he relented and said, "I pardon her. But I must set my mark on her, and it shall show on her all her life."

Then he ordered the slaves to drag me along the ground and lay me out at full length, after stripping me of all my clothes; and when the slaves had sat on me so that I could not move, he fetched a rod of quince wood and came down with it on my body, and went on beating me across the back and the sides until I lost consciousness from the pain, and I despaired of my life.

Then he ordered the slaves to take me away as soon as it was dark, along with the old woman to show them the way, and to throw me down on the floor of the house I had lived in before my marriage. They did their master's bidding, and threw me down in my old home, and went their way.

I did not come out of my faint until dawn appeared, when I set about dressing my wounds with ointments and other medicines; and I doctored myself — but my sides and my ribs still show the marks of the rod, as you have seen.

I lay weak and confined to my bed four months before I was able to get up, and my health came back to me. At the end of that time I went to the house where all this had happened, and found it a ruin; the whole street had been pulled down from end to end and heaps of rubbish stood where the building had been; and I could not learn how it had come about.

Then I went to this sister of mine on my father's side, and found her with these two black bitches. I greeted her and told her what had happened to me and the whole of my story, and she said, "Sister, who is safe from the spite of Time, and who is secure? Thanks be to Allah, who has brought you off safely." And she began to say:

	"Such is the world, so keep a patient heart
	when riches leave you and when friends depart."

Then she told me her own story, and what had happened to her with her two sisters, and how it had all ended. So we lived together, and the subject of marriage was never on our tongues in all these years.

After a while we were joined by our other sister, the caterer, who goes out every morning and buys everything we need for the day and the night; and we went on in that condition until last night.

In the morning our sister went out as usual to do her marketing, and then there happened to us what happened, from bringing the porter into the house and admitting these three kalandars.

We treated them kindly and honourably, and a quarter of the night had not gone by before three grave and respectable merchants from Mosul joined us and told us their adventures. We sat talking with them, but on one condition, which they broke; at which we treated them as suited their breach of promise, and made them repeat the account they had given of themselves. They did as we told them, and we forgave their offence; so they left us. And this morning we were unexpectedly summoned into your presence.

And such is our story.

The Caliph marvelled at her words and ordered the tale to be written down and put on record and laid up in his record rooms:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Nineteenth Night,

she went on: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Caliph commanded this story, and those of the sister and the kalandars, to be recorded in the archives and set in the royal record rooms.

Then he asked the eldest lady, the mistress of the house, "Do you know where the ifritah is who put your sisters under a spell?"

And she answered, "Commander of the Faithful, she gave me a ringlet of her hair, saying: whenever you want to see me, burn a couple of these hairs and I will be with you at once, even if I were beyond Mount Kaf."

Said the Caliph, "Bring me the hair."

So she brought it, and he threw the whole lock on the fire. And as soon as the smell of the burning hair spread, the palace shook and trembled, and everybody there heard a rumbling and rolling of thunder and a noise as of wings — and the jinniyah who had been a serpent stood in the Caliph's presence.

Now she was a Muslim, so she greeted him and said, "Peace be with you, Vicar of Allah"; to which he replied, "And with you also be peace, and the mercy of Allah and His blessing."

Then she went on, "Know that this girl sowed the seed of kindness for me, and I cannot repay her enough, in that she delivered me from death and destroyed my enemy. Now I had seen how her sisters dealt with her, and I felt bound to avenge her on them. At first I meant to kill them, but I was afraid it would grieve her, so I transformed them into bitches. But if you want them released, Commander of the Faithful, I will release them to please you and her, for I am one of the Muslims."

Said the Caliph, "Release them; and afterwards we will look into the affair of the beaten lady and consider her case carefully; and if the truth of her story is proved, I will exact retaliation from the man who wronged her."

Said the ifritah, "Commander of the Faithful, I will release them at once; and I will show you the man who did that deed to this lady and wronged her and took her property — and he is the nearest of all men to you."

So saying, she took a cup of water and muttered a spell over it and spoke words there was no understanding; and then she sprinkled some of the water over the faces of the two bitches, saying, "Return to your former human shape!" — at which they were restored to their natural forms and fell to praising their Creator.

Then said the ifritah, "Commander of the Faithful, the truth is that the man who scourged this lady with rods is your son Al-Amin, brother of Al-Ma'mun. For he had heard of her beauty and loveliness, and he played a lover's trick on her and married her according to the law, and committed the crime — such as it is — of scourging her.

"And yet he is not to be blamed for beating her, for he laid a condition on her and swore her by a solemn oath not to do a certain thing; and she was false to her vow. He meant to put her to death, but he feared Almighty Allah and contented himself with scourging her, as you have seen, and with sending her back to her own place. Such is the story of the second lady, and the Lord knows all."

When the Caliph heard these words from the ifritah, and knew who had beaten the girl, he marvelled with a mighty marvelling and said:

"Praise be to Allah, the Most High, the Almighty, who has shown me such exceeding mercy, letting me deliver these two girls from sorcery and torture, and granting me the knowledge of the secret of this lady's history! And now, by Allah, we will do a deed that shall be recorded of us after we are gone."

Then he summoned his son Al-Amin and questioned him about the story of the second lady, the doorkeeper; and he told it in the face of truth.

At which the Caliph had the judges and their witnesses called in, and the three kalandars, and the first lady with her full sisters who had been under the spell. And he married the three sisters to the three kalandars, whom he knew to be princes and the sons of kings, and appointed them chamberlains about his own person, assigning them stipends and allowances and everything they needed, and lodging them in his palace at Baghdad.

He returned the beaten lady to his son Al-Amin, renewing the marriage contract between them and giving her great wealth, and ordered the house rebuilt finer than it had been before.

As for himself, he took the caterer as his wife and lay with her that night; and next day he set apart an apartment for her in his own palace, with maids to serve her and a fixed daily allowance.

And the people marvelled at their Caliph's generosity and his natural kindness and his princely wisdom; nor did he forget to send all these histories to be recorded in his annals.

When Shahrazad stopped speaking, Dunyazad exclaimed, "Sister, by Allah, this is truly a most pleasant tale and a delightful one; the like of it was never heard. But please tell me another story now, to while away what is left of the waking hours of this night of ours."

She replied, "With love and gladness, if the King gives me leave."

And he said, "Tell your tale, and tell it quickly."

So she began, in these words,

The Hunchback's Tale

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that in the old days, and in the old time before them, there lived in a certain city of China a tailor, an open-handed man who loved pleasure and merrymaking, and who used to go out with his wife from time to time to amuse themselves at the public entertainments.

One day they went out at first light and were coming home in the evening when they fell in with a hunchback, whose appearance would raise a laugh out of care itself and drive off the horrors of despair. So they went over to enjoy the look of him, and invited him home to talk and drink with them that night.

He agreed, and walked home with them; at which the tailor went out to the market — night having just set in — and bought a fried fish and bread and lemons and dried sweets for dessert, and set the food in front of the hunchback, and they ate.

Presently the tailor's wife took a great chunk of fish and gave it to the hunchback in one lump, stopping his mouth with her hand and saying, "By Allah, you must get it down at a single gulp; I am not giving you time to chew it."

So he bolted it. But there was a stiff bone in it, which stuck in his throat; and his hour having come, he died:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Twenty-fifth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the tailor's wife gave the hunchback that mouthful of fish which ended his term of days, he died on the instant.

Seeing it, the tailor cried aloud, "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah! Alas that this poor wretch should have died in such a stupid way, and at our hands!"

And the woman answered, "Why all this idle talk? Have you not heard the man who said:

	Why then do I waste my time in grief, until I
	find no friend to carry my weight of woe?
	How am I to sleep on a fire that is never put out?
	To rest on the flames would be hard enough!"

Her husband asked, "And what am I to do with him?"

And she answered, "Get up and take him in your arms and spread a silk cloth over him; then I will go out with you following me, this very night; and if you meet anybody, say: this is my son, and his mother and I are carrying him to the doctor to have him looked at."

So he got up and took the hunchback in his arms and carried him along the streets, with his wife going in front of him crying, "My son, Allah keep you! Which part is hurting you, and where has this smallpox got at you?" So that everybody who saw them said, "It is a child sick with smallpox."

They went along asking for the doctor's house, until people directed them to the house of a physician who was a Jew. They knocked at the door, and a black slave girl came down and opened it; and seeing a man carrying a baby, with a woman beside him, she said, "What is the matter?"

"We have a little one with us," answered the tailor's wife, "and we want to show him to the physician. So take this quarter dinar and give it to your master and let him come down and see my son, who is very sick."

The girl went up to tell her master — at which the tailor's wife stepped into the hallway and said to her husband, "Leave the hunchback here and let us run for our lives."

So the tailor carried the dead man to the top of the stairs and propped him upright against the wall, and away he ran, he and his wife.

Meanwhile the girl went in to the Jew and said, "At the door there is a man and a woman with a sick child, and they have given me a quarter dinar for you, so that you will go down and look at the little one and prescribe for it."

As soon as the Jew saw the quarter dinar he was delighted, and got up quickly in his eagerness for the money, and went out in a hurry in the dark. But he had hardly taken a step before he tripped over the corpse and knocked it over, and it rolled to the bottom of the staircase.

So he shouted to the girl to hurry up with the light, and she brought it; and he went down and examined the hunchback and found him stone dead.

At which he cried out, "O Ezra! O Moses! O Aaron! O Joshua son of Nun! O the Ten Commandments! I have tripped over the sick man and he has fallen downstairs and he is dead! How am I to get this man I have killed out of my house? O by the hooves of the ass of Ezra!"

Then he picked the body up and carried it into the house and told his wife what had happened; and she said to him, "Why are you sitting still? If you keep him here till daybreak we shall both lose our lives. Let the two of us carry him up to the terrace roof and drop him over into the house of our neighbour the Muslim; for if he stays there a night the dogs will come down on him from the next-door terraces and eat him up."

Now this neighbour was a steward, the controller of the Sultan's kitchen, and he used to bring home a great store of oil and fat and scraps of meat; but the cats and the rats used to eat it, or if the dogs smelt a fat sheep's tail they would come down off the nearest roofs and tear at it; and in this way the animals had already done a good deal of damage to what he brought home.

So the Jew and his wife carried the hunchback up to the roof, and letting him down by his hands and feet through the ventilator shaft into the steward's house, propped him against the wall and went their way.

They had hardly done it when the steward, who had been spending the evening with friends listening to a recitation of the Koran, came home and opened the door; and going up with a lighted candle, found a son of Adam standing in the corner under the ventilator.

When he saw this he said, "Well! By Allah, very good indeed! So the thing that has been robbing my stores is nothing but a man."

Then he turned to the hunchback and said, "So it is you who steal the meat and the fat! I thought it was the cats and the dogs, and I kill the dogs and cats of the quarter and sin against them by killing them. And all the while it is you, coming down from the house terrace through the ventilator. But I will avenge myself on you with my own hand!"

So he snatched up a heavy hammer and set on him and struck him full in the chest, and he fell down. Then he examined him, and finding that he was dead, cried out in horror, thinking he had killed him, and said, "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great!"

And he was afraid for his own life, and added, "Allah curse the oil and the meat and the grease and the sheep's tails into the bargain! How has fate given this man his quietus at my hand?"

Then he looked at the body, and seeing it was a hunchback, said, "Was it not enough for you to be a hunchback, without being a thief as well and pinching meat and fat? O Thou the Veiler, deign to veil me with Thy curtain of concealment!"

So he took him up on his shoulders, and going out with him from his house towards the end of the night, carried him to the nearest end of the market, where he set him on his feet against the wall of a shop at the head of a dark lane, and left him and went away.

After a while up came a Christian, the Sultan's broker, who was very much the worse for drink and was heading for the baths, his drunkenness whispering in his ear, "Truly the call to morning prayer is close."

He came plodding along and staggering about until he got near the hunchback, and squatted down to relieve himself opposite him; when he happened to glance round and saw a man standing against the wall.

Now somebody had snatched the Christian's turban off him earlier in the night; so when he saw the hunchback close by, he imagined that this one meant to steal his headdress too. At which he clenched his fist and struck him on the neck, felling him to the ground, and called out for the market watchman; and he came down on the body in his drunken fury and went on pounding it and throttling it.

Presently the watchman came up and, finding a Christian kneeling on a Muslim and beating him, asked, "What harm has this man done?"

And the broker answered, "The fellow meant to snatch my turban off."

"Get up off him," said the watchman.

So he got up; and the watchman went over to the hunchback and, finding him dead, exclaimed, "By Allah, good indeed! A Christian killing a Muslim!"

Then he seized the broker and tied his hands behind his back and carried him off to the Governor's house — the Christian saying to himself all the way, "O Messiah! O Virgin! how did I come to kill this fellow? And what a hurry he must have been in to leave this life, dying of a single blow!"

Presently, as his drunkenness left him, misery came in its place.

So the broker and the body were kept at the Governor's place until the morning came, when the Governor came out and gave orders to hang the supposed murderer, and commanded the executioner to proclaim the sentence.

They set up a gallows at once and made the Christian stand under it, and the torch-bearer, who was also the hangman, threw the rope round his neck and passed one end through the pulley and was about to hoist him up — when the steward, passing by, saw the broker about to be hanged; and making his way through the crowd, shouted to the executioner, "Stop! Stop! I am the man who killed the hunchback!"

The Governor asked, "What made you kill him?"

And he answered, "I went home last night and found this man, who had come down the ventilator to steal my property; so I hit him on the chest with a hammer, and he died on the spot. Then I picked him up and carried him to the market and stood him against the wall in such a place, near such a lane." And he added, "Is it not enough for me to have killed a Muslim, without killing a Christian as well? So hang nobody but me."

When the Governor heard this he released the broker and said to the torch-bearer, "Hang this man, on his own confession."

So he loosed the cord from the Christian's neck and threw it round the steward's, and stood him under the gallows tree, and was about to string him up — when the Jewish physician pushed through the crowd and shouted to the executioner:

"Stop! Stop! It was I and nobody else who killed the hunchback! Last night I was sitting at home when a man and a woman knocked at the door carrying this hunchback, who was sick, and gave my maid a quarter dinar, telling her to hand me the fee and tell me to come down and see him.

"While she was gone, the man and the woman brought him into the house and set him on the stairs and went away; and presently I came down and did not see him, because I was in the dark, and tripped over him, and he fell to the foot of the staircase and died that instant.

"Then my wife and I took him up and carried him to the top terrace; and this steward's house being next door to mine, we let the body down through the ventilator. When he came home and found the hunchback in his house he thought he was a thief and hit him with a hammer, so that he fell to the ground, and our neighbour made certain he had killed him.

"Now is it not enough for me to have killed one Muslim without knowing it, without burdening myself with taking another Muslim's life knowingly?"

When the Governor heard this he said to the hangman, "Set the steward free and hang the Jew."

At which the torch-bearer took him and slung the cord round his neck — when the tailor pushed through the crowd and shouted to the executioner:

"Stop! Stop! It was I and nobody else who killed the hunchback, and this is how it happened. I had been out enjoying myself yesterday, and coming back for supper, fell in with this hunchback, who was drunk and drumming away and singing loudly to his tambourine.

"So I got talking to him and took him home and bought a fish, and we sat down to eat. Presently my wife took a chunk of fish and made a lump of it and crammed it into his mouth; but some of it went down the wrong way or stuck in his throat, and he died on the instant.

"So my wife and I lifted him up and carried him to the Jew's house, where the slave girl came down and opened the door to us, and I said to her: tell your master there is a man and a woman and a sick person for him to see. I gave her a quarter dinar and she went up to tell her master; and while she was gone I carried the hunchback to the top of the staircase and propped him against the wall, and went off with my wife. When the Jew came down he tripped over him and thought he had killed him."

Then he asked the Jew, "Is this the truth?"

And the Jew answered, "It is."

At which the tailor turned to the Governor and said, "Let the Jew go and hang me."

When the Governor heard the tailor's tale he marvelled at this business of the hunchback and exclaimed, "Truly this is an adventure that ought to be written down in books!"

Then he said to the hangman, "Let the Jew go and hang the tailor, on his own confession."

The executioner took the tailor and put the rope round his neck and said, "I am tired of this slow work. We bring out this one and change him for that one, and nobody gets hanged after all."

Now the hunchback in question, they say, was jester to the Sultan of China, who could not bear him out of his sight. So when the fellow got drunk and did not turn up that night or the next day until noon, the Sultan asked some of his courtiers about him, and they answered:

"Our lord, the Governor came upon him dead and has ordered his murderer to be hanged; but as the hangman was about to hoist him up there came a second man, and a third, and a fourth, and each of them said, 'It is I and nobody else who killed the hunchback!' and each gave a full and detailed account of how the jester came to be killed."

When the King heard this he called out to the chamberlain in waiting, "Go down to the Governor and bring me all four of them."

So the chamberlain went down at once to the place of execution, where he found the torch-bearer on the point of hanging the tailor, and shouted to him, "Stop! Stop!"

Then he gave the King's command to the Governor, who took the tailor, the Jew, the Christian and the steward — the hunchback's body being carried on men's shoulders — and went up with the whole lot of them to the King.

When he came into the presence he kissed the ground and told the ruler the whole story, which there is no need to repeat; for, as they say, there is no use in a tale told three times.

The Sultan, hearing it, marvelled and was moved to laughter, and commanded the story to be written down in letters of liquid gold, saying to the people about him, "Did you ever hear a more wonderful tale than that of my hunchback?"

At which the Christian broker came forward and said, "O King of the age, with your leave I will tell you something that happened to myself, and which is still more wonderful and marvellous and pleasing and delightful than the tale of the hunchback."

Said the King, "Tell us what you have to say."

So he began in these words

The Christian Broker's Story

O King of the age, I came to this country of yours with merchandise, and Destiny kept me here among you; but the place of my birth was Cairo in Egypt, where I was brought up as well, for I am one of the Copts, and my father was a broker before me. When I came of age he departed this life and I took over his business.

One day, as I was sitting in my shop, there came up to me a young man as handsome as could be, wearing sumptuous clothes and riding a fine donkey. When he saw me he greeted me, and I stood up to do him honour; and then he took out a handkerchief with a sample of sesame in it and asked, "How much is this worth an ardabb?" — which is the great Egyptian measure for grain.

I answered, "A hundred dirhams."

Said he, "Take porters and gaugers and measurers and come tomorrow to the Khan al-Jawali, by the Gate of Victory quarter, where you will find me."

Then he went off, leaving the sample of sesame with me in his handkerchief; and I went round my customers and established that every ardabb would fetch a hundred and twenty dirhams.
