Next day I took four measurers and walked with them to the khan, where I found him waiting for me. As soon as he saw me he got up and opened his storehouse, and we measured the grain until the store was empty; and we found the contents came to fifty ardabbs, making five thousand pieces of silver.

Then he said, "Let ten dirhams on every ardabb be your brokerage; so take the price and keep four thousand five hundred dirhams on deposit for me; and when I have finished selling the other goods in my warehouses I will come to you and collect the amount."

"Very good," I replied; and kissing his hand, I went away, having made a profit of a thousand dirhams that day.

He was gone a month, at the end of which he came to me and asked, "Where are the dirhams?"

I got up and greeted him and said, "Will you not eat something in my house?"

But he refused, with the remark, "Get the money ready and I will come back presently and take it." Then he rode away.

So I brought out the dirhams and sat down to wait for him; but he stayed away another month, and then came back and said, "Where are the dirhams?"

I got up and greeted him and asked, "Will you not eat something in my house?"

But again he refused, adding, "Get the money ready for me and I will come back presently and take it." Then he rode off.

So I brought out the dirhams and sat down to wait for him; but he stayed away from me a third month, and I said, "Truly this young man is generosity in human form."

At the end of the month he came up, riding a she-mule and wearing a suit of sumptuous clothes; and he was like the moon on the night of its fullness, and he seemed fresh from the baths, with his cheeks rosy bright and his brow flower-white and a mole like a grain of ambergris delighting the sight — as the poet said about such a man:

	The full moon and the sun rose in a single house
	and shone in the brightest splendour and good fortune,
	changing every spirit with their happy brilliance.
	Hail to the thing that rewards prayer with such a gift!
	Their charms and their grace have reached perfection's height;
	they have conquered every heart and won over every wit.
	Praise to the Lord for works so strange and wonderful,
	and for whatever the Almighty wills His hand has done.

When I saw him I rose and called down blessings on him and asked, "My lord, will you not take your money?"

"Why the hurry?" said he. "Wait till I have finished my business and then I will come and take it." And again he rode away.

And I said to myself, "By Allah, when he comes next time I really must make him my guest; for I have traded with his dirhams and made large profits by them."

At the end of the year he came again, dressed in a suit even more sumptuous than the last; and when I begged him, by the Gospel, to come down at my house and eat my guest-food, he said, "I agree, on condition that whatever you spend on me comes out of my own money that is still in your hands."

I answered, "So be it"; and I sat him down while I got ready everything necessary in the way of food and drink and the rest, and set the tray in front of him with the invitation, "In Allah's name!"

Then he drew up to the tray and put out his left hand and ate with me; and I wondered at his not using his right hand.

When we had finished eating I poured water over his hand and gave him something to dry it with. At which we sat down to talk, after I had set some sweets in front of him; and I said to him, "My master, please relieve my mind and tell me why you eat with your left hand. Is there something wrong with the other one?"

When he heard this he recited these lines:

	"Dear friend, do not ask what burns in my breast,
	in case you see fiery pains no eye ever saw.
	It is not that my heart chooses to house Salma
	in place of Layla's love — but need has never a law."

And he put his right arm out of his sleeve — and the hand was cut off, a wrist without a fist.

I was astounded at it; but he said, "Do not be surprised, and do not think I ate with my left hand out of conceit or bad manners, but out of necessity. And the cutting off of my right hand came about by the strangest adventure."

I asked, "And what caused it?"

And he answered: Know that I am one of the sons of Baghdad, and my father was among the notables of that city. When I came of age I heard the pilgrims and travellers, the wayfarers and the merchants, talking about the land of Egypt, and their words sank deep into my mind; until my father died, when I took a large sum of money and fitted myself out for trade with stuffs from Baghdad and Mosul, and packing them into bales, set out on my travels. And Allah decreed safety for me until I came into this city of yours.

Then he wept, and began repeating:

	The bleary-eyed escapes the pits
	that the lynx-eyed falls into.
	A word will kill the wise man
	and save the simpleton.
	The Muslim goes short of food
	while the unbeliever feasts in hall.
	What art or act belongs to a man?
	The will of God binds everybody.

Now when he had finished his verse he said:

So I came into Cairo and took off my loads and stored my goods in the Khan al-Masrur. Then I gave the servant a few silver pieces to buy me some food, and lay down to sleep a while. When I woke I went to the street called Bayn al-Kasrayn — Between the Two Palaces — and came back presently and spent the night at the khan.

When morning came I opened a bale and took out some cloth, saying to myself, "I will go off and walk through some of the markets and see the state of trade." So I loaded the stuff onto some of my slaves and went out until I reached the Exchange of Jaharkas, where the brokers, who knew I had come, came out to meet me.

They took the stuffs and cried them for sale, but could not get even the prime cost of them. I was vexed at this; however, the chief of the brokers said to me:

"My lord, I will tell you how you may make a profit on your goods. You should do as the merchants do, and sell your merchandise on credit for a fixed term, on a contract drawn up by a notary and properly witnessed; and employ a money-changer to collect your dues every Monday and Thursday. That way you will gain two dirhams and more for every one; and you will amuse yourself and pass the time seeing Cairo and the Nile."

Said I, "This is sound advice," and took the brokers back to the khan. They took my stuffs and went with them to the Exchange, where I sold them well, taking bonds for the value. These bonds I deposited with a money-changer, who gave me a receipt, and I went back to the khan with it.

Here I stayed a whole month, breaking my fast every morning with a cup of wine and making my meals on pigeon and mutton and sweets, until the time came for my receipts to fall due. So every Monday and Thursday I used to go to the Exchange and sit in the shop of one merchant or another, while the notary and the money-changer went round collecting the money from the traders, until after the hour of afternoon prayer, when they brought me the amount; and I counted it and sealed the bags and went back with them to the khan.

On a certain day, which happened to be a Monday, I went to the baths and from there back to my khan; and sitting in my own room, broke my fast with a cup of wine, after which I slept a little. When I woke I ate a chicken, and perfuming myself, went to the shop of a merchant called Badr al-Din the Gardener, who made me welcome; and we sat talking a while until the market should open.

And presently up came a lady of stately figure, wearing the most magnificent headdress, perfumed with the sweetest of scents and walking with a gracefully swaying step; and seeing me, she lifted her veil enough to let me glimpse her beautiful black eyes.

She greeted Badr al-Din, who returned her greeting and stood up and talked with her; and the moment I heard her speak, the love of her took hold of my heart.

Presently she said to Badr al-Din, "Have you by you a cut piece of cloth woven with thread of pure gold?"

So he brought out a piece from those he had bought from me, and sold it to her for a thousand two hundred dirhams; at which she said, "I will take the piece home with me and send you the price of it."

"That is impossible, my lady," the merchant replied, "for here is the owner of the cloth, and I owe him a share of the profit."

"Shame on you!" she cried. "Do I not regularly take whole rolls of costly stuff from you, and give you a greater profit than you expect, and send you the money?"

"Yes," he answered, "but I am in pressing need of the price this very day."

At which she took up the piece and threw it back into his lap, saying, "Out on you! Allah confound the whole tribe of you, who value nobody at their proper worth." And she turned to go.

I felt my very soul going with her; so I stood up and stopped her, saying, "I beg you by the Lord, my lady, do me the favour of retracing your gracious steps."

She turned back with a smile and said, "For your sake I will," and took a seat opposite me in the shop.

Then I said to Badr al-Din, "What is the price they asked you for this piece?"

And he said, "Eleven hundred dirhams."

I answered, "The odd hundred shall be your profit. Bring me a sheet of paper and I will write you a discharge for it." And I wrote him a receipt in my own hand and gave the piece to the lady, saying, "Take it away with you; and if you like, bring me the price of it next market day — or better still, accept it as my guest-gift to you."

"Allah reward you with good," she answered, "and make you my husband and lord and master of everything I have."

And Allah granted her prayer.

I saw the Gates of Paradise swing open in front of me, and said, "My lady, let this piece of cloth be yours now, and another like it is ready for you; only let me have one look at your face."

So she raised her veil, and I saw a face the sight of which left me a thousand sighs, and my heart was so captured by love of her that I was no longer master of my own reason.

Then she let her face veil fall, and taking up the piece of cloth, said, "My lord, do not make me desolate by staying away!" And she turned away and vanished from my sight.

I stayed sitting at the Exchange until past the hour of afternoon prayer, lost to the world by the love that had mastered me; and the violence of my passion forced me to ask the merchant about her, and he answered, "This is a lady and a rich one: she is the daughter of a certain emir who died lately and left her a large fortune."

Then I took my leave of him and went home to the khan, where they set supper in front of me; but I could not eat for thinking of her, and when I lay down to sleep, sleep did not come near me.

So I lay awake until morning, when I got up and put on a change of clothes and drank a cup of wine; and after breaking my fast on a trifle, I went to the merchant's shop, where I greeted him and sat down beside him.

Presently up came the lady as usual, followed by a slave girl and wearing a dress more sumptuous than before; and she greeted me without taking any notice of Badr al-Din, and said, in fluent graceful speech — I never heard a voice softer or sweeter — "Send somebody with me to take the thousand two hundred dirhams, the price of the piece."

"Why this hurry?" I asked.

And she answered, "May we never lose you!" and handed me the money.

Then I sat talking with her; and presently I signed to her in dumb show, so that she understood that I longed to enjoy her; and she got up in a hurry with a show of displeasure.

My heart clung to her, and I went out of the market and followed after her. As I was walking, a black slave girl suddenly stopped me and said, "My master, come and speak with my mistress."

At this I was surprised, and replied, "There is nobody who knows me here."

But she answered, "My lord, how quickly you have forgotten her! My lady is the same one who was at such a merchant's shop today."

Then I went with her to the money-changer's, where I found the lady, who drew me to her side and said, "My beloved, your image is firmly stamped on my imagination, and love of you has taken hold of my heart. From the hour I first saw you, neither sleep nor food nor drink has given me any pleasure."

I replied, "Double that suffering is mine, and my own state saves me the trouble of complaining."

Then she said, "My beloved — at your house, or at mine?"

"I am a stranger here and have no place to receive you but the khan; so by your leave, it shall be at your house."

"So be it. But this is Friday night, and nothing can be done till tomorrow after the public prayers. Go to the mosque and pray; then mount your donkey and ask for the Habbaniyah quarter; and when you are there, look for the mansion of Al-Nakib Barakat, who is generally known as Abu Shamah the Syndic — for that is where I live. So do not be late, as I shall be expecting you."

I rejoiced at this with still greater joy, and took my leave of her and went back to my khan, where I passed a sleepless night.

I had hardly made sure that morning had dawned when I got up and changed my clothes and perfumed myself with essences and sweet scents; and taking fifty dinars in a handkerchief, went from the Khan al-Masrur to the Zuwaylah gate, where I hired a donkey and said to its owner, "Take me to the Habbaniyah."

So he set off with me and brought up in the twinkling of an eye at a street called Darb al-Munkari, where I said to him, "Go in and ask for the Syndic's mansion."

He was gone a while and then came back and said, "Get down."

"Go in front of me to the house," said I, and added, "Come back at first light and take me home." And he answered, "In Allah's name"; at which I gave him a quarter dinar of gold, and he took it and went his way.

Then I knocked at the door, and out came two white slave girls, both young, high-bosomed maidens, and they were like two moons; and they said to me, "Come in, for our mistress is expecting you, and she has not slept all night for her delight in you."

I passed through the entrance hall into a great room with seven doors, floored with parti-coloured marbles and furnished with curtains and hangings of coloured silks. The ceiling was panelled with gold and corniced with inscriptions emblazoned in lapis lazuli; and the walls were plastered with Sultani gypsum that gave back the face of anybody looking at it.

Round the room were latticed windows overlooking a garden full of every kind of fruit, whose streams were railing and rilling and whose birds were trilling and shrilling; and in the heart of the hall was a jetting fountain, at whose corners stood birds fashioned in red gold, crusted with pearls and gems, spouting water crystal clear.

When I came in and took a seat:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Twenty-sixth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the young merchant went on:

When I came in and took a seat, the lady came in at once, crowned with a diadem of pearls and jewels; her face dotted with artificial moles in indigo, her eyebrows pencilled with kohl, and her hands and feet reddened with henna.

When she saw me she smiled into my face and took me into her arms and clasped me to her breast; then she put her mouth to my mouth and sucked my tongue, and I did the same; and she said, "Can it be true, my darling, that you have come to me?" And she added, "Welcome and good cheer to you! By Allah, from the day I saw you sleep has not been sweet to me and food has not been pleasant."

Said I, "That has been my case too; and I am your slave, your bondsman."

Then we sat down to talk, and I hung my head towards the ground out of bashfulness; but she did not wait long before she set a tray of the most exquisite food in front of me — marinated meats, fritters soaked in bees' honey, and chickens stuffed with sugar and pistachio nuts — and we ate our fill of them.

Then they brought a basin and a ewer, and I washed my hands; and we scented ourselves with musked rose water and sat down again to talk. And she began repeating these lines:

	"Had we known you were coming, your road would have been strewn
	with the blood of our hearts and the balls of our eyes;
	we would have thrown our cheeks down as a carpet to greet you,
	so that your step should land softly on our eyelids."

And she went on complaining of what had happened to her and I of what had happened to me; and love of her took such firm hold of my heart that all my wealth seemed nothing at all beside her.

Then we fell to playing and groping and kissing until nightfall, when the maids set food in front of us and a full wine service, and we sat drinking until midnight, when we lay down and I lay with her. Never in my life did I see a night like that night.

When morning came I got up and took my leave of her, throwing the handkerchief with the dinars in it under the bed; and as I went out she wept and said, "My lord, when shall I look on that lovely face again?"

"I will be with you at sunset," I answered.

And going out, I found the donkey boy who had brought me the day before waiting at the door. So I mounted and rode to the Khan al-Masrur, where I got down and gave the man half a dinar, saying, "Come back at sunset"; and he said, "I will."

Then I had my breakfast and went out to collect the price of my goods; after which I came back, and taking a roast lamb and some sweets, called a porter and put the provisions in his crate and sent them to the lady, paying the man his hire.

I went back to my business until sunset, when the donkey driver came for me; and I took fifty dinars in a handkerchief and rode to her house, where I found the marble floor swept, the brasses burnished, the branched lights burning, the wax candles already lit, the meat served up and the wine strained.

When my lady saw me she threw her arms round my neck and cried, "You have left me desolate by being away."

Then she set the tables in front of me and we ate our fill, and the slave girls carried the trays off and served the wine. We did not stop drinking until half the night was gone; and being well warmed with drink, we went into the bedchamber and lay there until morning.

Then I got up and left her, leaving the fifty dinars with her as before; and finding the donkey boy at the door, rode to the khan and slept a while.

After that I went out to get the evening meal ready, and took a brace of geese with gravy on two platters of dressed and peppered rice, and got ready taro roots fried and soaked in honey, and wax candles and fruit and preserves and nuts and almonds and sweet-scented flowers; and I sent the whole lot to her.

As soon as it was night I tied up fifty dinars in a handkerchief again, and mounting the donkey as usual, rode to the mansion, where we ate and drank and lay together till morning; when I threw her the handkerchief and the dinars and rode back to the khan.

I did not stop going on in this way until, after one sweet night, I woke up on a fine morning and found myself beggared, without a dinar or a dirham to my name.

So I said to myself, "All this is Satan's work," and began to recite these lines:

	"Poverty dims a man's brightness, whatever his wealth has been,
	just as the sun about to set shines with a yellowing light.
	Absent, he falls out of memory and is forgotten by his friends;
	present, he does not share their joys, for nobody delights in him.
	He walks the market avoided by everybody, glad enough to hide his head,
	and in lonely places he sheds tears and moans over his bitter state.
	By Allah, among his own kin a man, however good he is,
	is nothing but a stranger once want and poverty have waylaid him."

I went out from the khan and walked down the street called Between the Palaces until I came to the Zuwaylah Gate, where I found the crowd thick and the gateway blocked with people.

And by the decree of Destiny I saw there a trooper, against whom I pressed accidentally, so that my hand came against his breast pocket and I felt a purse inside it. I looked, and seeing a green silk string hanging out of the pocket, knew it for a purse.

The crush grew greater every minute; and just then a camel loaded with firewood happened to jostle the trooper on the other side, and he turned round to fend it off in case it tore his clothes. And Satan tempted me, so I pulled the string and drew out a little bag of blue silk with something in it that chinked like coin.

But the soldier, feeling his pocket suddenly lighter, put his hand to it and found it empty; at which he turned on me and, snatching his mace off his saddle bow, struck me on the head with it.

I fell to the ground, while the people gathered round us and seized the trooper's mare by the bridle and said to him, "Do you strike this young man a blow like that for a mere push?"

But the trooper shouted at them, "This fellow is a cursed thief!"

At which I came to myself and stood up; and the people looked at me and said, "No, he is a good-looking young man; he would not steal anything." And some of them took my part and others were against me, and question and answer grew loud and warm. The people pulled at me and would have rescued me out of his clutches — but as fate decreed, the Governor, the Chief of Police and the watch came in at the Zuwaylah Gate at that very moment; and seeing the people gathered round me and the soldier, the Governor asked, "What is the matter?"

"By Allah, Emir," answered the trooper, "this is a thief! I had a purse of blue silk in my pocket with twenty good gold pieces in it, and he took it while I was in the crush."

Said the Governor, "Was anybody beside you at the time?"

And the soldier said, "No."

At which the Governor called out to the Chief of Police, who seized me; and in this way the curtain of the Lord's protection was drawn back from me.

Then he said, "Strip him." And when they stripped me they found the purse in my clothes. The Governor took it and opened it and counted it; and finding twenty dinars in it, as the soldier had said, he grew extremely angry and ordered his guard to bring me before him.

Then he said to me, "Now, young man, speak the truth: did you steal this purse?"

At this I hung my head towards the ground and said to myself, "If I deny stealing it, I shall get myself into terrible trouble." So I raised my head and said, "Yes, I took it."

When the Governor heard this he wondered, and summoned witnesses, who came forward and attested my confession. All this happened at the Zuwaylah Gate.

Then the Governor ordered the torch-bearer to cut off my right hand, and he did so; after which he would have struck off my left foot as well — but the soldier's heart softened and he took pity on me and interceded for me with the Governor, so that I should not be killed.

At which the Governor left me and went away, and the people stayed round me and gave me a cup of wine to drink. As for the trooper, he pressed the purse on me and said, "You are a good-looking young man, and it does not suit you to be a thief."

So I recited these verses:

	"I swear by Allah's name, good sir, that I was no thief,
	nor, best of men, was I ever bred a bandit.
	But the chances and changes of Fortune overthrew me all at once,
	and care and trouble and poverty led me off my road.
	I did not shoot it, truly; it was Allah who shot the arrow
	that rolled the kingly crown from my head into the dust."

The soldier turned away after giving me the purse; and I too went my way, having wrapped my hand in a piece of rag and thrust it into my breast.

My whole appearance had changed, and my colour had gone yellow from the shame and the pain that had come on me. Even so, I went on to my mistress's house, where in extreme agitation of spirit I threw myself down on the bed.

She saw me in that state and asked, "What is the matter, and why do I see you so changed in your looks?"

And I answered, "My head is hurting me, and I am far from well."

At which she was upset and concerned on my account, and said, "Do not burn my heart, my lord; sit up and lift your head and tell me what has happened to you today, for your face tells me a story."

"Leave this talk," I replied.

But she wept and said, "It seems to me that you have grown tired of me, for I see you are not as you usually are."

But I was silent; and she went on talking to me although I gave her no answer, until night came on.

Then she set food in front of me; but I refused it, afraid she might see me eating with my left hand, and said to her, "I have no appetite to eat at present."

Said she, "Tell me what has happened to you today, and why you are so sorrowful and broken in spirit and in heart."

Said I, "Wait a while; I will tell you everything at my leisure."

Then she brought me wine, saying, "Down with it, this will drive off your grief. You really must drink, and tell me your news."

I asked, "Must I tell you?"

And she answered, "Yes."

Then I said, "If it must be so, then give it to me with your own hand."

She filled and drank, and filled again and gave me the cup; and I took it from her with my left hand, and wiped the tears from my eyelids and began repeating:

	"When Allah wills that something should befall a man
	who has his full share of ears and eyes and wits,
	He deafens his ears and He blinds his eyes
	and draws his wits out as we draw out a hair —
	until, having worked His purpose, He gives him back
	his wits, so that he may go more warily warned."

When I had finished my verses I wept; and she cried out with a very loud cry, "What is the cause of your tears? You are burning my heart! What makes you take the cup with your left hand?"

Said I, "The truth is I have a boil on my right hand."

And she said, "Put it out and I will open it for you."

"It is not time to open it yet," I replied, "so do not worry me with your words, for I will not take it out of the bandage at this hour."

Then I drank the cup off; and she did not stop plying me with drink until drunkenness overcame me and I fell asleep where I was sitting — at which she looked at my right hand and saw a wrist without a fist.

So she searched me closely, and found on me the purse of gold and my severed hand wrapped up in the piece of rag. At which such sorrow came over her as never came over anybody; and she did not stop lamenting on my account until the morning.

When I woke I found she had made me a dish of broth of four boiled chickens, which she brought me together with a cup of wine. I ate and drank; and laying down the purse, would have gone out — but she said to me, "Where are you going?"

And I answered, "Where my business calls me."

And she said, "You shall not go. Sit down."

So I sat down; and she went on, "Has your love for me so overpowered you that you have wasted all your wealth and lost your hand on my account? I call you to witness against me, and let Allah be my witness too, that I will never part with you, but will die under your feet; and you shall soon see that what I say is true."

Then she sent for the judge and the witnesses and said to them, "Write out my marriage contract with this young man, and bear witness that I have received the marriage settlement."

When they had drawn up the document she said, "Bear witness that all my money that is in this chest, and everything I have in slaves and maids and other property, is given as a free gift to this young man."

So they took a record of the statement, putting me in possession by right of marriage; and then they withdrew, after being paid their fees.

At which she took me by the hand and, leading me to a small room, opened a large chest and said, "Look at what is in here."

And I looked — and it was full of handkerchiefs.

Said she, "This is the money I had from you; and every handkerchief you gave me, with fifty dinars in it, I wrapped up and threw into this chest. So now take what is your own, for it comes back to you; and today you have become a man of high estate. Fortune and Fate afflicted you so that you lost your right hand for my sake, and I can never repay you; no, if I gave my life it would still be little, and I should remain in your debt."

Then she added, "Take charge of your property."

So I moved the contents of her chest into my chest, and added my wealth to her wealth, which I had given her; and my heart was eased and my sorrow ceased.

I stood up and kissed her and thanked her; and she said, "You have given your hand for love of me — and how am I able to give you anything equal to it? By Allah, if I offered my life for your love it would truly be a small thing and would not do justice to your claim on me."

Then she made over to me by deed everything she owned in clothes and ornaments of gold and pearls, and goods and farms and property; and she did not lie down to sleep that night, being so sorely grieved for my grief, until I had told her the whole of what had happened to me.

I spent the night with her. But before we had lived together a month she fell seriously ill, and her illness grew worse by reason of her grief over the loss of my hand; and she lasted only fifty days before she was numbered among the people of the world to come and the heirs of immortality.

So I laid her out and buried her body in the earth, and had a full reading of the Koran made for the health of her soul, and gave a great deal of money in alms for her; after which I turned away from the grave and went back to the house.

There I found she had left a great deal of property in ready money and slaves, houses, lands and estates; and among her storehouses was a granary of sesame seed, part of which I sold to you. And I had neither the time nor the inclination to settle accounts with you until I had sold the rest of the stock in store; nor indeed have I finished collecting the price even now.

So I want you not to baulk me in what I am about to say to you: twice I have eaten your food, and I wish to make you a present of the money for the sesame that you are holding.

Such is the cause of the cutting off of my right hand, and of my eating with my left.

"Truly," said I, "you have shown me the greatest kindness and generosity."

Then he asked me, "Why should you not travel with me to my own country, which I am about to go back to with Cairo and Alexandria goods? Tell me — will you come with me?"

And I answered, "I will."

So I agreed to go with him at the head of the month; and I sold everything I had and bought other merchandise. Then we set out and travelled, the young man and I, to this country of yours, where he sold his venture and bought another stock of country goods and went on with his journey to Egypt.

But it was my lot to stay here, so that these things happened to me in my exile which happened last night.

And is this tale, O King of the age, not more wonderful and more marvellous than the story of the hunchback?

"Not so," said the King. "I cannot accept it. There is no help for it: every one of you is to be hanged":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Twenty-seventh Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the King of China declared, "There is no help for it, every one of you is to be hanged," the steward of the Sultan's kitchen came forward and said, "If you will permit me, I will tell you a tale of what happened to me just before I found this hunchback; and if it is more wonderful than his story, then grant us our lives."

And when the King answered, "Yes," he began to recount

The Steward's Tale

Know, O King, that last night I was at a party where they made a full reading of the Koran and got together doctors of law and religion skilled in recitation and chanting; and when the readers had finished, the table was spread, and among other things they set in front of us was a marinated ragout flavoured with cumin seed.

So we sat down; but one of our number held back and refused to touch it. We begged him to eat some, but he swore he would not; and when we pressed him again, he said, "Do not press me. What has already happened to me through eating it is enough." And he began reciting:

	"Shoulder your tray and go straight to your goal;
	and if this kohl suits you — why, then, use this kohl."

When he had finished his verse we said to him, "In Allah's name, tell us your reason for refusing to eat the cumin ragout."

"If it must be so," he replied, "and I have to eat some of it, I will not do it unless I wash my hand forty times with soap, forty times with potash and forty times with galangal — a hundred and twenty washings in all."

At which our host told his slaves to bring water and everything else he needed; and the young man washed his hand as he had said. Then he sat down, looking disgusted and frightened at the same time, and dipping his hand into the ragout, began to eat, showing signs of anger as he did.

And we wondered at him beyond all wondering, for his hand trembled and the morsel in it shook, and we saw that his thumb had been cut off and he was eating with four fingers only.

So we said to him, "In Allah's name — what happened to your thumb? Is your hand like that by God's own creation, or has some accident happened to it?"

"My brothers," he answered, "it is not only this thumb, but the other one too, and both my great toes, as you shall see."

And saying that, he uncovered his left hand and his feet; and we saw that the left hand was like the right, and that each of his feet was likewise missing its great toe.

When we saw him like that our amazement grew greater still, and we said to him, "We have hardly the patience to wait for your history, and to hear how your thumbs came to be cut off, and why you wash both hands a hundred and twenty times."

Know then, said he, that my father was chief of the merchants and the wealthiest of them all in the city of Baghdad, in the reign of the Caliph Harun al-Rashid; and he was much given to wine drinking and to listening to the lute and the other instruments of pleasure, so that when he died he left nothing.

I buried him and had full readings of the Koran made for him, and mourned for him days and nights; then I opened his shop and found he had left few goods in it, while his debts were many. However, I made an arrangement with his creditors for time to settle their claims, and set about buying and selling, paying them something from week to week on account; and I did not stop doing this until I had cleared his obligations entirely and begun adding to my capital.

One day, as I was sitting in my shop, suddenly and unexpectedly there appeared in front of me a young lady, fairer than any I ever saw, wearing the richest clothes and ornaments and riding a she-mule, with one Black slave walking in front of her and another behind.

She drew rein at the head of the exchange market and came in, followed by a eunuch who said to her, "My lady, come out and away without telling anybody, in case you light a fire that burns the whole lot of us up." And he stood in front of her, keeping her from being seen, while she looked at the merchants' shops.

She found none open except mine; so she came up, with the eunuch behind her, and sat down in my shop and greeted me. I never heard anything fairer than her speech or sweeter than her voice.

Then she unveiled her face, and I saw that she was like the moon; and I stole a glance at her that cost me a thousand sighs, and my heart was captured with love of her; and I kept looking again and again at her face, repeating these lines:

	"Say to the charmer in the dove-coloured veil,
	death would be welcome if it eased your sorrow!
	Do me the favour of your favours, so that I may live:
	see, I hold out my palm to take what you give."

When she heard my verse she answered me, saying:

	"I have lost all patience through your unkindness;
	my heart knows nothing but its pledge of love to you.
	If I look on anything but those bright charms of yours,
	may my parting from you never end in the sight of you.
	I swear I will never forget what is owed to you,
	and this breast would gladly soar to the height of you.
	You made me drain the cup of love, and gladly
	would I hold a cup of love for your delight.
	Take this body of mine wherever you go, and when
	you die, bury me in the same place as you.
	Call to me in my grave, and you will hear my bones
	sigh their answers to the sound of your cry.
	And if I were asked, 'What would you have of God?'
	I would answer: first His will, and then your decree."

When she had finished her verse she asked me, "Young man, have you any fine stuffs by you?"

And I answered, "My lady, your slave is a poor man; but be patient until the merchants open their shops, and I will suit you with whatever you want."

Then we sat talking, she and I — and I was drowned in the sea of her love and lost in the desert of my passion — until the merchants opened their shops; when I got up and fetched her everything she wanted, to the tune of five thousand dirhams.

She gave the goods to the eunuch, and going out by the door of the Exchange, mounted her mule and rode away without telling me where she came from; and I was ashamed to speak about such a trifle.

When the merchants dunned me for the price, I made myself answerable for five thousand dirhams and went home, drunk with love of her. They set supper in front of me and I ate a mouthful, thinking of nothing but her beauty and loveliness, and tried to sleep, but sleep would not come.

And that was my condition for a whole week, when the merchants asked me for their money; but I persuaded them to be patient another week, at the end of which she appeared again, mounted on a she-mule and attended by her eunuch and two slaves.

She greeted me and said, "My master, we have been a long time bringing you the price of the goods; but now fetch the money-changer and take your money."

So I sent for the money-changer, and the eunuch counted out the coin in front of him and handed it over to me. Then we sat talking, she and I, until the market opened, when she said to me, "Get me this and that."

So I got her from the merchants whatever she wanted, and she took it and went away without saying a word to me about the price.

As soon as she was out of sight I regretted what I had done; for the value of the goods bought for her came to a thousand dinars, and I said in my soul, "What kind of love is this? She has brought me five thousand dirhams and has taken goods worth a thousand dinars."

I was afraid of being beggared by having to pay the merchants their money, and I said, "They know nobody but me; this lovely lady is nothing but a cheat and a swindler, who has diddled me with her beauty and her grace; for she saw I was a mere boy and laughed at me for not asking her address."

I did not stop being troubled by these doubts and fears, as she was gone more than a month, until the merchants pestered me for their money and were so hard on me that I put my property up for sale and stood on the very brink of ruin.

However, as I was sitting in my shop one day, drowned in melancholy thoughts, she suddenly rode up and, dismounting at the market gate, came straight over to me. When I saw her all my cares fell away from me and I forgot every trouble.

She came right up to me and greeted me in her sweet voice and pleasant speech, and presently said, "Fetch the money-changer and weigh your money."

So she gave me the price of the goods I had got for her, and more; and fell to talking freely with me, until I was ready to die of joy and delight.

Presently she asked me, "Have you a wife?"

And I answered, "Indeed no; I have never known a woman" — and began to shed tears.

Said she, "Why are you weeping?"

Said I, "It is nothing."

Then, giving the eunuch some of the gold pieces, I begged him to be a go-between in the matter; but he laughed and said, "She is more in love with you than you are with her. She has no use at all for the stuffs she has bought from you, and did the whole thing only for love of you; so ask her whatever you like and she will refuse you nothing."

When she saw me giving the dinars to the eunuch she came back and sat down again; and I said to her, "Be charitable to your slave and pardon him what he is about to say."

Then I told her what was in my mind; and she agreed, and said to the eunuch, "You shall carry my message to him" — adding to me, "And do whatever the eunuch tells you."

Then she got up and went away; and I paid the merchants their money and they all profited by it. But as for me, all I gained was regret at the breaking off of our meetings; and I did not sleep the whole of that night.

However, before many days had passed her eunuch came to me, and I treated him honourably and asked him after his mistress.

"Truly she is sick with love of you," he replied.

And I answered, "Tell me who and what she is."

Said he, "The Lady Zubaydah, queen consort of Harun al-Rashid, brought her up in her own household and has advanced her to be stewardess of the harem, and given her the right to come and go as she pleases. She spoke to her lady about you and begged her to marry her to you; but she said, 'I will not do it until I see the young man; and if he is worthy of you, I will marry you to him.'

"So now we are looking for the moment to smuggle you into the palace; and if you manage to get in secretly you will get your wish and marry her. But if the affair gets about, the Lady Zubaydah will strike your head off. What do you say to that?"

I answered, "I will go with you and take the risk you speak of."

Then he said, "As soon as it is night, go to the mosque the Lady Zubaydah built on the Tigris, and pray the night prayers and sleep there."

"With love and gladness," I cried.

So at nightfall I went to the mosque, where I prayed and passed the night. At the first light of dawn a number of eunuchs came in a skiff with a quantity of empty chests, which they set down in the mosque; and then they all went their way except one — and looking at him closely, I saw he was our go-between.

Presently in came the girl, my mistress, walking straight over to us; and I got up to her and embraced her, while she kissed me and shed tears. We talked a while; after which she made me get into one of the chests, which she locked on me.

Presently the other eunuchs came back with a quantity of packages, and she set about stowing them into the chests, which she locked down one by one until all were shut. When it was done the eunuchs loaded the chests into the boat and set off for the Lady Zubaydah's palace.

At this, misgivings began to trouble me and I said to myself, "Truly your lust and your recklessness will be the death of you; and after all this, the question is whether you get your wish or not."

And I began to weep, boxed up as I was in the box and suffering from cramp; and I prayed to Allah to deliver me from the dangerous position I was in — while the boat did not stop going on until it reached the palace gate, where they lifted out the chests, and mine among them.

Then they carried them in, passing a troop of eunuchs, the guardians of the harem and of the ladies behind the curtain, until they came to the post of the Chief Eunuch, who started up out of his sleep and shouted at the girl, "What is in those chests?"

"They are full of goods for the Lady Zubaydah."

"Open them, one by one, so that I can see what is in them."

"And what do you want to open them for?"

"Give me no words and do not overdo the talking! These chests must and shall be opened."

And saying that, he sprang to his feet; and the first one they brought him to open was the one I was in. And when I felt his hands on it my senses left me and I wet myself in my terror, so that the water ran out of the box.

Then she said to the Chief Eunuch, "Steward! You will get me killed and yourself too, for you have damaged goods worth ten thousand dinars. This chest holds coloured dresses and four gallon-flasks of Zamzam water; and now one of them has come unstoppered and the water is running out over the clothes and will spoil their colours."

The eunuch answered, "Take up your boxes and get out, to the curse of God!"

So the slaves carried off all the chests, mine included, and hurried on with them — when suddenly I heard a voice saying, "Alack, and alack! The Caliph! The Caliph!"

When that cry struck my ears I died in my skin, and said the saying that has never yet shamed the man who said it: "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great! I and nobody else have brought this calamity on myself."

Presently I heard the Caliph say to my mistress, "A plague on you — what is in those boxes?"

And she answered, "Dresses for the Lady Zubaydah."

At which he said, "Open them in front of me!"

When I heard this I died my death outright, and said to myself, "By Allah, today is the very last of my days in this world. If I come safely out of this I am to marry her and there is no more to be said; but discovery is staring me in the face and my head is as good as struck off."

Then I repeated the profession of faith, saying, "There is no god but God, and Mohammed is the Apostle of God!":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Twenty-eighth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the young merchant went on as follows:

Now when I had testified, "I bear witness that there is no god but God," I heard my mistress the handmaid declare to the Caliph, "These chests, Commander of the Faithful, have been committed to my charge by the Lady Zubaydah, and she does not want their contents seen by anybody."

"No matter," said the Caliph. "They must be opened; I will see what is in them." And he called out to the eunuchs, "Bring the chests here in front of me."

At this I made certain of death, beyond any doubt, and fainted away.

Then the eunuchs brought the chests up to him one after another and he set about inspecting the contents; but he saw in them nothing but perfumes and cloths and fine dresses. And they did not stop opening the chests and he did not stop looking at what was in them, finding nothing but clothes and such things, until none was left unopened but the box I was boxed in.

They put out their hands to open it — but my mistress made haste and said to the Caliph, "This one you shall see only in the presence of the Lady Zubaydah, for what is in it is her own secret."

When he heard this he gave orders to carry the chests in; so they took up the one I was in and carried it with the rest into the harem and set it down in the middle of the great room; and truly my spittle was dried up with sheer fear.

Then my mistress opened the box and took me out, saying, "Do not be afraid; no harm and no dread will come to you now. Broaden your chest and strengthen your heart and sit down until the Lady Zubaydah comes, and you shall certainly get your wish of me."

So I sat down; and after a while in came ten maids, virgins like moons, and ranged themselves in two rows, five facing five; and after them twenty other girls, high-bosomed virgins, surrounding the Lady Zubaydah, who could hardly walk for the weight of her clothes and her ornaments.

As she came near, the slave girls parted from around her, and I came forward and kissed the ground between her hands. She signed to me to sit; and when I had sat down in front of her chair, she began questioning me about my forebears and my family and my circumstances, to which I gave such answers as pleased her; and she said to my mistress, "Our raising of you, girl, has not disappointed us."

Then she said to me, "Know that this girl is to us as our own child, and she is a trust committed to you by Allah."

I kissed the ground before her again, well pleased that I should marry my mistress; and she told me to stay ten days in the palace.

So I stayed there ten days, in which time I saw neither my mistress nor anybody else except one of the concubines, who brought me my morning and evening meals.

After this the Lady Zubaydah consulted the Caliph about the marriage of her favourite handmaid, and he gave his leave and assigned her a wedding portion of ten thousand gold pieces. So the Lady Zubaydah sent for the judge and the witnesses, who wrote out our marriage contract; after which the women made ready sweets and rich dishes and distributed them among all the chambers of the harem.

They did this for another ten days, at the end of which my mistress went to the baths.

Meanwhile they set in front of me a tray of food with all sorts of meats on it; and among those dishes, which were enough to daze a man's wits, was a bowl of cumin ragout with chicken breasts in it, larded and flavoured with sugar, pistachios, musk and rose water.

Then, by Allah, good sirs, I did not hesitate long; but took my seat in front of the ragout and fell to and ate of it until I could eat no more. After this I wiped my hands, but forgot to wash them; and sat until it grew dark, when the wax candles were lit and the singing women came in with their tambourines and set about displaying the bride in one dress after another and carrying her in procession from room to room all round the palace, getting their palms crossed with gold as they went.

Then they brought her to me and undressed her.

When I found myself alone with her on the bed I put my arms round her, hardly able to believe we were together; but she smelled the strong odour of the ragout on my hands, and instantly cried out with a very loud cry, at which the slave girls came running to her from every side.

I trembled with alarm, not knowing what the matter was; and the girls asked her, "What is the matter, sister?"

She answered them, "Take this madman away from me. I thought he was a man of sense!"

Said I to her, "What makes you think me mad?"

Said she, "You madman! What made you eat cumin ragout and forget to wash your hand? By Allah, I will pay you back for your bad manners. Is a man like you to come to bed with a woman like me with unclean hands?"

Then she took a plaited scourge from her side and came down with it on my back and the place where I sit, until her forearms were numb and I had fainted away from the beating; when she said to the maids, "Take him and carry him to the Chief of Police, so that he may strike off the hand he ate the cumin ragout with and did not wash."

When I heard this I said, "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah! Will you cut off my hand because I ate a cumin ragout and did not wash?"

The maids interceded with her too, and kissed her hand, saying, "Sister, this man is a simpleton; do not punish him for what he has done this once."

But she answered, "By Allah, there is no help for it: I must dock him of something, and of the offending member above all."

Then she went away, and I saw no more of her for ten days, in which time she sent me food and drink by a slave girl, who told me she had fallen ill from the smell of the cumin ragout.

After that she came to me and said, "You disgrace! I will teach you how to eat cumin ragout without washing your hands."

Then she called out to the maids, who pinioned me; and she took a sharp razor and cut off my thumbs and my great toes, exactly as you see, good company.

At which I fainted away; and she sprinkled some powdered healing herbs on the stumps, and when the blood had been staunched I said, "Never again will I eat cumin ragout without washing my hands forty times with potash and forty times with galangal and forty times with soap!"

And she made me swear an oath and bound me by a covenant to that effect.

So when you brought me the cumin ragout my colour changed, and I said to myself, "This is the very dish that caused the cutting off of my thumbs and my great toes"; and when you forced me, I said, "I must fulfil the oath I have sworn."

"And what happened to you after that?" asked the people there.

And he answered: When I had sworn to her, her anger was appeased, and I slept with her that night.

We lived like that a while, until one day she said to me, "Truly the Caliph's palace is not a pleasant place for us to live in, and nobody ever entered it but you — and you only by the grace of the Lady Zubaydah. Now she has given me fifty thousand dinars," she added; "take this money and go out and buy us a fine house."

So I went out and bought a fine, spacious mansion, to which she moved all the wealth she owned and what riches I had made in cloth and costly rarities.

Such is the cause of the cutting off of my thumbs and my great toes.

We ate (the steward went on), and were going home when there happened to me with the hunchback that business you know about. That is my story, and peace be with you.

Said the King, "This story is in no way more delightful than the story of the hunchback; no, it is rather less so, and there is no help for it: the whole lot of you must be hanged."

Then the Jewish physician came forward and, kissing the ground, said, "O King of the age, I will tell you a history more wonderful than that of the hunchback."

"Tell on," said the King of China. So he began the

Tale of the Jewish Doctor

A truly marvellous thing happened to me in my youth. I was living in Damascus in Syria, studying my art; and one day, as I was sitting at home, a Mamluk came to me from the Viceroy's household and said, "Speak with my lord!"

So I followed him to the Viceroy's house; and going into the great hall, saw at the head of it a couch of cedar plated with gold, on which lay a sickly young man, and a handsome one at that — you could not see a fairer.

I sat down by his head and prayed to Heaven for a cure; and he made me a sign with his eyes. So I said to him, "My lord, favour me with your hand, and may safety be with you."

Then he put out his left hand; and I marvelled at it and said to myself, "By Allah, it is strange that this handsome young man, the son of a great house, should have so little in the way of manners. This can be nothing but pride and conceit."

However, I felt his pulse and wrote him a prescription, and went on visiting him for ten days, at the end of which he recovered and went to the baths; at which the Viceroy gave me a handsome robe of honour and appointed me superintendent of the hospital in Damascus.

I went with him to the baths, the whole of which they had kept private for his use; and the servants came in with him and took off his clothes inside; and when he was stripped I saw that his right hand had been cut off, and not long before — and this was the cause of his weakness.

At this I was amazed and grieved for him; and then, looking at his body, I saw on it the scars of scourge-strokes that he had been putting ointments on. I was troubled at the sight, and my concern showed in my face.

The young man looked at me and, understanding, said, "Physician of the age, do not marvel at my case; I will tell you my story as soon as we leave the baths."

Then we washed, and going back to his house, ate a little food and rested a while; after which he asked me, "What do you say to amusing yourself by looking over the supper hall?"

And I answered, "So let it be."

At which he ordered the slaves to carry out the necessary carpets and cushions, and to roast a lamb and bring us some fruit. They did as he said, and we ate together, he using his left hand for it.

After a while I said to him, "Now tell me your tale."

"Physician of the age," he replied, "hear what happened to me.

"Know that I am one of the sons of Mosul, where my grandfather died leaving nine children, of whom my father was the eldest. They all grew up and took wives, but not one of them was blessed with children except my father, to whom Providence granted me. So I grew up among my uncles, who rejoiced in me exceedingly, until I came of age.

"One day, which happened to be a Friday, I went to the cathedral mosque of Mosul with my father and my uncles, and we prayed the congregational prayers; after which the people went out, except my father and my uncles, who sat talking about wonderful things in foreign parts and the marvellous sights of strange cities.

"At last they mentioned Egypt, and one of my uncles said, 'Travellers tell us that there is nothing on the face of the earth finer than Cairo and her Nile' — and these words made me long to see Cairo.

"Said my father, 'Whoever has not seen Cairo has not seen the world. Her dust is golden and her Nile a miracle to behold; and her women are as fair as the maidens of Paradise, painted puppets, beautiful pictures; her houses are rare palaces; her water is sweet and light and her mud a commodity and a medicine beyond compare — just as the poet says in this poem of his:

	The Nile flood today is the gain you own;
	you alone dwell among such gains and bounties.
	The Nile is the flood of my own tears at separation,
	and here nobody is forlorn but I alone.

"'What is more, her air is temperate and mixed with a fragrance that surpasses aloes-wood in scent; and how should it be otherwise, she being the Mother of the World? And Allah favour the man who wrote these lines:

	If I leave Cairo and her pleasure gardens,
	where can I go to find such gladdening ways?
	Shall I abandon that place, whose grateful scents
	delight every soul and call for the loudest praise?
	Where every palace, like another Eden,
	displays its richly worked carpets and cushions;
	a city that woos the eye and the spirit to gladness,
	where Saint meets Sinner and each enjoys his craze;
	where friend meets friend, brought together by Providence
	in green gardens and in mazes of palm.
	People of Cairo — and by Allah's decree
	I travel — in my thoughts I live with you always.
	Do not whisper Cairo in the ear of the west wind,
	in case he robs her of her garden scents.

"'And if your eyes saw her earth, and how it is adorned with blossom and embroidered with every kind of flower, and the islands of the Nile and how much there is in them of wide and handsome prospect; and if you turned your sight on the Abyssinian Pond, your glance would not come back from the scene without wonder; for nowhere would you see the fellow of that lovely view. Indeed the two arms of the Nile embrace the most luxuriant green, as the white of the eye encloses its black, or like filigreed silver surrounding chrysolites. And a divinely gifted poet said these lines about it:

	By the Abyssinian Pond, O divine day,
	in the morning twilight and in the sunny shine!
	The water imprisoned in its green walls
	like the flash of a sabre before shrinking eyes.
	And in the Garden we sat while it drank
	a slow draught, its embroidered banks dyed the finest.
	The stream is rippled by the hands of the clouds,
	and we too go rippling as we lie back on our rugs,
	passing round pure wine; and whoever leaves us there
	shall never rise up from the fall his woes have designed.
	Draining long draughts from large and brimming bowls,
	administering the only medicine for thirst — wine.

"'And what is there to compare with the Observatory and its charms, of which every viewer says as he comes near it, "Truly this spot has every kind of excellence to itself"? And if you speak of the Night of the Nile at its full, then give away the rainbow and share it out! And if you saw the Garden in the evening, with the cool shadows sloping far and wide, you would see a marvel and would incline to Egypt in ecstasy. And if you were by Cairo's river when the sun is sinking and the stream puts on its coat of mail and its hauberk over its other clothes, you would be quickened to new life by its gentle breezes and by its all-sufficient shade.'

"So he spoke; and the rest of them fell to describing Egypt and her Nile. As I listened to their accounts my thoughts dwelt on the subject; and when they had talked their fill and all got up and went their ways, I lay down to sleep that night, but sleep would not come, because of my violent longing for Egypt; and neither food nor drink pleased me.

"After a few days my uncles fitted themselves out for a trading journey to Egypt; and I wept in front of my father until he got suitable merchandise ready for me, and consented to my going with them — saying, however, 'Do not let him enter Cairo, but leave him to sell his goods at Damascus.'

"So I said goodbye to my father, and we set out from Mosul and did not stop travelling until we reached Aleppo, where we halted some days. Then we marched on until we made Damascus; and we found her a city that might have been a Paradise, full of trees and streams and birds and fruit of every kind.

"We put up at one of the khans, where my uncles stayed a while selling and buying; and they bought and sold on my account too, each dirham turning a profit of five on the prime cost, which pleased me mightily.

"After this they left me alone and set their faces towards Egypt, while I stayed in Damascus, where I had rented from a jeweller, for two dinars a month, a house whose beauties would beggar the tongue. Here I stayed, eating and drinking and spending what money I had, until one day, as I was sitting at the door of my house, there came past a young lady in the costliest clothes my eyes ever saw.

"I gave her a look, and she stepped inside without hesitating and stood there. I went in with her and shut the door on the two of us; at which she raised her face veil and threw off her cloak — and I found her like a moon in a painting, of a rare and marvellous loveliness; and love of her took hold of my heart.

"So I got up and brought a tray of the most delicate food and fruit and whatever else suited the occasion; and we ate and played, and after that drank until the wine turned our heads. Then I lay with her the sweetest of nights; and in the morning I offered her ten gold pieces — at which her face darkened and her eyebrows drew together, and shaking with anger she cried, "Shame on you, my sweet companion! Do you think I want your money?"

"Then she took fifteen dinars out of the breast of her shift and laid them in front of me and said, "By Allah, unless you take these I will never come back to you."

"So I accepted them, and she said, "My beloved, expect me again in three days' time, when I will be with you between sunset and supper; and with these dinars prepare us the same entertainment as last night."

"And saying that, she took her leave and went away, and all my senses went with her.

"On the third day she came again, dressed in cloth woven with gold wire, and wearing clothes and ornaments finer than before. I had got the place ready for her before she arrived and the meal was waiting; so we ate and drank and lay together as we had done, until the morning, when she gave me another fifteen gold pieces and promised to come again in three days.

"So I got ready for her; and at the appointed time she appeared, more richly dressed than on the first and second occasions, and said to me, "My lord, am I not beautiful?"

"'Yes, by Allah, you are,' I answered.

"And she went on, 'Will you let me bring with me a young lady fairer than I am and younger in years, so that she can play with us, and you and she can laugh and make merry and gladden her heart? For she has been very sad this long while, and has asked me to take her out and let her spend the night away with me.'

"'Yes, by Allah!' I replied.

"And we drank until the wine turned our heads, and slept until morning, when she gave me another fifteen dinars, saying, 'Add something to your usual provision on account of the young lady who is coming with me.'

"Then she went away; and on the fourth day I got the house ready as usual, and soon after sunset she came, with another girl wrapped carefully in her cloak. They came in and sat down; and when I saw them I repeated these lines:

	'How dear our day is and how lucky our lot
	when the cynic is away with his spiteful tongue!
	When love and delight and the swimming of the head
	send cleverness trotting off — the best gift of wine.
	When the full moon shines out from the cloudy veil
	and the little branch sways in its shining greenery;
	when the red rose blooms in the freshest cheek
	and Narcissus opens his love-sick eyes;
	when pleasure with the people I love is so sweet
	and friendship with the people I love is complete.'

"I was delighted to see them, and lit the candles after welcoming them with gladness and delight. They took off their heavy outer clothes, and the new girl uncovered her face — and I saw she was like the moon at the full; I never saw anything more beautiful.

"Then I got up and set food and drink in front of them, and we ate and drank; and I kept giving mouthfuls to the newcomer and crowning her cup and drinking with her, until the first girl, growing inwardly jealous, asked me, 'By Allah, is she not more delicious than I am?'

"To which I answered, 'Yes, by the Lord.'

"'It is my wish that you lie with her tonight; for I am your mistress, but she is our guest. On my head be it, and on my eyes.'

"Then she got up and spread the carpets for our bed; and I took the young lady and lay with her that night until morning, when I woke and found myself wet, as I thought, with sweat.

"I sat up and tried to wake the girl; but when I shook her by the shoulders my hand came away crimson with blood, and her head rolled off the pillow.

"At which my senses left me and I cried out aloud, 'O All-powerful Protector, grant me Your protection!' And then, finding her neck had been cut through, I sprang up, and the world went black in front of my eyes; and I looked for the lady, my first love, and could not find her.

"So I knew it was she who had murdered the girl out of jealousy, and I said, 'There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great! What is to be done now?'

"I thought a while; then, taking off my clothes, I dug a hole in the middle of the courtyard, in which I laid the murdered girl with her jewellery and her gold ornaments; and throwing the earth back over her, replaced the slabs of the marble pavement.

"After this I made the full washing and put on clean clothes; then, taking what money I had left, I locked up the house and gathered my courage and went to its owner, to whom I paid a year's rent, saying, 'I am about to join my uncles in Cairo.'

"Presently I set out, and travelling to Egypt, met up with my uncles, who were delighted to see me; and I found they had finished selling their merchandise. They asked me, 'What is the reason for your coming?' And I answered, 'I longed for a sight of you' — but I did not let them know that I had any money with me.

"I stayed with them a year, enjoying the pleasures of Cairo and her Nile and squandering the rest of my money on feasting and carousing, until the time drew near for my uncles to leave, when I ran from them and hid myself. They made enquiries and searched for me; but hearing nothing, they said, 'He will have gone back to Damascus.'

"When they had gone I came out of my hiding place and stayed in Cairo three years, until nothing was left of my money.

"Now every year I used to send the rent of the Damascus house to its owner, until at last I had nothing left but enough to pay him one year's rent; and my chest was tight with worry. So I travelled to Damascus and put up at the house, whose owner the jeweller was glad to see me; and I found everything locked up as I had left it.

"I opened the cupboards and took out my clothes and necessaries, and came upon — underneath the bed where I had lain that night with the girl who was beheaded — a golden necklace set with ten gems of surpassing beauty.

"I picked it up and cleaned the blood off it, and sat gazing at it and weeping a while.

"Then I stayed in the house two days, and on the third went to the baths and changed my clothes. I had no money by me now; so Satan whispered temptation to me, that the Decree of Destiny might be carried out.

"Next day I took the jewelled necklace to the market and handed it to a broker, who sat me down in the shop of the jeweller, my landlord, and told me to be patient until the market filled up; when he carried the ornament off and cried it for sale, privately and without my knowledge.

"The necklace was priced as worth two thousand dinars; but the broker came back to me and said, 'This collar is copper, a mere counterfeit made after the fashion of the Franks, and a thousand dirhams have been bid for it.'

"'Yes,' I answered, 'I knew it was copper; we had it made for a certain person so as to play a joke on her. Now my wife has inherited it and we want to sell it; so go and take the thousand dirhams'":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Twenty-ninth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the handsome young man said to the broker, "Take the thousand dirhams"; and when the broker heard this, he knew the case was suspicious.

So he carried the collar to the head of the market, and the head of the market took it to the Governor, who was also prefect of police, and told him, falsely enough, "This necklace was stolen from my house, and we have found the thief dressed as a trader."

So before I knew anything about it the watch surrounded me and made me their prisoner and carried me before the Governor, who questioned me about the collar. I told him the tale I had told the broker; but he laughed and said, "These words are not true."

Then, before I knew what was happening, the guards stripped my clothes off and came down on my ribs with palm rods, until for the smart of the sticks I confessed, "It was I who stole it" — saying to myself, "It is better to say you stole it than to let them know its owner was murdered in your house, for then they would kill you to avenge her."

So they wrote down that I had stolen it, and they cut off my hand and scalded the stump in oil, at which I fainted away for the pain; but they gave me wine to drink and I recovered, and picking up my hand, was going back to my fine house — when my landlord said to me, "Since this has happened to you, my son, you must leave my house and look for another lodging, as you have been convicted of theft. You are a handsome young man, but who will pity you after this?"

"My master," I said, "bear with me two days or three, until I find another place."

He answered, "So be it," and went away and left me.

I went back into the house, where I sat weeping and saying, "How shall I go back to my own people with my hand cut off, when they do not know I am innocent? Perhaps even after this Allah may arrange something for me."

And I wept beyond all weeping; grief besieged me, and I stayed in bitter trouble for two days.

But on the third day my landlord came suddenly in to me, and with him some of the guards and the head of the market who had falsely accused me of stealing the necklace. I went up to them and asked, "What is the matter?" — but without any more talk they pinioned my arms and threw a chain round my neck, saying, "The necklace that was on you has turned out to be the property of the Wazir of Damascus, who is also her Viceroy." And they added, "It went missing from his house three years ago, at the same time as his younger daughter."

When I heard this my heart sank inside me, and I said to myself, "Your life is gone beyond any doubt! By Allah, I must tell the Chief my story; and if he likes let him kill me, and if he pleases let him pardon me."

So they carried me to the Wazir's house and stood me in front of him. When he saw me he glanced at me out of the corner of his eye and said to those present, "Why did you cut off his hand? This man is unfortunate, and there is no fault in him; indeed you have wronged him by cutting off his hand."

When I heard this I took heart, and my soul promising me something good, I said to him, "By Allah, my lord, I am no thief; but they slandered me with a vile slander, and they scourged me in the middle of the market, telling me to confess, until for the pain of the rods I lied against myself and confessed the theft, although I am entirely innocent of it."

"Do not be afraid," said the Viceroy. "No harm shall come to you."

Then he ordered the head of the market to be imprisoned, and said to him, "Give this man the blood money for his hand; and if you delay I will hang you and seize all your property."

What is more he called his guards, who took the man and dragged him away, leaving me with the Chief.

Then at his command they loosed the chain from my neck and unbound my arms; and he looked at me and said, "My son, be truthful with me, and tell me how this necklace came to you." And he recited these lines:

	"Truth suits you best, even though the truth
	should bring you to burn in the fire you were threatened with."

"By Allah, my lord," I answered, "I will tell you nothing but the truth."

Then I told him everything that had passed between me and the first lady, and how she had brought me the second and had killed her out of jealousy; and I set the tale out for him in full.

When he heard my story he shook his head and struck his right hand upon his left; and putting his handkerchief over his face, wept a while, and then recited:

	"I see the woes of the world in plenty,
	and worldly people sick with spleen and grief;
	there is One who will part the meeting of any two,
	and those who are not parted are few and far between."

Then he turned to me and said:

"Know, my son, that the elder girl who first came to you was my daughter, whom I used to keep closely guarded. When she grew up I sent her to Cairo and married her to her cousin, my brother's son. After a while he died and she came back — but she had learnt wantonness and bad manners from the people of Cairo; so she visited you four times, and at last brought her younger sister.

"Now they were full sisters and much attached to each other; and when that adventure happened to the elder, she disclosed her secret to her sister, who wanted to go out with her. So she asked your leave and brought her to you; after which she came back alone; and finding her weeping, I questioned her about her sister, but she said, 'I know nothing about her.'

"However, she presently told her mother privately what had happened and how she had cut off her sister's head; and her mother told me. Then she did not stop weeping and saying, 'By Allah, I shall cry for her till I die.' Nor did she leave off mourning until her heart broke and she died; and that is how things fell out.

"So you see, my son, what has come to pass. And now I want you not to cross me in what I am about to offer you: I mean to marry you to my youngest daughter, for she is a virgin and born of another mother; and I will take no dowry from you but on the contrary will settle an allowance on you, and you shall live with me in my house in the place of a son."

"So be it," I answered, "and how could I hope for such good fortune?"

Then he sent at once for the judge and the witnesses and had my marriage contract with his daughter written out, and I went in to her. What is more, he got me a large sum of money out of the head of the market, and I stood in high favour with him.

During that year news came to me that my father was dead; and the Wazir sent a courier with letters bearing the royal signature to fetch me the money my father had left behind. And now I am living in all the comfort of life.

Such was the manner of the cutting off of my right hand.

I marvelled at his story (the Jew went on), and I stayed with him three days, after which he gave me a great deal of wealth; and I set out and travelled eastwards until I reached this city of yours, and the place suited me very well; so I settled here — and there happened to me what you know about with the hunchback.

At this the King of China shook his head and said, "This story of yours is not stranger or more wonderful or more marvellous or more delightful than the tale of the hunchback; and so I must hang the whole number of you. However, there still remains the tailor, who is the head of the whole offence." And he added, "Tailor, if you can tell me anything more wonderful than the story of the hunchback, I will pardon you all your offences."

At which the man came forward and began to tell the

Tale of the Tailor

Know, O King of the age, that the most marvellous thing happened to me only yesterday, before I fell in with the hunchback.

It so happened that early in the day I was at the wedding feast of one of my friends, who had got together in his house some twenty of the craftsmen of this city — tailors and silk-spinners and carpenters and others of the same sort.

As soon as the sun had risen they set food in front of us so that we could eat; when in came the master of the house, and with him a young stranger, a good-looking man from Baghdad, wearing clothes as handsome as could be; and he was a very fine figure, except that he was lame in one leg.

He came and greeted us, and we stood up to receive him; but when he was about to sit down he caught sight among us of a certain man who was a barber, at which he refused to sit and would have gone away.

But we stopped him, and our host stopped him too, swearing he should not leave us, and asked, "What is the reason for your coming in and going straight out again?"

To which he answered, "By Allah, my lord, do not hinder me; the reason I am turning back is that barber over there — that man of ill omen, that disgrace, that good-for-nothing."

When the master of the house heard this he marvelled greatly and said, "How does this young man, who comes from Baghdad, come to be so troubled and put out by this barber?"

Then we looked at the stranger and said, "Explain the reason for your anger against the barber."

"Good company," said the young man, "I had a strange adventure with this barber in Baghdad, which is my native city. He was the cause of my leg being broken and of my lameness, and I have sworn never to sit in the same place as he does, nor even to stay in any town where he happens to be living. I said goodbye to Baghdad and travelled far from it and came to stay in this city of yours; and I had hardly passed one night before I meet him again. But not another day shall go by before I leave here."

Said we to him, "In Allah's name, tell us the tale."

And the young man began — the barber changing colour from brown to yellow as he spoke:

Know, good company, that my father was one of the chief merchants of Baghdad, and Almighty Allah had blessed him with no son but me. When I grew up and came of age my father was received into the mercy of Allah, whose Name be exalted, and left me money and eunuchs, servants and slaves; and I used to dress well and eat well.

Now Allah had made me a hater of womankind; and one day, as I was walking along a street in Baghdad, a party of women met me face to face on the footway; so I fled from them, and going into an alley that was a dead end, sat down on a stone bench at the far end of it.

I had not been sitting there long before the latticed window of one of the houses opposite was thrown open, and at it there appeared a young lady like the full moon at its fullest; I never in my life saw her like; and she began watering some flowers on the window sill.

She turned right and left, and seeing me watching her, shut the window and went away. At which a fire was suddenly kindled in my heart; my mind was possessed with her, and my hatred of women turned into love of women.

I went on sitting there, lost to the world, until sunset — when the judge of the city came riding by with his slaves in front of him and his eunuchs behind, and dismounted and went into the house where the girl had appeared.

By this I knew he was her father; so I went home miserable and threw myself down on my bed in grief. Then my maids came flocking in and sat about me, not knowing what was wrong with me; but I did not say a word to them, and they wept and wailed over me.
