Presently in came an old woman, who looked at me and saw at a glance what the matter was; so she sat down by my head and spoke kindly to me, saying, "My son, tell me all about it and I will be the means of your being joined with her."

So I told her what had happened; and she answered, "My son, this girl is the daughter of the judge of Baghdad, who keeps her in the closest seclusion; and the window where you saw her is her floor, while her father occupies the great hall on the lower storey. She is often there alone, and I am in the habit of visiting the house; so you will not get to her except through me. Now set your wits to work and take heart."

With these words she went away; and I took heart at what she had said, and my household rejoiced that day, seeing me get up in the morning safe and sound.

By and by the old woman came back looking crestfallen, and said, "My son, do not ask me how I got on with her! When I told her, she cried at me: 'If you do not hold your peace, you hag of ill omen, and leave off such talk, I will treat you as you deserve and put you to the foulest of deaths.' But I must have another try at her."

When I heard this it added illness to my illness; and the neighbours came to visit me and judged that I was not long for this world.

But after some days the old woman came to me and, putting her mouth close to my ear, whispered, "My son, I claim from you the gift for good news."

With this my soul came back into me and I said, "Whatever you want shall be yours."

At which she began: "Yesterday I went to the young lady, who, seeing me broken in spirit and shedding tears from reddened eyes, asked me, 'Auntie, what is the matter, that I see your chest so tight with trouble?'

"And I answered, weeping bitterly, 'My lady, I have just come from the house of a young man who loves you and who is about to die for your sake.'

"Said she — and her heart was softened — 'And who is this young man you speak of?'

"And I said, 'He is like a son to me and the fruit of my own body. He saw you some days ago at the window watering your flowers; and catching sight of your face and your wrists, he fell in love at first sight. I let him know what happened to me the last time I was with you, at which his illness grew worse; he took to his bed, and he is nothing now but a dead man, and there is no doubt about it at all.'

"At this she turned pale and asked, 'All this for my sake?'

"And I answered, 'Yes, by Allah! What would you have me do?'

"Said she, 'Go back to him and greet him for me and tell him that I am twice as heartsick as he is. And on Friday, before the hour of public prayer, tell him to come to the house, and I will come down and open the door for him. Then I will take him up to my room and be with him a while, and let him go before my father comes back from the mosque.'"

When I heard the old woman's words all my sickness suddenly fell away from me, my anguish stopped and my heart was comforted. I took off the clothes I had on and gave them to her; and as she turned to go she said, "Keep a good heart."

"I have not a jot of sorrow left," I replied.

My household and my friends rejoiced at my recovery; and I stayed like that until Friday, when the old woman came in and asked how I was, to which I answered that I was well and in good case.

Then I put on my clothes and perfumed myself and sat down to wait for the congregation to go in to prayers, so that I could go to her.

But the old woman said to me, "You have time and to spare; so you would do well to go to the baths and have your hair shaved off — especially after your illness — so as not to show the traces of it."

"That is the best way," I answered. "I have only just bathed in hot water, but I will have my head shaved."

Then I said to my page, "Go to the market and bring me a barber — a discreet fellow, and one not given to meddling or impertinent curiosity, or likely to split my head with too much talk."

The boy went out at once and came back with this wretched old man, this creature of ill omen.

When he came in he greeted me and I returned his greeting; and then he said, "Truly I see you are thin in the body."

And I said, "I have been ill."

He went on, "May Allah drive far away from you your woe and your sorrow and your trouble and your distress."

"Allah grant your prayer," said I.

He continued, "All gladness to you, my master, for recovery has certainly come to you. Do you wish to be shaved, or to be bled? For it was a tradition of Ibn Abbas — Allah accept of him — that the Apostle said, 'Whoever cuts his hair on a Friday, the Lord shall turn seventy calamities away from him.' And it is related of him also that he said, 'Cupping on a Friday preserves a man from loss of sight and from a host of diseases.'"

"Leave this talk," I cried. "Come and shave my head at once, for I cannot stand it."

So he got up and put out his hand in the most leisurely way and took out a handkerchief and unfolded it — and inside it was an astrolabe with seven parallel plates mounted in silver.

Then he went into the middle of the courtyard and raised his head and the instrument towards the sun's rays, and looked for a long while. When that was over he came back and said to me:

"Know that there have elapsed of this our day, which is Friday, and this Friday being the tenth of the month Safar in the six hundred and fifty-third year since the Flight of the Apostle — on whom be the best of blessings and peace — and the seven thousand three hundred and twentieth year of the era of Alexander: eight degrees and six minutes.

"Furthermore, the ascendant of this our day is, according to the most exact science of computation, the planet Mars; and it so happens that Mercury is in conjunction with him, indicating an auspicious moment for haircutting. And this also makes plain to me that you desire union with a certain person, and that your dealings with her will not be favourable. But after this there occurs a sign concerning a matter which will befall you, and of which I will not speak."

"You there," I cried, "by Allah, you weary me and scatter my wits, and your forecast is anything but good. I sent for you to shave my head and nothing else; so up and shave me, and do not draw out your speech."

"By Allah," he replied, "if you only knew what is about to happen to you, you would do nothing at all today; and I advise you to act as I tell you, by the computation of the constellations."

"By Allah," said I, "I never saw a barber who excelled in judicial astrology except you; but I think, and I know, that you are extremely prodigal of frivolous talk. I sent for you only to shave my head, and you come and pester me with this sorry prattle."

"What more would you have?" he replied. "Allah has generously bestowed on you a barber who is an astrologer; one learned in alchemy and white magic; in syntax, grammar and lexicology; in the arts of logic, rhetoric and elocution; in mathematics, arithmetic and algebra; in astronomy, astromancy and geometry; in theology, the Traditions of the Apostle and the Commentaries on the Koran.

"Furthermore I have read books by the score and digested them, and I have had experience of affairs and understood them. In short I have learned the theory and the practice of all the arts and sciences; I know them all by heart, and I am a past master in everything that can be known.

"Your father loved me for my lack of officiousness; therefore, to serve you is a religious duty laid on me. I am no busybody, as you seem to suppose; and on that account I am known as The Silent Man, and also The Modest Man. So it behoves you to give thanks to Allah Almighty and not to cross me, for I am a true counsellor to you and kindly disposed towards you. I only wish I were in your service a whole year, so that you might do me justice; and I would ask you no wage for any of it."

When I heard this flow of words I said to him, "You will certainly be the death of me today":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Thirtieth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the young man said to the barber, "You will certainly be the death of me this very day!"

"My good master," he replied, "I am the one called The Silent Man, by reason of the fewness of my words, to distinguish me from my six brothers. For the eldest is called Al-Bakbuk, the Prattler; the second Al-Haddar, the Babbler; the third Al-Fakik, the Gabbler; the fourth — his name is Al-Kuz al-Aswani, the Long-Necked Jug, from his everlasting chattering; the fifth is Al-Nashshar, the Tattler and Teller of Tales; the sixth is Shakashik, or Many Clamours; and the seventh is famous as Al-Samit, The Silent Man — and that is my noble self."

While he redoubled his talk I thought my gall bladder would burst; so I said to the servant, "Give him a quarter dinar and get rid of him, and let him go from me in the name of the God who made him. I will not have my head shaved today."

"What words are these, my lord?" he cried. "By Allah, I will accept no hire from you until I have served you and attended to your wants; and I do not care if I never take money from you at all. If you do not know my quality, I know yours; and I owe your father, an honest man — on whom Almighty Allah have mercy — a great many kindnesses, for he was a liberal soul and a generous one.

"By Allah, he sent for me one day, just as it might be this blessed day, and I went in to him and found a party of his intimates about him. Said he to me, 'Bleed me.' So I pulled out my astrolabe and, taking the sun's altitude for him, found that the ascendant was inauspicious and the hour unfavourable for bleeding. I told him so, and he did as I bade him and waited for a better opportunity. So I made these lines in his honour:

	I went to my patron to let a little blood,
	but found that the moment was far from good;
	so I sat and I talked of all sorts of strange things
	and wooed his goodwill with jests and with jokes.
	They pleased him, and he cried, 'O man of wit,
	you have proved yourself perfect in a merry mood!'
	Said I, 'O Lord of men, unless you lend me
	art and wisdom, I am a drunken fool;
	in you gather grace, gift, bounty and courtesy,
	and I reward the world with learning, science and gravity.'

"Your father was delighted and called out to the servant, 'Give him a hundred and three gold pieces with a robe of honour!' The man obeyed, and I waited for an auspicious moment and then bled him; and he did not baulk me — no, he thanked me, and I was thanked and praised by everybody there.

"When the bloodletting was over I had no power to keep silent, and asked him, 'By Allah, my lord, what made you say to the servant, Give him a hundred and three dinars?'

"And he answered, 'One dinar was for the astrological observation, another for your pleasant conversation, the third for the bloodletting, and the remaining hundred and the robe were for your verses in my praise.'"

"May Allah show small mercy to my father," I exclaimed, "for ever knowing the like of you!"

He laughed and said, "There is no god but God and Mohammed is the Apostle of God! Glory to Him that changes and is not changed! I took you for a man of sense, but I see you babble and wander from your illness. Allah has said in the Blessed Book, 'Paradise is prepared for the good, who bridle their anger and forgive men' — and so on; and in any case you are excused.

"Yet I cannot conceive the cause of your hurry and flurry; and you should know that your father and your grandfather did nothing without consulting me. Indeed it has been truly enough said, 'Let the adviser be prized'; and, 'There is no vice in advice'; and it is said too, in certain sayings, 'Whoever has no counsellor older than himself will never be an elder himself.' And the poet says:

	Whatever necessary thing you undertake,
	consult the experienced man and do not cross him.

"And truly you will never find a man better versed in affairs than I am; and here I stand on my feet to serve you. I am not vexed with you: why should you be vexed with me? But whatever happens I will bear with you patiently, in memory of the great kindness your father showed me."

"By Allah," I cried, "you with a tongue as long as a jackass's tail, you persist in pestering me with your prattle, and you grow longer and longer in your long speeches — when all I want of you is to shave my head and be on your way."

Then he lathered my head, saying, "I perceive you are vexed with me, but I will not take it ill of you, for your wits are weak and you are only a lad; it was no longer ago than yesterday that I used to take you on my shoulder and carry you to school."

"Brother," said I, "for Allah's sake do what I want and go your way!" And I tore my clothes.

When he saw me do that he took the razor and set about sharpening it, and did not leave off stropping it until my senses were very nearly leaving me. Then he came up to me and shaved part of my head; and then he stopped his hand, and then he said:

"My lord, haste is Satan's way, whereas patience is of Allah the Compassionate. But you, my master — I know you do not know my rank; for truly this hand comes down on the heads of kings and emirs and viziers, and sages and doctors learned in the law. And the poet said of a man like me:

	All crafts are like necklaces strung on a string,
	but this barber is the one great pearl of the row;
	he ranks high over every other craftsman, and why?
	Because the heads of kings are under his hand."

Then I said, "Do leave off talking about what does not concern you; indeed you have tightened my chest and distracted my mind."

Said he, "It seems to me you are a hasty man."

And said I, "Yes! Yes! Yes!"

And he, "I advise you to practise self-restraint, for haste is Satan's stock-in-trade, and bequeaths nothing but repentance and ruin; and He, upon whom be blessings and peace, has said, 'The best of works is the work that deliberation lurks in.' But by Allah, I have some doubt about this affair of yours; and so I should like you to let me know what it is you are in such haste to do, for I am afraid it is something other than good."

Then he went on, "It wants three hours yet to prayer time; but I do not wish to be in doubt about the matter — no, I must know the moment exactly; for truly, 'A guess shot in a time of doubt often brings harm about'; and especially in the case of a man like myself, a superior person whose merits are famous among mankind at large. It would not suit me to talk at random, as the common sort of astrologers do."

And saying that, he threw down the razor and took up the astrolabe and went out into the sun and stood there a long time; after which he came back and, counting on his fingers, said to me, "There remain to prayer time three full hours and complete, neither more nor less, according to the most learned astronomers and the wisest makers of almanacs."

"Allah upon you," I cried, "hold your tongue with me, for you are breaking my liver in pieces."

So he took the razor and, after sharpening it as before and shaving another two hairs off my head, stopped his hand again and said, "I am concerned about your hastiness, and truly you would do well to let me into the cause of it; it would be the better for you, as you know that neither your father nor your grandfather ever did a single thing except by my advice."

When I saw there was no escaping him I said to myself, "The time for prayer is drawing near, and I want to go to her before the people come out of the mosque. If I am held up much longer I do not know how I am to get to her."

Then I said aloud, "Be quick and cut short this talk and this impertinence, for I have to go to a party at the house of some friends of mine."

When he heard me speak of a party he said, "This day of yours is a blessed day for me! In very truth it was only yesterday that I invited a company of my friends, and I have forgotten to provide anything for them to eat. This very moment I was thinking about it. Alas, how disgraced I shall be in their eyes!"

"Do not be distressed about that," I answered. "Have I not told you that I am invited to an entertainment today? So everything in my house, food and drink both, shall be yours, if only you will get through your work and make haste to shave my head."

He replied, "Allah reward you with good! Tell me exactly what is in your house for my guests, so that I know about it."

Said I, "Five dishes of meat and ten chickens with browned breasts and a roast lamb."

"Set them in front of me," said he, "so that I can see them."

So I told my people to buy them, borrow them or steal them, and bring them in any way they could; and I had the lot set in front of him.

When he saw it he cried, "The wine is missing."

And I replied, "I have a flagon or two of good old grape juice in the house."

And he said, "Have it brought out."

So I sent for it, and he exclaimed, "Allah bless you for a generous disposition! But there are still the essences and the perfumes."

So I had a box set in front of him containing nadd, the best of compound perfumes, together with fine aloes-wood, ambergris and unmixed musk, the whole lot worth fifty dinars.

Now the time was growing short and my heart grew tight with it; so I said to him, "Take the whole of it, and finish shaving my head, by the life of Mohammed, whom Allah bless and keep."

"By Allah," said he, "I will not take it until I see everything that is in it."

So I told the page to open the box; and the barber laid down the astrolabe, leaving the greater part of my head unshaved, and sitting down on the ground, turned over the scents and the incense and the aloes-wood and the essences until I was very nearly out of my mind.

Then he took the razor and, coming up to me, shaved off a few more hairs and repeated these lines:

	"The boy will surely take after his father,
	as the tree grows out of its parent root."

Then he said, "By Allah, my son, I do not know whether to thank you or your father; for my entertainment today is entirely owing to your bounty and your kindness. And although not one of my company is worthy of it, still I have a set of honourable men — namely Zantut the bath-keeper; and Sali'a the corn-chandler; and Silat the bean-seller; and Akrashah the greengrocer; and Humayd the scavenger; and Sa'id the camel-man; and Suwayd the porter; and Abu Makarish the bathman; and Kasim the watchman; and Karim the groom.

"There is not among the whole lot of them a bore or a bully in his cups, nor a meddler, nor a man mean with his money; and every one of them has some dance of his own that he dances and some verses of his own that he sings. And the best of them is that, like your servant here, your slave, they do not know what too much talking is, nor what forwardness means.

"The bath-keeper sings to the drum a song that enchants you; and he stands up and dances and chants:

	I am going, O mother, to fill up my pot.

"As for the corn-chandler, he brings more skill to it than anybody; he dances and sings:

	O keening woman, O sweetheart, you fall not short —

and he leaves nobody's insides sound for laughing at him.

"But the scavenger sings so that the birds stop to listen to him, and dances and sings:

	What my wife knows is not locked up in a box!

"And he has the privilege of it, for he is a shrewd rogue and a witty one; and speaking of how good he is, I am in the habit of saying:

	My life for the scavenger! I love him well;
	like a waving bough he is sweet to my sight.
	Fate joined us one night, and I said to him
	— while I grew weak and love gained more might —
	'Your love burns my heart!' 'And no wonder,' said he,
	'when the drawer of dung turns into a stoker.'

"And truly each of them is perfect in whatever can charm a man's wits with joy and jollity." And presently he added, "But hearing is not seeing; and truly, if you would make up your mind to join us and put off going to your friends, it would be better for us and for you.

"The marks of your illness are still on you, and it may be that you are going among people who are mighty talkers, men who discuss together what does not concern them; or there may be among them some forward fellow who will split your head — and you half your size from sickness."

"This shall be for some other day," I answered, and laughed with my heart full of anger. "Finish your work and go, in Almighty Allah's keeping, to your friends, for they will be expecting you."

"My lord," he replied, "I am only trying to introduce you to these fellows of infinite mirth, the sons of men of worth, among whom there is neither impudence nor gossip nor chatter; for never, since I came to years of discretion, could I bear to keep company with anybody who asks questions about what does not concern him, nor have I ever spent time with any but men who are, like myself, men of few words. Truly, if you were to keep company with them, or even to see them once, you would give up all your own friends."

"Allah fulfil your enjoyment of them," said I. "I must certainly come among them some day or other."

But he said, "I wish it were this very day, for I had set my heart on your making one of us. Still, if you must go to your friends today, I will take these good things you have honoured and favoured me with to my guests and leave them to eat and drink and not wait for me; while I will come back to you in haste and go with you to your little party — for there is no ceremony between me and my intimates to stop me leaving them. Do not be afraid, I shall soon be back with you and go with you wherever you go. There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great!"

I shouted, "Go to your friends and make merry with them, and do let me go to mine and be with them today, for they are expecting me."

But the barber cried, "I will not let you go alone."

And I replied, "The truth is that nobody can go in where I am going except me."

He came back, "I suspect that today you have an assignation with some woman, or else you would have taken me with you. And yet I am the very man to take, one who could help you to the end you want. But I am afraid you are running after strange women and will lose your life over it; for in this city of Baghdad a man cannot do anything in that line, and especially on a day like Friday: our Governor is an angry man and a mighty sharp blade."

"Shame on you, you wicked, bad old man!" I cried. "Be off! What are these words you are giving me?"

"You cold-witted creature," he cried, "you say to me what is not true and you hide your mind from me. But I know the whole business for certain, and I only want to help you today with my best endeavours."

I was afraid my people or my neighbours would hear the barber's talk; so I kept quiet a long while, and in that time he finished shaving my head — by which time the hour of prayer had come and the sermon was about to follow.

When he had done I said to him, "Go to your friends with their meat and drink, and I will wait for you to come back. Then we will go together." I hoped in this way to pour oil on the troubled waters and trick the accursed fool, and so perhaps be rid of him.

But he said, "You are cozening me, and you mean to go alone to your appointment and throw yourself into a danger there will be no escaping from. Now by Allah, and again by Allah, do not go until I come back, so that I can go with you and watch how your business turns out."

"So be it," I replied. "Do not be gone long."

Then he took all the meat and drink I had given him, and the rest of it, and went out of my house — but the accursed fellow gave it to a porter to carry to his home and hid himself in one of the alleys.

As for me, I got up that instant, for the muezzins had already called the Friday salutation to the Apostle; and I dressed in a hurry and went out alone, and hurrying to the street, took up my position by the house where I had seen the young lady.

I found the old woman on guard at the door waiting for me, and went up with her to the upper storey, to the girl's rooms. I had hardly got there when the master of the house came back from prayers and, going into the great hall, shut the door.

I looked down out of the window and saw this barber — Allah's curse on him — sitting right opposite the door, and said, "How did this devil find me out?"

At that very moment, as Allah had decreed for the tearing of my veil of secrecy, one of the master's maids happened to commit some offence, for which he beat her. She shrieked out, and his slave ran in to intercede for her, at which the judge beat him too, and he roared out as well.

The damned barber imagined it was I who was being beaten; so he began shouting too, and tore his clothes and threw dust on his head and kept on shrieking and crying, "Help! Help!"

So the people gathered round him, and he went on yelling, "My master is being murdered in the judge's house!"

Then he ran off clamouring to my house with the crowd after him, and told my people and my servants and my slaves; and before I knew what was happening, up they came tearing their clothes and letting their hair down and shouting, "Alas, our master!" — with this barber leading the rout, his clothes torn and in the sorriest state, shouting like a madman and saying, "Alas for our murdered master!"

And the whole lot of them made an assault on the house I was in.

The judge, hearing the yelling and the uproar at his door, said to one of his servants, "See what the matter is"; and the man went out and came back and said, "My master, at the gate there are more than ten thousand souls, what with men and women, and all of them crying, 'Alas for our murdered master!' — and they keep pointing at our house."

When the judge heard this the matter looked serious, and he grew angry; so he got up and opened the door and saw a great crowd of people; at which he was astounded and said, "Good people! What is the matter?"

"You accursed thing! You dog! You hog!" my servants replied. "It is you who have killed our master!"

Said he, "Good people, and what has your master done to me that I should kill him?":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Thirty-first Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the judge said to the servants, "What has your master done to me that I should kill him? This is my house, and it is open to all of you."

Then the barber said, "You beat him, and I heard him cry out."

And the judge said, "But what was he doing that I should beat him? And what brought him into my house? And where did he come from and where did he go?"

"Do not be a wicked, perverse old man," cried the barber, "for I know the whole story. And the long and the short of it is that your daughter is in love with him and he loves her; and when you found out he had come into the house, you told your servants to beat him and they did. By Allah, nobody shall judge between us and you but the Caliph. Or else bring our master out so that his people can take him, before they go in and rescue him from your house by force and you are put to shame."

Then said the judge — his tongue bridled and his mouth stopped with confusion in front of all those people — "If you speak the truth, then come in yourself and fetch him out."

At which the barber pushed forward and went into the house.

When I saw this I looked about for some means of escape and flight, but could see no hiding place except a great chest in the upper room where I was. So I got into it and pulled the lid down over myself and held my breath.

The barber was hardly in the room before he began looking about for me; then he turned right and left and came straight to the place where I was, and stepped up to the chest and lifted it onto his head and made off as fast as he could go.

At this my reason left me, for I knew he would not leave me alone; so I took my courage in both hands and opened the chest and threw myself out onto the ground. My leg was broken in the fall; and the door being open, I saw a great crowd of people looking in.

Now I carried in my sleeve a good deal of gold and some silver, which I had put by against a bad day and just such an occasion as this; so I kept scattering it among the people to distract their attention from me, and while they were busy scrambling for it I set off, hopping as fast as I could through the back streets of Baghdad, shifting and turning right and left.

But wherever I went this damned barber would go in after me, crying aloud, "They would have robbed me of my ma-a-aster! They would have killed the man who was a benefactor to me and my family and my friends! Praise be to Allah, who made me prevail against them and delivered my lord out of their hands!"

And then to me: "Where will you go now? You would persist in following your own wicked devices, until you brought yourself to this pass; and if Allah had not granted me to you, you would never have escaped the strait you had fallen into, for they would have thrown you into a disaster you could never have got clear of. But I will not call you to account for your ignorance, since you are so little in your wits and so inconsequential and so given to hastiness."

Said I to him, "Is what you have brought on me not enough for you, without your running after me and talking such talk to me in the market streets?"

And I very nearly gave up the ghost for sheer rage against him.

Then I took refuge in a weaver's shop in the middle of the market and asked the owner's protection, and he drove the barber away; and sitting in the back room, I said to myself, "If I go home I shall never be able to get rid of this curse of a barber, who will be with me night and day; and I cannot bear the sight of him even for the space of a breath."

So I sent out at once for witnesses and made a will, dividing the greater part of my property among my people, and appointed a guardian over them, to whom I gave charge of great and small alike, directing him to sell my houses and my estates.

Then I set out on my travels, so as to be free of this pimp; and I came and settled in your town, where I have lived some time. When you invited me and I came here, the first thing I saw was this accursed pander sitting in the place of honour.

How, then, can my heart be glad and my stay be pleasant in the company of this fellow who brought all this on me, and who was the cause of the breaking of my leg and of my exile from my home and my native land?

And the young man refused to sit down, and went away.

When we heard his story (the tailor went on) we were amazed beyond measure, and amused; and we said to the barber, "By Allah, is it true, what this young man says about you?"

"By Allah," he replied, "I dealt with him like that out of my courtesy and my sound sense and my generosity. If it had not been for me he would have perished, and nobody but me was the cause of his escape. It was a good thing for him that he suffered in his leg and not in his life!

"If I had been a man of many words, a meddler, a busybody, I would never have acted so kindly by him. But now I will tell you a tale of something that happened to me, so that you may be quite satisfied that I am a man sparing of speech, in whom there is no forwardness, and a very different person from those six brothers of mine. And this is it."

The Barber's Tale of Himself

I was living in Baghdad in the time of Al-Mustansir Billah, son of Al-Mustazi Billah, who was Caliph then — a prince who loved the poor and the needy and kept company with the learned and the pious.

One day it happened that he was angry with ten men, highwaymen who robbed on the Caliph's own road; and he ordered the Prefect of Baghdad to bring them into his presence on the anniversary of the Great Festival.

So the Prefect went out and made them his prisoners and embarked with them in a boat. I caught sight of them as they were getting aboard, and said to myself, "These men are surely gathered for a wedding feast; I think they mean to spend their day in that boat eating and drinking, and nobody shall share their cups but me."

So I got up, good company; and out of the excess of my courtesy and the gravity of my understanding, I got aboard with them and fell into conversation with them.

They rowed across to the opposite bank, where they landed; and up came the watch and the guardians of the peace with chains, which they put round the robbers' necks. And they chained me among the rest of them.

And, good people, is it not a proof of my courtesy and my sparingness of speech that I held my peace and did not care to say a word?

Then they took us away in irons; and next morning they carried the whole lot of us before Al-Mustansir Billah, Commander of the Faithful, who ordered the necks of the ten robbers to be struck off.

So the executioner came forward after they had been seated on the leather mat of blood; and drawing his blade, struck off one head after another until he had struck the neck of the tenth — and I alone was left.

The Caliph looked at me and asked the headsman, "What is the matter with you, that you have struck off only nine heads?"

And he answered, "Allah forbid that I should behead only nine when you ordered me to behead ten."

Said the Caliph, "It seems to me you have struck the necks of only nine, and this man in front of you is the tenth."

"By your beneficence," replied the headsman, "I have beheaded ten."

"Count them," cried the Caliph. And when they counted the heads — there were ten.

The Caliph looked at me and said, "What made you keep silent at a time like this? And how did you come to be in the company of these men of blood? Tell me the cause of it all; for although you are a very old man, your wits are certainly weak."

Now when I heard these words from the Caliph I sprang to my feet and replied:

"Know, O Commander of the Faithful, that I am the Silent Old Man, and I am called so to distinguish me from my six brothers. I am a man of immense learning; while as for the gravity of my understanding, the wiliness of my wits and the sparingness of my speech, there is no end to them; and my calling is that of a barber.

"I went out early yesterday morning and saw these men making for a skiff; and imagining they were bound for a wedding feast, I joined them and mixed in with them. After a while up came the watch and the guardians of the peace, who put chains round their necks and round mine along with the rest; but in the excess of my courtesy I held my peace and did not say a word — and that was nothing but generosity on my part.

"They brought us into your presence, and you gave an order to strike off the necks of the ten; and yet I did not make myself known to you, and stayed silent in front of the executioner, purely out of the great generosity and courtesy that led me to share their death with them.

"But all my life long I have dealt so nobly with mankind, and they pay me back with the foulest and most evil payment there is."

When the Caliph heard my words and knew that I was a man of surpassing generosity and very few words, one with no forwardness in him — as this young man would have it, whom I rescued from mortal danger and who has repaid me so scurvily — he laughed with such excessive laughter that he fell over on his back.

Then he said to me, "Silent Man, do your six brothers take after you in wisdom and knowledge and sparingness of speech?"

I replied: "They were never like me! You put a reproach on me, Commander of the Faithful, and it does not become you to set my brothers on a level with me; for out of the abundance of their speech and the deficiency of their courtesy and their gravity, every one of them has got himself some injury or other.

"One of them is one-eyed; one is palsied; one is stone blind; one is cropped of both his ears; one is shorn of both his lips; and one is a hunchback and a cripple.

"And do not imagine, Commander of the Faithful, that I am prodigal of speech; but I am obliged to explain to you that I am a man of greater worth and fewer words than any of them. From every one of my brothers there hangs a tale of how he came by his bodily defect, and these I will relate to you."

So the Caliph gave ear to

The Barber's Tale of His First Brother

Know then, Commander of the Faithful, that my first brother, Al-Bakbuk the Prattler, is a hunchback who took to tailoring in Baghdad. He used to sew in a shop rented from a man of great wealth, who lived over the shop; and there was a flour mill in the basement as well.

One day, as my brother the hunchback was sitting in his shop tailoring, he happened to raise his head and saw a lady like the rising full moon at a balconied window of his landlord's house, looking out at the passers-by.

When my brother saw her his heart was taken with love of her, and he spent the whole day gazing at her and neglected his tailoring until evening.

Next morning he opened his shop and sat down to sew; but every time he made a stitch he looked up at the window and saw her as before, and his passion and his infatuation grew.

On the third day, as he sat in his usual place gazing at her, she caught sight of him; and seeing that he had been captivated with love of her, she laughed in his face, and he smiled back at her. Then she disappeared, and presently sent her slave girl to him with a bundle containing a piece of red flowered silk.

The maid came up to him and said, "My lady greets you, and asks that of your skill and goodwill you will make her a shift out of this piece, and sew it handsomely with your best sewing."

He replied, "Hearing and obedience"; and he cut out a chemise for her and finished sewing it that same day.

When the morning came the girl came back and said, "My lady greets you and asks how you passed last night; for she has not tasted sleep, her heart being so taken up with you."

Then she laid a piece of yellow satin in front of him and said, "My lady tells you to cut her two pairs of petticoat trousers out of this piece, and sew them this very day."

"Hearing and obedience," he replied. "Greet her for me with many greetings, and tell her: your slave is obedient to your order, so command him as you like."

Then he set about cutting out, and worked hard at sewing the trousers; and after an hour the lady appeared at the lattice and greeted him by signs, now casting her eyes down, now smiling into his face; and he began to assure himself that he would soon make a conquest.

She did not let him stir until he had finished both pairs of trousers; when she withdrew and sent the maid, to whom he handed them over; and she took them and went her way.

When night came he threw himself on his bed and lay tossing from side to side until morning, when he got up and sat down in his place.

Presently the girl came to him and said, "My master calls for you."

Hearing this he was extremely frightened; but the slave girl, seeing his fright, said, "No harm is meant to you: nothing but good is waiting for you. My lady wants you to make my lord's acquaintance."

So my brother the tailor, overjoyed, went with her; and when he came into the presence of his landlord, the lady's husband, he kissed the ground before him, and the master of the house returned his greeting and gave him a great piece of linen, saying, "Cut me shirts out of this stuff and sew them well."

And my brother answered, "To hear is to obey."

At which he fell to work at once, snipping, shaping and sewing, until he had finished twenty shirts by supper time, without stopping to taste food.

The master of the house asked him, "How much is the wage for this?"

And he answered, "Twenty dirhams."

So the gentleman called out to the slave girl, "Bring me twenty dirhams" — and my brother did not say a word; but the lady signed to him, "Take nothing from him"; at which my brother said, "By Allah, I will take nothing from your hand."

And he carried off his tailor's gear and went back to his shop, though he was destitute down to his last penny.

Then he applied himself to their work; eating, in his zeal and diligence, nothing but a bit of bread and drinking only a little water, for three days. At the end of that time the maid came and said to him, "What have you done?"

Said he, "They are finished" — and carried the shirts to the lady's husband, who would have paid him his hire; but he said, "I will take nothing," for fear of her; and going back to his shop, passed the night without sleep for hunger.

Now the lady had told her husband how things stood — my brother knowing nothing about it — and the two of them had agreed to make him their tailor for nothing, the better to mock him and laugh at him.

Next morning he went to his shop; and as he sat there the maid came and said, "Speak with my master."

So he went with her to the husband, who said to him, "I want you to cut me out five long-sleeved robes."

So he cut them out and took the stuff away. Then he sewed them and carried them to the gentleman, who praised his sewing and offered him a purse of silver. He put out his hand to take it — but the lady signed to him from behind her husband not to; and he replied, "My lord, there is no hurry, we have time enough for that."

Then he went out of the house meaner and meeker than a donkey; for truly five things were gathered together in him — love, beggary, hunger, nakedness and hard labour. Even so, he kept his spirits up with the hope of gaining the lady's favours.

When he had finished all their jobs they played him another trick, and married him to their slave girl; but on the night he expected to go in to her, they said, "Sleep tonight in the mill, and tomorrow all will go well."

My brother concluded there was some good reason for it, and spent the night alone in the mill.

Now the husband had set the miller on to make the tailor turn the mill; so when the night was half gone the man came in to him and began saying, "This bull of ours has become useless and stands still instead of going round; he will not turn the mill tonight, and yet we have a great store of corn to grind. However, I shall yoke him whether he likes it or not, and make him finish grinding it before morning, as the people are impatient for their flour."

So he filled the hoppers with grain; and going up to my brother with a rope in his hand, tied it round his neck and said, "Gee up! Round with the mill! You, bull, would do nothing but grub and stale and dung!"

Then he took a whip and laid it on my brother's shoulders and calves, and my brother began to howl and bellow; but nobody came to help him, and he was forced to grind the wheat until close on dawn, when the master of the house came in and, seeing my brother still tethered to the yoke and the man flogging him, went away again.

At daybreak the miller went home and left him still yoked and half dead; and soon afterwards in came the slave girl, who untied him and said, "My lady and I are very sorry for what has happened, and we have shared your grief with you."

But he had no tongue to answer her with, for the excess of beating and mill-turning.

Then he went off to his lodging; and the clerk who had drawn up the marriage deed came and greeted him, saying, "Allah give you long life! May your wedding be blessed! That face of yours tells of pleasant doings and dalliance and kissing and embracing from dusk to dawn."

"Allah grant the liar no peace, you thousandfold cuckold," my brother replied. "By Allah, I did nothing but turn the mill in the place of the bull all night till morning."

"Tell me your tale," said he. And my brother recounted what had happened to him; and he said, "Your star does not agree with her star; but if you like I can alter the contract for you" — adding, "Take care there is not another cheat in store for you."

And my brother answered, "See whether you have not another device."

Then the clerk left him; and he sat in his shop looking out for somebody to bring him a job, so that he could earn his day's bread.

Presently the maid came and said, "Speak with my lady."

"Be off, my good girl," he replied. "There shall be no more dealings between me and your lady."

The maid went back to her mistress and told her what my brother had said; and presently she put her head out of the window, weeping and saying, "Why, my beloved, are there to be no more dealings between me and you?"

But he made her no answer. Then she wept and begged him, swearing that everything that had happened to him in the mill was done without her knowledge, and that she was innocent of the whole business.

When he looked at her beauty and loveliness and heard the sweetness of her speech, the sorrow that had possessed him passed out of his heart; he accepted her excuse and rejoiced at the sight of her. So he greeted her and talked with her, and sat tailoring a while — after which the maid came and said, "My mistress greets you and informs you that her husband means to sleep out tonight at the house of some close friends of his; so when he has gone, come to us and spend the night with my lady in the most delightful enjoyment till the morning."

Now her husband had asked her, "How shall we manage to turn him away from you?" And she had answered, "Leave me to play him another trick and make him a laughing stock for the whole town." But my brother knew nothing of the malice of women.

As soon as it was dusk the slave girl came and took him to the house; and when the lady saw him she said, "By Allah, my lord, I have been longing for you terribly."

"By Allah," he cried, "kiss me quickly before you give me anything else."

He had hardly spoken when the lady's husband came in from the next room and seized him, saying, "By Allah, I will not let you go until I have handed you over to the chief of the town watch."

My brother humbled himself to him, but he would not listen, and carried him before the Prefect, who gave him a hundred lashes with a whip and, mounting him on a camel, paraded him round the city, while the guards proclaimed aloud, "This is the reward of the man who violates the households of honourable men!"

What is more, he fell off the camel and broke his leg, and so became lame. Then the Prefect banished him from the city; and he went off not knowing where to go. But I heard of him, and fearing for him, went out after him and brought him back secretly to the city and restored him to health, and took him into my house, where he is living still.

The Caliph laughed at my story and said, "You have done well, Samit — Silent Man, sparing of speech!" And he told me to take a present and go away.

But I said, "I will accept nothing from you until I have told you what happened to all my other brothers; and do not think me a man of many words."

So the Caliph gave ear to

The Barber's Tale of His Second Brother

Know, Commander of the Faithful, that my second brother's name was Al-Haddar, that is the Babbler, and he was the paralysed one.

It happened to him one day, as he was going about his business, that an old woman came up to him and said, "Stop a moment, my good man, so that I can tell you of something which, if it is to your liking, you may do for me; and I will pray Allah to give you good of it."

My brother stopped, and she went on, "I will put you in the way of a certain thing, provided you are not prodigal of speech."

"Go on with your talk," said he.

And she said, "What do you say to handsome quarters, and a fine garden with running water, flowers blooming and fruit growing and old wine going round, and a pretty young face whose owner you may hold in your arms from dark till dawn? If you do whatever I tell you, you will see something greatly to your advantage."

"And is all this in the world?" asked my brother.

And she answered, "It is, and it shall be yours — provided you are sensible and leave off idle curiosity and too much talk, and do as I say."

"I will indeed, my lady," said he. "But how is it you have chosen me for this before all other men, and what is it about me that pleases you so much?"

Said she, "Did I not tell you to be sparing of speech? Hold your peace and follow me. Know that the young lady I am taking you to loves to have her own way and hates being thwarted and hates anybody who contradicts her; so if you humour her, you will get what you want of her."

And my brother said, "I will not cross her in anything."

Then she went on and my brother followed her, hungering after everything she had described, until they came into a fine large house, handsome and choicely furnished, full of eunuchs and servants and showing signs of prosperity from top to bottom.

And she was taking him up to the upper storey when the people of the house said to him, "What are you doing here?"

But the old woman answered them, "Hold your peace and do not trouble him; he is a workman, and we have need of him."

Then she brought him into a fine great pavilion with a garden in the middle of it — eyes never saw a fairer — and sat him down on a handsome couch.

He had not been sitting long before he heard a loud noise, and in came a troop of slave girls surrounding a lady like the moon on the night of its fullness. When he saw her he got up and made her a bow, at which she welcomed him and told him to be seated.

So he sat down, and she said to him, "Allah advance you to honour! Is all well with you?"

"My lady," he answered, "all is very well with me."

Then she ordered food brought in, and they set delicate dishes before her; so she sat down to eat, making a show of affection towards my brother and joking with him — though the whole time she could not stop laughing; but every time he looked at her she made a sign towards her maids, as though she were laughing at them.

My brother, the ass, understood nothing of it; but in the excess of his ridiculous passion he imagined that the lady was in love with him and would soon grant him what he wanted.

When they had finished eating they set on the wine; and in came ten girls like moons, with lutes ready strung in their hands, and fell to singing with full voices, sweet and sad; at which delight took hold of him, and he took the cup from the lady's hands and drank it standing.

Then she drank a cup of wine, and my brother, still standing, said "Health!" to her and bowed. She handed him another cup and he drank it off — at which she slapped him hard on the back of the neck.

At this my brother would have gone out of the house in anger; but the old woman followed him and winked at him to come back. So he came back, and the lady told him to sit down, and he sat down without a word. Then she slapped him on the back of the neck again; and the second slapping was not enough for her — she had to make all her maids slap him and cuff him too, while he kept saying to the old woman, "I never saw anything nicer than this."

And she for her part kept exclaiming, "Enough, enough, I beg you, mistress!" — but the women slapped him until he very nearly fainted away.

Presently my brother got up and went out to relieve himself; but the old woman overtook him and said, "Be patient a little and you will get what you want."

"How much longer have I to wait?" my brother replied. "This slapping has made me feel faint."

"As soon as she is warm with the wine," she answered, "you shall have your desire."

So he went back to his place and sat down; at which all the maids stood up, and the lady told them to perfume him with pastilles and sprinkle his face with rose water.

Then she said to him, "Allah advance you to honour! You have come into my house and have put up with my conditions; for whoever thwarts me I turn away, and whoever is patient gets what he wants."

"My mistress," said he, "I am your slave and in the hollow of your hand."

"Know then," she went on, "that Allah has made me passionately fond of a frolic; and whoever falls in with my humour comes by whatever he wishes."

Then she ordered her maids to sing at the tops of their voices until the whole company was delighted; after which she said to one of them, "Take your lord and do what is necessary for him, and bring him straight back to me."

So the girl took my brother — and he not knowing what she meant to do with him. But the old woman overtook him and said, "Be patient; there is only a little more to do."

At this his face brightened, and he stood up in front of the lady while the old woman kept saying, "Be patient; you will get your wish this instant!" — until he said, "Tell me what she wants the girl to do with me."

"Nothing but good," she replied, "as I am your sacrifice! She only wants to dye your eyebrows and pluck out your moustaches."

Said he, "As for dyeing my eyebrows, that will come off with washing; but as for plucking out my moustaches, that is a somewhat painful business."

"Be careful how you cross her," cried the old woman, "for she has set her heart on you."

So my brother patiently let her dye his eyebrows and pluck out his moustaches; after which the girl went back to her mistress and told her.

Said she, "Now there is only one other thing to be done: you must shave off his beard and make him smooth-faced."

So the girl went back and told him what her mistress had ordered; and my brother, the blockhead, said, "How am I to do a thing that will disgrace me in front of everybody?"

But the old woman said, "She only wants it so that you may be like a beardless youth, and so that no hair is left on your face to scratch and prick her delicate cheeks; for truly she is passionately in love with you. So be patient and you will get what you are after."

My brother was patient and did as she said, and let his beard be shaved off. And when he was brought back to the lady — there he was, dyed red as to his eyebrows, plucked of both moustaches, shorn of his beard and rouged on both cheeks.

At first she was startled at him; and then she made a mockery of him, and laughing until she fell over on her back, said, "My lord, you have truly won my heart by your good nature!"

Then she begged him, by her own life, to stand up and dance; and he got up and capered about — and there was not a cushion in the house that she did not throw at his head, and all her women did the same, and they kept pelting him with oranges and lemons and citrons besides, until he fell down senseless from the cuffing on the neck, the cushions and the fruit.

"Now you have got what you wanted," said the old woman when he came round. "There are no more blows in store for you, and there is only one small thing left to do. It is her habit, when she is in her cups, to let nobody have her until she has taken off her dress and her trousers and is stark naked. Then she will tell you to take your clothes off and run; and she will run ahead of you as though she were flying from you; and you are to follow her from room to room until you are fully roused, when she will give herself to you." And she added, "Strip your clothes off at once."

So he got up, very nearly out of his mind with ecstasy, and taking off his clothes, showed himself stark naked:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Thirty-second Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the old woman said to the barber's second brother, "Take your clothes off," he got up very nearly out of his mind with ecstasy, and stripping off his clothes, showed himself stark naked.

At which the lady stripped too, and said to my brother, "If you want anything, run after me until you catch me."

Then she set off at a run and he ran after her, while she rushed into one room after another and out of one room after another, my brother scampering after her in a rage of desire like a downright madman, and fully roused.

After a good deal of this she dashed into a darkened place and he dashed in after her — but suddenly he trod on a spot that gave way under his weight; and before he knew where he was, he found himself in the middle of a crowded market, part of the leather-sellers' bazaar, where they were crying the prices of skins and hides and buying and selling.

When they saw him in that state — naked, roused, shorn of beard and moustaches, his eyebrows dyed red and his cheeks reddened with rouge — they shouted and clapped their hands at him, and set about flogging him with hides across his bare body until a faint came over him.

Then they threw him on the back of a donkey and carried him to the Chief of Police.

Said the Chief, "What is this?"

Said they, "This fellow fell suddenly on us out of the Wazir's house in this state."

So the Prefect gave him a hundred lashes and then banished him from Baghdad. However, I went out after him and brought him back secretly into the city and made him a daily allowance to live on — although, if it were not for my generous nature, I could not have put up with the likes of him.

Then the Caliph gave ear to

The Barber's Tale of His Third Brother

My third brother's name was Al-Fakik, the Gabbler, and he was blind.

One day Fate and Fortune drove him to a fine large house, and he knocked at the door, wanting a word with its owner so as to beg something of him.

Said the master of the house, "Who is at the door?"

But my brother did not say a word; and presently he heard him repeat in a loud voice, "Who is this?"

Still he made no answer; and immediately he heard the master walk to the door and open it and say, "What do you want?"

My brother answered, "Something for Almighty Allah's sake."

"Are you blind?" asked the man; and my brother answered, "I am."

Said the other, "Hold out your hand to me."

So my brother put out his hand, thinking he would give him something — but he took it and, drawing him into the house, carried him up from stair to stair until they reached the terrace on the roof, my brother thinking all the while that he would certainly give him something in the way of food or money.

Then he asked my brother, "What do you want, blind man?"

And he answered, "Something for the Almighty's sake."

"May Allah open some other door for you!"

"You there! Why not say so when I was down at the bottom of the stairs?"

"You beggar, why not answer me when I first called out to you?"

"And what do you mean to do for me now?"

"There is nothing in the house to give you."

"Then take me down the stairs."

"The way is in front of you."

So my brother got up and made his way downstairs, until he came within twenty steps of the door, when his foot slipped and he rolled to the bottom and broke his head open.

Then he went out, not knowing which way to turn; and presently he fell in with two other blind men, companions of his, who said to him, "What did you take today?"

He told them what had happened to him, and added, "Brothers, I want to take some of the money we have in hand and provide for myself out of it."

Now the master of the house had followed him and was listening to what they said; but neither my brother nor his companions knew anything about it.

So my brother went to his lodging and sat down to wait for his companions, and the owner of the house came in after him without being noticed.

When the other blind men arrived, my brother said to them, "Bolt the door and search the house, in case some stranger has followed us in."

The man, hearing this, caught hold of a cord that hung from the ceiling and clung to it, while they went round the house and searched and found nobody. So they came back and sat down beside my brother and brought out their money, which they counted — and it came to twelve thousand dirhams.

Each of them took what he wanted, and they buried the rest in a corner of the room. Then they set out food and sat down to eat.

Presently my brother, hearing a strange pair of jaws chewing beside him, said to his friends, "There is a stranger among us"; and putting out his hand, caught hold of the house-owner's.

At which they all fell on him and beat him; and when they were tired of belabouring him they shouted, "Muslims! A thief has got in among us and wants to take our money!"

A crowd gathered round them, at which the intruder clung to them and complained along with them, and shut his eyes as they did, so that nobody should doubt he was blind, and cried out, "Muslims! I take refuge with Allah and with the Governor, for I have a matter to lay before him!"

Suddenly up came the watch and, laying hands on the whole lot of them — my brother among them — drove them off to the Governor's, who set them in front of him and asked, "What is your news?"

Said the intruder, "Look and find out for yourself; not a word will be got out of us except by torture. So begin by beating me, and after me beat this man, our leader." And he pointed at my brother.

So they threw the man down at full length and gave him four hundred strokes on his backside. The beating hurt him, at which he opened one eye; and as they redoubled the blows, he opened the other.

When the Governor saw this he said, "What have we here, you accursed thing?"

To which he replied, "Give me the pledge of pardon! The four of us have shammed blindness, and we impose on people so as to get into their houses and look on the unveiled faces of their women and contrive to corrupt them. We have made a great deal of money this way, and our store comes to twelve thousand dirhams.

"I said to my companions, 'Give me my share, three thousand'; but they set on me and beat me and took my money away; and I take refuge with Allah and with you. Better you should have my share than they. So if you want to know whether what I say is true, beat each of the others more than you have beaten me, and he will certainly open his eyes."

The Governor gave orders for the questioning to begin with my brother; and they tied him to the whipping post, and the Governor said, "You scum of the earth, do you abuse the gracious gifts of Allah and pretend to be blind?"

"Allah! Allah!" cried my brother. "By Allah, there is not one of us who can see."

Then they beat him until he fainted away, and the Governor cried, "Leave him until he comes round, and then beat him again."

After this he had each of the companions given more than three hundred strokes, while the impostor kept saying to them, "Open your eyes, or you will be beaten again."

At last the man said to the Governor, "Send somebody with me to bring you the money; for these fellows will not open their eyes, in case they are disgraced in front of everybody."

So the Governor sent to fetch the money, and gave the man his pretended share, three thousand dirhams; and keeping the rest for himself, banished the three blind men from the city.

But I, Commander of the Faithful, went out and overtook my brother and questioned him about his case; at which he told me what I have told you. So I brought him secretly into the city and appointed him — in the strictest privacy — an allowance for meat and drink.

The Caliph laughed at my story and said, "Give him a gift and let him go."

But I said, "By Allah, I will take nothing until I have made known to the Commander of the Faithful what happened with the rest of my brothers; for truly I am a man of few words and sparing of speech."

Then the Caliph gave ear to

The Barber's Tale of His Fourth Brother

Now as for my fourth brother, Commander of the Faithful — Al-Kuz al-Aswani, called the Long-Necked Jug from his brimming over with words, the one who was blind in one eye — he became a butcher in Baghdad, and sold meat and fattened rams; and great men and rich men bought their meat from him, so that he amassed a good deal of wealth and got himself cattle and houses.

He went on like this a long while, until one day, as he was sitting in his shop, an old man with a long beard came up and laid down some silver and said, "Give me meat for this."

He gave him his money's worth of meat and the old man went his way. My brother examined the old man's silver, and seeing that the dirhams were white and bright, put them away in a place by themselves.

The greybeard kept coming back to the shop regularly for five months, and my brother did not stop laying up all the coin he got from him in its own box.

At last he thought he would take the money out and buy sheep with it; so he opened the box and found nothing in it but bits of white paper cut round to look like coins. At which he beat his own face and cried aloud until the people gathered round him; and then he told them his tale, which astonished them a great deal.

Then he got up as usual, and slaughtering a ram, hung it up inside his shop; after which he cut off some of the meat and hung it outside, saying to himself all the while, "O Allah, if only that ill-omened old fellow would come!"

And not an hour had passed before the old man came with his silver in his hand — at which my brother got up and caught hold of him, calling out, "Come and help me, Muslims, and hear my story about this villain!"

When the old man heard this he said to him quietly, "Which will be better for you — to let go of me, or to be disgraced by me in front of everybody?"

"And how will you disgrace me?"

"By showing that you sell human flesh for mutton."

"You lie, you accursed thing!"

"No — the accursed man is the one who has a human being hanging up in his shop by way of meat. If the matter is as you say, I give you lawful leave to take my money and my life."

Then the old man cried out aloud, "Ho, people! If you want to prove the truth of what I say, go into this man's shop."

The people rushed in — and found that the ram had become a dead man hung up for sale. So they set on my brother, crying out, "Infidel! Villain!"; and his best friends fell to cuffing and kicking him and kept saying, "Do you make us eat the flesh of the sons of Adam?"

What is more, the old man struck him in the eye and put it out.

Then they carried the carcass, with its throat cut, before the Chief of the city watch, to whom the old man said, "Emir, this fellow butchers men and sells their flesh for mutton, and we have brought him to you; so rise and carry out the judgements of Allah, to whom be honour and glory."

My brother would have defended himself, but the Chief refused to hear him, and sentenced him to receive five hundred strokes and to forfeit the whole of his property. And indeed, if it had not been for that same property, which he laid out in bribes, they would certainly have killed him.

Then the Chief banished him from Baghdad; and my brother travelled at random until he came to a great town, where he thought it best to set up as a cobbler; so he opened a shop and sat there doing what he could to make a living.

One day, as he went out about his business, he heard the distant tramp of horses; and asking what it was, was told that the King was going out hunting and coursing. So my brother stopped to look at the fine procession.

It so happened that the King's eye met my brother's — at which the King hung his head down and said, "I take refuge with Allah from the evil of this day!" And he turned his horse's reins and went home with his whole retinue.

Then he gave orders to his guards, who seized my brother and beat him with such a painful beating that he was very nearly dead; and my brother had no idea what the cause of his ill-treatment could be. After it he went back to his place in the sorriest state.

Soon afterwards he went to one of the King's household and told him what had happened; and the man laughed until he fell over on his back, and cried, "Brother, you must know that the King cannot bear the sight of a one-eyed man, and especially one blind in the right eye — in which case he never lets him go without killing him."

When my brother heard this he decided to fly from that city; so he went out of it to another, where nobody knew him, and there he stayed a long while.

One day, being full of sorrowful thoughts about what had happened to him, he went out to console himself; and as he was walking along he heard the distant tramp of horses behind him, and said, "The judgement of Allah is on me!" — and looked about for somewhere to hide, and could find nowhere.

At last he saw a closed door which he pushed hard; it gave way, and he went into a long gallery and took shelter there. But he had hardly done so when two men set on him, crying out, "Allah be thanked for delivering you into our hands, enemy of God! These three nights you have robbed us of our rest and our sleep, and truly you have made us taste the cup of death."

My brother asked, "Good people, what is the matter with you?"

And they answered, "You give us the slip and you go about to disgrace us, and you are planning some plot to cut the throat of the master of the house! Is it not enough that you have brought him to beggary, you and your fellows? But now hand over the knife you threaten us with every night."

Then they searched him and found in his belt the knife he used for shoe leather; and he said, "Good people, have the fear of Allah before your eyes and do not ill-treat me; for you must know that my story is a very strange one."

"And what is your story?" said they.

So he told them what had happened to him, hoping they would let him go; but they paid no attention to what he said, and instead of showing him any consideration, beat him grievously and tore his clothes off. And then, finding the scars of a beating with rods on his sides, they said, "You accursed thing! These marks are the plain signs of your guilt."

They carried him before the Governor, while he said to himself, "I am being punished now for my sins, and nobody can deliver me but Almighty Allah."

The Governor, addressing my brother, asked him, "You villain, what made you go into their house with the intention of murder?"

And my brother answered, "I beg you by Allah, Emir, hear my words and do not be hasty in condemning me."

But the Governor cried, "Are we to listen to the words of a robber who has beggared these people, and who carries the scars of the whip on his back?" And he added, "They would surely never have done that to you except for some great crime."

So he sentenced him to receive a hundred strokes of the scourge, after which they set him on a camel and paraded him round the city, proclaiming, "This is the reward, and only too small a reward, for the man who breaks into other people's houses."

Then they thrust him out of the city; and my brother wandered at random until I heard what had happened to him; and going to look for him, questioned him about his case. So he told me his story and all his misfortunes, and I carried him secretly to the city, where I made him an allowance for his meat and drink.

Then the Caliph gave ear to

The Barber's Tale of His Fifth Brother

My fifth brother, Al-Nashshar the Tattler, the one who was cropped of both ears, Commander of the Faithful, was a beggar, in the habit of asking from people by night and living on their alms by day.

Now when our father, who was an old man well on in years, fell sick and died, he left us seven hundred dirhams, of which each son took his hundred; but when my fifth brother got his share he was at a loss and did not know what to do with it.

While he was in this uncertainty he took it into his head to lay it out on glassware of all sorts and turn an honest penny on the price of it. So he bought a hundred dirhams' worth of glass and, putting it into a big tray, sat down to sell it on a bench at the foot of a wall, with his back leaning against the wall.

As he sat there with the tray in front of him he fell to musing, and said to himself:

"Know, my good self, that the head of my wealth, my capital invested in this glassware, is a hundred dirhams. I shall certainly sell it for two hundred, with which I shall buy other glass straight away and make four hundred by it; nor shall I stop selling and buying in this way until I have got four thousand, and soon find myself the master of a great deal of money.

"With these coins I shall buy merchandise and jewels and perfumes and make a great profit on them, until, Allah willing, I shall have made my capital a hundred thousand dirhams. Then I shall buy a fine house with white slaves and eunuchs and horses; and I shall eat and drink and enjoy myself; nor shall I leave a singing man or a singing woman in the city, but I shall summon them to my palace and make them perform in front of me."

All this he counted over in his mind, while the tray of glassware worth a hundred dirhams stood on the bench in front of him; and after looking at it he went on:

"And when, if Allah wills, my capital has become a hundred thousand dirhams, I shall send out marriage brokers to ask for me in marriage the daughters of kings and viziers; and I shall demand as my wife the eldest daughter of the Prime Minister, for it has reached me that she is perfect in beauty and first in loveliness and rare in accomplishments.

"I shall give a marriage settlement of a thousand dinars; and if her father consents, well and good; and if not, I shall take her by force from under his very nose.

"When she is safely housed with me, I shall buy ten little eunuchs, and for myself a robe such as kings and sultans wear; and get myself a saddle of gold and a bridle set thick with precious gems. Then I shall ride out with my Mamluks going in front of me and all round me, and I shall make a circuit of the city while the people salute me and bless me.

"After that I shall go to the vizier, the girl's father, with armed white slaves in front of me and behind me and on my right and my left. When he sees me the vizier will stand up and seat me in his own place and sit down well below me, since I am to be his son-in-law.

"Now I shall have two eunuchs with me carrying purses, each with a thousand dinars in it; and of these I shall hand him the thousand that is his daughter's marriage settlement, and make him a free gift of the other thousand, so that he may have reason to know my generosity and my liberality, and the greatness of my spirit and the littleness of the world in my eyes. And for every ten words he addresses to me I shall answer him two.

"Then back I go to my house; and if anybody comes to me from the bride's side, I shall make him a present of money and throw a robe of honour over him; but if he brings me a gift, I shall give it back to him and refuse to accept it, so that they may learn what a proud spirit is mine, which never condescends to lower itself. In this way I shall establish my rank and my standing.

"When that is done I shall appoint her wedding night and decorate my house showily and gloriously. And when the time comes for the bride to be paraded, I shall put on my finest clothes and sit down on a mattress of gold brocade, propping my elbow on a pillow and turning neither to the right nor to the left, but looking only straight ahead, out of the haughtiness of my mind and the gravity of my understanding.

"And there in front of me will stand my wife in her clothes and her ornaments, as lovely as the full moon; and I, in my loftiness and my dreadful lordliness, shall not glance at her until those present say to me, 'Our lord and master, your wife, your handmaid, is standing before you; grant her one look, for standing tires her.'

"Then they will kiss the ground in front of me a great many times; at which I shall raise my eyes and cast one single glance at her and turn my face down to the ground again.

"Then they will carry her off to the bridal chamber, and I shall get up and change my clothes for a far finer suit; and when they bring the bride in a second time, I shall not deign to throw her a look until they have begged me a great many times; after which I shall glance at her out of the corner of one eye, and then bend my head down.

"I shall go on behaving like this until the parading and displaying are finished":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Thirty-third Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the barber's fifth brother went on:

"Then I shall bend my head down and go on behaving like this until her parading and displaying are finished. At which I shall order one of my eunuchs to bring me a bag of five hundred dinars, which I shall give as a largesse to the dressing-women there, and tell them, all of them, to lead me into the bridal chamber.

"When they leave me alone with her I shall neither look at her nor speak to her, but lie down at her side with my face to the wall, showing my contempt, so that every one of them may remark again how high and haughty I am.

"Presently her mother will come in to me, and kissing my head and my hand, will say, 'My lord, look on your handmaid, who longs for your favour; heal her broken spirit!'

"I shall give her no answer; and when she sees this she will get up and kiss my feet a great many times and say, 'My lord, truly my daughter is a beautiful girl who has never known a man; and if you show her this coldness and dislike, her heart will break; so incline to her and speak to her and soothe her mind and her spirit.'

"Then she will get up and fetch a cup of wine, and say to her daughter, 'Take it and hand it to your lord.'

"But as she comes up to me I shall leave her standing between my hands, and sit propping my elbow on a round cushion edged with gold thread, leaning back lazily and not looking at her, in the majesty of my spirit, so that she may reckon me a very sultan and a mighty man.

"Then she will say to me, 'My lord, in Allah's name, do not refuse to take the cup from the hand of your handmaid, for truly I am your bondswoman.'

"But I shall not speak to her; and she will press me, saying, 'There is no help for it, you must drink it' — and she will put it to my lips.

"Then I shall shake my fist in her face and kick her with my foot — like this."

And he let out with his toe and knocked over the tray of glassware, which fell off the bench to the ground, and everything on it was broken to bits.

"You foulest of pimps, this comes of the pride of my spirit!" cried my brother. And then, Commander of the Faithful, he beat his own face and tore his clothes and went on weeping and beating himself.

The people who were flocking to their Friday prayers saw him; and some of them looked at him and pitied him, while others paid no attention; and in this way my brother lost both his capital and his profit.

He stayed there weeping a long while; and at last up came a beautiful lady with the scent of musk breathing off her, going to Friday prayers on a mule with a golden saddle and followed by several eunuchs.

When she saw the broken glass and my brother weeping, her kind heart was moved to pity for him, and she asked what was wrong with him, and was told that he had had a tray full of glassware which he hoped to make his living by selling, but it was broken; "and there happened to him," they said, "what you see."

At which she called up one of her eunuchs and said, "Give what you have with you to this poor fellow."

And he gave my brother a purse in which he found five hundred dinars; and when it touched his hand he was very nearly dying from the excess of his joy, and he called down blessings on her.

Then he went home a substantial man; and as he sat there thinking things over, somebody rapped at the door. So he got up and opened it and saw an old woman he had never seen before.

"My son," said she, "you should know that prayer time is near and I have not yet made my ritual washing; so kindly let me use your lodging for the purpose."

My brother answered, "To hear is to comply"; and going in, told her to follow him. So she came in and he brought her an ewer to wash with, and sat down ready to fly with joy on account of the dinars he had tied up in his belt for a purse.
