When the old woman had finished her washing she came over to where he was sitting and prayed a prayer of two prostrations; after which she blessed my brother with a godly benediction. And he, thanking her, put his hand to the dinars and gave her two, saying to himself, "These are my free offering."

When she saw the gold she cried, "Praise be to Allah! Why do you look on a woman who loves you as though she were a beggar? Take your money back: I have no need of it. Or if you do not want it, give it back to the woman who gave it to you when your glassware was broken. What is more, if you would like to be with her, I can arrange the matter, for she is my mistress."

"Mother," asked my brother, "by what means can I get to her?"

And she answered, "My son, she has an inclination for you; but she is a wealthy man's wife. So take all your money with you and follow me, and I will guide you to what you want; and when you are in her company, spare neither persuasion nor fair words, but bring the whole lot to bear on her; and so you shall enjoy her beauty and her wealth to your heart's content."

My brother took all his gold and got up and followed the old woman, hardly able to believe his luck.

She did not stop going on, and my brother following her, until they came to a tall gate at which she knocked; and a Greek slave girl came out and opened to them. Then the old woman led my brother into a great sitting room spread with wonderfully fine carpets and hung with curtains, where he sat down with his gold in front of him and his turban on his knee.

He had hardly taken his seat before there came in to him a young lady — eye never saw a fairer — dressed in the most sumptuous clothes; at which my brother rose to his feet, and she smiled in his face and welcomed him and signed to him to be seated.

Then she gave orders for the door to be shut; and when it was shut she turned to my brother and took his hand and led him to a private room furnished with all kinds of brocades and cloths of gold. Here he sat down and she sat beside him and played with him a while; after which she got up and said, "Do not stir from your seat until I come back to you" — and disappeared.

And while he was sitting like that, there came in to him a Black slave, big in body and bulk, holding a drawn sword in his hand, who said, "Curse you! Who brought you here, and what do you want here?"

My brother could not give him any reply, being tongue-tied with terror; so the man seized him and stripped his clothes off and beat him with the flat of his sword blade until he fell to the ground in a faint from the excess of the belabouring.

The slave supposed that was the end of him; and my brother heard him call out, "Where is the salt girl?"

At which in came a maid holding a large tray of salt, and the slave went on rubbing it into my brother's wounds; but he did not stir, for fear the slave might find out he was not dead and kill him outright.

Then the salt girl went away, and the slave cried, "Where is the keeper of the cellar?"

At which in came the old woman, and dragged my brother by his feet to a cellar and threw him down on a heap of dead bodies.

He lay in that place two full days; but Allah made the salt the means of preserving his life, by staunching the blood and stopping its flow.

Presently, feeling able to move, Al-Nashshar got up and opened the trapdoor in fear and trembling and crept out into the open; and Allah protected him, so that he went on in the darkness and hid himself in the entrance hall until dawn, when he saw the accursed old woman go out in search of other quarry.

He followed in her wake without her knowing it, and made for his own lodging, where he dressed his wounds and doctored himself until he was whole again.

Meanwhile he used to watch the old woman, tracking her at all times and seasons, and saw her accost one man after another and carry them to the house. However, he did not say a word; but as soon as he was hale and hearty again he took a piece of stuff and made it into a bag, which he filled with broken glass and tied round his middle.

He also disguised himself as a Persian so that nobody should know him, and hid a sword under his foreign-cut clothes.

Then he went out; and presently, falling in with the old woman, said to her, speaking Arabic with a Persian accent, "Venerable lady, I am a stranger, only arrived here today, and I know nobody. Have you a pair of scales where I might weigh eleven hundred dinars? I will give you something out of them for your pains."

"I have a son who is a money-changer, and he keeps all kinds of scales," she answered; "so come with me to him before he goes out, and he will weigh your gold."

My brother answered, "Lead the way."

She led him to the house, and the young lady herself came out and opened it; at which the old woman smiled in her face and said, "I am bringing you fat meat today."

Then the girl took my brother by the hand and led him to the same room as before, where she sat with him a while and then got up and went out, saying, "Do not stir from your seat until I come back to you."

Presently in came the accursed slave with the drawn sword, and cried to my brother, "Get up, and damnation to you."

So he got up; and as the slave walked ahead of him he drew the sword out from under his clothes and struck him with it, and sent his head flying off his body.

Then he dragged the corpse by the feet to the cellar and called out, "Where is the salt girl?"

Up came the girl carrying the tray of salt; and seeing my brother with a sword in his hand, turned to run; but he followed her and struck off her head.

Then he called out, "Where is the keeper of the cellar?" And in came the old woman, to whom he said, "Do you know me again, you ill-omened hag?"

"No, my lord," she replied.

And he said, "I am the owner of the five hundred gold pieces, whose house you came into to make your washing and say your prayers, and whom you snared here and betrayed."

"Fear Allah and spare me," she cried; but he paid no attention to her, and struck her with the sword until he had cut her into four.

Then he went to look for the young lady; and when she saw him her reason left her and she cried out piteously, "Mercy! Mercy!"

So he spared her, and asked, "What made you keep company with this slave?"

And she answered, "I was slave to a certain merchant, and the old woman used to visit me until I took a liking to her. One day she said to me, 'We have a marriage feast at our house the like of which was never seen, and I want you to enjoy the sight of it.' 'To hear is to obey,' I answered; and getting up, dressed myself in my finest clothes and ornaments and took with me a purse with a hundred gold pieces in it.

"Then she brought me here; and I had hardly got into the house before the Black man seized me — and I have stayed in this state three whole years, through the treachery of that accursed old woman."

Then my brother asked her, "Is there anything of his in the house?"

To which she answered, "A great store of wealth; and if you are able to carry it away, do so, and Allah give you good of it."

My brother went with her, and she opened various chests for him with money bags in them, at which he was astounded; then she said to him, "Go now and leave me here, and fetch men to move the money."

He went out and hired ten men; but when he came back he found the door wide open, the girl gone, and nothing left except some small matter of coin and the household stuff. By this he knew that the girl had outwitted him; so he opened the storerooms and seized everything in them, together with the rest of the money, and left nothing in the house.

He passed the night rejoicing; but when morning dawned he found some twenty troopers at the door, who laid hands on him saying, "The Governor wants you."

My brother begged them hard to let him go back to his house, and even offered them a large sum of money; but they refused, and binding him fast with cords, carried him off.

On the way they met a friend of my brother's, who clung to his skirt and begged his protection and asked him to stand by him and help to get him out of their hands. The man stopped and asked them what the matter was, and they answered, "The Governor has ordered us to bring this fellow before him, and, look you, that is what we are doing."

My brother's friend urged them to release him and offered them five hundred dinars to let him go, saying, "When you get back to the Governor, tell him you could not find him."

But they would not listen to what he said, and took my brother and dragged him along on his face, and set him in front of the Governor, who asked, "Where did you get these goods and this money?"

And he answered, "I ask for mercy!"

So the Governor gave him the pledge of mercy; and he told him everything that had happened to him from first to last with the old woman, and how the girl had run off; ending with, "Whatever I have taken, take what you like of it, so long as you leave me enough to live on."

But the Governor took all the goods and all the money for himself; and fearing that the affair might come to the Sultan's ears, he summoned my brother and said, "Leave this city, or I will hang you."

"Hearing and obedience," said my brother, and set out for another town.

On the road thieves fell on him and stripped him and beat him and docked his ears; but I heard news of his misfortunes and went out after him, taking him clothes, and brought him secretly into the city, where I assigned him an allowance for meat and drink.

And presently the Caliph gave ear to

The Barber's Tale of His Sixth Brother

My sixth brother, Commander of the Faithful — Shakashik, or Many Clamours, the one shorn of both his lips — was once rich and became poor; so one day he went out to beg something to keep body and soul together.

As he was on the road he suddenly caught sight of a large and handsome mansion, with a wide, lofty building standing separate at the entrance, where a number of eunuchs sat giving orders and forbidding.

My brother asked one of the men idling there, and he replied, "The palace belongs to a member of the house of Barmecide."

So he went up to the doorkeepers and asked them for alms.

"Go in," said they, "by the great gate, and you will get what you are after from our master the Wazir."

Accordingly he went in; and passing through the outer entrance, walked on a while and presently came to a hall of the utmost beauty and elegance, paved with marble, hung with curtains, and with a flower garden in the middle of it whose like he had never seen.

My brother stood a while bewildered, not knowing which way to turn his steps; then, seeing somebody at the far end of the sitting room, he walked up to it and found a man of handsome presence and a comely beard.

When this personage saw my brother he stood up to him and welcomed him and asked how things stood with him; to which he replied that he was in want and needed charity.

Hearing this, the great man showed great concern and, putting his hand to his fine robe, tore it, exclaiming, "What! Am I in a city, and you standing here hungry? I have not the patience to bear such a disgrace!"

Then he promised him all manner of good cheer and said, "There is no help for it, you must stay with me and eat of my salt."

"My lord," answered my brother, "I can wait no longer; for indeed I am dying of hunger."

So he cried, "Ho, boy! Bring the basin and the ewer!" And turning to my brother, said, "My guest, come forward and wash your hands."

My brother got up to do it — but he saw neither ewer nor basin; and yet his host went on washing his hands with invisible soap in imperceptible water, and cried, "Bring the table!"

But again my brother saw nothing.

Then said the host, "Honour me by eating some of this meat, and do not be shy."

And he kept moving his hand to and fro as though he were eating, and saying to my brother, "I am surprised to see you eating so sparingly. Do not stint yourself, for I am sure you are famished."

So my brother began to make as though he were eating, while his host kept saying, "Fall to — and notice especially how excellent this bread is, and how white!"

But still my brother saw nothing. Then he said to himself, "This man is fond of making fun of people"; and replied, "My lord, in all my days I never knew anything more winsome than the whiteness of it or sweeter than its taste."

The Barmecide said, "This bread was baked by a maid of mine whom I bought for five hundred dinars."

Then he called out, "Ho, boy, bring in the meat pudding for our first dish, and let there be plenty of fat in it." And turning to my brother, said, "My guest — in Allah's name, did you ever see anything better than this meat pudding? Now by my life, eat, and do not be embarrassed."

Presently he cried out again, "Ho, boy, serve up the marinated stew with the fattened sand grouse in it." And he said to my brother, "Up and eat, my guest, for truly you are hungry and you need food."

So my brother began wagging his jaws and making as if he were champing and chewing, while the host went on calling for one dish after another and yet producing nothing but orders to eat.

Presently he cried, "Ho, boy, bring us the chickens stuffed with pistachio nuts." And he said to my brother, "By your life, my guest, I have fattened these chickens on pistachios; eat, for you have never eaten their like."

"My lord," replied my brother, "they are indeed first rate."

Then the host began motioning with his hand as though he were putting a mouthful into my brother's mouth; and he did not stop enumerating the various dishes and expatiating on them to the hungry man, whose hunger grew more violent still, so that his soul lusted after a bit of bread, even a barley scone.

Said the Barmecide, "Did you ever taste anything more delicious than the seasoning of these dishes?"

And said my brother, "Never, my lord."

"Eat heartily and do not be ashamed," said the host.

And the guest said, "I have eaten my fill of meat."

So the host cried, "Take it away and bring in the sweets." And turning to my brother, said, "Eat some of this almond conserve, for it is first rate; and some of these honey fritters. Take this one — by my life, the syrup is running out of it."

"May I never be bereaved of you, my lord," replied the hungry man; and he began asking him about the abundance of musk in the fritters.

"That is my custom," he answered. "They put a dinar's weight of musk in every honey fritter for me, and half that quantity of ambergris."

All this time my brother kept wagging his head and his jaws, until the master cried, "Enough of that. Bring us the dessert!"

Then he said to him, "Eat some of these almonds and walnuts and raisins; and of this and that" — naming various kinds of dried fruit — "and do not be embarrassed."

But my brother replied, "My lord, indeed I am full: I can eat no more."

"My guest," the host repeated, "if you have a mind to these good things, eat. Allah! Allah! Do not stay hungry."

But my brother answered, "My lord, a man who has eaten of all these dishes — how can he be hungry?"

Then he thought it over and said to himself, "I will do something that will make him regret these tricks of his."

Presently the host called out, "Bring me the wine"; and moving his hands in the air as though they had set it in front of them, he gave my brother a cup and said, "Take this cup, and if it pleases you, let me know."

"My lord," he replied, "it is remarkably good in the nose; but I am used to drinking wine some twenty years old."

"Knock at this door, then," said the host, "for you cannot drink of anything better."

"By your kindness," said my brother, motioning with his hand as though he were drinking.

"Health and joy to you," exclaimed the master of the house; and he pretended to fill a cup and drink it off, and then handed another to my brother, who drank it down and made as though he were drunk.

Presently he caught the host off guard; and raising his arm until the white of his armpit showed, dealt him such a cuff on the back of the neck that the palace echoed with it. And then he came down on him with a second cuff.

The host cried aloud, "What is this, you scum of the earth?"

"My lord," replied my brother, "you have shown great kindness to your slave, and let him into your house and given him your food to eat; and then you made him drink your old wine until he became drunk and rowdy. But you are too noble not to bear with his ignorance and pardon his offence."

When the Barmecide heard my brother's words he laughed his loudest and said, "For a long time I have been in the habit of making mock of men and playing the madcap among my friends; but I have never yet come across a single one who had the patience and the wit to fall in with all my humours except you. So I forgive you; and you shall be my drinking companion in good earnest, and never leave me."

Then he ordered the servants to lay the table in earnest, and they set on every dish he had spoken of in sport; and he and my brother ate until they were satisfied. After which they moved to the drinking room, where they found girls like moons who sang every kind of song and played on every kind of instrument.

There they stayed drinking until the wine got the better of them; and the host treated my brother like a familiar friend, so that he became like a brother to him, and gave him a robe of honour and loved him with a great love.

Next morning the two fell to feasting and carousing again, and they did not stop living like this for a term of twenty years — at the end of which the Barmecide died, and the Sultan took possession of all his wealth and squeezed my brother of his savings, until he was left a pauper without a penny to handle.

So he left the city and fled away, going wherever his face led him; but when he was halfway between two towns the desert Arabs fell on him and bound him and carried him to their camp, where the man who had taken him set about torturing him, saying, "Buy your life from me with your money, or else I will kill you."

My brother began to weep and replied, "By Allah, I have nothing, neither gold nor silver; but I am your prisoner, so do what you like with me."

Then the Bedouin drew a knife, broad-bladed and ground so sharp that if it were plunged into a camel's throat it would sever it clean across from one side to the other, and cut off my brother's lips, and grew more insistent still in demanding money.

Now this Bedouin had a beautiful wife, who in her husband's absence used to make advances to my brother and offer herself to him; but he held off from her.

One day she began tempting him as usual, and he played with her and made her sit on his lap — when in came the Bedouin, who, seeing this, cried out, "Curse you, you accursed villain, would you debauch my wife for me?"

Then he took out a knife and cut off my brother's manhood; after which he tied him on the back of a camel and carried him to a mountain and left him there.

He was found at last by people who recognised him and gave him food and drink, and let me know how he was; at which I went out to him and brought him back to Baghdad, where I made him an allowance enough to live on.

This, then, Commander of the Faithful, is the history of my six brothers; and I was afraid to go away without telling you all of it and leaving you in the error of judging me to be like them. And now you know that I have six brothers on my hands, and that being more upright than they are, I support the whole family.

When the Caliph heard my story and everything I told him about my brothers, he laughed and said, "You speak the truth, Silent Man! You are indeed sparing of speech, and there is nothing of forwardness in you; but now go out of this city and settle in some other."

And he banished me by decree.

I left Baghdad and travelled in foreign parts until I heard of his death and of another man's accession to the Caliphate. Then I went back to Baghdad, where I found all my brothers dead, and came upon this young man, to whom I rendered the kindliest service — for without me he would certainly have been killed.

Indeed he slanders me and accuses me of a fault which is not in my nature; and what he reports about impudence and meddling and forwardness is idle and false. For truly it was on his account that I left Baghdad and travelled through a great many countries until I came to this city and met him here in your company.

And was not all this, worthy company, the mark of the generosity of my nature?

The End of the Tailor's Tale

Then said the tailor to the King of China:

When we had heard the barber's tale, and seen the excess of his talkativeness and the way he had wronged this young man, we laid hands on him and shut him up; after which we sat down in peace, and ate and drank and enjoyed the good things of the wedding feast until the call to afternoon prayer, when I left the party and went home.

My wife received me with sour looks and said, "You go off enjoying yourself among your friends and leave me sitting sorrowing here alone. So now, unless you take me out and give me some amusement for the rest of the day, I shall cut the rope between us, and that will be the cause of my parting from you."

So I took her out and we amused ourselves until supper time, when we came home and fell in with this hunchback, who was brimful of drink and trolling out these rhymes:

	"Clear is the wine and the cup is fine;
	like to like the two combine.
	It is wine and not a cup!
	It is a cup and not wine!"

So I invited him to have supper with us, and went out to buy fried fish; after which we sat down to eat; and presently my wife took a piece of bread and a chunk of fish and stuffed them into his mouth, and he choked; and though I slapped him long and hard between the shoulders, he died.

Then I carried him off and contrived to leave him at the house of this doctor, the Jew; and the doctor contrived to drop him into the house of the steward; and the steward contrived to set him up in the way of the Christian broker.

This, then, is my adventure, which happened to me only yesterday. Is it not more wonderful than the story of the hunchback?

When the King of China heard the tailor's tale he shook his head for pleasure; and showing great surprise, said, "What passed between the young man and that busybody of a barber is truly more pleasant and more wonderful than the story of my lying rogue of a hunchback."

Then he told one of his chamberlains to go with the tailor and bring the barber out of jail, saying, "I want to hear the talk of this Silent Man, and it shall be the cause of your deliverance, every one of you; then we will bury the hunchback, since he has been dead since yesterday, and set up a tomb over him":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Thirty-fourth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the King of China ordered, "Bring me the barber, who shall be the cause of your deliverance; then we will bury this hunchback, since he has been dead since yesterday, and set up a tomb over him."

So the chamberlain and the tailor went to the jail and released the barber, and presently came back with him to the King.

The Sultan of China looked at him and considered him carefully — and he was an ancient man, past his ninetieth year; dark of face, white of beard, and hoary of eyebrow; lop-eared and with a nose like a trunk, and a vacant, silly, conceited expression on his face.

The King laughed at this figure of fun and said to him, "Silent Man, I want you to tell me something of your history."

Said the barber, "O King of the age, allow me first to ask you: what is the story of this Christian and this Jew and this Muslim and this hunchback — the corpse — that I see among you? And pray, what may be the object of this gathering?"

Said the King of China, "And why do you ask?"

"I ask," he replied, "so that the King's majesty may know that I am no forward fellow or busybody or impertinent meddler, and that I am innocent of their slanderous charges of too much talk; for I am the man whose name is the Silent Man, and my nickname is particularly happy, as the poet says:

	When men design a nickname or a pet name,
	know that nature will often fall in with the name."

Then the King said, "Explain to the barber the case of this hunchback and what happened to him at supper time; and repeat to him the stories told by the Christian, the Jew, the steward and the tailor. A twice-told tale is of no use to me."

They did as he ordered; and the barber shook his head and said, "By Allah, this is a marvel of marvels! Now uncover the body of that hunchback for me."

They undid the winding sheet, and he sat down and took the hunchback's head in his lap and looked at his face, and laughed and guffawed until he fell over on his back, and said, "There is a wonder in every death; but the death of this hunchback is worth writing down and recording in letters of liquid gold!"

The bystanders were astounded at his words, and the King marvelled and said to him, "What is the matter with you, Silent Man? Explain your words to us."

"O King of the age," said the barber, "I swear by your beneficence that there is still life in this hunchback."

At which he pulled a barber's kit out of his belt, and took from it a pot of ointment and anointed the hunchback's neck with it, and the arteries of it. Then he took a pair of iron tweezers and, putting them into the hunchback's throat, drew out the chunk of fish with its bone; and when it came into sight, it was soaked in blood.

At which the hunchback gave a hearty sneeze and jumped up as though nothing had happened, and passing his hand over his face, said, "I testify that there is no god but God, and I testify that Mohammed is the Apostle of God."

At this sight everybody there wondered; the King of China laughed until he fainted, and so did the rest of them.

Then said the Sultan, "By Allah, this is truly the most marvellous thing I ever saw! Muslims! Soldiers, all of you! Did you ever in your lives see a man die and be brought back to life? Truly, if Allah had not granted him this barber, he would have been a dead man."

Said they, "By Allah, it is a marvel of marvels."

Then the King of China ordered this tale to be recorded; so they recorded it and placed it in the royal record rooms. After which he bestowed costly robes of honour on the Jew, the Christian and the steward, and told them to go on their way with every mark of esteem.

Then he gave the tailor a sumptuous robe and appointed him his own tailor, with suitable pay and allowances; and made peace between him and the hunchback, to whom he also presented a splendid and expensive suit with a suitable stipend.

He dealt as generously with the barber, giving him a gift and a robe of honour; what is more, he settled a handsome salary on him and created him Barber-Surgeon of State and made him one of his drinking companions.

So they did not stop living the most pleasurable and delightful of lives, until there came to them the Destroyer of all delights and the Sunderer of all societies, the Depopulator of palaces and the Garnerer for graves.

And yet, O most fortunate King (Shahrazad went on), this tale is by no means more wonderful than the tale of Sindbad the Seaman and Sindbad the Landsman.

Said her sister Dunyazad, "And what may that be?"

At which she began to tell the following tale of

Sindbad the Seaman and Sindbad the Landsman

There lived in the city of Baghdad, in the reign of the Commander of the Faithful, Harun al-Rashid, a man named Sindbad the Porter, a poor man who carried burdens on his head for hire.

It happened to him one day of great heat that while he was carrying a heavy load he grew extremely tired and sweated profusely, the heat and the weight oppressing him alike. Presently, as he was passing the gate of a merchant's house, in front of which the ground had been swept and watered and the air was temperate, he caught sight of a broad bench beside the door; so he set his load down on it to rest and take the air:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Thirty-seventh Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the porter had set his load on the bench to rest and take the air, there came out to him from the courtyard door a pleasant breeze and a delicious fragrance.

He sat down on the edge of the bench, and at once heard from inside the melodious sound of lutes and other stringed instruments, and voices singing and reciting to stir up mirth, together with the song of birds warbling and glorifying Almighty Allah in all sorts of tunes and tongues — turtle doves, mockingbirds, blackbirds, nightingales, wood pigeons and stone-curlews; at which he marvelled to himself and was moved to a mighty joy and comfort.

Then he went up to the gate and saw inside a great flower garden, in which were pages and Black slaves and such a train of servants and attendants and the rest as is only found with kings and sultans; and his nostrils were greeted with the savoury smells of every kind of meat, rich and delicate, and of delicious and generous wines.

So he raised his eyes to heaven and said:

"Glory to You, O Lord, O Creator and Provider, who provide for whom You will without counting or stinting! O my Holy One, I beg Your pardon for all my sins and turn to You in repentance for all my offences!

"O Lord, there is no gainsaying You in Your ordinance and Your dominion, nor will You be questioned about what You do, for You are indeed Almighty over all things. Extolled be Your perfection: whom You will You make poor, and whom You will You make rich; whom You will You exalt and whom You will You abase; and there is no god but You.

"How mighty is Your majesty and how enduring Your dominion and how excellent Your government! Truly You favour whom You will among Your servants, so that the owner of this place lives in all the joyance of life and delights himself with pleasant scents and delicious food and exquisite wines of every kind.

"For indeed You appoint for Your creatures whatever You will and whatever You have foreordained for them; and so some are weary and others are at rest, and some enjoy good fortune and plenty while others suffer the last extremity of toil and misery — as I do."

And he fell to reciting:

	How many, by my labours that go on and on for ever,
	enjoy every good thing in life and lie back in the cool shade?
	Every morning that dawns I wake to toil and to grief,
	and my condition is strange and my burden makes me pine.
	Plenty of others are in luck and free of every misery,
	and Fortune never loads them with loads like mine.
	They live out their happy days in comfort and delight;
	they eat, drink and live in honour among the noble and the worthy.
	Every living thing was made out of a little drop of seed;
	your origin is mine and my beginning is yours;
	and yet the difference and the distance between the two of us
	are as far apart as the taste of vinegar and the taste of wine.
	But at You, O all-wise God, I do not venture to rail,
	whose ordinance is just and whose justice cannot fail.

When Sindbad the Porter had finished reciting his verses, he took up his burden and was about to go on his way, when there came out to him from the gate a little page boy, fair of face and shapely of figure and dainty in his dress, who caught him by the hand and said, "Come in and speak with my lord, for he is calling for you."

The porter would have excused himself to the page, but the boy would take no refusal; so he left his load with the doorkeeper in the entrance hall and followed the boy into the house, which he found to be a fine mansion, radiant and full of majesty — until he brought him into a grand sitting room, where he saw a company of nobles and great lords seated at tables decked with all sorts of flowers and sweet-scented herbs, besides great plenty of dainty dishes and fruit, dried and fresh, and sweets, and wines of the choicest vintages.

There too were instruments of music and mirth, and lovely slave girls playing and singing. The whole company was ranged according to rank; and in the highest place sat a man of a worshipful and noble aspect, whose beard was touched at the sides with grey; and he was stately in stature and handsome in his face, agreeable to look at and full of gravity and dignity and majesty.

So Sindbad the Porter was confounded at what he saw, and said to himself, "By Allah, this must be either a piece of Paradise or some king's palace!"

Then he greeted the company with great respect, praying for their prosperity; and kissing the ground before them, stood with his head bowed down in a humble attitude:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Thirty-eighth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Porter, after kissing the ground between their hands, stood with his head bowed in a humble attitude.

The master of the house told him to come nearer and be seated, and spoke to him kindly and made him welcome. Then he set various kinds of food in front of him, rich and delicate and delicious; and the porter, after saying "In Allah's name," fell to and ate his fill; after which he exclaimed, "Praised be Allah, whatever our condition!" and washing his hands, thanked the company for entertaining him.

Said the host, "You are welcome, and your day is a blessed one. But what is your name and your calling?"

Said the other, "My lord, my name is Sindbad the Porter, and I carry people's goods on my head for hire."

The master of the house smiled and answered, "Know, porter, that your name is the same as mine, for I am Sindbad the Seaman. And now, porter, I should like you to let me hear the verses you were reciting at the gate just now."

The porter was embarrassed and replied, "In Allah's name, excuse me! Toil and travail and lack of luck, when the hand is empty, teach a man bad manners and boorish ways."

Said the host, "Do not be ashamed; you have become my brother. But repeat the verses to me, for they pleased me when I heard you recite them at the gate."

At which the porter repeated the lines, and they delighted the merchant, who said to him:

Know, porter, that my story is a wonderful one; and you shall hear everything that happened to me and everything I went through before I rose to this state of prosperity and became the lord of this place where you see me. For I did not come to this high estate except after grievous toil and perils in plenty; and how much labour and trouble have I not suffered in days gone by!

I have made seven voyages, and by each one of them hangs a marvellous tale, such as confounds the reason; and all of it came about by the doom of fortune and fate, for from what destiny writes there is neither refuge nor flight.

Know then, my good lords (he went on), that I am about to relate the

The First Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman

My father was a merchant, one of the notables of my native place, a moneyed man and ample of means, who died while I was still a child, leaving me a great deal of wealth in money and lands and farmhouses.

When I grew up I laid hands on the whole of it and ate of the best and drank freely and wore rich clothes and lived lavishly, keeping company with young men of my own age and reckoning that this way of living would go on for ever and never know any change.

I went on like that a long time; but at last I woke out of my heedlessness, and coming back to my senses, found that my wealth had become no wealth and my condition an ill condition, and that everything I had once held had gone out of my hand.

And recovering my reason, I was struck with dismay and confusion, and remembered a saying of our lord Solomon son of David, on whom be peace, which I had heard from my father in the old days: "Three things are better than three others: the day of death is better than the day of birth, a live dog is better than a dead lion, and the grave is better than want."

Then I got together the remains of my estates and property and sold everything, even my clothes, for three thousand dirhams, with which I resolved to travel to foreign parts, remembering the poet's saying:

	By means of hard work a man shall climb the height;
	whoever aspires to fame must not sleep at night.
	Whoever looks for pearls in the deep must dive,
	winning wealth and welfare by his own main strength;
	and whoever looks for Fame without toil and struggle
	is looking for the impossible and wasting his life.

So, taking heart, I bought myself goods and merchandise and everything needed for a voyage; and impatient to be at sea, I embarked with a company of merchants on board a ship bound for Basra.

There we embarked again and sailed many days and nights, and we passed from island to island and sea to sea and shore to shore, buying and selling and bartering everywhere the ship touched; and we kept on our course until we came to an island like a garden out of the gardens of Paradise.

Here the captain cast anchor, and making fast to the shore, put out the landing planks. So everybody aboard landed and made furnaces and lit fires in them and busied themselves in various ways, some cooking and some washing, while others walked about the island for their amusement; and the crew fell to eating and drinking and playing and sporting.

I was one of the walkers. But while we were occupied like this, the master, who was standing on the gunwale, called out to us at the top of his voice:

"Ho there, passengers! Run for your lives and hurry back to the ship, and leave your gear and save yourselves from destruction, Allah preserve you! For this island you are standing on is no true island, but a great fish lying still in the middle of the sea, on which the sand has settled and trees have sprung up in the old days, so that it has become like an island. But when you lit fires on it, it felt the heat and moved; and in a moment it will sink with you into the sea and you will all be drowned. So leave your gear and look to your safety before you die!":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Thirty-ninth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the ship's master cried out to the passengers, "Leave your gear and look to your safety, before you die!" — all who heard him left their gear and their goods, clothes washed and unwashed, fire pots and brass cooking pots, and fled back to the ship for their lives; and some reached it and others, myself among them, did not.

For suddenly the island shook and sank into the depths of the sea with everything that was on it, and the dashing sea surged over it with clashing waves.

I sank with the rest, down and down into the deep; but Almighty Allah preserved me from drowning and threw in my way a great wooden tub, one of those the ship's company had used for washing. I gripped it for the sweetness of life; and getting astride it like a man riding, paddled with my feet like oars while the waves tossed me right and left as though in sport.

Meanwhile the captain made sail and went off with the men who had got aboard, without a thought for the drowning and the drowned; and I did not stop following the vessel with my eyes until she was out of sight, and I made certain of death.

Darkness closed in on me while I was in this plight, and the winds and the waves carried me on all that night and the next day, until the tub brought up with me under the lee of a high island with trees hanging out over the water.

I caught hold of a branch and by its help clambered up onto the land, after coming close to death; but when I reached the shore I found my legs cramped and numb, and my feet showed the traces of fish nibbling at their soles — though I had felt nothing, for the excess of my anguish and exhaustion.

I threw myself down on the ground of the island like a dead man, and drowned in desolation, fainted away; and I did not come back to my senses until next morning, when the sun rose and revived me.

But I found my feet swollen, so I made shift to move by shuffling on my backside and crawling on my knees; for on that island there was a store of fruit and springs of sweet water. I ate the fruit, which strengthened me; and so I stayed days and nights, until my life seemed to come back to me and my spirits began to revive and I was better able to move about.

So, after due consideration, I set about exploring the island and amusing myself with gazing at everything Almighty Allah had created there; and I rested under the trees, and cut myself a staff from one of them to lean on.

One day, as I walked along the shore, I caught sight of something in the distance and took it for a wild animal or one of the monstrous creatures of the sea; but as I came nearer, looking hard at it all the while, I saw it was a noble mare, tethered on the beach.

Presently I went up to her; but she cried out against me with a great cry, so that I trembled with fear and turned to go away — when a man came out from under the earth and followed me, shouting, "Who are you and where do you come from, and what brought you here?"

"My lord," I answered, "I am truly a waif and a stranger, and I was left to drown with several others by the ship we were voyaging in; but Allah graciously sent me a wooden tub, so I saved myself on it, and it floated with me until the waves cast me up on this island."

When he heard this he took my hand and said, "Come with me"; and he carried me into a great underground chamber, as spacious as a hall. He made me sit down at the upper end of it; and then he brought me something to eat, and being famished, I ate until I was satisfied and refreshed.

And when he had put me at my ease he questioned me about myself, and I told him everything that had happened to me from first to last. And as he was marvelling at my adventure, I said, "By Allah, my lord, excuse me; I have told you the truth of my case and the accident that came to me; and now I should like you to tell me who you are, and why you live here under the earth, and why you have tethered that mare on the edge of the sea."

He answered, "Know that I am one of several men stationed in different parts of this island. We are the grooms of King Mihrjan, and all his horses are under our hands.

"Every month, about the time of the new moon, we bring our best mares here that have never been covered, and picket them on the seashore and hide ourselves in this place under the ground, so that nobody can see us.

"Presently the stallions of the sea scent the mares and come up out of the water; and seeing nobody, mount the mares and have their will of them. When they have covered them they try to drag them away, but cannot, because of the leg-ropes; so they cry out at them and butt at them and kick them. Hearing which, we know that the stallions have dismounted; so we run out and shout at them, at which they take fright and go back into the sea.

"Then the mares conceive by them and bear colts and fillies worth a mint of money, whose like is not to be found on the face of the earth. This is the season for the sea stallions to come out; and, Allah willing, I shall take you to King Mihrjan":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fortieth Night,

she went on: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the groom said to Sindbad the Seaman, "I shall take you to King Mihrjan and show you our country. And know that if you had not happened on us you would have perished miserably and nobody would ever have known of you; but I shall be the means of saving your life and of your getting back to your own land."

I called down blessings on him and thanked him for his kindness and courtesy; and while we were still talking, up came the stallion out of the sea and, giving a great cry, sprang on the mare and covered her.

When he had had his will of her he dismounted and would have carried her away with him, but could not because of the tether. She kicked and cried out at him, at which the groom took a sword and a shield and ran out of the underground room, striking the shield with the blade and calling to his companions, who came up shouting and brandishing spears; and the stallion took fright at them and plunged into the sea like a buffalo and disappeared under the waves.

After this we sat a while, until the rest of the grooms came up, each leading a mare; and seeing me with their fellow groom, they asked about my situation and I repeated my story to them. At which they came up to me and spread the table and ate, and invited me to eat; so I ate with them.

After which they took horse and, mounting me on one of the mares, set out with me and travelled on without stopping until we came to the capital city of King Mihrjan; and going in to him, they told him my story.

Then he sent for me; and when they had set me before him and greetings had been exchanged, he gave me a cordial welcome, and wishing me a long life, told me to tell him my tale.

So I related to him everything I had seen and everything that had happened to me from first to last; at which he marvelled and said, "By Allah, my son, you have truly been preserved by a miracle! If the term of your life were not a long one, you would never have escaped these straits. But praise be to Allah for your safety!"

Then he spoke cheerfully to me and treated me with kindness and consideration; what is more, he made me his agent for the port and registrar of all the ships that came into the harbour.

I attended him regularly to receive his commands, and he favoured me and did me every kind of kindness and invested me with costly and splendid robes. Indeed I stood high in his favour, as an intercessor for the people and a go-between for them and him when they wanted anything of him.

I stayed like that a great while; and whenever I passed through the city to the port I used to question the merchants and travellers and sailors about the city of Baghdad, in the hope of hearing of some chance of getting back to my own country; but I could find nobody who knew it or who knew anybody who went there.

At this I was distressed, for I was weary of being a stranger so long; and my disappointment went on for a time — until one day, going in to King Mihrjan, I found him with a company of Indians. I greeted them and they returned my greeting, and welcomed me politely and asked me about my country:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-first Night,

she went on: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman said:

When they asked me about my country I asked them about theirs, and they told me that they were of various castes: some called the Shakiriyah, who are the noblest of their castes and neither oppress nor offer violence to anybody; and others Brahmans, a people who abstain from wine but live in delight and comfort and merriment and own camels and horses and cattle.

What is more, they told me that the people of India are divided into seventy-two castes, and I marvelled at this beyond all marvelling.

Among the other things I saw in King Mihrjan's dominions was an island called Kasil, where all night long you can hear the beating of drums and tabors; but we were told by the neighbouring islanders and by travellers that the inhabitants are people of diligence and judgement.

In that sea I also saw a fish two hundred cubits long, which the fishermen are afraid of; so they knock pieces of wood together and put it to flight. I saw another fish too, with a head like an owl's — besides many other wonders and rarities which it would be tedious to recount.

I occupied myself in visiting the islands like this until one day, as I stood in the port with a staff in my hand as usual, a great ship with many merchants aboard came sailing for the harbour.

When it reached the small inner port where the ships anchor below the city, the master furled his sails, and making fast to the shore, put out the landing planks; at which the crew fell to breaking bulk and landing cargo, while I stood by taking written note of it all.

They were a long while bringing the goods ashore, so I asked the master, "Is there anything left in your ship?"

And he answered, "My lord, there are several bales of merchandise in the hold whose owner was drowned from among us at one of the islands on our course; so his goods have remained in our charge as a trust, and we mean to sell them and note the price, so as to convey it to his people in the city of Baghdad, the House of Peace."

"What was the merchant's name?" said I.

And he said, "Sindbad the Seaman."

At which I looked hard at him and, recognising him, cried out to him with a great cry, saying:

"Captain, I am that same Sindbad the Seaman who travelled with the other merchants; and when the fish heaved and you called out to us, some saved themselves and others sank, and I was one of them. But Almighty Allah threw in my way a great wooden tub, one of those the crew had used for washing; and the winds and the waves carried me to this island, where by Allah's grace I fell in with King Mihrjan's grooms, and they brought me here to the King their master.

"When I told him my story he treated me with favour and made me his harbour master; and I have prospered in his service and found acceptance with him. These bales, therefore, are mine — the goods that God has given me":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-second Night,

she went on: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when Sindbad the Seaman said to the captain, "These bales are mine, the goods that Allah has given me," the other exclaimed, "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great! Truly there is neither conscience nor good faith left among men!"

Said I, "Captain, what do you mean by these words, seeing that I have told you my case?"

And he answered, "Because you heard me say that I had goods with me whose owner was drowned, you think to take them without any right; but this is forbidden you by law, for we saw him drown before our eyes, together with many other passengers, and not one of them was saved. So how can you pretend to be the owner of the goods?"

"Captain," said I, "listen to my story and pay attention to my words, and my truthfulness will be plain to you; for lying and falsehood are the marks of hypocrites."

Then I recounted to him everything that had happened to me since I sailed from Baghdad with him, up to the time we came to the fish-island where we were nearly drowned; and I reminded him of certain matters that had passed between us — at which both he and the merchants were satisfied of the truth of my story and recognised me and wished me joy of my deliverance, saying, "By Allah, we did not think you had escaped drowning! But the Lord has granted you a new life."

Then they handed my bales over to me, and I found my name written on them, and nothing was missing from them.

So I opened them and, making up a present for King Mihrjan of the finest and costliest of the contents, had the sailors carry it up to the palace; where I went in to the King and laid my present at his feet, telling him what had happened, and particularly about the ship and my goods.

At which he marvelled beyond all marvelling, and the truth of everything I had told him was made plain to him. His affection for me redoubled after that, and he showed me great honour and bestowed a great present on me in return for mine.

Then I sold my bales and the other things I owned, making a great profit on them, and bought myself other goods and gear of the growth and fashion of that island city.

When the merchants were about to start on their homeward voyage I put everything I had aboard the ship; and going in to the King, thanked him for all his favours and his friendship and begged his leave to go back to my own country and my own friends. He said goodbye to me and bestowed on me a great store of the country's stuffs and produce; and I took my leave of him and embarked.

Then we set sail and travelled on nights and days by the permission of Almighty Allah; and Fortune served us and Fate favoured us, so that we arrived safely at the city of Basra, where I landed, rejoicing at my safe return to my native soil.

After a short stay I set out for Baghdad, the House of Peace, with a store of goods and commodities of great price. Reaching the city in due time, I went straight to my own quarter and into my own house, where all my friends and relations came to greet me.

Then I bought myself eunuchs and concubines, servants and Black slaves, until I had a large household; and I bought houses and lands and gardens, until I was richer and better off than before; and I went back to enjoying the society of my friends and companions more assiduously than ever, forgetting everything I had suffered of exhaustion and hardship and exile and every peril of travel. And I gave myself up to every kind of joy and comfort and delight, eating the daintiest food and drinking the most delicious wines; and my wealth allowed this state of things to go on.

This, then, is the story of my first voyage; and tomorrow, Allah willing, I shall tell you the tale of the second of my seven voyages.

(Says the teller of the tale:) Then Sindbad the Seaman made Sindbad the Landsman have supper with him, and gave orders to give him a hundred gold pieces, saying, "You have cheered us with your company today."

The porter thanked him and, taking the gift, went his way, turning over what he had heard and marvelling mightily at the things that happen to mankind.

He passed the night in his own place, and with the early morning went back to the house of Sindbad the Seaman, who received him with honour and seated him at his side. As soon as the rest of the company had assembled, he set food and drink in front of them; and when they had eaten and drunk well and were merry and in a cheerful frame of mind, he took up his discourse and recounted to them, in these words, the narrative of

The Second Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman

Know, my brother, that I was living a most comfortable and enjoyable life, in all comfort and delight, as I told you yesterday:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-third Night,

she went on: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when Sindbad the Seaman's guests were all gathered together he spoke to them like this:

I was living a most enjoyable life, until one day my mind became possessed with the thought of travelling about the world of men and seeing their cities and their islands; and a longing took hold of me to trade and make money by commerce.

On this resolve I took a great store of cash and, buying goods and gear fit for travelling, tied them up in bales. Then I went down to the riverbank, where I found a noble ship, brand new and about to sail, fitted with sails of fine cloth and well manned and provisioned; so I took passage in her with a number of other merchants, and after loading our goods we weighed anchor the same day.

Our voyage was a very fine one, and we sailed from place to place and from island to island; and whenever we anchored we met a crowd of merchants and notables and customers, and set about buying and selling and bartering.

At last Destiny brought us to an island, fair and green, in trees abundant, with yellow-ripe fruit luxuriant and flowers fragrant and birds warbling a soft descant, and streams crystalline and radiant — but no sign of a man showed to anyone looking, not so much as a blower of a fire.

The captain made fast with us at this island, and the merchants and the sailors landed and walked about, enjoying the shade of the trees and the song of the birds, which chanted the praises of the One, the Victorious, and marvelling at the works of the Omnipotent King.

I landed with the rest; and sitting down by a spring of sweet water that welled up among the trees, took out some provisions I had with me and ate what Almighty Allah had allotted me. And the breeze was so sweet and the flowers so fragrant that presently I grew drowsy, and lying down in that place, was soon drowned in sleep.

When I woke I found myself alone, for the ship had sailed and left me behind, and not one of the merchants or the sailors had given me a thought.

I searched the island right and left, but found neither man nor jinn; at which I was troubled beyond measure and my gall was ready to burst for the stress of my chagrin and anguish and worry, because I was left entirely alone, without any worldly goods or food or drink, weary and broken-hearted.

So I gave myself up for lost and said, "The crock does not always escape the shock. I was saved the first time by finding somebody who brought me from a desert island to an inhabited place; but now there is no hope for me."

Then I fell to weeping and wailing and gave myself up to a fit of rage, blaming myself for having ventured again on the perils and hardships of a voyage when I was at my ease in my own house in my own country, taking my pleasure with good food and good drink and good clothes and wanting for nothing, neither money nor goods.

And I repented of having left Baghdad — the more so after all the troubles and dangers I had gone through on my first voyage, in which I had so narrowly escaped destruction — and exclaimed, "Truly we are Allah's and to Him we are returning!"

I was indeed like a man mad and jinn-struck; and presently I got up and walked about the island, right and left and every way, unable for trouble of mind to sit still or stay in any one place.

Then I climbed a tall tree and looked out in every direction, but saw nothing except sky and sea and trees and birds and islands and sand.

However, after a while my eager glances fell on some great white thing, a long way off in the interior of the island; so I came down from the tree and made for what I had seen — and it was a huge white dome, rising high into the air and of vast compass.

I walked all round it, but found no door to it, nor could I muster the strength or the nimbleness to climb it, because it was so exceedingly smooth and slippery. So I marked the spot where I stood and went round the dome to measure its circumference, which I found to be fifty good paces.

And as I stood there, casting about for a way to get inside — the day being near its close and the sun near the horizon — the sun was suddenly hidden from me and the air went dull and dark.

I thought a cloud had come over the sun; but it was the season of summer, so I marvelled at it, and lifting my head, looked steadily at the sky — and saw that the cloud was nothing else than an enormous bird, of gigantic girth and inordinately wide of wing, which, as it flew through the air, veiled the sun and hid it from the island.

At this sight my wonder redoubled, and I remembered a story:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-fourth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on:

My wonder redoubled, and I remembered a story I had heard in the old days from pilgrims and travellers: how on a certain island there lives a huge bird called the roc, which feeds its young on elephants. And I was certain that the dome which had caught my eye was nothing else than a roc's egg.

As I looked and marvelled at the wonderful works of the Almighty, the bird alighted on the dome and brooded over it, its wings covering it and its legs stretched out behind it on the ground; and in that posture it fell asleep — glory be to Him who never sleeps!

When I saw this I got up and, unwinding my turban from my head, doubled it and twisted it into a rope, with which I girded my middle and tied my waist fast to the legs of the roc, saying to myself, "Perhaps this bird will carry me to a land of cities and inhabitants, and that will be better than staying on this desert island."

I passed the night watching and afraid to sleep, in case the bird flew away with me unawares; and as soon as the dawn broke and the morning shone, the roc rose off its egg and, spreading its wings with a great cry, flew up into the air, dragging me with it. Nor did it stop soaring and towering until I thought it had reached the limit of the firmament; after which it came down towards the earth little by little, until it landed on the top of a high hill.

As soon as I found myself on hard ground I made haste to untie myself, quaking with fear of the bird — though it took no notice of me and did not even feel me; and loosing my turban from its feet, I made off at my best speed.

Presently I saw it catch up something from the ground in its huge claws and rise with it high into the air; and looking narrowly at it, I saw it was a serpent, big of bulk and gigantic of girth, with which it flew clean out of sight.

I marvelled at this; and going forward, found myself on a peak overlooking a valley, exceedingly great and wide and deep, bounded by vast mountains that towered up into the air: nobody could make out their summits, for the excess of their height, nor was anybody able to climb up to them.

When I saw this I blamed myself for what I had done, and said, "Would to Heaven I had stayed on the island! It was better than this wild desert; for there I had at least fruit to eat and water to drink, and here there are neither trees nor fruit nor streams. But there is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great! Truly, as often as I get clear of one peril I fall into a worse danger and a more grievous."

However, I took courage; and walking along the valley, found that its soil was diamond — the stone they use for boring minerals and precious stones and porcelain and onyx, since it is a dense stone and a hard one, on which neither iron nor steel has any effect, and we cannot cut anything from it or break it except by means of lead.

What is more, the valley swarmed with snakes and vipers, each as big as a palm tree, that would have made one gulp of an elephant; and they came out by night and hid during the day, in case the rocs and the eagles pounced on them and tore them to pieces, as was their habit — why, I do not know.

And I repented of what I had done, and said, "By Allah, I have hurried to bring destruction on myself."

The day began to wane as I went along, and I looked about for a place to pass the night, being afraid of the serpents; and I took no thought of food or drink in my concern for my life.

Presently I caught sight of a cave nearby with a narrow doorway; so I went in, and seeing a great stone close to the mouth, rolled it up and stopped the entrance, saying to myself, "I am safe here for the night; and as soon as it is day I will go out and see what destiny will do."

Then I looked inside the cave and saw at the far end a great serpent brooding on her eggs — at which my flesh quaked and my hair stood on end; but I raised my eyes to Heaven and, committing my case to fate and lot, stayed there all that night without sleeping until daybreak, when I rolled the stone back from the mouth of the cave and went out, staggering like a drunken man and giddy with watching and fear and hunger.

As I walked along the valley in this sore state, there fell down in front of me a slaughtered beast — but I could see nobody; at which I marvelled greatly, and presently remembered a story I had heard in the old days from traders and pilgrims and travellers.

How the mountains where the diamonds are, are full of perils and terrors, and nobody can travel through them; but the merchants who deal in diamonds have a device by which they get them. That is to say, they take a sheep and slaughter it and skin it and cut it in pieces, and throw the pieces down from the mountain tops into the floor of the valley, where the meat, being fresh and sticky with blood, has some of the gems cling to it.

There they leave it until midday, when the eagles and the vultures swoop down on it and carry it in their claws to the mountain tops; at which the merchants come and shout at them and scare them off the meat. Then they come and take the diamonds they find sticking to it and go their way with them, and leave the meat to the birds and the beasts; and nobody can come at the diamonds except by this device:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-fifth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on with his account of what happened to him in the Valley of Diamonds, and told them that the merchants cannot come at the diamonds except by the device already described.

So when I saw the slaughtered beast fall (he went on) and remembered the story, I went up to it and filled my pockets and my belt-shawl and my turban and the folds of my clothes with the choicest diamonds; and while I was busy at it, down fell another great piece of meat in front of me.

Then, with my turban unrolled, and lying on my back, I set the piece of meat on my chest, so that I was hidden by it and it was held up off the ground.

I had hardly gripped it when an eagle swooped down on the flesh and, seizing it in his talons, flew up with it high into the air, and me clinging to it; nor did he stop flying until he landed on the top of one of the mountains, where he dropped the carcass and fell to tearing at it.

But there arose behind him a great noise of shouting and clattering of wood, at which the bird took fright and flew away.

Then I loosed the meat off myself, my clothes daubed with blood from it, and stood up beside it; at which up came the merchant who had shouted at the eagle, and seeing me standing there, did not speak to me, but was frightened of me and shook with fear.

However, he went up to the carcass and, turning it over, found no diamonds sticking to it; at which he gave a great cry and exclaimed, "Alas, my disappointment! There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, with whom we take refuge from Satan the stoned!"

And he bemoaned himself and beat one hand on the other, saying, "Alas, the pity of it! How has this come about?"

Then I went up to him, and he said to me, "Who are you, and what has brought you here?"

And I said, "Do not be afraid; I am a man, and a good man, and a merchant. My story is a wonderful one and my adventures marvellous, and the manner of my coming here is prodigious. So be of good cheer; you shall get from me what will make you glad, for I have a great plenty of diamonds with me and I will give you enough of them to satisfy you — and each one is better than anything you could get otherwise. So fear nothing."

The man was delighted at this and thanked me and blessed me; then we talked together until the other merchants, hearing me in conversation with their fellow, came up and greeted me, for each of them had thrown down his own piece of meat.

And as I went off with them I told them my whole story, how I had suffered hardships at sea and the manner of my reaching the valley. But I gave the owner of the meat a number of the stones I had by me; so they all wished me joy of my escape, saying, "By Allah, a new life has been decreed for you; for nobody ever reached that valley and came away alive before you. But praise be to Allah for your safety!"

We passed the night together in a safe and pleasant place, and I was beyond measure glad at my deliverance from the Valley of Serpents and my arrival in an inhabited land.

Next day we set out and journeyed over the mighty range of mountains, seeing many serpents in the valley, until we came to a fine great island where there was a grove of huge camphor trees, under each one of which a hundred men might take shelter.

When the people want to get camphor, they bore into the upper part of the trunk with a long iron; at which the liquid camphor, which is the sap of the tree, flows out and they catch it in vessels, where it hardens like gum. But after this the tree dies and becomes firewood.

What is more, on this island there is a kind of wild beast called the rhinoceros, which grazes as our steers and buffaloes do; but it is a huge brute, bigger in the body than a camel, and like the camel it feeds on the leaves and twigs of trees.

It is a remarkable animal with a great thick horn, ten cubits long, in the middle of its head, in which, when it is split in two, there is the likeness of a man.

Voyagers and pilgrims and travellers declare that this beast, called the karkadan, will carry off a great elephant on its horn and graze about the island and the seacoast with it and take no notice of it, until the elephant dies and its fat, melting in the sun, runs down into the rhinoceros's eyes and blinds him, so that he lies down on the shore. Then comes the roc and carries off both the rhinoceros and what is on its horn, to feed its young with.

Besides this I saw on this island many kinds of oxen and buffaloes whose like is not found in our country.

Here I sold some of the diamonds I had by me for gold dinars and silver dirhams, and bartered others for the produce of the country; and loading them on beasts of burden, travelled on with the merchants from valley to valley and town to town, buying and selling and seeing foreign countries and the works and the creatures of Allah, until we came to the city of Basra, where we stayed a few days, after which I went on with my journey to Baghdad:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-sixth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when Sindbad the Seaman came back from his travels to Baghdad, the House of Peace, he arrived home with a great store of diamonds and money and goods.

(He went on:) I met up with my friends and my relations, and gave alms and largesse and bestowed curious gifts and made presents to all my friends and companions.

Then I took to eating well and drinking well and wearing fine clothes and making merry with my fellows, and forgot all my sufferings in the pleasures of coming back to the comfort and delight of life, with a light heart and a broadened chest.

And everybody who heard of my return came and questioned me about my adventures and about foreign countries; and I told them everything that had happened to me and all I had suffered, at which they marvelled and wished me joy of my safe return.

This, then, is the end of the story of my second voyage; and tomorrow, Allah willing, I shall tell you what happened to me on my third voyage.

The company marvelled at his story and had supper with him; after which he ordered a hundred gold dinars to be given to the porter, who took the sum with many thanks and blessings — which he did not stint even when he got home — and went his way, wondering at what he had heard.

Next morning, as soon as the day came in its brightness and shone, he got up and prayed the dawn prayer and went to the house of Sindbad the Seaman, as he had told him to; and he went in and gave him good morning.

The merchant welcomed him and made him sit with him until the rest of the company arrived; and when they had eaten and drunk well and were merry with joy and jollity, their host began by saying, "Listen, my brothers, to what I am about to tell you; for it is even more wonderful than what you have heard already. But Allah alone knows what things His Omniscience has concealed from man. And listen to

The Third Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman

As I told you yesterday, I came back from my second voyage overjoyed at my safety and with a great increase of wealth, Allah having repaid me everything I had wasted and lost; and I stayed a while in the city of Baghdad enjoying the utmost ease and prosperity and comfort and happiness — until the flesh took hold of me once more with a longing for travel and diversion and adventure, and I yearned after trade and profit and gain; for the human heart is naturally inclined to what is bad for it.

So, making up my mind, I laid in a great plenty of goods suitable for a sea voyage, and going to Basra, went down to the shore and found a fine ship there ready to sail, with a full crew and a large company of merchants, men of worth and substance, of faith and piety and consideration.

I embarked with them, and we set sail on the blessing of Almighty Allah and on His aid and His favour to bring our voyage to a safe and prosperous end; and already we were congratulating one another on our good fortune and our fine voyage.

We travelled on from sea to sea and island to island and city to city, in all delight and contentment, buying and selling wherever we touched and taking our comfort and our pleasure — until one day, as we sailed across the dashing sea, swollen with clashing billows, the master, who was standing on the gunwale examining the ocean in every direction, cried out with a great cry, and beat his face and plucked out his beard and tore his clothes, and ordered the sails furled and the anchors cast.

So we said to him, "Captain, what is the matter?"

"Know, my brothers — Allah preserve you — that the wind has got the better of us and driven us off our course into the middle of the ocean; and destiny, for our ill luck, has brought us to the Mountain of the Zughb, a hairy people like apes, among whom no man ever fell and came out alive. And my heart tells me that we are all dead men."

The master had hardly finished speaking when the apes were on us. They surrounded the ship on all sides, swarming like locusts and crowding the shore.

They were the most frightful of wild creatures, covered with black hair like felt, foul of face and small of stature, being only four spans high, yellow-eyed and black-faced; nobody knows their language or what they are, and they shun the company of men.

We were afraid to kill them or strike them or drive them off, because of their inconceivable numbers, in case, if we hurt one, the rest fell on us and killed us — for numbers prevail over courage. So we let them do as they liked, although we were afraid they would plunder our goods and our gear.

They swarmed up the cables and gnawed them through, and did the same with all the ropes of the ship, so that she fell off from the wind and stranded on their mountainous coast.

Then they laid hands on all the merchants and the crew, and landing us on the island, made off with the ship and its cargo and went their way, we knew not where.

So we were left on the island, eating its fruit and its pot-herbs and drinking from its streams — until one day we caught sight of something in the middle of it that looked like an inhabited house.

So we made for it as fast as our feet would carry us; and it was a castle, strong and tall, surrounded by a high wall and having a two-leaved gate of ebony wood, both leaves of which stood open.

We went in and found inside a wide bare space like a great square, round which stood a number of tall doors thrown open; and at the far end a long stone bench and braziers, with cooking gear hanging on them and a great plenty of bones about them. But we saw nobody, and marvelled at it beyond all wondering.

Then we sat down in the courtyard a little while, and presently fell asleep, and slept from the forenoon until sundown — when the earth trembled under our feet and the air rumbled with a terrible sound.

And there came down on us, from the top of the castle, a huge creature in the likeness of a man, black in colour, tall and big of bulk as though he were a great date palm, with eyes like coals of fire and eye-teeth like a boar's tusks and a vast wide mouth like the mouth of a well.

What is more, he had long loose lips like a camel's, hanging down on his chest, and ears like two boats falling over his shoulder blades; and the nails of his hands were like a lion's claws.

When we saw this frightful giant we were ready to faint, and every moment our fear and terror increased; and we became like dead men for the excess of our horror and fright:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-seventh Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on:

When we saw this frightful giant we were struck with the utmost terror and horror. And after trampling about on the ground he sat a while on the bench; then he got up and came over to us and seized me by the arm, choosing me out from among my comrades the merchants.

He took me up in his hand and, turning me over, felt me as a butcher feels a sheep he is about to slaughter — and I was no more than a little mouthful in his hands. But finding me lean and fleshless from the stress of toil and trouble and weariness, he let me go and took up another, whom he turned over and felt in the same way and let go. Nor did he stop feeling and turning over the rest of us, one after another, until he came to the master of the ship.

Now he was a sturdy, stout, broad-shouldered fellow, fat and in full vigour; so he pleased the giant, who seized him as a butcher seizes a beast and, throwing him down, set his foot on his neck and broke it; after which he fetched a long spit and, thrusting it up through him, brought it out at the crown of his head.

Then, lighting a fierce fire, he set the spit over it with the captain on it, and turned it over the coals until the flesh was roasted; when he took the spit off the fire and set it down in front of him like a kebab skewer.

Then he tore the body limb from limb as a man joints a chicken, and rending the flesh with his nails, fell to eating it and gnawing the bones, until there was nothing left but some of them, which he threw down beside the wall.

This done, he sat a while; then he lay down on the stone bench and fell asleep, snorting and snoring like the gurgling of a lamb or a cow with its throat cut; nor did he wake until morning, when he got up and went out and went his way.

As soon as we were certain he was gone we began talking to one another, weeping and bemoaning ourselves for the danger we were in, and saying, "Would to Heaven we had been drowned in the sea, or that the apes had eaten us! That would be better than being roasted over the coals. By Allah, this is a vile, foul death! But whatever the Lord wills must come to pass, and there is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Him, the Glorious, the Great. We shall certainly perish miserably and nobody will ever know of us, for there is no escape for us from this place."

Then we got up and roamed about the island, hoping we might find somewhere to hide or some means of flight; for indeed death was a light matter to us, provided we were not roasted over the fire and eaten. However, we could find no hiding place, and the evening overtook us; so out of the excess of our terror we went back to the castle and sat down a while.

Presently the earth trembled under our feet, and the black ogre came up to us and, turning us over, felt one after another until he found a man to his liking, whom he took and served as he had served the captain, killing and roasting and eating him; after which he lay down on the bench and slept all night, snorting and snoring like a beast with its throat cut, until daybreak, when he got up and went out as before.

Then we drew together and talked, and said to one another, "By Allah, we had better throw ourselves into the sea and be drowned than die roasted; for this is an abominable death."
