Said one of us, "Hear what I say! Let us cast about to kill him and be at peace from the grief of him, and rid the Muslims of his barbarity and his tyranny."

Then said I, "Hear me, my brothers. If there is nothing for it but to kill him, let us carry some of this firewood and these planks down to the seashore and make ourselves a boat, in which — if we manage to kill him — we can either embark and let the water carry us wherever Allah wills, or else stay here until some ship passes and take passage in her.

"And if we fail to kill him, we will get into the boat and put out to sea; and if we are drowned, we shall at least have escaped being roasted over a kitchen fire with our throats cut. And if we escape, we escape; and if we are drowned, we die martyrs."

"By Allah," they all said, "this advice is sound." And we agreed on it and set about carrying it out.

So we hauled the pieces of wood that lay about the bench down to the beach and, making a boat, moored it to the shore; after which we stowed some provisions in it and went back to the castle.

As soon as evening fell the earth trembled under our feet and in came the ogre on us, snarling like a dog about to bite. He came up to us and, feeling us and turning us over one by one, took one of us and did with him as he had done before and ate him; after which he lay down on the bench and snored and snorted like thunder.

As soon as we were sure he was asleep we got up and, taking two of the iron spits that stood there, heated them in the fiercest part of the fire until they were red hot like burning coals; when we gripped them fast and, going up to the giant as he lay snoring on the bench, thrust them into his eyes and pressed on them, all of us together with our united strength, so that his eyeballs burst and he was stone blind.

At which he cried out with a great cry that made our hearts tremble; and springing up off the bench, fell to groping after us, blindfolded.

We fled from him right and left and he could not see us, for his sight was altogether gone; but we were in terrible fear of him and made certain we were dead men, despairing of any escape.

Then he found the door, feeling for it with his hands, and went out roaring aloud; and the earth shook under us with the noise of his roaring, and we quaked with fear.

As he left the castle we followed him and made for the place where we had moored our boat, saying to one another, "If this accursed creature stays away until sundown and does not come back to the castle, we shall know he is dead; and if he comes back, we will get into the boat and paddle until we escape, committing our affair to Allah."

But even as we spoke, up came the ogre with two others, like ghouls, fouler and more frightful than he was, with eyes like red-hot coals. Seeing which, we hurried into the boat and, casting off the moorings, paddled away and pushed out to sea.

As soon as the ogres caught sight of us they cried out at us and, running down to the seashore, fell to pelting us with rocks, some of which fell among us and others into the sea. We paddled with all our might until we were beyond their reach; but most of us were killed by the rock-throwing, and the winds and the waves played with us and carried us into the middle of the dashing sea, swollen with clashing billows.

We had no idea where we were going, and my companions died one after another, until there were only three of us left, myself and two others:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-eighth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on:

Most of us were killed by the rock-throwing, and only three of us were left aboard the boat; for as often as one died we threw him into the sea.

We were badly exhausted with the stress of hunger, but we took courage and heartened one another and worked for dear life and paddled with main strength, until the winds cast us up on an island, and we were like dead men for exhaustion and fear and famine.

We landed on the island and walked about it a while, and found it abounded in trees and streams and birds; and we ate its fruit and rejoiced at our escape from the black ogre and our deliverance from the perils of the sea. And so we went on until nightfall, when we lay down and fell asleep from sheer exhaustion.

But we had hardly closed our eyes before we were roused by a hissing sound like the sighing of the wind; and waking, saw a serpent like a dragon — a rarely seen sight — of monstrous make and with a belly of enormous bulk, lying in a circle around us.

Presently it reared its head and, seizing one of my companions, swallowed him down to his shoulders; then it gulped down the rest of him, and we heard his ribs crack in its belly. Presently it went its way; and we were left in bitter amazement and grief for our comrade and in mortal fear for ourselves, saying:

"By Allah, this is a marvellous thing! Every kind of death that threatens us is more terrible than the last. We were rejoicing at our escape from the black ogre and our deliverance from the perils of the sea; and now we have fallen into something worse. There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah! By the Almighty, we have escaped from the ogre and from drowning — but how are we to escape from this abominable, viperish monster?"

Then we walked about the island, eating its fruit and drinking from its streams until dusk, when we climbed up into a high tree and went to sleep there, myself on the topmost bough.

As soon as it was dark night up came the serpent, looking right and left; and making for the tree we were in, climbed up to my comrade and swallowed him down to his shoulders. Then it coiled about the trunk with him — while I, who could not take my eyes off the sight, heard his bones crack in its belly — and it swallowed him whole, after which it slid down out of the tree.

When the day broke and the light showed me that the serpent was gone, I came down like a dead man for the stress of my fear and anguish, and thought of throwing myself into the sea and being at rest from the woes of the world; but I could not bring myself to it, for truly life is dear.

So I took five pieces of wood, broad and long, and bound one crosswise to the soles of my feet, and others in the same way on my right and left sides and over my chest; and the broadest and largest of them I bound across my head, and made them all fast with ropes.

Then I lay down on the ground on my back, so that I was completely fenced in by the pieces of wood, which enclosed me like a bier.

So as soon as it was dark, up came the serpent as usual and made towards me, but could not get at me to swallow me because of the wood that fenced me in. So it wriggled round me on every side while I looked on like a dead man for terror; and every now and then it would glide away and come back — but as often as it tried to get at me it was hindered by the pieces of wood I had tied round myself on every side.

It did not stop besetting me like this from sundown until dawn; but when the light of day shone on the beast, it made off in the utmost fury and the extremity of disappointment.

Then I put out my hand and untied myself, very nearly down among the dead men for fear and suffering; and went down to the shore of the island — where a ship far off in the middle of the waves suddenly struck my sight.

So I tore off a great branch of a tree and made signs with it to the crew, shouting all the while; which when the ship's company saw, they said to one another, "We must stand in and see what this is; perhaps it is a man."

So they made for the island and presently heard my cries, at which they took me aboard and questioned me about my case. I told them all my adventures from first to last, at which they marvelled mightily, and covered my nakedness with some of their clothes.

What is more, they set some food in front of me, and I ate my fill and drank cold sweet water and was greatly refreshed; and Almighty Allah brought me back to life after I had been virtually dead. So I praised the Most High and thanked Him for His favours and His exceeding mercies; and my heart revived in me after utter despair, until it seemed to me that everything I had suffered was only a dream I had dreamed.

We sailed on with a fair wind the Almighty sent us until we came to an island called Al-Salahitah, which abounds in sandalwood, where the captain cast anchor:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-ninth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on:

And when we had cast anchor, the merchants and the sailors landed with their goods to sell and to buy. Then the captain turned to me and said:

"Listen — you are a stranger and a pauper, and you tell us you have gone through frightful hardships; and so I have a mind to do you some good that may help you towards your own country, so that you will always bless me and pray for me."

"So be it," I answered. "You shall have my prayers."

Said he, "Know then that there was a man with us, a traveller, whom we lost, and we do not know whether he is alive or dead, for we have had no news of him. So I mean to commit his bales of goods to your charge, so that you may sell them on this island. We will give you a part of the proceeds as a payment for your pains and your service, and the rest we will keep until we get back to Baghdad, where we will ask after his family and hand it over to them, together with any goods left unsold. Tell me, then — will you take on the charge and land them and sell them as the other merchants do?"

I replied, "Hearing and obedience to you, my lord; and great is your kindness to me" — and thanked him; at which he told the sailors and the porters to carry the bales in question ashore and hand them over to my charge.

The ship's clerk asked him, "Master, what bales are these, and what merchant's name shall I write on them?"

And he answered, "Write on them the name of Sindbad the Seaman, the man who was with us in the ship and whom we lost at the roc's island, and of whom we have had no news; for we mean this stranger to sell them, and we will give him a part of the price for his pains and keep the rest until we get back to Baghdad, where, if we find the owner, we will hand it over to him, and if not, to his family."

And the clerk said, "Your words are apt and your advice is right."

Now when I heard the captain give orders for the bales to be inscribed with my name, I said to myself, "By Allah, I am Sindbad the Seaman!"

So I armed myself with courage and patience and waited until all the merchants had landed and were gathered together, talking and haggling about buying and selling; and then I went up to the captain and asked him, "My lord, do you know what manner of man this Sindbad was, whose goods you have committed to me for sale?"

And he answered, "I know nothing about him except that he was a man from the city of Baghdad, called Sindbad the Seaman, who was drowned with a number of others when we lay at anchor at such and such an island; and I have heard nothing of him since."

At this I cried out with a great cry and said:

"Captain — whom Allah keep! — know that I am that same Sindbad the Seaman, and that I was not drowned. When you cast anchor at the island I landed with the rest of the merchants and the crew; and I sat down in a pleasant place by myself and ate some of the food I had with me and enjoyed myself, until I grew drowsy and was drowned in sleep; and when I woke I found no ship and nobody near me.

"These goods are my goods and these bales are my bales; and all the merchants who fetch jewels from the Valley of Diamonds saw me there and will bear me witness that I am the very same Sindbad the Seaman. For I told them everything that had happened to me, and told them how you forgot me and left me sleeping on the island, and what happened to me happened."

When the passengers and the crew heard my words they gathered round me, and some of them believed me and others did not. But presently one of the merchants, hearing me mention the Valley of Diamonds, came up and said to them:

"Hear what I say, good people! When I told you the most wonderful thing in all my travels, and told you that at the time we threw down our slaughtered animals into the Valley of Serpents — I throwing one with the rest, as was my custom — there came up a man hanging onto mine, you did not believe me and gave me the lie."

"Yes," said they, "you did tell us some such tale, but we had no reason to believe you."

He went on, "Now this is that very man; and the proof of it is that he gave me diamonds of great value and high price, whose like is not to be found, repaying me more than would ever have come up sticking to my quarter of meat. And I kept company with him as far as the city of Basra, where he took leave of us and went on to his native place, while we went back to our own country.

"This is he; and he told us his name, Sindbad the Seaman, and how the ship left him on the desert island. And you should know that Allah has sent him here so that the truth of my story might be made plain to you. What is more, these are his goods; for when he first fell in with us he told us about them, and the truth of what he said is obvious."

Hearing the merchant's speech, the captain came up to me and considered me closely a while, after which he said, "What was the mark on your bales?"

"Such and such," I answered; and I reminded him of something that had passed between him and me when I shipped with him from Basra.

At which he was convinced that I really was Sindbad the Seaman, and took me round the neck and wished me joy of my safety, saying, "By Allah, my lord, your case is truly wondrous and your tale marvellous; but praised be Allah, who has brought you and me together again, and who has restored your goods and your gear to you!":—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fiftieth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on:

"Praise be to Allah," said the captain, "who has restored your goods and your gear to you."

Then I disposed of my merchandise as skilfully as I could, and made a large profit on it; at which I rejoiced exceedingly and congratulated myself on my safety and on the recovery of my goods.

We did not stop buying and selling at the various islands until we came to the land of India, where we bought cloves and ginger and all kinds of spices; and from there we went on to the land of Sind, where we also bought and sold.

In those Indian seas I saw wonders without number or count — among others a fish like a cow, which brings forth its young and suckles them as human beings do, and out of whose skin shields are made. There were fish like donkeys and camels too, and tortoises twenty cubits across. And I saw a bird as well that comes out of a seashell and lays its eggs and hatches its chicks on the surface of the water, and never comes up out of the sea onto the land.

Then we set sail again with a fair wind and the blessing of Almighty Allah; and after a prosperous voyage arrived safe and sound at Basra.

Here I stayed a few days and presently went back to Baghdad, where I went straight to my own quarter and my own house, and greeted my family and my household and my friends.

I had gained on this voyage more than could be counted or reckoned; so I gave alms and largesse and clothed the widow and the orphan by way of thanksgiving for my happy return, and fell to feasting and making merry with my companions and my intimates; and forgot, in eating well and drinking well and dressing well, everything that had happened to me and all the perils and hardships I had suffered.

These, then, are the most remarkable things I saw on my third voyage; and tomorrow, if it be the will of Allah, you shall come to me and I will relate the adventures of my fourth voyage, which is still more wonderful than those you have heard already.

(Says the teller of the tale:) Then Sindbad the Seaman ordered a hundred golden dinars to be given to Sindbad the Landsman as usual, and called for food. So they spread the tables and the company ate the evening meal and went their ways, marvelling at the tale they had heard.

The porter, after taking his gold, passed the night in his own house, also wondering at what his namesake the Seaman had told him; and as soon as day broke and the morning showed with its brightness and shone, he got up and prayed the dawn prayer and went to Sindbad the Seaman, who returned his greeting and received him with an open heart and a cheerful face, and made him sit with him until the rest of the company arrived; when he had food set on, and they ate and drank and made merry.

Then Sindbad the Seaman spoke to them and related to them the narrative of

The Fourth Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman

Know, my brothers, that after I came back from my third voyage and met up with my friends, and forgot all my perils and hardships in the enjoyment of ease and comfort and rest, I was visited one day by a company of merchants, who sat down with me and talked of foreign travel and trade — until the old bad man inside me yearned to go with them and enjoy the sight of strange countries, and I longed for the society of the various races of mankind and for trade and profit.

So I resolved to travel with them; and buying the necessaries for a long voyage, and a great store of costly goods, more than ever before, transported them from Baghdad to Basra, where I took ship with the merchants in question, who were among the chief men of the town.

We set out trusting in the blessing of Almighty Allah; and with a favouring breeze and the best of conditions we sailed from island to island and sea to sea — until one day a contrary wind rose against us, and the captain cast out his anchors and brought the ship to a standstill, afraid she might founder in mid-ocean.

Then we all fell to praying and humbling ourselves before the Most High; but while we were doing it a furious squall struck us that tore the sails to rags and tatters. The anchor cable parted, and the ship foundering, we were thrown into the sea, goods and all.

I kept myself afloat by swimming for half the day, until, when I had given myself up for lost, the Almighty threw in my way one of the ship's planks, which I and some of the other merchants scrambled onto:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-first Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on as follows:

And when the ship foundered I scrambled onto a plank with some of the other merchants; and mounting it as we would a horse, we paddled with our feet in the sea.

We stayed like that a day and a night, the wind and the waves helping us along; and on the second day, shortly before the middle of the morning, the breeze freshened and the sea worked and the rising waves cast us up on an island, very nearly dead bodies for weariness and want of sleep, cold and hunger and fear and thirst.

We walked about the shore and found plenty of herbs, of which we ate enough to keep breath in our bodies and steady our failing spirits; then we lay down and slept until morning close by the sea.

And when the morning came with its brightness and shone, we got up and walked about the island to right and left, until we came in sight of an inhabited house a long way off. So we made towards it, and did not stop walking until we reached its door — when a number of naked men came out of it and, without greeting us or a word said, laid hold of us and mastered us and carried us off to their king, who signed to us to sit down.

So we sat down, and they set food in front of us of a kind we did not know and whose like we had never seen in all our lives. My companions ate some of it out of the stress of their hunger; but my stomach revolted at it and I would not eat — and my refusing it was, by Allah's favour, the reason I am alive today.

For no sooner had my comrades tasted it than their reason left them and their condition changed, and they began to devour it like madmen possessed by an evil spirit.

Then the savages gave them coconut oil to drink and anointed them with it; and straight after drinking it their eyes turned up in their heads and they fell to eating greedily, quite against their habit.

When I saw this I was confounded and concerned for them, and no less anxious about myself for fear of the naked people. So I watched them closely, and it was not long before I discovered that they were a tribe of Magian cannibals, whose King was a ghoul.

Everybody who came to their country, or whoever they caught in their valleys or on their roads, they brought to this King and fed on that food and anointed with that oil, at which their stomachs would swell so that they could eat a great deal, while their reason left them and they lost the power of thought and became idiots.

Then they stuffed them with coconut oil and the food I have described until they became fat and gross; when they slaughtered them by cutting their throats and roasted them for the King to eat. But as for the savages themselves, they ate human flesh raw.

When I saw this I was badly dismayed for myself and my comrades, who by now had become so stupefied that they did not know what was being done with them; and the naked people committed them to a man who used to lead them out every day and pasture them on the island like cattle. And they wandered among the trees and rested as they pleased, and so grew very fat.

As for me, I wasted away and grew sickly with fear and hunger, and my flesh shrivelled on my bones. Seeing which, the savages left me alone and took no notice of me, and so far forgot about me that one day I gave them the slip; and walking out of their place, made for the beach, which was a long way off.

There I caught sight of a very old man sitting on a high place, ringed about by the water. I looked at him and knew him for the herdsman who had charge of pasturing my companions; and with him were many others in the same state.

As soon as he saw me he knew I was still in possession of my reason and not afflicted like the rest he was pasturing; so he signed to me from a distance, as much as to say, "Turn back and take the right-hand road, for that will bring you to the King's highway."

So I turned back as he directed, and followed the right-hand road, now running for fear and now walking at leisure to rest myself, until I was out of the old man's sight.

By this time the sun had gone down and the dark had set in; so I sat down to rest, and would have slept, but sleep would not come to me that night for the stress of fear and famine and fatigue.

When the night was half gone I got up and walked on, until the day broke in all its beauty and the sun rose over the heads of the lofty hills and across the low gravelly plains.

Now I was weary and hungry and thirsty; so I ate my fill of the herbs and grasses that grew on the island and kept life in my body and stayed my stomach; after which I set out again and travelled all that day and the next night, staying my hunger with roots and herbs.

Nor did I stop walking for seven days and their nights, until the morning of the eighth, when I caught sight of a faint object in the distance. So I made towards it, though my heart quaked for everything I had suffered first and last — and it was a company of men gathering peppercorns.

As soon as they saw me they hurried up to me and surrounded me on all sides and said, "Who are you and where do you come from?"

I replied, "Know, good people, that I am a poor stranger" — and told them my case and all the hardships and perils I had suffered:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-second Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on:

And the men gathering pepper on the island questioned me about my case, when I told them all the hardships and perils I had suffered and how I had fled from the savages; at which they marvelled and wished me joy of my safety, saying:

"By Allah, this is wonderful! But how did you escape from these savages, who swarm all over the island and devour everybody who falls in with them? Nobody is safe from them, and nobody gets out of their clutches."

And after I had told them the fate of my companions they made me sit with them until they had finished their work; and fetched me some good food, which I ate, for I was hungry, and rested a while.

After which they took ship with me and, carrying me to their island home, brought me before their King, who returned my greeting and received me honourably and questioned me about my case.

I told him everything that had happened to me from the day I left the city of Baghdad; at which he wondered greatly at my adventures, he and his courtiers, and told me to sit beside him. Then he called for food, and I ate with him as much as I needed and washed my hands and gave thanks to Almighty Allah for all His favours, praising Him and glorifying Him.

Then I left the King and walked about the city to amuse myself, and found it wealthy and populous, abounding in market streets well stocked with food and merchandise and full of buyers and sellers.

So I rejoiced at having reached such a pleasant place, and took my ease there after my exhaustion; and I made friends among the townspeople, and before long I stood higher in honour and favour with them and with their King than any of the chief men of the realm.

Now I saw that all the citizens, great and small, rode fine horses, high-priced and thoroughbred, without saddles or housings; at which I wondered, and said to the King, "Why, my lord, do you not ride with a saddle? There is comfort in it for the rider and an increase of control."

"What is a saddle?" he asked. "I never saw one or used one in all my life."

And I answered, "With your permission I will make you a saddle, so that you may ride on it and see how comfortable it is."

And he said, "Do so."

So I said to him, "Furnish me with some wood"; which being brought, I looked out a clever carpenter and sat with him and showed him how to make the saddle tree, drawing the shape of it for him in ink on the wood.

Then I took wool and teased it and made felt of it; and covering the saddle tree with leather, stuffed it and polished it and attached the girth and the stirrup leathers.

After which I fetched a blacksmith and described to him the shape of the stirrups and the bit. So he forged a fine pair of stirrups and a bit, and filed them smooth and tinned them. What is more, I fastened silk fringes to them and fitted bridle leathers to the bit.

Then I fetched one of the best of the royal horses and, saddling and bridling him, hung the stirrups on the saddle and led him to the King.

The thing took his fancy and he thanked me; then he mounted and was delighted with the saddle, and rewarded me handsomely for my work.

When the King's vizier saw the saddle he asked me for one like it, and I made it for him. And after that all the grandees and officers of state came to me for saddles; so I fell to making saddles — having taught the craft to the carpenter and the blacksmith — and selling them to everybody who wanted one, until I amassed great wealth and stood in high honour and great favour with the King and his household and his grandees.

I lived like this until one day, as I was sitting with the King in all respect and contentment, he said to me:

"Know, my friend, that you have become one of us, dear as a brother; and we hold you in such regard and affection that we cannot part with you or allow you to leave our city. And so I want your obedience in a certain matter, and I will not have you cross me in it."

I answered, "O King, what is it you want of me? Far be it from me to cross you in anything, for I am indebted to you for many favours and bounties and much kindness; and, praise be to Allah, I have become one of your servants."

Said he, "I have a mind to marry you to a fair, clever, agreeable wife who is as wealthy as she is beautiful, so that you may be naturalised and settled among us. I will lodge you with me in my palace; so do not oppose me or cross me in this."

When I heard this I was abashed and held my peace, and could not answer him at all for my great bashfulness in front of him.

He asked, "Why do you not answer me, my son?"

And I answered, "My master, it is yours to command, O King of the age."

So he summoned the judge and the witnesses and married me straight away to a lady of a noble family and a high pedigree; wealthy in money and in means; the flower of an ancient race; of surpassing beauty and grace, and the owner of farms and estates and many a dwelling place:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-third Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on in these words:

Now after the King my master had married me to this choice wife, he also gave me a great and handsome house standing on its own, together with slaves and officers, and assigned me pay and allowances.

So I lived in all ease and contentment and delight, and forgot everything that had happened to me of weariness and trouble and hardship; for I loved my wife with the fondest love and she loved me no less, and we were as one, and lived in the utmost comfort of life and in its happiness.

And I said to myself, "When I go back to my own country I will take her with me." But whatever is predestined for a man, that must happen, and nobody knows what will befall him.

We lived like this a great while, until Almighty Allah bereaved one of my neighbours of his wife. Now he was a friend of mine; so hearing the cry of the mourners, I went in to condole with him on his loss, and found him in a very bad way, full of trouble and weary in soul and mind.

I condoled with him and comforted him, saying, "Do not mourn for your wife, who has now found the mercy of Allah; the Lord will surely give you a better one in her place, and your name shall be great and your life shall be long in the land, Allah willing."

But he wept bitter tears and replied, "My friend, how can I marry another wife, and how shall Allah replace her with a better than she was, when I have only one day left to live?"

"Brother," said I, "come back to your senses, and do not announce the glad tidings of your own death, for you are well and sound and in good case."

"By your life, my friend," he answered, "tomorrow you will lose me and will never see me again till the Day of Resurrection."

I asked, "How so?"

And he answered, "This very day they bury my wife, and they bury me with her in one tomb; for it is the custom with us, if the wife dies first, to bury the husband alive with her, and likewise the wife if the husband dies first, so that neither may enjoy life after losing the other."

"By Allah," I cried, "this is a most vile and wicked custom, and not to be endured by anybody!"

Meanwhile most of the townspeople came in and fell to condoling with my friend for his wife and for himself. Presently they laid the dead woman out, as was their custom; and setting her on a bier, carried her and her husband out of the city until they came to a place in the side of the mountain at the end of the island by the sea.

And here they raised a great rock and uncovered the mouth of a stone-lined pit or well, leading down into a vast underground cavern that ran beneath the mountain.

Into this pit they threw the corpse; then, tying a rope of palm fibre under the husband's armpits, they let him down into the cavern, and with him a great pitcher of fresh water and seven scones by way of provisions.

When he reached the bottom he loosed himself from the rope and they drew it up; and stopping the mouth of the pit with the great stone, went back to the city, leaving my friend in the cavern with his dead wife.

When I saw this I said to myself, "By Allah, this fashion of death is more grievous than the other!"

And I went in to the King and said, "My lord, why do you bury the living with the dead?"

Said he, "You must understand that it has been the custom of our forefathers and of our old kings from time out of mind: if the husband dies first, to bury his wife with him, and the same with the wife — so that we may not sever them, alive or dead."

I asked, "O King of the age, if the wife of a foreigner like myself dies among you, do you deal with him as you did with that man?"

And he answered, "Certainly; we do with him exactly as you have seen."

When I heard this my gall bladder was ready to burst for the violence of my dismay and my concern for myself. My wits were dazed; I felt as if I were in a foul dungeon; and I hated their society, for I went about in fear that my wife might die before me and they would bury me alive with her.

However, after a while I comforted myself, saying, "Perhaps I shall die before her, or shall have gone back to my own country before she dies; for nobody knows which will go first and which last."

Then I applied myself to turning my mind from this thought with various occupations; but it was not long before my wife fell ill and complained and took to her bed, and after a few days went to the mercy of Allah.

And the King and the rest of the people came, as was their custom, to condole with me and with her family and console us for her loss — and no less to condole with me for my own death.

Then the women washed her and, dressing her in her richest clothes and her golden ornaments, necklaces and jewellery, laid her on the bier and carried her to the mountain I have described, where they lifted the cover of the pit and threw her in.

After which all my intimates and acquaintances and my wife's family gathered round me, to say goodbye to me in my own lifetime and console me for my own death — while I cried out among them, saying:

"Almighty Allah never made it lawful to bury the living with the dead! I am a stranger and not one of your kind; and I cannot bear your custom; and if I had known of it I would never have married among you!"

They did not hear me and paid no attention to my words, but laying hold of me, bound me by force and let me down into the cavern with a large jar of sweet water and seven cakes of bread, according to their custom.

When I reached the bottom they called out to me to cast myself loose from the cords, but I refused to do it; so they threw them down on me, and closing the mouth of the pit with the stones I have described, went their ways:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-fourth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on:

When they had left me in the cavern with my dead wife and closed the mouth of the pit and gone their ways, I looked about me and found myself in a vast cave full of dead bodies, which gave off a foul and loathsome smell; and the air was heavy with the groans of the dying.

At this I fell to blaming myself for what I had done, saying:

"By Allah, I deserve everything that has happened to me and everything that is going to happen! What curse was on me, to take a wife in this city? There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great! As often as I say I have escaped from one calamity, I fall into a worse. By Allah, this is an abominable death to die! Would to Heaven I had died a decent death and been washed and shrouded like a man and a Muslim. I wish I had been drowned at sea or had perished in the mountains — it would be better than dying this miserable death."

And so I went on blaming my own folly and my greed for gain, in that black hole where I could not tell night from day; and I did not stop cursing the Foul Fiend and blessing the Almighty Friend.

Then I threw myself down on the bones of the dead and lay there imploring Allah's help; and in the violence of my despair I called on death, which did not come to me — until the fire of hunger burned my stomach and thirst set my throat aflame, when I sat up and, feeling for the bread, ate a morsel of it and swallowed a mouthful of water on top of it.

After this, the worst night I ever knew, I got up and explored the cavern, and found that it ran a long way, with hollows in its sides; and its floor was strewn with dead bodies and rotten bones that had lain there since ancient times. So I made myself a place in one of the hollows of the cave, far from the corpses lately thrown down, and slept there.

I stayed like that a long while, until my provisions were close to running out; and even so I ate only once every day or every second day, and did not drink more than an occasional mouthful, for fear my food should fail me before my death; and I said to myself, "Eat little and drink little; perhaps the Lord will grant you deliverance."

One day, as I sat there pondering my case and wondering what I should do when my bread and water were finished, the stone that covered the opening was suddenly rolled away and the light streamed down on me.

Said I, "I wonder what the matter is; perhaps they have brought another corpse."

Then I saw people standing about the mouth of the pit, who presently let down a dead man and a living woman, weeping and bemoaning herself, and with her a fuller supply of bread and water than usual. I saw her, and she was a beautiful woman; but she did not see me. And they closed up the opening and went away.

Then I took the leg-bone of a dead man and, going up to the woman, struck her on the crown of the head; and she gave one cry and fell down in a faint. I struck her a second and a third time, until she was dead; when I laid hands on her bread and water, and found on her a great quantity of ornaments and rich clothes, necklaces, jewels and gold trinkets — for it was their custom to bury women in all their finery.

I carried the provisions to my sleeping place in the side of the cavern and ate and drank of them sparingly, no more than was enough to keep the life in me, in case the food should run out quickly and I should die of hunger and thirst. And yet I never entirely lost hope in Almighty Allah.

I stayed there a great while, killing everybody they let down alive into the cavern and taking their provisions of food and drink — until one day, as I slept, I was woken by something scratching and burrowing among the bodies in a corner of the cave; and I said, "What can this be?" — being afraid of wolves or hyenas.

So I sprang up and, seizing the leg-bone I have mentioned, made for the noise. As soon as the thing was aware of me it fled from me into the depths of the cavern; and it was a wild animal.

However, I followed it to the far end, until I saw a long way off a point of light no bigger than a star, now appearing and now disappearing. So I made for it; and as I came nearer it grew larger and brighter, until I was certain that it was a crevice in the rock leading out into the open country.

And I said to myself, "There must be some reason for this opening: either it is the mouth of a second pit, like the one they let me down by, or else it is a natural fissure in the rock."

So I thought a while; and coming closer to the light, found that it came from a break in the far side of the mountain, which the wild animals had enlarged by burrowing, so that they could get in and devour the dead and come and go freely.

When I saw this my spirits revived and hope came back to me and I made certain of life, after having died a death. So I went on as though in a dream; and managing to scramble through the gap, found myself on the slope of a high mountain overlooking the salt sea and cutting off all access to it from the island, so that nobody could reach that part of the beach from the city.

I praised my Lord and thanked Him, rejoicing greatly and heartening myself with the prospect of deliverance; then I went back through the crack into the cavern and brought out all the food and water I had saved up, and put on some of the dead people's clothes over my own.

After which I gathered together all the collars and necklaces of pearls and jewels, and the trinkets of gold and silver set with precious stones, and the other ornaments and valuables I could find on the corpses; and making them into bundles with the grave clothes and the garments of the dead, carried them out to the back of the mountain facing the seashore, where I settled myself, meaning to wait there until it should please Almighty Allah to send me relief by some passing ship.

I visited the cavern every day; and as often as I found people buried alive there I killed them all without distinction, men and women alike, and took their food and their valuables and carried them to my place on the seashore.

So I stayed a long while:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-fifth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on:

And after carrying all my food and my valuables from the cavern to the coast, I stayed a long while by the sea, pondering my case — until one day I caught sight of a ship passing in the middle of the clashing sea, swollen with dashing billows.

So I took a piece of a white shroud I had with me and, tying it to a staff, ran along the seashore making signals with it and calling out to the people in the ship, until they saw me and, hearing my shouts, sent a boat to fetch me off.

When it drew near the crew called out to me, saying, "Who are you, and how did you come to be on this mountain, where we have never seen anybody in all our born days?"

I answered, "I am a gentleman and a merchant who was shipwrecked and saved himself on one of the ship's planks with some of his goods; and by the blessing of the Almighty and the decrees of Destiny, and by my own strength and skill, after a great deal of toil and trouble I have landed with my gear in this place, where I have been waiting for some passing ship to take me off."

So they took me into their boat, together with the bundles I had made of the jewels and the valuables from the cavern, tied up in clothes and shrouds, and rowed back with me to the ship; where the captain said to me:

"How did you come, man, to that place on that mountain, behind which lies a great city? All my life I have sailed these seas and passed to and fro close by these heights, and yet I never saw any living thing here except wild animals and birds."

I repeated to him the story I had told the sailors, but told him nothing of what had happened to me in the city and the cavern, in case there should be any of the islanders aboard the ship.

Then I took out some of the best pearls I had with me and offered them to the captain, saying, "My lord, you have been the means of saving me off that mountain. I have no ready money; but take this from me in return for your kindness and your good offices."

But he refused to accept it from me, saying, "When we find a shipwrecked man on the seashore or on an island, we take him up and give him food and drink; and if he is naked we clothe him; and we take nothing from him. On the contrary, when we reach a safe port we set him ashore with a present of our own money and treat him kindly and charitably, for the love of Allah the Most High."

So I prayed that his life might be long in the land, and rejoiced at my escape, trusting to be delivered from my troubles and to forget my past misfortunes; for every time I remembered being let down into that cave with my dead wife I shuddered with horror.

Then we went on with our voyage and sailed from island to island and sea to sea, until we came to the Island of the Bell, which contains a city two days' journey across; from where, after a six-day run, we reached the Island of Kala, close to the land of India.

This place is governed by a powerful and mighty King, and it produces excellent camphor and an abundance of Indian rattan; there is a lead mine here too.

At last, by the decree of Allah, we arrived safely at the town of Basra, where I stayed a few days and then went on to the city of Baghdad; and finding my own quarter, went into my house with lively pleasure.

There I met up with my family and my friends, who rejoiced at my happy return and wished me joy of my safety. I laid up in my storehouses all the goods I had brought with me, and gave alms and largesse to holy beggars and the poor, and clothed the widow and the orphan.

Then I gave myself up to pleasure and enjoyment, going back to my old merry way of living.

Such, then, are the most marvellous adventures of my fourth voyage; but tomorrow, if you will kindly come to me, I will tell you what happened to me on my fifth voyage, which was rarer still and more marvellous than the ones before it. And you, my brother Sindbad the Landsman, shall have supper with me as usual.

(Says the teller of the tale:) When Sindbad the Seaman had finished his story he called for supper; so they spread the table and the guests ate the evening meal; after which he gave the porter a hundred dinars as usual, and he and the rest of the company went their ways, glad at heart and marvelling at the tales they had heard — for every story was more extraordinary than the one before it.

Sindbad the Porter passed the night in his own house in all joy and cheer and wonderment; and as soon as morning came with its brightness and shone, he prayed the dawn prayer and went to the house of Sindbad the Seaman, who welcomed him and told him to sit with him until the rest of the company arrived; when they ate and drank and made merry, and the talk went round among them.

Presently their host began the narrative of the fifth voyage:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-sixth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the host began, in these words, the narrative of

The Fifth Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman

Know, my brothers, that when I had been a while ashore after my fourth voyage — and when, in my comfort and my pleasures and my merrymaking, and in my rejoicing over my large gains and profits, I had forgotten everything I had endured of perils and sufferings — the flesh took hold of me again with the longing to travel and see foreign countries and islands.

Accordingly I bought costly merchandise suited to my purpose, and making it up into bales, went to Basra; where I walked about the river quay until I found a fine tall ship, newly built, with unused gear and fitted out ready for sea.

She pleased me; so I bought her, and putting my goods aboard, hired a master and a crew and set some of my slaves and servants over them as inspectors. A number of merchants also brought their goods aboard and paid me freight and passage money; and then, after reciting the opening chapter of the Koran, we set sail over Allah's pool in all joy and cheer, promising ourselves a prosperous voyage and a good profit.

We sailed from city to city and from island to island and from sea to sea, viewing the cities and countries we passed, and selling and buying in a good many of them — until one day we came to a great uninhabited island, deserted and desolate, on which was a white dome of the biggest bulk, half buried in the sand.

The merchants landed to examine this dome, leaving me in the ship; and when they came near it — it was a huge roc's egg. They fell to beating it with stones, not knowing what it was, and presently broke it open; at which a great deal of water ran out of it and the young roc appeared inside. So they pulled it out of the shell and cut its throat and took a great store of meat off it.

Now I was in the ship and did not know what they were doing; but presently one of the passengers came up to me and said, "My lord, come and look at the egg we took for a dome."

So I looked, and seeing the merchants beating it with stones, called out to them, "Stop! Stop! Do not meddle with that egg, or the roc will come out and break our ship and destroy us."

But they paid no attention to me and did not leave off striking the egg — when the day grew dark and dun and the sun was hidden from us, as though some great cloud had passed over the sky.

So we raised our eyes, and saw that what we had taken for a cloud was the roc, poised between us and the sun; and it was his wings that darkened the day.

When he came and saw his egg broken he cried a loud cry, at which his mate came flying up; and the two of them began circling round the ship, crying out at us with voices louder than thunder.

I called to the captain and the crew, "Put out to sea and look for safety in flight, before we are all destroyed!"

So the merchants came aboard and we cast off and made haste away from the island to reach the open sea. When the rocs saw this they flew off, and we crowded all sail on the ship, thinking to get clear of their country; but presently the two of them reappeared and flew after us and stood over us, each carrying in its claws a huge boulder it had brought from the mountains.

As soon as the male roc came up with us he let fall the rock he held in his talons; but the master put the ship about, so that the rock missed her by a very little and plunged into the waves with such violence that the ship pitched high and then sank into the trough of the sea, and the bottom of the ocean appeared to us.

Then the female roc let fall her rock, which was bigger than her mate's; and as Destiny had decreed, it fell on the poop of the ship and crushed it, the rudder flying into twenty pieces; at which the vessel foundered and everything and everybody aboard was thrown into the sea.

As for me, I struggled for sweet life until Almighty Allah threw in my way one of the ship's planks, which I clung to; and getting astride it, fell to paddling with my feet.

Now the ship had gone down close to an island in the middle of the sea, and the winds and the waves carried me on until, by permission of the Most High, they cast me up on the shore of that island, at my last gasp from toil and distress and half dead with hunger and thirst.

So I landed more like a corpse than a living man, and throwing myself down on the beach, lay there a while until I began to revive and recover my spirits; when I walked about the island and found it like one of the enclosed gardens of Paradise.

Its trees, in abundance dressed, bore ripe yellow fruit for their freight; its streams ran clear and bright; its flowers were fair to smell and to sight, and its birds warbled with delight the praises of Him to whom belong permanence and all might.

So I ate my fill of the fruit and slaked my thirst with the water of the streams until I could take no more; and I gave thanks to the Most High and glorified Him:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-seventh Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on:

So when I had escaped drowning and reached the island, which gave me fruit to eat and water to drink, I gave thanks to the Most High and glorified Him; after which I sat until nightfall, hearing no voice and seeing no inhabitant.

Then I lay down, very nearly dead with labour and trouble and terror, and slept without a break until morning; when I got up and walked about under the trees, until I came to the channel of a draw-well fed by a spring of running water; and by this well sat an old man of venerable appearance, girt about with a waistcloth made of the fibre of palm fronds.

I said to myself, "Perhaps this old man is one of the people who were wrecked in the ship and has made his way to this island."

So I came up to him and greeted him, and he returned my greeting by signs but did not speak; and I said to him, "Uncle, what makes you sit here?"

He shook his head and moaned and signed to me with his hands, as much as to say, "Take me on your shoulders and carry me across to the other side of the well channel."

And I said in my mind, "I will deal kindly with him and do what he wants; perhaps I shall earn a reward in Heaven for it, since he may be a paralytic."

So I took him on my back and carried him to the place he pointed at, and said, "Get down at your leisure."

But he would not get off my back, and wound his legs about my neck. I looked at them, and seeing that they were like a buffalo's hide for blackness and roughness, I was frightened and would have thrown him off; but he clung to me and gripped my neck with his legs until I was very nearly choked, and the world went black in my sight and I fell senseless to the ground like a dead man.

But he still kept his seat; and raising his legs, drummed with his heels and beat my back and shoulders harder than palm rods, until he forced me to get up for the excess of the pain.

Then he signed to me with his hand to carry him this way and that among the trees that bore the best fruit; and if ever I refused to do what he wanted, or loitered, or took my time, he beat me with his feet more grievously than if I had been beaten with whips.

He did not stop signalling with his hand wherever he had a mind to go; so I carried him about the island like a captive slave, and he fouled my shoulders and my back, and never dismounted night or day; and when he wanted to sleep he wound his legs about my neck and leaned back and slept a while, then got up and beat me — at which I sprang up in a hurry, unable to gainsay him because of the pain he inflicted on me.

And indeed I blamed myself and bitterly regretted having taken pity on him; and I went on in this condition, suffering an exhaustion beyond describing, until I said to myself, "I did him a good turn and he has paid me back with harm. By Allah, never again will I do any man a service as long as I live!"

And again and again I begged the Most High that I might die, for the stress of my weariness and my misery. And so I went on a long while — until one day I came with him to a place where there were plenty of gourds, many of them dry.

So I took a great dry gourd and, cutting the head open, scooped out the inside and cleaned it; after which I gathered grapes from a vine that grew close by and squeezed them into the gourd until it was full of the juice.

Then I stopped up the mouth and set it in the sun, where I left it some days, until it became strong wine; and every day I used to drink some of it, to comfort and sustain me under my labours with that perverse and obstinate fiend. And as often as I drank myself drunk I forgot my troubles and took new heart.

One day he saw me drinking and signed to me with his hand, as much as to say, "What is that?"

Said I, "It is an excellent cordial, which cheers the heart and revives the spirits."

Then, being heated with the wine, I ran and danced with him among the trees, clapping my hands and singing and making merry; and I staggered under him on purpose.

When he saw this he signed to me to give him the gourd so that he could drink; and I was afraid of him and gave it to him. So he took it and, draining it to the dregs, threw it on the ground; at which he grew frolicsome and began to clap his hands and jig to and fro on my shoulders, and he made water over me so copiously that all my clothes were drenched.

But presently the fumes of the wine rose to his head and he became helplessly drunk, and the muscles of his sides and his limbs relaxed and he swayed to and fro on my back.

When I saw that he had lost his senses with drunkenness I put my hand to his legs and, loosing them from my neck, stooped down almost to the ground and threw him off at full length:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-eighth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on:

So I threw the devil off my shoulders, hardly able to believe in my deliverance from him and afraid he might shake off his drunkenness and do me a mischief.

Then I took up a great stone from among the trees and, coming up to him, struck him on the head with it with all my might and crushed in his skull as he lay dead drunk. At which his flesh and his fat and his blood being all in a pulp, he died and went to what he deserved, the Fire — no mercy of Allah be on him.

I then went back, with an easy heart, to my old station on the seashore, and stayed on that island many days, eating its fruit and drinking its water and keeping a lookout for passing ships — until one day, as I sat on the beach recalling everything that had happened to me and saying, "I wonder whether Allah will keep me alive and restore me to my home and my family and my friends" — a ship came making for the island through the dashing sea and the clashing waves.

Presently it cast anchor and the passengers landed; so I made for them, and when they saw me they all hurried up to me and, gathering round me, questioned me about my case and how I came to be there.

I told them everything that had happened to me, at which they marvelled beyond all marvelling and said, "The one who rode on your shoulder is called the Shaykh al-Bahr, the Old Man of the Sea; and nobody has ever felt his legs on his neck and come off alive except you; and those who die under him he eats. So praise be to Allah for your safety!"

Then they set some food in front of me, of which I ate my fill; and gave me some clothes, with which I clothed myself afresh and covered my nakedness; after which they took me up into the ship.

And we sailed days and nights, until fate brought us to a place called the City of Apes, built with lofty houses, all of which looked out on the sea, and having a single gate studded and strengthened with iron nails.

Now every night, as soon as it is dusk, the people who live in this city come out through the gates and, putting out to sea in boats and ships, pass the night on the water for fear the apes should come down on them from the mountains.

Hearing this I was badly troubled, remembering what I had suffered before from the ape-kind.

Presently I landed to amuse myself in the city; but meanwhile the ship set sail without me, and I regretted having gone ashore; and calling to mind my companions and what had happened to me with the apes, first and last, I sat down and fell to weeping and lamenting.

Presently one of the townspeople came up to me and said, "My lord, it seems to me you are a stranger to these parts?"

"Yes," I answered, "I am indeed a stranger, and a poor one, who came here in a ship that cast anchor here; and I landed to see the town, but when I would have gone aboard again, I found they had sailed without me."

Said he, "Come and embark with us; for if you spend the night in the city the apes will destroy you."

"Hearing and obedience," I replied; and getting up, embarked at once with him in one of the boats; at which they pushed off from the shore, and anchoring a mile or so from land, passed the night there.

At daybreak they rowed back to the city and landed and went each about his business. They did this every night; for if anybody stayed in the town by night the apes came down on him and killed him. As soon as it was day the apes left the place and ate the fruit in the gardens, then went back to the mountains and slept there until nightfall, when they came down on the city again.

Now this place was in the farthest part of the Land of the Blacks; and one of the strangest things that happened to me during my stay in the city was this.

One of the company I passed the night with in the boat asked me, "My lord, you are plainly a stranger in these parts; have you any trade you can work at?"

And I answered, "By Allah, brother, I have no trade and I know no handicraft; for I was a merchant and a man of money and substance, and had a ship of my own loaded with a great store of goods and merchandise. But it foundered at sea and everybody was drowned except me, who saved myself on a piece of plank that Allah granted me of His favour."

At this he brought me a cotton bag and, giving it to me, said, "Take this bag and fill it with pebbles from the beach, and go out with a company of the townspeople, to whom I will give instructions about you. Do as they do, and perhaps you will earn something that may help you towards the voyage home to your own country."

Then he carried me to the beach, where I filled my bag with pebbles large and small; and presently we saw a company of people come out of the town, each carrying a bag like mine filled with pebbles.

To these he committed me, commending me to their care and saying, "This man is a stranger; take him with you and teach him how to gather, so that he may earn his daily bread, and you will earn your reward and recompense in Heaven."

"On our head and eyes be it," they answered; and bidding me welcome, went on with me until we came to a spacious valley, full of tall trees with trunks so smooth that nobody could climb them.

Now sleeping under these trees were a great many apes, which when they saw us got up and fled from us and swarmed up among the branches; at which my companions began pelting them with what they had in their bags, and the apes fell to plucking the fruit off the trees and throwing it at the people.

I looked at the fruit they were throwing at us and found it to be coconuts; so I picked out a great tree full of apes, and going up to it, began pelting them with stones; and they pelted me back with nuts, which I collected as the rest did — so that even before I had finished my bagful of pebbles I had got a great plenty of nuts.

And as soon as my companions had likewise got as many nuts as they could carry, we went back to the city, where we arrived at the tail end of the day.

Then I went in to the kindly man who had put me in company with the nut-gatherers, and gave him everything I had got, thanking him for his kindness; but he would not accept them, saying, "Sell them and make a profit on the price."

And presently he added, giving me the key of a storeroom in his house, "Store your nuts in this safe place, and go out every morning and gather them as you have done today; and pick out the worst of them for sale and for your own keep, and lay up the rest here — so that perhaps you may collect enough to serve you for your journey home."

"Allah reward you!" I answered; and I did as he advised me, going out every day with the coconut gatherers, who recommended me to one another and showed me the best-stocked trees.

I did this for some time, until I had laid up a great store of excellent nuts, besides a large sum of money from the price of those I had sold. So I became comfortably off, and bought everything I saw and had a mind to, and passed my time pleasantly, greatly enjoying my stay in the city — until one day, as I stood on the beach, a great ship steering through the heart of the sea presently cast anchor by the shore and landed a company of merchants, who set about selling and buying and bartering their goods for coconuts and other commodities.

Then I went to my friend and told him the ship had come and that I had a mind to go back to my own country; and he said, "It is for you to decide."

So I thanked him for his kindnesses and took my leave of him; then, going to the captain of the ship, I agreed with him for my passage and put my coconuts and everything else I had aboard.

We weighed anchor:—

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-ninth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on:

So I left the City of the Apes and put my coconuts and everything else I had aboard. We weighed anchor the same day and sailed from island to island and sea to sea; and wherever we stopped I sold and traded with my coconuts, and the Lord repaid me more than I had before and lost.

Among other places we came to an island abounding in cloves and cinnamon and pepper; and the country people told me that beside every bunch of pepper there grows a great leaf which shades it from the sun and casts the water off it in the wet season, but that when the rain stops the leaf turns over and droops down at the side of the bunch.

Here I took in a great store of pepper and cloves and cinnamon in exchange for coconuts; and from there we passed to the Island of Al-Usirat, where the Comorin aloes-wood comes from, and then to another island five days' journey in length, where the Chinese aloes-wood grows, which is better than the Comorin. But the people of this island are fouler in their conduct and their religion than those of the other, for they love fornication and wine-bibbing, and know neither prayer nor the call to prayer.

From there we came to the pearl fisheries, and I gave the divers some of my coconuts and said to them, "Dive for my luck and my lot!"

They did so, and brought up from the deep water a great store of large and priceless pearls; and they said to me, "By Allah, my master, your luck is a lucky one!"

Then we sailed on with the blessing of Allah, whose name be exalted; and did not stop sailing until we arrived safely at Basra.

There I stayed a little and then went on to Baghdad, where I came into my own quarter and found my house and met up with my family and greeted my friends, who wished me joy of my safe return; and I laid up all my goods and valuables in my storehouses.

Then I distributed alms and largesse and clothed the widow and the orphan and made presents to my relations and my comrades; for the Lord had repaid me fourfold what I had lost. After which I went back to my old merry way of living, and forgot everything I had suffered, in the great profit and gain I had made.

Such, then, is the history of my fifth voyage and its wonders; and now to supper. And tomorrow come again, and I will tell you what happened to me on my sixth voyage; for it was more wonderful still than this.

(Says the teller of the tale:) Then he called for food; and the servants spread the table; and when they had eaten the evening meal, he ordered a hundred golden dinars to be given to Sindbad the porter; and the Landsman went home and lay down to sleep, marvelling greatly at everything he had heard.

Next morning, as soon as it was light, he prayed the dawn prayer; and after blessing Mohammed, the Cream of all creatures, went to the house of Sindbad the Seaman and wished him a good day.

The merchant told him to sit down and talked with him until the rest of the company arrived. Then the servants spread the table; and when they had eaten and drunk well and were mirthful and merry, Sindbad the Seaman began, in these words, the narrative of

The Sixth Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman

Know, my brothers and friends and companions all, that after I came home from my fifth voyage I lived some time in great comfort and satisfaction, in mirth and merriment, in joy and enjoyment; and I forgot everything I had suffered, seeing what a great profit I had made by it.

Then one day, as I sat making merry with my friends, there came in to me a company of merchants with the look of travel about them, who talked to me of voyages and adventures and of the greatness of money and gain. And at that I remembered the days of my return from abroad, and my delight at seeing my native land again and being back among my family and my friends; and my soul began to yearn for travel and trade.

So, driven by Fate and Fortune, I made up my mind to undertake another voyage; and, buying fine and costly merchandise suitable for foreign trade, I made it up into bales and carried it from Baghdad to Basra. There I found a great ship ready for sea, full of merchants and men of standing who had valuable goods with them; so I put my bales aboard, and we left Basra in safety and good spirits under the protection of the King, the Preserver.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixtieth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on:

And after loading my bales and leaving Basra in safety and good spirits, we continued our voyage from place to place and from city to city, buying and selling and making a profit and amusing ourselves with the sight of countries where strange people live. And Fortune and the voyage both smiled on us — until one day, as we went along, the captain suddenly gave a great cry and flung his turban down on the deck. Then he beat his own face like a woman and tore out his beard, and fell down in the waist of the ship half fainting with grief and rage, calling out, "Oh, alas for the ruin of my house and the orphaning of my poor children!"

So all the merchants and the sailors gathered round him and asked, "Master, what is the matter?" — for the daylight had turned to night before their eyes.

And he answered, "Know, good people, that we have wandered off our course and left the sea whose ways we know, and come into a sea whose ways I do not know at all; and unless Allah grants us some means of escape, we are all dead men. So pray to the Most High that He deliver us out of this strait. Perhaps there is one righteous man among you whose prayers the Lord will accept."

Then he got up and climbed the mast to see whether there was any way out of the strait, and he would have loosed the sails; but the wind blew twice as hard against the ship and spun her round three times and drove her backwards, so that her rudder broke and she fell away towards a high mountain.

At this the captain came down from the mast, saying, "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great! No man can prevent what fate has laid down beforehand. By Allah, we have fallen upon a place of certain destruction; there is no way of escape for us, and not one of us can be saved."

Then we all began to weep over ourselves and to bid one another farewell, for our days were at an end and we had given up all hope of life. And presently the ship struck the mountain and broke up, and everything and everybody aboard her was plunged into the sea. Some of the merchants were drowned and others managed to reach the shore and save themselves on the mountain, myself among them.

When we got ashore we found a great island — or rather a peninsula — whose base was strewn with the wreckage of ships and with goods and gear cast up by the sea out of broken vessels whose passengers had drowned; and the quantity of it defeated counting and reckoning.

So I climbed the cliffs into the interior of the island and walked on inland, until I came to a stream of sweet water that welled up at the nearest foot of the mountains and disappeared into the earth under the range of hills on the opposite side. But all the other passengers went over the mountains into the inner parts of the island, and, scattering here and there, were bewildered by what they saw and became like madmen at the sight of the wealth and the treasures strewn along the shores.

As for me, I looked into the bed of the stream I have mentioned, and saw in it a great abundance of rubies, and great royal pearls, and every kind of jewel and precious stone, lying like gravel in the beds of the rivulets that ran through the fields; and the sands sparkled and glittered with gems and precious ores. Moreover we found on the island a great quantity of the finest aloes-wood, both Chinese and Comorin.

And there is a spring of raw ambergris there too, which flows out like wax or gum over the banks of the stream in the great heat of the sun, and runs down to the seashore, where the monsters of the deep come up and swallow it and go back into the sea. But it burns in their bellies, so they bring it up again, and it hardens on the surface of the water, and by this its colour and its quantity are changed; and at last the waves throw it ashore, and the travellers and merchants who know it collect it and sell it. But as for the raw ambergris which is not swallowed, it flows over the channel and hardens on the banks; and when the sun shines on it, it melts and scents the whole valley with a fragrance like musk, and then, when the sun leaves it, it hardens again. But nobody can get to the place where the raw ambergris is, because of the mountains that shut in the island on every side, which no man's foot can climb.

We went on exploring the island in this way, marvelling at the wonderful works of Allah and at the riches we found there, but badly troubled about our own case and dismayed at our prospects. Now we had picked up a little food on the beach from the wreck, and we hoarded it carefully, eating only once every day or two out of fear that it would fail us and we should die miserably of hunger or of terror. Moreover we were weak with the cramps that come of seasickness and poor food, and my companions died one after another, until only a small company of us was left.

Each man who died we washed and wrapped in some of the clothes and linen the tide had cast ashore; and after a little the rest of my fellows perished too, one by one, until I had buried the last of the party and was left alone on the island with very little food remaining — I, who had been used to having so much.

And I wept over myself, saying, "I wish to Heaven I had died before my companions, and that they had washed me and buried me. It would have been better than this, that I should die and nobody wash me and shroud me and bury me. But there is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great!"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-first Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on, in these words:

Now, after I had buried the last of my party and was left alone on the island, I got up and dug myself a deep grave on the seashore, saying to myself, "When I grow weak and know that death is coming to me, I will get down into the grave and die there, and the wind will drift the sand over me and cover me, and I shall be buried."

Then I fell to reproaching myself for my lack of sense, in leaving my own country and taking to travel again after everything I had suffered on my first five voyages — not one of which I had made without meeting more horrible dangers and worse hardships than the one before it — and now with no hope at all of getting out of my present trouble. And I repented my folly and lamented over myself, all the more because I had no need of money, seeing that I had enough and more than enough, and could not have spent what I had, no, nor half of it, in a whole lifetime.

However, after a while Allah put a thought into my head, and I said to myself, "By God, this stream must have an end as well as a beginning, and so it must come out somewhere; and very likely its course leads to some inhabited place. So my best plan is to make myself a little boat, just big enough to sit in, and carry it down and launch it on the river and get in and drift with the stream. If I escape, I escape, by God's leave; and if I die, better to die in the river than here."

Then, sighing for myself, I set to work gathering a number of pieces of Chinese and Comorin aloes-wood, and bound them together with ropes from the wreckage; then I picked out from the broken-up ships straight planks of an even size and fixed them firmly on top of the aloes-wood, making myself a boat-raft a little narrower than the channel of the stream; and I tied it as tightly and firmly as if it had been nailed.

Then I loaded it with the goods, the precious ores and the jewels, and the pearls that lay about like gravel, and the best of the ambergris, raw and pure, together with what I had collected on the island and what was left to me of food and wild herbs. Last of all I lashed a piece of wood on either side to serve me for oars, and launched it and got aboard, doing as the poet says:

	Run for your life when the danger is on you;
	let the house stand and tell how its builder died.
	Land after land you may look for and find,
	but no second life is waiting on the far side.
	Do not wear out your soul with your thoughts in the night;
	every sorrow comes to an end, soon or late.
	The man born in one country will die in that country,
	and nowhere else, and there he will meet his fate.
	Never trust the great business of your life to another:
	the soul has only the soul for a confederate.

My boat-raft drifted along with the stream while I sat pondering how the business would end; and it went on drifting until it came to the place where the water disappeared under the mountain. I rowed my craft into the opening, where it was intensely dark, and the current carried the raft with it down the underground channel. The narrow stream bore me on through a tunnel so tight that the raft touched both sides at once and my head rubbed against the roof, and there was no possibility of turning back.

Then I blamed myself for having risked my life like this, and said, "If this passage gets any narrower the raft will hardly get through, and I cannot turn round; so I shall certainly die a miserable death in this place." And I threw myself down flat on my face on the raft, because the channel was so low, while the stream carried me along, and I could not tell night from day for the thickness of the gloom all around me and my terror and dread for myself.

And so I went on down the channel, which now widened and now grew tighter, until, worn out with a darkness you could feel, I fell asleep as I lay face-down on the raft; and I slept, not knowing whether the time was long or short.

When I woke at last, I found myself in the light of Heaven; and opening my eyes I saw that I was on a broad river, with the raft moored to an island among a number of Indians and Abyssinians. As soon as they saw that I was awake they came up to me and spoke to me in their own language; but I did not understand what they said, and I thought this was a dream and a vision that had come to me out of my anxiety and misery. But I was delighted to have escaped from the river.

When they saw that I did not understand them and gave them no answer, one of them came forward and said to me in Arabic, "Peace be with you, brother! Who are you, and where have you come from? How did you get into this river, and what sort of land lies behind those mountains? For we never knew anybody make his way from there to us."

I said, "And peace be upon you, and the mercy of Allah and His blessing! Who are you, and what country is this?"

"Brother," he answered, "we are farmers and tillers of the soil, who came out to water our fields and our plantations; and, finding you asleep on this raft, we took hold of it and made it fast beside us, to wait until you should wake in your own good time. So tell us how you came here."

I answered, "For Allah's sake, sir, before I speak give me something to eat, for I am starving; and afterwards ask me what you like."

So he hurried to fetch me food, and I ate my fill until I was refreshed and my fear was quieted by a full stomach and my life came back to me. Then I gave thanks to the Most High for mercies great and small, glad to be out of the river and glad to be among these people; and I told them all my adventures from first to last, and especially my troubles in the narrow channel.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-second Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on:
