When I had landed and found myself among the Indians and Abyssinians and had taken some rest, they consulted among themselves and said to one another, "There is nothing for it but to take him with us and present him to our King, so that he may hear his adventures."

So they took me, together with the raft and its cargo of money and merchandise, jewels, minerals and golden gear, and brought me to their King, who was the King of Sarandib, telling him what had happened; and he greeted me and made me welcome. Then he questioned me about my situation and my adventures through the man who had spoken Arabic, and I repeated my story to him from beginning to end, at which he marvelled greatly and congratulated me on my escape.

After that I went and fetched from the raft a great store of precious ores and jewels and ambergris and aloes-wood and presented them to the King, who accepted them and treated me with the utmost honour, giving me a lodging in his own palace. So I kept company with the chief men of the islanders, and they showed me the greatest respect; and I did not leave the royal palace.

Now the island of Sarandib lies under the equator, its night and its day both measuring twelve hours. It is eighty leagues long by thirty broad, and its breadth is bounded by a lofty mountain and a deep valley. The mountain can be seen from three days' distance, and it contains many kinds of rubies and other minerals, and spice trees of every sort. Its surface is covered with emery, the stuff gems are cut and shaped with; diamonds are in its rivers and pearls are in its valleys. I climbed that mountain and refreshed myself with a view of its marvels, which are beyond describing, and afterwards came back to the King.

After that, all the travellers and merchants who came to the place questioned me about the affairs of my native land and about the Caliph Harun al-Rashid and his rule; and I told them about him and about the things he was famous for, and they praised him because of it; while I in my turn questioned them about the manners and the customs of their own countries and got the knowledge I wanted.

One day the King himself asked me about the fashions and the form of government of my country, and I told him how the Caliph ruled in the city of Baghdad and how just his rule was. The King marvelled at my account of his arrangements and said, "By Allah, the Caliph's ordinances are wise indeed and his ways are praiseworthy, and you have made me love him by what you tell me; so I have a mind to make him a present and send it by you."

I said, "To hear is to obey, my lord; I will carry your gift to him and tell him that you are his sincere admirer and his true friend."

Then I stayed with the King in great honour and regard and consideration for a long while, until one day, as I sat in his palace, I heard news of a company of merchants who were fitting out a ship for Basra; and I said to myself, "I cannot do better than sail with these men."

So I got up without pause or delay and kissed the King's hand and told him how I longed to set out with the merchants, since I was pining for my own people and my own country.

He said, "You are your own master; and yet, if you will stay with us, it shall be on our head and eyes, for you gladden us with your company."

"By Allah, my lord," I answered, "you have overwhelmed me with your favours and your kindnesses; but I am hungry for a sight of my friends and my family and my native country."

When he heard this, he sent for the merchants in question and commended me to their care, paying my freight and my passage money. Then he bestowed great riches on me out of his treasuries and charged me with a magnificent present for the Caliph Harun al-Rashid. Moreover he gave me a sealed letter, saying, "Carry this with your own hand to the Commander of the Faithful, and give him many greetings from us!"

"To hear is to obey," I replied.

The letter was written on the skin of the khawi, which is finer than lambskin parchment and yellow in colour, with ink of ultramarine; and the contents were as follows:

	Peace be with you from the King of Al-Hind, before whom stand a thousand elephants, and upon whose palace battlements are a thousand jewels. And after that (praise be to the Lord and blessings on His Prophet): we send you a trifling gift, which we hope you will be pleased to accept. You are a brother to us and a sincere friend, and great is the love we bear you in our heart; so favour us with a reply. The gift is not worthy of your dignity; but we beg you, our brother, to be gracious and accept it. And peace be with you.

And the present was: a cup of ruby a span high, the inside of it set all over with precious pearls; and a bed covered with the skin of the serpent that swallows the elephant, a skin whose spots are each of them the size of a gold dinar, and whoever sits on it never falls sick; and a hundred thousand miskals of Indian aloes-wood; and a slave girl like a shining moon.

Then I took leave of him and of all my friends and acquaintances on the island, and embarked with the merchants I have mentioned. We sailed with a fair wind, committing ourselves to the care of Allah (be He extolled and exalted!), and by His leave arrived at Basra, where I spent a few days and nights getting myself equipped and packing up my bales.

Then I went on to Baghdad, the House of Peace, where I asked for an audience with the Caliph and laid the King's presents before him. He asked me where they came from, and I said, "By Allah, Commander of the Faithful, I do not know the name of the city, nor the way there!"

Then he asked, "Sindbad, is this true, what the King writes?"

And I answered, after kissing the ground, "My lord, I saw in his kingdom a great deal more than he has written in his letter. On state occasions a throne is set for him on the back of a huge elephant eleven cubits high; and on this he sits, with his great lords and his officers and his guests standing in two ranks, on his right hand and on his left. At his head is a man holding a golden javelin, and behind him another with a great mace of gold whose head is an emerald a span long and as thick as a man's thumb. And when he takes horse, a thousand horsemen mount with him, dressed in gold brocade and silk; and as the King goes by, a man walks in front of him crying, 'This is the King of great dignity, of high authority!' And he goes on repeating his praises in words I do not remember, saying at the end of the speech, 'This is the King who owns the crown whose like neither Solomon nor the Mihrjan ever possessed.' Then he falls silent, and one behind him proclaims, saying, 'He will die! Again I say, he will die!' And the other adds, 'Extolled be the perfection of the Living One who does not die!' Moreover, by reason of his justice and his good ordering and his intelligence, there is no judge in his city at all, and every one of his subjects can tell truth from falsehood for himself."

The Caliph said, "How great this King is! His letter has shown me that; and as for the might of his dominion, you have told us what you saw with your own eyes. By Allah, he has been endowed with wisdom as well as with wide rule."

Then I related to the Commander of the Faithful everything that had happened to me on my last voyage, at which he wondered exceedingly, and gave orders to his historians to write my story down and store it up in his treasuries for the instruction of everybody who might see it. After that he conferred very great favours on me, and I went back to my own quarter and into my own house, where I warehoused all my goods and possessions. Presently my friends came to me, and I distributed presents among my family and gave alms and largesse; after which I gave myself up to joy and enjoyment, mirth and merrymaking, and forgot everything I had suffered.

Such, then, my brothers, is the history of what happened to me on my sixth voyage; and tomorrow, God willing, I will tell you the story of my seventh and last voyage, which is more wonderful and marvellous still than any of the first six.

(Says the teller of the tale:) Then he ordered the table to be laid, and the company had supper with him; after which he gave the porter a hundred dinars, as usual, and they all went their ways, marvelling beyond measure at what they had heard.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-third Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when Sindbad the Seaman had related the history of what happened to him on his sixth voyage, and all the company had scattered, Sindbad the Landsman went home and slept as usual. Next day he got up and prayed the dawn prayer and went to his namesake's house, where, after the company had all assembled, the host began to relate

The Seventh Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman

Know, my friends, that after I came home from my sixth voyage, which brought me abundant profit, I took up my old life again in every possible joy and enjoyment and mirth and merrymaking, day and night; and I stayed a while in this comfort and satisfaction, until my soul began once more to long to sail the seas and see foreign countries and keep company with merchants and hear new things.

So, having made up my mind, I packed up in bales a quantity of costly stuffs suitable for sea trade, and carried them from Baghdad to Basra, where I found a ship ready for sea with a company of substantial merchants aboard her. I took passage with them, and we became friends, and we set out on our venture in health and safety, sailing with a fair wind until we came to a city called Madinat al-Sin, the City of China.

But after we had left it, as we went along in all cheerfulness and confidence, talking of trade and travel, there sprang up a violent head wind and a storm of rain fell on us and soaked us and our goods through. So we covered the bales with our cloaks and our clothes and coarse cloth and canvas, so that the rain should not spoil them, and gave ourselves up to prayer and supplication to Almighty Allah, humbling ourselves before Him to be delivered from the danger we were in.

But the captain got up and tightened his belt and tucked up his skirts and, after taking refuge with Allah from Satan the stoned, climbed to the masthead, from where he looked out to the right and to the left; and then, gazing down at the passengers and the crew, he fell to beating his face and tearing out his beard.

So we cried out to him, "Captain, what is the matter?"

And he answered, "Ask the Most High to deliver you out of the strait we have fallen into, and mourn for yourselves and take leave of one another; for you must know that the wind has got the mastery of us and has driven us into the uttermost of all the seas of the world."

Then he came down from the masthead and, opening his sea chest, pulled out a bag of blue cotton, from which he took a powder like ashes. This he put in a saucer wetted with a little water, and after waiting a short time he smelt it and tasted it; and then he took a small book out of the chest and read in it a while, and said, weeping:

"Know, passengers, that in this book there is a marvellous matter set down, which shows that whoever comes to this place will surely die, with no hope of escape; for this ocean is called the Sea of the Region of the King, and in it is the tomb of our lord Solomon son of David (on both be peace!); and in it are serpents of enormous size and dreadful appearance. And whatever ship comes into these waters, there rises to her a great fish out of the sea and swallows her up with everything and everybody on board her."

When we heard these words from the captain we were greatly astonished; but he had hardly finished speaking when the ship was lifted clean out of the water and dropped back again, and we set about praying the prayer for the dying and committing our souls to Allah.

Presently we heard a terrible great cry like a loud peal of thunder, at which we were struck with terror and became like dead men, giving ourselves up for lost. And then there came up to us a huge fish, as big as a tall mountain, at the sight of which we went wild with fright and, weeping bitterly, made ready to die, marvelling at its vast size and its grim shape — when a second fish appeared, and we had never seen anything more monstrous than that. So we mourned for our lives and said farewell to one another; and then suddenly up came a third fish, bigger than the first two; at which we lost the power of thought and reason altogether and were stupefied with the excess of our fear and horror.

Then the three fish began circling round the ship, and the third and biggest opened his mouth to swallow it; and we looked into his mouth, and it was wider than the gate of a city, and his throat was like a long valley. So we called upon the Almighty and cried out for help to His Apostle (on whom be blessing and peace!) — when all at once a violent squall of wind rose and struck the ship, which lifted out of the water and came down on a great reef, the haunt of sea monsters, where she broke up and fell apart into planks, and everything and everybody aboard was plunged into the sea.

As for me, I tore off all my clothes except my gown and swam a little way, until I came upon one of the ship's planks, which I clung to and then got astride like a horse, while the winds and the waters played with me and the waves lifted me up and threw me down; and I was in a most pitiable state for fear and misery and hunger and thirst.

Then I reproached myself for what I had done, and my soul was sick after a life of ease and comfort; and I said to myself, "Sindbad, Sindbad the Seaman, you never repent, and yet you are always suffering hardships and disasters; and still you will not give up sea travel — or if you do say, 'I give it up,' you lie when you say it. Bear patiently, then, what you suffer, for you deserve every bit of what happens to you!"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-fourth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on:

But when I had got astride the plank, I said to myself, "You deserve everything that happens to you. All this is decreed for me by Allah (whose name be exalted!) to turn me away from my greed for gain, which is the source of everything I endure — for I have wealth and to spare."

Then I came to my senses and said, "Truly, this time I repent to the Most High, with a sincere repentance, of my hunger for profit and adventure; and never again will I so much as name travel with my tongue or in my thoughts." And I went on humbling myself before Almighty Allah and weeping and lamenting over myself, remembering my former condition of comfort and satisfaction and mirth and merriment and joy.

So I remained two days, at the end of which I came to a great island with plenty of trees and streams on it. There I landed and ate of the fruit of the island and drank of its waters, until I was refreshed and my life came back to me and my strength and spirits were restored; and I recited:

	When your affairs show a knotted and tangled skein,
	Fate comes down out of Heaven and straightens every ply.
	Hold your soul in patience till your lot comes clear:
	He who ties the knot can also untie.

Then I walked about until I found, on the far side, a great river of sweet water running with a strong current; and this brought to my mind the boat-raft I had made before, and I said to myself, "I must make another; perhaps I can get myself out of this strait. If I escape, I have what I want, and I vow to Almighty Allah to swear off travelling; and if I die, I shall be at peace and shall rest from all my toil and trouble."

So I got up and gathered a great quantity of pieces of wood from the trees, which were all of the finest sandalwood, the like of which is not to be found — though at the time I did not know it; and I managed to twist creepers and tree twigs into a kind of rope, with which I bound the logs together and so contrived a raft.

Then, saying, "If I am saved, it is by God's grace," I got aboard it and committed myself to the current; and it carried me on for the first day and the second and the third after I left the island, while I lay on the raft, eating nothing and drinking, when I was thirsty, the water of the river, until I was as weak and giddy as a chicken with the stress of exhaustion and starvation and fear.

At the end of this time I came to a high mountain with the river running underneath it; and when I saw it I feared for my life, remembering how narrow a passage I had suffered through on my last journey; and I would gladly have stopped the raft and got ashore on the mountainside. But the current was too strong for me and drew the raft into the underground passage like an archway; at which I gave myself up for lost and said, "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great!"

However, after a little the raft slid out into the open air, and I saw before me a wide valley into which the river fell with a noise like rolling thunder and a swiftness like the rushing of the wind. I held on to the raft for fear of falling off it, while the waves tossed me right and left; and the craft went on down with the current, and I could neither stop it nor turn it towards the bank, until it came to a halt with me at a great and handsome city, splendidly built and full of people.

And when the townspeople saw me on the raft, coming down with the current, they threw me ropes, which I had not the strength to hold; then they tossed a net over the craft and drew it ashore with me on it, whereupon I fell on the ground in the middle of them like a dead man, from sheer fear and hunger and lack of sleep.

After a while there came up to me out of the crowd an old man of dignified appearance, well on in years, who welcomed me and threw over me a quantity of handsome clothes, with which I covered myself. Then he took me to the baths and brought me refreshing sherbets and delicious perfumes; and when I came out, he carried me to his house, where his people made much of me and, seating me in a pleasant place, set rich food in front of me, of which I ate my fill and gave thanks to God the Most High for my deliverance.

Then his pages fetched me hot water and I washed my hands, and his handmaids brought me silk napkins with which I dried them and wiped my mouth. The old gentleman also set aside a room for me in a part of his house, and instructed his pages and his slave girls to wait on me and do whatever I wanted and supply whatever I needed. They were diligent in my service, and I stayed with him in the guest chamber three days, taking my ease with good food and good drink and good scents, until life came back to me and my terrors quieted down and my heart grew calm and my mind was at rest.

On the fourth day my host came in to me and said, "You cheer us with your company, my son, and praise be to Allah for your safety! Tell me: will you come down with me now to the shore and the bazaar and sell your goods and take the price of them? You might buy something to trade with. I have told my servants to bring your stock in trade up out of the sea, and they have piled it on the beach."

I was silent for a while, and said to myself, "What does he mean by this, and what goods do I have?"

Then he said, "My son, do not be troubled or anxious, but come with me to the market; and if anyone offers a price for your goods that satisfies you, take it; and if you are not satisfied, I will store them for you in my warehouse until a better occasion for selling comes round."

So I thought over my situation and said to myself, "Do as he says, and see what these goods are." And I said to him, "Uncle, I hear and I obey; I cannot go against you in anything, for Allah's blessing is upon everything you do."

So he led me to the market street, where I found that he had taken to pieces the raft that had carried me, which was made of sandalwood, and I heard the broker calling it up for sale.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-fifth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman took up his tale in these words:

I found that the old gentleman had taken my raft to pieces where it lay on the beach, and that the broker was crying the sandalwood for sale. Then the merchants came and opened the bidding for the wood, and bid against one another until the price reached a thousand dinars, when they stopped bidding.

And my host said to me, "Listen, my son: this is the going rate for your goods in hard times like these. Will you sell them for this, or shall I store them for you in my warehouses until prices go up?"

"My lord," I answered, "the business is in your hands: do as you think best."

Then he asked, "Will you sell the wood to me, my son, for a hundred gold pieces over and above what the merchants have bid for it?"

And I answered, "Yes, I have sold it to you, and the money is received."

So he ordered his servants to carry the wood off to his warehouses and, taking me back to his house, sat me down and counted out the purchase money to me; after which he put it away in bags and, setting them in a private place, locked them up with an iron padlock and gave me the key.

Some days after this the old gentleman said to me, "My son, I have something to put to you, and I hope you will do as I ask."

I said, "What is it?"

He said, "I am a very old man and I have no son; but I have a daughter who is young in years and lovely to look at, and endowed with great wealth and beauty. Now I have a mind to marry her to you, so that you may live with her here in this country of ours; and I will make you master of everything I have in hand, for I am an old man and you shall stand in my place."

I was silent for shame and gave him no answer, so he went on: "Do as I wish in this, my son, for I want nothing but your good; and if you will only do as I say, you shall have her at once and be as a son to me, and everything that is in my hands or that comes to me shall be yours. And if you have a mind to trade and travel to your own country, nobody shall stop you, and your property will be entirely at your own disposal; so do as you please."

"By Allah, uncle," I answered, "you have become like a father to me; and I am a stranger here and have gone through a great many hardships, and with the stress of everything I have suffered I have no judgment or understanding left. It is for you, then, to decide what I should do."

At this he sent his servants for the judge and the witnesses, and married me to his daughter, making us a noble wedding feast and a great celebration. When I went in to her I found her perfect in beauty and loveliness and grace and proportion, dressed in rich clothes and covered with a profusion of ornaments and necklaces and other trinkets of gold and silver and precious stones, worth a mint of money, a price nobody could pay. She pleased me and we loved each other; and I lived with her in comfort and delight of life, until her father was taken to the mercy of Almighty Allah.

So we washed him and shrouded him and buried him, and I took possession of the whole of his property, and all his servants and slaves became mine. Moreover, the merchants installed me in his office, for he had been their headman and their chief, and none of them bought anything except with his knowledge and by his leave; and now his rank passed to me.

When I came to know the townspeople better, I found that at the beginning of each month they were transformed: their faces changed and they became like birds, and they put out wings on which they flew up into the upper regions of the sky, and nobody was left in the city but the women and the children.

And I said in my mind, "When the first of the month comes, I will ask one of them to carry me with them, wherever it is they go."

So when the time came and their colour changed and their shapes altered, I went to one of the townspeople and said to him, "Allah be upon you! Carry me with you, so that I may enjoy myself with the rest and come back with you."

"That cannot be done," he answered; but I would not stop pressing him, and I kept at him until he agreed.

Then I went out in his company, without telling any of my family or my servants or my friends; and he took me on his back and flew up with me so high in the air that I heard the angels glorifying God in the dome of heaven, at which I marvelled and cried out, "Praised be Allah! Extolled be the perfection of Allah!"

I had hardly finished pronouncing the tasbih — praised be Allah! — when there came a fire out of heaven that all but consumed the whole company; whereupon they fled from it and came down cursing me, and, throwing me down on a high mountain, went away in great anger and left me there alone.

Finding myself in this plight, I repented of what I had done and reproached myself for having taken on something I was not equal to, saying, "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great! No sooner am I delivered out of one affliction than I fall into a worse one."

And I stayed there in this state, not knowing where I ought to go, when two young men came up, as beautiful as two moons, each of them using a rod of red gold for a staff. So I went over to them and greeted them; and when they had returned my greeting I said, "Allah be upon you both! Who are you, and what are you?"

They said, "We are servants of Allah the Most High, living on this mountain"; and, giving me a rod of red gold that they had with them, they went on their way and left me.

I walked along the mountain ridge, steadying my steps with the staff and thinking about the two young men, when a serpent came out from under the mountain with a man in her jaws, whom she had swallowed as far as below his navel, and he was calling out and saying, "Whoever delivers me, Allah will deliver him from every adversity!"

So I went up to the serpent and struck her on the head with the golden staff, at which she threw the man out of her mouth.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-sixth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Sindbad the Seaman went on in these words:

When I struck the serpent on the head with my golden staff she threw the man out of her mouth. Then I struck her a second time and she turned and fled; whereupon he came up to me and said, "Since it was at your hands that I was delivered from that serpent, I will never leave you, and you shall have me for your comrade on this mountain."

"And welcome," I answered. So we went on together along the mountain until we fell in with a company of people; and I looked and saw among them the very man who had carried me and thrown me down there. I went up to him and spoke him fair, apologising to him and saying, "Comrade, this is not how a friend should treat a friend."

He said, "It was you who nearly destroyed us all with your tasbih and your glorifying God on my back."

I said, "Forgive me, for I knew nothing about this business; but if you will take me with you, I swear not to say a word."

So he relented and agreed to carry me with him, but he made it an express condition that as long as I was on his back I should say no tasbih and do no glorifying of God at all.

Then I gave the golden wand to the man I had delivered from the serpent and said goodbye to him, and my friend took me on his back and flew with me as before, until he brought me to the city and set me down in my own house.

My wife came to meet me and greeted me and congratulated me on my safety, and then said, "Take care not to go out with those people again, and do not keep company with them, for they are brothers of the devils, and they do not know how to speak the name of Almighty Allah, nor do they worship Him."

"And how did your father get on with them?" I asked.

And she answered, "My father was not one of them and did not do as they do. And now that he is dead, I think you would do better to sell everything we have and buy merchandise with the price of it and travel to your own country and your own people, and I will go with you; for I have no wish to stay on in this city, now that my father and my mother are both dead."

So I sold off the old gentleman's property piece by piece, and looked out for somebody who might be travelling from there to Basra, so that I could join him. And while I was doing this I heard of a company of the townspeople who had a mind to make the voyage but could not find a ship; so they bought timber and built themselves a great ship, in which I took passage with them and paid the whole of the hire.

Then we embarked, my wife and I, with all our movable goods, leaving our houses and our lands and the rest of it, and set sail; and we went on sailing from island to island and from sea to sea, with a fair and favouring wind, until we arrived at Basra safe and sound.

I made no stay there, but chartered another vessel and, transferring my goods to her, set out at once for Baghdad, where I arrived safely; and going into my own quarter and to my own house, I met up with my family and my friends and my familiars, who stored my goods away in my warehouses.

Now my people, reckoning up how long I had been away on this seventh voyage, had made it twenty-seven years, and had given up all hope of me; so when they heard of my return they came to welcome me and congratulate me on my safety, and I told them everything that had happened to me, at which they marvelled exceedingly.

Then I swore off travel and vowed to Allah the Most High that I would venture no more by land or by sea, for this seventh and last voyage had given me a surfeit of travel and adventure; and I thanked the Lord (be He praised and glorified!) and blessed Him for having restored me to my kith and kin and my country and my home.

"Consider, then, Sindbad the Landsman," Sindbad the Seaman went on, "what sufferings I have gone through and what dangers and hardships I endured before I came to my present state."

"Allah be upon you, my lord!" answered Sindbad the Landsman. "Forgive me the wrong I did you."

And they never left off friendship and fellowship, living in all cheerfulness and pleasure and comfort of life, until there came to them the Destroyer of Delights and the Sunderer of Companies, the Leveller of palaces and the Filler of graveyards — that is to say, the Cup of Death. And glory be to the Living One who does not die!

The Seventh Voyage of Sindbad the Seaman: The Calcutta Version

[Editor's note: The seventh voyage is the one place where the manuscripts part company outright. What follows is not a variant reading of the tale just told but a different story altogether, told in the Calcutta edition of the Nights in place of the flying men and the sandalwood raft. Burton printed both. So does this edition.]

Know, my brothers and friends and companions all, that when I gave up voyaging and trading I said to myself, "What has happened to me is enough"; and I spent my time in comfort and pleasure.

Then one day, as I sat at home, there came a knock at the door, and when the doorkeeper opened it a page came in and said, "The Caliph summons you."

I went with him to His Majesty and kissed the ground and greeted him; and he welcomed me and treated me with honour and said, "Sindbad, I have a piece of business for you: will you do it?"

So I kissed his hand and asked, "My lord, what business has the master for the slave?"

And he answered, "It is my wish that you should travel to the King of Sarandib and carry him our letter and our gift, since he has sent a present and a letter to us."

I trembled at these words and replied, "By Allah the Omnipotent, my lord, I have come to loathe travelling; when I so much as hear the words 'voyage' or 'journey' my limbs shake with the memory of the hardships and horrors I have been through. I have no desire for this whatever — the more so as I have bound myself by an oath never to leave Baghdad."

Then I told the Caliph everything I had gone through from first to last, and he marvelled exceedingly and said, "By the Almighty, Sindbad, in all the ages of the world such misfortunes as happened to you were never known to happen to any man, and you do quite right never even to speak of travel. But for our sake you will go this one time and carry our present and our letter to the King of Sarandib; and, God willing, you shall be back quickly, and in this way we shall be under no obligation to him."

I answered that I heard and obeyed, since I could not oppose his command; so he gave me the gifts and the letter, with money for my expenses, and I kissed his hands and left his presence.

Then I went down from Baghdad to the Gulf and embarked with some other merchants, and our ship sailed before a fair wind many days and nights until, by Allah's help, we reached the island of Sarandib. As soon as we had made fast we landed, and I took the present and the letter and went in with them to the King and kissed the ground before him.

When he saw me he said, "Welcome, Sindbad! By Allah the Omnipotent, we have been longing to see you; and glory be to God, who has shown us your face again!"

Then he took me by the hand and made me sit beside him, delighted, and welcomed me with familiar kindness and treated me as a friend. After this he began to talk with me and addressed me courteously and asked, "What was the reason for your coming to us, Sindbad?"

So, after kissing his hand and thanking him, I answered, "My lord, I have brought you a present from my master, the Caliph Harun al-Rashid"; and I offered him the present and the letter, which he read and was overjoyed at.

The present was: a mare worth ten thousand dinars, with a golden saddle set with jewels; a book; a sumptuous suit of clothes; a hundred different kinds of white Cairo cloths and silks of Suez, Kufa and Alexandria; Greek carpets; and a hundred maunds weight of linen and raw silk. Moreover there was a wonderful rarity — a marvellous cup of crystal, in the middle of which was the figure of a lion facing a kneeling man who grasped a bow with the arrow drawn back to the head — together with the food tray of Solomon son of David (on whom be peace!).

The letter ran as follows:

	Peace from King al-Rashid, whom Allah has aided (and has granted to him and to his forefathers noble rank and wide-spread glory), be upon the fortunate Sultan. And after: your letter came to our hands and we rejoiced at it; and we have sent you the book entitled Delight of the Intelligent and, for Friends, the Rare Present, together with various curiosities suitable for Kings; so be so good as to accept them. And peace be with you.

Then the King heaped wealth on me and treated me with every honour; so I prayed for him and thanked him for his generosity.

Some days later I asked his leave to depart, but could not get it except by a great deal of pressing; whereupon I said goodbye to him and set out from his city with merchants and other companions, bound for home with no desire at all for travel or for trade.

We went on voyaging and coasting along a good many islands; but when we were half-way we were surrounded by a number of canoes full of men like devils, armed with bows and arrows, swords and daggers, and dressed in mail coats and other armour. They fell on us and wounded and killed everybody who resisted them; and then, having captured the ship and everything in her, they carried us off to an island, where they sold us for the meanest price.

Now I was bought by a wealthy man, who took me to his house and gave me food and drink and clothing and treated me in the friendliest way; so I took heart, and rested a little.

One day he asked me, "Do you know any art or trade?"

And I answered, "My lord, I am a merchant, and I know nothing but buying and selling."

"Do you know," he asked, "how to use a bow and arrow?"

"Yes," I said, "I know that much."

At this he brought me a bow and arrows and mounted me behind him on an elephant; then he set out when the night was nearly over and, passing through a forest of huge trees, came to a tall and sturdy one, up which he made me climb. Then he gave me the bow and the arrows, saying, "Sit here now; and when the elephants come trooping past in the early morning, shoot at them. You may well hit one; and if he falls, come and tell me." And with that he left me.

I hid myself in the tree, in great terror, and trembled there until the sun rose; and when the elephants appeared and wandered about among the trees I shot my arrows at them, and kept on until I had shot one of them down. In the evening I reported my success to my master, who was delighted with me and treated me with great honour; and next morning he took the dead elephant away.

I went on like this, shooting an elephant every morning which my master would carry off, until one day, as I sat hidden up in the tree, there came on suddenly and without warning a countless host of elephants, whose screaming and trumpeting were such that I thought the earth was shaking under them. They all surrounded my tree, which was some fifty cubits round, and one enormous monster came up to it and wound his trunk about the trunk of it and hauled it up by the roots and dashed it to the ground.

I fell down in a faint among the beasts, and then the monster elephant wound his trunk about me and, setting me on his back, went off with me, the others going along with us. He carried me, still unconscious, until he reached the place he was making for, when he rolled me off his back and presently went his way, and the others followed him.

So I rested a little; and when my terror had died down I looked about me, and found myself among the bones of elephants — from which I concluded that this was their burial place, and that the monster elephant had brought me here on account of the tusks.

So I got up and walked a whole day and night until I came to my master's house. He saw how my colour was changed with fright and hunger, and he rejoiced at my return and said, "By Allah, you have made my heart sore! I went to look when you were missing and found the tree torn up, and I thought the elephants had killed you. Tell me how it went with you."

I told him everything that had happened to me, at which he wondered greatly and was very glad; and at last he asked, "Do you know the place?"

"Yes, master," I answered.

So we mounted an elephant and went until we came to the spot; and when my master saw the heaps of tusks he rejoiced greatly, and, carrying away as many as he wanted, went home with me.

After this he treated me with even greater favour and said, "My son, you have shown us the way to great riches, and may Allah reward you for it! You are free, for the Almighty's sake and before His face! The elephants used to destroy a great many of us, because we hunted them for their ivory; but Allah has preserved you from them, and you have made our fortunes with the heaps you have led us to."

"Master," I answered, "may God free your neck from the fire! And do you, master, graciously give me leave to go back to my own country."

"Yes," he said, "you shall have that permission. But we hold a fair once a year, when merchants come to us from all quarters to buy up this ivory. The time is drawing near; and when they have finished their business I will send you in their charge and give you what you need to reach your home."

So I blessed him and thanked him and stayed with him, treated with respect and honour, for some days; and then the merchants came as he had said, and bought and sold and bartered. And when they had made ready to go back, my master came to me and said, "Get up and prepare yourself to travel with the traders on their way to your country."

They had bought a great many tusks, which they had tied up together in loads and were putting aboard, when my master sent me off with them, paying for my passage and settling all my debts; and besides that he made me a large present in goods.

We set out and voyaged from island to island until we had crossed the sea and landed on the shores of the Persian Gulf, where the merchants brought out their stores and sold them. I sold what I had at a high profit too, and bought some of the prettiest things in the place for presents, and beautiful curiosities, and everything else I wanted. I also bought myself a mount; and we set off and crossed the deserts from country to country until I reached Baghdad.

Here I went in to the Caliph and, after greeting him and kissing his hands, told him everything that had happened to me; whereupon he rejoiced at my safety and thanked Almighty Allah, and ordered my story to be written down in letters of gold.

Then I went into my house and met my family and my brothers; and that is the end of the history of what happened to me in the course of my seven voyages. Praise be to Allah, the One, the Creator, the Maker of all things in Heaven and Earth!

Now when Shahrazad had finished her story of the two Sindbads, Dunyazad exclaimed, "Sister, how pleasant your tale is, and how tasteful! How sweet and how welcome!"

She answered, "And what is this compared with what I could tell you tomorrow night?"

The King said, "What might that be?"

And she said: It is a tale touching

The City of Brass

It is told that long ago, in years and ages long gone by, there was at Damascus in Syria a Caliph called Abd al-Malik bin Marwan, the fifth of the house of Umayya.

As this Commander of the Faithful sat one day in his palace, talking with his sultans and kings and the great men of his empire, the conversation turned upon the legends of past peoples and the traditions of our lord Solomon, son of David (on the two of them be peace!), and upon what Almighty Allah had given him of lordship and dominion over men and jinn and birds and beasts and reptiles and the wind and all other created things.

And the Caliph said, "Truly we hear from those who went before us that the Lord (extolled and exalted be He!) granted to nobody the like of what He granted to our lord Solomon, and that he attained to what no other man ever attained — in that he used to imprison jinn and marids and satans in jars of copper, and stop them with lead, and seal them with his ring."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-seventh Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Caliph Abd al-Malik bin Marwan sat talking with the great men of his court about our lord Solomon, and they remarked upon what Allah had given him of lordship and dominion, the Commander of the Faithful said, "Indeed he attained to what no other man ever attained, in that he used to imprison jinn and marids and satans in jars of copper, and stop them with lead, and seal them with his ring."

Then Talib bin Sahl spoke up — a man who hunted for treasure, and had books that revealed to him hoards and wealth hidden under the earth — and said:

"Commander of the Faithful — may Allah make your dominion endure and exalt your dignity in this world and the next! — my father told me, on the authority of my grandfather, that he once took ship with a company bound for the island of Sicily, and sailed until a contrary wind rose against them and drove them off their course and brought them, after a month, to a great mountain in one of the lands of Allah the Most High; though what land it was they did not know.

"My grandfather said: This was in the darkness of the night; and as soon as it was day there came out to us from the caves of the mountain a people black-skinned and naked, who understood not one word that was said to them; nor was there one of them who knew Arabic except their King, who was of their own kind.

"When he saw the ship he came down to it with a company of his followers and greeted us and made us welcome, and asked us about our condition and our faith. We told him everything about ourselves, and he said, Be of good cheer, for no harm shall come to you. And when we in our turn asked them about their faith, we found that each of them held one of the many creeds that were current before the preaching of Islam and the mission of Mohammed, whom may Allah bless and keep. So my shipmates said, We do not know what you are talking about.

"Then the King said, No son of Adam has ever come to our land before you; but do not be afraid, and be assured of your safety and of your return to your own country. Then he entertained us three days, feeding us on the flesh of birds and wild beasts and fishes, for they had no other meat; and on the fourth day he took us down to the beach so that we might amuse ourselves watching the fishermen.

"There we saw a man casting his net for fish; and presently he pulled it up, and in it was a jar of copper, stopped with lead and sealed with the seal ring of Solomon son of David, on whom be peace! He brought the vessel ashore and broke it open, and there came out of it a smoke which rose twisting and blue to the top of the sky, and we heard a horrible voice saying, I repent! I repent! Pardon, Prophet of Allah! Never again will I go back to what I did before.

"Then the smoke became a terrible giant, frightful in shape, whose head was level with the mountaintops; and he vanished from our sight, while our hearts were nearly torn out of us for terror. But the black people thought nothing of it.

"So we went back to the King and asked him about the matter; and he said, Know that this was one of the jinn whom Solomon son of David, being angry with them, shut up in these vessels and threw into the sea, after stopping their mouths with molten lead. Our fishermen often bring up such bottles in their nets; and when they are broken open, out come jinn who, supposing that Solomon is still alive and can pardon them, make their submission to him and say, I repent, Prophet of Allah!"

The Caliph marvelled at Talib's story and said, "Glory be to God! Truly, a mighty dominion was given to Solomon."

Now al-Nabighah al-Zubyani was present, and he said, "Talib has spoken the truth, as the words of the All-wise, the Everlasting One, prove:

	And Solomon, when Allah said to him,
	Rise, be my Caliph, rule with righteous sway;
	Honour the man who honours and obeys you,
	And whoever rebels, imprison him for aye —

so he used to put them in copper bottles and throw them into the sea."

The poet's words pleased the Caliph, and he said, "By Allah, I long to look on some of these vessels of Solomon's, which must be a warning to anyone willing to be warned."

"Commander of the Faithful," replied Talib, "it is in your power to do so without stirring from home. Send to your brother Abd al-Aziz bin Marwan, so that he may write to Musa bin Nusayr, governor of the Maghrib, telling him to ride from there to the mountains I have spoken of and fetch you as many of these jars as you have a mind for; for those mountains adjoin the frontiers of his province."

The Caliph approved his advice and said, "You have spoken the truth, Talib; and I wish you to be my messenger to Musa bin Nusayr in this matter. You shall have the White Flag, and whatever you like of money and honours and the rest; and I will look after your family while you are away."

"With love and gladness, Commander of the Faithful!" answered Talib.

"Go, with the blessing of Allah and His help," said the Caliph; and he ordered a letter written to his brother Abd al-Aziz, his viceroy in Egypt, and another to Musa bin Nusayr, his viceroy in North-West Africa, telling him to go himself in search of the bottles of Solomon, leaving his son to govern in his place. Moreover he charged him to engage guides, and to spare neither men nor money, and not to be slack in the business, since he would accept no excuse.

Then he sealed the two letters and handed them to Talib bin Sahl, telling him to have the royal ensigns carried before him and to make all possible speed; and he gave him treasure and horsemen and footmen to help him on his way, and provided for the needs of his household while he was gone.

So Talib set out, and arrived in due course at Cairo.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-eighth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Talib bin Sahl set out with his escort and crossed the desert country between Syria and Egypt, where the Governor came out to meet him and treated him and his company with high honour while they stayed with him. Then he gave them a guide to bring them up to the Sa'id, which is Upper Egypt, where the Emir Musa had his residence.

And when the son of Nusayr heard that Talib was coming, he went out to meet him and was delighted with him. Talib gave him the Caliph's letter, and he took it reverently and laid it on his head and cried, "I hear and I obey the Commander of the Faithful!"

Then he thought it best to call his chief officers together; and when they were all present he told them what was in the Caliph's letter and asked their advice about how he should act.

"Emir," they answered, "if you are looking for somebody to guide you to the place, send for the Shaykh Abd al-Samad, son of Abd al-Kuddus, al-Samudi; for he is a man of wide learning, who has travelled far and knows from experience all the seas and deserts and lands and countries of the world, and the peoples and the wonders in them. Send for him, and he will surely guide you to what you want."

So Musa sent for him; and he proved to be a very ancient man, far gone in years and broken down with the passage of time. The Emir greeted him and said, "Shaykh Abd al-Samad, our lord the Commander of the Faithful, Abd al-Malik bin Marwan, has given me such and such an order. I have little knowledge of the country where the thing he wants is to be found; but I am told that you know it well, and the roads to it. Will you come with me, then, and help me to accomplish the Caliph's need? If it please Allah the Most High, your trouble and your travelling shall not go for nothing."

The Shaykh replied, "I hear and obey the command of the Commander of the Faithful. But know, Emir, that the road there is long and difficult, and there are few ways to it."

"How far is it?" asked Musa.

And the Shaykh answered, "It is a journey of two years and some months going, and as long coming back; and the way is full of hardships and terrors and things wonderful and strange. Now you are a champion of the Faith, and our country lies close to the enemy's; and it may be that the Christians will come out against us while you are gone. So you ought to leave somebody to govern in your place."

"That is well said," answered the Emir; and he appointed his son Harun governor for the time of his absence, requiring the troops to swear allegiance to him and ordering them to obey him in everything he commanded. And they heard his words and promised obedience. Now this Harun was a man of great prowess, a renowned warrior and a formidable knight.

And the Shaykh Abd al-Samad let Harun believe that the place they were making for was only four months' journey away along the seashore, with camping places all the way, one adjoining the next, and grass and springs; adding, "Allah will certainly make the matter easy for us, through your blessing, deputy of the Commander of the Faithful!"

The Emir Musa said, "Do you know whether any of the kings have trodden this land before us?"

And the Shaykh said, "Yes; it belonged in the old days to Darius the Greek, King of Alexandria." But he said to Musa privately, "Emir, take with you a thousand camels loaded with food, and a great store of porous earthenware water jars."

The Emir asked, "And what are we to do with those?"

And the Shaykh answered, "On our way lies the desert of Kayrawan, which is a vast waste four days' journey across and has no water in it; nor does the sound of a voice ever sound there, nor is a living soul ever to be seen. Moreover the simoom blows there, and the other hot winds they call al-Juwayb, which dry up the waterskins; but if the water is in earthenware, no harm can come to it."

"Right," said Musa; and he sent to Alexandria and had a great quantity of the jars brought from there.

Then he took with him his vizier and two thousand cavalry, in mail from head to foot, and set out, with no other guide but Abd al-Samad, who went before them riding on his hackney.

The party pressed on, now passing through inhabited lands, now through ruins, now crossing frightful wastes and thirsty deserts, and now mountains that towered up into the air; and they did not leave off travelling for a whole year, until one morning, at daybreak, after they had journeyed all night, the Shaykh found himself in a country he did not know, and said, "There is no Majesty and there is no Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great!"

The Emir said, "What is the matter, Shaykh?"

And he answered, "By the Lord of the Kaaba, we have wandered off our road!"

"How did that happen?" asked Musa.

And Abd al-Samad replied, "The stars were covered with cloud, and I could not steer by them."

"Where on God's earth are we now?" asked the Emir.

And the Shaykh answered, "I do not know; for I never set eyes on this land until this moment."

Musa said, "Guide us back to the place where we went astray."

But the other said, "I know it no longer."

Then Musa said, "Let us push on; perhaps Allah will guide us to it, or set us right by His power."

So they went on until the hour of the noon prayer, when they came out on a fine open plain, wide and level and smooth as the sea in a calm; and presently there appeared to them on the horizon something great and high and black, in the middle of which was what looked like smoke rising to the edge of the sky.

They made for this, and did not stop until they came near it — and behold, it was a lofty castle, firm-founded and huge and grim, like a towering mountain, built all of black stone, with frowning battlements and a door of gleaming Chinese steel that dazzled the eyes and dazed the wits. Round about it were a thousand steps; and the thing that had looked like smoke from far off was a central dome of lead, a hundred cubits high.

When the Emir saw this he marvelled greatly, and marvelled that the place should be empty of inhabitants; and the Shaykh, when he had satisfied himself about it, said, "There is no god but God, and Mohammed is the Apostle of God!"

Musa said, "I hear you praising the Lord and calling Him holy, and it seems to me you are glad."

"Emir," answered Abd al-Samad, "be glad; for Allah (extolled and exalted be He!) has delivered us out of the frightful wastes and the thirsty deserts."

"How do you know that?" said Musa.

And the other said, "I know it because my father told me, on the authority of my grandfather, that he said: We were once travelling in this country and strayed from the road, and came to this palace, and from it to the City of Brass; and between that city and the place you are seeking is two full months' travel. But you must take to the seashore and not leave it, for there are watering places and wells and camping grounds along it, established by King Alexander the Two-Horned, who, when he went to the conquest of Mauretania, found thirsty deserts and wastes and wilds on the way, and dug water pits in them and built cisterns."

Musa said, "May Allah gladden you for your good news!"

And the Shaykh said, "Come, let us go and look at that palace and its marvels, for it is a lesson to anybody willing to be taught."

So the Emir went up to the palace with the Shaykh and his officers; and coming to the gate, they found it open. Now this gate was built with lofty columns and porticoes whose walls and ceilings were inlaid with gold and silver and precious stones; and there were flights of steps leading up to it, among them two wide staircases of coloured marble the like of which was never seen; and over the doorway was a tablet with letters of gold graven on it in the old Ionian character.

"Emir," asked the Shaykh, "shall I read?"

And Musa answered, "Read, and God bless you; for everything that happens to us on this journey depends upon your blessing."

So the Shaykh, who was a very learned man and versed in all tongues and scripts, went up to the tablet and read what was written on it, and it was verse like this:

	The signs that here portray their mighty works
	warn us that all must tread the selfsame way.
	You who stand in this place to hear the news
	of a people whose power has passed for ever away:
	enter this palace gate, and ask what became
	of greatness fallen into dust and clay.
	Death has destroyed them and scattered their might,
	and in the dust they lost their rich display —
	as if they had only set their burdens down
	to rest a while, and then had ridden away.

When the Emir Musa heard these lines he wept until he lost his senses, and said, "There is no god but God, the Living, the Eternal, who does not cease!"

Then he entered the palace and was astounded at its beauty and the excellence of its building. He amused himself a while looking at the pictures and figures in it, until he came to another door, over which verses were written too; and he said to the Shaykh, "Come, read me these."

So he went forward and read as follows:

	Under these domes how many a company
	halted of old, and went on without stay.
	See what a power Time shows over other men,
	Time with his changes, that could such lords waylay.
	They shared out among them everything they had gathered,
	then left their joys behind and went the way of decay.
	What joys they had! What food they ate! And now
	in the dust they are eaten, and the worm has his prey.

At this the Emir Musa wept bitterly, and the world turned yellow before his eyes, and he said, "Truly, we were created for a mighty matter!"

Then they went on exploring the palace and found it deserted and empty of any living thing, its courtyards desolate and its dwellings laid waste. In the middle of it stood a lofty pavilion with a dome rising high into the air, and around it were four hundred tombs built of yellow marble.

The Emir went up to these, and among them was a great tomb, wide and long, with a tablet of white marble standing at the head of it, on which these lines were graven:

	How often have I fought, and how many have I killed!
	How much have I seen of blessing and of bane!
	How much have I eaten, and how much have I drunk!
	How often have I listened to a singing girl's strain!
	How much have I commanded, how much have I forbidden!
	How many a castle, and how many a castellain
	have I besieged and searched, and the cloistered maids
	deep in its walls were taken as my captives then!
	But it was in ignorance that I sinned, to win rewards
	that, once won, proved nothing and brought me no gain.
	So reckon your reckoning, man, and be wise,
	before you drain the cup of death and doom;
	for it is only a little while before they strew
	the dust on your head, and your life goes down to the tomb.

The Emir and his companions wept; then, going up to the pavilion, they saw that it had eight doors of sandalwood, studded with nails of gold and stars of silver and inlaid with every kind of precious stone. On the first door these verses were written:

	What I left, I did not leave out of nobility of soul,
	but by the sentence and decree appointed to every man.
	While I lived happy, with a haughty and lofty temper,
	defending my hoard like a lion in the fight,
	I took no rest, and greed forbade me to give away
	one grain of mustard seed to save my soul from the fire —
	until I was struck one day, as by an arrow, by the decree
	of the Maker, the Fashioner, the Lord of Might and Right.
	When my death was appointed, I could not keep my life
	by all my stratagems, my cunning and my sleight;
	the troops I had gathered availed me nothing, and none
	of my friends and my neighbours had power to mend my plight.
	All my life long I was weaned by journeying towards death,
	in hardship or in comfort, in joy or in despite.
	So when the money bags are bloated, and you add
	dinar to dinar, all of it may leave you in a night;
	and the driver of a camel and the digger of a grave
	are what your heirs shall fetch before the morning is bright.
	And on the Day of Judgment you shall stand alone before your Lord,
	overloaded with your sins and your crimes and your fright.
	Do not let the world seduce you with its luring, but look
	at the measure it has dealt out to your family and your neighbours.

When Musa heard these verses he wept so hard that he fainted away; then, coming to himself, he went into the pavilion and saw in it a long tomb, awesome to look at, on which was a tablet of Chinese steel; and the Shaykh Abd al-Samad drew near it and read this inscription:

	In the name of the Everlasting Allah, the Never-beginning, the Never-ending; in the name of Allah, who does not beget and is not begotten, and to whom there is no like; in the name of Allah, the Lord of Majesty and Might; in the name of the Living One who is never appointed to death!

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-ninth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Shaykh Abd al-Samad, having read what is set down above, found this written also:

	You who come to this place, take warning from what you see of the accidents of Time and the turns of Fortune, and do not be deceived by the world and its pomps and vanities and fallacies and falsehoods and empty lures; for it is flattering and deceitful and treacherous, and the things in it are only a loan to us, which it will borrow back from every borrower.
	It is like the dreams of a dreamer and the visions of a sleeper, or like the mirage in the desert, which the thirsty man takes for water; and Satan makes it seem fair to men, right up to their death. These are the ways of the world; so do not put your trust in it, nor lean towards it, for it betrays the man who leans on it and commits his affairs to it. Do not fall into its snares, nor take hold of its skirts, but take warning from my example.
	I owned four thousand bay horses and a proud palace, and I had a thousand daughters of kings to wife, high-bosomed girls like so many moons. I was blessed with a thousand sons like fierce lions, and I lived a thousand years, glad in heart and mind, and I amassed treasures beyond the means of all the kings of all the regions of the earth, supposing that my delight would go on for ever.
	But there fell on me unawares the Destroyer of Delights and the Sunderer of Companies, the Desolator of dwellings and the Spoiler of inhabited places, the Murderer of great and small, of babies and children and mothers; who has no pity on the poor man for his poverty, and no fear of the King for all his commanding and forbidding.
	Truly, we lived safe and secure in this palace until there came down on us the judgment of the Lord of the Three Worlds, the Lord of the Heavens and the Lord of the Earths, and the vengeance of the Manifest Truth overtook us; when two of us died every day, until a great company of us had perished.
	When I saw that destruction had come into our houses and settled down with us, and had drowned us in the sea of deaths, I called for a writer and told him to compose these verses and lessons and warnings, which I had graven, with rule and compass, on these doors and tablets and tombs.
	Now I had an army of a thousand thousand bridles, men of warlike bearing with strong keen forearms, armed with spears and shining mail coats and swords that gleamed; so I ordered them to put on their long hauberks and gird on their biting blades and mount their high-mettled horses and level their dreadful lances. And when the doom of the Lord of heaven and earth fell on us, I said to them: Ho, all you soldiers and troopers, can you turn aside what has fallen on me from the Omnipotent King?
	But the soldiers and the troopers could do nothing, and they said: How shall we do battle with Him whom no chamberlain bars access to — the Lord of the door that has no doorkeeper?
	Then I said to them: Bring me my treasures. Now I had in my treasuries a thousand cisterns, and in each of them a thousand hundredweight of red gold and as much white silver, besides pearls and jewels of every kind and other precious things beyond the reach of the kings of the earth. So they did as I said; and when they had laid all the treasure before me, I said to them: Can you ransom me with all this treasure? Can you buy me one single day of life with it?
	But they could not. So they resigned themselves to Fate and Fortune as they had been ordained, and I submitted to the judgment of Allah, bearing patiently the affliction He decreed for me, until He took my soul and made me dwell in my grave.
	And if you ask my name: I am Kush, son of Shaddad, son of Ad the Greater.

And on the tablets these lines were engraved:

	If you would know my name, whose day is done
	with the shifts of time and the chances under the sun:
	know that I am the son of Shaddad, who ruled mankind
	and held dominion over all the earth as one.
	Every stubborn people was made abject to me,
	from Syria to Cairo and the lands of Adnan;
	I reigned in glory and conquered many kings,
	and every people went in fear of my mischief.
	Yes, I saw tribes and armies in my hand,
	and the whole world dreaded me, both friend and foe.
	When I took horse, I looked upon my numbered troops:
	a million bridles on neighing steeds in a row.
	And I had wealth that nobody could tell or count,
	all of it hoarded against the day of woe.
	Gladly would I have bought my life with all my wealth,
	and shunned my death for the space of a breath or so;
	but God would have nothing except what His purpose willed,
	and so I was cut off from my brothers and left alone.
	And Death, who sunders men, exchanged my lot
	for a pauper's hut, out of a mansion's grandeur;
	and there I found all my actions gone and past,
	for which I stand pledged, and by my own sin undone.
	So fear, O man, who walk along the edge of a brink,
	the turns of Fortune and the chances of Change.

The Emir Musa was wounded to the heart and sick of his own life for what he saw of the places where these people had been cut down; and as they went about the highways and byways of the palace, looking at its sitting rooms and its pleasure grounds, they came upon a table of yellow onyx supported on four feet of juniper wood, with these words graven on it:

	At this table have eaten a thousand kings blind in the right eye, and a thousand blind in the left, and yet another thousand sound in both eyes — all of whom have left the world and taken up their lodging in the tombs and the catacombs.

The Emir wrote all this down, and left the palace, carrying away nothing with him but the table.

Then he went on with his troops for three days under the guidance of the Shaykh Abd al-Samad, until they came to a high hill on which stood a horseman of brass. In his hand he held a lance with a broad head, bright as blinding lightning, on which was graven:

	You who come to me: if you do not know the way to the City of Brass, rub the hand of this rider, and he will turn round and presently stop. Then take the direction he faces, and go without fear, for it will bring you, without hardship, to the city.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventieth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Emir Musa rubbed the horseman's hand, he spun round like dazzling lightning and stopped facing in a different direction from the one they had been travelling in. So they took the road he pointed to — which was the right way — and, finding it a beaten track, went on through their days and nights until they had covered a wide stretch of country.

Then they came upon a pillar of black stone like the chimney of a furnace, in which there was somebody sunk up to his armpits. He had two great wings and four arms — two of them like the arms of the sons of Adam, and the other two like a lion's paws with claws of iron — and he was black and tall and frightful to look at, with hair like horses' tails and eyes like blazing coals set upright in his face. Moreover he had in the middle of his forehead a third eye, like a lynx's, out of which flew sparks of fire; and he was crying out and saying, "Glory to my Lord, who has adjudged me this grievous torment and this sore punishment until the Day of Doom!"

When the party saw him they lost their reason with fright and turned to run; so the Emir Musa asked the Shaykh Abd al-Samad, "What is this?"

And he answered, "I do not know."

Musa said, "Go closer and question him about his condition; perhaps he will tell you his case."

"Allah keep you, Emir! Indeed, I am afraid of him," replied the Shaykh.

But the Emir answered, "Do not be afraid; he is prevented from reaching you, or anybody else, by the thing he is in."

So Abd al-Samad went up to the pillar and said to the one who was inside it, "Creature, what is your name, and what are you, and how did you come to be here like this?"

"I am an ifrit of the jinn," he replied, "and my name is Dahish, son of al-A'amash; and I am confined here by the Almighty, imprisoned here by Providence and punished by the judgment of Allah, until it pleases Him, to whom belong Might and Majesty, to release me."

Then Musa said, "Ask him why he is shut up in this column."

So the Shaykh asked him about it, and the ifrit replied:

Truly, my tale is a wonder and my case a marvel, and it is this. One of the sons of Iblis had an idol of red carnelian, of which I was the guardian; and there served that idol a King of the Kings of the sea, a prince of great power and famous for his prowess, who ruled over a thousand thousand warriors of the jann, who struck with swords before him and answered his summons in time of need. All of these were under my command and obeyed my orders, and every one of them was a rebel against Solomon son of David, on whom be peace! And I used to get inside the belly of the idol, and give them their orders from there.

Now this King's daughter loved the idol and was constant in bowing down to it and diligent in its service; and she was the loveliest woman of her day, perfect in beauty and grace, in elegance and charm. She was described to Solomon, and he sent to her father, saying, "Give me your daughter in marriage, and break your idol of carnelian, and bear witness, saying: There is no god but God, and Solomon is the Prophet of Allah! If you do this, what is due to us shall be due to you, and your debt shall be our debt. But if you refuse, prepare to answer the summons of the Lord and put on your grave clothes, for I will come against you with an army nothing can resist, which shall fill the waste places of the earth and make you like yesterday, which is past and will never come back."

When this message reached the King he grew insolent and rebellious, full of pride and defiance, and he cried out to his viziers, "What do you say to this? You know that Solomon son of David has sent demanding that I give him my daughter in marriage, and break my idol of carnelian, and enter his faith!"

And they answered, "Mighty King, how shall Solomon do such a thing to you? Even if he could come at you in the middle of this vast ocean, he could not prevail against you; for the marids of the jann will fight on your side, and you will ask help of your idol whom you serve, and he will help you and give you victory over him. So you would do well to consult your Lord about this matter" — meaning the idol — "and hear what he says. If he says, Fight him, then fight him; and if not, not."

So the King went in to his idol without pause or delay and offered up sacrifices and slaughtered victims; after which he fell down before it, prostrate and weeping, and repeated these verses:

	O my Lord, well I know your powerful hand:
	Solomon would break you and see you banned.
	O my Lord, I stand here to beg your aid;
	command, and I bow to your high command.

Then I — the ifrit went on, addressing the Shaykh and those around him — out of my ignorance and my want of wit, and my recklessness about Solomon's commandment and my lack of any knowledge of his power, got inside the belly of the idol and answered as follows:

	As for me, of him I feel no fright,
	for my learning and my wisdom are infinite.
	If he wants war, I will show him a fight,
	and out of his body I will tear his sprite!

When the King heard my boastful answer he hardened his heart and resolved to make war on the Prophet and offer him battle; so he beat the messenger with a severe beating and returned a foul answer to Solomon, threatening him and saying, "Truly, your soul has suggested a vain thing to you. Do you threaten me with lying words? Gird yourself for battle; for if you do not come to me, I shall certainly come to you."

So the messenger went back to Solomon and told him everything that had passed and everything that had happened to him. And when the Prophet heard it, he raged like Doomsday and set himself to the fight, and raised armies of men and jann and birds and reptiles. He commanded his vizier al-Dimiryat, King of the Jann, to gather together the marids of the jinn from every quarter, and he collected six hundred thousand thousand devils for him. Moreover, by his order, his vizier Asaf bin Barkhiya raised him an army of men to the number of a thousand thousand and more. All these he furnished with arms and armour; and mounting, with his host, upon his carpet, he took flight through the air, while the beasts went along under him and the birds flew overhead, until he came down on the island of the rebel King and encircled it about, filling the earth with his hosts.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-first Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the ifrit went on:

So when Solomon the prophet (on whom be peace!) had come down with his host on the island, he sent to our King, saying, "Behold, I am come. Defend your life against what has fallen on you, or else make your submission to me and confess that I am the Apostle of Allah, and give me your daughter in lawful marriage, and break your idol and worship the one God, who alone is worthy of worship; and bear witness, you and yours, and say: There is no god but God, and Solomon is the Apostle of Allah! If you do this you shall have pardon and peace; and if not, it will do you no good to fortify yourself on this island, for Allah (extolled and exalted be He!) has commanded the wind to obey me, and I will order it to carry me to you on my carpet and make you a warning and an example to deter others."

But the King answered his messenger, saying, "It cannot be in any way as he demands of me; so tell him I am coming out to him."

With this answer the messenger went back to Solomon, who thereupon gathered together all the jinn under his hand, to the number of a thousand thousand, and added to them others besides — marids and satans from the islands of the sea and the tops of the mountains — and, drawing them up on parade, opened his armouries and distributed arms and armour to them.

Then the Prophet drew up his host in order of battle, dividing the beasts into two bodies, one on the right wing of the men and the other on the left, and ordering them to tear the enemies' horses apart. Furthermore, he ordered the birds that were on the island to hover over their heads, and, when the assault was made, to swoop down and tear out the enemy's eyes with their beaks and beat their faces with their wings; and they answered, "We hear and we obey Allah and you, Prophet of Allah!"

Then Solomon seated himself on a throne of alabaster studded with precious stones and plated with red gold; and, commanding the wind to lift him into the air, set his vizier Asaf bin Barkhiya and the kings of mankind on his right, and his vizier al-Dimiryat and the kings of the jinn on his left, and arrayed the beasts and the vipers and the serpents in the van.

Then they all fell on us together, and we gave them battle for two days over a vast plain; but on the third day disaster came upon us and the judgment of Allah the Most High was carried out on us. Now the first to charge them were my troops and I; and I said to my companions, "Stay where you are, while I go out to them and challenge al-Dimiryat to single combat."

And behold, he came out to the duel like a vast mountain, with his fires flaming and his smoke going up in a spire, and shot a falling star of fire at me; but I swerved aside from it and it missed me. Then I cast a flame of fire at him in my turn, and struck him; but his shaft overcame my fire, and he gave such a terrible cry at me that it seemed to me the skies had fallen flat on top of me, and the mountains trembled at his voice.

Then he ordered his hosts to charge; and they rushed on us and we rushed on them, each side crying out against the other; and the battle reared its crest, rising in volumes with the smoke going up in columns and hearts nearly splitting. The birds and the flying jinn fought in the air, and the beasts and the men and the foot-going jann in the dust; and I fought with al-Dimiryat until I was worn out, and he no less.

At last I grew weak and turned to flee from him, whereupon my companions and my tribesmen took to flight as well, and my hosts were routed; and Solomon cried out, saying, "Take that furious tyrant, the accursed, the infamous!"

Then man fell on man and jinni on jinni, and the armies of the Prophet charged down on us, with the wild beasts and the lions on their right hand and on their left, tearing our horses apart and rending our men; while the birds hovered overhead in the air, pecking out our eyes with their claws and beaks and beating our faces with their wings, and the serpents struck us with their fangs, until most of our people lay flat on the face of the earth like the trunks of date palms. So defeat came upon our King, and we became a spoil for Solomon.

As for me, I fled before al-Dimiryat, but he followed me for three months' journey, until I fell down from weariness and he overtook me and pounced on me and made me his prisoner.

I said, "By the virtue of Him who has exalted you and abased me, spare me and bring me into the presence of Solomon, on whom be peace!"

So he carried me before Solomon, who received me in the foulest fashion and ordered this pillar to be brought and hollowed out. Then he put me inside it and chained me and sealed me with his seal ring; and al-Dimiryat carried me to this place where you see me. Moreover, he charged a great angel to guard me; and this pillar is my prison until the Day of Judgment.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-second Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the jinni imprisoned in the pillar had told them his tale from first to last, the party marvelled at his story and at the frightfulness of his appearance, and the Emir Musa said, "There is no god but God! Truly Solomon was gifted with a mighty dominion."

Then the Shaykh Abd al-Samad said to the jinni, "You there! I should like to ask you about something; tell us about it."

"Ask what you like," answered the ifrit Dahish.

And the Shaykh said, "Are there anywhere hereabouts any of the ifrits imprisoned in jars of copper from the time of Solomon, on whom be peace?"
