"Yes," replied the jinni. "There are such in the sea of al-Karkar, on the shores of which lives a people descended from Noah, on whom be peace; for their country was not reached by the Flood, and they are cut off there from the other sons of Adam."

Abd al-Samad said, "And which is the way to the City of Brass and the place where the jars of Solomon are, and what distance is there between us and it?"

The ifrit said, "It is near at hand"; and he directed them on the way there.

So they left him and went forward, until there appeared to them far off a great blackness with two fires in it facing one another; and the Emir Musa asked the Shaykh, "What is that vast blackness and its twin fires?"

And the guide answered, "Rejoice, Emir, for this is the City of Brass, as it is described in the Book of Hidden Treasures which I have with me. Its walls are of black stone, and it has two towers of Andalusian brass, which look to anybody in the distance like two fires; and that is why it is called the City of Brass."

Then they went on without stopping until they drew near the city — and behold, it was like a piece of a mountain, or a mass of iron cast in a mould, impenetrable for the height of its walls and bulwarks; while nothing could be more beautiful than its buildings and the ordering of them.

So they dismounted and looked for a way in, but saw none, and could not find a trace of any opening in the walls — for although there were twenty-five gates to the city, not one of them was visible from outside.

Then the Emir said, "Shaykh, I can see no sign of any gate to this city."

And he said, "Emir, so it is described in my Book of Hidden Treasures. It has twenty-five gates, but not one of them can be opened except from inside the city."

Musa asked, "And how shall we manage to get into the city and see its wonders?"

And Talib son of Sahl, his vizier, answered, "Allah keep the Emir! Let us rest here two or three days, and, God willing, we shall find a way to get inside the walls."

Then Musa said to one of his men, "Mount your camel and ride round the city; perhaps you may come upon a gate, or some place a little lower than this in front of us, or, God willing, a breach we can get in by."

So he mounted his beast, taking water and food with him, and rode round the city for two days and two nights without drawing rein to rest; but he found the wall of it like a single block, with no breach and no way in. And on the third day he came in sight of his companions again, dazed and astonished at what he had seen of the size and the height of the place, and said, "Emir, the easiest place to get at is the one where you have halted."

Then Musa took Talib and Abd al-Samad and climbed the highest hill overlooking the city. When they reached the top they saw below them a city — and eyes never saw a greater or a finer — with dwellings and mansions of towering height, and palaces and pavilions and domes gleaming gloriously bright, and lamps and bulwarks of infinite strength; and its streams were flowing and its flowers blowing and its fruits glowing. It was a city with impregnable gates; but empty and still, without a voice and without one living soul to cheer it. The owl hooted in its quarters; the bird went skimming in circles over its squares; and the raven croaked in its great thoroughfares, weeping and lamenting for the people who once lived there.

The Emir stood a while, marvelling and grieving over the desolation of the city, and saying, "Glory to Him whom no ages and no changes and no times can wither — Him who created all things by His Might!"

Presently he happened to look aside and caught sight of seven tablets of white marble a long way off. So he went up to them, and finding inscriptions graven on them, called the Shaykh and told him to read them. So he came forward, and examining the inscriptions, found that they held matter of admonition and warning, and examples and restraint for people of understanding.

On the first tablet was inscribed, in the ancient Greek character:

	Son of Adam, how heedless you are of what lies before you! Truly your years and your months and your days have distracted you from it. Do you not know that the cup of death is filled for your undoing, and that in a little while you shall drain it to the dregs? Look to your doom before you go into your tomb. Where are the Kings who held dominion over the lands and humbled the servants of Allah and built these palaces and had armies under their command? By Allah, the Destroyer of Delights and the Sunderer of Companies and the Devastator of dwelling places came down on them and carried them from the spaciousness of their palaces to the narrowness of their burial places.

And at the foot of the tablet these verses were written:

	Where are the kings who peopled the earth — where are they?
	They left what they had built and settled, for ever and aye.
	They are entombed, and still pledged for actions past,
	and after their death decay came upon them to stay.
	Where are their troops? They failed to ward and guard.
	Where is the wealth that in their treasuries lay?
	The Lord of the Highest Heaven surprised them with one word,
	and neither wealth nor refuge could their doom delay.

When the Emir heard this he cried out, and the tears ran down his cheeks, and he exclaimed, "By Allah, to abstain from the world is the wisest course and the only cure!" And he called for a pen case and paper and wrote down what was graven on the first tablet.

Then he went up to the second tablet and found these words graven on it:

	Son of Adam, what has seduced you away from the service of the Ancient of Days, and made you forget that one day you must pay the debt of death? Do you not know that this is a place you pass through, in which nobody stays? And yet you give your thought to the world and cling fast to it. Where are the kings who peopled Iraq and possessed the four quarters of the globe? Where are those who lived in Isfahan and the land of Khorasan? The voice of the Summoner of Death called them and they answered him, and the Herald of Destruction hailed them and they replied, Here we are! Truly, what they built and fortified profited them nothing; nor did what they had gathered and laid by serve for their defence.

And at the foot of the tablet these verses were graven:

	Where are the men who built and fortified
	high places whose like no man ever espied?
	In fear of Fate they levied troops and hosts,
	which availed them nothing when the time and the tide
	came round. Where are the Chosroes in their strongest walls?
	As though they had never been in the homes they tried.

The Emir Musa wept and exclaimed, "By Allah, we are indeed created for a grave matter!" Then he copied the inscription and passed on to the third tablet.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-third Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Emir Musa passed on to the third tablet, on which was written:

	Son of Adam, the things of this world you love and prize, and the command of your Lord you spurn and despise. All the days of your life go by, and you are content to have it so. Make ready your provision for the journey against the day appointed for you to see, and prepare to answer the Lord of every creature that shall be.

And at the foot were written these verses:

	Where is the man who peopled, in the years gone past,
	the lands of Hind and Sind, and played the tyrant there?
	Who bound Zanj and Abyssinia beneath his yoke,
	and curbed Nubia and laid its power bare?
	Do not look for news of what is in his grave:
	he is too far off to help your seeing there.
	The stroke of death fell on him sharp and sure,
	and neither palace saved him nor the lands he swayed.

At this Musa wept bitterly, and going on to the fourth tablet he read inscribed on it:

	Son of Adam, how long shall your Lord bear with you, while every day you are sunk in the sea of your own folly? Has it been established, then, that some day you shall not die? Son of Adam, do not let the deceits of your days and nights and times and hours delude you with their delights; but remember that death lies ready for you in ambush, eager to spring on your shoulders; and not a day passes but he wakes with you in the morning and lies down with you at night. Beware, then, of his onslaught, and make provision against it. As it was with me, so it is with you: you waste your whole life and squander the joys your days are full of. Listen, then, to my words and put your trust in the Lord of Lords; for in the world there is no stability — it is no more to you than a spider's web.

And at the foot of the tablet these couplets were written:

	Where is the man who plied all this labour,
	who founded and built and reared these walls on high?
	Where are the lords of the castles? Those who dwelt in them
	went out and left them lying in decay.
	They are all entombed, in pledge against the day
	when every sin shall show to every eye.
	None but the Lord Most High has endurance,
	whose Might and Majesty shall never die.

When the Emir read this he fainted away, and presently, coming to himself, marvelled greatly and wrote it down. Then he went up to the fifth tablet, and behold, on it was graven:

	Son of Adam, what is it that distracts you from obedience to your Creator and the Author of your being — Him who raised you when you were little, and fed you when you were grown? You are ungrateful for His bounty, although He watches over you with His favours and lets down the curtain of His protection over you. There must come to you an hour bitterer than aloes and hotter than live coals. Provide against it, then; for who shall sweeten its gall or quench its fires? Think of the peoples and the heroes who went before you, and take warning by them, before you perish.

And at the foot of the tablet these couplets were graven:

	Where are the kings of the earth, who from the place they lived
	sped off to the graveyards with their hoardings in tow?
	Once, on their days of mounting, you would have seen
	hosts that hid the ground they rode on, row on row.
	How many a king they humbled in their day!
	How many a host they led and laid on low!
	But from the Lord of the Highest Heaven there came
	one word in haste, and joy turned grief before the morning's glow.

The Emir marvelled at this and wrote it down; after which he passed on to the sixth tablet, and behold, on it was inscribed:

	Son of Adam, do not think that safety will last for ever and always, seeing that death is sealed to your head at every hour. Where are your fathers, where are your brothers, where are your friends and the people you loved? They have all gone to the dust of the tombs and presented themselves before the Glorious One, the Forgiving, as if they had never eaten or drunk; and they are held in pledge for what they earned. So look to yourself, before your tomb comes upon you.

And at the foot of the tablet were these couplets:

	Where are the kings who ruled the Franks of old?
	Where is the king who peopled the land of Tangier?
	Their works are written down in a book, and He,
	the One, the Father of all, shall hold it as witness there.

At this the Emir Musa marvelled and wrote it down, saying, "There is no god but God! Indeed, how fine these people were!"

Then he went up to the seventh tablet, and behold, on it was written:

	Glory to Him who has fore-ordained death for everything He creates, the Living One, who does not die! Son of Adam, do not let your days and their delights delude you, nor your hours and the pleasures of their time; and know that death is coming to you and sits upon your shoulder. Beware, then, of his assault, and be ready for his onslaught. As it was with me, so it is with you: you are wasting the sweetness of your life and the joy of your hours. Give ear, then, to my counsel and put your trust in the Lord of Lords, and know that in the world there is no stability, but it is like a spider's web to you, and everything in it shall die and cease to be. Where is the man who laid the foundation of Amid and built it, and built Farikin and exalted it? Where are the peoples of the strong places? When they had lived in them, after all their might they went down into the tombs. They have been carried off by death, and we shall be afflicted by doom in the same way. Nobody remains except Allah the Most High, for He is Allah the Forgiving One.

The Emir Musa wept and copied all this; and indeed the world had grown small in his eyes.

Then he came down the hill and rejoined his host, with whom he spent the rest of the day casting about for a way into the city. And he said to his vizier Talib bin Sahl and to the chief officers about him, "How shall we manage to get into this city and see its marvels? Perhaps we shall find in it something to win us the favour of the Commander of the Faithful."

"Allah prolong the Emir's fortune!" replied Talib. "Let us make a ladder and climb the wall with it; then perhaps we may get at the gate from the inside."

The Emir said, "That is exactly what occurred to me too, and it is admirable advice!"

Then he called for carpenters and blacksmiths and told them to shape wood and build a ladder plated and banded with iron. So they made a strong ladder, and a great many men worked at it for a whole month.

Then the whole company took hold of it and set it up against the wall, and it reached the top as exactly as if it had been built for it beforehand. The Emir marvelled and said, "The blessing of Allah be upon you! It looks as though you had taken the measure of the wall, so excellent is your work."

Then he said to his men, "Which of you will go up the ladder and walk along the wall and look for a way of getting down into the city, so as to see how things stand and let us know how we may open the gate?"

At which one of them said, "I will go up, Emir, and go down and open it for you."

And Musa answered, "Go, and the blessing of Allah go with you!"

So the man climbed the ladder; but when he came to the top of the wall he stood up and gazed steadily down into the city, and then clapped his hands and cried out at the top of his voice, "By Allah, you are fair!" — and threw himself down into the place.

And Musa cried, "By Allah, he is a dead man!"

But another came up to him and said, "Emir, this man was mad, and no doubt his madness got the better of him and destroyed him. I will go up and open the gate for you, if it be the will of Allah the Most High."

"Go up," replied Musa, "and Allah be with you! But take care not to lose your head, as your comrade did."

Then the man climbed the ladder; but no sooner had he reached the top of the wall than he laughed aloud, saying, "Well done! Well done!" and, clapping his hands, threw himself down into the city and died on the spot.

When the Emir saw this he said, "If that is what a reasonable man does, what will a madman do? If all our men behave like this we shall have none left, and we shall fail in our errand and in the errand of the Commander of the Faithful. Get ready to march: we have no business with this city."

But a third man of the company said, "Perhaps somebody else may be steadier than they were." So a third climbed the wall, and a fourth and a fifth, and every one of them cried out and threw himself down, exactly as the first had done; nor did they leave off doing so until a dozen had perished in the same way.

Then the Shaykh Abd al-Samad came forward and took heart and said, "This business is for nobody but me; for a man with experience is not like a man without it."

The Emir said, "Indeed you shall not do it, and I will not have you go up. If you die, we shall all be cut off to the last man, since you are our guide."

But he answered, "It may be that what we are looking for will be accomplished at my hands, by the grace of God Most High."

So the whole company agreed to let him climb the ladder; and he got up and took heart and said, "In the name of Allah, the Compassionating, the Compassionate!" and went up the ladder, calling on the name of the Lord and reciting the Verses of Safety.

When he reached the top of the wall he clapped his hands and gazed steadily down into the city; at which the people below all cried out to him with one voice, saying, "Shaykh Abd al-Samad, for the Lord's sake, do not throw yourself down!" and they added, "Truly, we belong to Allah and to Him we are returning! If the Shaykh falls, we are all dead men."

Then he laughed beyond all measure, and sat for a long hour reciting the names of Almighty Allah and repeating the Verses of Safety; and then he got up and cried out at the top of his voice, saying, "Emir, have no fear; no harm shall come to you, for Allah (to whom belong Might and Majesty!) has turned aside from me the wiles and the malice of Satan, by the blessing of the words, In the name of Allah, the Compassionating, the Compassionate!"

Musa asked, "What did you see, Shaykh?"

And Abd al-Samad answered, "I saw ten girls like the houris of Heaven, calling to me with their hands."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-fourth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Shaykh Abd al-Samad answered:

"I saw ten girls like the houris of Heaven, calling and signalling, Come to us! And it seemed to me there was a lake of water below me. So I thought I would throw myself down — when I caught sight of my twelve companions lying dead; so I held myself back and recited something of Allah's Book, whereupon He dispelled the girls' witching wiles and malicious guiles, and they disappeared. And no doubt this was an enchantment devised by the people of the city, to drive off anybody who should try to look into the place or enter it. And it has succeeded in killing our companions."

Then he walked on along the wall until he came to the two towers of brass, and saw in them two gates of gold, without padlocks or any visible means of opening. Here he paused as long as Allah pleased, and looked about him a while, until he caught sight, in the middle of one of the gates, of a horseman of brass with his hand stretched out as if pointing, and something written on his palm. So he went up to it and read these words:

	You who come to this place: if you would enter, turn the pin in my navel twelve times, and the gate will open.

So he examined the horseman, and finding in his navel a pin of gold, firmly set and fast fixed, he turned it twelve times; whereupon the horseman revolved like blinding lightning and the gate swung open with a noise like thunder.

He went in and found himself in a long passage, which brought him down some steps into a guardroom furnished with fine wooden benches, on which sat men who were dead, with handsome shields hanging over their heads, and keen blades, and bent bows, and arrows ready notched.

From there he came to the main gate of the city; and finding it secured with iron bars and elaborately worked locks and bolts and chains and other fastenings of wood and metal, he said to himself, "Very likely the keys are with those dead men."

So he went back to the guardroom, and seeing among the dead an old man sitting on a high wooden bench who seemed to be the chief of them, he said in his mind, "Who knows but the keys are with this Shaykh? No doubt he was the warden of the city and these others were under his hand."

So he went up to him and lifted his gown — and behold, the keys were hanging at his belt; at which he rejoiced exceedingly and was ready to fly for gladness.

Then he took them and went to the gateway and undid the padlocks and drew back the bolts and the bars, whereupon the great leaves flew open with a crash like a peal of thunder, so huge and so terrible were they. At this he cried out, "Allahu akbar — God is most great!" And the people outside answered him with the same words, rejoicing and thanking him for what he had done.

The Emir Musa was delighted too at the Shaykh's safety and at the opening of the city gate, and the troops all pressed forward to go in; but Musa cried out to them, "Good people, if we all go in at once we shall not be safe from some mishap that may befall us. Let half go in and the other half wait outside."

So he pushed forward with half his men, carrying their weapons of war; and finding their comrades lying dead, they buried them. And they saw the doorkeepers and the eunuchs and the chamberlains and the officers reclining on couches of silk, and every one of them a corpse.

Then they went on until they came to the chief market place, full of lofty buildings, not one of which overtopped the others; and they found all its shops open, with the scales hung out and the brass vessels set in order and the caravanserais full of goods of every kind. And they saw the merchants sitting on the shop boards, dead, with shrivelled skin and rotted bones — a warning to those who can take warning; and here they saw four separate markets, all of them full of wealth.

Then they left the great bazaar and went on until they came to the silk market, where they found silks and brocades embroidered with red gold and figured with white silver on every kind of colour, and the owners lying dead on mats of scented goatskin, looking as if they were about to speak.

After that they crossed the market street of pearls and rubies and other jewels, and came to the street of the money-changers, whom they saw sitting dead on carpets of raw silk and dyed stuffs, in shops full of gold and silver.

From there they passed on to the perfumers' bazaar, where they found the shops filled with drugs of all kinds, and bladders of musk and ambergris and nadd-perfume and camphor and other scents, in vessels of ivory and ebony and khalanj-wood and Andalusian copper, which is equal in value to gold; and various kinds of rattan and Indian cane. But the shopkeepers all lay dead, and there was nothing whatever of food with them.

And close by this drug market they came upon a palace, imposingly built and magnificently decorated; so they went in and found in it banners displayed and drawn sword blades and strung bows and shields hanging by chains of gold and silver, and helmets gilded with red gold. In the vestibules stood benches of ivory plated with glittering gold and covered with silken stuffs, on which lay men whose skin had dried on their bones; a fool would have thought they were asleep, but for want of food they had perished and tasted the cup of death.

Now when the Emir Musa saw this he stood still, glorifying Allah the Most High and calling Him holy, and contemplating the beauty of the palace and the massiveness of its masonry and the fine perfection of its ordering; for it was built in the finest and most solid fashion, and most of its decoration was of green lapis lazuli. And on the inner door, which stood open, these couplets were written in characters of gold and ultramarine:

	Consider, man, what these places have shown you,
	and be on your guard before you travel the same road;
	and make ready good provision that may serve your turn some day,
	for every dweller in the house must go with those who have gone.
	Consider how this people adorned their palaces,
	and in the dust have been held in pledge for the seed of the acts they sowed.
	They built, but their building did not avail them, and their hoards
	neither saved their lives nor put off the day of Destiny.
	How often they hoped for things that were not decreed,
	and passed on to their tombs before Hope had shown its bounty!
	And from a high and awful state, all of a sudden, they were sent
	to the narrowness of the grave — and oh, how base is their abode!
	Then a Crier came to them after burial and cried:
	What good were the thrones to you, or the crowns, or the gold you were given?
	Where now are the faces that were hidden by curtain and by veil,
	whose charms were told in proverbs — those beauties in the fashion?
	The tombs reply aloud to the questioners, and cry:
	The canker and decay of Death corrode those rosy cheeks.
	Long they ate and drank, but their rejoicing had a term;
	and the eater in his turn was eaten, and the worm ate him.

When the Emir read this he wept until he was nearly fainting.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-fifth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Emir wept until he was nearly fainting, and gave orders for the verses to be written down; after which he passed on into the inner palace and came to a vast hall, at each of whose four corners stood a pavilion, lofty and spacious, washed with gold and silver and painted in various colours.

In the heart of the hall was a great jetting fountain of alabaster, surmounted by a canopy of brocade; and in each pavilion was a sitting place, and each place had its richly worked fountain and its tank paved with marble, and streams running in channels along the floor and meeting in a great and splendid cistern of many-coloured marbles.

The Emir said to the Shaykh Abd al-Samad, "Come, let us visit that pavilion!"

So they went into the first and found it full of gold and silver and pearls and jacinths and other precious stones and metals, besides chests filled with brocades, red and yellow and white.

Then they went to the second pavilion, and, opening a closet there, found it full of arms and armour — gilded helmets and Davidean hauberks and Indian swords and Arabian spears and Khwarazmian maces and other gear of fight and fray.

From there they passed to the third pavilion, where they saw closets padlocked and covered with curtains worked with every kind of embroidery. They opened one of these and found it full of weapons elaborately ornamented with openwork and with gold and silver damascening and jewels.

Then they went into the fourth pavilion, and opening one of the closets there, saw in it a great store of eating and drinking vessels of gold and silver, with platters of crystal and goblets set with fine pearls and cups of carnelian and the like. So they all fell to taking whatever suited their taste, and each of the soldiers carried off what he could.

When they left the pavilions they saw, in the middle of the palace, a door of teak inlaid with ivory and ebony and plated with glittering gold, over which hung a silk curtain bordered with every kind of embroidery; and on this door were locks of white silver that opened by a trick, without a key. The Shaykh Abd al-Samad went boldly up to it and by the help of his knowledge and skill opened the locks, whereupon the door let them into a corridor paved with marble and hung with veil-like tapestries embroidered with figures of every kind of beast and bird, whose bodies were of red gold and white silver and their eyes of pearls and rubies, amazing everybody who looked at them.

Going on, they came to a hall built all of polished marble inlaid with jewels, which looked to anybody standing there as if the floor were running water, so that whoever walked on it slipped. The Emir told the Shaykh to strew something over it, so that they could walk across; and when this was done they managed to get forward, until they came to a great domed pavilion of stone gilded with red gold and crowned with a cupola of alabaster, around which were set lattice windows, carved and jewelled with rods of emerald beyond the means of any king.

Under this dome was a canopy of brocade, resting on pillars of red gold and worked with figures of birds whose feet were of emerald, and beneath each bird was a network of fresh-coloured pearls. The canopy was spread over a jetting fountain of ivory and carnelian, plated with glittering gold; and beside it stood a couch set with pearls and rubies and other jewels, and beside the couch a pillar of gold. On the capital of the column stood a bird made of red rubies, holding in his bill a pearl that shone like a star.

And on the couch lay a girl like the shining sun, and eyes never saw a fairer. She wore a close-fitting robe of fine pearls, with a crown of red gold on her head, banded with gems; and on her forehead were two great jewels whose light was like the light of the sun. On her breast she wore a jewelled amulet, filled with musk and ambergris and worth the empire of the Caesars; and round her neck hung a collar of rubies and great pearls, hollowed and filled with sweet-smelling musk. And it seemed as though she looked at them, to the right and to the left.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-sixth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the girl seemed to be gazing at the party to the right and to the left. The Emir Musa marvelled at her extraordinary beauty and was astonished at the blackness of her hair and the redness of her cheeks, which made anybody looking at her think she was alive and not dead; and he said to her, "Peace be with you, girl!"

But Talib ibn Sahl said to him, "Allah preserve you, Emir! This girl is dead and there is no life in her; so how should she return your greeting?" And he added, "Indeed, she is only a corpse embalmed with extraordinary art. Her eyes were taken out after her death and quicksilver set under them, after which they were put back in their sockets. That is why they glisten; and when the air moves her lashes she seems to blink, and it looks to anybody watching as though she were looking at him, dead though she is."

At this the Emir marvelled beyond measure and said, "Glory be to God, who subjects His creatures to the dominion of Death!"

Now the couch the girl lay on had steps, and on them stood two statues of Andalusian copper representing slaves, one white and the other black. The first held a mace of steel and the second a sword of watered steel that dazzled the eye; and between them, on one of the steps of the couch, lay a golden tablet, on which these words were written in characters of white silver:

	In the name of God, the Compassionating, the Compassionate! Praise be to Allah, the Creator of mankind; and He is the Lord of Lords, the Causer of Causes! In the name of Allah, the Never-beginning, the Everlasting, the Ordainer of Fate and Fortune!
	Son of Adam, what has fooled you into this long hoping? What has made you forget the mischance of the Day of Death? Do you not know that Death is calling for you and hurrying to seize your soul? Be ready, then, for the road, and provide yourself for your departure from the world; for you shall certainly leave it without delay.
	Where is Adam, the first of mankind? Where is Noah with his descendants? Where are the Kings of India and the plain of Iraq, and those who reigned over the widest regions of the earth? Where do the Amalekites live now, and the giants and the tyrants of old? Truly, the dwelling places are empty of them, and they have departed from their kindred and their homes. Where are the Kings of the Arabs and of the Persians? They are dead, every one, and gone, and have become rotten bones. Where are the lords who stood so high? They are all done and dead. Where are Korah and Haman? Where is Shaddad son of Ad? Where are Canaan and the Lord of the Stakes? By Allah, the Reaper of lives has reaped them and emptied the lands of them. Did they provide against the Day of Resurrection, or make ready to answer the Lord of men?
	You there — if you do not know me, I will tell you my name. I am Tadmurah, daughter of the Kings of the Amalekites, of those who held dominion over the lands in fairness and brought low the necks of mankind. I possessed what no king ever possessed, and I was righteous in my rule and did justice among my subjects; yes, I gave gifts and largesse, and freed slaves both men and women. So I lived many years in all the ease and delight of life, until Death knocked at my door and calamities beyond counting fell on me and on my people. And it happened in this way.
	There came upon us seven successive years of drought, in which not a drop of rain fell on us from the skies and not a green thing sprouted for us on the face of the earth. So we ate what food we had by us, and then we fell upon the cattle and ate them, until nothing was left. Then I had my treasures brought out and measured by the measure, and sent out trusted men to buy food. They went round all the lands looking for it and left no city unsearched, but they did not find it to be bought, and came back to us with the treasure after a long absence, and let us know that they had not been able to barter fine pearls for poor wheat, bushel for bushel, weight for weight.
	So when we despaired of help, we displayed all our riches and things of price and, shutting the gates of the city and its strong places, resigned ourselves to the judgment of our Lord and committed our case to our King. And then we all died, as you see us, and left everything we had built and everything we had hoarded. This, then, is our story; and after the substance nothing remains but the trace.

Then they looked at the foot of the tablet and read these couplets:

	Child of Adam, do not let hope mock you and jeer at you:
	from everything your hands have treasured you shall be removed.
	I see you coveting the world and the fleeting charms of the world,
	and the races that are past and gone did the same as you, I see.
	They got wealth lawful and unlawful; but all their hoarded store,
	when their term was accomplished, delayed nothing of Destiny's decree.
	They led armies and mighty men and won themselves gold in plenty;
	then left their wealth and their palaces, compelled by Fate to flee
	to the narrowness of the graveyard and the humble bed of dust,
	from which, held in pledge for every word and deed, they never win free.
	They are like a company of travellers who had unloaded in the night
	at a house that lacked food and was not overfond of company,
	whose owner says, Good people, there is no lodging here for you;
	so those who had just unpacked packed up and went off hurriedly,
	disliking the march, and neither the journey nor the halt
	had anything of pleasant chance or anything of a good greeting.
	So make ready good provision, stored up for tomorrow's journey:
	nothing but a righteous and honest life shall avail you with the Lord.

And the Emir Musa wept as he read on:

	By Allah, the fear of the Lord is the best of all property, the pillar of certainty and the only sure support. Truly, Death is the manifest truth and the sure command, and in it, O you, is the goal and the plain place of return. Take warning, then, by those who went off into the dust and hurried along the road to the appointed end. Do you not see that grey hairs are summoning you to the tomb, and that the whiteness of your locks is lamenting your doom? So be awake and ready for your departure and for the settling of your account.
	Son of Adam, what has hardened your heart in this hateful way? What has seduced you from the service of your Lord? Where are the peoples of the old time? They are a warning to whoever will be warned. Where are the Kings of China and the lords of majestic bearing? Where is Shaddad son of Ad and everything he built and established? Where is Nimrod, who revolted against Allah and defied Him? Where is Pharaoh, who rebelled against God and denied Him? Death followed hard on the trail of all of them and laid them low, sparing neither great nor small, male nor female; and the Reaper of Mankind cut them off — yes, by Him who makes the night come round upon the day!
	Know, you who come to this place, that the woman you see here was not deluded by the world and its frail delights, for it is faithless and treacherous, a house of ruin, empty and false; and it is good for a creature to remember his sins. So she feared her Lord and made her dealings fair and provided herself with provisions against the appointed day of marching.
	Whoever comes to our city, and Allah grants him the means to enter it, let him take of the treasure all he can; but let him not touch anything that is on my body, for it is the covering of my shame and the outfit for the last journey. So let him fear Allah and strip none of it away, or else he will destroy his own self. This I have set out for him as a warning from me and a solemn trust to keep. And with that, peace be with you; and I pray Allah to keep you from sickness and calamity.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-seventh Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Emir Musa read this he wept exceedingly until he fainted away; and presently, coming to himself, he wrote down everything he had seen and took to heart everything he had witnessed.

Then he said to his men, "Fetch the camels and load them with these treasures and vases and jewels."

"Emir," asked Talib, "are we to leave our girl here with all that is on her — things that have no equal, whose like is not to be found, and more perfect than anything else you are taking? You could not find a finer offering to win the favour of the Commander of the Faithful."

But Musa answered, "Man, did you not hear what the lady says on this tablet? All the more since she gives it in trust to us, and we are no traitors."

"And are we," retorted the vizier Talib, "because of these words, to leave all these riches and jewels behind, seeing that she is dead? What should she do with things that are the adornment of the world and the ornament of the worldly, when a single garment of cotton would be enough to cover her? We have more right to them than she has."

And so saying he mounted the steps of the couch between the pillars; but when he came within reach of the two slaves, the mace-bearer struck him on the back and the other struck him with the sword he held in his hand and cut off his head, and he dropped down dead.

The Emir said, "Allah have no mercy on your resting place! Indeed, there was enough in these treasures; and greed for gain certainly degrades a man."

Then he ordered the troops to be let in; so they came in and loaded the camels with those treasures and precious ores; after which they went out, and the Emir ordered them to shut the gate as it had been before.

They travelled along the seashore a whole month, until they came in sight of a high mountain overlooking the sea and full of caves, in which lived a tribe of black people, dressed in hides with hooded cloaks of hide as well, and speaking a language nobody knew. When they saw the troops they started like shying horses and fled into the caves, while their women and children stood at the cave mouths looking at the strangers.

"Shaykh Abd al-Samad," asked the Emir, "who are these people?"

And he answered, "They are the people we are looking for, on behalf of the Commander of the Faithful."

So they dismounted and set down their loads and pitched their tents; and almost before they had finished, down came the King of these people from the mountain and drew near the camp. Now he understood Arabic; so when he came to the Emir he greeted him with the salaam, and Musa returned his greeting and treated him with honour.

Then the King said to the Emir, "Are you men, or jinn?"

"We are men, certainly," said Musa; "but no doubt you are jinn, to judge by your living apart on this mountain, which is cut off from mankind, and by your enormous size."

"Not at all," answered the King. "We too are children of Adam, of the lineage of Ham, son of Noah (on whom be peace!); and this sea is called al-Karkar."

Musa asked, "King, what is your religion, and what do you worship?"

And he answered, "We worship the God of the heavens, and our religion is the religion of Mohammed, whom Allah bless and preserve!"

"And how did you come by the knowledge of that," asked the Emir, "seeing that no prophet was ever inspired to visit this country?"

"Know, Emir," replied the King, "that a long while ago there appeared to us out of the sea a man from whom came a light that lit up the horizons, and he cried out in a voice that was heard by men far and near, saying: Children of Ham, reverence Him who sees and is not seen, and say: There is no god but God, and Mohammed is the messenger of God! And he added: I am Abu al-Abbas al-Khizr.

"Before that we used to worship one another, but he called us to the service of the Lord of all creatures; and he taught us to repeat these words: There is no god but God alone, who has no partner; His is the kingdom and His is the praise. He gives life and death, and He is Almighty over all things. Nor do we draw near to Allah (be He exalted and extolled!) except with these words, for we know no others. But every eve before Friday we see a light on the face of the earth, and we hear a voice saying: Holy and glorious, Lord of the Angels and the Spirit! What He wills, is; and what He does not will, is not. Every blessing is of His grace, and there is neither Majesty nor is there Might save in Allah, the Glorious, the Great!

"But you," said the King, "who and what are you, and what brings you to this land?"

Musa said, "We are officers of the Sovereign of Islam, the Commander of the Faithful, Abd al-Malik bin Marwan, who has heard tell of the lord Solomon, son of David (on whom be peace!) and of the supreme dominion the Most High gave him: how he held sway over jinn and beast and bird, and how, when he was angry with one of the marids, he used to shut him in a jar of copper and stop its mouth on him with lead, on which he stamped his seal ring, and throw it into the sea of al-Karkar. Now we have heard that this sea is near your land; so the Commander of the Faithful has sent us here to bring him some of these jars, that he may look at them and take pleasure in the sight of them. Such is our case, then, and what we want of you, King; and we hope you will help us to accomplish the errand the Commander of the Faithful has laid on us."

"With love and gladness," replied the King; and taking them to the guest house, he treated them with the utmost honour and provided them with everything they needed, feeding them on fish.

They stayed like this three days, and then he ordered his divers to fetch some of the vessels of Solomon up out of the sea. So they dived and brought up twelve jars, at which the Emir and the Shaykh and all the company rejoiced that the Caliph's need had been met.

Then Musa gave the King many great gifts; and he in his turn made him a present of one of the wonders of the deep — fishes in human form — saying, "Your food these three days has been the flesh of these fish."

The Emir said, "We must certainly carry some of these to the Caliph, for the sight of them will please him more than the jars of Solomon."

Then they took their leave of the King and, setting out on their homeward journey, travelled until they came to Damascus, where Musa went in to the Commander of the Faithful and told him everything he had seen and heard of verses and legends and examples, and how Talib bin Sahl had died.

And the Caliph said, "I wish I had been with you, so that I might have seen what you saw!"

Then he took the copper vessels and opened them one after another, whereupon the devils came out of them, saying, "We repent, Prophet of Allah! Never again will we go back to the like of this — never!" And the Caliph marvelled at it.

As for the daughters of the deep that the King had presented to them, they made them cisterns of planks full of water and laid them in there; but they died of the great heat.

Then the Caliph sent for the spoils of the City of Brass and divided them among the Faithful.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-eighth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Caliph marvelled greatly at the jars and their contents; and then he sent for the spoils and divided them among the Faithful, saying, "Never did Allah give to anybody the like of what He bestowed upon Solomon son of David!"

Thereupon the Emir Musa asked his leave to appoint his son governor of the province in his place, so that he might take himself off to the Holy City of Jerusalem and worship Allah there. So the Commander of the Faithful invested his son Harun with the government, and Musa went off to the Glorious and Holy City, where he died.

This, then, is all that has come down to us of the story of the City of Brass; and God is All-knowing.

Now, said Shahrazad, I have another tale to tell, about

Aladdin; Or, the Wonderful Lamp

[Editor's note: Aladdin and Ali Baba, which close this selection, are the two most famous stories in the Nights and the two that are not in it. Neither appears in any Arabic manuscript older than the eighteenth century. Both reached Europe through Antoine Galland, who took them down in Paris in 1709 from a young Syrian traveller named Hanna Diyab, and only afterwards were they written back into Arabic and printed. Burton translated them from that later Arabic. They carry their own night numbering, which is why the count starts again here instead of going on from the tale before.]

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that there lived in a city of the cities of China a man who was a tailor, and a poor one; and he had one son, whose name was Aladdin.

Now this boy had been a good-for-nothing and a scapegrace from his babyhood; and when he reached his tenth year his father wanted to teach him his own trade — for he was too poor to spend money on having him taught any other work or craft or apprenticeship — and took the lad into his shop to learn tailoring.

But as Aladdin was a scapegrace and a good-for-nothing, and used to play at all hours with the gutter boys of the quarter, he would not sit in the shop for a single day. He would wait for his father to leave it on some errand or other, such as going to meet a creditor, and then he would run straight off and away to the gardens with the other scapegraces and low companions who were his friends.

That was how things stood; advice and beatings were no use, and he would not obey either parent in anything, nor learn any trade at all. And presently, out of sadness and sorrow at his son's shiftless idleness, the tailor fell ill and died.

Aladdin carried on in his old bad ways; and when his mother saw that her husband was dead and her son was a scapegrace and good for nothing whatever, she sold the shop and everything in it and took to spinning cotton yarn. By this hard work she fed herself and found food for her son Aladdin the scapegrace — who, finding himself free of his father's severities, grew more idle and low in his habits than ever, and would never stay at home except at mealtimes, while his poor wretched mother lived on nothing but what her hands could spin. And so it went on until the boy had reached his fifteenth year.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifteenth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when Aladdin had come to his fifteenth year, it happened one day, as he was hanging about the quarter playing with the vagabond boys, that a dervish from the Maghrib, the Land of the Setting Sun, came up and stood watching the lads for his amusement; and he looked hard at Aladdin and studied his face carefully, hardly noticing his companions at all.

Now this dervish was a Moor from the interior of Morocco, and he was a magician who could heap hill upon hill by his magic, and he was an adept in astrology too. So after examining Aladdin closely he said to himself, "This is truly the lad I need, and the one I left my native country to find."

Presently he drew one of the children aside and questioned him about the scapegrace, saying, "Whose son is he?" And he asked for every scrap of information about his circumstances and everything to do with him.

After that he walked up to Aladdin and, taking him aside, asked, "My son, are you not the child of such-and-such a tailor?"

And the lad answered, "Yes, sir; but he died a long time ago."

When the Moroccan magician heard these words he threw himself upon Aladdin and wound his arms round his neck and fell to kissing him, weeping all the while, with the tears running down his cheeks.

But when the lad saw the state the Moroccan was in he was greatly surprised, and questioned him, saying, "What is making you weep, sir? And how did you come to know my father?"

"How can you ask me such a question, my son," replied the Moroccan, in a soft voice full of feeling, "after telling me that your father — my brother — is dead? For he was my own brother; and now I have come from my adopted country, and after a long exile I was rejoicing at the hope of seeing him once more and talking over old times with him — and now you tell me he is gone. But blood does not hide from blood, and it revealed to me that you are my nephew, my brother's son; and I knew you out of all the lads, although your father, when I parted from him, was not yet married."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixteenth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Moroccan magician said to the tailor's orphan, "My son Aladdin, I have missed the mourning ceremonies now, and lost the joy I looked for in meeting your father, my brother, whom after my long banishment I had hoped to see once more before I die. But the great distance did me this injury; and a creature has no refuge from the Creator, and no trick to play against the commandments of Almighty Allah."

Then he clasped Aladdin to his bosom again, crying, "My son, I have nobody left to grieve with now except yourself; and you stand in your father's place, being his offspring and his representative — and whoever leaves offspring does not die, my child!"

So saying, the magician put his hand to his purse and pulled out ten gold pieces and gave them to the lad, asking, "My son, where is your house, and where does she live — your mother, my brother's widow?"

Aladdin got up with him at once and showed him the way to their home; and as they went, the wizard said, "My son, take this money and give it to your mother, with my greetings, and let her know that your uncle, your father's brother, has come back from his exile; and that tomorrow, God willing, I will visit her and greet her with the salaam, and see the house my brother lived in, and look at the place where he lies buried."

At this Aladdin kissed the Moroccan's hand, and then ran in his joy at top speed to his mother's house and went in to her, quite contrary to his custom, since he never came near her except at mealtimes. And when he found her, the lad exclaimed in his delight, "Mother, I bring you good news of my uncle, who has come back from his exile and who now sends me to greet you!"

"My son," she replied, "it seems to me you are making fun of me. Who is this uncle? How can you have an uncle in the land of the living?"

He answered, "How can you say, mother, that I have no living uncles and no kinsmen, when this man is my father's own brother? Indeed he embraced me and kissed me, shedding tears all the while, and told me to let you know about it."

She retorted, "My son, I know very well that you had an uncle; but he is dead now, and I am not aware that you have another."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventeenth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Moroccan magician went out the next morning and set about finding Aladdin, for his heart would no longer let him be parted from the lad; and as he was going to and fro about the city streets he came face to face with him, amusing himself as usual among the vagabonds and the scapegraces.

So he went up to him and, taking his hand, embraced him and kissed him; then he pulled two dinars out of his pocket and said, "Off you go to your mother and give her these two gold pieces, and tell her that your uncle would like to have supper with you. So take the two coins and get us a good supper ready. But before anything else, show me the way to your house once more."

"On my head and on my eyes be it, uncle," replied the lad, and went in front of him, pointing out the street that led to the house. Then the Moroccan left him and went his way, and Aladdin ran home and gave his mother the news and the two coins, saying, "My uncle is coming to supper with us."

So she got up at once and went to the market street and bought everything she needed; then, coming back to the house, she borrowed from the neighbours whatever was wanted in the way of pans and dishes and so on. And when the meal was cooked and suppertime came, she said to Aladdin, "My child, the food is ready, but perhaps your uncle does not know the way to our house; so go out and meet him on the road."

He answered, "To hear is to obey"; and before the two of them had finished talking there was a knock at the door.

Aladdin went out and opened it, and there was the Moroccan magician, with a servant carrying the wine and the dessert fruit; so the lad led them in, and the servant went off about his business.

The Moroccan, on entering, greeted his sister-in-law with the salaam, and then began to shed tears and to question her, saying, "Where is the place where my brother used to sit?"

She showed it to him, and he went up to it and prostrated himself in prayer and kissed the floor, crying, "Ah, how small my satisfaction is and how luckless my lot, that I have lost you, my brother, vein of my eye!" And he went on in this fashion, weeping and wailing, until he fainted away from the violence of his sobbing and lamenting; so that Aladdin's mother was quite convinced he was telling the truth.

So she came up to him and raised him from the floor and said, "What good is there in killing yourself?"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Eighteenth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin's mother set about consoling the Moroccan magician and settled him on the divan; and as soon as he was comfortably seated, and before the food trays were brought in, he fell to talking with her and saying:

"Wife of my brother, it must seem a wonder to you that in all your days you never saw me, nor heard anything about me during the lifetime of my brother, who has found mercy. The reason is that forty years ago I left this town and exiled myself from my birthplace, and wandered over all the lands of India and Sind, and went into Egypt and settled a long time in its magnificent city, which is one of the wonders of the world; until at last I made my way to the regions of the Setting Sun and lived thirty years in the interior of Morocco.

"Now one day, sister-in-law, as I was sitting alone at home, I fell to thinking of my own country and my birthplace and my brother, who has found mercy; and my longing to see him grew so strong that I wept and bewailed being a stranger and so far away from him. And at last my longings drove me homewards, until I made up my mind to travel to the country where my head shall fall and where my homestead is, so that I might see my brother again.

"And I said to myself: Man, how long will you wander like a desert Arab, away from your birthplace and your native soil? Moreover, you have one brother and no more; so up with you and travel and look at him before you die, for who knows the woes of the world and the changes of the days? It would be the saddest regret if you lay down to die without ever seeing your brother — and Allah (praise be to the Lord!) has granted you ample wealth; and it may be that he is in straitened and poor circumstances, and then you will be able to help your brother as well as see him.

"So I got up at once and equipped myself for the journey and recited the Fatihah; and then, when Friday prayers were over, I mounted and travelled to this town, after suffering all sorts of toils and troubles which I bore patiently, while the Lord (to whom be honour and glory!) covered me with the veil of His protection.

"So I arrived; and while I was wandering about the streets, the day before yesterday, I saw my brother's son Aladdin playing with the boys. And by God the Great, sister-in-law, the moment I saw him this heart of mine went out to him — for blood yearns to blood — and my soul felt and told me that he was my very nephew. So I forgot all my toils and troubles at once at the sight of him, and I was ready to fly for joy. But when he told me that the dear one had departed to the mercy of Almighty Allah, I fainted away from the shock of my grief and disappointment. Perhaps my nephew has told you of the pains that overcame me. But I am consoled after a fashion by the sight of Aladdin, the legacy left to us by him who has found mercy; for whoever leaves offspring is not wholly dead."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Nineteenth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Moroccan magician said to Aladdin's mother, "Whoever leaves offspring is not wholly dead." And when he looked at his sister-in-law she wept at these words of his; so he turned to the lad, to make her forget the mention of her husband — as a way of comforting her, and also of completing his deception — and asked him, "My son Aladdin, what have you learned in the way of work, and what is your business? Tell me, have you mastered any trade by which you can earn a living for yourself and for your mother?"

The lad was abashed and put to shame, and he hung his head and bowed his face towards the ground. But his mother spoke out: "How, indeed? By Allah, he knows nothing at all. Such an ungracious child I never yet saw — no, never! All day long he idles away his time with the boys of the quarter, vagabonds like himself; and his father — oh, my grief! — died of nothing but sorrow over him. And I am now in a pitiful state myself: I spin cotton and toil at my distaff night and day, so that I may earn a couple of loaves of bread which we eat together. That is how things are, brother-in-law; and, by your life, he never comes near me except at mealtimes, and at no other. Indeed, I am thinking of locking the house door and never opening to him again, but leaving him to go and find a living he can live on; for I am a woman getting on in years now and have no strength left to work and go about earning a keep in this way. O Allah, I am forced to provide him with his daily bread when it is I who need providing for!"

At this the Moroccan turned to Aladdin and said, "Why is this, son of my brother? Why do you go about so ungraciously? It is a disgrace to you and unbecoming in a man like yourself. You are a lad with sense, my son, and the child of honest folk; so it is a shame for you that your mother, a woman in years, should struggle to support you. And now that you have grown to a man's estate it is for you to contrive some way of living, my child.

"Look around you — and praise be to Allah, in this town of ours there are many teachers of every kind of craft, and nowhere are there more of them. So choose some calling that pleases you, and I will set you up in it; and when you are grown, my son, you shall have a business to live by. Perhaps your father's trade is not to your liking; and if so, choose some other handicraft that suits your fancy, and let me know, and I will help you with everything I can, my son."

But when the Moroccan saw that Aladdin kept silence and made him no answer, he knew that the lad wanted no occupation but the life of a scapegrace; so he said to him, "Son of my brother, do not let my words seem hard and harsh to you; for if, in spite of everything I say, you still dislike learning a trade, I will open you a merchant's shop stocked with the costliest stuffs, and you shall become famous among people and take and give and buy and sell and be well known in the city."

Now when Aladdin heard his uncle the Moroccan's words, and his plan of making him a merchant and a gentleman, he was overjoyed, knowing that such people dress handsomely and live delicately. So he looked at the Moroccan, smiling and drooping his head towards the ground, and saying, in the language of the situation, that he was content.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Twentieth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Moroccan magician looked at Aladdin and saw him smiling, by which he understood that the lad was content to become a trader. So he said to him, "Since you are content that I should open you a merchant's shop and make a gentleman of you, then, son of my brother, prove yourself a man; and, God willing, tomorrow I will take you to the bazaar in the first place and have a fine suit of clothes cut out for you, the sort of thing merchants wear; and in the second place I will look out a shop for you and keep my word."

Now Aladdin's mother had had some doubts about the Moroccan being her brother-in-law; but as soon as she heard him promise to open a merchant's shop for her son and set him up with goods and capital and the rest of it, the woman decided and determined in her mind that this Moroccan was truly her husband's brother, seeing that no stranger would do such a good turn for her son.

So she began directing the lad into the right road, and teaching him to cast the ignorance out of his head and prove himself a man; moreover, she told him always to obey his excellent uncle as though he were his son, and to make up for the time he had wasted in wilfulness with his friends.

After this she got up and spread the table and served the supper; so they all sat down and fell to eating and drinking, while the Moroccan talked with Aladdin about matters of business and the like, delighting him to such a degree that he got no sleep that night.

But when the Moroccan saw that the dark hours were passing and the wine was drunk, he got up and hurried off to his own place; but before he went he agreed to come back next morning and take Aladdin and see to a suit of merchant's clothes being cut out for him.

And as soon as it was dawn, there was the Moroccan rapping at the door, which was opened by Aladdin's mother. He would not come in, though, but asked to take the lad with him to the market street. So Aladdin went out to his uncle and wished him good morning and kissed his hand; and the Moroccan took him by the hand and went with him to the bazaar.

There he went into a clothier's shop stocked with all kinds of clothes, and asked for the most sumptuous suit in it; and the merchant brought out what he wanted, all fashioned and ready sewn, and the Moroccan said to the lad, "Choose whatever pleases you, my child."

Aladdin was overjoyed to see that his uncle had given him his choice, so he picked out the suit that most took his fancy, and the Moroccan paid the merchant the price of it in ready money. Then he took the lad to the baths, where they bathed; and then they came out and drank sherbets, after which Aladdin got up and put on his new clothes in enormous joy and delight, and went up to his uncle and kissed his hand and thanked him for his kindness.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Twenty-first Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Moroccan magician, after leaving the baths with Aladdin, took him and walked with him to the merchants' bazaar; and, having entertained him by showing him the market and its buying and selling, said to him, "My son, it becomes you to get to know people, and merchants especially, so that you may learn the merchant's trade from them, seeing that it is your calling now."

Then he led him out and showed him the city and its great mosques, along with all the pleasant sights in it; and last of all he took him into a cook's shop. Here dinner was served to them on plates of silver, and they dined well and ate and drank their fill, after which they went on their way.

Presently the Moroccan pointed out to Aladdin the pleasure grounds and the noble buildings, and went in with him to the Sultan's palace and entertained him by showing him all the apartments, which were exceedingly fine and grand; and finally he led him to the merchants' caravanserai where he was lodging himself. Then he invited several of the traders who were staying there; and they came and sat down to supper, when he informed them that the youth was his nephew, Aladdin by name.

And after they had eaten and drunk and night had fallen, he got up and took the lad with him and led him back to his mother; who, the moment she saw her boy looking like one of the merchants, was out of her wits and grew almost sad from sheer gladness.

Then she fell to thanking her supposed relative, the Moroccan, for all his kindnesses, and said to him, "Brother-in-law, I could never say enough if I thanked you for the rest of your days and praised you for the good deeds you have done to this child of mine."

At which the Moroccan said, "Wife of my brother, do not think this mere kindness on my part; the lad is my own son, and it is my duty to stand in the place of my brother, his father. So be quite satisfied."

And she said, "I pray Allah, by the honour of the saints, the ancients and the moderns, that He preserve you and let you continue, brother-in-law, and prolong your life for my sake; so that you shall be a wing spread over this orphan boy, and he shall always be obedient to your orders and do nothing except what you tell him."

The Moroccan replied, "Wife of my brother, Aladdin is a young man of sense now, and the son of good people, and I hope to Allah that he will follow in his father's footsteps and be a comfort to your eyes. But I am sorry that tomorrow, being Friday, I shall not be able to open his shop, since it is the day of assembly, when all the merchants go out to the gardens and pleasure grounds after congregational prayer. On Saturday, though, God willing, we will do our business. Meanwhile I will come to you early tomorrow and take Aladdin for a pleasant walk to the gardens and pleasure grounds outside the city, which he may perhaps not have seen before. There he shall see the merchants and the notables who go out to amuse themselves, so that he may get to know them and they him."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Twenty-second Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Moroccan went away and slept that night in his lodgings; and early next morning he came to the tailor's house and rapped at the door.

Now Aladdin — what with the joy of the new clothes he had put on, and the previous day's enjoyment in the baths and in eating and drinking and looking at the people, and what with expecting his uncle to come at dawn and carry him off on an outing to the gardens — had not slept a wink that night nor closed his eyelids, and could hardly believe it when the day broke. But hearing the knock at the door he went out at once in a great hurry, like a spark of fire, and opened it and saw his uncle the magician, who embraced him and kissed him.

Then, taking his hand, the Moroccan said to him as they set off together, "Son of my brother, today I will show you a sight you never saw in all your life"; and he began to make the lad laugh and to cheer him with pleasant talk.

So they went out of the city gate, and the Moroccan took to walking about the gardens with Aladdin, pointing out for his pleasure the exceedingly fine pleasure grounds and the marvellous tall pavilions. And whenever they stopped to stare at a garden or a mansion or a palace, the Moroccan would say to his companion, "Does this please you, son of my brother?"

Aladdin was nearly flying with delight at seeing sights he had never seen in all his born days; and they went on strolling about and enjoying themselves until they grew tired, when they came into a very grand garden nearby, a place that delighted the heart and lit up the sight, for its swift-running rills flowed among the flowers and the water jetted from the jaws of lions moulded in yellow brass like gold.

So they sat down opposite a little lake and rested a while; and Aladdin enjoyed himself exceedingly and fell to joking with his uncle and making merry with him, as though the magician really were his father's brother.

Presently the Moroccan got up and, loosening his belt, drew out from under it a bag full of food, dried fruit and so on, saying to Aladdin, "Nephew, perhaps you have grown hungry; so come and eat what you need."

So the lad fell on the food and the Moroccan ate with him, and they were gladdened and cheered by the rest and the good cheer.

Then the magician said, "Get up, son of my brother, if you are rested, and let us stroll on a little and reach the end of our walk."

So Aladdin got up, and the Moroccan walked with him from garden to garden until they had left them all behind and reached the foot of a high, bare hill; when the lad — who had never in all his days been outside the city gate, and had never in his life walked such a walk as this — said to the Moroccan, "Uncle, where are we going? We have left the gardens behind us one and all and got into barren hill country; and if the way is still long, I have no strength left for walking. Indeed I am ready to drop with tiredness. There are no gardens ahead of us, so let us turn back and go home to town."

The magician said, "No, my son, this is the right road, and the gardens are not ended; for we are going to look at one that has no equal among the gardens of kings, and everything you have seen is nothing beside it. So screw up your courage to walk; you are a man now, praise be to Allah!"

Then the Moroccan fell to soothing Aladdin with soft words and telling him wonderful tales, lies as well as truth, until they reached the spot the African magician had in mind — the spot he had travelled from the Land of the Setting Sun to the regions of China for.

And when they got there the Moroccan said to Aladdin, "Son of my brother, sit down and take your rest, for this is the place we have been looking for; and, God willing, I will soon entertain you by showing you marvels the like of which nobody in the world ever saw, and no one has ever had the pleasure of gazing on what you are about to see."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Twenty-third Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Moroccan wizard said to Aladdin, "No created being has ever enjoyed the sights you are about to see. But when you are rested, get up and look for some wood chips and kindling sticks, small ones and dry, so that we may light a fire; and then I will show you, son of my brother, matters beyond the range of matter."

Now when the lad heard these words he longed to see what his uncle was going to do; and, forgetting how tired he was, he got straight up and fell to gathering small wood chips and dry sticks, and went on until the Moroccan called to him, "That is enough, son of my brother!"

Presently the magician brought out from his breast pocket a casket, which he opened, and took out of it as much incense as he needed; and then he fumigated and conjured and pronounced spells, muttering words nobody could understand. And immediately the ground split apart, after a thick gloom and a quaking of the earth and bellowings of thunder.

At this Aladdin was startled, and so terrified that he tried to run away. But when the African magician saw what he meant to do, he flew into a terrible rage; for without the lad his work would profit him nothing, since the hidden hoard he was trying to open could not be opened except by means of Aladdin.

So, noticing this attempt to run off, the magician got up and raised his hand and struck Aladdin such a blow on the head that his back teeth were nearly knocked out, and he fell to the ground in a faint. But after a time he came round by the magician's magic, and cried out, weeping all the while, "Uncle, what have I done to deserve a blow like that from you?"

At this the Moroccan fell to soothing him, and said, "My son, my intention is to make a man of you; so do not go against me, for I am your uncle and like a father to you. Obey me, then, in everything I tell you, and very soon you will forget all this labour and toil, when you look at the marvels I am about to show you."

And soon after the ground had split apart in front of the Moroccan, it showed a marble slab with a copper ring set in it. The Moroccan struck a geomantic table and turned to Aladdin and said, "If you do everything I tell you, you shall certainly become richer than any of the kings. And this, my son, is the reason I struck you: because there lies a hoard here that is stored in your name, and yet you meant to leave it and make off. But now collect your thoughts, and see how I have opened the earth by my spells and my conjurations."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Twenty-fourth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Moroccan magician said to Aladdin:

"My son, now collect your thoughts! Under that stone with the ring set in it lies the treasure I told you about. So put your hand on the ring and lift the slab; for nobody among all the people except yourself has the power to open it, and no mortal born but you may set foot inside this enchanted treasury, which has been kept for you. But you must learn from me everything I am going to charge you with, and not go against a single syllable of my words. All this, my child, is for your own good; the hoard is of immense value, such as the kings of the world never gathered — and remember that it is for you and for me."

So poor Aladdin forgot his weariness and the blow and his tears; and he was struck dumb and dazzled by the Moroccan's words, and rejoiced that he was fated to become rich in such measure that not even the Sultans would be richer than he was. So he cried, "Uncle, tell me to do whatever you please, for I will be obedient to your bidding."

The Moroccan replied, "Nephew, you are to me like my own child and even dearer, being my brother's son, and since I have no other kith or kin except yourself; and you, my child, are my heir and my successor."

So saying, he went up to Aladdin and kissed him and said, "Who is it I intend all this labour of mine for? Truly, every bit of it is for your sake, my son, so that I may leave you a rich man and one of the very greatest. So do not go against me in anything I say to you. And now go up to that ring and lift it up as I told you."

Aladdin answered, "Uncle, this ring is too heavy for me: I cannot lift it single-handed, so come forward yourself and lend me your strength and your help in lifting it, for indeed I am young in years."

The Moroccan replied, "Son of my brother, we shall find it impossible to do anything at all if I help you, and all our efforts will be wasted. But put your hand on the ring and pull it up, and you shall raise the slab at once — and indeed I told you that nobody can touch it except yourself. But while you are hauling at it, do not stop saying your own name and the names of your father and your mother, and it will come up to you immediately and you will not feel the weight of it."

At this the lad summoned up his strength and girded the loins of resolution and did as the Moroccan had told him, and heaved up the slab with perfect ease when he pronounced his own name and the names of his parents, exactly as the magician had bidden him. And as soon as the stone was up, he threw it aside.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Twenty-fifth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that after Aladdin had raised the slab from over the entrance to the hoard, there appeared before him an underground vault, with a flight of some twelve stairs leading down into it; and the Moroccan said:

"Aladdin, collect your thoughts, and do whatever I tell you down to the smallest detail, and do not fail in any part of it.

"Go down into that vault with all care until you reach the bottom, and there you will find a space divided into four halls; and in each of these you will see four jars of gold, and others of pure gold and silver. Take care, though, not to take anything from them or touch them, and do not even let your gown or its skirts so much as brush the jars or the walls. Leave them alone and go forward until you reach the fourth hall, without pausing for a single moment on the way; and if you do anything contrary to this, you will be transformed on the spot and become a black stone.

"When you reach the fourth hall you will find a door in it, which you must open; and, pronouncing the names you spoke over the slab, go through it into a garden planted everywhere with fruit-bearing trees. You must cross this by a path you will see in front of you, about fifty cubits long, beyond which you will come upon an open hall with a ladder in it of some thirty rungs. And you will also see, hanging from its ceiling —"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Twenty-sixth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Moroccan magician went on teaching Aladdin how he was to go down into the hoard, and continued:

"When you reach the hall you will find there a Lamp hanging from the ceiling. So climb the ladder and take that Lamp and put it in your breast pocket, after pouring out what is in it; and have no fear of harm to your clothes from it, because what is in it is not ordinary oil. And on your way back you are allowed to pick from the trees whatever you please, for it is all yours so long as the Lamp is in your hand."

Now when the Moroccan had finished his instructions to Aladdin, he drew off a seal ring and put it on the lad's forefinger, saying, "My son, this ring will free you from all hurt and all fear that may threaten you — but only on condition that you keep in mind everything I have told you.
