So get up straight away and go down the stairs, strengthening your purpose and girding the loins of resolution; and moreover have no fear, for you are a man now and no longer a child. And in a very short time, my son, you shall win yourself immense riches and become the wealthiest man in the world."

So Aladdin got up and went down into the vault, where he found the four halls, each with its four jars of gold; and these he passed by, as the Moroccan had told him, with the utmost care and caution. From there he went on into the garden and walked along the length of it until he came into the hall, where he climbed the ladder and took the Lamp, which he put out, pouring away the oil that was in it, and placed it in his breast pocket.

Then, coming down the ladder, he went back into the garden, where he fell to gazing at the trees, on which birds sat glorifying their great Creator with loud voices. Now he had not noticed them as he went in; but all these trees bore costly gems for fruit, and each had its own kind of growth and jewels of its own particular sort. And these were of every colour — green and white, yellow, red and other brilliant hues — and the radiance flashing from these gems put the rays of the mid-morning sun in the shade. Furthermore, the size of each stone was so far beyond describing that no king among the kings of the world owned a single gem equal to the larger sort, nor could boast of even one half the size of the smaller kind.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Twenty-seventh Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin walked among the trees and gazed at them and at other things that surprised the sight and bewildered the wits; and as he studied them, he saw that instead of ordinary fruit their produce was of very fine jewels and precious stones — emeralds and diamonds, rubies, spinels and balas rubies, pearls and other such gems, astounding to the mind's eye of any man.

And since the lad had never in all his born days seen anything like these, nor reached the years of discretion that would have taught him what such valuables were worth — he being still only a little lad — he supposed that all these jewels were made of glass or crystal.

So he collected them until he had filled his breast pockets, and began to satisfy himself as to whether they were or were not ordinary fruits, such as grapes and figs and other things one could eat. But finding them to be of a glassy substance, and being ignorant of precious stones and their prices, he gathered into his breast pockets every kind of growth the trees had to offer; and, having failed in his purpose of finding them to be food, he said in his mind, "I will collect a lot of these glass fruits to play with at home."

So he fell to picking them in quantities and cramming them into his pockets and his breast pockets until they were stuffed full; after which he picked more, which he put in his waist shawl, and then, girding himself with it, he carried off all he could manage, meaning to put them about the house as ornaments — and, as has been said, never imagining that they were anything but glass.

Then he hurried his pace, for fear of his uncle the Moroccan, until he had passed through the four halls and finally, on his way back, reached the vault, where he did not cast a glance at the jars of gold, although he was able and permitted to take some of what was in them on his way out.

But when he came to the vault stairs and climbed the steps until there was nothing left but the last one, he found this one higher than all the others, and he was unable, alone and unassisted and loaded down as he was, to get up it. So he said to the Moroccan, "Uncle, give me your hand and help me to climb."

But the Moroccan answered, "My son, give me the Lamp and lighten your load; it may well be that that is what is weighing you down."

The lad answered, "Uncle, it is not the Lamp weighing me down at all; but do give me a hand, and as soon as I reach the ground I will give it to you."

At this the Moroccan magician, whose only object was the Lamp and nothing else, began to insist on Aladdin giving it to him at once. But the lad, having put it at the bottom of his breast pocket, and his other pouches being full of gems and bulging outwards, could not get his fingers to it to hand it over. So the wizard, after a great deal of useless insistence on being given what his nephew was unable to give, fell to raging with a furious rage and demanding the Lamp, while Aladdin could not get at it.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Twenty-eighth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin could not get at the Lamp to hand it to his uncle the Moroccan, that false villain; so the magician grew foolish with fury at being unable to get what he wanted. And yet the lad had promised truthfully that he would give it up as soon as he could reach the ground, with no lying thought and no ill intent.

But when the Moroccan saw that he would not hand it over, he grew exceedingly angry and gave up all hope of winning it; so he conjured and pronounced spells and threw incense into the middle of the fire, and immediately the slab made a lid of itself and by the power of magic closed the entrance; the earth buried the stone as it had been before, and Aladdin, unable to get out, was left underground.

Now the sorcerer was a stranger and, as we have said, no uncle of Aladdin's at all; he had misrepresented himself and put forward a lying claim, so that he might get hold of the Lamp by means of the lad for whom the hoard had been stored up. So the accursed man heaped the earth over him and left him to die of hunger.

For this Moroccan was an African of Africa proper, born in the interior of the Land of the Setting Sun; and from his earliest years he had been addicted to witchcraft and had studied and practised every kind of occult science, for which unholy learning the city of Africa is notorious. And he never left off reading and hearing lectures until he had become a past master of all such knowledge.

And out of the abounding skill in spells and conjurations that he had acquired by forty years of reading and being taught, one day he discovered by devilish inspiration that there lay in a far city of the cities of China, named al-Kalas, an immense hoard, the like of which none of the kings of this world had ever gathered; and, moreover, that the most marvellous article in this enchanted treasure was a wonderful Lamp, of which whoever had possession could not possibly be surpassed by any man on earth, either in high rank or in wealth and riches; nor could the mightiest monarch in the universe attain to the all-sufficiency of this Lamp with all its magical power.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Twenty-ninth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Moroccan had assured himself by his science and had seen that this hoard could only be opened by the presence of a lad named Aladdin, of a poor family and living in that very city, and had learned how easy the taking of it would be and free of hardships, he immediately and without pause or delay equipped himself for the voyage to China, as we have already told; and he did what he did with Aladdin, fancying that he would become Lord of the Lamp.

But his attempt and his hopes were baffled and his work was entirely wasted; whereupon, determining to put the lad to death, he heaped the earth over him by sorcery, so that the unfortunate boy might perish, reflecting that a live man has nobody to murder him. And secondly, he did it with the intention that, since Aladdin could not come out from underground, he would also be powerless to bring the Lamp out of the vault.

So presently he went his way and retired to his own country, Africa, a sadder man, and disappointed of all his expectations.

Such was the case with the wizard. But as for Aladdin, when the earth was heaped over him he began shouting to the Moroccan, whom he still believed to be his uncle, begging him to lend a hand so that he might get out of the vault and come back up to the surface of the earth; but however loudly he cried, nobody was found to answer.

At that moment he understood the trick the Moroccan had played on him, and that the man was no uncle but a liar and a wizard. Then the unhappy boy despaired of life, and learned to his sorrow that there was no way out for him; so he fell to weeping bitterly at the calamity that had come upon him.

And after a while he stood up and went down the stairs to see whether Almighty Allah had lightened his load of grief by leaving a way out. So he turned to the right and to the left, but he saw nothing except darkness, and four walls shut upon him; for the magician had by his magic locked all the doors and had even shut up the garden the lad had walked through, in case it should offer him some means of getting out onto the surface of the earth, so that he should be sure to die.

Then Aladdin's weeping grew more bitter and his wailing louder, when he found all the doors fast shut; for he had thought to console himself for a while in the garden. But when he found that everything was locked, he fell to shedding tears and lamenting like a man who has lost his every hope, and went back to sit on the stairs of the flight he had come down into the vault by.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Thirtieth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin sat down on the stair of the vault, weeping and wailing and wanting all hope.

But it is a light matter for Allah (be He exalted and extolled!), when He intends anything, to say "Be", and it comes to be; for He creates joy in the middle of annoyance. And so it was with Aladdin.

While the Moroccan magician was sending him down into the vault, he had put a seal ring on his finger by way of a gift, and had said, "Truly, this ring shall save you out of every strait, if you fall into calamity and the ill turns of time; and it shall take away from you all hurt and harm, and help you with a strong arm wherever you may be set down."

Now this was by the destiny of God the Great, that it might be the means of Aladdin's escape. For while he sat wailing and weeping over his situation, and had thrown away all hope of life, and utter misery had overwhelmed him, he rubbed his hands together in the excess of his sorrow, as unhappy people do; and then, raising them in supplication to Allah, he cried:

"I testify that there is no God but You alone, the Most Great, the Omnipotent, the All-Conquering, the Quickener of the dead, the Creator of man's need and the Granter of it, the Resolver of his difficulties and his distress and the Bringer of joy and not of annoyance. You are my sufficiency, and You are the Truest of Trustees. And I bear witness that Mohammed is Your servant and Your Apostle; and I beg You, my God, by his favour with You, to free me from this foul plight I am in."

And while he was imploring the Lord and chafing his hands in the soreness of his sorrow for what had happened to him, his fingers happened to rub the Ring — when, lo and behold, its familiar rose up before him and cried, "Here I am! Your slave stands between your hands. Ask whatever you want, for I am the servant of him who has the Ring on his hand, the seal ring of my lord and master."

At this the lad looked at him and saw standing in front of him a marid like one of the ifrits of our lord Solomon's jinn. He trembled at the terrible sight; but, hearing the Slave of the Ring say, "Ask whatever you want; truly I am your servant, seeing that my lord's ring is on your finger," he got his spirits back and remembered the Moroccan's words when he gave him the Ring.

So he rejoiced greatly and grew brave, and cried, "You there, Slave of the Lord of the Ring, I want you to set me on the face of the earth."

And he had hardly finished speaking when the ground split apart and he found himself at the door of the hoard, outside it and in full view of the world.

Now for three whole days he had been sitting in the darkness of the treasury underground, and when the light of day and the shining of the sun struck his face he found he could not keep his eyes open; so he began to open the lids a little and shut them a little, until his eyeballs got their strength back and grew used to the light and were purged of the foul murk.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Thirty-first Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell me one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin, having come out of the treasury, opened his eyes after a short time and saw himself on the surface of the earth, which delighted him exceedingly. And yet he was astonished to find himself outside the hoard door he had gone in by when it was opened by the Moroccan magician — especially as the opening had been lidded over and the ground smoothed out, with no sign at all of any entrance.

At this his surprise grew until he half thought he was in some other place, and his mind was not convinced that the spot was the same until he saw the place where they had kindled the fire of wood chips and dried sticks, and where the African wizard had conjured over the incense. Then he turned to right and left and caught sight of the gardens far off, and his eyes recognised the road he had come by.

So he gave thanks to Almighty Allah, who had restored him to the face of the earth and freed him from death after he had given up all hope of life. Then he got up and walked along the way to the town, which he now knew well, until he came into the streets and went on to his own home.

Then he went in to his mother; and at the sight of her, with the overwhelming stress of joy at his escape, and the memory of his past fright and the hardships he had endured and the pangs of hunger, he fell to the ground in front of her in a dead faint.

Now his mother had been utterly wretched since the time he left her, and he found her moaning and crying about him; and on seeing him come into the house she rejoiced exceedingly, but was at once overwhelmed with grief when he sank to the ground in a swoon before her eyes.

Still, she did not neglect the matter or treat it lightly, but hurried at once to sprinkle water on his face, and afterwards asked the neighbours for some scents, which she made him breathe in.

And when he had come round a little, he begged her to bring him something to eat, saying, "Mother, it is three days now since I ate anything at all."

At this she got up and brought him what she had by her; and then, setting it in front of him, said, "Come along, my son; eat and be cheered; and when you have rested you shall tell me what has happened to you and upset you so, my child. Just now I will not question you, for you are truly worn out."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Thirty-second Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell me one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin ate and drank and was cheered; and after he had rested and got his spirits back, he cried:

"Ah, mother, I have a bitter grievance against you for leaving me to that accursed creature who tried to bring about my destruction and meant to take my life. Know that I saw Death with my own eyes at the hand of this damned wretch, whom you assured me was my uncle; and if Almighty Allah had not rescued me from him, both you and I, mother, would have been cheated by the excess of this accursed man's promises to do me good, and by the great show of affection he made to us.

"Understand, mother, that this fellow is a sorcerer, a Moor, an accursed man, a liar, a traitor and a hypocrite; nor do I believe that the devils under the earth are as damnable as he is. Allah abase him in his every book!

"Listen, then, mother, to what this abominable man did; and everything I tell you will be true and certain. See how the damned villain broke every promise he made, assuring me that he would soon bring me nothing but good; and consider the fondness he showed me and the things he did for me — and all of it only to get what he wanted, for his design was to destroy me. And praise be to the Lord for my deliverance! Listen and learn, mother, how this accursed man treated me."

Then Aladdin told his mother everything that had happened to him, weeping all the while for the stress of his gladness — how the Moroccan had led him to a hill in which the hoard was hidden, and how he had conjured and fumigated. And he added:

"After that, mother, a mighty fear took hold of me when the hill split and the earth gaped in front of me by his wizardry; and I trembled with terror at the rolling of the thunder in my ears and the murk that fell on us when he fumigated and muttered spells. Seeing these horrors, in my fright I meant to run away; but when he understood what I intended he abused me and struck me such a blow that it made me faint.

"However, seeing that the treasury could only be opened by means of me, mother, he could not go down into it himself, it being in my name and not in his; and since he is an ill-omened magician, he understood that I was necessary to him, and that was his need of me."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Thirty-third Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell me one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin acquainted his mother with everything that had happened to him at the hands of the Moroccan magician, and said:

"After he had struck me, he thought it best to soothe me so that he could send me down into the enchanted treasury; and first he drew a Ring off his own finger and put it on mine. So I went down and found four halls, all full of gold and silver, which counted for nothing, and the accursed man had charged me not to touch any of it. Then I went into a very fine flower garden, decked out everywhere with tall trees whose leaves and fruit bewildered the wits — for all of them, mother, were of many-coloured glass — and at last I reached the hall where this Lamp was hanging. So I took it straight away and put it out and poured out what was in it."

And so saying, Aladdin drew the Lamp out of his breast pocket and showed it to his mother, along with the gems and jewels he had brought from the garden; and there were two large bagfuls of precious stones, not one of which was to be found among the kings of the world. But the lad knew nothing about their worth, supposing them to be glass or crystal.

And presently he went on: "After this, mother, I reached the hoard door carrying the Lamp, and shouted to the accursed sorcerer, who called himself my uncle, to give me a hand and haul me up, since I could not get up the last step by myself for the great weight of my load. But he would not, and only said, 'First hand me the Lamp!' However, as I had put it at the bottom of my breast pocket, and the other pouches bulged out beyond it, I could not get at it, and said, 'Uncle, I cannot reach you the Lamp, but I will give it to you when I am outside the treasury.'

"His only need was the Lamp, and he meant, mother, to snatch it from me and after that kill me — as indeed he did his best to do, by heaping the earth over my head. That, then, is what happened to me at the hands of this foul sorcerer."

At this Aladdin fell to abusing the magician in hot anger and with a burning heart, crying, "Away with him! I take refuge from this damned creature, the ill-omened, the wrongdoer, the perjurer, the man lost to all humanity, the arch-traitor, the hypocrite, the annihilator of pity and mercy!"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Thirty-fourth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when Aladdin's mother heard his words and what had happened to him at the hands of the Moroccan magician, she said, "Yes indeed, my son, he is a miscreant and a hypocrite who murders people by his magic; but it was the grace of Almighty Allah, my child, that saved you from the tricks and the treachery of this accursed sorcerer, whom I took to be truly your uncle."

Then, as the lad had not slept a wink for three days and found himself nodding, he went to get his natural rest, and his mother did the same; nor did he wake until about noon on the second day.

As soon as he had shaken off his sleep he called for something to eat, being very hungry indeed; but his mother said, "My son, I have no food for you, since yesterday you ate everything there was in the house. But wait patiently a while: I have spun a little yarn which I will carry to the market street and sell, and buy you some food with whatever it fetches."

"Mother," said he, "keep your yarn and do not sell it; but fetch me the Lamp I brought here, so that I may go and sell it and buy provisions with the price of it; for I think it will bring in more money than the spinning."

So Aladdin's mother got up and fetched the Lamp for her son; but while she was doing it she saw that it was exceedingly dirty, and so she said, "My son, here is the Lamp, but it is very filthy: once we have washed it and polished it, it will sell better."

Then, taking a handful of sand, she began to rub it — and she had hardly begun when there appeared to her one of the jann, whose face was frightful and whose bulk was horribly big, and he was gigantic as one of the giants. And straight away he cried to her, "Say what you want of me! Here I am, your slave, and the slave of whoever holds the Lamp — and not I alone, but all the Slaves of the Wonderful Lamp you have there in your hand."

She quaked, and terror was heavy on her when she looked at that frightful figure; and her tongue was tied so that she could make no reply at all, never having been used to seeing anything of the sort.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Thirty-fifth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin's mother was too terrified to make any answer to the marid; indeed she fell to the ground, overcome with fright.

Now her son was standing a little way off, and he had already seen the jinni of the Ring which he had rubbed inside the treasury; so when he heard the slave speaking to his mother he hurried forward and, snatching the Lamp out of her hand, said, "Slave of the Lamp, I am hungry, and it is my wish that you fetch me something to eat — and let it be something tasty, beyond our means."

The jinni disappeared for the twinkling of an eye and came back with a very fine tray and a costly one, for it was all of virgin silver; and on it stood twelve golden dishes of all kinds of meats and delicate dainties, with bread whiter than snow; also two silver cups and two flagons of wine, clear-strained and long-stored. And after setting all these in front of Aladdin, he vanished out of sight.

At this the lad went and sprinkled rose water on his mother's face and made her breathe in pure sharp perfumes, and said to her when she came round, "Get up, mother, and let us eat some of this food, with which Almighty Allah has eased our poverty."

But when she saw that very fine silver tray she fell to marvelling at the business, and said, "My son, who is this generous, this open-handed person who has taken away our hunger pains and our poverty? We are truly under an obligation to him; and it seems to me it is the Sultan who, hearing of our mean condition and our misery, has sent us this tray of food."

He said, "Mother, this is no time for questions: get up, and let us eat, for we are both starving."

So they sat down to the tray and fell to eating; and Aladdin's mother tasted meats whose like she had never touched in all her life. So they devoured them with sharpened appetites and with all the capacity that comes of extreme hunger; and, besides, the food was such as marks the tables of kings. But neither of them knew whether the tray was valuable or not, for never in their born days had they set eyes on anything like it.

As soon as they had finished the meal — leaving enough food, all the same, for supper and for the next day too — they got up and washed their hands and sat down to talk; and the mother turned to her son and said, "Tell me, my child, what happened to you with the slave, the jinni? For now, praise be to the Lord, we have eaten our fill of the good things He has favoured us with, and you have no excuse for saying to me, 'I am hungry.'"

So Aladdin told her everything that had passed between him and the slave while she had lain on the ground in a faint from sheer terror; and at this she was seized with great astonishment, and said, "That is true; for the jinn do present themselves before the sons of Adam. But I, my son, never saw them in all my life; and it seems to me that this is the same one who saved you when you were inside the enchanted hoard."

"This is not he, mother: this one who appeared to you is the Slave of the Lamp!"

"And who may that be, my son?"

"This is a slave of another kind and shape from him. That one was the familiar of the Ring; and this fellow of his that you saw was the slave of the Lamp you were holding in your hand."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Thirty-sixth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin said, "Truly, mother, the jinni who appeared to you was the slave of the Lamp."

And when his mother heard these words she cried, "There! There! So this accursed creature who showed himself to me and came near to killing me with fright is attached to the Lamp!"

"Yes," he replied.

And she answered, "Now I beg you, my son, by the milk I suckled you with, to throw this Lamp and this Ring away from you; because they can bring us nothing but the most extreme terror, and I in particular can never bear to set eyes on them a second time. Besides, all dealings with them are unlawful, for the Prophet (whom Allah save and keep!) warned us against them with threats."

He replied, "Your commands, mother, are upon my head and my eyes; but as for this thing you have said, it is impossible for me to part either with the Lamp or with the Ring. You have seen yourself what good the slave did us when we were starving. And understand, mother, that the Moroccan, the liar, the magician, when he sent me down into the hoard, wanted neither the silver nor the gold that filled the four halls, but charged me to bring him the Lamp and nothing else — because in truth he had learned what its priceless value was. And if he had not been certain of it, he would never have endured all that toil and trouble, nor travelled from his own country to ours in search of it; nor would he have shut me up in the treasury when he despaired of the Lamp I would not hand over to him.

"So it becomes us, mother, to keep this Lamp and take every care of it, and not to disclose its secrets to anybody; for this is our means of living now, and this is what shall make us rich. And as for the Ring, I will never take it off my finger, seeing that but for this you would never have seen me alive again — no, I should have died inside the hoard underground. How then could I possibly take it off my finger? And who knows what may happen to me as time goes by, what slips or calamities or injurious mishaps this Ring may deliver me from? However, out of regard for your feelings I will put the Lamp away, and never let it be seen by you again."

Now when his mother heard his words and thought them over she knew they were true, and said to him, "Do whatever you like, my son; for my part I never wish to see them again, nor ever to set eyes on that frightful spectacle I saw before."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Thirty-seventh Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin and his mother went on eating the food the jinni had brought them for two full days, until it was finished. But when he found that no food was left for them, he got up and took one of the dishes the slave had brought on the tray. Now they were all of the finest gold, but the lad knew nothing about that.

So he carried it to the bazaar, and there, seeing a dealer, a Jewish man, he offered it to him for sale. When the dealer caught sight of it he took the lad aside where nobody could see him, and looked the dish over and studied it until he was certain that it was of refined gold. But he did not know whether Aladdin was aware of its value or was a raw boy in such matters, so he asked him, "How much for this dish, sir?"

And the other answered, "You know what it is worth."

The dealer debated with himself how much he should offer, since Aladdin had given him a tradesman's answer; and he thought of the lowest possible valuation, while at the same time he was afraid that the lad might know its worth and expect a considerable sum. So he said in his mind, "Very likely the fellow is an ignoramus in these matters and does not know the price of the dish."

Whereupon he pulled a dinar out of his pocket; and Aladdin, seeing the gold piece lying in his palm, took it hastily and went his way — by which the dealer was assured that his customer knew nothing whatever about such things, and repented with entire repentance that he had given him a gold dinar instead of a copper coin, a bright-polished groat.

Aladdin, however, made no delay, but went straight to the baker's, where he bought bread and got change for the coin; and then, going to his mother, he gave her the loaves and the small change that was left, and said, "Mother, off you go and buy everything we need."

So she got up and walked to the bazaar and laid in the necessary stock; after which they ate and were cheered.

And whenever the price of the dish was spent, Aladdin would take another and carry it to the same dealer, who bought every one of them at a pitiful price; and he would have paid even less, only that, having given a dinar for the first, he was afraid to offer a smaller sum in case the lad should go and sell to some rival in the trade and so lose him his profits.

Now when all the golden dishes had been sold there remained only the silver tray they had stood on; and, as it was large and heavy, Aladdin brought the dealer to his house and produced the article, and the buyer, seeing the size of it, gave him ten dinars; and these being accepted, he went his way.

Aladdin and his mother lived on the coins until they were spent; and then he brought out the Lamp and rubbed it, and immediately there appeared the slave who had shown himself before.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Thirty-eighth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the jinni, the slave of the Lamp, on appearing to Aladdin said, "Ask, my lord, whatever you want; for I am your slave and the servant of whoever has the Lamp."

And the lad said, "I want you to bring me a tray of food like the one you brought me before, for I am starving."

So in the glance of an eye the slave produced a similar tray carrying twelve dishes of the most sumptuous kind, furnished with everything required; and on it stood clean bread and several glass bottles of strained wine.

Now Aladdin's mother had gone out when she knew he was about to rub the Lamp, so that she should not have to look at the jinni again; but after a while she came back, and when she caught sight of the tray covered with silver dishes and smelt the savour of the rich meats spreading through the house, she marvelled and rejoiced.

At this he said, "Look, mother! You told me to throw the Lamp away — see now what its virtues are."

And she said, "My son, Allah increase his welfare; but I would rather not look at him."

Then the lad sat down with his mother to the tray, and they ate and drank until they were satisfied; after which they put away what was left for the next day.

As soon as the food was eaten, Aladdin got up and stowed one of the dishes away under his clothes and went out to find the dealer, meaning to sell it to him. But by the decree of Fate he passed the shop of an old jeweller, an honest man and a pious one who feared Allah.

When the old man saw the lad he asked him, "My son, what is it you want? For I have seen you pass this way many times and do business with that dealer, and I have watched you hand over various articles to him; and now I fancy you have something for sale and are looking for him as a buyer. But you do not know, my child, that this man holds it lawful to take the goods of anybody who comes to him, and always defrauds them; and you have fallen into his hands. If, then, my son, you have anything you want to sell, show it to me and have no fear, for I will give you the full price of it, by the truth of Almighty Allah."

At this Aladdin brought out the dish; and when the old goldsmith saw it he took it and weighed it in his scales and asked the lad, "Was it the fellow of this that you sold to him?"

"Yes, its fellow and its brother," he answered.

And the old man said, "What price did he pay you?"

And the lad said, "One dinar."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Thirty-ninth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the old goldsmith heard from Aladdin that the dealer used to give him only one dinar as the price of a dish, he cried, "Ah! I take refuge from a man who cheats the servants of Almighty Allah!"

Then, looking at the lad, he exclaimed, "My son, that tricky fellow has swindled you and laughed at you; for this dish is pure silver and virgin, and I have weighed it and found it worth seventy dinars. And if you care to take its value, take it."

At this the old man counted out seventy gold pieces to him, which he accepted; and presently he thanked him for his kindness in exposing the dealer's rascality.

And after this, whenever the price of a dish was spent he would bring another; and in this way he and his mother were soon in better circumstances. Yet they went on living in their old style, as middle-class people, without spending too much on food or squandering money.

But Aladdin had now thrown off the ungraciousness of his boyhood: he shunned the company of scapegraces and began to keep company with good men and true, going every day to the merchants' market street and there associating with the great and the small of them, asking about matters of merchandise and learning the price of investments and so on. He also frequented the bazaars of the goldsmiths and the jewellers, where he would sit and amuse himself by inspecting their precious stones and by noting how jewels were bought and sold there.

And so presently he became aware that the fruits of those trees, which he had filled his pockets with when he went into the enchanted treasury, were neither glass nor crystal but gems, rich and rare; and he understood that he had come by immense wealth, such as kings can never possess. He then considered all the precious stones there were in the jewellers' quarter, and found that their biggest was not worth his smallest.

In this way he went on, going to the bazaar every day and making himself familiar with the people and winning their good will, and asking about selling and buying, giving and taking, the dear and the cheap — until one day, when, after getting up at dawn and putting on his clothes, he went out as usual to the jewellers' bazaar; and as he was passing along it he heard the crier crying as follows:

"By command of our magnificent master, the King of the Time and the Lord of the Age and the Tide: let all the people lock up their shops and their stores and go inside their houses, for the Lady Badr al-Budur, the Sultan's daughter, intends to visit the baths; and whoever disobeys the order shall be punished with the death penalty, and his blood be on his own neck!"

But when Aladdin heard the proclamation he longed to look upon the King's daughter, and said in his mind, "Indeed, all the people talk of her beauty and loveliness, and the end of my desires is to see her."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fortieth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin fell to contriving some way of getting a look at the Princess Badr al-Budur, and at last judged it best to take up his station behind the door of the baths, where he could see her face as she went in.

So without pause or delay he went off to the baths before she was expected, and stood at the back of the entrance, in a place where none of the people happened to be looking.

Now when the Sultan's daughter had gone the rounds of the city and its main streets, and had enjoyed herself sightseeing, she came at last to the baths; and as she was going in she raised her veil, and her face rose before the sight like a pearl of price or a shining sun; and she was one of whom the poet sang:

	Magic kohl enchants the bright glances of her;
	we pluck roses in posies from the rosy cheeks of her.
	The gloom of the hair of her is the gloomiest hue of night,
	and her bright brow lights up all the murk of the night of her.

(Says the reciter:) when the Princess raised the veil from her face and Aladdin saw her looks, he said, "In very truth her fashioning magnifies her Almighty Fashioner; and glory be to Him who created her and adorned her with this beauty and loveliness."

His strength was struck down from the moment he saw her, and his thoughts were scattered; his gaze was dazzled and the love of her took hold of the whole of his heart; and when he went home to his mother he was like a man in a trance.

His mother spoke to him, but he neither answered nor denied; and when she set the morning meal before him he was still the same. So she said, "My son, what can have happened to you? Tell me, is anything wrong with you? Let me know what harm has come to you; for, quite unlike your custom, you do not speak when I speak to you."

At this Aladdin — who used to think that all women were like his mother, and who, although he had heard of the charms of Badr al-Budur, the Sultan's daughter, had no idea what "beauty" and "loveliness" might mean — turned to his mother and exclaimed, "Let me be!"

However, she went on begging him to come and eat; so he did as she asked, but hardly touched the food; after which he lay at full length on his bed all night long, deep in thought, until the morning came. And he was in the same condition the next day, when his mother was perplexed at the state of her son and unable to find out what had happened to him.

So, thinking that perhaps he was ill, she came close to him and asked, "My son, if you feel any pain or anything of that kind, let me know, so that I may go out and fetch you the doctor; and today there is in this city of ours a physician from the Land of the Arabs, whom the Sultan has sent to summon, and rumour has it he is exceedingly skilful. So if you are ill, let me go and bring him to you."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-first Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin, hearing his mother offer to send for the physician, said, "Mother, I am well in body and in no way ill. But I always thought that all women were like you, until yesterday, when I saw the Lady Badr al-Budur, the Sultan's daughter, as she was going to the baths."

Then he told her everything that had happened to him, and added, "Perhaps you too heard the crier crying, 'Let no man open a shop or stand in the street, so that the Lady Badr al-Budur may go to the baths without an eye seeing her.' But I have looked upon her just as she is, for she raised her veil at the door; and when I saw her face and beheld that noble work of the Creator, a violent fit of ecstasy fell on me, mother, for love of her; and a firm resolve to win her has opened its way into every limb of me, and there is no rest possible for me unless I win her. So I intend to ask the Sultan her father for her hand in lawful marriage."

When Aladdin's mother heard her son's words she thought little of his wits, and cried, "My child, the name of Allah be upon you! It seems to me you have lost your senses. Be rightly guided, my son, and do not be like the men the jinn have maddened!"

He replied, "No, mother, I am not out of my mind, nor am I one of the madmen; and what you say will not alter one jot of what is in my thoughts, for rest is impossible to me until I have won the darling of my heart's core, the beautiful Lady Badr al-Budur. And now I am resolved to ask her of her father the Sultan."

She answered, "My son, by my life upon you, do not talk like this, in case anybody overhears you and says you are insane; so throw such nonsense away from you! Who would undertake a business like this, or make such a request of the King? Indeed, supposing this talk of yours were serious, I do not know how you would manage to beg such a favour of the Sultan, or through whom you would want to put it forward."

He retorted, "Through whom should I ask it, mother, when you are here? And who is there who loves me and is more faithful to me than you are? So my plan is that you yourself shall put forward this petition of mine."

She said, "My son, Allah keep me far from it! What — have I lost my wits like you? Throw the thought away, and a long way from your heart. Remember whose son you are, my child — the orphan boy of a tailor, the poorest and meanest of all the tailors working in this city; and I, your mother, come of poor and needy people too. How then do you dare ask for the Sultan's daughter in marriage, when her father would not condescend to marry her to the sons of kings and sovereigns unless they were his peers in honour and grandeur and majesty — and if they were even one degree lower, he would refuse her to them?"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-second Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin waited patiently until his mother had said her say, and then said, "Mother, everything you have called to mind is known to me; and moreover I know perfectly well that I am the child of poor parents. Nevertheless these words of yours do not turn me from my purpose at all, not at all. And I still hope of you, if I am your son and you truly love me, that you will grant me this favour; otherwise you will destroy me, for present Death is hovering over my head unless I win my will of my heart's darling; and I, mother, am your child whatever happens."

Hearing these words, his mother wept out of her sorrow for him and said, "My child! Yes, indeed I am your mother, and I have no son and no lifeblood of my liver except yourself, and the end of my wishes is to get you a wife and take joy in you. But suppose I looked for a bride among our own likes and equals: her people would at once ask whether you had any land or garden, any merchandise or trade, by which you could support her; and what answer could I make?

"Then, if I cannot possibly answer poor people like ourselves, how shall I be bold enough, my son, to ask for the daughter of the Sultan of China, who has no equal either behind him or before him? So weigh this matter in your mind. And who is to ask her in marriage for the son of a tailor? I know very well that saying anything of the sort will only increase our misfortunes; for it may be the cause of our falling into mortal danger from the Sultan — perhaps even death, for you and for me.

"And as far as I am concerned, how am I to venture on such a rash and perilous deed, my son? In what way am I to ask the Sultan for his daughter to be your wife; and, indeed, how am I ever to get near him at all? And if I do succeed in that, what am I to answer if they ask me about your means? Very likely the King will take me for a madwoman. And, last of all, suppose I do get an audience with the Sultan — what offering is there that I can lay before the King's majesty?"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-third Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin's mother went on to her son: "It is true, my child, that the Sultan is mild and merciful, and never turns away anybody who comes to him asking for justice or pity or protection, nor anybody who begs him for a present; for he is generous and lavishes his favours on far and near. But he deals out his gifts to those who deserve them — to men who have done some daring deed in battle before his eyes, or have rendered some great service to his state as civilians.

"But you! Tell me what feat you have performed in his presence or before the public, that you should deserve such a favour from him? And, secondly, this boon you are ambitious for is not for one of our condition, nor is it possible that the King should grant you the goal of your aspiration. For whoever goes to the Sultan and begs a favour of him ought to take in hand something that suits the royal majesty, as indeed I warned you before. How, then, are you to risk yourself standing before the Sultan and asking for his daughter in marriage, when you have nothing with you to offer him that befits his exalted station?"

To this Aladdin replied, "Mother, you speak to the point and have reminded me rightly, and it is proper that I should turn over in my mind everything you have reminded me of. But, mother, the love of Princess Badr al-Budur has entered into the core of my heart, and I cannot rest unless I win her. However, you have also called back to my mind something I had forgotten, and it is this that emboldens me to ask the King for his daughter. Although you declare, mother, that I have no gift I can lay before the Sultan, as the way of the world is, yet in very truth I have an offering and a present whose equal, mother, I do not believe any of the kings possesses — no, nor anything like it."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-fourth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin said to his mother:

"Because in fact what I took for glass or crystal was nothing but precious stones; and I hold that all the kings of the world have never possessed anything like one of the smallest of them. For by going about among the jewellers I have learned that they are the costliest gems, and these are what I brought back in my pockets from the hoard; so, if you please, set your mind at rest.

"We have in the house a bowl of Chinese porcelain; so get up and fetch it, and I will fill it with these jewels, which you shall carry as a gift to the King; and you shall stand in his presence and ask him for what I want. I am certain that by this means the business will become easy for you. And if you are unwilling, mother, to make the effort to win what I wish for as regards the Lady Badr al-Budur, know that I shall certainly die.

"And do not imagine that this gift is anything but the costliest of stones; and be assured, mother, that in my many visits to the jewellers' bazaar I have watched the merchants selling, for sums beyond a man's judgment, jewels whose beauty is not worth a quarter of a carat of what we have. Seeing which, I was certain that ours are beyond all price. So get up, mother, as I asked you, and bring me that porcelain bowl, so that I may arrange some of these gems in it and we can see what they look like."

So she brought him the Chinese bowl, saying to herself, "I shall know what to do when I find out whether my child's words about these jewels are true or not"; and she set it in front of her son, who pulled the stones out of his pockets and arranged them in the bowl, and went on arranging gems of all sorts in it until he had filled it.

And when it was brimful she could not fix her eyes steadily on it; on the contrary, she winked and blinked at the dazzle of the stones and their radiance and the excess of their lightning-like flash; and her wits were bewildered by it. Only, she was not convinced that their value was really as enormous as she had been told. And yet she reflected that possibly her son had spoken rightly when he declared that their like was not to be found with kings.

Then Aladdin turned to her and said, "You have seen, mother, that this present intended for the Sultan is magnificent, and I am certain it will get you high honour with him, and that he will receive you with all respect. And now, mother, you have no excuse; so compose your thoughts and get up; take this bowl and away with it to the palace."

His mother answered, "My son, it is true that the present is exceedingly high-priced and the costliest of the costly, and also that, as you say, nobody owns its like. But who would have the boldness to go and ask the Sultan for his daughter, the Lady Badr al-Budur? I certainly dare not say to him, 'I want your daughter!' when he asks me, 'What is it you want?' — for you must understand, my son, that my tongue will be tied.

"And granting that Allah helps me and I embolden myself to say to him, 'My wish is to become a connection of yours by the marriage of your daughter, the Lady Badr al-Budur, to my son Aladdin' — they will certainly decide on the spot that I am demented, and will throw me out in disgrace and despised. I will not tell you that I shall thereby fall into danger of death, for it will not only be me but you as well.

"However, my son, out of regard for your inclination, I must embolden myself and go there. And yet, my child, if the King receives me and honours me on account of the gift, and asks me what it is you want —"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-fifth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin's mother said to her son, "— and in answer I ask him for what you want in the matter of your marriage with his daughter, how am I to answer him if he asks me, as men do, What estates have you, and what income? And perhaps, my son, he will ask me that before he asks me about you."

Aladdin replied, "It is not possible that the Sultan should make such a demand at the moment when he is looking at the jewels and their magnificence; nor is it right to think about things like these which may never happen. Now just get up and set this present of precious stones before him and ask him for his daughter for me, and do not sit there making so much of the difficulty in your imagination.

"You have learned by now, mother, that this Lamp of ours has become a steady income to us, and that whatever I want of it is supplied to me; and my hope is that by means of it I shall learn how to answer the Sultan, if he asks me about what you say."

Then Aladdin and his mother went on talking the subject over all that night; and when morning came the good woman got up and heartened her heart, especially as her son had explained to her a little of the powers of the Lamp and its virtues — namely, that it would supply everything they asked of it.

Aladdin, however, seeing his mother take courage when he explained to her the workings of the Lamp, was afraid she might chatter to people about it; so he said to her, "Mother, take care how you speak to anybody about the properties of the Lamp and the profit of it, for this is our one great blessing. Guard your thoughts, in case you say too much about it in front of others, whoever they may be; or we may lose it, and lose the good fortune we have and the benefits we look for, since they come from it."

His mother replied, "Have no fear of that, my son"; and she got up and took the bowl full of jewels, which she wrapped in a fine kerchief, and went out early so as to reach the Divan before it got crowded.

When she came into the palace the reception was not yet fully attended, and she saw the viziers and various lords of the land going into the presence chamber; and after a short time, when the Divan was made complete by the ministers and high officials and chieftains and emirs and grandees, the Sultan appeared, and the viziers made their obeisance and so did the nobles and the notables.

The King seated himself on the throne of his kingship, and everybody present at the reception stood before him with folded arms, waiting for his command to sit; and when they got it, each took his place according to his rank. Then the petitioners came before the Sultan, who gave judgment in his usual way, until the Divan came to an end; when the King got up and withdrew into the palace and all the rest went their ways.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-sixth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin's mother, having come earliest of all, found means of getting in without anybody speaking to her or offering to lead her to the presence; and she went on standing there until the Divan ended, when the Sultan got up and withdrew into the palace and all the rest went about their business.

And when she saw the throne empty and the King going into his harem, she went off too, and returned home. But as soon as her son caught sight of her, bowl in hand, he thought that perhaps something unfortunate had happened to her; but he would not ask anything until she had set the bowl down, when she told him what had occurred, and ended by adding:

"Praise be to the Lord, my child, that I found courage enough and secured myself a standing place at the reception today. And although I was too frightened to speak to the King, yet, God willing, I will address him tomorrow. Even today there were many who, like me, could not get an audience with the Sultan. But be of good cheer, my son; tomorrow I really must speak to him for your sake. And what has not happened may yet happen."

When Aladdin heard his mother's words he was overjoyed; and although, in the excess of his love and longing for the Lady Badr al-Budur, he expected the business to be settled from one hour to the next, yet he possessed his soul in patience.

They slept well that night; and early next morning Aladdin's mother got up and went with her bowl to the King's court, which she found shut. So she asked the people, and they told her that the Sultan did not hold a reception every day, but only three times a week; so she decided to go home again.

And after this, whenever she saw the court open she would stand before the King until the reception ended; and when it was shut she would go to make sure of it; and this went on for a whole month.

The Sultan noticed her presence at every reception; but on the last day, when she took up her station as usual before the Council, she let it close and lacked the boldness to come forward and speak a single syllable.

Now as the King, having risen, was making for his harem in the company of the Grand Vizier, he turned to him and said, "Vizier, for the last six or seven reception days I have seen that old woman present herself at every audience, and I have also noticed that she always carries something under her cloak. Tell me, Vizier, do you know anything about her and what she intends?"

"My lord the Sultan," said the other, "women are truly weak of wit, and very likely this good woman comes here to complain to you against her husband or somebody of her family."

But this answer was far from satisfying the Sultan; on the contrary, he ordered the Vizier to set her before him if she should come again; and the minister immediately put his hand on his head and exclaimed, "To hear is to obey, my lord the Sultan!"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-seventh Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin's mother made a practice of going to the Divan every day and passing into the room and standing opposite the King; and although she was sorrowful and thoroughly worn out, still, for her son's sake, she did her best to make light of all her difficulties.

Now one day, when she was doing as she usually did, the Sultan cast his eyes on her as she stood before him and said to his Grand Vizier, "This is the very woman I spoke to you about yesterday; so bring her before me at once, that I may see what her suit is and grant her what she needs."

So the minister introduced her immediately; and when she was in the presence she saluted the King by kissing her fingertips and raising them to her forehead, and, praying for the Sultan's glory and long continuance and the permanence of his prosperity, kissed the ground before him.

At this he said, "Woman, for several days I have seen you attending the reception without a word said; so tell me if you have some request that I may grant."

She kissed the ground a second time, and after blessing him answered, "Yes indeed, as your head lives, O King of the Age, I have a want; but before anything else, be pleased to grant me a promise of safety, so that I may put my suit to the ears of our lord the Sultan; for your Highness may perhaps find it a strange one."

The King, wanting to know what she needed, and being a man of unusual mildness and clemency, gave his word for her safety and ordered everybody about him to be dismissed at once, so that nobody was left but the Grand Vizier. Then he turned to his petitioner and said, "Tell me your suit: you have the safeguard of Almighty Allah."

"O King of the Age," she replied, "I ask your pardon too."

And he said, "Allah pardon you, even as I do."

Then she said, "Our lord the Sultan, I have a son called Aladdin; and one day, having heard the crier ordering all men to shut up their shops and keep off the streets, because the Lady Badr al-Budur, the Sultan's daughter, was going to the baths, he felt an uncontrollable longing to look at her, and hid himself in a place where he could see her very well; and that place was behind the door of the baths.

"When she came in he saw her and studied her as much as he wished — and only too well; for from the time he looked at her, O King of the Age, until this hour, life has not been pleasant to him. And he has required of me that I ask your Highness for her as his wife; nor could I drive this fancy out of his head, because love of her has mastered his vitals, and to such a degree that he said to me, 'Understand, mother, that if I do not get my wish I shall certainly die.'

"And so I hope that your Highness will be pleased to be mild and merciful and pardon this boldness on my part and my child's, and refrain from punishing us for it."

When the Sultan heard her tale he looked at her kindly, and, laughing aloud, asked her, "What is that you are carrying, and what is in that kerchief?"

And she, seeing the Sultan laugh instead of growing angry at her words, opened the wrapper at once and set the bowl of jewels before him — at which the audience hall was lit up as though by chandeliers and candelabra; and he was dazed and amazed at the radiance of the rare gems, and fell to marvelling at their size and beauty and excellence.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-eighth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the King saw the gems he was seized with surprise and cried, "Never at all until this day have I seen anything like these jewels for size and beauty and excellence; nor do I believe there is a single one like them to be found in my treasury."

Then he turned to his minister and asked, "What do you say, Vizier? Tell me, have you ever in your time seen such very fine jewels as these?"

The other answered, "Never have I seen the like, our lord the Sultan; nor do I think there is in the treasuries of my lord the Sultan the fellow of the least of them."

The King went on, "Now indeed, whoever has presented me with such jewels deserves to become the bridegroom of my daughter Badr al-Budur; because, as far as I can see, nobody is more deserving of her than he is."

When the Vizier heard the Sultan's words he was tongue-tied with worry and grieved bitterly, for the King had promised to give the Princess in marriage to his son. So after a little while he said, "O King of the Age, your Highness was pleased to promise me that the Lady Badr al-Budur should be my son's wife; so it is only right that your exalted Highness should grant us a delay of three months, during which time, God willing, my son may obtain and present an offering costlier still than this."

So the King, although he knew that such a thing could not be done, either by the Vizier or by the greatest of his grandees, yet out of his grace and kindness granted him the delay he asked for.

Then he turned to the old woman, Aladdin's mother, and said, "Go to your son and tell him I have pledged my word that my daughter shall be in his name; only, I must make the necessary preparations of wedding furniture for her use, and so it is only proper that he should be patient for the next three months."

Getting this answer, Aladdin's mother thanked the Sultan and blessed him; and then, going out in the greatest haste, like one flying for joy, she went home. And when her son saw her come in with a smiling face he was gladdened at the sign of good news, especially as she had come back without delay, as she did on the days when the court was shut, and had not brought the bowl back with her.

Presently he asked her, "God willing, you bring me good news, mother? Perhaps the jewels and their value have done their work, and perhaps you have been kindly received by the King, and he has shown you favour and listened to your request?"

So she told him the whole tale — how the Sultan had treated her well and had marvelled at the extraordinary size of the gems and their surpassing water, as had the Vizier too — and added, "And he promised that his daughter should be yours. Only, my child, the Vizier spoke of a secret agreement made with him by the Sultan before he pledged himself to me; and, after speaking privately, the King put me off to the end of three months. So I have grown fearful that the Vizier may be ill-disposed towards you, and may perhaps try to change the Sultan's mind."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Forty-ninth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when Aladdin heard his mother's words, and how the Sultan had promised him his daughter — putting the wedding off, however, until after the third month — his mind was gladdened and he rejoiced exceedingly, and said, "Since the King has given his word for three months' time — well, it is a long while! — at any rate my gladness is very great."

Then he thanked his mother, showing her how her good work had gone beyond all her toil and trouble; and said to her, "By Allah, mother, until now I was as it were in my grave, and you have drawn me out of it; and I praise Almighty Allah, because at this moment I am certain that no man in the world is happier than I am, or more fortunate."

Then he possessed himself in patience until two of the three months had gone by.

Now one day his mother went out about sundown to the bazaar to buy some oil, and she found all the market shops fast shut and the whole city decorated, and people putting wax tapers and flowers in their windows; and she saw the soldiers and the household troops and the officers riding in procession, and torches and lamps flaming and flaring; and she wondered at the marvellous sight and the glamour of the scene.

So she went into an oil seller's shop that was still open and bought what she needed from him, and said, "By your life, uncle, tell me what the news in town is today, that people have made all these decorations, and every house and market street is adorned, and the troops are all standing on guard?"

The oil seller asked her, "Woman, I suppose you are a stranger and not one of this city?"

And she answered, "No, I am your fellow townswoman."

He retorted, "You a townswoman, and yet you do not know that this very night the son of the Grand Vizier is going in to the Lady Badr al-Budur, the Sultan's daughter! He is at the baths now, and all this force of soldiery is on guard and standing under arms to wait for him to come out, when they will carry him in bridal procession to the palace, where the Princess is expecting him."

As Aladdin's mother heard these words she grieved, and was distracted in her mind and perplexed how to tell her son of this sorrowful event, knowing well that the poor youth was looking, hour by hour, to the end of the three months.

But she went straight home to him, and when she had come in she said, "My son, I have some news for you, but the sorrow it will cause you will be hard for me."

He cried, "Let me know what your news is."

And she replied, "Truly the Sultan has broken his promise to you in the matter of the Lady Badr al-Budur, and this very night the Grand Vizier's son is going in to her. And for some time, my son, I have suspected that the minister would change the King's mind, just as I told you how he had spoken privately to him in front of me."

Aladdin asked, "How did you learn that the Vizier's son is to pay his first visit to the Princess tonight?"

So she told him the whole tale — how, when she went to buy oil, she had found the city decorated and the eunuch officials and lords of the land with the troops under arms waiting for the bridegroom to come from the baths, and that the first visit was appointed for that very night.

Hearing this, Aladdin was seized with a fever of jealousy brought on by his grief; but after a short while he remembered the Lamp, and, recovering his spirits, said, "By your life, mother, believe me that the Vizier's son will not enjoy her as you think. But let us leave this subject now; get up and serve the supper, and after we have eaten let me go to my own room, and all will be well and happy."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fiftieth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that after Aladdin had eaten his supper he went to his room and, locking the door, brought out the Lamp and rubbed it; whereupon its familiar appeared to him at once and said, "Ask whatever you want, for I am your slave and the slave of him who holds the Lamp in his hand — I and all the Slaves of the Lamp."

He replied, "Listen to me. I begged the Sultan for his daughter in marriage, and he promised her to me after three months; but he has not kept his word — no, he has given her to the Vizier's son, and this very night the bridegroom will go in to her. Therefore I order you, if you are a trustworthy servant of the Lamp, when you see bride and bridegroom bedded together tonight, to take them up at once and carry them here, bed and all; and this is what I want of you."

The marid replied, "Hearing and obeying; and if you have any other service besides this, ask me for everything you want."

Aladdin said, "At present I require nothing except what I have told you to do."

Whereupon the slave disappeared, and Aladdin went back to spend the rest of the evening with his mother.

But at the hour when he knew the servant would be coming, he got up and went to his room; and after a little while, behold, the marid came, bringing him the newly wedded couple on their bridal bed.

Aladdin was overjoyed to see them; then he cried to the slave, "Carry that gallows bird away and lay him out at full length in the privy."

His order was carried out at once; but before leaving him the slave blew such a cold blast upon the bridegroom that it shrivelled him, and the plight of the Vizier's son was pitiful.

Then the servant, coming back to Aladdin, said to him, "If you need anything else, tell me of it."

And Aladdin said, "Come back in the morning, so that you may put them back where they belong."

To which the marid said, "I hear and obey," and vanished.

Presently Aladdin got up, hardly able to believe that the affair had gone so well for him; but when he looked at the Lady Badr al-Budur lying under his own roof, although he had long burned with love of her, still he kept his respect for her, and said, "Princess of fair ones, do not think that I brought you here to lessen your honour. Heaven forbid! No, it was only to prevent the wrong man having you, since your father the Sultan promised you to me. So rest here in peace."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-first Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Lady Badr al-Budur, the Sultan's daughter, saw herself in that mean and dark lodging, and heard Aladdin's words, she was seized with fear and trembling and became utterly distraught, and could make no reply at all.

Presently the youth got up and, stripping off his outer clothes, laid a sword between them and lay down on the bed beside the Princess; and he did nothing villainous, for it was enough for him to have prevented the consummation of her marriage with the Vizier's son.

The Lady Badr al-Budur, on the other hand, passed the worst night of all nights, nor had she seen a worse in all her born days; and it was the same with the minister's son, who lay in the privy and dared not stir for the fear of the jinni that overwhelmed him.

As soon as it was morning the slave appeared before Aladdin, without the Lamp having been rubbed, and said to him, "My lord, if you require anything, command me, and I will do it upon my head and my eyes."

He said, "Go, take up the bride and bridegroom and carry them to their own apartment."

So the servant did as he was told in the glance of an eye, and bore the pair away and put them in the palace where they had been before, without anybody seeing them; but they both nearly died of fright when they found themselves being carried from place to place.

And the marid had barely time to set them down and go on his way before the Sultan came on a visit of congratulation to his daughter; and when the Vizier's son heard the doors thrown open he sprang out of bed at once and put his clothes on, for he knew that nobody but the King could come in at that hour. And yet it was exceedingly hard for him to leave his bed, in which he had wanted to warm himself a little after the cold night in the water closet he had just come from.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-second Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Sultan went in to his daughter Badr al-Budur and, kissing her between the eyes, bade her good morning and asked her about her bridegroom, and whether she was pleased and satisfied with him.

But she made no reply whatever, and looked at him with an angry eye; and although he repeated his words again and again, she held her peace and did not speak a single syllable to him.

So the King left her and, going to the Queen, told her what had passed between him and his daughter; and the mother, not wanting to leave the Sultan angry with their child, said to him, "O King of the Age, this is the way with most newly married couples, at least during their first days of marriage, for they are bashful and rather shy. So be pleased to excuse her, and after a little while she will become herself again and talk to people as she did before; whereas now, O King of the Age, it is her shyness that keeps her silent. However, I should like to go and see her."

At this the Queen got up and put on her clothes; then, going to her daughter, she wished her good morning and kissed her between the eyes. But still the Princess would make no answer at all; whereupon the Queen said to herself, "No doubt something strange has happened to trouble her like this."

So she asked her, "My daughter, what has brought you to this state? Let me know what has happened to you, that when I come and bid you good morning you have not a word to say to me?"

At this the Lady Badr al-Budur raised her head and said, "Forgive me, mother; it was my duty to meet you with all respect and honour, seeing that you have honoured me with this visit. But I beg you to hear the cause of my condition, and to see how the night I have just spent has been the worst of nights to me.

"Hardly had we lain down, mother, when somebody — whose shape I do not know — lifted up our bed and carried it to a dark place, foul and mean."

Then the Princess related to the Queen mother everything that had happened to her that night: how they had taken her bridegroom away and left her alone and lonely; and how after a while another young man came and lay down beside her in the bridegroom's place, after putting his sword between her and himself.

"And in the morning," she went on, "the one who carried us off came back and took us straight back to our own place. But the moment he got here he left us; and suddenly my father the Sultan came in at the very hour and moment of our arrival, and I had neither heart nor tongue to speak to him with, for the stress of the terror and trembling that had come over me. Perhaps such a want of duty may have seemed hard to him; so I hope, mother, that you will tell him the cause of my condition, and that he will pardon me for not answering him, and will not blame me but rather accept my excuses."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-third Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Queen heard these words from Princess Badr al-Budur she said to her, "My child, compose your thoughts. If you tell such a tale in front of anybody, he will very likely say, 'Truly, the Sultan's daughter has lost her wits.' And you did quite right not to choose to tell your adventure to your father; and beware, and again I say beware, my daughter, of letting him know about it."

The Princess replied, "Mother, I have spoken to you like somebody sound in her senses, and I have not lost my wits: this is what happened to me; and if you do not believe it coming from me, ask my bridegroom."

To which the Queen replied, "Get up at once, my daughter, and banish such fancies from your thoughts; and dress yourself and come out to look at the wedding feasts and festivities they are holding in the city for your sake and your marriage; and listen to the drumming and the singing and look at the decorations, all of them meant to honour your marriage, my daughter."

So saying, the Queen at once summoned the tirewomen, who dressed and prepared the Lady Badr al-Budur; and presently she went in to the Sultan and assured him that their daughter had suffered all through her wedding night from bad dreams and nightmares, and said to him, "Do not be severe with her for not answering you."

Then the Queen sent privately for the Vizier's son and asked him about the matter, saying, "Tell me, are these words of the Lady Badr al-Budur true or not?"

But he, in his fear of losing his bride there and then, answered, "My lady, I know nothing of what you are speaking about."

And so the mother made sure that her daughter had been seeing visions and dreams.

The marriage feasts lasted all that day, with dancing girls and singers and the striking of every kind of instrument of mirth and merriment, while the Queen and the Vizier and his son strove their hardest to enhance the festivities so that the Princess might enjoy herself; and that day they left nothing that excites pleasure unperformed in her presence, so that she might forget what was on her mind and take more joy in it all.

Yet none of this had any effect on her at all; on the contrary, she sat in silence, sad in her thoughts and badly perplexed at what had happened to her the night before.
