It is true that the Vizier's son had suffered even more, because he had spent his sleeping hours lying in the water closet; he, however, had lied about the story and had cast the memory of the night out of his mind — in the first place for fear of losing his bride, and with her the honour of a connection that brought him so much consideration and for which men envied him so much; and, secondly, on account of the wonderful loveliness of the Lady Badr al-Budur and her marvellous beauty.

Aladdin also went out that day and looked at the merrymaking that ran through the whole city as well as the palace; and he fell to laughing, especially when he heard people chattering about the high honour that had come to the son of the Vizier and the prosperity of his fortunes in becoming son-in-law to the Sultan, and the great consideration shown by the wedding celebrations. And he said in his mind, "Indeed you have no idea, you miserable creatures, what happened to him last night, that you should envy him!"

But after darkness fell and it was time for sleep, Aladdin got up and, going to his room, rubbed the Lamp; whereupon the slave appeared immediately.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-fourth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the slave appeared before Aladdin he was ordered to bring him the Sultan's daughter along with her bridegroom, as on the night before, before the Vizier's son could take her maidenhead.

So the marid vanished without pause or delay for a little while, until the appointed time, when he came back carrying the bed on which the Lady Badr al-Budur and the Vizier's son were lying; and he did with the bridegroom as he had done before — that is, he took him up and laid him at full length in the privy, and left him there dried up with the excess of his fear and trembling.

Then Aladdin got up and, laying the sword between himself and the Princess, lay down beside her; and when day broke the slave restored the pair to their own place, leaving Aladdin filled with delight at the state of the minister's son.

Now when the Sultan woke that morning he resolved to visit his daughter and see whether she would treat him as she had the day before; so, shaking off his sleep, he sprang up and dressed himself and, going to the Princess's apartment, ordered the door opened.

At this the Vizier's son got up at once and came down out of bed and began putting his clothes on, while his ribs were wrung with cold; for the slave had only just brought him back when the King came in.

The Sultan, raising the curtain, went up to his daughter as she lay in bed and bade her good morning; then, kissing her between the eyes, he asked her how she was. But he saw her looking sour and sad, and she did not answer him at all, only glowering at him like somebody angry; and her condition was pitiable.

At this the Sultan grew furious with her for not replying, and he suspected that something evil had happened to her; whereupon he bared his sword and cried to her, blade in hand, "What is this that has come over you? Either tell me what has happened, or this very moment I will take your life! Is this the sign of honour and respect I expect of you — that I speak to you and you do not answer me a word?"

When the Lady Badr al-Budur saw her father in high indignation, with the naked blade in his grip, she was freed from her earlier fear; so she raised her head and said to him, "My beloved father, do not be angry with me, and do not be hasty in your hot passion, for I am excusable in what you shall see of my case. So lend an ear to what has happened to me; and I know well that after hearing my account of what befell me these last two nights, you will pardon me, and your Highness will be softened into pitying me, as I claim of you affection for your child."

Then the Princess told her father everything that had happened to her, and added, "Father, if you do not believe me, ask my bridegroom, and he will tell your Highness the whole adventure; for I did not know what they would do with him when they carried him away from my side, nor where they would put him."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-fifth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Sultan heard his daughter's words he was saddened, and his eyes brimmed with tears; then he sheathed his sword and kissed her, saying, "My daughter, why did you not tell me what happened the night before, so that I might have guarded you against this torture and terror that visited you a second time? But it is no matter now. Get up and throw off all such care; and tonight I will set a watch to guard you, and no mishap shall ever make you miserable again."

Then the Sultan went back to his palace and immediately ordered the Grand Vizier summoned, and asked him, as he stood before him in attendance, "Vizier, how do you look at this business? Perhaps your son has told you what happened to him and to my daughter."

The minister replied, "O King of the Age, I have not seen my son either yesterday or today."

At this the Sultan told him everything that had afflicted the Princess, and added, "It is my wish that you go at once and get news from your son about the facts of the case: it may be that out of her fear my daughter is not fully aware of what really happened to her — although I hold every word she said to be truthful."

So the Grand Vizier got up and, going out, ordered his son summoned and asked him whether everything his lord had told him was true or untrue.

The youth replied, "My father the Vizier, Heaven forbid that the Lady Badr al-Budur should speak falsely: indeed everything she said was true, and these two nights proved to us the worst of our nights instead of being nights of pleasure and marriage joys. But what happened to me was the greater evil, because instead of sleeping in bed with my bride I lay in the wardrobe — a black hole, frightful, foul-smelling, truly damnable; and my ribs were bursting with cold."

In short, the young man told his father the whole tale, and added as he finished it, "Dear father, I beg you to speak to the Sultan and have him set me free from this marriage. Yes indeed, it is a high honour for me to be the Sultan's son-in-law, and especially since love of the Princess has got hold of my vitals; but I have no strength left to endure a single night like these last two."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-sixth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Vizier, hearing his son's words, was exceedingly saddened and sorrowful, for it had been his plan to advance and promote his child by making him son-in-law to the Sultan. So he became thoughtful and perplexed about the affair and about how to manage it; and it was very grievous to him to break off the marriage, since it had been a rare pleasure to him to have fallen upon such high good fortune.

So he said, "Be patient, my son, until we see what may happen tonight, when we will set watchmen to guard you; and do not give up the exalted distinction that has fallen to nobody but yourself."

Then the Vizier left him and, going back to his sovereign, reported that everything the Lady Badr al-Budur had told him was a true tale; whereupon the Sultan said, "Since the affair stands like this, we need no delay"; and he at once ordered all the rejoicings to stop and the marriage to be broken off.

This made the people and the citizens marvel at the business, especially when they saw the Grand Vizier and his son leaving the palace in a pitiable state for grief and stress of feeling; and everybody fell to asking, "What has happened, and what is the reason for the wedding being made null and void?" Nor did anybody know a thing about the truth of it except Aladdin, the lover who laid claim to the Princess's hand; and he laughed in his sleeve.

But even after the marriage was dissolved, the Sultan forgot, and never even called to mind, the promise he had made to Aladdin's mother; and it was the same with the Grand Vizier, while neither of them had the least inkling of where the thing that had happened to them had come from.

So Aladdin waited patiently for the three months to pass, after which the Sultan had pledged himself to give him his daughter in marriage; but the moment the term came round, he sent his mother to the Sultan to require him to keep his covenant.

So she went to the palace; and when the King appeared in the Divan and saw the old woman standing before him, he remembered his promise to her about the marriage after a term of three months, and he turned to the minister and said, "Vizier, this is the old lady who presented me with the jewels, and to whom we pledged our word that when the three months had gone by we would summon her to our presence before all others."

So the minister went out and fetched her; and when she came into the Sultan's presence she saluted him and prayed for his glory and the permanence of his prosperity. At this the King asked her whether she needed anything, and she answered, "O King of the Age, the three months' term you assigned me is finished, and this is the time for you to marry my son Aladdin to your daughter, the Lady Badr al-Budur."

The Sultan was thrown into confusion by this demand, especially when he saw the old woman's poverty-stricken condition, one of the meanest of her kind; and yet the offering she had brought him had been of the most magnificent, far beyond his power to pay the price of. So he turned to the Grand Vizier and said, "What plan have you? Truly I did pass my word; and yet it seems to me they are poor people and not persons of high condition."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-seventh Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Grand Vizier, who was dying of envy and who was particularly saddened by what had happened to his son, said to himself, "How shall a man like this marry the King's daughter, and my son lose this highest of honours?"

So he answered his sovereign, speaking privately, "My lord, it is an easy matter to keep off a poor devil like this, for he is not worthy that your Highness should give your daughter to a fellow whom nobody knows anything about."

"By what means," asked the Sultan, "shall we put the man off, when I have pledged my promise? And the word of kings is their bond."

The Vizier replied, "My lord, my advice is that you demand of him forty platters made of pure gold and full of gems, such as the woman brought you before, with forty white slave girls to carry the platters and forty black eunuch slaves."

The King answered, "By Allah, Vizier, you have spoken to the purpose, seeing that such a thing is not possible, and by this means we shall be free of him."

Then he said to Aladdin's mother, "Go and tell your son that I am a man of my word, just as I pledged it to him — but on condition that he has the power to pay the dowry of my daughter. And what I require of him is a settlement consisting of forty platters of virgin gold, all brimming with gems like the ones you brought me, and as many white handmaids to carry them, and forty black eunuch slaves to attend and escort the bearers. If your son can manage this, I will marry him to my daughter."

At this she went home wagging her head and saying in her mind, "Where can my poor boy get these platters and jewels? And granting that he went back to the enchanted treasury and picked them off the trees — which, however, I hold to be impossible — yet even if he brought them, where is he to come by the girls and the black slaves?"

Nor did she stop communing with herself until she reached her house, where she found Aladdin waiting for her; and she lost no time in saying, "My son, did I not tell you never to imagine that your power would stretch as far as the Lady Badr al-Budur, and that such a thing is not possible for people like ourselves?"

"Tell me the news," he said.

So she said, "My child, truly the Sultan received me with all honour, as he usually does, and it seems to me his intentions towards us are friendly. But your enemy is that accursed Vizier. For after I addressed the King in your name, as you told me to say — 'In very truth the promised term is past,' adding, 'It would be well if your Highness would be pleased to give the order for the betrothal of your daughter the Lady Badr al-Budur to my son Aladdin' — he turned and spoke to the minister, who answered him privately; after which the Sultan gave me his reply."

Then she went through the King's demands and said, "My son, he certainly expects an immediate answer from you; but I fancy we have no answer for him."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-eighth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when Aladdin heard these words he laughed and said, "Mother, you declare that we have no answer, and you think the case exceedingly difficult; but compose your thoughts and get up and bring me something to eat; and after we have dined, if the Compassionate is willing, you shall see my reply.

"The Sultan too thinks, as you do, that he has demanded a prodigious dowry in order to turn me away from his daughter — whereas the fact is that he has asked me for a great deal less than I expected. But go out at once and buy the provisions, and leave me to get you an answer."

So she went out to fetch what she needed from the bazaar, and Aladdin went to his room and, taking the Lamp, rubbed it; whereupon its slave appeared to him at once and said, "Ask, my lord, whatever you want."

He replied, "I have asked the Sultan for his daughter in marriage, and he has required of me forty bowls of the purest gold, each weighing ten pounds and all to be filled with gems such as we find in the gardens of the hoard; and furthermore, that they be carried on the heads of as many white handmaids, each attended by her black eunuch slave, forty of them in full number. So I want you to bring all these into my presence."

"Hearing and obeying, my lord," said the slave; and, disappearing for the space of an hour or so, he presently came back bringing the platters and the jewels, the handmaids and the eunuchs; and, setting them before him, the marid said, "This is what you demanded of me: tell me now if you want any other matter or service besides this."

Aladdin answered, "I need nothing else; but if I do, I will summon you and let you know."

The slave now disappeared; and after a little while Aladdin's mother came home, and on entering the house saw the black slaves and the handmaids. At this she marvelled and exclaimed, "All this comes from the Lamp — which may Allah preserve to my son!"

But before she could take off her cloak Aladdin said to her, "Mother, this is your moment, before the Sultan goes into his private palace: carry him what he asked for, and go with it at once, so that he may know that I can supply everything he wants and more; and also that he has been misled by his Grand Vizier, and that the two of them vainly imagined they would baffle me."

Then he got up at once and opened the house door, and the handmaids and black slaves paced out two by two, each girl with her eunuch beside her, until they crowded the whole quarter, with Aladdin's mother going in front of them.

And when the people of that district caught sight of such a very fine sight and marvellous spectacle, they all stood and gazed, and studied the forms and figures of the handmaids and marvelled at their beauty and loveliness; for every one of them wore robes worked with gold and studded with jewels, no dress being worth less than a thousand dinars. They stared just as hard at the bowls; and although these were covered with pieces of brocade, themselves embroidered with gold and set with precious stones, yet the brilliance that shot out from them dulled the shine of the sun.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Fifty-ninth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the people, and especially the people of the quarter, stood marvelling at this extraordinary scene.

Then Aladdin's mother walked forward, and all the handmaids and eunuchs paced behind her in the best of order and arrangement, and the citizens gathered to gaze at the beauty of the girls and glorify God the Most Great, until the train reached the palace and went into it in the company of the tailor's widow.

Now when the officers and chamberlains and army officers saw them, they were all seized with surprise, particularly at the sight of the handmaids, any one of whom would have ravished the reason of a hermit. And although the royal chamberlains and officials were men of family, the sons of grandees and emirs, still they could not help wondering at the costly dresses of the girls and the platters carried on their heads; nor could they look at them with their eyes open, because of the exceeding brilliance and radiance.

Then the officials went in and reported to the King, who immediately ordered them admitted to the presence chamber; and Aladdin's mother went in with them.

When they stood before the Sultan they all saluted him with every sign of respect and honour and prayed for his glory and prosperity; then they set the bowls down from their heads at his feet and, having taken off the brocade covers, stood with their arms folded behind them.

The Sultan marvelled exceedingly and was distracted by the beauty of the handmaids and their loveliness, which was beyond praise; and his wits were bewildered when he looked at the golden bowls brimful of gems that captured a man's sight; and he was so perplexed at the marvel of it that he became like a dumb man, unable to utter a syllable for the excess of his wonder. And his senses were stupefied still more when he considered that within an hour or so all these treasures had been collected.

Presently he ordered the slave girls to carry their loads inside, as the Princess's dowry; and when they had done as he bade them, Aladdin's mother came forward and said to the Sultan, "My lord, this is not much with which to honour the Lady Badr al-Budur, for she deserves all these things multiplied many times over."

At this the sovereign turned to the minister and asked, "What do you say, Vizier? Is not a man who could produce such wealth in so short a time — is he not, I say, worthy to become the Sultan's son-in-law and take the King's daughter to wife?"

Then the minister — although he marvelled at these riches even more than the Sultan did — whose envy was killing him and growing greater by the hour, seeing his liege lord satisfied with the money and the dowry, and yet being unable to fight against fact, answered, "It is not worthy of her."

And with that he fell to devising a scheme against the King, so that he might keep the Lady Badr al-Budur from Aladdin; and accordingly he went on, "My liege, all the treasures of the universe are not worth a nail-paring of your daughter: indeed your Highness has valued these things far too highly in comparison with her."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixtieth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the King heard the words of his Grand Vizier he knew that the speech was prompted by excess of envy; so, turning to the mother of Aladdin, he said, "Woman, go to your son and tell him that I have accepted the dowry from him and stand by my bargain, and that my daughter shall be his bride and he my son-in-law. Furthermore, tell him to come and present himself at once, so that I may become acquainted with him: he shall see nothing from me but honour and consideration, and this night shall be the beginning of the marriage festivities. Only, as I said to you, let him come to me and not delay."

At this Aladdin's mother went home with the speed of a storm wind, so as to hurry as fast as she could to congratulate her son; and she flew with joy at the thought that her boy was about to become son-in-law to the Sultan.

After she had gone, the King dismissed the Divan and, going into the Princess's palace, ordered the bowls and the handmaids to be brought before him and before her, so that she might inspect them too.

But when the Lady Badr al-Budur looked at the jewels she was overcome and cried, "It seems to me that in all the treasuries of the world there is not one jewel to rival these!"

Then she looked at the handmaids and marvelled at their beauty and loveliness, and knew that all this came from her new bridegroom, who had sent them to serve her. So she was gladdened, although she had been grieved and saddened on account of her former husband, the Vizier's son; and she rejoiced exceedingly as she gazed at the girls and their charms. Nor was her father the Sultan less pleased and heartened when he saw his daughter relieved of all her mourning and melancholy; and his own vanished at the sight of her enjoyment.

Then he asked her, "My daughter, do these things divert you? Indeed I think this suitor of yours is more suitable for you than the Vizier's son; and very soon, God willing, my daughter, you shall have fuller joy of him."

So it was with the King. But as for Aladdin, as soon as he saw his mother coming into the house with her face laughing from the stress of her joy, he rejoiced at the sign of good news and cried, "To Allah alone be praise! Everything I desired is accomplished."

His mother answered, "Be glad at my good news, my son, and hearten your heart and cool your eyes at the winning of your wish. The Sultan has accepted your offering — I mean the money and the dowry of the Lady Badr al-Budur, who is now your betrothed bride; and this very night, my child, is your marriage and your first visit to her. For the King, so as to assure me of his word, has proclaimed to the world that you are his son-in-law, and has promised this night for the going in. But he also said to me, 'Let your son come here at once, so that I may become acquainted with him and receive him with all honour and respect.' And now here I am, my son, at the end of my labours; and whatever happens, the rest is upon your shoulders."

At this Aladdin got up and kissed his mother's hand and thanked her and praised her kindly service; then he left her and, going into his room, took the Lamp and rubbed it — when, lo and behold, its slave appeared and cried, "Here I am! Ask whatever you want."

The young man replied, "It is my desire that you take me to a bath whose like is not in the world; and then fetch me a suit of clothes so costly and so kingly that no royalty ever owned its fellow."

The marid replied, "I hear and I obey"; and carried him off to baths such as were never seen by the kings of Persia, for the building was all of alabaster and carnelian and it contained marvellous paintings that captured the sight; and the great hall was studded with precious stones. There was not a soul in it; but when Aladdin went in, one of the jann in human shape washed him and bathed him exactly as he wished.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-first Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin, after being washed and bathed, left the baths and went into the great hall, where he found that his old clothes had been taken away and replaced by a suit of the most precious and princely kind. Then he was served with sherbets and coffee scented with ambergris; and after drinking he got up, and a party of black slaves came forward and dressed him in the costliest of clothing, and then perfumed him and fumigated him.

It is known that Aladdin was the son of a tailor, a poor man; yet now nobody would have thought him anything of the kind — no, everybody would have said, "This is the greatest of the offspring of kings: praise be to Him who changes and who is not changed!"

Presently the jinni came and lifted him up and carried him to his home, and asked, "My lord, tell me, do you need anything?"

He answered, "Yes. It is my wish that you bring me forty-eight mamelukes, of whom two dozen shall go before me and the rest follow me, the whole number with their war chargers and their clothing and accoutrements; and everything upon them and their horses must be of nothing but the highest worth and the costliest kind, such as is not to be found in the treasuries of kings.

"Then fetch me a stallion fit for the riding of the kings of Persia, and let his furniture, every bit of it, be of gold crusted with the finest gems. Fetch me also forty-eight thousand dinars, so that each white slave may carry a thousand gold pieces. It is my intention now to go to the Sultan, so do not delay; for without all the requisites I have told you of I cannot visit him.

"Moreover, set before me a dozen slave girls, unique in beauty and dressed in the most magnificent clothes, to go with my mother to the royal palace; and let every handmaid be robed in clothing that befits a queen's wearing."

The slave replied, "To hear is to obey"; and, disappearing for the twinkling of an eye, brought everything he had been told to bring, and led by the hand a stallion that had no rival among the Arabs of Arabia, whose saddlecloth was of splendid brocade worked with gold.

At this, without pause or delay, Aladdin sent for his mother and gave her the clothes she was to wear, and put in her charge the twelve slave girls who were to form her suite to the palace. Then he sent one of the mamelukes whom the jinni had brought to see whether the Sultan had left the palace or not. The white slave went off lighter than the lightning, and coming back just as fast, said, "My lord, the Sultan is waiting for you!"

At this Aladdin got up and took horse, his mamelukes riding in front of him and behind him; and they were such that everybody had to cry out, "Praise to the Lord who created them and clothed them with such beauty and loveliness!" And they scattered gold among the crowd in front of their master, who surpassed them all in comeliness and good looks — and there is no need to ask about the sons of kings; praise be to the Bountiful, the Eternal!

All this came of the virtues of the Wonderful Lamp, which gifted whoever possessed it with the fairest face and the finest figure, with wealth and with wisdom.

The people admired Aladdin's liberality and exceeding generosity, and everybody was distracted by his charm and elegance, his gravity and his good manners; they glorified the Creator for this noble creation, and blessed him one and all; and, although they knew him for the son of such-and-such a tailor, still not a man envied him — no, everybody agreed that he deserved his great good fortune.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-second Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the people were bewildered at Aladdin and his liberality and generosity; and everybody, high and low, blessed him and prayed for him as he rode towards the palace with the mamelukes before and behind him, scattering gold over the heads of the crowd.

Now the Sultan had assembled the lords of the land and, telling them of the promise he had passed to Aladdin about the marriage of his daughter, had ordered them to await his arrival and then go out, one and all, to meet him and greet him. So the emirs and viziers, the chamberlains, the officials and the army officers took their stations, waiting for him at the palace gate.

Aladdin would gladly have dismounted at the outer entrance; but one of the nobles whom the King had appointed to the duty came up to him and said, "My lord, it is the royal command that you ride in and not dismount until you reach the door of the Divan."

Then they all went before him in a body and escorted him to the appointed place, where they crowded round him, some to hold his stirrup and some supporting him on either side, while others took him by the hands and helped him dismount; after which all the emirs and nobles went ahead of him into the Divan and led him right up to the royal throne.

At this the Sultan came down at once from his seat of state and, forbidding him to kiss the carpet, embraced and kissed him and seated him at his own right hand, beside him.

Aladdin did whatever is proper in the case of kings, by way of salutation and offering of blessings, and said, "Our lord the Sultan, truly the generosity of your Highness required that you should be pleased to grant me the hand of your daughter, the Lady Badr al-Budur, although I am undeserving of the greatness of such a gift, being only the humblest of your slaves. I pray Allah grant you prosperity and long continuance; but in very truth, O King, my tongue is helpless to thank you for the fullness of the favour, beyond all measure, that you have bestowed on me. And I hope of your Highness that you will give me a piece of ground suitable for a pavilion that shall befit your daughter, the Lady Badr al-Budur."

The Sultan was struck with admiration when he saw Aladdin in his princely suit and looked at him and considered his beauty and loveliness, and noticed the mamelukes standing to serve him in their comeliness and good looks; and his wonder grew still more when Aladdin's mother came up to him in costly and sumptuous clothes, dressed as though she were a queen, and when he gazed at the twelve handmaids standing before her with folded arms, doing her service with all respect and reverence.

He noticed too Aladdin's eloquence and his delicacy of speech, and he was astounded at it, he and all his court who were present at the reception.

At this a fire was kindled in the Grand Vizier's heart out of envy of Aladdin, until he was ready to die of it; and it was worse when the Sultan, after hearing the youth's succession of prayers and seeing his high dignity of bearing — respectful with it — and his eloquence and elegance of language, clasped him to his bosom and kissed him and cried, "Alas, my son, that I have not enjoyed your conversation before this day!"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-third Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Sultan saw Aladdin in this fashion, he rejoiced in him with very great joy and immediately ordered the music and the bands to strike up; then he got up and, taking the youth, led him into the palace where supper had been prepared, and the eunuchs at once laid the tables.

So the sovereign sat down and seated his son-in-law at his right side, and the viziers and high officials and lords of the land took their places, each according to his rank; whereupon the bands played and a very fine wedding feast was spread out in the palace.

The King now applied himself to making friends with Aladdin and talked with the youth, who answered him with all courtesy and eloquence, as though he had been brought up in the palaces of kings or had lived among them all his life. And the longer the talk went on between them, the more the Sultan's pleasure and delight increased, hearing his son-in-law's readiness of reply and his sweet flow of language.

But after they had eaten and drunk and the trays had been taken away, the King ordered the judges and witnesses summoned; and they presently attended and knitted the knot and wrote out the contract between Aladdin and the Lady Badr al-Budur.

And presently the bridegroom got up and would have gone out, when his father-in-law held him back and asked, "Where are you off to, my child? The bridal feasts have begun and the marriage is made and the tie is tied and the deed is written."

He replied, "My lord the King, it is my wish to build for the Lady Badr al-Budur a pavilion befitting her station and high degree, nor can I visit her before I have done so. But, God willing, the building shall be finished in the shortest possible time, by the utmost efforts of your slave and by the kindly regard of your Highness. And although I do — yes indeed! — long to enjoy the society of the Lady Badr al-Budur, still it is my duty to serve her first, and it becomes me to set about the work at once."

"Look around you, my son," replied the Sultan, "for whatever ground you think suitable to your design, and take everything into your own hands; but I think the best for you will be that broad plain facing my palace, and, if it pleases you, build your pavilion on it."

"And this," answered Aladdin, "is the sum of my wishes, that I may be near your Highness."

So saying, he said farewell to the King and took horse, with his mamelukes riding before him and behind him, and all the world blessed him and cried, "By Allah, he deserves it!" until he reached his home.

Then he got down from his stallion and, going to his room, rubbed the Lamp; and behold, the slave stood before him and said, "Ask, my lord, whatever you want."

And Aladdin answered, "I require of you a grave and important service, which you must do for me; and it is that you build me, with all urgency, a pavilion facing the palace of the Sultan; and it must be a marvel, for it shall be provided with every requisite, such as royal furniture and so forth."

The slave replied, "To hear is to obey."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-fourth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the slave vanished, and before the next dawn broke came back to Aladdin and said, "My lord, the pavilion is finished to the utmost of your fancy; and if you would like to inspect it, get up at once and come with me."

So he rose, and the slave carried him in the glance of an eye to the pavilion; which, when Aladdin looked at it, struck him with surprise at such building, all its stones being of jasper and alabaster and porphyry and mosaic work.

Then the slave led him into the treasury, which was full of gold and silver and costly gems of every kind, past counting or computing, pricing or estimating. From there to another place, where Aladdin saw everything needed for the tables — plates and dishes, spoons and ladles, basins and covers, cups and goblets, the whole of precious metal. From there to the kitchen, where they found the cooks provided with everything they needed and with cooking pans, likewise of gold and silver. From there to a storehouse piled with chests packed full of royal clothing, stuffs that captured the reason, such as gold-worked brocades from India and China and cloths embroidered with gold. From there to many apartments furnished beyond describing. From there to the stables, containing horses whose like was not to be met with among the kings of the universe; and lastly they went to the harness rooms, all hung with saddlecloths and costly saddles and other gear, studded everywhere with pearls and precious stones.

And all this was the work of a single night.

Aladdin was wonder-struck and astounded by that magnificent display of wealth, which not even the mightiest monarch on earth could have produced; and more so to see his pavilion fully provided with eunuchs and handmaids whose beauty would have seduced a saint.

Yet the chief marvel of the pavilion was an upper belvedere with twenty-four windows, all made of emeralds and rubies and other gems; and one window was left unfinished, at Aladdin's own requirement, so that the Sultan might prove himself unable to complete it.

When the youth had inspected the whole building he was exceedingly pleased and gladdened; then, turning to the slave, he said, "I require one thing more of you, which is still wanting and which I forgot to tell you of."

"Ask what you want, my lord," said the servant.

And the other said, "I ask of you a carpet of the finest brocade, all worked with gold, which, when it is unrolled and stretched out, shall reach from here to the Sultan's palace, so that the Lady Badr al-Budur, when she comes here, may walk upon it and not tread on the common earth."

The slave went away for a short while and said on his return, "My lord, truly what you asked for is here."

Then he took him and showed him a carpet that bewildered the wits, and it stretched from palace to pavilion; and after this the servant carried Aladdin off and set him down in his own home.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-fifth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the slave, after showing Aladdin the carpet, carried him home.

Now the day was brightening, so the Sultan rose from his sleep and, throwing open the casement, looked out and saw, opposite his palace, a palatial pavilion ready built. At this he fell to rubbing his eyes and opening them their widest and studying the scene; and he was soon certain that the new building was very fine and grand enough to bewilder the wits. And with just as much amazement he saw the carpet spread out between palace and pavilion; and, like their lord, the royal doorkeepers and the whole household were dazed and amazed at the spectacle.

Meanwhile the Vizier came in, and as he entered he caught sight of the newly built pavilion and the carpet, at which he wondered too; and when he went in to the Sultan the two of them fell to talking about this marvellous matter, with great surprise at a sight that distracted the gazer and attracted the heart. They said at last, "In very truth, we think that none of the royalties could build the fellow of this pavilion."

And the King, turning to the minister, asked him, "Do you see now that Aladdin is worthy to be the husband of the Princess my daughter? Have you looked at and considered this right royal building, this magnificence of wealth, which the thought of man cannot contain?"

But the Vizier, in his envy of Aladdin, replied, "O King of the Age, truly this foundation and this building and this wealth cannot be except by means of magic; nor can any man in the world, be he the richest in goods or the greatest in power, manage to found and finish such a building as this in a single night."

The Sultan retorted, "I am surprised to see how you go on harping continually on your evil opinion of Aladdin; but I hold that it is caused by your envy and jealousy. You were present when I gave him the ground at his own request for a place where he might build a pavilion to lodge my daughter, and I myself favoured him with a site for it, and that too before your very face. But however that may be — shall a man who could send me such a store of such stones for the Princess's dowry, of which kings have never obtained even a few, shall he, I say, be unable to build a building like this?"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-sixth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Vizier heard the Sultan's words he knew that his lord loved Aladdin exceedingly; so his envy and malice increased; only, as he could do nothing against the youth, he sat silent and powerless to make any reply.

But Aladdin, seeing that it was broad day and that the appointed time had come for him to go to the palace — where his wedding was being celebrated, and where the emirs and viziers and grandees were gathered about the Sultan to be present at the ceremony — got up and rubbed the Lamp; and when its slave appeared and said, "My lord, ask whatever you want, for I stand before you and at your service," he said, "I mean to go to the palace at once, this day being my wedding festival, and I want you to supply me with ten thousand dinars."

The slave vanished for the twinkling of an eye and came back bringing the money; whereupon Aladdin took horse with his mamelukes before and behind him and rode on his way, scattering gold pieces among the people as he went, until they were all fondly disposed towards him and his dignity was enhanced.

But when he drew near the palace, and the emirs and officers and army officers who were standing to await him noticed his approach, they hurried straight to the King and gave him the news; whereupon the Sultan rose and went to meet his son-in-law, and after embracing and kissing him led him, still holding his hand, into his own apartment, where he sat down and seated him at his right side.

The city was all decorated, and music rang through the palace and the singers sang, until the King ordered the midday meal brought, when the eunuchs and mamelukes hurried to spread the tables and trays, which were such as are served to kings.

Then the Sultan and Aladdin and the lords of the land and the grandees of the realm took their seats and ate and drank until they were satisfied. And it was a very fine wedding, in city and palace alike, and the high nobles all rejoiced in it and the common people of the kingdom were just as gladdened, while the governors of provinces and rulers of districts flocked in from far regions to see Aladdin's marriage and its processions and festivities.

The Sultan too marvelled in his mind to look at Aladdin's mother and to remember how she used to visit him in her poverty-stricken state, while her son could command all this wealth and magnificence.

And when the spectators who crowded the royal palace to enjoy the wedding feasts looked at Aladdin's pavilion and the beauties of the building, they were seized with immense surprise that so vast a building as this could have been raised up in a single night; and they blessed the youth and cried, "Allah gladden him! By Allah, he deserves all this! Allah bless his days!"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-seventh Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when dinner was over, Aladdin rose and, taking his leave of the Sultan, took horse with his mamelukes and rode to his own pavilion to prepare to receive his bride, the Lady Badr al-Budur, in it.

And as he passed, all the people shouted their good wishes with one voice, and their words were, "Allah gladden you! Allah increase your glory! Allah grant you length of life!" while immense crowds gathered to swell the marriage procession; and they escorted him to his new home, he showering gold on them the whole time.

When he reached his pavilion he dismounted and walked in and sat down on the divan, while his mamelukes stood before him with folded arms; and after a short delay they brought him sherbets; and when these had been drunk, he ordered his white slaves and handmaids and eunuchs and everybody in the pavilion to make ready to receive the Lady Badr al-Budur.

Moreover, as soon as mid-afternoon came and the air had cooled and the great heat of the sun had lessened, the Sultan ordered his army officers and emirs and viziers to go down to the plain of the maydan, where he rode too. And Aladdin also took horse with his mamelukes, mounting a stallion whose like was not among the horses of the Arabs of Arabia; and he showed his horsemanship on the parade ground and so played at the javelin game that nobody could withstand him — while his bride sat watching him from the latticed balcony of her bower and, seeing in him such beauty and such horsemanship, fell headlong in love with him and was ready to fly for joy.

And after they had ridden their horses in rings on the maydan, and each had displayed what he could of horsemanship, and Aladdin had proved himself the best man of them all, they rode in a body to the Sultan's palace, and the youth went back to his own pavilion.

But when evening came, the viziers and nobles took the bridegroom and, falling into order, escorted him to the royal baths, where he was bathed and perfumed. As soon as he came out he put on a dress more magnificent than the last and took horse, with the emirs and the officers riding before him and forming a grand procession, in which four of the viziers carried naked swords about him. All the citizens and the strangers and the troops marched before him in ordered throng, carrying wax candles and kettledrums and pipes and other instruments of mirth and merriment, until they escorted him to his pavilion.

Here he dismounted and walked in and took his seat, and seated the viziers and emirs who had escorted him; and the mamelukes brought sherbets and sugared drinks, which they also passed to the people who had followed in his train. It was a world of people, past all telling; and with it all Aladdin ordered his mamelukes to stand outside the pavilion doors and shower gold on the crowd.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-eighth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Sultan came back from the plain of the maydan to his palace, he ordered the household, men and women alike, to form a cavalcade at once for his daughter, with all ceremony, and carry her to her bridegroom's pavilion.

So the nobles and officers who had followed and escorted the bridegroom mounted at once, and the handmaids and eunuchs went out with wax candles and made a very fine procession for the Lady Badr al-Budur; and they paced on in front of her until they came into Aladdin's pavilion, with Aladdin's mother walking beside the bride. In front of the Princess went the wives of the viziers and emirs, grandees and notables; and in attendance on her were the forty-eight slave girls presented to her before by her bridegroom, each holding in her hand a huge candle scented with camphor and ambergris and set in a candlestick of gem-studded gold.

And reaching Aladdin's pavilion they led her to her bower in the upper storey and changed her robes and enthroned her; then, as soon as the displaying was over, they took her to Aladdin's apartments, and presently he paid her the first visit.

Now his mother was with the bride; and when the bridegroom came up and took off her veil, the old lady fell to studying the beauty of the Princess and her loveliness; and she looked around at the pavilion, which was all lit up by gold and gems, besides the many candelabra of precious metals encrusted with emeralds and jacinths. So she said in her mind, "Once upon a time I thought the Sultan's palace was very fine; but this pavilion is a thing apart. Nor do I believe that any of the greatest kings of Persia ever attained anything like it in his day; and I am certain that all the world together could not build a match for it."

And no less did the Lady Badr al-Budur fall to gazing at the pavilion and marvelling at its magnificence.

Then the tables were spread, and they all ate and drank and were gladdened; after which eighty girls came before them, each holding an instrument of mirth and merriment in her hand; and then they moved their fingertips deftly and touched the strings, striking them into song, most musical and most melancholy, until they tore the hearts of the hearers.

At this the Princess marvelled more than ever, and said to herself, "In all my life I never heard songs like these" — until she left off eating, the better to listen.

And at last Aladdin poured out wine for her and passed it to her with his own hand; so great joy and jubilation went round among them, and it was a notable night, such a one as Alexander, Lord of the Two Horns, never spent in his time.

When they had finished eating and drinking and the tables had been taken away from before them, Aladdin got up and went in to his bride.

As soon as morning came he left his bed, and the treasurer brought him a costly suit and a very fine one, of the most sumptuous robes worn by kings. Then, after drinking coffee flavoured with ambergris, he ordered the horses saddled and, mounting with his mamelukes before and behind him, rode to the Sultan's palace; and as he came into its courtyard the eunuchs went in and reported his coming to their lord.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Sixty-ninth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Sultan heard of Aladdin's approach he got up at once to receive him, and embraced and kissed him as though he were his own son; then, seating him at his right, he blessed and prayed for him, as did the viziers and emirs, the lords of the land and the grandees of the realm.

Presently the King ordered the morning meal brought, which the attendants served up; and they all broke their fast together; and when they had eaten and drunk their fill and the tables had been taken away by the eunuchs, Aladdin turned to the Sultan and said, "My lord, would your Highness be pleased to honour me today at dinner in the house of the Lady Badr al-Budur, your beloved daughter, and to come accompanied by all your ministers and the grandees of the realm?"

The King replied — and he was delighted with his son-in-law — "You are surpassing in liberality, my son!"

Then he gave orders to all those invited and rode out with them, Aladdin riding beside him, until they reached the pavilion; and as he went in and considered its construction, its architecture and its stonework, all jasper and carnelian, his sight was dazed and his wits amazed at such grandeur and magnificence of wealth.

Then, turning to the minister, he said, "What do you say? Tell me, have you ever in all your time seen anything like this among the mightiest of earth's monarchs, for the abundance of gold and gems we are looking at now?"

The Grand Vizier replied, "My lord the King, this is a feat that cannot be accomplished by the might of any monarch among the sons of Adam; nor could all the peoples of the whole world put together build a palace like this; no, not even builders could be found to make anything resembling it, except — as I said to your Highness — by force of sorcery."

These words made the King certain that his minister spoke from nothing but envy and jealousy of Aladdin, and wanted to establish in the royal mind that all this splendour was not made by man but by means of magic and with the aid of the black art. So he said to him, "That is enough from you, Vizier: you have no other word to say, and I know very well what cause drives you to say what you say."

Then Aladdin went ahead of the Sultan until he had led him to the upper belvedere, where he saw its skylights, windows and latticed casements and shutters wholly made of emeralds and rubies and other costly gems; at which his mind was perplexed and his wits bewildered and his thoughts distracted.

Presently he took to strolling round the belvedere and enjoying these sights that captured the eye, until he happened to cast a glance at the window that Aladdin had deliberately left unworked and unfinished like the rest; and when he noticed that it was incomplete he cried, "Woe and alas for you, window, for your imperfection!"

And, turning to his minister, he asked, "Do you know the reason for leaving this window and its frame incomplete?"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventieth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Vizier said to the Sultan, "My lord, I imagine that the want of finish in this window comes of your Highness having pushed on Aladdin's marriage, so that he had no leisure to complete it."

Now at that time Aladdin had gone in to his bride, the Lady Badr al-Budur, to tell her that her father was there; and when he came back the King asked him, "My son, what is the reason that the window of this belvedere was not made perfect?"

"O King of the Age, seeing how sudden my wedding was," he answered, "I could not find craftsmen to finish it."

The Sultan said, "I have a mind to complete it myself."

And Aladdin said, "Allah perpetuate your glory, O King; so shall your memory endure in your daughter's pavilion."

The Sultan immediately ordered jewellers and goldsmiths summoned, and gave orders that they should be supplied from the treasury with everything they needed of gold and gems and precious ores; and when they were gathered together he commanded them to complete the work still wanting in the belvedere window.

Meanwhile the Princess came out to meet her father the Sultan, who noticed her smiling face as she drew near; so he embraced her and kissed her, and then led her into the pavilion, and they all went in together.

Now this was the hour of the midday meal, and one table had been spread for the sovereign, his daughter and his son-in-law, and a second for the viziers, the lords of the land, the grandees of the realm, the chief officers of the army, the chamberlains and the officials.

The King took his seat between the Princess and her husband; and when he put out his hand to the food and tasted it, he was struck with surprise at the flavour of the dishes and their savoury and sumptuous cooking. Moreover, there stood before him the eighty girls, each and every one of them saying to the full moon, "Get up, and let me sit in your place!" All held instruments of mirth and merriment, and they tuned them and deftly moved their fingertips and struck the strings into song, most musical and most melodious, which expanded the heart of any mourner.

At this the Sultan was gladdened and the time was good to him; and in his high enjoyment he exclaimed, "In very truth this thing is beyond the compass of King or Caesar."

Then they fell to eating and drinking, and the cup went round until they had drunk enough, when sweetmeats and fruits of all sorts and other such things were served, the dessert being laid out in a different room, to which they moved and enjoyed these pleasures to their satisfaction.

Presently the Sultan got up to see whether the work of his jewellers and goldsmiths matched that of the pavilion; so he went upstairs to them and inspected their work and how they had done it; but he noticed a very great difference, and his men were far from being able to make anything like the rest of Aladdin's pavilion.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-first Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that after the King had inspected the work of his jewellers and goldsmiths, they told him how all the gems stored in the Lesser Treasury had been brought to them and used, and that the whole lot had proved insufficient; whereupon he ordered the Greater Treasury opened and gave the workmen everything they wanted of him. Moreover he allowed them, if that was not enough, to take the jewels Aladdin had given him.

They carried off the whole lot and pushed on with their labours, but they found the gems failing them, even though they had not yet finished half of what was wanting to the belvedere window. At this the King ordered them to seize all the precious stones owned by the viziers and grandees of the realm; but although they did as he bade them, the supply still fell short of what they needed.

Next morning Aladdin got up to look at the jewellers' work, and noticed that they had not finished half of what was wanting to the belvedere window; so he ordered them at once to undo everything they had done and give the jewels back to their owners.

So they pulled out the precious stones and sent the Sultan's to the Sultan and the viziers' to the viziers. Then the jewellers went to the King and told him what Aladdin had ordered; so he asked them, "What did he say to you, and what was his reason, and why was he not content to have the window finished, and why did he undo the work you had done?"

They answered, "Our lord, we have no idea at all; he simply told us to take out everything we had done."

At this the Sultan called for his horse at once and, mounting, took the road to the pavilion; while Aladdin, having dismissed the goldsmiths and jewellers, had gone into his private room and rubbed the Lamp.

At this its servant appeared to him at once and said, "Ask whatever you want: your slave is between your hands."

And Aladdin said, "It is my wish that you finish the window that was left unfinished."

The marid replied, "On my head be it, and on my eyes!" — and then vanished, and after a little while came back saying, "My lord, truly what you commanded me to do is done."

So Aladdin went upstairs to the belvedere and found the whole window in a wholly finished state; and while he was still studying it, behold, a eunuch came in to him and said, "My lord, the Sultan has ridden out to visit you and is coming through the pavilion gate."

So Aladdin went straight down and received his father-in-law.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-second Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Sultan, on catching sight of his son-in-law, cried to him, "Why, my child, have you done this, and not let the jewellers complete the belvedere window, leaving an unfinished place in the pavilion?"

Aladdin replied, "O King of the Age, I left it imperfect only for a design of my own; nor was I incapable of perfecting it, nor could I intend that your Highness should honour me by visiting a pavilion in which there was anything deficient. And so that you may know I am not unable to make it perfect, let your Highness be pleased to walk upstairs with me and see whether anything remains to be done to it or not."

So the Sultan went up with him and, entering the belvedere, fell to looking right and left; but he saw no fault at all in any of the windows — no, he noticed that they were all perfect. So he marvelled at the sight and embraced Aladdin and kissed him, saying, "My son, what is this extraordinary feat? You can do in a single night what the jewellers could not do in months. By Allah, I believe you have neither brother nor rival in this world."

Aladdin said, "Allah prolong your life and preserve you for ever! Your slave does not deserve such praise."

And the King said, "By Allah, my child, you deserve all praise for a feat that all the craftsmen of the world were incapable of."

Then the Sultan came down and went into the apartments of his daughter the Lady Badr al-Budur to take a rest beside her, and he saw that she was exceedingly joyful at the glory and grandeur she lived in; and then, after resting a while, he went back to his palace.

Now Aladdin used to go through the city streets every day with his mamelukes riding in front of him and behind him, showering gold right and left upon the people; and all the world, stranger and neighbour, far and near, was filled with love of him for the excess of his liberality and generosity.

Moreover he increased the pensions of the poor religious and the paupers, and he would distribute alms to them with his own hand; by which good deed he won a high reputation throughout the realm; and most of the lords of the land and the emirs would eat at his table, and men swore by nothing except his precious life.

Nor did he leave off going out to the chase and to the parade ground, and riding horses and playing at the javelin game in the Sultan's presence; and whenever the Lady Badr al-Budur watched him disporting himself on horseback, she loved him all the more, and thought to herself that Allah had done her abundant good by causing what happened with the Vizier's son to happen, and by preserving her virginity intact for her true bridegroom, Aladdin.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-third Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin won for himself a fairer fame and a rarer reputation day by day, while affection for him increased in the hearts of all the people and he grew greater in the eyes of men.

Moreover it happened in those days that certain enemies took horse and attacked the Sultan, who armed and equipped an army to drive them off and made Aladdin its commander. So he marched out with his men and did not stop marching until he drew near the enemy, whose forces were exceedingly many; and presently, when the action began, he bared his sword and charged home upon them.

Then battle and slaughter broke out and violent was the uproar; but at last Aladdin broke the hostile host and put them all to flight, killing the best part of them and plundering their money and cattle, their property and possessions; and he despoiled them of spoils that could not be counted or computed.

Then he came back victorious after a noble victory, and entered the capital, which had decorated herself in his honour out of her delight in him; and the Sultan went out to meet him and, congratulating him, embraced him and kissed him; and throughout the kingdom high festival was held with great joy and gladness.

Presently the sovereign and his son-in-law went to the pavilion, where they were met by the Princess Badr al-Budur, who rejoiced in her husband and, after kissing him between the eyes, led him to her apartments. After a time the Sultan came too, and they sat down while the slave girls brought them sherbets and confections, which they ate and drank.

Then the Sultan commanded that the whole kingdom be decorated for the triumph of his son-in-law and his victory over the invader; and the subjects and the soldiery and all the people knew only Allah in heaven and Aladdin on earth; for their love, won by his liberality, was increased by his noble horsemanship and his successful fighting for the country and putting the enemy to flight.

Such, then, was the high fortune of Aladdin. But as for the Moroccan magician, after going back to his own country he spent all this time bewailing what he had endured of toil and travail to win the Lamp, and above all that his trouble had gone for nothing and that the morsel, when it was almost at his lips, had flown out of his grasp.

He pondered all this and mourned and reviled Aladdin out of the excess of his rage against him; and at times he would exclaim, "I am well satisfied with this bastard's death underground, and I only hope that at some time or other I may get hold of the Lamp, seeing how it is still safe."

Now one day he struck a table of sand and dotted down the figures and carefully considered what they came to; then he transferred them to paper so that he might study them and make sure of Aladdin's destruction and of the safety of the Lamp preserved beneath the earth. Presently he firmly established the sequence of the figures, mothers as well as daughters, but still he did not see the Lamp.

At this rage overrode him, and he made another trial to be sure of Aladdin's death; but he did not see him in the enchanted treasure. At this his anger grew still more, and it grew greater when he ascertained that the youth had come up out of the ground and was now on the surface of the earth alive and alert — and furthermore, that he had become the owner of the Lamp, for which he himself had endured such toil and travail and troubles as a man cannot bear except for so great an object.

So he said to himself, "I have suffered pains and penalties that nobody else could have endured, for the sake of the Lamp, only for somebody other than me to carry it off; and this accursed boy has taken it without any difficulty. And who knows whether he knows the virtues of the Lamp, than whose owner nobody in the world should be wealthier?"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-fourth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Moroccan magician, having considered and ascertained that Aladdin had escaped from the vault and had got the prize of the Lamp, said to himself, "There is nothing for it but that I work for his destruction."

He then struck another geomantic table and, examining the figures, saw that the lad had won himself immeasurable riches and had married the daughter of his King; so, out of envy and jealousy, he was fired with the flame of wrath; and, getting up without let or delay, he equipped himself and set out for China, where he arrived in due season.

Now when he had reached the King's capital, where Aladdin was, he put up at one of the caravanserais; and when he had rested from the weariness of the journey he put on his clothes and went down to wander about the streets, where he never passed a group without hearing them chattering about the pavilion and its grandeur and praising Aladdin's beauty, his good looks, his liberality and generosity, his fine manners and his good morals.

Presently he went into an establishment where men were drinking a certain warm beverage; and, going up to one of those who were loud in their praises, he said to him, "Fine young man, who may this be that you all describe and commend?"

"Evidently you are a foreigner," answered the other, "and you have come from a far country. But even granting that, how does it happen that you have not heard of the Emir Aladdin, whose renown, I fancy, has filled the universe, and whose pavilion, known by report to far and near, is one of the Wonders of the World? How, then, has nothing of this ever come to your ears, nor the name of Aladdin — whose glory and enjoyment may our Lord increase! — nor his fame?"

The Moroccan replied, "The sum of my wishes is to look upon this pavilion; and if you would do me a favour, please guide me to it, for I am a foreigner."

The man answered, "To hear is to obey"; and, going ahead of him, pointed out Aladdin's pavilion; whereupon the Moroccan fell to studying it and understood at once that it was the work of the Lamp.

So he cried, "Ah! Ah! I must dig a pit for this accursed boy, this son of a tailor, who could not once earn himself so much as an evening meal; and if the Fates help me, I will certainly destroy his life and send his mother back to spinning at her wheel, as she used to do before."

So saying, he went back to his caravanserai in a sorry state of grief and melancholy and regret, bred by his envy and hatred of Aladdin.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-fifth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Moroccan magician got back to his caravanserai he took his astrological gear and his geomantic table to discover where the Lamp might be; and he found that it was in the pavilion and not on Aladdin's person. So he rejoiced at this exceedingly and exclaimed, "Now indeed it will be an easy task to take the life of this accursed boy, and I see my way to getting the Lamp."

Then he went to a coppersmith and said to him, "Make me a set of lamps, and take the full price of them from me and more; only I would have you hurry to finish them."

The smith replied, "Hearing and obeying," and fell to work to keep his word; and when they were ready the Moroccan paid him what price he asked; then, taking them, he carried them to the inn and set them in a basket.

Presently he began wandering about the highways and market streets of the capital, crying aloud, "New lamps for old! Ho! Who will give old lamps for new lamps?"

But when people heard him crying in this fashion they laughed at him and said, "No doubt this man is jinn-mad, going about offering new for old"; and a whole world followed him, and the children of the quarter chased him from place to place laughing at him, and he neither forbade them nor cared how they treated him.

And he did not stop strolling about the streets until he came under Aladdin's pavilion, where he shouted at the top of his voice, and the boys screamed after him, "A madman! A madman!"

Now Destiny had decreed that the Lady Badr al-Budur should be sitting in her belvedere, from which she heard somebody crying like a crier and the children bawling at him; only she did not understand what was going on. So she gave orders to one of her slave girls, saying, "Go and see who it is that is crying, and what his cry is."

The girl went out and looked, and saw a man crying, "New lamps for old! Ho! Who will give old lamps for new lamps?" — and the little ones chasing him and laughing at him; and the Princess laughed as loudly when this strange business was told to her.

Now Aladdin had carelessly left the Lamp in his pavilion without hiding it and locking it up in his strongbox; and one of the slave girls who had seen it said, "My lady, I think I noticed an old lamp in my lord Aladdin's apartment; so let us give it in exchange for a new lamp to this man, and see whether his cry is truth or a lie."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-sixth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that at this the Princess said to the slave girl, "Bring me the old lamp you say you saw in your lord's apartment."

Now the Lady Badr al-Budur knew nothing about the Lamp and its peculiar properties, which had raised Aladdin her husband to such high rank and grandeur; and her only end and aim was to find out by experiment what was in the mind of a man who would give new in exchange for old.

So the handmaid went out and up to Aladdin's apartment and came back with the Lamp to her lady, who, like all the rest of them, knew nothing of the Moroccan's cunning tricks and his crafty device.

Then the Princess ordered one of the eunuch officers to go down and barter the old lamp for a new one. So he obeyed her order and, after taking a new lamp from the man, came back and laid it before his lady; who, looking at it and seeing that it was brand new, fell to laughing at the Moroccan's wits.

But the Moroccan, when he had the thing in his hand and recognised it for the Lamp of the enchanted treasury, put it at once into his breast pocket and left all the other lamps to the people who were bartering with him.

Then he went off running until he was clear of the city, when he walked at leisure over the level ground; and he waited patiently until night fell on him in open country where there was nobody but himself.

There he brought out the Lamp, when suddenly the marid appeared to him and said, "Here I am! Your slave stands between your hands: ask of me whatever you want."

"It is my desire," the Moroccan replied, "that you lift up Aladdin's pavilion from where it is now, with the people in it and everything it contains — not forgetting me — and set it down in my own land, Africa. You know my town, and I want the building placed in the gardens close by it."

The marid slave replied, "Hearing and obedience: shut your eyes and open your eyes, and you will find yourself together with the pavilion in your own country."

This was done; and in the twinkling of an eye the Moroccan and the pavilion and everything in it were carried away to the land of Africa.

Such, then, was the work of the Moroccan magician. But now let us go back to the Sultan and his son-in-law.

It was the custom of the King, because of his attachment to his daughter and his affection for her, every morning when he had shaken off sleep to open the latticed casement and look out from it, so that he might catch sight of where she lived. So that day he got up and did as he always did.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-seventh Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Sultan came up to the latticed casement of his palace and looked out towards Aladdin's pavilion, he saw nothing at all: no, the site was smooth as a well-trodden highway and just as it had been before, and he could find neither building nor outbuildings.

So astonishment covered him like a garment, and his wits were bewildered, and he began rubbing his eyes in case they were dimmed or darkened, and gazing intently; but at last he was certain that no trace of the pavilion remained and no sign that it had ever been, nor did he know the why or the wherefore of its disappearance.

So his surprise increased and he struck hand upon hand, and the tears trickled down his cheeks over his beard, because he did not know what had become of his daughter. Then he sent out officials at once and summoned the Grand Vizier, who attended immediately; and, seeing him in this pitiable state, said, "Pardon, O King of the Age; may Allah keep every ill from you! Why are you in such sorrow?"

The sovereign exclaimed, "I suppose you do not know what has happened to me?"

And the minister said, "Not at all, our lord: by Allah, I know nothing whatever about it."

"Then," resumed the Sultan, "it is plain you have not looked in the direction of Aladdin's pavilion today."

"True, my lord," said the Vizier; "it must still be locked and fast shut."

And the King said, "Since you have no inkling of anything, get up and look out of the window and see Aladdin's pavilion, that you say is locked and fast shut."

The minister obeyed him, but he could see nothing at all, neither pavilion nor anything else; so, with mind and thoughts sorely perplexed, he came back to his liege lord, who asked him, "Have you learned the reason of my distress now, and noticed that palace of yours, locked and fast shut?"

The Vizier answered, "O King of the Age, some time ago I represented to your Highness that this pavilion and all these matters were magic."

At this the Sultan, fired with anger, cried, "Where is Aladdin?"

And the minister replied, "He has gone hunting."

Whereupon the King commanded, without pause or delay, that certain of his officers and army officers should go and bring his son-in-law to him chained and with his elbows pinioned.

So they went out until they found Aladdin, when they said to him, "Our lord Aladdin, excuse us and do not be angry with us; for the King has commanded that we carry you before him pinioned and fettered, and we hope for pardon from you, because we are under royal orders which we cannot go against."

Aladdin, hearing these words, was seized with surprise; and, not knowing the reason for it, remained tongue-tied for a time; after which he turned to them and asked, "Good people, do you know nothing at all about the motive for the royal command? I know very well that my soul is innocent, and that I have never sinned against king or against kingdom."

"Our lord," they answered, "we have no idea whatever."

So Aladdin got down from his horse and said to them, "Do whatever the Sultan told you to do, for the King's command is upon the head and the eyes."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-eighth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the officers, having bound Aladdin and pinioned his elbows behind his back, dragged him along in chains and carried him into the city.

But when the people saw him pinioned and in irons, they understood that the Sultan meant to strike off his head; and, since they loved him exceedingly, they all gathered together and seized their weapons; and then, swarming out of their houses, followed the soldiers to see what was going on.

And when the troops arrived with Aladdin at the palace they went in and informed the Sultan, whereupon he immediately commanded the executioner to cut off his son-in-law's head.

Now as soon as the subjects knew of this order they barricaded the gates and shut the doors of the palace and sent a message to the King, saying, "At this very moment we will level your house over the heads of everybody in it and over your own, if the least hurt or harm comes to Aladdin."

So the Vizier went in and reported to the Sultan, "O King of the Age, your command is about to seal the roll of our lives; and it would be better if you pardoned your son-in-law, in case some sore mischance comes upon us; for the people love him far more than they love us."

Now the executioner had already spread out the carpet of blood and, having seated Aladdin on it, had bandaged his eyes; moreover he had walked round him several times, waiting for his lord's last orders, when the King looked out of the window and saw his subjects — who had suddenly attacked him — swarming up the walls and meaning to tear them down.

So he immediately ordered the executioner to stay his hand from Aladdin, and commanded the crier to go out to the crowd and cry aloud that he had pardoned his son-in-law and taken him back into favour.

But when Aladdin found himself free and saw the Sultan seated on his throne, he went up to him and said, "My lord, since your Highness has favoured me all my life, be pleased of your grace to let me know now how and in what I have sinned against you."
