"Traitor," cried the King, "until this moment I knew of no sin of yours"; then, turning to the Vizier, he said, "Take him and make him look out of the window, and afterwards let him tell us where his pavilion is."

And when the royal order was obeyed, Aladdin saw the place as level as a well-trodden road, exactly as it had been before the foundation of the building was laid, without the faintest trace of any building at all.

At this he was astonished and perplexed, not knowing what had happened; but when he came back into the presence the King asked him, "What is it you have seen? Where is your pavilion, and where is my daughter, the core of my heart, my only child, than whom I have no other?"

Aladdin answered, "O King of the Age, I know nothing of it, nor anything of what has happened."

And the Sultan retorted, "You must understand, Aladdin, that I have pardoned you only so that you may go out and look into this affair and enquire after my daughter for me. And never show yourself in my presence unless she is with you; and if you do not bring her, by the life of my head I will cut off your head."

The other replied, "To hear is to obey: only grant me a delay and respite of forty days; after which, if I do not produce her, strike off my head and do with me whatever you wish."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Seventy-ninth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Sultan said to Aladdin, "Truly I have granted your request, a delay of forty days; but do not imagine you can fly out of my hand, for I would bring you back even if you were above the clouds instead of only on the surface of the earth."

Aladdin replied, "My lord the Sultan, as I said to your Highness, if I fail to bring her within the appointed term I will present myself to have my head struck off."

Now when the people and all the subjects saw Aladdin at liberty they rejoiced exceedingly and were delighted at his release; but the shame of his treatment, and his embarrassment before his friends, and the envious exultation of his enemies had bowed down Aladdin's head; so he went off wandering through the streets of the city, perplexed about his situation and not knowing what had happened to him.

He lingered about the capital for two days in the saddest state, not knowing what to do to find his wife and his pavilion; and during this time various people privately brought him food and drink.

When the two days were over he left the city to wander about the waste and open lands outside the walls, with no notion where he ought to go; and he walked on aimlessly until the path brought him beside a river, where, under the stress of the sorrow that overwhelmed him, he gave himself up to despair and thought of throwing himself into the water.

Being, however, a good Muslim who professed the unity of the Godhead, he feared Allah in his soul; and, standing on the bank, he prepared to perform the ritual ablution. But as he was scooping up the water in his right hand and rubbing his fingers, it so happened that he also rubbed the Ring.

At this its marid appeared and said to him, "Here I am! Your slave stands between your hands: ask of me whatever you want."

Seeing the marid, Aladdin rejoiced exceedingly and cried, "Slave, I want you to bring my pavilion before me, and my wife the Lady Badr al-Budur in it, together with everything it contains."

"My lord," replied the marid, "it is very hard on me that you ask a service I cannot manage: this matter depends on the Slave of the Lamp, and I dare not even attempt it."

Aladdin answered, "Since the matter is beyond your competence, I do not require it of you; but at least take me up and set me down beside my pavilion, in whatever land that may be."

The slave exclaimed, "Hearing and obeying, my lord"; and, lifting him high in the air, in the space of a glance set him down beside his pavilion in the land of Africa, at a spot facing his wife's apartment.

Now this was at nightfall; yet one look was enough for him to recognise his home; whereby his cares and worries were cleared away, and he recovered his trust in Allah, after having cut off all hope of ever seeing his wife again.

Then he fell to pondering the secret and mysterious favours of the Lord (glorified be His omnipotence!), and how, after despair had mastered him, the Ring had come to gladden him; and how, when all his hopes were cut off, Allah had been pleased to bless him with the services of its slave.

So he rejoiced and his melancholy left him; and then, since he had gone four days without sleep for the excess of his cares and sorrows and the stress of his thoughts, he went up close to his pavilion and slept under a tree beside the building, which, as we said, had been set down among the gardens outside the city of Africa.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Eightieth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin lay that night under a tree beside his pavilion in complete restfulness; but a man who carries his head next door to the headsman cannot sleep at night except when slumber gets the better of him.

He slumbered until Morning showed her face; and when he was woken by the warbling of the small birds he got up and went down to the bank of the river that ran past there into the city; and here he washed his hands and face again and afterwards finished his ablution. Then he prayed the dawn prayer; and when he had ended his devotions he came back and sat down under the windows of the Princess's bower.

Now the Lady Badr al-Budur, out of her extreme sorrow at being parted from her husband and her father the Sultan, and at the great misfortune that had come upon her from the accursed Moroccan magician, had got into the habit of rising in the darkness before dawn and sitting in tears, since she could not sleep at nights and had sworn off food and drink.

Her favourite slave girl used to come into her chamber at the hour of the prayer salutation in order to dress her; and this time, by the decree of Destiny, when she threw open the window to let her lady comfort and console herself by looking at the trees and the streams, and peered out of the lattice herself, she caught sight of her master sitting below, and told the Princess, saying, "My lady! My lady! Here is my lord Aladdin sitting at the foot of the wall!"

So her mistress got up hurriedly and, gazing from the casement, saw him; and her husband, raising his head, saw her; so she greeted him and he greeted her, both of them ready to fly for joy.

Presently she said, "Up and come in to me by the private side door, for the accursed man is not here now"; and she gave orders to the slave girl, who went down and opened it for him.

Then Aladdin came through it and was met by his wife, and they embraced and exchanged kisses with all delight until they wept for sheer joy.

After this they sat down, and Aladdin said to her, "My lady, before anything else it is my wish to ask you a question. I used to keep an old copper lamp in a certain part of my pavilion; what became of it?"

When the Princess heard these words she sighed and cried, "My darling, it was that very Lamp that made us fall into this calamity!"

Aladdin asked her, "How did the affair happen?"

And she answered by recounting to him everything that had passed, first and last, and especially how they had given an old lamp in exchange for a new one, adding, "And the next day we had hardly seen one another at dawn before we found ourselves in this country; and the man who deceived us and took the lamp by way of barter told me that he had done the deed by the might of his magic and by means of the Lamp; that he is a Moor from Africa; and that we are now in his native country."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Eighty-first Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Lady Badr al-Budur had finished speaking, Aladdin went on, "Tell me what this accursed man intends with regard to you; also what he says to you, and what he wants of you."

She replied, "He comes to visit me once every day and no more. He would woo me to his love, and he begs me to take him for my husband instead of you, and to forget you and console myself for the loss of you. And he tells me that the Sultan my father has cut off my husband's head, adding that you, the son of poor parents, were made rich by him. And he coaxes me with talk; but he never gets anything from me except weeping and wailing, nor has he heard one sugar-sweet word from me."

Aladdin said, "Tell me where he has put the Lamp, if you know anything about it."

And she said, "He carries it about on his body always, nor is it possible for him to leave it for a single hour; and moreover, once, when he was telling me what I have just told you, he brought it out of his breast pocket and let me look at it."

When Aladdin heard these words he rejoiced exceedingly and said, "My lady, listen to me. It is my plan to go away from you at once, and to come back only after changing these clothes of mine; so do not be surprised when you see me altered, but tell one of your women to stand by the private side door all the time, and to open it the moment she sees me coming. And now I will contrive a scheme for killing this damned fool."

With that he got up and, going out of the pavilion door, walked on until he met a farm labourer on the way, to whom he said, "Man, take my clothes and give me your garments."

But the peasant refused; so Aladdin stripped him of his clothes by force and put them on, leaving the man his own rich gear by way of a gift.

Then he followed the highway leading to the neighbouring city, and, entering it, went to the perfumers' bazaar, where he bought from one of them some rarely potent bhang, the kind that works in a minute, paying two dinars for two drams of it; and he came back in disguise by the same road until he reached the pavilion.

Here the slave girl opened the private side door to him, and he went in to the Lady Badr al-Budur.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Eighty-second Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when Aladdin came in disguised to his wife he said:

"Listen to me. I want you to dress and adorn yourself in your best and cast off every outward show and appearance of care; and when the accursed Moroccan visits you, receive him with a 'Welcome and fair welcome,' and meet him with a smiling face, and invite him to come and have supper with you. Moreover, let him see that you have forgotten Aladdin your beloved, and your father too, and that you have learned to love him with a great love, showing him every kind of joy and pleasure.

"Then ask him for wine, which must be red, and pledge him to his secret wishes in a meaningful draught; and when you have given him two or three cupfuls and made him careless, then drop these drops into his cup and fill it up with wine. He will no sooner drink it than he will fall on his back senseless as a dead man."

Hearing these words, the Princess exclaimed, "It is exceedingly hard for me to do such a thing; and yet I must do it, so that we may escape the defilement of this accursed man who tortured me by parting me from you and from my father. So the killing of this accursed man is lawful and right."

Then Aladdin ate and drank with his wife enough to keep off his hunger, and then, getting up without pause or delay, went out of the pavilion.

So the Lady Badr al-Budur summoned her tirewoman, who robed her and arrayed her in her finest clothes and adorned her and perfumed her; and while she was like this, behold, the accursed Moroccan came in.

He was greatly delighted to see her in such a state, and more delighted still when she faced him, quite against her custom, with a laughing face; and his love-longing increased, and his desire to have her.

Then she took him and, seating him beside her, said, "My darling, do come to me tonight, if you are willing, and let us have supper together. My sorrow has been enough for me; for if I were to sit mourning for a thousand years or even two thousand, Aladdin would never come back to me from the tomb. And I rely on what you said yesterday, namely that my father the Sultan killed him in his stress of sorrow at being parted from me.

"And do not be surprised that I am changed today from what I was yesterday; the reason for it is that I have decided to take you for my friend and companion in Aladdin's place and succession, for now I have no other man but you. So I hope for your company tonight, that we may have supper together and drink a little wine with one another; and especially I should like you to let me taste the wine of your native soil, the land of Africa, because it may well be better than any of the wine of China that we drink. I have some wine by me, but it is the growth of my own country, and I very much want to taste what yours produces."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Eighty-third Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Moroccan saw the love lavished on him by the Lady Badr al-Budur, and noticed how changed she was from the sorrowful, melancholy woman she used to be, he thought she had cut off all hope of Aladdin; and he was overjoyed and said to her, "I hear and obey, my lady, whatever you wish and everything you command. I have at home a jar of our country's wine, which I have carefully kept and stored deep in the earth for eight years; and I will go now and fill our need from it and come back to you in all haste."

But the Princess, so as to wheedle him more and more, replied, "My darling, do not go and leave me alone; send one of the eunuchs to fill some for us, and stay sitting here beside me, so that I may find my consolation in you."

He answered, "My lady, nobody knows where the jar is buried but myself, and I will not be long away from you."

So saying, the Moroccan went out, and after a short time brought back as much wine as they wanted; whereupon the Princess said to him, "You have taken pains and trouble to serve me, and I have suffered for your sake, my beloved."

He said, "Not at all, eyes of mine; I hold myself honoured by serving you."

Then the Lady Badr al-Budur sat down with him at table, and the two fell to eating; and presently the Princess said she would like to drink, when the handmaid filled her a cup at once and then crowned another for the Moroccan. So she drank to his long life and his secret wishes, and he drank to her life too.

Then the Princess, who was unmatched in eloquence and delicacy of speech, fell to making a drinking companion of him, and beguiled him by addressing him in the sweetest terms, full of hidden meaning. This was done only so that he might become more madly in love with her; but the Moroccan thought it came of a real inclination for him, and did not know it was a snare set to kill him.

So his longing for her increased, and he was dying of love for her when he saw her speaking to him with such tenderness of words and thoughts, and his head began to swim and all the world seemed as nothing in his eyes.

But when they came to the end of the supper, and the wine had mastered his brains, and the Princess saw this in him, she said, "With us there is a custom throughout our country, but I do not know whether it is the usage of yours or not."

The Moroccan replied, "And what may that be?"

So she said to him, "At the end of supper each lover in turn takes the cup of the beloved and drinks it off"; and at once she crowned one with wine and told the handmaid to carry him her own cup, in which the drink was mixed with the bhang.

Now she had taught the slave girl what to do; and all the handmaids and eunuchs in the pavilion longed for the sorcerer's slaughter and were at one with the Princess in that matter.

So the girl handed him the cup; and when he heard her words and saw her drinking from his cup and passing hers to him, and noticed all this show of love, he fancied himself Alexander, Lord of the Two Horns.

Then she said to him, swaying gracefully from side to side and putting her hand in his hand, "My life, here is your cup with me and my cup with you; and this is how lovers drink from each other's cups."

Then she kissed the brim and drained it to the dregs, and again kissed its lip and offered it to him.

At this he flew for joy, and meaning to do the same, raised her cup to his mouth and drank off the whole contents, without considering whether there was anything harmful in it or not.

And immediately he rolled over on his back in a deathlike condition, and the cup dropped out of his grasp; whereupon the Lady Badr al-Budur and the slave girls ran hurriedly and opened the pavilion door to their lord Aladdin, who came in disguised as a labourer.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Eighty-fourth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin, entering his pavilion, went up to his wife's apartment, where he found her still sitting at table, and facing her lay the Moroccan like a man slaughtered; so he went straight up to her and kissed her and thanked her for it.

Then, rejoicing exceedingly, he turned to her and said, "Take yourself and your handmaids to the inner rooms, and leave me alone for the present so that I may take counsel about my business."

The Princess did not hesitate but went away at once, she and her women; then Aladdin got up and, after locking the door on them, walked up to the Moroccan and put his hand to his breast pocket and drew out the Lamp; after which he unsheathed his sword and killed the villain.

Presently he rubbed the Lamp, and the marid slave appeared and said, "Here I am, my lord; what is it you want?"

"I want you," said Aladdin, "to take up my pavilion out of this country and carry it to the land of China, and there set it down on the site where it stood before, facing the Sultan's palace."

The marid replied, "Hearing and obeying, my lord."

Then Aladdin went and sat down with his wife and, throwing his arms round her neck, kissed her, and she kissed him; and they sat talking together, while the jinni carried the pavilion and everything in it to the appointed place.

Presently Aladdin told the handmaids to spread the table before him, and he and the Lady Badr al-Budur took their seats at it and fell to eating and drinking in all joy and gladness, until they had enough; when, moving to the room of wine and conversation, they sat there and caroused in fair companionship and each kissed the other with all the gladness of love.

It had been long and long since they had enjoyed any pleasure; so they went on like this until the sun of the wine rose in their heads and sleep took hold of them, at which point they went to their bed in all ease and comfort.

Early next morning Aladdin woke and woke his wife, and the slave girls came in and put on her dress and prepared her and adorned her, while her husband arrayed himself in his costliest clothes; and the two of them were ready to fly for joy at their reunion after being parted. Moreover the Princess was especially joyful and glad because that day she expected to see her beloved father.

Such was the case with Aladdin and the Lady Badr al-Budur. But as for the Sultan, after he had driven his son-in-law away he never stopped grieving for the loss of his daughter; and every hour of every day he would sit and weep for her as women weep, because she was his only child and he had nobody else to take to his heart. And as he shook off sleep, morning after morning, he would hurry to the window and throw it open and peer in the direction where Aladdin's pavilion used to stand, and pour out tears until his eyes were dried up and their lids were ulcerated.

Now on that day he got up at dawn and, as he always did, looked out — when, lo and behold, he saw a building in front of him; so he rubbed his eyes and studied it curiously until he became certain that it was his son-in-law's pavilion.

So he called for a horse without let or delay; and as soon as his beast was saddled he mounted and made for the place. And Aladdin, when he saw his father-in-law coming, went down and met him halfway; then, taking his hand, helped him up the stairs to his daughter's apartment.

And the Princess, being just as eager to see her father, came down and greeted him at the foot of the staircase facing the ground-floor hall. At this the King folded her in his arms and kissed her, shedding tears of joy; and she did the same, until at last Aladdin led them up to the upper hall, where they took their seats and the Sultan fell to asking her how she was and what had happened to her.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Eighty-fifth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Lady Badr al-Budur began to inform the Sultan of everything that had happened to her, saying, "My father, I did not come back to life until yesterday, when I saw my husband; and it was he who freed me from the bondage of that Moroccan, that magician, that accursed man, than whom I believe there is nobody viler on the face of the earth. And but for my beloved, I should never have escaped him, nor would you have seen me for the rest of my days.

"But great sadness and sorrow got hold of me, father, not only for losing you but for the loss of a husband under whose kindness I shall live all my life long, seeing that he freed me from that foul sorcerer."

Then the Princess began repeating to her father everything that had happened to her, and telling him how the Moroccan had tricked her in the guise of a lamp seller who offered new for old; how she had given him the Lamp, whose worth she did not know; and how she had bartered it away only to laugh at the lamp man's folly.

"And next morning, father," she went on, "we found ourselves and everything the pavilion contained in the land of Africa — until my husband came to us and contrived a scheme by which we escaped; and if it had not been for Aladdin hurrying to our aid, the accursed man was determined to have me by force."

Then she told him of the drops of bhang given to the African in his wine, and concluded, "Then my husband came back to me; and how I do not know, but we were moved from the land of Africa to this place."

Aladdin in his turn recounted how, finding the wizard dead drunk, he had sent his wife and her women away out of the polluted place into the inner apartments; how he had taken the Lamp out of the sorcerer's breast pocket, where his wife had told him to look; how he had killed the villain; and finally how, making use of the Lamp, he had summoned its slave and ordered him to carry the pavilion back to its proper site — ending his tale with, "And if your Highness has any doubt about my words, come with me and look at the accursed magician."

The King did so; and, having examined the Moroccan, ordered the body to be carried away at once and burnt and its ashes scattered in the air.

Then he took to embracing Aladdin and kissing him, and said, "Pardon me, my son, for I was about to destroy your life through the foul deeds of this damned enchanter, who threw you into such a pit of peril; and I may be excused, my child, for what I did to you, because I found myself bereft of my daughter, my only one, who is dearer to me than my very kingdom. You know how the hearts of parents yearn towards their children, especially when, as with me, they have one and no other to love."

And in this fashion the Sultan went on excusing himself and kissing his son-in-law.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Eighty-sixth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin said to the Sultan, "O King of the Time, you did nothing to me contrary to Holy Law, and I did not sin against you either; but all the trouble came from that Moroccan, the impure, the magician."

Thereupon the Sultan ordered the city decorated, and they obeyed him and held high feast and festivities. He also commanded the crier to cry about the streets, saying, "This day is a mighty great festival, on which public rejoicings must be held throughout the realm for a full month of thirty days, in honour of the return home of the Lady Badr al-Budur and her husband Aladdin."

So it happened with Aladdin and the Moroccan. But for all that, the King's son-in-law had not escaped entirely from the accursed man, although his body had been burnt and its ashes scattered in the air.

For the villain had a brother, more villainous still than himself, and a greater adept in necromancy, geomancy and astrology; and, as the old saying has it, "a bean, and it was split" — so each of them lived in his own quarter of the globe, that he might fill it with his sorcery, his fraud and his treason.

Now one day it happened that the Moroccan's brother wanted to learn how things fared with him; so he brought out his sandboard and dotted it and produced the figures; which, when he had considered them and studied them carefully, gave him to know that the man he was looking for was dead and housed in the tomb.

So he grieved and was certain of his death; but he dotted a second time, seeking to learn the manner of the death and where it had happened; and so he found that the place was the land of China and the manner the foulest kind of slaughter; and furthermore, that the man who had killed him was a young man named Aladdin.

Seeing this, he got up at once and equipped himself for the journey; then he set out and crossed wilds and woods and heights for the space of many months, until he reached China and the capital of the Sultan, where the slayer of his brother was.

He put up at the so-called Strangers' Inn and, hiring himself a cell, rested there a while; then he went out and wandered about the highways so that he might find some path that would help him to win his ill-minded wish, which was to take blood-revenge upon Aladdin for his brother.

Presently he went into a coffee house, a fine building that stood in the marketplace and that gathered a throng of people to play, some at mankalah, others at backgammon, others at chess and whatever else.

There he sat down and listened to the men sitting beside him; and they happened to be talking about an ancient and holy dame named Fatimah, who lived always at her devotions in a hermitage outside the town, and never came into it except two days in each month. They mentioned too that she had performed many saintly miracles.

When the Moroccan necromancer heard this he said to himself, "Now I have found what I was looking for. God willing, by means of this old woman I shall win my wish."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Eighty-seventh Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Moroccan necromancer went up to the people who were talking about the miracles performed by the devout old woman and said to one of them, "Uncle, I heard you all talking about the wonders of a certain holy woman named Fatimah: who is she, and where might she live?"

"Marvellous!" exclaimed the man. "How can you be in our city and yet never have heard about the miracles of the Lady Fatimah? Evidently, you poor fellow, you are a foreigner, since the fastings of this devout woman and her asceticism in worldly matters and the beauties of her piety have never come to your ears."

The Moroccan answered, "That is true, sir: yes, I am a stranger, and I only came to this city of yours last night. And I hope you will tell me about the saintly miracles of this virtuous woman and where she lives, for I have fallen into a calamity, and it is my wish to visit her and beg for her prayers; so that perhaps Allah, to whom be honour and glory, may through her blessings deliver me from my trouble."

At this the man recounted to him the marvels of Fatimah the devout and her piety and the beauties of her worship; and then, taking him by the hand, went with him outside the city and showed him the way to where she lived, which was a cave on the top of a hill.

The necromancer acknowledged his kindness in many words and, thanking him for his good offices, went back to his cell in the caravanserai.

Now by the decree of Fate, the very next day Fatimah came down into the city; and the Moroccan necromancer happened to leave his lodging in the morning, when he saw the people swarming and crowding; so he went up to find out what was going on, and found the holy woman standing in the middle of the throng, with everybody who suffered from pain or sickness flocking to her, asking a blessing and begging for her prayers; and every one she touched became whole of his illness.

The Moroccan necromancer followed her about until she went back to her cave; then, waiting until the evening had drawn in, he got up and went to a wine seller's shop, where he drank a cup of wine.

After this he went out of the city and, finding the holy woman's cave, went in and saw her lying flat on her back on a strip of matting. So he came forward and mounted upon her belly; then he drew his dagger and shouted at her; and when she woke and opened her eyes she saw a Moorish man with an unsheathed dagger sitting on her middle as though about to kill her.

She was troubled and badly terrified; but he said to her, "Listen! If you cry out or say a word I will kill you this very moment. Get up now and do everything I tell you." Then he swore her an oath that if she obeyed his orders, whatever they might be, he would not put her to death.

So saying, he got up off her, and Fatimah got up too; when he said to her, "Give me your gear and take my clothes"; whereupon she gave him her clothing and her headbands, her face veil and her cloak.

Then he said, "It is also necessary that you rub me with something that will make the colour of my face like yours."

So she went into the inner part of the cave and, bringing out a jar of ointment, spread some of it on her palm and with it smeared his face until its colour matched her own; then she gave him her staff and, showing him how to walk and what to do when he went into the city, hung her rosary round his neck.

Last of all she handed him a mirror and said, "Now look! You are no different from me at all"; and he saw himself the double of Fatimah, as though she had never gone or come.

But having got everything he wanted, he broke his oath and asked for a cord, which she brought him; then he seized her and strangled her in the cave; and presently, when she was dead, dragged the body outside and threw it into a pit nearby.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Eighty-eighth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Moroccan, after murdering Fatimah, threw her body into a pit and went back to sleep in her cave; and when the day broke he got up and, going to the town, took his stand under the walls of Aladdin's pavilion.

At this the people flocked about him, all of them certain that he was Fatimah the devout; and he fell to doing whatever she used to do: he laid hands on these in pain, and recited a chapter of the Koran for those, and made prayers for a third.

Presently the thronging of the people and the clamour of the crowd were heard by the Lady Badr al-Budur, who said to her handmaids, "Look and see what is going on and what the cause of this uproar is."

At this the chief of the eunuchs went out to see what the matter might be, and came back presently and said, "My lady, this clamour is caused by the Lady Fatimah; and if you are pleased to command it, I will bring her to you, and so you may gain a blessing through her."

The Princess answered, "Go and bring her; for many a day now I have kept hearing of her miracles and her virtues, and I long to see her and get a blessing by her intervention, for people tell of her manifestations in many cases of difficulty."

The eunuch went out and brought in the Moroccan necromancer, dressed in Fatimah's clothing; and when the wizard stood before the Lady Badr al-Budur he began, at first sight, to bless her with a string of prayers; nor did any one of those present doubt for a moment that he was the holy woman herself.

The Princess got up and greeted him with the salaam; then, seating him beside her, said, "My Lady Fatimah, it is my wish that you should stay with me always, so that I may be blessed through you, and may also learn from you the paths of worship and piety and follow your example, which makes for salvation."

Now all this was a foul deception on the part of the accursed African, and he planned to complete his trickery; so he went on, "My lady, I am a poor woman and a religious, who lives in the desert; and one like me does not deserve to live in the palaces of kings."

But the Princess replied, "Have no worry at all, my Lady Fatimah; I will set aside an apartment of my pavilion for you, so that you may worship in it and nobody shall ever come and trouble you; and you will be able to worship Allah in my house better than in your cave."

The Moroccan answered, "Hearing and obedience, my lady; I will not oppose your order, for the commands of the children of kings may not be gainsaid or refused. Only I hope that my eating and drinking and sitting may be inside my own room, which shall be kept wholly private; nor do I require or wish for delicacies of diet, but do me the favour of sending your handmaid every day with a bit of bread and a sup of water; and when I feel like food, let me eat by myself in my own room."

Now what the accursed man meant by this was to avoid the danger of having to raise his face veil at mealtimes, when his purpose might be defeated by his beard and moustaches showing that he was a man.

The Princess replied, "My Lady Fatimah, be of good heart; nothing shall happen except what you wish. But now get up and let me show you the apartment in the palace that I would prepare for your stay with us."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Eighty-ninth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Lady Badr al-Budur got up and, taking the necromancer who had disguised himself as the holy woman, showed him into the place she had kindly promised him for a home, and said, "My Lady Fatimah, here you shall live with every comfort about you, in all privacy and repose; and the place shall be named after your name."

Whereupon the Moroccan acknowledged her kindness and prayed for her.

Then the Princess showed him the lattices and the jewelled belvedere with its twenty-four windows, and said to him, "What do you think, my Lady Fatimah, of this marvellous pavilion?"

The Moroccan replied, "By Allah, my daughter, it is indeed exceedingly fine and wondrous; nor do I believe its equal is to be found in the whole universe. But alas for the lack of one thing that would enhance its beauty and its decoration!"

The Princess asked, "My Lady Fatimah, what does it lack, and what is this thing that would add to its adornment? Tell me about it, for I always believed it to be wholly perfect."

The Moroccan answered, "My lady, all it wants is that there should be hanging from the middle of the dome the egg of a bird called the roc; and if that were done, the pavilion would have no equal anywhere in the world."

The Princess asked, "What is this bird, and where can we find her egg?"

And the Moroccan answered, "My lady, the roc is indeed a giant bird, which carries off camels and elephants in her claws and flies away with them, such is her size and her strength; and this bird is mostly found on Mount Kaf; and the architect who built this pavilion is able to bring you one of her eggs."

Then they left off such talk, since it was the hour for the midday meal; and when the handmaid had spread the table, the Lady Badr al-Budur sent down to invite the accursed African to eat with her. But he would not accept, and for a good reason would on no account agree; no, he got up and retired to the room the Princess had assigned him, and the slave girls carried his dinner there.

Now when evening came on, Aladdin got back from the chase and met his wife, who greeted him with the salaam; and he clasped her to his bosom and kissed her. Presently, looking at her face, he saw a shade of sadness on it, and he noticed that, contrary to her custom, she did not laugh; so he asked her, "What has happened to you, my darling? Tell me — has anything happened to trouble your thoughts?"

"Nothing whatever," she answered; "but, my beloved, I used to imagine that our pavilion lacked nothing at all; and yet, eyes of mine, Aladdin, if the dome of the upper storey were hung with an egg of the bird called the roc, there would be nothing like it in the universe."

Her husband answered, "And you are saddened over this trifle, when it is the easiest of all matters to me! So cheer yourself; and whatever you want, it is enough that you tell me of it, and I will bring it from the depths of the earth in the quickest time and at the earliest hour."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Ninetieth Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Aladdin, after refreshing his Princess's spirits by promising her everything she could wish for, went straight to his room and, taking the Lamp, rubbed it; when the marid appeared without let or delay, saying, "Ask whatever you want."

The other said, "I want you to fetch me an egg of the bird roc and hang it from the crown of the dome of this pavilion of mine."

But when the marid heard these words his face grew fierce, and he shouted with a mighty loud and frightful voice, and cried:

"Denier of kindly deeds! Is it not enough for you that I and all the Slaves of the Lamp are for ever at your service, but you must also require me to bring you our Liege Lady for your pleasure, and hang her up at the dome of your pavilion for the enjoyment of you and your wife? Now by Allah, you deserve, you and she, that I should reduce you to ashes this very moment and scatter you on the air. But since the two of you are ignorant of this matter, and do not know its inner meaning from its outer, I will pardon you, for indeed you are only innocents.

"The offence comes from that accursed necromancer, brother to the Moroccan magician, who is living here representing himself to be Fatimah the devout, after taking her dress and her belongings and murdering her in the cave. Indeed he came here seeking to kill you by way of blood-revenge for his brother; and it is he who taught your wife to require this thing of me."

So saying, the marid vanished.

But when Aladdin heard these words his wits fled his head and his joints trembled at the marid's terrible shout; and yet he strengthened his purpose and, getting up at once, went out of his room and into his wife's.

There he pretended to have an aching head, since he knew how famous Fatimah was for the art and mystery of healing all such pains; and when the Lady Badr al-Budur saw him sitting with his hand to his head and complaining of feeling unwell, she asked him the cause, and he answered, "I know of nothing else, except that my head aches exceedingly."

At this she immediately ordered Fatimah summoned, so that the holy woman might lay her hand on his head; and Aladdin asked her, "Who may this Fatimah be?"

So she told him it was Fatimah the devout, to whom she had given a home in the pavilion.

Meanwhile the slave girls had gone out and summoned the Moroccan; and when the accursed man made his appearance, Aladdin got up to him and, acting like a man who knew nothing of his purpose, greeted him as though he were the real Fatimah and, kissing the hem of his sleeve, welcomed him and treated him with honour and said, "My Lady Fatimah, I hope you will bless me with a favour, for I know well how you practise the healing of pains: I have got a mighty ache in my head."

The accursed Moroccan could hardly believe he was hearing such words, this being all he had wanted.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Five Hundred and Ninety-first Night,

Dunyazad said, "Sister, if you are not sleepy, do tell us one of your pleasant tales." And Shahrazad replied, "With love and good will."

It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Moroccan necromancer, dressed as Fatimah the devout, came up to Aladdin to put his hand on his head and heal his ache; so he laid on one hand and, putting the other under his gown, drew out a dagger to kill him with.

But Aladdin was watching him and, waiting patiently until he had wholly unsheathed the weapon, seized him with a powerful grip; and, wrenching the dagger out of his grasp, plunged it deep into his heart.

When the Lady Badr al-Budur saw him do this she shrieked and cried out, "What has this virtuous and holy woman done, that you have loaded your neck with the heavy burden of her blood, wrongfully shed? Have you no fear of Allah, that you kill Fatimah, this saintly woman, whose miracles are famous far and wide?"

"No," replied Aladdin. "I have not killed Fatimah. I have killed only Fatimah's killer, the man who is the brother of the accursed Moroccan magician who carried you off by his black art and transported my pavilion to the land of Africa. And this damnable brother of his came to our city and worked these wiles, murdering Fatimah and taking her clothes, only so that he might avenge his brother's blood on me; and it was he too who taught you to require a roc's egg of me, so that my death might come of the request. But if you doubt what I say, come here and look at the person I have killed."

At this Aladdin drew aside the Moroccan's face veil, and the Lady Badr al-Budur saw the likeness of a man with a full beard that nearly covered his features. She knew the truth at once and said to her husband, "My beloved, twice now I have cast you into risk of death!"

But he answered, "No harm in that, my lady, by the blessing of your loving eyes: I accept with all joy everything you bring me."

The Princess, hearing these words, hurried to fold him in her arms and kissed him, saying, "My darling, all this comes of my love for you, and I knew nothing about it; but truly I do not think lightly of your affection."

So Aladdin kissed her and pressed her to his breast, and the love between them grew greater still.

At that moment the Sultan appeared, and they told him everything that had happened and showed him the body of the Moroccan necromancer; whereupon the King ordered it to be burned and the ashes scattered on the air, exactly as had been done with the wizard's brother.

And Aladdin lived with his wife, the Lady Badr al-Budur, in all pleasure and joy of life, and from then on escaped every danger; and after a while, when the Sultan died, his son-in-law was seated on the throne of the kingdom; and he ruled and dealt justice to the people, so that they all loved him; and he lived with his wife in all comfort and happiness, until there came to him the Destroyer of Delights and the Sunderer of Companies.

Dunyazad said, "Sister, how rare and delightful your tale is!"

And Shahrazad said, "And what is this compared with what I could tell you tomorrow night, if my lord the King is pleased to leave me alive?"

So Shahryar said to himself, "Indeed I will not kill her until she has told me the whole tale."

When it was the Five Hundred and Ninety-second Night,

Shahrazad began to relate the adventures of

Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves

In days of old, and in times and tides long gone before, there lived in a certain town of Persia two brothers, one named Kasim and the other Ali Baba, who at their father's death had divided the little wealth he left them fairly between them, and had lost no time in wasting and spending all of it.

The elder, however, presently took a wife, the daughter of a wealthy merchant; so that when his father-in-law went to the mercy of Almighty Allah he became the owner of a large shop full of rare goods and costly wares, and of a storehouse stocked with precious stuffs, and likewise of a great deal of gold buried in the ground. And so he was known throughout the city as a man of substance.

But the woman Ali Baba had married was poor and needy; so they lived in a mean hovel, and Ali Baba scraped a scanty living by selling firewood, which he gathered every day in the jungle and carried about the town to the bazaar on his three donkeys.

Now it happened one day that Ali Baba had cut as many dead branches and as much dry fuel as he needed, and had put the load on his beasts, when suddenly he saw a cloud of dust spiralling high in the air to his right and moving rapidly towards him; and when he looked at it closely he made out a troop of horsemen riding hard and about to reach him.

At this sight he was badly alarmed; and, fearing that they might perhaps be a band of robbers who would kill him and drive off his donkeys, in his fright he began to run. But since they were close at hand and he could not get out of the forest, he drove his animals with their loads of fuel into a side path among the bushes and swarmed up the thick trunk of a huge tree to hide himself in it; and he sat on a branch from which he could see everything below him, while nobody below could catch a glimpse of him above; and that tree grew close beside a rock that towered high overhead.

The horsemen — young, active, hardy riders — came right up to the rock face and all dismounted; at which Ali Baba took good note of them, and he was soon quite persuaded, by their look and their manner, that they were a troop of highwaymen who had fallen on a caravan and robbed it and carried off the spoil, and had brought their booty to this place meaning to hide it safely in some cache.

Moreover he observed that there were forty of them.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Six Hundred and Twenty-seventh Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Ali Baba saw the robbers, as soon as they came under the tree, each unbridle his horse and hobble it; and then all of them took off their saddlebags, which proved to be full of gold and silver.

The man who seemed to be the captain presently pushed forward, load on shoulder, through thorns and thickets, until he came to a certain spot, where he spoke these strange words: "Open, Sesame!"

And immediately a wide doorway appeared in the face of the rock. The robbers went in, and last of all their chief, and then the door shut of itself.

They stayed inside the cave a long while, and Ali Baba was obliged to stay perched up in the tree, reflecting that if he came down the band might perhaps come out that very moment and seize him and kill him. At last he had determined to mount one of the horses and, driving on his donkeys, to head back to town — when suddenly the door flew open.

The robber chief was the first to come out; then, standing at the entrance, he watched and counted his men as they came out; and lastly he spoke the magic words, "Shut, Sesame!" — whereupon the door closed of itself.

When they had all passed muster and review, each slung on his saddlebags and bridled his own horse; and as soon as they were ready they rode off, led by their leader, in the direction they had come from.

Ali Baba stayed perched in the tree and watched them go; nor would he come down until they were completely out of sight, in case one of them should come back and look around and spot him.

Then he thought to himself, "I too will try the virtue of those magic words, and see whether the door will open and close at my bidding." So he called out loudly, "Open, Sesame!"

And no sooner had he spoken than the door flew open at once, and he went inside.

He saw a large vaulted cavern, as high as the height of a full-grown man, hewn out of the living stone and lit by light that came through air holes and skylights in the upper surface of the rock that formed the roof. He had expected to find nothing but outer darkness in this robbers' den, and he was surprised to see the whole room filled with bales of every kind of stuff, and heaped from floor to ceiling with camel-loads of silks and brocades and embroidered cloths, and mound upon mound of many-coloured carpets; besides which he saw coins of gold and silver beyond measure or reckoning, some piled on the ground and others tied up in leather bags and sacks.

Seeing these goods and moneys in such abundance, Ali Baba decided in his mind that not for a few years only, but for many generations, thieves must have been storing their gains and their spoils in this place.

When he was standing inside the cave the door had closed behind him; and yet he was not dismayed, since he had kept the magic words in his memory. And he took no notice of the precious stuffs around him, but applied himself only and entirely to the sacks of gold coins. Of these he carried out as many as he judged a sufficient load for his beasts; then he loaded them on his animals and covered the plunder with sticks and firewood, so that nobody might see the bags, but might think he was carrying home his usual goods.

Last of all he called out, "Shut, Sesame!" — and immediately the door closed; for the spell worked in such a way that whenever anybody went into the cave the door shut of itself behind him, and when he came out of it, it would neither open nor close again until he had pronounced the words.

Presently, having loaded his donkeys, Ali Baba drove them ahead of him with all speed to the city; and reaching home he drove them into the yard and, shutting the outer door fast, took down first the sticks and then the bags of gold, which he carried in to his wife.

She felt them, and finding them full of coin suspected that Ali Baba had been robbing, and fell to scolding and blaming him for doing such an ill thing.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Six Hundred and Twenty-eighth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Ali Baba said to his wife, "Indeed I am no robber; you had far better rejoice with me at our good fortune."

At this he told her of his adventure and began to pour the gold out of the bags in heaps before her; and her sight was dazzled by the sheen of it and her heart delighted by his story and his adventures. Then she began counting the gold; at which Ali Baba said, "Silly woman, how long will you go on turning over the coin? Let me dig a hole now to hide this treasure in, so that nobody may learn the secret of it."

She said, "Your advice is right! Still, I should like to weigh the money and have some idea of the amount of it."

And he replied, "As you please — but see that you tell nobody."

So she hurried off to Kasim's house to borrow weights and scales with which she might balance the gold coins and make some reckoning of their value; and when she could not find Kasim she said to his wife, "Lend me your scales, I beg you, for a moment."

Her sister-in-law replied, "Do you need the bigger balance, or the smaller?"

And the other answered, "I do not need the large scales; give me the little ones."

And her sister-in-law cried, "Wait here a moment while I look about and find what you want."

With this excuse Kasim's wife went aside and secretly smeared wax and suet over the pan of the balance, so that she might learn what it was that Ali Baba's wife wanted to weigh; for she felt sure that whatever it might be, some bit of it would stick to the wax and the fat. So the woman took this chance to satisfy her curiosity; and Ali Baba's wife, suspecting nothing of it, carried the scales home and began to weigh the gold, while Ali Baba went on digging; and when the money had been weighed, the two of them stowed it into the hole, which they carefully filled up with earth.

Then the good wife took the scales back to her kinswoman, not knowing at all that a gold coin had stuck to the cup of the scales; but when Kasim's wife spotted the gold coin she seethed with envy and anger, saying to herself, "So ho! They borrowed my balance to weigh out gold coins?" And she marvelled greatly where a man as poor as Ali Baba could have got such a store of wealth that he had to weigh it with a pair of scales.

Now after pondering the matter a long while, when her husband came home at evening she said to him, "Husband, you think yourself a man of wealth and substance; but look — your brother Ali Baba is an emir beside you, and far richer than you are. He has such heaps of gold that he has to weigh his money out with scales, while you, forsooth, are satisfied to count your coin."

"How do you know this?" asked Kasim.

And in answer his wife told him all about the pair of scales, and how she had found a gold coin stuck to them, and showed him the coin, which bore the mark and inscription of some ancient king.

Kasim got no sleep at all that night, out of envy and jealousy and covetousness; and next morning he got up early and, going to Ali Baba, said, "Brother, to all appearances you are poor and needy; but in fact you have a store of wealth so abundant that you are obliged to weigh your gold with scales."

Ali Baba said, "What is this you are saying? I do not understand you; make your meaning plain."

And Kasim said, with ready anger, "Do not pretend to be ignorant of what I am saying, and do not think to deceive me." Then, showing him the gold coin, he cried, "You have laid by thousands of gold coins like this one; and meanwhile my wife found this one stuck to the cup of the scales."

Then Ali Baba understood that both Kasim and his wife knew he had a store of gold, and said in his mind that it would do him no good to keep the matter hidden, but would rather cause ill-will and mischief; and so he was induced to tell his brother every bit of it, about the bandits and about the treasure found in the cave.

When he had heard the story, Kasim exclaimed, "I want you to tell me exactly where you found the money; and the magic words too, by which the door opened and closed. And I warn you: if you do not tell me the whole truth, I will give notice of those gold coins to the governor, and then you will forfeit all your wealth and be disgraced and thrown into gaol."

Thereupon Ali Baba told him his tale, not forgetting the magic words; and Kasim, who kept careful note of all these matters, set out the next day driving ten mules he had hired, and readily found the place Ali Baba had described to him.

And when he came to the rock and the tree Ali Baba had hidden himself in, and had made sure of the door, he cried in great joy, "Open, Sesame!"

The door yawned wide at once, and Kasim went in and saw the piles of jewels and treasures ranged all around; and as soon as he was standing among them the door shut behind him, as it always did.

He walked about in ecstasy, marvelling at the treasures; and when he was weary of admiring he gathered together bags of gold coins, a sufficient load for his ten mules, and put them by the entrance ready to be carried outside and loaded on the beasts.

But by the will of Almighty Allah he had clean forgotten the magic words, and cried out, "Open, Barley!" — whereupon the door refused to move.

Astonished and confused beyond measure, he named the names of every kind of grain except sesame, which had slipped out of his memory as though he had never heard the word; and in his dire distress he paid no attention to the gold coins heaped at the entrance, but paced to and fro, backwards and forwards, inside the cave, sorely puzzled and perplexed. The wealth whose sight had a little while before filled his heart with joy and gladness was now the cause of bitter grief and sadness.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Six Hundred and Twenty-ninth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Kasim gave up all hope of the life he had put in such peril by his greed and his envy.

It happened that at noon the robbers, coming back that way, saw from a distance some mules standing beside the entrance, and they marvelled much at what had brought the beasts to that place; for, since Kasim had by mischance failed to tether or hobble them, they had strayed about the jungle and were browsing here and there.

However, the thieves paid little attention to the strays and did not care to secure them, but only wondered by what means they had wandered so far out of the town. Then, reaching the cave, the captain and his troop dismounted and, going up to the door, repeated the formula, and at once it flew open.

Now Kasim had heard from inside the cave the hooves of the horses drawing nearer and nearer, and he had fallen to the ground in a fit of fear, never doubting that this was the clatter of the bandits, who would kill him without fail. Even so, he presently took heart of grace, and at the moment when the door flew open he rushed out, hoping to make good his escape.

But the unhappy man ran full tilt into the captain, who was standing in front of the band, and knocked him to the ground; whereupon a robber standing near his chief at once bared his sword and with one cut clove Kasim clean in two.

Thereupon the robbers rushed into the cavern and put back where they had been the bags of gold that Kasim had heaped up at the doorway ready for taking away; nor did they take any notice of the ones Ali Baba had removed, so dazed and amazed were they to discover by what means the strange man had got in.

They all knew it was not possible for anybody to drop through the skylights, so tall and steep was the rock's face and so slippery to climb; and also that nobody could come in by the door unless he knew the magic words that opened it.

However, they presently quartered Kasim's dead body and hung it up on the door inside the cavern, two parts to the right jamb and two to the left, so that the sight might be a warning of coming doom to anybody who dared to enter the cave. Then, coming out, they shut the door of the hoard and rode away about their usual work.

Now when night fell and Kasim did not come home, his wife grew uneasy and, running round to Ali Baba, said, "Brother, Kasim has not come back: you know where he went, and I am sorely afraid some misfortune has come to him."

Ali Baba also guessed that some mishap had happened to prevent his return; but nonetheless he tried to comfort his sister-in-law with cheering words, and said, "Wife of my brother, very likely Kasim is being cautious and, avoiding the city, is coming by a roundabout road and will be here soon. That, I do believe, is the reason he is so long."

At this, comforted in her spirits, Kasim's wife went home and sat waiting for her husband's return; but when half the night was gone and still he had not come, she was like one out of her mind. She was afraid to cry aloud in her grief, in case the neighbours should hear her and come and learn the secret; so she wept in silence, and, reproaching herself, fell to thinking, "Why did I tell him this secret, and breed envy and jealousy of Ali Baba? This is the fruit of it, and this is the disaster that has come down on me."

She spent the rest of the night in bitter tears, and early next morning hurried in the greatest haste to Ali Baba and begged him to go out in search of his brother; so he tried to console her and set out at once with his donkeys for the forest.

Presently, reaching the rock, he wondered to see stains of freshly shed blood; and, not finding his brother or the ten mules, he foresaw a calamity from so evil a sign. Then he went to the door and, saying, "Open, Sesame!", pushed in and saw Kasim's dead body, two parts hanging to the right and the rest to the left of the entrance.

Although he was frightened beyond all measure of fright, he wrapped the quarters in two cloths and laid them on one of his donkeys, hiding them carefully with sticks and firewood so that nobody should see them. Then he put the bags of gold on the two other animals and covered them just as carefully; and when everything was ready he closed the cave door with the magic words and set off homewards with all care and watchfulness.

The donkeys with the load of gold he handed over to his wife, telling her to bury the bags diligently; but he did not tell her the condition he had found his brother Kasim in.

Then he went with the other donkey — the one with the body on its back — to the widow's house and knocked gently at the door.

Now Kasim had a slave girl, shrewd and sharp-witted, named Morgiana. She undid the bolt just as softly and let Ali Baba and the donkey into the courtyard of the house, where he let the body down from the beast's back and said, "Morgiana, hurry and make ready to perform the rites for your master's burial. I am going now to tell the news to your mistress, and I will come back quickly to help you in the business."

At that moment Kasim's widow, seeing her brother-in-law, exclaimed, "Ali Baba, what news do you bring me of my husband? Alas, I see the tokens of grief written on your face. Tell me quickly what has happened."

Then he recounted to her how it had gone with her husband, and how he had been killed by the robbers, and in what way he had brought the dead body home.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Six Hundred and Thirtieth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Ali Baba went on: "My lady, what was to happen has happened; but we must keep this matter secret, for our lives depend upon its being kept private."

She wept bitterly and answered, "It has gone with my husband according to the decree of Fate; and now, for your own safety's sake, I give you my word to keep the affair concealed."

He replied, "Nothing can avail when Allah has decreed. Rest patiently until the days of your widowhood are accomplished; after which time I will take you to wife, and you shall live in comfort and happiness; and have no fear that my first wife will vex you or show any jealousy, for she is kindly and tender-hearted."

The widow, lamenting her loss noisily, cried, "Let it be just as you please."

Then Ali Baba took his leave of her, weeping and wailing for her husband; and, joining Morgiana, took counsel with her about how to manage his brother's burial. So, after much consultation and many warnings, he left the slave girl and went off home, driving his donkey before him.

As soon as Ali Baba had gone, Morgiana went quickly to a druggist's shop; and, so as to deceive him the better and not make the matter known, she asked him for a drug often given to men who are ill with a dangerous fever. He gave it, saying, "Who is there in your house so ill as to need this medicine?"

And she said, "My master Kasim is sick almost to death: for many days he has neither spoken nor tasted any food, so that we almost despair of his life."

Next day Morgiana went again and asked the druggist for more medicine and for the essences that are given to the sick when they are at death's door, so that a dying man may perhaps rally before his last breath. The man gave her the potion, and she, taking it, sighed aloud and wept, saying, "I am afraid he may not have the strength to drink this draught: I think everything will be over with him before I get back to the house."

Meanwhile Ali Baba was anxiously waiting to hear the sounds of wailing and lamentation in Kasim's house, so that at that signal he might hurry there and take part in the funeral ceremonies.

Early on the second day Morgiana went with her face veiled to one Baba Mustafa, a tailor well on in years whose trade was making shrouds and grave clothes; and as soon as she saw him open his shop she gave him a gold piece and said, "Bind a bandage over your eyes and come along with me."

Mustafa acted as though he would not go; whereupon Morgiana put a second gold coin in his palm and begged him to come with her. The tailor presently consented, for greed of gain; so, tying a kerchief tightly over his eyes, she led him by the hand to the house where her master's dead body lay.

Then, taking off the bandage in the darkened room, she told him to sew the quarters of the corpse together, limb to limb; and, throwing a cloth over the body, said to the tailor, "Make haste and sew a shroud to the size of this dead man, and I will give you yet another gold piece for it."

Baba Mustafa quickly made the grave cloth of the right length and breadth, and Morgiana paid him the promised coin; then, bandaging his eyes once more, she led him back to the place she had brought him from.

After this she hurried home and, with Ali Baba's help, washed the body in warm water and, putting on the shroud, laid the corpse in a clean place ready for burial.

This done, Morgiana went to the mosque and gave notice to an imam that a funeral was waiting for the mourners at a certain house, and begged him to come and read the prayers for the dead; and the imam went back with her.

Then four neighbours took up the bier and carried it on their shoulders and set out with the imam and the others who were used to helping at such funerals. After the funeral prayers were ended, four other men carried off the coffin; and Morgiana walked in front of it bare-headed, striking her breast and weeping and wailing with exceedingly loud lamentation, while Ali Baba and the neighbours came behind.

In this order they came into the cemetery and buried him; and then, leaving him to Munkar and Nakir, the Questioners of the Dead, they all went their ways.

Presently the women of the quarter, according to the custom of the city, gathered together in the house of mourning and sat an hour with Kasim's widow, comforting her and condoling with her, and presently left her somewhat resigned and cheered.

Ali Baba stayed forty days at home in ceremonial mourning for the loss of his brother; so that nobody in the town except himself and his wife and Kasim's widow and Morgiana knew anything about the secret.

And when the forty days of mourning were over, Ali Baba moved all the dead man's property to his own quarters and openly married the widow; and then he appointed his nephew, his brother's eldest son — who had lived a long time with a wealthy merchant and was thoroughly knowledgeable in all matters of trade, in selling and buying — to take charge of the dead man's shop and carry on the business.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Six Hundred and Thirty-first Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that it chanced one day, when the robbers came to the treasure cave as they usually did, that they marvelled exceedingly to find no sign or trace of Kasim's body, while they noticed that a great deal of the gold had been carried off.

The captain said, "Now we must make enquiry into this matter; or else we shall suffer great loss, and this treasure of ours, which we and our forefathers have amassed over the course of many years, will be wasted and spoiled little by little."

To this they all assented, and with one mind agreed that the man they had killed had known the magic words by which the door was made to open; and moreover, that somebody besides him knew the spell too, and had carried off the body and a great deal of the gold as well; and so they must make diligent search and find out who the man might be.

Then they took counsel and decided that one of them, who should be shrewd and quick-witted, must put on the clothes of some merchant from foreign parts; and then, going to the city, must go about from quarter to quarter and from street to street and learn whether any townsman had lately died, and if so where he had lived, so that with this clue they might be able to find the man they were looking for.

At this one of the robbers said, "Give me leave to go and find out such news in the town and bring you word of it; and if I fail in my purpose, I hold my life forfeit."

So that bandit, after disguising himself in his dress, pushed into the town at night; and early next morning he went to the market square and saw that none of the shops had been opened yet, except only that of Baba Mustafa the tailor, who sat on his working stool with thread and needle in hand.

The thief bade him good day and said, "It is still dark: how can you see to sew?"

The tailor said, "I can tell you are a stranger. In spite of my years my eyesight is so keen that only yesterday I sewed a dead body together while sitting in a room that was quite dark."

At this the bandit said to himself, "I shall get something of what I want out of this tailor"; and to get a further clue he said, "It seems to me you are joking with me, and that you mean a shroud for a corpse was stitched by you and that your business is sewing shrouds."

The tailor answered, "It is no matter to you: ask me no more questions."

Thereupon the robber placed a gold coin in his hand and went on, "I do not wish to uncover anything you are hiding — my breast, like every honest man's, is the grave of secrets; and this only would I learn from you: in what house did you do that job? Can you direct me to it, or take me there yourself?"

The tailor took the gold greedily and cried, "I have not seen the way to that house with my own eyes. A certain slave woman led me to a place I know very well, and there she bandaged my eyes and guided me to some building, and finally took me into a darkened room where the dead body lay dismembered. Then she unbound the kerchief and told me to sew first the corpse and then the shroud; which having done, she blindfolded me again and led me back to the place she had brought me from and left me there. So you see I am not able to tell you where you will find the house."

The robber said, "Even though you do not know the dwelling you speak of, still you can take me to the place where you were blindfolded; then I will tie a kerchief over your eyes and lead you as you were led — and in this way you may perhaps hit upon the spot. If you will do me this favour, look: here is another gold coin for you."

Thereupon the bandit slipped a second gold coin into the tailor's palm, and Baba Mustafa thrust it into his pocket with the first; then, leaving his shop as it was, he walked to the place where Morgiana had tied the kerchief round his eyes, and with him went the robber, who, after binding on the bandage, led him by the hand.

Baba Mustafa, who was clever and keen-witted, presently struck the street he had walked along with the handmaid, and walked on counting step by step; then, stopping suddenly, he said, "This far I came with her"; and the two of them stopped in front of Kasim's house, where his brother Ali Baba now lived.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Six Hundred and Thirty-second Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the robber then made marks with white chalk on the door, so that he might find it easily at some future time; and, taking the bandage off the tailor's eyes, said, "Baba Mustafa, I thank you for this favour; and may Almighty Allah reward you for your goodness. Tell me now, I beg you, who lives in that house?"

He said, "In very truth I do not know, for I have little knowledge of this quarter of the city."

And the bandit, understanding that he could get no further clue from the tailor, sent him back to his shop with abundant thanks, and hurried back to the meeting place in the jungle where the band was waiting for him.

Not long afterwards it happened that Morgiana, going out on some errand, marvelled exceedingly at seeing the chalk marks showing white on the door. She stood a while deep in thought and presently guessed that some enemy had made the signs so that he might recognise the house and play some trick on her lord. So she chalked the doors of all her neighbours in the same way, and kept the matter secret, never confiding it either to her master or to her mistress.

Meanwhile the robber told his comrades the tale of his adventure and how he had found the clue; so the captain, and the whole band with him, went one after another by different ways until they came into the city; and the man who had put the mark on Ali Baba's door went with the chief to point out the place.

He led him straight to the house and, pointing at the sign, exclaimed, "Here lives the man we are looking for!"

But when the captain looked around him he saw that all the houses bore chalk marks in the same fashion; and he wondered and said, "By what means do you know which house, of all these houses that bear the same signs, is the one you spoke of?"

At this the robber guide was confounded beyond all measure of confusion and could make no answer; then with an oath he cried, "I certainly did set a sign on a door; but I do not know where all the marks on the other doors came from, nor can I say for certain which was the one I chalked."

Thereupon the captain went back to the marketplace and said to his men, "We have toiled and laboured in vain, and we have not found the house we came to look for. Let us go back to the forest, our rendezvous; I shall go there too."

Then they all trooped off and gathered together inside the treasure cave; and when the robbers had all met, the captain judged that the man who had spoken falsely and led them through the city to no purpose deserved punishment. So he imprisoned him in the presence of them all; and then he said, "I will show special favour to the one among you who will go to town and bring me intelligence by which we may lay hands on the plunderer of our property."

At this another of the company came forward and said, "I am ready to go and enquire into the case; and it is I who will bring you to your wish."

The captain, after giving him presents and promises, sent him off on his errand; and by the decree of Destiny, which nobody may gainsay, this second robber went first to the house of Baba Mustafa the tailor, exactly as the thief before him had done. In the same way he persuaded the tailor with gifts of gold coin to be led blindfold; and so he too was guided to Ali Baba's door.

Here, noting his predecessor's work, he fixed a mark on the doorpost in red chalk, the better to distinguish it from the others, which still showed white. Then he made his way back in stealth to his company; but Morgiana on her part also spotted the red sign on the door and, with subtle forethought, marked all the others in the same fashion; nor did she tell anybody what she had done.

Meanwhile the bandit rejoined his band and said boastfully, "Captain, I have found the house and put a mark on it by which I shall tell it clearly from all its neighbours."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Six Hundred and Thirty-third Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the captain sent another of his men to the city, and he found the place; but, as before, when the troop went there they saw every single house marked with signs of red chalk. So they came back disappointed, and the captain, growing exceedingly displeased and distracted, clapped this spy into gaol too.

Then the chief said to himself, "Two men have failed in their attempt and have got their rightful reward of punishment; and I imagine none of the rest of my band will try to follow up their search; so I will go and find this fellow's house myself."

So he went along and, helped by the tailor Baba Mustafa, who had gained a good deal of gold in this business, he hit upon the house of Ali Baba; and here he made no outward show or sign, but marked it on the tablet of his heart and impressed the picture of it on the page of his memory.

Then, returning to the jungle, he said to his men, "I have full knowledge of the place and have drawn it clearly in my mind, so that now there will be no difficulty in finding it. Go out straight away and buy and bring here nineteen mules, together with one large leather jar of mustard oil and thirty-seven vessels of the same kind quite empty.

"Not counting me and the two locked up in gaol, you number thirty-seven souls; so I will stow you away, armed and equipped, each inside his jar, and will load two on each mule; and on the nineteenth mule there shall be a man in an empty jar on one side, and on the other the jar full of oil.

"I for my part, in the guise of an oil merchant, will drive the mules into the town, arriving at the house by night, and will ask leave of its master to stay there until morning. After this we shall find our chance during the dark hours to get up and fall on him and kill him."

And the captain went on to say, "When we have made an end of him we shall recover the gold and treasure he robbed us of, and bring it back on the mules."

This plan pleased the robbers, who went out at once and bought mules and huge leather jars, and did as the captain had told them. And after a delay of three days, shortly before nightfall, they got up; and, smearing all the jars over with mustard oil, each hid himself inside an empty vessel.

The chief then disguised himself in a trader's clothes and placed the jars on the nineteen mules — that is, the thirty-seven vessels, in each of which lay a robber armed and equipped, and the one that was full of oil.

This done, he drove the beasts before him, and presently reached Ali Baba's place at nightfall; when it happened that the master of the house was strolling to and fro in front of his home after supper.

The captain greeted him with the salaam and said, "I come from such and such a village with oil; and I have often been here selling oil, but now, to my grief, I have arrived too late, and I am sorely troubled and perplexed about where I shall spend the night. If you have pity on me, I beg you to let me stay here in your courtyard and ease the mules by taking down the jars and giving the beasts a little fodder."
