Although Ali Baba had heard the captain's voice when he was perched in the tree, and had seen him go into the cave, still, because of the disguise, he did not know him for the leader of the thieves, and granted his request with a hearty welcome and gave him full leave to stop there for the night.

He then pointed out an empty shed to tether the mules in, and told one of the slave boys to go and fetch grain and water. He also gave orders to the slave girl Morgiana, saying, "A guest has come here and is staying tonight. Busy yourself with all speed about his supper and make the guest bed ready for him."

Presently, when the captain had let down all the jars and had fed and watered his mules, Ali Baba received him with all courtesy and kindness, and, summoning Morgiana, said in his presence, "See that you do not fail in the service of this stranger of ours, nor let him lack for anything. Tomorrow early I want to go to the baths and bathe; so give my slave boy Abdullah a suit of clean white clothes that I may put on after washing; and moreover make ready some broth overnight, that I may drink it after I get home."

She replied, "I will have everything ready as you have told me."

So Ali Baba went off to his rest; and the captain, having had his supper, went to the shed and saw that all the mules had their food and drink for the night.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Six Hundred and Thirty-fourth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the captain, after seeing to the mules and to the jars, which Ali Baba and his household believed to be full of oil, and finding himself completely private, whispered to his men who were lying in ambush, "Tonight at midnight, when you hear my voice, open the leather jars quickly from top to bottom with your sharp knives and come out without delay."

Then, passing through the kitchen, he reached the room where a bed had been spread for him, Morgiana showing the way with a lamp.

She said, "If you need anything else, I beg you to command your servant, who is always ready to obey what you say."

He answered, "I need nothing else"; and then, putting out the light, he lay down on the bed to sleep a while before the time came to rouse his men and finish off the work.

Meanwhile Morgiana did as her master had told her: she first took out a suit of clean white clothes and handed it over to Abdullah, who had not yet gone to bed; then she put the pot on the hearth to boil the broth, and blew the fire until it burnt briskly.

After a short while she needed to see whether the broth was boiling; but by that time all the lamps had gone out, and she found that the oil was spent and there was nowhere she could get a light.

The slave boy Abdullah noticed that she was troubled and perplexed at this, and said to her, "Why make such a fuss? In that shed there are plenty of jars of oil: go now and take as much of it as you like."

Morgiana thanked him for the suggestion; and Abdullah, who was lying at his ease in the hall, went off to sleep so that he might wake early and attend Ali Baba at the bath.

So the handmaid got up and, with the oil can in her hand, walked to the shed where the leather jars stood ranged in rows. Now as she drew near one of the vessels, the thief who was hidden in it, hearing the tread of footsteps, thought it must be his captain, whose summons he was waiting for; so he whispered, "Is it time for us to come out now?"

Morgiana started back, frightened at the sound of a human voice; but since she was bold and quick-witted she replied, "The time is not yet come" — and said to herself, "These jars are not full of oil, and I perceive some mystery here. Perhaps the oil merchant is hatching some treacherous plot against my lord; so may Allah, the Compassionating, the Compassionate, protect us from his snares!"

So she answered in a voice made like the captain's, "Not yet; the time has not come." Then she went to the next jar and gave the same reply to the man inside it, and so on to all the vessels, one by one.

Then she said to herself, "Praise be to the Lord! My master took this fellow in, believing him to be an oil merchant; but look — he has let in a band of robbers, who are only waiting for the signal to fall on him and plunder the place and put him to death."

Then she went on to the furthest jar and, finding it brimming with oil, filled her can and, going back to the kitchen, trimmed the lamp and lit the wicks; then, bringing out a large cauldron, she set it on the fire and, filling it with oil out of the jar, heaped wood on the hearth and fanned it into a fierce flame, the more readily to boil what was in it.

When this was done she baled it out in potfuls and poured it, seething hot, into the leather vessels one by one — while the thieves, unable to escape, were scalded to death, and every jar held a corpse.

So did this slave girl by her subtle wit make a clean end of them all, noiselessly and without even the people in the house knowing about it.

Now when she had satisfied herself that every one of the men had been killed, she went back to the kitchen and, shutting the door, sat brewing Ali Baba's broth.

Hardly an hour had passed before the captain woke from his sleep; and, opening his window wide, saw that everything was dark and silent; so he clapped his hands as a signal for his men to come out, but not a sound was heard in return. After a while he clapped again and called aloud, but got no answer; and when he cried out a third time with no reply, he was perplexed and went out to the shed where the jars stood.

He thought to himself, "Perhaps they have all fallen asleep, when the time for action is at hand; so I must wake them without pause or delay."

Then, going up to the nearest jar, he was startled by a smell of oil and seething flesh; and touching it on the outside he felt it reeking hot; then, going to the others one by one, he found them all in the same condition.

At this he knew for certain what fate had befallen his band; and, fearing for his own safety, he climbed onto the wall and, dropping from there into a garden, made his escape in high dudgeon and sore disappointment.

Morgiana waited a while to see the captain come back from the shed, but he did not come; at which she knew that he had scaled the wall and taken to flight, since the street door was double-locked; and, the thieves being all disposed of in this way, Morgiana lay down and slept in perfect ease and peace of mind.

When two hours of darkness were still left, Ali Baba woke and went to the baths, knowing nothing of the night's adventure, for the gallant slave girl had not woken him — nor indeed had she thought such a thing wise, because if she had looked for a chance to report her plan to him she might well have lost her opportunity and spoiled the whole project.

The sun was high over the horizon when Ali Baba walked back from the baths; and he marvelled greatly to see the jars still standing under the shed, and said, "How does it come about that the oil merchant, my guest, has not taken his mules and his jars of oil to market?"

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Six Hundred and Thirty-fifth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Ali Baba presently asked Morgiana what had become of the oil merchant, his guest, whom he had put in her charge; and she answered, "Almighty Allah grant you a hundred and twenty years of safety! I will tell you about this merchant in private."

So Ali Baba went aside with his slave girl, who, taking him outside the house, first locked the courtyard door; then, showing him a jar, said, "Please look into this and see whether there is oil in it or something else."

At this, peering inside it, he saw a man; at which sight he cried out and would gladly have run away in his fright.

Morgiana said, "Do not fear him; this man no longer has the strength to do you harm. He is dead, and stone dead."

Hearing such words of comfort and reassurance, Ali Baba asked, "Morgiana, what evils have we escaped, and by what means has this wretch become the quarry of Fate?"

She answered, "Praise be to Almighty Allah! I will tell you all about the case; but hush, do not speak aloud, in case the neighbours learn the secret and it ends in our ruin. Now look into all the jars, one by one from first to last."

So Ali Baba examined them each in turn and found in each a man fully armed and equipped, all of them scalded to death.

At this, speechless with sheer amazement, he stared at the jars; but presently, recovering himself, he asked, "And where is he, the oil merchant?"

She answered, "I will tell you about him too. The villain was no trader but a treacherous assassin, whose honeyed words would have trapped you to your doom; and now I will tell you what he was and what has happened. But meanwhile you are fresh from the baths, and you should first drink some of this broth for your stomach's sake and your health's."

So Ali Baba went inside and Morgiana served up the dish; after which her master said, "I should very much like to hear this wonderful story: please tell it to me and set my heart at ease."

At this the handmaid fell to relating everything that had happened, in these words:

"Master, when you told me to boil the broth and went off to bed, your servant, obeying your command, took out a suit of clean white clothes and gave it to the boy Abdullah; then kindled the fire and set the broth on. As soon as it was ready I needed to light a lamp so that I could see to skim it; but all the oil was spent, and, learning this, I told the slave boy Abdullah what I needed, and he advised me to draw some from the jars standing under the shed.

"So I took a can and went to the first vessel, when suddenly I heard a voice inside it whisper very cautiously, 'Is it time for us to come out now?' I was amazed at this and judged that the pretended merchant had laid some plot to kill you; so I replied, 'The time is not yet come.' Then I went to the second jar and heard another voice, to which I made the same answer, and so on with all of them.

"By now I was certain that these men were only waiting for some signal from their chief, whom you had taken in as a guest within your walls, supposing him to be a merchant in oil; and that, after you had received him hospitably, the wretch had brought these men to murder you and plunder your goods and spoil your house. But I gave him no opportunity to win his wish.

"The last jar I found full of oil; and, taking some from it, I lit the lamp; then, putting a large cauldron on the fire, I filled it up with oil that I brought from the jar and made a fierce blaze under it; and when the contents were seething hot I took out several cansful, meaning to scald them all to death, and, going to each jar in due order, poured boiling oil into them one by one.

"Having destroyed them utterly in this way, I went back to the kitchen and, putting out the lamps, stood by the window watching what might happen and how that false merchant would act next.

"Not long after I had taken up my station, the robber captain woke and signalled to his thieves several times. Then, getting no reply, he came downstairs and went out to the jars; and, finding that all his men were dead, he fled through the darkness — where, I do not know. So when he had completely disappeared I was sure that, the door being double-locked, he had scaled the wall and dropped into the garden and made his escape. And then, with my heart at rest, I slept."

And Morgiana, after telling her story to her master, presently added, "This is the whole truth that I have told you. For some days indeed I have had an inkling of something of this kind, but I kept it from you, thinking it unwise to risk the chance of its reaching the neighbours' ears; now, however, there is nothing for it but to tell you.

"One day, as I came to the house door, I saw a white chalk mark on it; and the next day a red sign beside the white. I did not know what the marks were made for; nevertheless I put others on the doors of several neighbours, judging that some enemy had done this in order to bring about my master's destruction. So I made the marks on all the other doors in such perfect conformity with those I had found that it would be hard to tell them apart."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Six Hundred and Thirty-sixth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Morgiana went on to Ali Baba:

"Judge now and see whether these signs and all this villainy are not the work of the bandits of the forest, who marked our house so that they might know it again. Of these forty thieves there are still two others left, about whose case I know nothing; so beware of them, but chiefly of the third one still remaining, their captain, who fled from here alive. Take good heed and be cautious of him; for if you fall into his hands he will in no way spare you, but will certainly murder you. I will do everything in my power to save your life and your property from hurt and harm, nor shall your servant be found wanting in any service to my lord."

Hearing these words, Ali Baba rejoiced exceedingly and said to her, "I am well pleased with you for this conduct of yours; and tell me what you would have me do on your behalf. I shall not fail to remember your brave deed as long as I have breath in me."

She said, "Before everything else, we must bury these bodies in the ground at once, so that the secret may not become known to anybody."

At this Ali Baba took his slave boy Abdullah with him into the garden, and there under a tree they dug a deep pit for the corpses of the thieves, of a size to fit its contents; and they dragged the bodies to the trench — having first carried off their weapons — and threw them in; and then, covering up the remains of the thirty-seven robbers, they made the ground look level and clean as it usually was.

They also hid the leather jars and the gear and the arms; and presently Ali Baba sent the mules by ones and twos to the bazaar and sold them all, with the able help of his slave boy Abdullah.

So the matter was hushed up and did not reach anybody's ears; and yet Ali Baba never stopped being uneasy, in case the captain or the two surviving robbers should wreak their vengeance on his head. He kept himself private with all caution and took care that nobody should learn a word of what had happened, or of the wealth he had carried off from the bandits' cave.

Meanwhile the captain of the thieves, having escaped with his life, fled to the forest in hot anger and sore vexation of mind, and his senses were scattered and the colour of his face vanished like rising smoke.

Then he thought the matter over again and again, and at last firmly resolved that he must take Ali Baba's life, or else he would lose all the treasure, which his enemy, knowing the magic words, would carry away and turn to his own use. Furthermore, he determined that he would undertake the business single-handed; and that, after getting rid of Ali Baba, he would gather another band of robbers together and carry on his career of brigandage, as indeed his forefathers had done for many generations.

So he lay down to rest that night, and, getting up early in the morning, put on a suitable-looking outfit; then, going to the city, he put up at a caravanserai, thinking to himself, "No doubt the murder of so many men has reached the governor's ears, and Ali Baba has been seized and brought to justice, and his house is levelled and his goods confiscated. The townsfolk must surely have heard news of all this."

So he asked the keeper of the inn straight away, "What strange things have happened in the city these last few days?" — and the man told him everything he had seen and heard; but the captain could not learn a jot of what most concerned him.

By this he understood that Ali Baba was wary and wise, and that he had not only carried off such a store of treasure but had also destroyed so many lives and come off unscathed into the bargain; and furthermore, that he himself would need to have all his wits about him not to fall into his enemy's hands and perish.

With this resolve the captain hired a shop in the bazaar, to which he brought whole bales of the finest stuffs and fine merchandise from his forest treasure house; and presently he took his seat in the store and fell to doing a merchant's business.

By chance his place faced the shop of the late Kasim, where his son, Ali Baba's nephew, now traded; and the captain, who called himself Khwajah Hasan, soon struck up an acquaintance and friendship with the shopkeepers around him and treated them all with lavish civilities — but he was especially gracious and cordial to Kasim's son, a handsome and well-dressed youth, and would often sit and chat with him for a long while.

A few days later it happened that Ali Baba, as he sometimes did, came to see his nephew, whom he found sitting in his shop. The captain saw and recognised him at sight; and one morning he asked the young man, "Tell me, please: who is the man who comes to you now and then at your place of business?"

To which the youth answered, "He is my uncle, my father's brother."

Whereupon the captain showed him greater favour and affection still, the better to deceive him for his own purposes, and gave him presents and had him sit at meat with him and fed him with the daintiest of dishes.

Presently Ali Baba's nephew thought it was only right and proper that he should invite the merchant to supper in his turn; but since his own house was small, and he was cramped for room and could not put on a show of splendour as Khwajah Hasan did, he took counsel with his uncle about it.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Six Hundred and Thirty-seventh Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Ali Baba replied to his nephew:

"You are quite right: you ought to entertain your friend as handsomely as he has entertained you. Tomorrow, which is Friday, shut your shop as all merchants of repute do; then, after the early meal, take Khwajah Hasan out to smell the air, and as you walk lead him here without his knowing. Meanwhile I will give orders that Morgiana shall make ready the best of dishes and everything needful for a feast against his coming. Do not trouble yourself in any way, but leave the matter in my hands."

So the next day, that is Friday, Ali Baba's nephew took Khwajah Hasan to walk about the garden; and as they were coming back he led him along the street where his uncle lived.

When they came to the house the youth stopped at the door and, knocking, said, "My lord, this is my second home: my uncle has heard a great deal about you and about your goodness to me, and wants exceedingly to meet you; so if you would consent to come in and visit him, I should be truly glad and grateful to you."

Although Khwajah Hasan rejoiced in his heart that he had found a means of getting into his enemy's house and household, and although he hoped soon to gain his end by treachery, still he hesitated to go in, and stood there making his excuses and preparing to walk away.

But when the door was opened by the slave porter, Ali Baba's nephew seized his companion's hand and, after a great deal of persuasion, led him in; at which he entered with a great show of cheerfulness, as though much pleased and honoured.

The master of the house received him with all favour and respect and asked after his welfare, and said to him, "My lord, I am obliged and grateful to you for having shown favour to my brother's son; and I perceive that you regard him with an affection even fonder than my own."

Khwajah Hasan replied with pleasant words and said, "Your nephew greatly takes my fancy, and I am well pleased with him; for although he is young in years, Allah has endowed him with a great deal of wisdom."

So the two of them talked together in friendly conversation; and presently the guest rose to leave and said, "My lord, your servant must now say goodbye to you; but on some future day, God willing, he will wait upon you again."

Ali Baba, however, would not let him go, and asked, "Where are you off to, my friend? I would invite you to my table, and I beg you to sit at meat with us and afterwards go home in peace. Perhaps the dishes are not as delicate as those you are used to eating; still, be pleased to grant me this request, I beg you, and refresh yourself with my food."

Khwajah Hasan said, "My lord, I am beholden to you for your gracious invitation, and I would gladly sit at meat with you; but for a particular reason I must excuse myself. Allow me, then, to go, for I may not stay any longer nor accept your gracious offer."

To this the host replied, "I beg you, my lord, tell me what this reason may be, that is so urgent and weighty."

And Khwajah Hasan answered, "The cause is this: by order of the physician who lately cured me of my complaint, I must not eat any food prepared with salt."

Ali Baba said, "If that is all, do not deprive me, I beg you, of the honour your company will do me: since the dishes are not yet cooked, I will forbid the cook to use any salt at all. Stay here a while and I will come back to you presently."

So saying, Ali Baba went in to Morgiana and told her not to put salt into any one of the dishes; and she, busy with her cooking, fell to marvelling greatly at such an order and asked her master, "Who is this man who eats food with no salt in it?"

He answered, "What does it matter to you who he is? Just do as I tell you."

She replied, "Very well; everything shall be as you wish" — but in her mind she wondered at the man who made such a strange request, and very much wanted to get a look at him.

So when all the dishes were ready to be served up, she helped the slave boy Abdullah to lay the table and set out the meal; and no sooner did she see Khwajah Hasan than she knew who he was, although he had disguised himself in the dress of a foreign merchant. And furthermore, when she looked at him attentively she spotted a dagger hidden under his robe.

"So ho!" she said to herself. "This is the reason the villain does not eat salt — because he is looking for an opportunity to kill my master, whose mortal enemy he is. But I will be beforehand with him and finish him off before he finds a chance to harm my lord."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Six Hundred and Thirty-eighth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Morgiana, having spread a white cloth on the table and served up the meal, went back to the kitchen and thought out her plot against the robber captain.

Now when Ali Baba and Khwajah Hasan had eaten their fill, the slave boy Abdullah brought Morgiana word to serve the dessert; and she cleared the table and set out fruit, fresh and dried, in dishes; then she placed beside Ali Baba a small stand with three cups and a flagon of wine; and lastly she went off with the slave boy Abdullah into another room, as though she meant to have her own supper.

Then Khwajah Hasan — that is, the captain of the robbers — perceiving that the coast was clear, exulted mightily, saying to himself, "The time has come for me to take my full revenge. With one thrust of my dagger I will finish this fellow off, then escape across the garden and go my way. His nephew will not venture to stay my hand; for if he so much as moves a finger or a toe with that intent, another stab will settle his earthly account. Still, I must wait a while until the slave boy and the cook maid have eaten and lain down to rest in the kitchen."

Morgiana, however, was watching him closely, and, guessing his purpose, said in her mind, "I must not let this villain get the advantage of my lord; and by some means I must make his plan come to nothing and put an end to his life at once."

So the trusty slave girl changed her clothes with all haste and put on the sort of dress that dancers wear; she veiled her face with a costly kerchief; round her head she bound a fine turban, and about her middle she tied a waist cloth worked with gold and silver, in which she stuck a dagger whose hilt was rich with filigree and jewels.

Disguised in this way, she said to the slave boy Abdullah, "Take your tambourine now, so that we may play and sing and dance in honour of our master's guest."

So he did as she told him, and the two of them went into the room, the lad playing and the girl following. Then, making a low bow, they asked leave to perform and entertain and play; and Ali Baba gave them permission, saying, "Dance now, and do your best, so that this guest of ours may be mirthful and merry."

Khwajah Hasan said, "My lord, you do indeed provide very pleasant entertainment."

Then the slave boy Abdullah, standing by, began to strike the tambourine, while Morgiana rose up and showed her perfect art and pleased them greatly with her graceful steps and her sportive motion; and suddenly, drawing the dagger from her belt, she brandished it and paced from side to side — a spectacle that pleased them most of all. At times, too, she stood in front of them, now clapping the sharp-edged dagger under her armpit and now setting it against her breast.

Lastly she took the tambourine from the slave boy Abdullah and, still holding the dagger in her right hand, went round for largesse, as is the custom among entertainers. First she stood in front of Ali Baba, who threw a gold coin into the tambourine, and his nephew put in a gold coin too; then Khwajah Hasan, seeing her about to come up to him, fell to pulling out his purse — when she heartened her heart and, quick as blinding lightning, plunged the dagger into his vitals, and the villain fell back on the instant, stone dead.

Ali Baba was dismayed and cried out in his anger, "Wretched girl, what is this deed you have done, to bring about my ruin!"

But she replied, "No, my lord — it was to save you and not to do you harm that I killed this man. Loosen his clothes and see what you find underneath."

So Ali Baba searched the dead man's dress and found a dagger hidden in it.

Then Morgiana said, "This wretch was your deadly enemy. Look at him well: he is none other than the oil merchant, the captain of the band of robbers. When he came here meaning to take your life, he would not eat your salt; and when you told me that he wanted none in the food I suspected him, and at first sight I was sure that he would certainly put you to death. Almighty Allah be praised — it is just as I thought."

Then Ali Baba lavished thanks and expressions of gratitude on her, saying, "See now, twice you have saved me from his hand"; and, falling on her neck, he cried, "You are free; and as a reward for this loyalty of yours, I have married you to my nephew."

Then, turning to the youth, he said, "Do as I tell you and you shall prosper. I want you to marry Morgiana, who is a model of duty and loyalty. You see now that this Khwajah Hasan sought your friendship only so that he might find an opportunity to take my life; but this girl, with her good sense and her wisdom, has killed him and saved us."

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Six Hundred and Thirty-ninth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that Ali Baba's nephew consented at once to marry Morgiana.

After which the three of them raised the dead body and carried it out with all care and vigilance and buried it privately in the garden; and for many years nobody knew anything about it.

In due time Ali Baba married his brother's son to Morgiana with great pomp, and spread a wedding feast in the most sumptuous fashion for his friends and neighbours, and made merry with them and enjoyed singing and every kind of dancing and amusement.

He prospered in every undertaking, and Time smiled on him, and a new source of wealth was opened to him.

For fear of the thieves he had not once visited the cave in the jungle where the treasure lay, since the day he had carried out his brother Kasim's body. But some time afterwards he mounted his horse one morning and rode there with all care and caution; and, finding no sign of man or horse, and reassured in his mind, he ventured to go up to the door.

Then, dismounting from his beast, he tied it to a tree and, going to the entrance, spoke the words he had not forgotten: "Open, Sesame!"

At this, as it always did, the door flew open; and, going in by it, he saw the goods and the hoard of gold and silver untouched and lying just as he had left them. So he was assured that not one of all the thieves was left alive, and that apart from himself there was not a soul who knew the secret of the place.

At once he tied up in his saddlecloth a load of gold coins, as much as his horse could carry, and brought it home; and in later days he showed the hoard to his sons and his sons' sons, and taught them how the door could be made to open and shut.

So Ali Baba and his household lived all their lives in wealth and gladness in that city where once he had been a pauper; and by the blessing of that secret treasure he rose to high rank and dignity.

And Shahrazad saw the dawn breaking, and fell silent.

When it was the Six Hundred and Fortieth Night,

she said: It has reached me, O fortunate King — and so Shahrazad went on telling the King her tales, night after night, until the thousand nights and a night were fulfilled.

Conclusion

Now during all this time Shahrazad had borne the King three boy children; so when she had made an end of her tales she rose to her feet and, kissing the ground before him, said:

"O King of the time, and unique one of the age and the tide: I am your handmaid, and for these thousand nights and a night I have entertained you with stories of the people who went before us and with cautionary instances of the men of old. May I then make bold to beg a boon of your Highness?"

He replied, "Ask, Shahrazad, and it shall be granted you."

Whereupon she cried out to the nurses and the eunuchs, saying, "Bring me my children."

So they brought them to her in haste, and they were three boy children, one walking, one crawling and one at the breast. She took them and, setting them before the King, kissed the ground again and said:

"O King of the age, these are your children; and I beg you to release me from the doom of death, as a gift to these infants; for if you kill me they will be motherless, and will find no woman to rear them as they ought to be reared."

When the King heard this he wept and, pressing the boys to his bosom, said, "By Allah, Shahrazad, I pardoned you before ever these children came, because I found you chaste, pure, honest and pious. Allah bless you, and your father and your mother, and your root and your branch! I take the Almighty to witness against me that I exempt you from anything that could harm you."

So she kissed his hands and his feet and rejoiced exceedingly, saying, "May the Lord make your life long and increase you in dignity and majesty!" — and presently added:

"You marvelled at what happened to you at the hands of women; and yet greater and more grievous misfortunes than yours befell the kings of Persia before you. Indeed I have set out for you what happened to caliphs and kings and others with their women; but the telling is long and the hearing of it grows tedious, and in what I have told there is warning enough for the man of wits and admonishment enough for the wise."

Then she stopped speaking; and when King Shahryar had heard her words and profited by what she said, he summoned up his powers of reason and cleansed his heart and made his understanding come back to him, and turned to Almighty Allah and said to himself:

"Since more than has befallen me befell the kings of Persia, never, while I live, shall I stop blaming myself for the past. As for this Shahrazad, her like is not to be found in the lands; so praise be to Him who appointed her a means of delivering His creatures from oppression and slaughter!"

Then he rose from where he sat and kissed her head; at which she rejoiced exceedingly, she and her sister Dunyazad.

When the morning came, the King went out and, sitting down on the throne of his kingship, summoned the lords of his land; whereupon the chamberlains and officials and captains of the army came in to him and kissed the ground before him.

He distinguished the vizier, Shahrazad's father, with special favour, and bestowed on him a costly and splendid robe of honour, and treated him with the utmost kindness, and said to him, "Allah protect you, for that you gave me your noble daughter to wife, who has been the means of my repenting of killing other people's daughters. Indeed I have found her pure and pious, chaste and honest; and Allah has granted me three boy children by her; so praised be He for His surpassing favour."

Then he bestowed robes of honour on his viziers and emirs and chief officers, and set out briefly to them what had happened to him with Shahrazad, and how he had turned from his former ways and repented of what he had done, and how he intended to take the vizier's daughter Shahrazad to wife and have the marriage contract drawn up with her.

When those who were present heard this they kissed the ground before him and blessed him and his betrothed Shahrazad, and the vizier thanked her.

Then Shahryar brought his sitting to an end in all well-being, whereupon the people dispersed to their homes, and the news was noised abroad that the King intended to marry the vizier's daughter Shahrazad.

Then he set about making ready the wedding gear, and presently sent for his brother, King Shah Zaman, who came; and King Shahryar went out to meet him with his troops.

Furthermore they decorated the city in the finest fashion and spread scents from censers and burnt aloes-wood and other perfumes in all the markets and thoroughfares, and rubbed themselves with saffron, while the drums beat and the flutes and pipes sounded and mimes and mountebanks played and plied their arts, and the King lavished gifts and largesse on them; and indeed it was a notable day.

When they came to the palace, King Shahryar gave orders to spread the tables with beasts roasted whole and sweetmeats and every kind of food, and told the crier to cry to the people that they should come up to the Divan and eat and drink, and that this should be a means of reconciliation between him and them. So high and low, great and small, came up to him; and they stayed like that, eating and drinking, seven days and seven nights.

Then the King shut himself up with his brother and told him what had happened to him with the vizier's daughter Shahrazad over the past three years, and told him what he had heard from her of proverbs and parables, chronicles and pleasantries, quips and jests, stories and anecdotes, dialogues and histories and elegies and other verses; at which King Shah Zaman marvelled with the uttermost marvel and said:

"I should like to take her younger sister to wife, so that we may be two brothers married to two sisters, and they in the same way sisters to us. For the calamity that befell me was the cause of our discovering what had befallen you; and all this time, these three years past, I have taken no delight in any woman, except that I lie each night with a girl of my kingdom and every morning I put her to death. But now I want to marry your wife's sister Dunyazad."

When King Shahryar heard his brother's words he rejoiced exceedingly and, getting up at once, went in to his wife Shahrazad and told her what his brother intended, namely that he sought her sister Dunyazad in marriage.

Whereupon she answered, "O King of the age, we ask one condition of him, and that is that he take up his home with us; for I cannot bear to be parted from my sister for an hour, since we were brought up together and cannot endure to be separated from one another. If he accepts this bargain, she is his servant."

King Shahryar went back to his brother and told him what Shahrazad had said; and he replied, "Indeed, this is exactly what was in my mind; for I wish never again to be parted from you for a single hour. As for the kingdom, Allah the Most High shall send it whomever He chooses, for I have no desire for kingship any longer."

When King Shahryar heard his brother's words he rejoiced exceedingly and said, "Truly this is what I wished, my brother. So praised be Allah, who has brought about union between us."

Then he sent for the judges and the learned men, the captains and the notables, and they married the two brothers to the two sisters. The contracts were written out, and the two kings bestowed robes of honour of silk and satin on all who were present, while the city was decorated and the rejoicings were renewed.

The King commanded every emir and vizier and chamberlain and officer to decorate his palace, and the people of the city were gladdened by the promise of happiness and contentment. King Shahryar also ordered sheep slaughtered and kitchens set up, and made wedding feasts and fed all comers, high and low; and he gave alms to the poor and needy and extended his bounty to great and small.

Then the eunuchs went out to perfume the baths for the brides; so they scented them with rosewater and willow-flower water and pods of musk, and fumigated them with eaglewood and ambergris.

Then Shahrazad went in, she and her sister Dunyazad, and they cleansed their heads and trimmed their hair. When they came out of the baths they put on clothes and ornaments such as men used to prepare for the kings of Persia; and among Shahrazad's clothes was a dress bordered with red gold and worked with images of birds and beasts.

And the two sisters encircled their necks with necklaces of precious jewels, the like of which Alexander never rejoiced in, for in them were great jewels that amazed the wit and dazzled the eye; and the imagination was bewildered at their charms, for indeed each of them was brighter than the sun and the moon.

Before them they lit brilliant torches of wax in candelabra of gold; but their faces outshone the torches, for they had eyes sharper than unsheathed swords, and the lashes of their eyelids bewitched all hearts. Their cheeks were rosy red and their necks and their figures swayed gracefully, and their eyes played like a gazelle's; and the slave girls came to meet them with instruments of music.

Then the two kings went into the baths, and when they came out they sat down on a couch set with pearls and gems, whereupon the two sisters came up and stood between their hands, like two moons, bending and leaning from side to side in their beauty and loveliness.

Presently they brought Shahrazad forward and displayed her, in the first dress, in a suit of red; whereupon King Shahryar rose to look at her, and the wits of everybody present, men and women alike, were bewitched; for she was just as one of those who described her said of her:

	A sun on a wand in a knoll of sand she showed,
	clad in her crimson-coloured chemisette;
	of the honey-dew of her lips she gave me drink,
	and with her rosy cheeks quenched the fire she set.

Then they dressed Dunyazad in a dress of blue brocade, and she became like the full moon when it shines out. So they displayed her in this, in the first dress, before King Shah Zaman, who rejoiced in her and nearly fainted away with love-longing and desire; yes, he was distracted with passion for her the moment he saw her, because she was as one of those who described her said of her in these lines:

	She comes dressed in a vest of azure,
	ultramarine, as the skies are decked and dight;
	I viewed the unparalleled sight, which showed my eyes
	a summer moon upon a winter night.

Then they went back to Shahrazad and displayed her in the second dress, a suit of surpassing fineness, and veiled her face with her hair like a chin-veil. Moreover they let down her side locks, and she was as one of those who described her said of her in these lines:

	Hail to him whose locks overshadow his cheeks,
	who slew my life by cruel hard despite!
	I said, "Have you veiled the Morning in Night?"
	He said, "No — I veil the Moon in the hue of Night."

Then they displayed Dunyazad in a second and a third and a fourth dress, and she paced forward like the rising sun, and swayed to and fro in the insolence of her beauty; and she was as the poet says of her in these lines:

	The sun of beauty she to all appears,
	and, lovely and coy, she mocks all loveliness;
	and when he meets her face and her smile
	in the morning, the sun of day must dress in clouds.

Then they displayed Shahrazad in the third dress and the fourth and the fifth, and she became like a supple willow branch or a thirsting gazelle, lovely of face and perfect in every attribute of grace, just as one says of her in these lines:

	She comes like the fullest moon on a happy night,
	taper of waist, with a shape of magic might;
	she has an eye whose glances quell mankind,
	and the ruby on her cheeks reflects its light.
	The blackness of her hair enveils her hips —
	beware of curls that bite with a viper's bite!
	Her sides are silken-soft, and all the while the heart
	behind that surface is mere rock, escaping sight.
	From the fringed curtains of her eyes she shoots
	shafts that at the furthest range still strike the white.

Then they went back to Dunyazad and displayed her in the fifth dress and in the sixth, which was green; and she surpassed with her loveliness the fair ones of the four quarters of the world, and outdid, with the brightness of her face, the full moon at its rising; for she was as the poet says of her in these lines:

	A girl she was whom the dresser's art had decked with snare and sleight,
	and robed with rays as though the sun had borrowed her own light.
	She came before us wondrously clad in a chemisette of green,
	as, veiled behind his leafy screen, the pomegranate hides from sight.
	And when he said, "What do you call the fashion of your dress?"
	she answered us in a pleasant way, with a double meaning dight:
	"We call this garment heartbreak; and rightly is it named,
	for many a heart we broke with this, and harried many a sprite."

Then they displayed Shahrazad in the sixth and seventh dresses and clad her in a young man's clothes; whereupon she came forward swaying from side to side and moving coquettishly, and indeed she ravished wits and hearts and bewitched all eyes with her glances. She shook her sides and swayed her haunches, then put her hair up under a sword hilt and went up to King Shahryar, who embraced her as a hospitable host embraces his guest, and threatened her in her ear with the taking of the sword; and she was as the poet says of her in these words:

	Were the darkness of a beard not male,
	and fairer than the feminine,
	the tirewomen would have grudged the bride
	who made herself a beard and whiskers wear.

And they did the same with her sister Dunyazad; and when they had made an end of the display, the King bestowed robes of honour on everybody present and sent the brides to their own apartments.

Then Shahrazad went in to King Shahryar and Dunyazad to King Shah Zaman, and each of them solaced himself with the company of his beloved wife, and the hearts of the people were comforted.

When morning came, the vizier came in to the two kings and kissed the ground before them; and they thanked him and were generous in their bounty to him. Presently they went out and sat down on the couches of kingship, while all the viziers and emirs and grandees and lords of the land presented themselves and kissed the ground. King Shahryar ordered them robes of honour and largesse, and they prayed for the permanence and prosperity of the King and his brother.

Then the two sovereigns appointed their father-in-law the vizier to be viceroy in Samarkand and assigned him five of the chief emirs to go with him, charging them to attend him and do him service. The minister kissed the ground and prayed that they might be granted length of life; then he went in to his daughters, with the eunuchs and ushers walking before him, and greeted them and said goodbye to them. They kissed his hands and gave him joy of his kingship and bestowed immense treasures on him; after which he took his leave of them and set out, and travelled days and nights until he came near Samarkand, where the townspeople met him three days' journey out and rejoiced in him exceedingly.

So he entered the city, and they decorated the houses, and it was a notable day. He sat down on the throne of his kingship, and the viziers did him homage, and the grandees and emirs of Samarkand, and they all prayed that he might be granted justice and victory and long continuance. So he bestowed robes of honour on them and treated them with distinction, and they made him Sultan over them.

As soon as his father-in-law had left for Samarkand, King Shahryar summoned the grandees of his realm and made them a stupendous banquet of every kind of delicious food and exquisite sweetmeat. He also bestowed robes of honour on them and rewarded them, and divided the kingdoms between himself and his brother in their presence; at which the people rejoiced.

Then the two kings lived on, each ruling a day in turn, and they were always in harmony with one another; while in the same way their wives continued in the love of Almighty Allah and in thanksgiving to Him; and the peoples and the provinces were at peace, and the preachers prayed for them from the pulpits, and their fame was noised abroad, and travellers carried news of them to every land.

In due time King Shahryar summoned chroniclers and copyists and told them to write down everything that had happened to him with his wife, first and last; so they wrote it, and named it The Stories of the Thousand Nights and a Night. The book came to thirty volumes, and these the King laid up in his treasury.

And the two brothers lived with their wives in all pleasure and comfort of life and its delights, for indeed Allah the Most High had changed their annoyance into joy; and in this way they went on until there took them the Destroyer of Delights and the Sunderer of Companies, the Desolator of dwelling places and the Garnerer of graveyards; and they were carried away to the mercy of Almighty Allah. Their houses fell into waste and their palaces lay in ruins, and other kings inherited their riches.

Then there reigned after them a wise ruler, who was just and keen-witted and accomplished, and who loved tales and legends, and especially those that chronicle the doings of sovereigns and sultans; and he found in the treasury these marvellous stories and wonderful histories, contained in the thirty volumes.

So he read in them a first book and a second and a third, and so on to the last of them; and each book astounded and delighted him more than the one before it, until he came to the end of them. Then he admired everything he had read in them of description and discourse and rare traits and anecdotes and moral instances and reminiscences, and ordered the people to copy them and spread them over all lands and climes; and so their fame was noised abroad, and the people named them The Marvels and Wonders of the Thousand Nights and a Night.

This is all that has come down to us of the origin of this book, and Allah is All-knowing.

So glory be to Him whom the shifts of Time do not waste away, nor does anything of chance or change affect His sway; whom one case does not divert from another case, and who is alone in the attributes of perfect grace. And prayer and peace be upon the Lord's Pontiff and Chosen One among His creatures, our lord Mohammed, the Prince of mankind, through whom we beg of Him a goodly and a godly end.
